additional_notes: Used for garments, shoes, or figuratively for roles/situations that suit someone very well. Equivalent to English 'to fit like a glove.' Often appears in constructions like 'Ça lui va comme un gant' or with an infinitive 'aller comme un gant' after a subject.
target_language_example: Cette veste va aller comme un gant pour toi.
native_language_example: That jacket will fit you like a glove.

meaning: to move forward; to move on (emotionally or in life)
additional_notes: Used to say someone should progress, stop dwelling on the past, or continue with life/projects. Common in both personal and professional contexts. Often followed by no object. Literal components: 'aller' = to go, 'de l'avant' = of/from the front.
target_language_example: Après cette mauvaise nouvelle, il faut aller de l'avant.
native_language_example: After that bad news, we must move on.

meaning: 'to go without saying' — to be obvious or taken for granted
additional_notes: Used impersonally to say that something is obvious or naturally expected. Often appears in constructions like "Il va de soi que..." (It goes without saying that...). Formal or neutral register; common in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Il va de soi que cela doit aller de soi dans une situation professionnelle.
native_language_example: It goes without saying that this should go without saying in a professional situation.

meaning: 'to go then' / a prompt or mild exclamation used to encourage action, urge someone to go, express impatience or surprise depending on context.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom with one meaning. More commonly used in conjugated imperatives (va/allez donc) rather than the infinitive phrase 'aller donc' in isolation; however 'aller donc' can appear in spoken or literary contexts to urge someone to go or to comment on someone's going. Tone, context and verb form determine force (e.g., encouragement, dismissal, surprise).
target_language_example: Si tu veux changer d'air, tu devrais aller donc voir ta famille pour un week-end.
native_language_example: If you want a change of scenery, you should go then see your family for a weekend.

meaning: to come and go; to move back and forth or move freely between places.
additional_notes: Used to describe the ability to move freely, to go back and forth, or to circulate within a place or situation. Often appears in expressions meaning 'as one pleases' (aller et venir à son gré / comme bon te semble). Literal components are transparent (aller = to go, venir = to come).
target_language_example: Tu peux aller et venir librement dans la maison.
native_language_example: You can come and go freely in the house.

meaning: to go far; literally to travel a long distance, figuratively to get far in life, career, a project, or to achieve great success.
additional_notes: Used both literally and figuratively. Common conjugations: aller loin (infinitive), il/elle ira loin (future), tu es allé(e) loin (past). Often used with modalities or reasons (e.g., « avec ce talent, tu vas aller loin »). Can be followed by context specifying area of success (career, studies, projet).
target_language_example: Avec ton travail et ta détermination, tu vas aller loin.
native_language_example: With your work and determination, you're going to go far.

meaning: to go nowhere / to be unable to go anywhere
additional_notes: Usually appears with 'part' as 'aller nulle part' meaning 'to go nowhere' or in negative sentences ('ne ... nulle part') to mean 'nowhere'. In everyday French, speakers often say 'nulle part' alone after a verb (Je ne peux aller nulle part) or prefer 'part' with 'nulle' omitted in casual speech ('Je ne peux aller nulle part' is common). Affirmative sentence 'Je peux aller nulle part' is uncommon and sounds odd — normally you'd say 'Je peux aller n'importe où' (I can go anywhere).
target_language_example: Avec ce temps, on ne peut aller nulle part.
native_language_example: With this weather, we can't go anywhere.

meaning: to go and get/take a (something) — expresses going somewhere to pick up, obtain, or have something (follow with a noun).
additional_notes: Construction: aller (to go) + prendre (to take/get) + an object. It implies moving with the intention of obtaining or consuming something (e.g., aller prendre un café). Conjugate aller as needed: je vais aller prendre un is the future-ish periphrasis but commonly use aller + prendre directly (je vais prendre un, nous allons prendre un, il/elle va prendre un). Often used for food/drink, quick errands, appointments, or actions where you go to get something. Use the appropriate article (un/une/des/le/la) and noun after it. Informal and neutral registers both use it.
target_language_example: Je vais aller prendre un café avant la réunion.
native_language_example: I'm going to go get a coffee before the meeting.

meaning: to go without saying; to be obvious or unnecessary to state
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is so obvious it doesn't need to be said. Often appears in expressions like "aller sans dire" or the more common fixed phrase "ça va sans dire". Formality: neutral; common in both spoken and written French. Note: "aller sans dire" is less commonly used on its own than "ça va sans dire", but it is grammatically correct in contexts where the verb "aller" refers to a situation or conclusion.
target_language_example: Que cela aille sans dire, je respecterai votre décision.
native_language_example: Let it go without saying, I will respect your decision.

meaning: A fragment used before an infinitive in reflexive constructions meaning 'to go and have/get [something done to oneself]' (neutral) or as part of idiomatic/rude expressions 'aller se faire + [infinitive]' telling someone to 'go and [do something to yourself]' (offensive).
additional_notes: Not a complete phrase by itself; it precedes an infinitive (e.g. aller se faire opérer, aller se faire voir, aller se faire foutre). In neutral contexts it describes going to obtain a service or undergo something (aller se faire opérer = to go to have surgery). In colloquial/insulting contexts it forms vulgar commands and should be used with caution. Register varies from neutral (medical/services) to highly informal and offensive (insults).
target_language_example: Il lui a dit d'aller se faire voir après la dispute.
native_language_example: He told her to go and get lost after the argument.

meaning: to go by oneself; to go alone (without company)
additional_notes: Used when someone goes somewhere without other people. Can refer to a person going alone (no companion) or a child going alone depending on context. Commonly used in conversational French. Verb aller is conjugated; e.g. Il va tout seul = He goes alone.
target_language_example: Je peux y aller tout seul.
native_language_example: I can go there by myself.

meaning: to go too far; to exceed acceptable limits (in words or actions).
additional_notes: Used when someone crosses a boundary — e.g., says something offensive, takes an action that's excessive, or pushes a situation beyond what's acceptable. Can refer to literal excess but most commonly figurative. Common responses: «Tu vas trop loin» (You're going too far) or «Il a tout simplement été trop loin».
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas aller trop loin dans ces accusations.
native_language_example: You must not go too far with these accusations.

meaning: go see
additional_notes: A common, compositional phrase meaning to go and see someone or something. With a person, it often means "go see" or "go visit"; with a film or show, it means "go watch"; and without a direct object, it can mean "go check" or "go see for oneself."
target_language_example: Je vais aller voir le médecin demain.
native_language_example: I'm going to go see the doctor tomorrow.

meaning: to go look elsewhere; to leave and seek something/someone in another place. Often used figuratively to tell someone to go away or to suggest finding alternatives.
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning either (1) literally go look somewhere else, or (2) figuratively tell someone to go away or advise seeking alternatives. Tone depends on context — can be neutral (advice) or blunt/rude (dismissal). Can be followed by a noun (aller voir un autre médecin) or stand alone (Va/Allez voir ailleurs).
target_language_example: Si le magasin n'a pas ta taille, tu peux aller voir ailleurs.
native_language_example: If the store doesn't have your size, you can go look elsewhere.

meaning: to go there
additional_notes: In standard French, the usual form is « y aller », not « aller y ». The sequence « aller y » is generally not used in normal sentence word order, so this entry is best understood as a reference to the components of the expression rather than a standard standalone phrase. In commands, related forms like « vas-y » or « allez-y » can mean « go ahead ».
target_language_example: On dit « y aller », pas « aller y » en français standard.
native_language_example: People say "y aller," not "aller y" in standard French.

meaning: to go to the gym / to go to the sports hall
additional_notes: Used when talking about going to a place for exercise — 'la salle' is short for 'la salle de sport' (the gym). Commonly used in everyday speech. You can change the article and noun for other places (e.g. aller au stade, aller à la piscine).
target_language_example: Je vais aller à la salle cet après‑midi.
native_language_example: I am going to go to the gym this afternoon.

meaning: will be
additional_notes: A future construction using the present tense of aller + infinitive être. Used to say someone will become or will be in a certain state or situation (emotion, condition, location, role). Common in spoken and written French to express near future. Use with different subjects by conjugating aller (e.g., je vais être, il/elle va être, nous allons être).
target_language_example: Ça va bien se passer — vous allez être surpris.
native_language_example: It will go well — you are going to be surprised.

meaning: go ahead
additional_notes: A polite/neutral imperative form meaning 'go' or 'go ahead'. Used with vous (plural or formal you). Can encourage someone to start, to proceed, to go somewhere, or to give permission. Often repeated for emphasis (allez-y, allez-y). If speaking informally to one person, use 'vas-y'.
target_language_example: Allez-y, faites-le !
native_language_example: Go ahead, do it!

meaning: Who knows / go figure / nobody knows (used to express uncertainty or resignation).
additional_notes: Informal expression often used conversationally to shrug off a question or admit you don't know the reason. Literally 'go know', but functionally equivalent to English 'who knows', 'beats me', or 'go figure'. Can stand alone or be followed by a clause (e.g. 'allez savoir pourquoi' = 'who knows why').
target_language_example: Allez savoir pourquoi il est parti si tôt.
native_language_example: Who knows why he left so early.

meaning: come on
additional_notes: Informal spoken expression used to encourage someone, to urge them to do something, or to express impatience/disbelief. Combines allez (imperative of aller) and va (imperative of aller) — redundant but common in casual speech for emphasis (similar to 'oh, come on' or 'go on then'). Tone and context determine whether it's encouraging, dismissive, or incredulous.
target_language_example: Allez va, dis-lui ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: Come on, tell her what you think.

meaning: 'go fuck yourself' (very strong insult)
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Used to angrily tell someone to go away or express extreme contempt. Should not be used in polite company. Literal components: 'allez' (go, imperative plural/formal), 'vous' (you), 'faire foutre' (to get fucked) — the phrase is emphatic and directed at one or more people.
target_language_example: Allez vous faire foutre, je ne veux plus vous voir.
native_language_example: Go fuck yourself, I never want to see you again.

meaning: Let's go / come on / let's do it (encouraging others to start moving or begin an action).
additional_notes: Contraction of 'allons' (we go) + 'y' (there/it). Common informal expression used to urge people to leave, begin something, or encourage action. Tone depends on context: can be enthusiastic, impatient, or dismissive (e.g. 'laisse tomber' = 'never mind, let's go'). Often used with an exclamation mark or a short pause.
target_language_example: Allons-y, il est déjà tard.
native_language_example: Let's go, it's already late.

meaning: went into
additional_notes: Past participle aller (allé) + preposition dans. Used to say someone went to or into a place. In spoken/written French you'd normally include the subject and auxiliary (être) for past tense (il est allé). Can be followed by a location (une chambre, un endroit, un pays) or a building; implies motion toward and entering or visiting the place.
target_language_example: Je suis allé dans le jardin ce matin.
native_language_example: I went into the garden this morning.

meaning: went to do
additional_notes: Past form of aller faire, usually used with être: je suis allé(e) faire..., nous sommes allé(e)s faire.... It means someone went somewhere in order to do an activity, errand, or pastime. In natural English, it is often translated more idiomatically as 'went shopping', 'went surfing', 'went for a walk', etc., rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Je suis allé faire du vélo ce matin.
native_language_example: I went biking this morning.

meaning: went to bed / went to sleep.
additional_notes: A reflexive construction: aller + se coucher (here in past: 'je suis allé me coucher' for a male speaker; a female speaker would say 'je suis allée me coucher'). Used to say you went to bed or went to sleep, often after something else. Can include details (e.g. 'avec mes vêtements' = went to bed with my clothes on).
target_language_example: Après la fête, je suis allé me coucher très tard.
native_language_example: After the party, I went to bed very late.

meaning: went to a (masculine or general) — past participle of 'aller' used with the auxiliary être + the indefinite article 'un'. Indicates that someone went to a masculine or unspecified place/event.
additional_notes: 'Allé' appears with the correct agreement (allé / allée / allés / allées) depending on the subject when used in compound tenses (e.g., Il est allé, Elle est allée). In casual speech you may hear the full form with the auxiliary (je suis allé(e) à un ...). If the noun is masculine and definite you would use 'au' instead (au concert). Use 'à une' for feminine nouns (à une réunion).
target_language_example: Il est allé à un centre islamique hier.
native_language_example: He went to an Islamic center yesterday.

meaning: 'went to buy a' (used with a feminine subject: she went somewhere to purchase a ...).
additional_notes: This phrase is the passé composé construction using être + allé(e) + infinitive acheter and the indefinite article un for a masculine singular noun. It requires agreement of the past participle with a feminine subject (elle est allée). Change the article and noun as needed (une, des) and adjust past-participle agreement for gender/number (il est allé, ils sont allés, elles sont allées).
target_language_example: Elle est allée acheter un cartable.
native_language_example: She went to buy a schoolbag.

meaning: a conversational prompt: 'so, what...' used to ask what (we/you) have, do, say, or will do next.
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase that combines 'alors' (so/then) with the start of 'qu'est-ce que' (what). Often used to move a conversation forward, ask for the next step, or request information/decisions. Informal to neutral spoken register; in writing you might see the full form 'Alors, qu'est-ce que...' or shorter 'Alors, qu'est-ce qu'on...'. The phrase usually continues with a verb or noun (ex.: '...on fait ?' = '...we do?').
target_language_example: Alors, qu'est-ce qu'on fait ce soir ?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing tonight?

meaning: while / whereas / even though (contrast or simultaneous actions)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast (whereas) or to indicate two actions happening at the same time (while). Context determines meaning: often contrasts two facts (Mes chaussures sont vieilles, alors que les siennes sont neuves) or points out simultaneity or surprise (Tu es resté planté alors que mon fils me mentait). Can be followed by indicative tense. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il travaille tard, alors que sa sœur rentre tôt.
native_language_example: He works late, whereas his sister comes home early.

meaning: 'fine for' (a penalty given because of something)
additional_notes: Used to say someone received or paid a monetary penalty for a specific offense (e.g. 'amende pour excès de vitesse' = fine for speeding). Typically followed by the reason introduced by a noun or an infinitive phrase (pour + noun / pour + infinitive). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a reçu une amende pour stationnement interdit.
native_language_example: She received a fine for illegal parking.

meaning: 'my/your/her/etc. friend is' (a feminine friend) — used to describe or ask about a female friend.
additional_notes: Amie = female friend (feminine noun). The verb est is the third-person singular of être (to be). Together they appear in sentences like 'Mon amie est...' or questions 'Ton amie est-elle...?' Change the possessive (mon/ton/votre) to match the speaker and the friend. Use 'ami est' for a male friend. Common in simple descriptions, nationality, condition, or questions.
target_language_example: Mon amie est professeur.
native_language_example: My (female) friend is a teacher.

meaning: my friends like / friends like
additional_notes: A combination of the plural noun 'amis' (friends) and the verb 'aiment' (they like). Use 'mes amis aiment' to say 'my friends like ...' or 'tous mes amis aiment' for 'all my friends like ...'. The verb 'aimer' followed by a noun means 'to like' (or 'to love' in stronger contexts with people). For likes/preferences, 'aimer' + noun is common. Make sure subject and verb agree: 'amis aiment' (they like).
target_language_example: Mes amis aiment les films comiques.
native_language_example: My friends like comedy movies.

meaning: 'English with' — used to say someone speaks English accompanied by something (often an accent) or to speak English with someone.
additional_notes: The phrase combines the noun anglais (English) + avec (with). Common uses: 'parler anglais avec un accent...' = 'to speak English with an ... accent'; or 'parler anglais avec quelqu'un' = 'to speak English with someone' (i.e., use English when speaking to them). Word order: 'parler anglais avec + [noun/pronoun/phrase]'.
target_language_example: Elle parle anglais avec un léger accent irlandais.
native_language_example: She speaks English with a light Irish accent.

meaning: pet (an animal kept for companionship).
additional_notes: Used to refer to animals kept in the home for companionship (dog, cat, rabbit, etc.). Common in questions (As-tu un animal de compagnie ?) and statements (C'est mon animal de compagnie.). In French the adjective 'de compagnie' follows 'animal'.
target_language_example: Nous avons adopté un chien comme animal de compagnie.
native_language_example: We adopted a dog as a pet.

meaning: pet; a domesticated animal kept for companionship or work.
additional_notes: Used for animals that live with or are tamed by humans (pets like cats and dogs, or domesticated animals like horses). Can be used in questions (As-tu un animal domestique?) and in definitions (Le chat est un animal domestique). Formal/neuter phrase suitable for spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Nous avons adopté un animal domestique, un chien.
native_language_example: We adopted a pet, a dog.

meaning: '...'s birthday / anniversary of'. Used to say whose birthday or whose anniversary it is.
additional_notes: Followed by a person or event (name/pronoun/noun) to indicate possession: l'anniversaire de Marie (Marie's birthday), l'anniversaire de mariage (wedding anniversary). In English you often use 'of' or possessive 's. For dates use 'c'est l'anniversaire de...' or 'l'anniversaire de...' to say an event is someone's birthday/anniversary.
target_language_example: C'est l'anniversaire de ma mère demain.
native_language_example: It's my mother's birthday tomorrow.

meaning: 'in (month/year)' when giving age or time with a month or point in time; or part of the expression indicating duration followed by a time unit (e.g., 'ans en une année' = 'years in one year').
additional_notes: Commonly used when saying someone will be a certain age in a given month or time (e.g., 'aura dix-huit ans en mai' = 'will be 18 in May'). It also appears in constructions about durations combined with a time reference (e.g., 'cinq ans en une année' = 'five years in one year') and in past-tense phrases indicating time spent ('a passé seize ans en prison' = 'spent sixteen years in prison'). The meaning depends on the surrounding words: with 'aura' it's 'will be ... in (month)', with 'a passé' it's 'spent ... in (place)'.
target_language_example: Elle aura sept ans en août.
native_language_example: She will be seven in August.

meaning: 'years have' (part of the expression meaning '... years have passed')
additional_notes: Used with a number + ans + ont passé to say that a number of years have gone by. The full common pattern is "X ans ont passé" or "X ans se sont passés" / "X années se sont écoulées". In spoken/written French you will often see "Il y a X ans" or "X ans se sont écoulés" as alternatives. Agreement: when using "ans" as a time expression with the auxiliary, you usually keep "passé" invariable (passé) after a numeral (spoken/written variation exists).
target_language_example: Cinq ans ont passé depuis ma dernière visite.
native_language_example: Five years have passed since my last visit.

meaning: belongs to (used in questions or statements about possession)
additional_notes: Comes from the verb appartenir (to belong). In questions it is commonly used as 'À qui appartient + noun ?' = 'Who does ... belong to?'. Word order in French places the noun after appartient in some constructions (e.g., 'À qui appartient le chien ?'). In statements you'd say 'Le livre appartient à Paul.'
target_language_example: À qui appartient le vélo garé devant la maison ?
native_language_example: Who does the bike parked in front of the house belong to?

meaning: 'you call that a...' — a skeptical or critical way to question whether something deserves the name given to it
additional_notes: Used to express disbelief, sarcasm, or surprise about whether something should be called what the speaker or another person calls it. Often appears in questions starting with 'Tu' (Tu appelles ça...?) but can be used with other subjects: 'Vous appelez ça...?', 'On appelle ça...?'. Tone is usually incredulous; intonation and context convey criticism or mockery.
target_language_example: Tu appelles ça un repas ?
native_language_example: You call that a meal?

meaning: called a / named a (feminine singular).
additional_notes: Past participle 'appelé' (masculine form) + article 'une' introduces a feminine noun that names or describes something. Used to say something was called/named or someone phoned (when 'appeler' means 'to call' a person or service) — context decides meaning. For phone actions use subject + 'a appelé une amie/ambulance' = 'called a friend/an ambulance.' For naming use passive-like or descriptive constructions: 'peut être appelé une langue' = 'can be called a language.'
target_language_example: Elle a appelé une copine hier soir.
native_language_example: She called a friend last night.

meaning: brings (some/of) — indicates bringing or causing something (often followed by partitive or plural).
additional_notes: Common uses: literal 'bring' (someone brings something to someone) and figurative 'bring/produce' (something brings/causes results, questions, benefits). Often appears with partitive 'de + noun' (de l'eau, de bonnes choses) or with plural nouns. Conjugated form of apporter (j'apporte, il apporte, il nous apporte).
target_language_example: Elle apporte de la nourriture pour le pique-nique.
native_language_example: She brings some food for the picnic.

meaning: brought to (someone) / brought (something) for (someone).
additional_notes: Past participle form of apporter used with an indirect object introduced by à (to/for someone). Often followed by what was brought: 'apporté à manger' = brought food (to someone). Subject and indirect object pronouns change: Je t'ai apporté à manger = I brought you something to eat. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je lui ai apporté à manger ce midi.
native_language_example: I brought him something to eat this noon.

meaning: learned everything / was told everything
additional_notes: Appris is the past participle of apprendre (to learn / to be told). The phrase 'appris tout' can mean either that someone learned all information or skills or that someone was told everything; context and word order affect nuance. More idiomatic word order in full sentences often places 'tout' before the past participle when using compound tenses (e.g., «Il a tout appris»), but 'appris tout' can appear in contexts like reported speech, ellipsis, or after negation/emphasis: «J'ai finalement appris tout» or «Elle a appris tout ce qui s'est passé».
target_language_example: J'ai appris tout seulement hier soir.
native_language_example: I learned (found out) everything only last night.

meaning: 'after the fact' / 'later on' (referring to something felt or realized after an event).
additional_notes: Used to say that something (regret, realization, consequence) happens or is noticed only after an action or event. Often followed by verbs like regretter, se sentir, or used as an adverbial phrase. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Je lui ai parlé sans réfléchir, et j'ai regretté après coup.
native_language_example: I spoke to him without thinking, and I regretted it afterward.

meaning: depends on context: either 'after you' (sequence/location) or 'in your opinion' when used as 'd'après toi'.
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) Literal/time/place: après toi = after you (e.g. letting someone go first, or something happening later than someone). 2) As part of the phrase 'd'après toi' it means 'in your opinion' or 'according to you'. Also appears in the idiomatic sentence 'il en a après toi' meaning 'he's got it in for you' (i.e. he's angry at you). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: D'après toi, on part maintenant ?
native_language_example: In your opinion, should we leave now?

meaning: depending on you / after you (literal: after you).
additional_notes: Has two common uses: 1) As a polite phrase meaning 'after you' (i.e., go ahead, you first). 2) As part of a longer expression meaning 'according to you' or 'in your opinion' when placed before a clause (often written 'd'après vous'). Context determines meaning: with 'd'' (d'après vous) = 'in your opinion'; alone 'après vous' = 'after you' (sequence/politeness) or 'after you doing something' when used with an infinitive (après vous être lavé = after you washed).
target_language_example: D'abord vous passez, après vous, je viendrai.
native_language_example: You go first, then I'll come.

meaning: after all; in spite of everything; when all is said and done.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a reminder, justification, or a conciliatory comment — often to downplay objections or to point out an obvious/final reason. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence, or alone as a short remark. Neutral register; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de problème — après tout, nous pouvons revenir demain.
native_language_example: There's no problem — after all, we can come back tomorrow.

meaning: 'after' (introduces a clause indicating that one action occurred later than another).
additional_notes: Connects two clauses: the 'après que' clause refers to an event that happened earlier; the main clause describes what followed. In standard/formal French, the verb after 'après que' is normally in an indicative tense (passé composé, passé simple, imparfait, plus-que-parfait, etc.), though some speakers use the subjunctive colloquially (e.g., après que + subjunctive). Do not confuse with 'après' + noun/pronoun (e.g., 'après le dîner').
target_language_example: Après que sa femme mourut, il vécut encore quelques années supplémentaires.
native_language_example: After his wife died, he lived on for a few more years.

meaning: 'the money belongs to' or 'the money is with/held by' (indicates possession or location of money).
additional_notes: Combines 'argent' (money) with the construction 'être à' which expresses possession ('belongs to') or, in context, where money is held (e.g. 'à la banque' = 'in the bank'). Use 'argent est à moi/toi/lui' to say the money belongs to someone, or 'argent est à la banque' to say the money is at the bank. Word order: 'Cet argent est à moi.'
target_language_example: Tout l'argent est à elle; elle l'a mis à la banque.
native_language_example: All the money belongs to her; she put it in the bank.

meaning: firearm; a weapon that fires projectiles using an explosive charge (gun).
additional_notes: Common term for guns, rifles, pistols, etc. Used in both formal and everyday contexts. Plural: armes à feu. Can appear in questions about ownership or descriptions (e.g., powerful firearm).
target_language_example: Il a été arrêté pour port d'une arme à feu.
native_language_example: He was arrested for carrying a firearm.

meaning: arrive at / reach (the) — used with a masculine singular noun.
additional_notes: Combination of the verb arriver (to arrive/reach) + the contraction au (à + le). Use before a masculine singular place or thing: arriver au cinéma, arriver au sommet. For feminine nouns use arriver à la; for plural use arriver aux. Can mean physically reaching or figuratively reaching a point/state.
target_language_example: Si on arrive au sommet, on pourra sauter.
native_language_example: If we reach the top, we can jump.

meaning: arrive at; reach; manage to
additional_notes: With a place or abstract noun, arriver à often means "arrive at" or "reach" (for example, arriver à la station, arriver à une conclusion). With an infinitive, it often means "manage to" or "succeed in" doing something: je n'arrive pas à comprendre = "I can't manage to understand."
target_language_example: Combien de temps cela prend-il pour arriver à la station ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to arrive at the station?

meaning: 'arrived in/by' (depends on context) — past participle arrivé followed by preposition en; with places it means 'arrived in' a country/region (use en for feminine places or before a vowel), with vehicles it means 'arrived by' that transport, and with expressions like 'en premier' or 'en toute sécurité' it forms adverbial phrases ('arrived first', 'arrived safely').
additional_notes: Agreement: arrivé agrees in gender/number when used with être (elle est arrivée, nous sommes arrivés). Use en for feminine countries/regions or before a vowel (en France, en Espagne). With modes of transport use en + vehicle (arrivé en taxi, arrivé en voiture). Can also appear in set phrases: arrivé en premier (arrived first), arrivé en toute sécurité (arrived safely).
target_language_example: Il avait dix ans quand il est arrivé en France.
native_language_example: He was ten years old when he arrived in France.

meaning: 'arrived too' — the past participle arrivé (from arriver) combined with trop to indicate someone arrived too (late/early) when followed by an adverb (e.g., tard/tôt). Note that in full sentences the past participle agrees in gender/number with the subject when used with être in passé composé (arrivé / arrivée / arrivés / arrivées).
additional_notes: This entry shows the sequence 'arrivé trop' as part of common patterns like 'arrivé trop tard' (arrived too late) or 'arrivé trop tôt' (arrived too early). In isolation 'arrivé trop' is typically followed by an adverb (tard/tôt) or clause. Adjust arrivé for gender/number when appropriate.
target_language_example: Vous êtes arrivé trop tard.
native_language_example: You arrived too late.

meaning: 'happened to your' (used to ask what happened to someone's body part or possession).
additional_notes: Common in questions asking what has happened to someone or something: Qu'est-il arrivé à votre ...? = What happened to your ...? 'Arriver à' here means 'happen to'. Formal/polite because of 'votre' (your, formal or plural). Use with body parts, objects, or people.
target_language_example: Qu'est-il arrivé à votre voiture ?
native_language_example: What happened to your car?

meaning: arrived there
additional_notes: Past participle 'arrivés' agrees in number/gender with the subject (they arrived). 'Là-bas' means 'over there' or 'there' (emphatic, indicating a location at some distance). Commonly used to say someone reached a place before someone else (arrivés là-bas avant ...).
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés là-bas avant nous.
native_language_example: They arrived there before us.

meaning: bus stop
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning the place where buses pick up and drop off passengers. Use l'arrêt (masculine) with definite/indefinite articles: un arrêt de bus, l'arrêt de bus. Can be used with prepositions: à l'arrêt de bus, près de l'arrêt de bus.
target_language_example: Où est l'arrêt de bus le plus proche ?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest bus stop?

meaning: don't stop / keeps (on) — depending on context: either an imperative 'don't stop' or part of a negative present ('doesn't stop / keeps on').
additional_notes: Colloquial. 'Arrête pas' is a contraction of 'n'arrête pas' (imperative negative) or of 'n'arrête pas de ...' meaning 'keeps on (doing something)'. In spoken French the initial 'ne' is often dropped. Use 'arrête' alone for 'stop' (imperative) and include 'de' + verb when saying 'keeps on doing something' (e.g. 'Il n'arrête pas de parler' → 'He keeps talking').
target_language_example: Arrête pas de te comparer aux autres.
native_language_example: Don't keep comparing yourself to others.

meaning: stop ...-ing
additional_notes: From arrêter de + infinitive, used to say someone stops doing something: arrêter de fumer = 'to stop smoking'. arrêtiez is the vous form; after que, it is often the subjunctive ('that you stop').
target_language_example: Je préférerais que vous arrêtiez de parler si fort.
native_language_example: I'd prefer that you stop talking so loudly.

meaning: martial art; a system or tradition of combat practices (e.g., karate, judo, kung-fu).
additional_notes: Used to refer to any organized fighting discipline or combat sport. In French, 'art' is singular and 'martial' agrees (masculine). Commonly used with national adjectives (art martial chinois, japonais) or specific names (le kung-fu est un art martial).
target_language_example: Le karaté est un art martial que je pratique depuis trois ans.
native_language_example: Karate is a martial art that I've practiced for three years.

meaning: did ... properly
additional_notes: This is the second-person singular (tu) form of the verb avoir + bien. 'Bien' modifies the verb to mean 'well', 'properly', or 'indeed' (emphasizing success or thoroughness). Use with different verbs: 'tu as bien dormi ?' = 'did you sleep well?', 'tu as bien réussi' = 'you did well / succeeded'. In spoken French 'bien' can also add emphasis: 'tu l'as bien eu' = 'you really got him/it' or 'you got away with it'.
target_language_example: Tu as bien préparé le repas ?
native_language_example: Did you prepare the meal properly?

meaning: 'have slept with' / 'slept with' (i.e., had sex with).
additional_notes: Past participle construction of the verb 'coucher' used in the passé composé: 'tu as couché' = 'you slept with' (informal, refers to sexual intercourse). Common in spoken French; can be blunt or offensive depending on context. Not literal 'to lie down' here — in these sentences it means 'to have had sex with'.
target_language_example: Tu as couché avec qui hier soir ?
native_language_example: Who did you sleep with last night?

meaning: you told (someone) to
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé of dire + a clause introduced by de + infinitive or de + question/amount. Structure: "tu as dit de + (infinitive or clause)" means "you told (someone) to..." or "you said to (someone) ..." In spoken French the indirect object (to whom) is often expressed earlier in the sentence (tu leur as dit de...). With verbs of telling, use "dire à + personne + de + infinitive"; in passé composé the past participle (dit) stays the same. If the sentence lacks an explicit indirect object, context tells who was addressed.
target_language_example: Tu leur as dit de fermer la porte.
native_language_example: You told them to close the door.

meaning: 'you have ... again' (the familiar/neutral 2nd person singular 'tu as' + 'encore' meaning 'again' or 'still')
additional_notes: This is the combination of the verb form 'tu as' (you have) with 'encore' (again/still). In many examples it's used in short spoken comments: pointing out that someone has done something again (often with slight annoyance or surprise) or that a state continues. The exact meaning depends on the main verb that follows: e.g. 'tu as encore dormi' = 'you slept again' (or 'you slept like that again'), 'tu as encore oublié' = 'you forgot again'.
target_language_example: Tu as encore laissé tes clés sur la table.
native_language_example: You left your keys on the table again.

meaning: 'did you hear that' or 'have you heard that' (used to ask if someone heard what was just said).
additional_notes: This is an informal spoken structure combining the auxiliary 'as' (tu as) + past participle 'entendu' + demonstrative 'ce' as the start of a reported clause (often completed by 'que...' or embedded as 'ce qu'il a dit'). In everyday speech the subject 'tu' is often contracted to 't'' (T'as entendu ce...). Use it to ask whether someone heard a statement or news just mentioned. The full clause is usually 'tu as entendu ce qu'il/elle a dit ?' or 'tu as entendu ce qu'ils ont dit ?'.
target_language_example: T'as entendu ce qu'il vient de dire ?
native_language_example: Did you hear what he just said?

meaning: 'you had (some)'. Often used in the expression "tu as eu de la chance" = "you were (lucky)" or more literally "you had some luck".
additional_notes: This is the 2nd person singular passé composé (avoir + past participle) followed by the partitive article 'de la' + a noun (e.g. chance). In casual speech the subject and auxiliary may be contracted (T'as eu de la...). Commonly used in set phrases like 'tu as eu de la chance' (you were lucky) or 'tu as eu de la patience' (you showed some patience). The phrase itself is not idiomatic beyond forming 'you had some + noun'.
target_language_example: T'as eu de la chance hier soir.
native_language_example: You were lucky last night.

meaning: 'have done this' (second-person singular, past) — literally 'you have done this.'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a short sequence of words: 'as' = second-person singular of 'avoir' in the present (tu as), 'fait' = past participle of 'faire', 'ce' = 'this' or 'it'. In natural French you'd usually see 'tu as fait ça/ceci' or 'tu as fait cela' (more common) or 'tu as fait ce [nom]' when followed by a noun (e.g. 'tu as fait ce travail'). Without context it looks like a clipped part of a sentence. Pronoun order: spoken/written: 'tu as fait ça.'
target_language_example: Tu as fait ce gâteau ?
native_language_example: Did you make this cake?

meaning: 'have done of' — part of constructions like "tu as fait de ton mieux" (you have done your best) or "qu'est-ce que tu as fait de... ?" (what did you do with.../what happened to...).
additional_notes:
This phrase is not a fixed idiom by itself but a sequence: "as" (2nd person singular of avoir) + "fait" (past participle of faire) + "de" introducing a complement. Common patterns:
- "tu as fait de ton mieux" = "you did/you have done your best" ("de" + "ton mieux").
- "Qu'est-ce que tu as fait de X ?" = "What did you do with X? / What happened to X?" ("de" + noun/pronoun). Context determines translation (action performed vs. whereabouts). Use with other subjects by changing the auxiliary: "il a fait de...", "nous avons fait de...".
The sequence is compositional (its parts keep their meanings) and not informal.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu as fait de mon livre ?
native_language_example: What did you do with my book?

meaning: 'have done for' (part of the phrase 'ce que tu as fait pour moi' = 'what you have done for me').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase but a sequence of words: as (2nd person singular of avoir), fait (past participle of faire), pour (for). It appears in sentences like "ce que tu as fait pour moi" meaning "what you have done for me". Use with a subject pronoun (tu, il, elle, etc.) and possibly an object (pour moi, pour nous).
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu as fait pour elle.
native_language_example: I know what you have done for her.

meaning: you closed the (feminine noun) — informal spoken/short form of "est-ce que tu as fermé la... ?" or "tu as fermé la... ?"
additional_notes: Used to ask whether the listener has closed something feminine (la fenêtre, la porte, la voiture — though "la voiture" is feminine but often you'd say "la portière" or "la voiture" depending on context). This is the familiar/neutral spoken way; in full questions you might hear "Est-ce que tu as fermé la fenêtre ?" or the inversion "As-tu fermé la fenêtre ?" The phrase is compositional (meaning comes from the words) and not slang, but it's informal/conversational rather than very formal.
target_language_example: Tu as fermé la fenêtre avant de partir ?
native_language_example: Did you close the window before leaving?

meaning: to have done something badly / to have (verb) poorly (you did ... badly).
additional_notes: This construction uses the auxiliary 'avoir' + 'mal' + past participle (here shown as 'as mal' + past participle) to say someone performed an action poorly or made a mistake (e.g., 'tu as mal entendu' = you heard incorrectly). It often appears with verbs of perception, action, or education (entendre, lire, agir, élever). 'Mal' modifies the verb and means 'badly' or 'wrongly'.
target_language_example: Tu as mal compris la question.
native_language_example: You understood the question badly / You misunderstood the question.

meaning: 'you forgot your...' (informal/tu form)
additional_notes: This is the familiar second-person singular (tu) form of the perfect tense: as (avoir) + oublié (past participle). Use it to tell someone they forgot something that belongs to them (ton = your, masculine or before a vowel). For feminine nouns use "ta" (tu as oublié ta clé). For plural use "tes" (tu as oublié tes chaussures). Pronunciation: [a z‿u bli e tɔ̃].
target_language_example: Tu as oublié ton sac à dos.
native_language_example: You forgot your backpack.

meaning: 'have not ... yet' (informal spoken contraction used with tu)
additional_notes: This is the familiar/informal spoken form of 'tu n'as pas encore ...' (you haven't ... yet). It combines 'tu as' (you have) with the negation 'pas' and 'encore' (yet/still) but often drops the 'ne' in everyday speech: 'T'as pas encore fini ?' = 'Tu n'as pas encore fini ?'. Use with the pronoun tu in casual contexts. For formal or written French, use 'tu n'as pas encore ...' or 'vous n'avez pas encore ...' for polite/plural.
target_language_example: T'as pas encore répondu ?
native_language_example: You haven't answered yet?

meaning: did spend
additional_notes: This is the compound form of the passé composé with the auxiliary avoir + the past participle 'passé' (tu as passé). It translates as 'did spend' or 'have spent' depending on context. Commonly used with time expressions (un après‑midi, la nuit, de bonnes vacances) or to mean 'to pass' time (passer du temps). For questions use inversion or est-ce que as in the examples.
target_language_example: Tu as passé un bon week‑end ?
native_language_example: Did you have a good weekend?

meaning: have taken a
additional_notes: This is part of the present perfect (passé composé) with tu + avoir + past participle + indefinite article. It literally appears in questions or statements: "tu as pris un..." meaning "you took/have taken a..." or in questions "as-tu pris un..." In English use "have/ did + you + take" depending on context. The phrase requires an object after "un" (e.g. bain, avocat, petit-déjeuner).
target_language_example: Tu as pris un café ce matin ?
native_language_example: Did you have a coffee this morning?

meaning: 'you have' + 'so/so much' (emphasis: 'you have ... so much' or 'you are so...')
additional_notes: Combines the 2nd-person singular of avoir (tu as) with the adverb tellement meaning 'so' or 'so much.' Used to emphasize a change, amount, or degree: Tu as tellement changé = You have changed so much / You are so different. Can modify verbs (as tellement + past participle) or adjectives (as tellement + adjective).
target_language_example: Tu as tellement grandi depuis la dernière fois !
native_language_example: You have grown so much since the last time!

meaning: you have always
additional_notes: 'as' is the tu form of avoir, so this phrase means 'you have always'. In these examples, it is followed by a past participle (like fait, voulu, été) to form the passé composé and express that something has always been the case or has always happened.
target_language_example: Tu as toujours aimé les chats.
native_language_example: You have always loved cats.

meaning: have everything
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of "tu as tout..." = "you have everything...". In many beginner sentences, "as" is also the auxiliary verb in the passé composé, so "tu as tout + past participle" means "you ... everything": for example, "tu as tout trouvé" = "you found everything". Here, "tout" means "everything".
target_language_example: Tu as tout compris ?
native_language_example: Did you understand everything?

meaning: 'have you seen this/that' (informal spoken French: tu as vu ce ...?)
additional_notes: Common colloquial expression used to draw attention to a person, thing, or situation—often followed by a noun or demonstrative (ce type, ce bâtiment, ce ciel). Usually spoken as 'Tu as vu ce...?' or contracted 'T'as vu ce...?' It can express surprise, disapproval, or to point something out to the listener.
target_language_example: T'as vu ce café là-bas ?
native_language_example: Have you seen that café over there?

meaning: "have seen this" (informal, spoken contraction within a question or clause)
additional_notes: This sequence looks like parts of the compound verb plus demonstrative: 'as' = second-person singular of 'avoir' in the present (tu as), 'vu' = past participle of 'voir', and 'ce' = this/it. It appears in spoken or clipped written forms inside larger sentences (e.g. 'Tu as vu ce…' or 'T'as vu ce…') and often begins a question meaning 'Did you see this…?' or introduces something the speaker points out. In standard writing, keep the subject 'tu' before 'as' and place 'ce' after: 'Tu as vu ce film ?' Contractions like 'T'as vu ce… ?' are very common in speech. Use for informal contexts.
target_language_example: T'as vu ce film hier soir ?
native_language_example: Did you see that movie last night?

meaning: 'have you seen it' (familiar form: 'tu as vu la...').
additional_notes: This is the familiar 2nd-person singular past (passé composé) form 'tu as vu' + 'la' (feminine direct object pronoun or demonstrative article). 'Tu as vu la...' can mean 'have you seen the...' or 'have you seen her/it' depending on context. In the example, 'la lumière du jour' = 'daylight' (feminine), so 'tu as vu la lumière' = 'have you seen daylight'. Pronunciation and word order are same as in standard French; 'la' refers to a feminine noun mentioned or understood. For politeness or formality, use 'avez-vous vu la...' with 'vous'.
target_language_example: Tu as vu la nouvelle exposition au musée ?
native_language_example: Have you seen the new exhibit at the museum?

meaning: 'have you seen the...' (informal second-person singular question)
additional_notes: Contraction of 'tu as vu les...'. Used in spoken or casual written French to ask if someone has seen specific things (news, people, objects, places). Followed by a noun or noun phrase: 'as vu les infos?', 'as vu les plans?'. The subject is 'tu' (you, singular informal). For polite/formal or plural 'you' use 'avez-vous vu les...' or 'vous avez vu les...'.
target_language_example: Tu as vu les photos de la soirée ?
native_language_example: Have you seen the photos from the party?

as besoin de quoi que ce

target_language_multi_word_term: as besoin de quoi que ce
meaning: This string is ungrammatical in French. It appears to be a scrambled form of phrases meaning “do you need anything” (e.g., «Tu as besoin de quoi ?», «As-tu besoin de quelque chose ?», «As-tu besoin de quoi que ce soit ?»). It should not be used as written.
additional_notes:
Correct alternatives:
- «Tu as besoin de quoi ?» (informal) — “What do you need?”
- «As-tu besoin de quelque chose ?» (neutral/formal) — “Do you need something/anything?”
- «As-tu besoin de quoi que ce soit ?» (emphatic) — “Do you need anything at all?”

The form «as besoin de quoi que ce» mixes parts of these expressions and is not grammatically valid. Use one of the correct alternatives above depending on register and emphasis.
target_language_example: — Tu as besoin de quoi que ce pour la tarte ? (incorrect; ungrammatical)
native_language_example: — You 'as besoin de quoi que ce' for the pie? (incorrect; ungrammatical)

meaning: 'do you have any...?' (informal spoken question: 'tu as de l'... ?')
additional_notes: Contraction of 'tu as de l'' used in informal speech (often written 't'as de l''). It introduces an uncountable noun or a singular noun starting with a vowel: e.g. alcool, argent, eau. Use to ask if someone has some/any of something. For polite or formal contexts, use 'avez-vous' or 'est-ce que vous avez'.
target_language_example: T'as de l'eau ?
native_language_example: Do you have any water?

meaning: you have done the
additional_notes: Combination of the auxiliary 'as' (tu as) + past participle 'fait' + definite article 'le' starting a noun phrase. It appears in spoken and written French when saying someone 'has done' something (e.g. le bon choix, le boulot, le calcul). In casual speech 'tu as' often becomes 't'as'. The exact English auxiliary (have/did) depends on context; use present perfect ('you have done the') for completed actions with relevance to now, or simple past ('you did the') in narrative contexts.
target_language_example: Tu as fait le bon choix.
native_language_example: You have done the right choice. / You did the right choice.

meaning: 'you have done your' (followed by a noun): indicates someone has completed a specific task or obligation.
additional_notes: This is the second-person singular (tu) passé composé of faire + a possessive adjective 'ton' plus a noun. Use to say someone has completed something that belongs to or concerns them (e.g., ton boulot, ton choix, ton devoir). In English you'd typically say 'you've done your...' or 'you've made your...' depending on the noun (faire un choix = make a choice). Verb agreement: 'tu as fait' remains the same regardless of the following noun.
target_language_example: Tu as fait ton devoir ?
native_language_example: Have you done your homework?

meaning: 'have something better' — used in questions like 'Do you have something better to do/say/propose?'
additional_notes: Colloquial; often appears in spoken French with inversion/ellipses (T'as mieux ? / Tu as mieux à faire ?). Used to challenge what someone is doing or saying, implying there's a better option or that the current action/idea is not worthwhile. Can be followed by 'à faire', 'à proposer', etc. Contraction 'T'as' is common in speech.
target_language_example: Tu as mieux à proposer que ça ?
native_language_example: Do you have something better to suggest than that?

meaning: 'don't you have a...?' (informal way to ask if someone has or can give something or an idea)
additional_notes: Colloquial/informal contraction of 'n'as pas une' or 'tu n'as pas une' used in spoken French. Often appears as 'T'as pas une...' or 'Tu n'as pas une...'. Used to ask if someone has something on them (e.g., a cigarette) or to request a suggestion/idea. Tone is casual; use in familiar contexts. The full formal version would be 'Tu n'as pas une...'.
target_language_example: T'as pas une pièce pour le bus ?
native_language_example: Don't you have a coin for the bus?

meaning: you may/might have (something or be something).
additional_notes: Combines the second-person singular present of 'avoir' (tu as) with 'peut-être' to express possibility or uncertainty about possession, condition, or a state. In spoken French, 'tu as' often contracts to 't'as' (as in examples). Common uses: possibilities (tu as peut-être le choix = you might have a choice), suggestions about someone’s condition (tu as peut-être une commotion = you may have a concussion), or cautiously agreeing (tu as peut-être raison = you might be right).
target_language_example: Tu as peut-être besoin d'aide pour finir ce projet.
native_language_example: You might need help to finish this project.

target_language_multi_word_term: as quoi / t'as quoi / tu as quoi
meaning: 'what do you have' or more generally 'what's wrong/what's up' depending on context.
additional_notes: Informal spoken French. Often used to ask what someone is wearing or holding (literal: 'what do you have on your arm/feet/hand'), or to ask what's the matter ('Tu as quoi ?' = 'What's wrong?'). Frequently contracted to 'T'as quoi ?' in speech. Word order differs from English but is natural in French questions.
target_language_example: T'as quoi au bras ?
native_language_example: What's on your arm?

meaning: 'you have' (informal contraction; 'tu as tes' = 'do you have your / you have your')
additional_notes: T'as is the spoken/informal contraction of 'tu as'. Combined with 'tes' (your, plural possessions or things) it means 'you have your ...' or is used in questions like 'T'as tes règles?' ('Do you have your period?'). Common in colloquial spoken French. Use 'tu as tes' in writing or more formal contexts. Word order: t'as tes + [noun].
target_language_example: T'as tes clés ?
native_language_example: Do you have your keys?

meaning: 'do you have everything' or 'you have everything (that...)' — used to ask or state that someone possesses all they need or everything required.
additional_notes: This sequence appears in colloquial questions or statements built with avoir + tout + relative pronoun (ce que / ce dont / ce qu'il faut). Common spoken forms: «Tu as tout ce qu'il te faut?», «T'as tout ce qu'il faut?» or «Tu as tout ce dont tu as besoin?» «T'as» is the contracted informal form of «tu as». Use to ask if someone has everything they need or to say someone has everything desirable. The exact follow-up changes the nuance: «ce qu'il te faut» = what you need, «ce dont tu as besoin» = that of which you are in need, «ce qu'un homme peut désirer» = what one could desire.
target_language_example: T'as tout ce qu'il te faut pour partir?
native_language_example: Do you have everything you need to leave?

meaning: have three
additional_notes: Combines the verb 'avoir' (tu as = you have) with the number 'trois' (three). Used to say someone has three of something. In English you usually say 'you have three' or 'there are three' depending on context. Subject 'tu' (you, singular informal) is implied; in other contexts the verb form changes (j'ai, il/elle a, nous avons...).
target_language_example: Tu as trois pommes dans ton sac.
native_language_example: You have three apples in your bag.

meaning: you have a good (something) — 'tu as un bon' begins a sentence meaning 'you have a good [noun]'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb tu as ('you have') + the indefinite article un + the adjective bon before a noun (e.g. avocat, cœur, plan, travail). In spoken French the adjective can appear before the noun when emphasizing quality (Tu as un bon avocat) or the adjective may follow depending on the noun (un bon cœur = a good heart). Use 'tu' for informal singular you.
target_language_example: Tu as un bon professeur.
native_language_example: You have a good teacher.

meaning: 'have one' (informal spoken form: 'tu as une')
additional_notes: This is the spoken/informal sequence where 'tu as une' becomes 't'en as une' when referring back to something introduced with 'de' (informal 't'' = 'tu', 'en' = 'of it'/'one'). Often used in questions: 'T'en as une ?' = 'Do you have another one / one of those?'. Context determines whether it means 'one' (une) or 'another'. Grammatical components: 'tu' (you), 'en' (of it / some / one), 'as' (have, 2nd person singular of avoir), 'une' (feminine 'one').
target_language_example: T'en as une pour moi ?
native_language_example: Do you have one for me?

meaning: Enough talking; let's stop talking about (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to cut off a topic or end a discussion. Can stand alone (Assez parlé!) or be followed by de + topic/person (Assez parlé de moi). Polite to firm depending on tone; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Assez parlé de travail, parlons de tes vacances.
native_language_example: Enough talking about work, let's talk about your vacation.

meaning: seated in (a formation or arrangement, e.g. 'seated in a circle').
additional_notes: Used after a plural subject (ils/elles/se sont) or with nouns to describe how people are sitting — usually followed by a noun indicating the shape or arrangement (en cercle, en demi-cercle, en rangées, etc.). Commonly appears as 's'asseoir' past participle agreement: ils se sont assis en + [arrangement].
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes assis en demi-cercle pour écouter le conteur.
native_language_example: We sat in a semicircle to listen to the storyteller.

meaning: 'to wait in/inside' (followed by a place).
additional_notes: Used with a location introduced by an article or noun (e.g. la voiture, le bar, le couloir). Common in everyday speech to tell or ask someone to wait somewhere. The verb attendre can take a person as a direct object (Je t'attends) or be followed by 'dans' + place to indicate where the waiting happens. Word order: attendre + dans + [place].
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu veux attendre dans la voiture ?
native_language_example: Do you want to wait in the car?

meaning: literally 'to wait a' — part of phrases used to ask someone to wait briefly (e.g. 'attendre un peu', 'attendre un instant'). The verb attendre is transitive; when followed by 'un' + noun it means 'to wait a/an [noun]'.
additional_notes: 'attendre un' on its own is incomplete in French and normally appears with a following word (peu, instant, peu plus longtemps, etc.). Common in polite requests: 'Attendre un instant', 'attendre un peu'. Can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on phrasing.
target_language_example: Est-ce que vous pouvez attendre un peu ?
native_language_example: Can you wait a bit?

meaning: to wait and see; to wait to find out what will happen.
additional_notes: Used to express taking a wait-and-see attitude about an uncertain situation. Often appears in the imperative or future context: «On va attendre voir» or colloquially «attendons de voir». More common written form is «attendre de voir» or simply «attendre» + «voir» in speech. Informal/colloquial phrasing.
target_language_example: On va attendre voir avant de décider.
native_language_example: We'll wait and see before deciding.

meaning: 'given that' / 'considering that' / 'whereas' (used to introduce a fact or reason)
additional_notes: Formal or legal phrase used to introduce a premise, reason, or fact. Common in written French (laws, official documents, formal letters) and in formal speech. It often appears at the start of a clause explaining why something is the case. In everyday spoken French you might instead hear 'comme' or 'étant donné que'.
target_language_example: Attendu que les travaux sont terminés, la route sera rouverte demain.
native_language_example: Given that the work is finished, the road will be reopened tomorrow.

meaning: be careful not to / take care not to (warns someone to avoid something)
additional_notes: Used to warn someone; usually appears in the imperative with 'Fais attention de ne pas...' or 'Faites attention de ne pas...'. Followed by an infinitive verb introduced by 'pas' for the negative (ne... pas). More common alternative: 'Fais attention à ne pas...' (both are correct; 'à' is very frequent).
target_language_example: Fais attention de ne pas te brûler.
native_language_example: Be careful not to burn yourself.

meaning: attention to
additional_notes: Used with a person or thing that receives focus or care. In affirmative contexts (porter attention à) it means to pay close attention to or be careful about something. In commands with ne...pas, "ne fais/ne faites pas attention à" means "don't pay attention to" or "ignore" someone/something. Verb agreement: often appears after verbs like porter (porter attention à), faire (faire attention à), or as a standalone noun phrase.
target_language_example: Fais attention à la marche en descendant.
native_language_example: Watch your step when going down.

meaning: to bring (trouble, problems) on someone or oneself; to cause someone to get into trouble.
additional_notes: Often used with nouns like "ennuis" (trouble) to mean 'to get into trouble' or 'to cause trouble for (someone)'. Common constructions: "s'attirer des ennuis" (to get oneself into trouble) or "attirer des ennuis à quelqu'un" (to bring trouble on someone). Usually followed by a plural noun (des ennuis, des problèmes).
target_language_example: Il risque de s'attirer des ennuis s'il continue comme ça.
native_language_example: He risks getting himself into trouble if he keeps going like that.

meaning: 'caught my' (as in 'caught my attention').
additional_notes: Used with a noun (usually 'attention') to say something attracted or drew the speaker's notice. Most common full expression: 'attirer mon attention' (to catch my attention). Tense changes (a attiré, a attirent, a attirera) depending on subject/time. Often followed by 'sur' + object to indicate what was noticed (e.g., 'attiré mon attention sur...').
target_language_example: Cette couleur a attiré mon attention.
native_language_example: That color caught my attention.

meaning: 'to catch a cold' or 'to get sick from being cold'.
additional_notes: Common French expression meaning to become ill (usually a cold) after being exposed to cold weather or getting chilled. Often used as a warning: "Tu vas attraper froid" = "You'll catch a cold." Can also be used more generally for getting sick because of cold exposure.
target_language_example: Si tu ne prends pas de veste, tu vas attraper froid.
native_language_example: If you don't take a jacket, you'll catch a cold.

meaning: 'beyond' or 'on the other side' (can be literal or figurative, also 'afterlife' in some contexts).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something beyond a place, limit, time, or concept. In everyday use it means 'beyond' (e.g., beyond that point, beyond expectations). In philosophical or spiritual contexts it can refer to the afterlife or another dimension. Often appears with de/du (au-delà de + noun) or alone as a noun (l'au-delà = the afterlife).
target_language_example: Au-delà de la montagne, il y a un petit village.
native_language_example: Beyond the mountain, there is a small village.

meaning: beyond; on the other side of; more than
additional_notes: Used to indicate something that is farther, exceeds a limit, or goes past a point in space, ability, duty, time, or degree. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g. au-delà de vos capacités = beyond your abilities). Can be literal (beyond the hill) or figurative (beyond expectations).
target_language_example: Son travail va au-delà de ce qu'on attendait.
native_language_example: His work goes beyond what was expected.

meaning: under, below (in position or level).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something or someone is beneath something else (physically or on a list/diagram). Often followed by de + noun (au-dessous de) when specifying what it's below. Can be used alone in context (e.g., 'ma chambre est juste au-dessous' = my room is just below).
target_language_example: Le chat dort au-dessous de la table.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping under the table.

meaning: above; over; higher than (in space, level, or amount).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something is physically higher or exceeds a limit/level (e.g., temperature, height, amount). Often followed by de + noun (au-dessus de) when specifying what it's above. Can be used both literally and figuratively.
target_language_example: Le tableau est accroché au-dessus de la cheminée.
native_language_example: The painting is hung above the fireplace.

meaning: right in the middle of (time or place); in the very middle of
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens in the exact middle of a period or place (often time: night, day). Adds a stronger, slightly dramatic emphasis than just 'au milieu de'. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il a quitté la fête au beau milieu de la nuit.
native_language_example: He left the party right in the middle of the night.

meaning: if necessary; when needed; as required.
additional_notes: Used to say something can be done or used when necessary. Common in instructions or offers of help: 'Je suis là, au besoin' = 'I'm here if needed.' Often follows the clause it modifies. Can be interchangeable with 'si besoin' or 'si nécessaire'.
target_language_example: Appelle-moi, au besoin.
native_language_example: Call me if necessary.

meaning: 'in the right' (as part of expressions like 'au bon endroit' = 'in the right place' or 'au bon moment' = 'at the right time').
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase—'au' (à + le) + adjective 'bon' combines with a noun (endroit, moment, etc.) to mean 'in/at the right [noun]'. Common in expressions indicating correctness of place, time, choice, etc. Use with singular masculine nouns; for feminine nouns use 'à la bonne' (e.g. 'à la bonne adresse').
target_language_example: Nous sommes au bon étage.
native_language_example: We are on the right floor.

meaning: at the right time; at a good/appropriate moment.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or should happen at an appropriate or timely moment. Can be literal (arriving at the right time) or figurative (speaking or acting when it's appropriate). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Merci, tu arrives au bon moment pour m'aider.
native_language_example: Thanks, you arrive at the right time to help me.

meaning: at the edge of; on the shore of; close to (a limit or place).
additional_notes: Used with abstract limits (e.g. au bord de la famine = on the verge of starvation) and with physical edges or shores (au bord de la mer / d'un lac / d'une route). Followed by 'de' + noun. Commonly expresses location at a boundary or being on the verge of something.
target_language_example: Nous étions assis au bord de la mer pour écouter les vagues.
native_language_example: We were sitting at the edge of the sea to listen to the waves.

meaning: 'at work' or 'to work' (informal).
additional_notes: Informal way to say 'at work' or 'to work' (standard: 'au travail' or 'au travail' / 'au bureau'). Used both to tell someone to get to work (e.g. 'Allez, au boulot' = 'Come on, get to work') and to state being or going to one's workplace ('Je suis au boulot', 'Il va au boulot').
target_language_example: Allez, au boulot, on a encore beaucoup à faire.
native_language_example: Come on, get to work, we still have a lot to do.

meaning: at the end of / at the tip of / after (a period) / at the end (figurative).
additional_notes: Used with physical locations (end/tip of something), positions (end of a line/table), time periods (after a few days), or figuratively (at the end of one's life/road or when a thought is fully carried out). Often followed by de + noun (au bout de la rue, au bout de quelques jours) or by a noun alone (au bout de la table).
target_language_example: Il habite au bout de la rue.
native_language_example: He lives at the end of the street.

meaning: in the end; ultimately; when all is said and done.
additional_notes: Used to summarize a result or final outcome after considering everything. Often interchangeable with "en fin de compte" or "finalement." Common in spoken and written French to introduce a conclusion or final judgment.
target_language_example: Au bout du compte, elle a accepté l'offre.
native_language_example: In the end, she accepted the offer.

meaning: completely exhausted, worn out (physically or mentally).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning to be at the end of one's strength or patience. Used for people feeling very tired, stressed, or emotionally drained. Common in spoken and informal contexts but acceptable in writing. Can refer to physical exhaustion or burnout.
target_language_example: Après trois nuits sans dormir, je suis au bout du rouleau.
native_language_example: After three nights without sleep, I'm completely exhausted.

meaning: 'in case' / 'in case that' (used to talk about a possible future situation).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to introduce a precaution or a possible situation. Often followed by a conditional (e.g. 'au cas où vous voudriez...') but can also appear with other tenses in informal speech. Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je te donne une clé au cas où tu oublierais la tienne.
native_language_example: I'll give you a key in case you forget yours.

meaning: warm; in a warm place or kept warm.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is warm or should be kept warm (physically). Common in everyday speech—can be short as a standalone phrase (e.g., "Au chaud." meaning "Keep warm" or "Stay warm"). Often follows verbs like garder (garder au chaud), rester (restez au chaud), or être (être au chaud).
target_language_example: Mets un manteau pour rester au chaud.
native_language_example: Put on a coat to stay warm.

meaning: unemployed; out of work.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does not have a job. Commonly used with être (être au chômage, rester au chômage). Can refer to temporary or longer-term unemployment. Not informal; neutral everyday expression.
target_language_example: Depuis six mois, elle est au chômage.
native_language_example: She has been unemployed for six months.

meaning: 'at the cinema or' — a short phrase combining 'at the cinema' with the conjunction 'or'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom on its own but a sequence you might see in a sentence offering an alternative involving the cinema. "Au cinéma" = 'at the cinema'; "ou" = 'or'. Expect it to be followed by another option (e.g. "au cinéma ou à la maison"). Word order: "au cinéma" (preposition + article + noun), then "ou" (conjunction).
target_language_example: On va au cinéma ou on reste à la maison ?
native_language_example: Are we going to the cinema or staying at home?

meaning: clear; in a clear, understandable state (used in expressions meaning 'clarify' or 'make clear').
additional_notes: Commonly appears in fixed expressions like 'mettre les choses au clair' or 'tirer quelque chose au clair' meaning 'to clarify something' or 'to clear things up'. Not used alone; paired with verbs like mettre, tirer, mettre au clair = to clarify. Literal sense 'in the clear' but used idiomatically.
target_language_example: Il faut mettre les choses au clair avant de décider.
native_language_example: We need to clear things up before deciding.

meaning: 'at the corner' or 'on the corner' (location); can also mean 'around the corner'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a place at the corner of a street or next to a nearby corner. Often appears with de/du/la to specify which corner (au coin de la rue, au coin du bois). Can also be used more figuratively (e.g. 'voir la mort au coin du bois' — 'see death around the corner'). Common in directions: 'Tourne au coin' / 'Tourne à gauche au coin suivant'.
target_language_example: La boulangerie est juste au coin de la rue.
native_language_example: The bakery is right on the corner of the street.

meaning: around the corner / at the corner of the street (very near).
additional_notes: Used to say something or someone is very close by — either literally at the street corner or nearby. Common in directions and to describe location. Can be followed by 'de la rue' (this phrase) or by a specific street name: 'au coin de la rue X'.
target_language_example: Le café est au coin de la rue, on y va à pied.
native_language_example: The café is around the corner, we can walk there.

meaning: 'full' or 'sold out' / 'at full capacity'
additional_notes: Used to say that something is full, complete or operating at full strength/capacity. Common in contexts like events, venues, teams, staffing, or inventory. Can be used impersonally (On est au complet) or as a short reply (Au complet.).
target_language_example: Le restaurant est au complet ce soir.
native_language_example: The restaurant is full tonight.

meaning: on the account of; charged to; attributed to (used in financial/administrative contexts)
additional_notes: Used in banking, billing, accounting or official records to indicate that an amount, a charge or a record is assigned to someone or something (e.g., an account, a budget line, or a person). Often appears in phrases like «au compte de X» meaning 'debited/credited to X' or 'listed under X'. Formal/administrative register.
target_language_example: Le paiement a été enregistré au compte de la société.
native_language_example: The payment was recorded on the company's account.

meaning: 'on the contrary' / 'quite the opposite' (used to disagree or correct a statement).
additional_notes: Used to contradict or counter what was just said. Can stand alone as a short reply (e.g. "Au contraire !"). Often followed by a full sentence that presents the opposing view. Equivalent to English 'on the contrary' or 'quite the opposite.'
target_language_example: Tu penses qu'il est paresseux ? Au contraire, il travaille très dur.
native_language_example: You think he's lazy? On the contrary, he works very hard.

meaning: informed
additional_notes: Used to say someone is informed or will be kept informed. Common in phrases like "tenir quelqu'un au courant" (to keep someone informed). Can be used as an adjective: "être au courant" = to be aware/know about something.
target_language_example: Tiens-moi au courant si les plans changent.
native_language_example: Keep me informed if the plans change.

meaning: during; in the course of; over (a period of).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something happening within a period or event. Common in formal and neutral contexts. Can be followed by a noun indicating time (ex: au cours de la nuit, au cours de la discussion) or a period (au cours de ce siècle).
target_language_example: Au cours de la réunion, elle a présenté de nouvelles idées.
native_language_example: During the meeting, she presented new ideas.

meaning: 'to hell with' / 'damn' (used to reject, dismiss or express anger/frustration)
additional_notes: An idiomatic exclamation used to dismiss someone/something or show strong annoyance. Can precede a noun (Au diable X) to mean 'to hell with X' or stand alone as 'To hell with it!' Not polite — avoid in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Au diable les règles, faisons comme on veut.
native_language_example: To hell with the rules, let's do what we want.

meaning: 'at the beginning' or 'at first'.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the start of a time period, situation, story, or process. Can mean 'initially' or 'at first' (contrasting with later changes). Common in spoken and written French. Often followed by a clause or used alone as a time marker.
target_language_example: Au début, je ne comprenais pas la chanson.
native_language_example: At first, I didn't understand the song.

meaning: at first; initially
additional_notes: Used to talk about what was true in the beginning or originally. Can mean 'initially' or 'to start with'. In contexts like sentence 3 (On se remet au départ), it can mean 'back to the start' or 'to the starting point' (more literal).
target_language_example: Au départ, je pensais que ce serait difficile, mais ça va.
native_language_example: At first, I thought it would be difficult, but it's okay.

meaning: by the way
additional_notes: Used to introduce a new topic or a question related to the conversation—often to ask for information or to remind someone of something. Common in spoken and informal written French. Can appear at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: Au fait, tu as reçu mon message ?
native_language_example: By the way, did you get my message?

meaning: 'to/at the fire' or 'in the fire' depending on context; can mean 'into the fire' (placing something to burn) or 'over/at a fire' (near flames), and is also used in set phrase 'au feu de bois' (roasted over wood fire).
additional_notes: Context determines meaning: when used with verbs like mettre/jeter, 'au feu' means 'into the fire' (to burn something). With verbs of position or description (détendre face au feu; rôti au feu de bois) it means 'by/at the fire' or 'over the fire' (cooked on/near fire). 'Au feu de circulation' is unrelated: it means 'at the traffic light' (French 'feu' also means traffic light).
target_language_example: Elle a mis les vieux journaux au feu pour les brûler.
native_language_example: She put the old newspapers into the fire to burn them.

meaning: over the course of; as (time or events) pass/by
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens gradually or during a period (au fil du temps = over time; au fil des années = as the years go by). Followed by a noun introduced by de/du/des. Common in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Au fil des semaines, il a appris à mieux gérer son stress.
native_language_example: Over the weeks, he learned to manage his stress better.

meaning: 'in the end' / 'ultimately'.
additional_notes: Used to sum up or give the final outcome or conclusion of a situation. Common in spoken and written French. Can be followed by a clause or stand alone as a short comment (e.g. 'Au final, oui.' = 'In the end, yes.'). Slightly more neutral than 'en fin de compte' but interchangeable in many contexts.
target_language_example: Au final, nous avons choisi un autre hôtel.
native_language_example: In the end, we chose a different hotel.

meaning: at the back / deep down / basically (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common multi-use phrase.
