target_language_example: Il a fait une bonne action en aidant la voisine à porter ses courses.
native_language_example: He did a good deed by helping the neighbor carry her groceries.

meaning: 'a good year' or used as 'Happy New Year' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is 'good year'. Used to wish someone a Happy New Year when said alone or as a greeting around New Year's. In other contexts it describes a period of a year that was good (une bonne année) or roughly 'for about a year' in informal uses (e.g. 'pendant une bonne année' = 'for a good year/about a year').
target_language_example: Nous avons passé une bonne année ensemble.
native_language_example: We had a good year together.

meaning: good luck
additional_notes: Used to wish someone success or luck in a situation. Commonly said when parting or before an event (exam, trip, challenge). Polite and neutral — appropriate in most contexts. Can be addressed to one person or a group (bonne chance à tous).
target_language_example: Bonne chance pour ton examen demain.
native_language_example: Good luck for your exam tomorrow.

meaning: informal/pejorative: 'woman' or 'wife' (often dismissive; can mean 'old woman' or 'mistress' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in informal or colloquial speech. Can be neutral in some contexts to mean 'woman' or 'wife' (e.g., 'sa bonne femme' = his wife), but often carries a dismissive, derogatory, or old-fashioned tone ('la bonne femme' = some woman/old woman). Context determines whether it means 'wife', 'some woman', 'old woman', or 'mistress'. Avoid in polite speech.
target_language_example: Il est parti avec une bonne femme, et ils ne sont jamais revenus.
native_language_example: He left with some woman, and they never came back.

meaning: a good/good-natured girl; used to describe a well-behaved, kind, or obedient girl.
additional_notes: Commonly used to praise behavior (kindness, obedience, politeness). Can be literal (a well-behaved girl) or used playfully/affectionately by adults toward children. Tone depends on context — sometimes slightly patronizing if said to an adult. Agreement: 'bonne' matches feminine singular 'fille'.
target_language_example: Sois une bonne fille et aide ta sœur.
native_language_example: Be a good girl and help your sister.

meaning: Happy [holiday/celebration] or Happy birthday (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to wish someone a happy celebration. In many contexts in France it commonly means "Happy birthday" when said to a person; in other contexts it means "Happy [name of holiday]" (e.g. Bonne fête du Canada = Happy Canada Day). Can be followed by the name of the holiday (Bonne fête de la lune) or directed at a person (Bonne fête à toi). Tone is neutral and appropriate in both formal and informal settings.
target_language_example: Bonne fête, profite bien de ta journée !
native_language_example: Happy birthday, enjoy your day!

meaning: good mood; cheerful mood.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is cheerful, in a pleasant or positive mood. Often used with être (être de bonne humeur / être en bonne humeur). Can be used generally (Il est de bonne humeur) or about a specific time (être en très bonne humeur). The opposite is 'mauvaise humeur' (bad mood).
target_language_example: Elle est de bonne humeur ce matin.
native_language_example: She is in a good mood this morning.

meaning: 'have a good day' (a polite farewell) or 'a good day' (noun phrase).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a polite goodbye: 'Bonne journée.' = 'Have a good day.' Can also describe a day as being good: 'une bonne journée.' Context tells whether it's a farewell or a description. Formality: neutral/polite and appropriate in most situations. Pronunciation tip: the final 'e' in 'bonne' is pronounced, and 'journée' stresses the -ée.
target_language_example: Bonne journée, à demain !
native_language_example: Have a good day, see you tomorrow!

meaning: good news; a piece of positive information
additional_notes: Used to announce or react to positive information. Can stand alone as an exclamation ("Bonne nouvelle!") or be followed by details. Gender: 'nouvelle' is feminine, but English translation is invariant. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Bonne nouvelle : le train est à l'heure.
native_language_example: Good news: the train is on time.

meaning: good news for (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say that some information is positive or beneficial to a person, group, or situation. Commonly followed by a noun or a pronoun (toi, vous, le clan, etc.). Can be used as 'Il y a une bonne nouvelle pour...' (There is good news for...) or 'J'ai une bonne nouvelle pour...' (I have good news for...).
target_language_example: J'ai une bonne nouvelle pour toi : ton examen est réussi.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: you passed your exam.

meaning: good night
additional_notes: Used to say farewell in the evening or before someone goes to sleep. Commonly used alone or followed by a name/term of address (e.g., "Bonne nuit, Marie"). Can be polite or familiar depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Bonne nuit, à demain.
native_language_example: Good night, see you tomorrow.

meaning: Safe travels / Have a good trip (literally: 'good road').
additional_notes: Used to wish someone a pleasant or safe journey when they are traveling by road or leaving on a trip. Can be said informally to friends, family or acquaintances. Also appears in questions when talking about the correct route (e.g. "C'est la bonne route ?" = "Is this the right road?").
target_language_example: Bonne route et à bientôt !
native_language_example: Safe travels and see you soon!

meaning: Have a good evening / Enjoy the rest of your evening.
additional_notes: Polite farewell used in the evening or at night. Appropriate in both formal and informal contexts; you can say it to one person or a group. Often said when parting ways or ending a conversation (in person, by phone, or in messages). If addressing a single male you might also hear "bonne soirée, monsieur"; for friends you can use simply "bonne soirée !"
target_language_example: Merci pour ton aide — bonne soirée !
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — have a good evening!

meaning: good manners; polite behavior
additional_notes: Used to refer to polite behavior, etiquette, or social rules. Often plural in French. Can be used generally (les bonnes manières) or in questions/addresses to scold someone (e.g. Où sont tes bonnes manières ? meaning 'Where are your manners?').
target_language_example: Apprends les bonnes manières à table.
native_language_example: Learn good manners at the table.

meaning: 'have a good holiday' / 'have a nice vacation' (wished to someone).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to wish someone an enjoyable holiday or vacation period. 'Bonnes' agrees in gender/number with 'vacances' (always plural). Use 'Passe de bonnes vacances' (informal singular you) for friends/family, and 'Passez de bonnes vacances' (formal or plural you) for polite or multiple people. Often said as a short goodbye before a holiday.
target_language_example: Passez de bonnes vacances et profitez bien du soleil !
native_language_example: Have a nice vacation and enjoy the sun!

meaning: an exclamation like 'good heavens!' or 'goodness gracious!'.
additional_notes: Used to express surprise, shock, disbelief or strong emotion. Polite/old-fashioned tone — not vulgar; can be emphatic on its own. Equivalent to English mild oaths such as 'good heavens' or 'for heaven's sake'.
target_language_example: Bonté divine, tu as vu la taille de ce gâteau ?
native_language_example: Good heavens, did you see the size of that cake?

meaning: an intense swear/exclamation like 'fucking hell' or 'goddamn it'.
additional_notes: Very vulgar and strong. Used to express anger, frustration, shock or to insult someone. Avoid in polite company or formal situations. Can be directed at a person (as an insult) or used alone as an exclamation. Equivalent to combining 'bordel' (mess/whorehouse, used as strong expletive) with 'merde' (shit).
target_language_example: Bordel de merde, j'ai encore perdu mes clés !
native_language_example: Fucking hell, I lost my keys again!

meaning: to kick someone's butt; to beat someone up (informal, aggressive).
additional_notes: Very informal/colloquial and vulgar. Used to threaten or promise physical punishment or a strong beating; can also be used figuratively to mean 'defeat' or 'dominate' someone. Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Si tu continues, je vais te botter le cul.
native_language_example: If you keep going, I'm going to kick your butt.

meaning: 'speechless' or 'open-mouthed' (astonished, unable to speak).
additional_notes: Used as an adjective or fixed expression after a noun/pronoun (often with être or rester) to describe someone so surprised or impressed that they can't speak. Literally 'mouth open.' Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Elle est restée bouche bée devant le spectacle.
native_language_example: She stood there speechless in front of the show.

meaning: a job/work at (somewhere) or 'work to' (something) depending on context.
additional_notes: Boulot = informal for 'job' or 'work'. With 'à' it can mean: 1) 'un boulot à faire' = 'a job/task to do' (à + infinitive or faire = to be done); 2) 'un boulot à New York' = 'a job in/at New York' (location); or 3) in colloquial imperatives it can appear in phrases like 'demande du boulot à X' = 'ask X for a job'. 'Boulot' is informal — prefer 'emploi' or 'travail' in formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il cherche un boulot à Paris cet été.
native_language_example: He's looking for a job in Paris this summer.

meaning: 'the end of the world' or 'a very remote place'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a place that is extremely far away or isolated. Can be literal (the end of the world) but is commonly used figuratively in everyday speech to mean 'in the middle of nowhere' or 'the back of beyond'. Often appears in phrases like «au bout du monde» (at the end of the world / in a very remote place).
target_language_example: Ils habitent au bout du monde, il faut des heures pour y arriver.
native_language_example: They live at the end of the world; it takes hours to get there.

meaning: mailbox; the physical receptacle for receiving mail (also email inbox in some contexts).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a physical mailbox at home or on the street (letterbox). Can also mean an email inbox in modern contexts, but in everyday spoken French 'boîte aux lettres' usually means the physical box for postal mail. Feminine noun phrase: 'la boîte aux lettres'. Plural: 'les boîtes aux lettres'.
target_language_example: J'ai relevé le courrier dans la boîte aux lettres.
native_language_example: I collected the mail from the mailbox.

meaning: nightclub; a place for dancing, music and late-night socializing.
additional_notes: Commonly shortened to "boîte" in spoken French. Often implies late hours, DJs or live music, dancing and drinks. Used as a feminine noun: "une boîte de nuit". To enter some clubs you may need to meet age or dress requirements.
target_language_example: On va en boîte de nuit ce soir ?
native_language_example: Shall we go to a nightclub tonight?

meaning: glove compartment (the small storage compartment in a car dashboard).
additional_notes: Commonly shortened in speech to "boîte" in some contexts, but full form is clear. Used to indicate where items (gloves, documents, keys, etc.) are stored in a car. Masculine or feminine? "La boîte à gants" (feminine).
target_language_example: La clé de secours est dans la boîte à gants.
native_language_example: The spare key is in the glove compartment.

meaning: 'toolbox' — a container for tools.
additional_notes: Used literally to refer to a physical box that holds tools (hammer, pliers, etc.). Can also be used metaphorically in contexts like software or skill sets (e.g., "une boîte à outils numérique"), but examples here are literal. Feminine noun phrase (la boîte à outils).
target_language_example: La boîte à outils est sous l'établi.
native_language_example: The toolbox is under the workbench.

meaning: 'right arm' (literal) / 'right-hand man' or 'assistant' (figurative)
additional_notes: Used literally to refer to the physical right arm. Figuratively, it means a trusted helper or key assistant (English: 'right-hand man/woman'). Context tells which meaning applies. Gender agreement: bras is masculine; 'bras droit' stays the same for a male or neutral referent, but you may see 'sa bras droit' (incorrect) — correct: 'son bras droit' because 'bras' is masculine. Can refer to either gender as the assistant (e.g., 'Elle est son bras droit').
target_language_example: Le ministre a présenté sa nouvelle collaboratrice comme son bras droit.
native_language_example: The minister introduced his new collaborator as his right-hand person.

meaning: to break someone's heart; to deeply hurt or sadden someone emotionally.
additional_notes: Used figuratively to describe causing strong emotional pain, disappointment, or sadness. Commonly followed by an indirect object (e.g., me, la, lui) or a clause describing what caused the hurt. Not literal (not about physically breaking a heart). Can be used in both serious and emotional everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Cette trahison a vraiment réussi à briser le cœur de Marie.
native_language_example: This betrayal really succeeded in breaking Marie's heart.

meaning: toothbrush.
additional_notes: Common everyday noun meaning the tool used to clean teeth. Always feminine singular: 'une brosse à dents' (a toothbrush), 'la brosse à dents' (the toothbrush). Use with reflexive verb 'se brosser les dents' to say 'to brush one's teeth' (e.g., 'Je me brosse les dents').
target_language_example: J'ai pris ma brosse à dents avant de partir.
native_language_example: I took my toothbrush before leaving.

meaning: noise/sound in (somewhere); used to say there is or isn't noise inside a place, or figuratively that something will make a public stir.
additional_notes: Common collocation: faire du bruit dans + lieu = to make noise in a place. Can be literal (physical sound inside a room or building) or figurative (an event causing attention or gossip: ça a fait du bruit dans le monde). Often appears with négation: pas un bruit dans la maison = not a sound in the house.
target_language_example: Il n'y avait pas un bruit dans la salle pendant la conférence.
native_language_example: There wasn't a sound in the hall during the lecture.

meaning: 'noise of' or 'sound of' (used to describe the noise produced by something).
additional_notes: Followed by a noun to indicate the source or type of a sound (e.g. bruit de moteur = engine noise). Can be used in literal descriptions and in figurative expressions (bruit de couloir = rumor, though that uses the full phrase). Common in descriptions and reports.
target_language_example: J'entends un bruit de moteur dehors.
native_language_example: I hear an engine noise outside.

meaning: drank a
additional_notes: Past participle + indefinite article: 'bu' is the past participle of boire (to drink). 'bu un' commonly appears before a beverage or 'verre' (glass). In English you would usually say 'drank a' or 'had a (drink)'. Context determines what was drunk: e.g. 'bu un verre (de vin)' = 'had a glass (of wine)'.
target_language_example: Hier soir, j'ai bu un verre de jus d'orange.
native_language_example: Last night I had a glass of orange juice.

meaning: post office
additional_notes: Used to refer to the local post office building or branch. Common in directions and when asking where to send/collect mail or buy stamps. 'Bureau' here means 'office' and 'de poste' specifies postal service.
target_language_example: Le bureau de poste est ouvert jusqu'à 17h.
native_language_example: The post office is open until 5 PM.

meaning: the phrase 'bureau en' isn't a fixed expression by itself; it's 'bureau' (office/desk) followed by a preposition like 'en' to form phrases such as 'au bureau en voiture' or 'bureau en partant' — meaning depends on the following word (e.g. 'bureau en voiture' = 'office by/with car' is actually ungrammatical; more common patterns are 'se rendre au bureau en voiture' = 'go to the office by car', or 'le bureau en dessous' = 'the office below').
additional_notes: There is no standalone idiom 'bureau en'. In your examples 'bureau' (office/desk) combines with different structures: - 'au/au bureau' (to/at the office) + mode of transport introduced by 'en' (en voiture, en train) → 'go to the office by car/train'. - 'le bureau en dessous' uses 'en dessous' (below) to mean 'the office below'. - 'quitter le bureau en toute hâte' and 'en partant' use 'en' to form adverbial phrases ('in/with great haste', 'upon leaving'). Learn 'bureau' (office/desk) and the various uses of 'en' separately; then combine: 'aller au bureau en train' = 'go to the office by train', 'quitter le bureau en toute hâte' = 'leave the office in great haste', 'le bureau en dessous (de notre appartement)' = 'the office below (our apartment)'.
target_language_example: Elle est allée au bureau en bus ce matin.
native_language_example: She went to the office by bus this morning.

meaning: 'the bus is' (used to describe the bus — its state, location, or condition).
additional_notes: A simple subject–verb phrase: bus (le bus) + est (3rd person singular of être). Use to state facts about the bus (late, broken down, full, dirty, expensive ticket, present, etc.). Replace 'bus' by another noun to form similar sentences. For negative or different tenses, modify the verb (n'est pas, était, sera, etc.).
target_language_example: Le bus est arrivé en retard ce matin.
native_language_example: The bus arrived late this morning.

meaning: 'don't drink' (plural/formal or polite imperative + negation)
additional_notes: A negative imperative formed with the verb boire (to drink): 'Ne buvez pas' is the standard command telling one or more people (or one person formally) not to drink something or not to drink alcohol. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped, giving ' buvez pas' or 'N'oubliez pas' style; writing should keep 'Ne buvez pas'. Use 'Ne bois pas' for one person in informal singular, and 'Ne buvons pas' for 'let's not drink.'
target_language_example: Ne buvez pas cette eau, elle est contaminée.
native_language_example: Don't drink this water, it's contaminated.

meaning: 'the baby has' (third-person singular of avoir used in present or as auxiliary in compound tenses).
additional_notes: bébé = the baby. a is the third-person singular present of avoir (to have). Used to describe what the baby has or to form compound past tenses (e.g., 'le bébé a crié' = the baby cried / the baby has cried). In simple present contexts it means 'the baby has' (possession) or functions as an auxiliary: 'le bébé a commencé...' = the baby has started / the baby started. Pronunciation: [be-be a].
target_language_example: Le bébé a faim et pleure.
native_language_example: The baby is hungry and is crying.

meaning: 'the baby has' or 'the baby did' (bébé + third-person singular of avoir).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the noun bébé followed by the verb avoir (to have) in the 3rd person singular: "bébé a" = "the baby has". In French, avoir is also used in some expressions where English uses different verbs (e.g. "a fait" = "did/made", "a droit à" = "is entitled to/has the right to"). Context determines the English translation.
target_language_example: Le bébé a faim et veut manger.
native_language_example: The baby is hungry and wants to eat.

meaning: "a baby with" (literal) — appears in two uses: 1) talking about having a baby with someone (romantic/parenting meaning); 2) as part of the idiom "jeter/le bébé avec l'eau du bain" meaning "to throw the baby out with the bathwater."
additional_notes: This pair of words can occur simply as the literal combination "a baby with [someone]" (e.g., "avoir un bébé avec toi" = "to have a baby with you"). However, many example sentences show the fixed idiom "jeter le bébé avec l'eau du bain," meaning to discard something valuable along with the undesirable. The idiom is not compositional (its figurative meaning doesn't follow from the words). When used literally, it's neutral; when used in the idiom, it's a common proverb-like expression.
target_language_example: Elle veut avoir un bébé avec lui, mais ils attendent d'être prêts.
native_language_example: She wants to have a baby with him, but they're waiting until they're ready.

meaning: the baby (with negation or emphasis using 'ne'); appears as 'the baby does not...' or in expressions about the baby
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the word bébé followed by the negative particle ne (often paired with pas, plus, que, or another negative word). In spoken French, the 'ne' is frequently dropped (e.g. «Le bébé ne parle pas» → «Le bébé parle pas»). Sometimes examples show 'bébé ne' inside a clause or sentence where the rest of the negative element comes later (e.g. ne...pas, ne...que). Also watch for informal/special uses like 'Ne dis pas' directed at the baby.
target_language_example: Le bébé ne mange pas encore de solides.
native_language_example: The baby does not eat solids yet.

meaning: this is
additional_notes: Very common expression used to identify, present, or point out someone or something. Depending on context, it can mean 'this is', 'that is', or 'it's'. It is the contracted form of 'ce est'.
target_language_example: C'est mon ami.
native_language_example: This is my friend.

meaning: 'that is' / 'that is to say' — used to clarify, restate, or give a more precise explanation.
additional_notes: Use to introduce a clarification, explanation, rephrasing, or specification of what was just said. Can precede a simple restatement (C'est-à-dire moi = that is, me) or a more detailed explanation. Often contracted in speech (c'est-à-dire → 'c'est-à-dire' pronounced quickly).
target_language_example: Il arrivera demain, c'est-à-dire vers midi.
native_language_example: He will arrive tomorrow, that is to say around noon.

meaning: that's it
additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with something, or to indicate that something just said is correct. Can be used alone as a short response (like "exactly" or "that's it"). Tone and context determine whether it is emphatic or neutral.
target_language_example: — Tu veux dire que le train partira à six heures ? — C'est cela.
native_language_example: — You mean the train leaves at six? — That's it.

meaning: This exact phrase is not a fixed French expression; literal meaning: 'it's of the other' or 'it's from the other one.'
additional_notes: Without context, this sequence is not a common set phrase in French. It could appear in sentences like "C'est de l'autre côté" (it's on the other side) with a missing word, or in contrasts: "Ce livre est à Paul, c'est de l'autre" (colloquial/incomplete) — but that latter would be nonstandard. If you encounter it, check surrounding words: likely a word is missing (e.g. côté, part, personne). Do not use 'c'est de l'autre' by itself as a set phrase.
target_language_example: Ce sac n'est pas à moi, c'est de l'autre côté du magasin.
native_language_example: This bag isn't mine; it's on the other side of the store.

meaning: 'that is to say' / 'which means' (used to rephrase or emphasize what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clarification, explanation, consequence or to emphasize a point already mentioned. Often followed by a short clause or a phrase giving the effect/implication of the previous statement. Common in spoken and written French. Not literal 'it is to say' in English—use 'which means' or 'meaning' or 'that is to say'.
target_language_example: Il n'a pas dormi de la nuit, c'est dire à quel point il était stressé.
native_language_example: He didn't sleep all night, which shows how stressed he was.

meaning: 'that's life' — used to accept or resign oneself to something disappointing or unchangeable.
additional_notes: A common French expression used to shrug off misfortune, setbacks, or inevitabilities. Can be used on its own (Mais c'est la vie) or with a question tag (C'est la vie, hein?) to invite agreement. Tone ranges from resigned to slightly humorous. Not formal or slang — it's neutral and widely used in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Il a raté le train, mais c'est la vie.
native_language_example: He missed the train, but that's life.

meaning: it's me
additional_notes: Used to identify oneself as the person responsible or involved; often followed by a clause introduced with qui or qu' to emphasize 'I' did something (e.g. "c'est moi qui l'ai fait" = "I'm the one who did it"). Can be used simply to answer "Who?" ("C'est moi." = "It's me.").
target_language_example: C'est moi qui ai oublié les clés.
native_language_example: I'm the one who forgot the keys.

meaning: 'let's go' / 'here we go' / 'it's started'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is starting or that you're ready to begin. Common in spoken French: can announce the start of an action, a trip, a meeting, or that something happened on its own (depending on context). Tone can be enthusiastic or neutral.
target_language_example: OK, c'est parti pour la réunion !
native_language_example: OK, let's go for the meeting!

meaning: that's why; therefore; for that reason.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a result or explanation. Common in spoken and written French. It connects a cause (previous idea) to its consequence. Can be followed by a clause or a short phrase. Formality: neutral—works in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, c'est pourquoi nous sommes restés à la maison.
native_language_example: It was raining, that's why we stayed home.

meaning: It's started again / here we go again.
additional_notes: Used when something restarts or repeats (often with a sense of resignation, amusement, or inevitability). Commonly appears as the fuller phrase "C'est reparti pour un tour." Can be used for events restarting, repetitive situations, or when something happens again unexpectedly.
target_language_example: Oh non, la réunion dépasse encore le temps prévu — c'est reparti.
native_language_example: Oh no, the meeting is running over again — here we go again.

meaning: that's all
additional_notes: Used to indicate that nothing more needs to be said or done, or to downplay/explain something briefly. Can be added at the end of a sentence to close a topic or to minimize an explanation ('I'm just... that's all'). Tone depends on context and intonation: neutral, dismissive, or final.
target_language_example: Je voulais juste aider, c'est tout.
native_language_example: I just wanted to help, that's all.

meaning: that's it
additional_notes: Very common conversational phrase. Can confirm something ("that's right"), indicate you've identified something or finished ("that's it"), or emphasize what you mean ("that's what I mean"). Context and intonation determine the exact sense. Often used alone as a short response.
target_language_example: C'est ça, tu as compris.
native_language_example: That's right, you understood.

meaning: 'to hide the' (followed by a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Verbe 'cacher' (to hide) + article 'la' (feminine singular). Use 'cacher le' for masculine, 'cacher les' for plural. Can refer to hiding physical objects or abstract things (la vérité). Verb appears in different tenses (essayer de cacher, a caché, essaya de cacher, etc.). Ensure correct agreement and placement of pronouns and negation (e.g. je ne vais pas cacher la vérité).
target_language_example: Tom a essayé de cacher la vérité.
native_language_example: Tom tried to hide the truth.

meaning: 'a gift from my' (used before a male family member or masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that something was given to the speaker by a male person (e.g., mon père, mon mari, mon grand-père). Follow with the person who gave the gift. If the giver is feminine, use 'cadeau de ma'. For plural or formal constructions you might use 'cadeau de mes' or 'cadeau de M.' (Monsieur). Commonly appears in spoken and written French to indicate origin/possession.
target_language_example: C'est un cadeau de mon frère.
native_language_example: It's a gift from my brother.

meaning: black coffee (coffee without milk or cream).
additional_notes: Common phrase in cafés and everyday speech. Implies coffee served without milk; sugar may or may not be added depending on context (you can say 'sans sucre' to specify no sugar). Also used as a short request: 'Un café noir' = 'I'll have a black coffee.'
target_language_example: Je prendrai un café noir, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a black coffee, please.

meaning: Not a correct fixed phrase. It appears to combine 'café' (coffee) and 'tous' (every).
additional_notes: French does not use 'café tous' as a set phrase. In the example sentences you would say 'café tous les matins' (coffee every morning) or 'tous les matins, je bois du café' (every morning I drink coffee). 'Tous' must be followed by a time period with the definite article (e.g., 'tous les matins', 'tous les jours').
target_language_example: Je bois du café tous les matins.
native_language_example: I drink coffee every morning.

meaning: captain of / leader of (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the captain, leader or person in charge of a group, team, ship, or metaphorically in charge of one's life. Followed by the thing or group they lead (e.g., capitaine de bateau, capitaine de l'équipe, capitaine de soirée). Formal in neutral contexts; can be used figuratively.
target_language_example: Elle est la capitaine de l'équipe de volley.
native_language_example: She is the captain of the volleyball team.

meaning: 'because I' — gives a reason involving the speaker (I).
additional_notes: Car is a formal/neutral conjunction meaning 'because' or 'for'. When followed by je it introduces a reason about the speaker. Car is a bit more literary or written than parce que and is less common in casual speech. Word order: car + clause (no que). Can appear mid-sentence (after a comma) or at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: Je reste ici, car je dois aider ma sœur.
native_language_example: I'm staying here, because I have to help my sister.

meaning: 'map of' or 'map showing' when followed by a noun (e.g. carte au trésor = map of/for treasure); can also mean 'map on/at' in some contexts (carte au tableau = the map on the board).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a combination 'carte au/à la/aux' used before a noun to indicate the map relates to that noun. Gender/number of the following noun affects the article: 'carte au' = carte + à + le (used before masculine singular nouns like 'trésor' if 'le trésor' is intended). You will also see 'carte à' + noun in other uses (e.g. 'carte à jouer' = playing card) or 'carte sur'/'carte du' depending on meaning. Context decides whether it means 'map of', 'map for', or 'map on'.
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé une carte au trésor dans le grenier.
native_language_example: I found a treasure map in the attic.

meaning: complete freedom or full permission to act as one chooses.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they may do whatever they think best; similar to 'free rein' or 'full authority'. Often preceded by 'avoir' (to have carte blanche) or used alone as an imperative/statement. Formality: neutral — appropriate in both spoken and written contexts.
target_language_example: Ils m'ont donné carte blanche pour organiser l'événement.
native_language_example: They gave me carte blanche to organize the event.

meaning: identity card (official ID).
additional_notes: Refers to an official identity document (national ID card) used to prove name, photo, date of birth, nationality, etc. Used when asking to see someone's ID (formal situations: police, administration, age verification). In casual contexts foreigners might show a passport instead. The phrase is literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Montrez-moi votre carte d'identité, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Show me your identity card, please.

meaning: credit card
additional_notes: Common phrase for a bank-issued payment card used to borrow funds up to a limit. Used in contexts about payment method (en espèces ou par carte de crédit?), lending/borrowing (prêter sa carte) or possession (avoir la carte).
target_language_example: Je paye la facture par carte de crédit.
native_language_example: I pay the bill by credit card.

meaning: business card; a small card with a person's name and contact details.
additional_notes: Commonly used when giving someone your contact information in a professional or social context. In French, always feminine singular: 'une carte de visite'. Can also mean an old-fashioned visiting card (same idea).
target_language_example: Tenez, voici ma carte de visite.
native_language_example: Here, this is my business card.

meaning: postcard (a card sent by mail, often from travel).
additional_notes: Common tangible item: a single card with a picture on one side and space for a message and address on the other. Used for short messages from trips or as a souvenir. Can also refer to a specific postcard previously mentioned (la carte postale).
target_language_example: Envoie-moi une carte postale de Paris !
native_language_example: Send me a postcard from Paris!

meaning: 'a map for' or 'a card for' (depends on context); here: 'a map for...'
additional_notes: carte = map or (payment) card; 'pour' = for. Together they mark that the map/card is intended for someone or some purpose (e.g. "une carte pour votre trajet" = a map for your route). Use context to know whether 'carte' means map or card. To ask someone to make a map, use "tracer une carte pour moi" = "draw/plot a map for me."
target_language_example: Peux-tu préparer une carte pour notre randonnée ?
native_language_example: Can you prepare a map for our hike?

meaning: fire station (building where firefighters and fire engines are based).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the local firehouse or fire station. Common in everyday speech and formal contexts. Often preceded by articles (la/une) or location words (à la, près de).
target_language_example: La caserne de pompiers est au bout de la rue.
native_language_example: The fire station is at the end of the street.

meaning: to beat someone up; to smash someone's face (colloquial, violent threat)
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. literally 'break the mouth/face' (gueule = slang for mouth/face/animal's muzzle). Used as a threat or to say you'll physically attack someone. Avoid in polite contexts; strong aggression implied.
target_language_example: Si tu continues, je vais te casser la gueule.
native_language_example: If you keep going, I'm going to beat you up.

meaning: to annoy/harass someone badly; to be a pain in the neck (very vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar — literally 'to break the balls'. Used to say someone or something is extremely annoying or bothersome. Avoid in polite/company or formal contexts. Can be directed at a person (Tu me casses les couilles) or used impersonally (Ça me casse les couilles).
target_language_example: Arrête de me casser les couilles, j'essaie de travailler.
native_language_example: Stop pissing me off, I'm trying to work.

meaning: broke a (feminine noun) — short for 'a cassé une ...' meaning 'broke a/an ...'
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own; it's the past tense verb phrase 'a cassé' (has/have broken) or 'cassé' used in context with the feminine noun that follows. In correct full French you'd usually see 'a cassé une...' (e.g. 'a cassé une assiette' = 'broke a plate') or 'j'ai cassé une...' ('I broke a...'). Alone, 'cassé une' is incomplete. Use it when referring to breaking one (singular feminine) object. The past participle agrees with a preceding direct object only in compound tenses with 'être' or when 'avoir' plus preceding object — beginners can keep it simple: 'J'ai cassé une fenêtre.'
target_language_example: J'ai cassé une assiette hier.
native_language_example: I broke a plate yesterday.

meaning: because of
additional_notes: Short for "à cause de" followed by a vowel or mute 'h' where the 'de' contracts to d' (e.g. "à cause d'elle", "à cause d'hier"). Used to give the reason or blame for something (can be neutral or express blame). Common structure: "C'est à cause de + noun/pronoun". Informal spoken and written French both use it when the following word begins with a vowel.
target_language_example: C'est à cause d'elle que nous sommes en retard.
native_language_example: It's because of her that we're late.

meaning: caused a lot (of)...
additional_notes: Used after a subject to say it produced or brought about many of something (problems, damage, etc.). Usually followed by 'de' + noun (e.g. 'beaucoup de problèmes', 'beaucoup de dommages'). 'Causé' is the past participle of 'causer' (to cause).
target_language_example: La pluie a causé beaucoup de dégâts dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The rain caused a lot of damage in the garden.

meaning: all this way to / go to the trouble of coming to (in order) — expresses making a long trip or effort for a purpose.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like faire (faire tout ce chemin) to emphasize that someone traveled a long distance or went to great effort 'for' a reason. Often appears in questions or surprise (Tu as fait tout ce chemin pour ça ?). The phrase is compositional: 'ce chemin' = 'this/that way' and 'pour' = 'for'.
target_language_example: Tu as fait tout ce chemin pour m'aider ?
native_language_example: You went all this way to help me?

meaning: tonight
additional_notes: Refers to the evening of the current day. In English, "tonight" is often the most natural translation, though the literal meaning is "this evening."
target_language_example: On dîne ensemble ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are we having dinner together tonight?

meaning: what... (that/of which)
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something introduced earlier when the verb or expression requires the preposition de. It combines ce + dont and is followed by a clause. English translations depend on context: 'what', 'that ... of which', or 'what ... about'. Example: 'Je sais ce dont vous voulez parler' = 'I know what you want to talk about.'
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas ce dont elle a besoin.
native_language_example: I don't understand what she needs.

meaning: 'what (we/one) have/need' — roughly 'what one has/needs' or 'what we have/need'.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something needed or possessed. 'Dont' replaces 'de + (relative clause)' after verbs that take 'de' (e.g. avoir besoin de, manquer de). The subject can be 'on', 'nous', 'il/elle', etc.: Ce dont on a besoin = what we/one needs. Word order: Ce dont + subject + verb.
target_language_example: Nous avons déjà ce dont on a besoin pour le voyage.
native_language_example: We already have what we need for the trip.

meaning: by doing so
additional_notes: A linking phrase used to show that one action causes or accompanies another. Often placed at the start or middle of a sentence to indicate consequence or simultaneous action. Formal to neutral register; common in written and spoken French.
target_language_example: Il a accéléré, et ce faisant, il a perdu le contrôle.
native_language_example: He sped up, and in doing so, he lost control.

meaning: 'it was a pleasure' (formal/polite).
additional_notes: Used to politely close an interaction or express that an experience was enjoyable. Often used in customer/service, business, or formal contexts. More formal than 'ce fut un plaisir' can also be expressed as 'ça a été un plaisir' or the present 'c'est un plaisir.'
target_language_example: Ce fut un plaisir de vous aider aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to help you today.

ce là tout ce que tu

target_language_multi_word_term: Est-ce là tout ce que tu ... ?
meaning: Is that all (that) you ...? / Is that all you have to say?
additional_notes: Polite/neutral way to ask whether what was just said is everything the speaker intends. Often used to check if the person has finished speaking or to express surprise/disappointment at brevity. The structure combines the question marker 'Est-ce', the demonstrative 'là' (there/that), 'tout ce que' (all that/everything that) and the verb referring to the person (tu + verb). Replace the ellipsis with the appropriate verb form (peux dire, veux dire, voulais dire, etc.).
target_language_example: Est-ce là tout ce que tu voulais me dire ?
native_language_example: Is that all you wanted to tell me?

ce là tout ce que vous

target_language_multi_word_term: Est-ce là tout ce que vous...
meaning: Is that all you... / Is that all you have to say...?
additional_notes: Polite/formal question used to ask whether the speaker has finished saying something or whether there is more to add. Often followed by verbs like pouvez dire, voulez dire, vouliez me dire, etc. Uses formal 'vous' and can sound slightly incredulous or confirmatory depending on tone.
target_language_example: Est-ce là tout ce que vous vouliez me dire ?
native_language_example: Is that all you wanted to tell me?

meaning: what (for) / that for which; the thing/reason for which (something is done).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a purpose, reason, or thing previously mentioned or implied. It is a relative expression combining 'ce' (that/what) + 'pour quoi' (for which). In English it often becomes 'what (for)' or 'that for which' and may be rendered naturally as 'what' or 'the thing/reason for which'. Common in formal or written French; speakers may also use simpler alternatives like 'ce que' or 'pour quoi' depending on context.
target_language_example: Je repars avec ce pour quoi je suis venu.
native_language_example: I'm leaving with what I came for.

meaning: 'what' or 'that which' (used before a vowel sound; contraction of ce que).
additional_notes: ce qu' is the elided form of ce que used before a following vowel or mute h (e.g., ce qu'elle). It introduces a subordinate clause and can mean 'what,' 'that which,' or be part of expressions like jusqu'à ce que ('until'). It is not a question word when used in phrases like 'je tiens à ce qu'elle...'; there it introduces a clause expressing desire, obligation, or condition.
target_language_example: Je veux ce qu'il a décidé.
native_language_example: I want what he decided.

meaning: 'what she said' (referring to something a female person has said).
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to the content of a woman's or girl's speech. It combines ce que ('what/that which') + elle a dit (she said). Commonly appears in questions (Qu'est-ce qu'elle a dit ? / Est-ce qu'elle a dit quelque chose ?) and can be adapted for other subjects (ce que j'ai dit, ce qu'il a dit).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas entendu — dis-moi ce qu'elle a dit.
native_language_example: I didn't hear — tell me what she said.

meaning: 'what he said' (referring to something a male person said).
additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer back to the content of someone's words. Can appear in questions (e.g. Qu'est-ce qu'il a dit ?) or embedded in longer sentences (e.g. Dis-moi ce qu'il a dit). 'Il' can be replaced by other pronouns/nouns (ce qu'elle a dit, ce que tu as dit).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas entendu la réunion — tu peux me dire ce qu'il a dit ?
native_language_example: I didn't hear the meeting — can you tell me what he said?

meaning: 'what he did' or 'what he has done' (referring to actions someone did).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask about a man's (or a person's when gender is unspecified) actions. Often appears inside qu'est-ce que... (e.g. Qu'est-ce qu'il a fait ?) and can be adapted for other subjects (ce que j'ai fait, ce qu'elle a fait). Tense is normally passé composé here (a fait) meaning a completed action.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'il a fait pour réparer la voiture ?
native_language_example: What did he do to fix the car?

meaning: 'what (is) happening' or 'what's going on' (part of the phrase "ce qu'il se passe").
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common expression "ce qu'il se passe" (or more formally "ce qui se passe"). It introduces a subordinate clause meaning "what is happening" or "what's going on." In spoken French you will often hear "ce qu'il se passe" instead of the more grammatical "ce qui se passe." Use it to ask or tell about a situation (e.g. "Dis‑moi ce qu'il se passe").
target_language_example: Dis‑moi ce qu'il se passe ici.
native_language_example: Tell me what's going on here.

meaning: what we
additional_notes: qu'on is the shortened form of que + on before a vowel. on often means 'we' in everyday French, but it can also mean 'people/one'. In your examples, ce qu'on appears inside jusqu'à ce qu'on..., and the whole expression means 'until we/someone...' and is followed by the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Je sais ce qu'on doit faire.
native_language_example: I know what we have to do.

meaning: 'what we are' or 'what one is' (depends on context); often used in questions like 'what are we (doing)?' or 'where are we?'.
additional_notes: Ce qu'on est combines ce que + on + être. 'On' can mean 'we', 'people in general', or 'one'. The phrase appears in several question patterns: 'Est-ce qu'on est d'accord ?' (Are we in agreement?), 'Où est-ce qu'on est ?' (Where are we?), and 'Qu'est-ce qu'on est censés/supposés faire ?' (What are we supposed to do?). Use depends on context—translate 'on' as we/you/one accordingly. The phrase is compositional and literal.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on est censés apporter ?
native_language_example: What are we supposed to bring?

meaning: 'what (we/people) know' or 'what is known'.
additional_notes: Literally combines ce que (what/that which) + on sait (one/we/people know). 'On' is commonly used in spoken French to mean 'we' or 'people' in general. Use to ask or talk about information that is known so far. Can be followed by de/à/pour/... depending on what's being asked (e.g. "Qu'est-ce qu'on sait de lui ?" = What do we know about him?).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on sait sur le projet pour l'instant ?
native_language_example: What do we know about the project so far?

meaning: 'what (we) ... to each other' or part of questions like 'what do we...' / 'when will we...'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in spoken questions using est-ce que + on + reflexive verbs (se connaître, se raconter, se marier, se revoir, se voir). 'On' is an informal substitute for 'nous' (we). 'Se' signals a reflexive or reciprocal action (each other). The full structures in the examples are: «Est-ce qu'on se connaît?» (Do we know each other?), «Qu'est-ce qu'on se raconte?» (What do we tell each other / what's the gossip?), «Quand est-ce qu'on se marie?» (When are we getting married?), «Quand est-ce qu'on se revoit/voit?» (When will we see each other again?).
target_language_example: Quand est-ce qu'on se parle?
native_language_example: When are we going to talk to each other?

meaning: 'what are we going to do' (asks about the next action or plan)
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase built from 'ce que' + 'on' (we/people) + 'aller' (future proche) + 'faire' (to do). Used to ask for a plan, express worry or seek suggestions about what to do next. Can be formalized as 'qu'est-ce que nous allons faire' but 'qu'est-ce qu'on va faire' is more natural in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qu'on va faire si la voiture ne démarre pas ?
native_language_example: What are we going to do if the car won't start?

meaning: what
additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing or idea: often after verbs like voir, savoir, dire, or faire. It can mean both direct 'what' and more formal 'that which.' In patterns like 'X est à Y ce que A est à B,' it means 'what' in a comparison: 'X is to Y what A is to B.'
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean.

meaning: 'what I want (someone) to ...' — introduces something the speaker wants another person to do.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause expressing the speaker's request, desire, or instruction about another person's action. It is usually followed by a subject and a verb in the subordinate clause (e.g. 'tu fasses', 'vous fassiez'). In English this often becomes 'what I want you to (do)'. The phrase is compositional and not idiomatic; the verb tense/mood in the subordinate clause often uses the subjunctive in French (e.g. 'que tu fasses').
target_language_example: Ce que je veux que tu fasses, c'est appeler ta mère.
native_language_example: What I want you to do is call your mother.

meaning: 'ce que' = 'what' or 'that which'; 'tout' = 'all/every' — together they could start phrases like 'ce que tout le monde...' (what everyone...)
additional_notes: Alone, 'ce que tout' is not a complete fixed phrase in French. It typically appears at the start of longer expressions such as 'ce que tout le monde pense' (what everyone thinks) or 'ce que tout le monde sait' (what everybody knows). 'Ce que' is a relative/neutral pronoun meaning 'what' or 'that which', and 'tout' modifies a following noun or phrase (e.g. 'tout le monde' = everybody, 'tout cela' = all that).
target_language_example: Ce que tout le monde veut, c'est la paix.
native_language_example: What everyone wants is peace.

ce que vous avez à faire est

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que vous avez à faire est
meaning: 'all you have to do is' or 'what you need to do is'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple instruction or required action. Often appears as 'tout ce que vous avez à faire est de + infinitive' (formal/plural or polite 'you'). Can be shortened in casual speech to 'tout ce que vous avez à faire, c'est de...' or 'tout ce que tu as à faire, c'est de...' for familiar singular.
target_language_example: Tout ce que vous avez à faire est de signer ici.
native_language_example: All you have to do is sign here.

meaning: 'what ... is' or 'what ... means' (used to ask or explain the nature/identity of something).
additional_notes: This phrase combines ce que + c'est + que and is used in informal spoken French to ask about or emphasize the nature/identity of something (often followed by a noun or clause). It appears in questions like «Qu'est-ce que c'est ?» but with extra emphasis or in longer structures: «Tu sais ce que c'est que... ?» = 'Do you know what ... is?' It can be reduced or reorganized in formal French (e.g. «Qu'est-ce que c'est ?» or «ce que c'est»).
target_language_example: Tu sais ce que c'est que ce bruit ?
native_language_example: Do you know what that noise is?

meaning: 'what this' or 'what this (thing) ...' — introduces a clause asking or stating what a particular thing means or does.
additional_notes: Combines 'ce que' (what/that which) + 'ceci' (this). Used when referring to a specific thing or phrase nearby and asking about its meaning or significance. Slightly formal/neutral; more common spoken alternatives: 'ce que ça signifie' or 'ce que cela signifie'.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous m'expliquer ce que ceci veut dire ?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me what this means?

meaning: what I
additional_notes: A fragment meaning "ce que" + "j'" (short for "je"). It is used before a verb starting with a vowel or mute h, as in "ce que j'aime" or "ce que j'ai vu." It usually introduces what the speaker does, thinks, likes, knows, etc., and is not normally used on its own.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que j'entends.
native_language_example: I understand what I hear.

meaning: 'what I ...' used to start a clause where the speaker refers to something they do to/for themselves (incomplete fragment).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the beginning of a relative/indirect clause: 'ce que' = 'what/that which' and 'je me' is the reflexive pronoun for 'I (myself)'. It will be followed by a verb (e.g. 'dis' -> 'ce que je me dis' = 'what I tell myself'). Common in reflexive verbs and expressions about thoughts, feelings, or actions directed at oneself. Pay attention to word order: reflexive pronoun comes before the verb (je me + verb).
target_language_example: Ce que je me dis, c'est que tout ira bien.
native_language_example: What I tell myself is that everything will be fine.

ce que je peux te parler

target_language_multi_word_term: Est-ce que je peux te parler ?
meaning: Can I speak to you? / May I talk to you?
additional_notes: A polite way to ask to speak with someone, often used to request a private or brief conversation. Replace 'te' with 'vous' for formal/plural: «Est-ce que je peux vous parler ?». You can add time words (un instant, une minute, en privé) to specify length or privacy.
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux te parler un instant ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a moment?

meaning: 'could I have' — polite request asking to receive something or to obtain something.
additional_notes: Used in polite questions (often with Est-ce que) to ask for objects, information, access, or a short private word. The conditional 'pourrais' makes it more polite/less direct than 'je veux' or 'est-ce que je peux avoir'. Can be shortened in speech to 'je pourrais avoir...' or 'est-ce que je pourrais...'.
target_language_example: Est-ce que je pourrais avoir l'addition, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could I have the bill, please?

meaning: 'what I have just' (used to introduce something you just did or said).
additional_notes: This is the start of a clause meaning 'what I have just (done / said / seen...)'. It's followed by an infinitive or a clause: e.g. 'ce que je viens de dire' = 'what I have just said'. Common in spoken and written French to refer to a very recent action. The literal components are compositional ('ce que' = 'what/that which', 'je viens de' = 'I have just').
target_language_example: Ce que je viens de dire n'était pas clair, je vais répéter.
native_language_example: What I have just said wasn't clear, I'll repeat it.

meaning: "ce que" + "tes" — literally 'what your' (incomplete phrase)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed multiword expression. It looks like the start of a sentence combining the relative pronoun 'ce que' (what/that which) and the possessive adjective 'tes' (your, plural or plural objects). It is incomplete and must be followed by a noun or verb phrase (e.g. 'ce que tes parents pensent', 'ce que tes amis savent'). Alone it has no full meaning.
target_language_example: Ce que tes amis pensent est important pour toi ?
native_language_example: What your friends think—is that important to you?

meaning: Is everything okay? / Is everything all right?
additional_notes: A polite, neutral way to ask if things are fine or if someone is all right. Commonly used to check on people or situations; can be directed at a person (Est-ce que tout va bien, José ?) or a place (Est-ce que tout va bien là-bas ?). You can shorten to "Tout va bien ?" in casual speech. Pronunciation tip: the full form starts with a rising question intonation.
target_language_example: Est-ce que tout va bien chez toi ?
native_language_example: Is everything okay at your place?

meaning: 'what you bought' (used to ask about specific items someone purchased).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'ce que' (what/that which) with the perfect tense 'tu as acheté' (you bought). Common in questions introduced by 'Est‑ce que' or 'Pourquoi/Quand/Quel...' to ask about the things someone purchased. Can be used standalone in reported questions: «Dis‑moi ce que tu as acheté.»
target_language_example: Tu peux me montrer ce que tu as acheté ?
native_language_example: Can you show me what you bought?

meaning: 'what you drank' (referring to the drink or amount someone consumed).
additional_notes: This is a short clause meaning 'what you drank'. It is often used inside questions (e.g. 'Dis‑moi ce que tu as bu' or 'Combien de verres est‑ce que tu as bu ?') or to ask about the content or amount someone consumed. Word order is standard for past tense: 'tu as bu' = 'you have drunk/you drank'.
target_language_example: Dis‑moi ce que tu as bu hier soir.
native_language_example: Tell me what you drank last night.

meaning: 'what you have to' or 'what you need to (do/have)'.
additional_notes: This phrase is often followed by an infinitive or a noun and is used to refer to something the listener possesses, must do, or has available. Context determines whether it means obligation (what you have to do), possession (what you have), or availability (what you have on you). It's informal/neutral spoken style when addressing one person (tu).
target_language_example: Dis‑moi ce que tu as à faire demain.
native_language_example: Tell me what you have to do tomorrow.

meaning: 'what you must' / 'what you have to'.
additional_notes: Combines ce que (what/that which) + tu dois (you must / you have to). Used to refer to something the listener is required or expected to do. Can introduce a clause or be part of a larger sentence: e.g. explaining duties, instructions, or reminders.
target_language_example: Voici ce que tu dois faire avant de partir.
native_language_example: Here is what you have to do before leaving.

meaning: 'ce que' = 'what/that which'; 'tu le' = 'you it' (you + direct object pronoun). The exact sequence 'ce que tu le' is not a grammatical standalone phrase in standard French; it typically appears only as part of a larger, corrected sentence or in nonstandard/regional speech. Often one must reorder or add words: use 'ce que tu fais' (what you do) or 'tu le fais' (you do it).
additional_notes: This three-word string mixes two common pieces: the relative/introductory 'ce que' and the subject + object pronoun 'tu le'. In standard French they do not occur directly adjacent in a well-formed clause. If you encounter 'ce que tu le' in writing or speech, it's likely a mistake, ellipsis, or dialectal phrasing. Correct alternatives: 'ce que tu fais' (what you do), 'tu le fais' (you do it), or rephrase the clause so the pronoun is in the right position (e.g., 'Ce que tu fais, tu le fais bien.' contains both parts but with punctuation and additional words).
target_language_example: Ce que tu le penses ne change rien. (non standard / incorrect)
native_language_example: 'What you think it' changes nothing. (illustrates incorrect sequence)

meaning: 'what you (to) them' — used to refer to what you said, gave, or did to them.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a short sequence combining the relative pronoun 'ce que' (what), the subject 'tu' (you), and the indirect object pronoun 'leur' (to them). It appears in reported-content or object clauses: 'ce que tu leur as dit' = 'what you told them'; 'ce que tu leur as donné' = 'what you gave them'. Use 'leur' for 'to them' (plural or polite). The verb and tense follow after these words.
target_language_example: Je veux savoir ce que tu leur as écrit.
native_language_example: I want to know what you wrote to them.

meaning: 'what you could' or 'what you might (do)'.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the relative pronoun ce que ('what' / 'that which') with the conditional form tu pourrais ('you could' / 'you might'). It is used to introduce a suggestion, possibility or hypothetical action that the listener could do. Often followed by an infinitive or a clause: ce que tu pourrais faire, ce que tu pourrais dire, etc.
target_language_example: Ce que tu pourrais faire, c'est appeler Marie pour demander de l'aide.
native_language_example: What you could do is call Marie to ask for help.

ce que tu sais comment aller

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu sais comment aller
meaning: 'do you know how to get (to)...' (literal: 'what that you know how to go')
additional_notes: This string is a fragment; the natural question in French is 'Est-ce que tu sais comment aller...' or the informal 'Tu sais comment aller... ?' The provided phrase begins with 'ce que' which often appears in 'Est-ce que...' constructions; standing alone as 'ce que tu sais comment aller' is ungrammatical. To form a correct question, use 'Est-ce que tu sais comment aller au/à la/à l'/aux ...' or 'Tu sais comment aller à... ?' For destinations: 'au' = à + le (masculine), 'à la' (feminine), 'à l'' before a vowel, 'aux' (plural).
target_language_example: Est-ce que tu sais comment aller au supermarché ?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get to the supermarket?

meaning: 'what' (that) + 'you are going to' + indirect object 'me' — used to introduce something the speaker expects someone will say, ask, do, or give to them.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common fragment inside sentences like "Je sais ce que tu vas me dire" (I know what you are going to tell me) or questions using "est-ce que tu vas me..." (Are you going to... me?). It combines: "ce que" (what/that which) + future/immediate-future construction "tu vas" (you are going to) + indirect object pronoun "me" (to me). Use it before verbs (dire, demander, rendre, le dire, le sauver, etc.).
target_language_example: Je sais ce que tu vas me demander demain.
native_language_example: I know what you are going to ask me tomorrow.

meaning: Not a correct or natural French phrase; likely a mistaken mix of structures. It does not form a grammatical clause in French. The intended expressions are probably «ce que tu veux» (what you want) or «où tu veux aller» (where you want to go).
additional_notes:
This exact string is ungrammatical. Possible correct alternatives depending on meaning:
- «ce que tu veux» = "what you want".
- «où tu veux aller» = "where you want to go".
- «ce que tu veux faire» = "what you want to do".
To ask where someone wants to go: «Où veux-tu aller ?» (inversion), «Tu veux aller où ?» (casual), or «Où voulez-vous aller ?» (formal).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas compris «ce que tu veux aller» — on dirait une erreur; dis plutôt «ce que tu veux» ou «où tu veux aller».
native_language_example: I didn't understand "ce que tu veux aller" — it looks like a mistake; say instead "ce que tu veux" or "où tu veux aller".

ce que tu veux que je te

target_language_multi_word_term: ce que tu veux que je te
meaning: 'what you want me to (do/say/bring) to you' — start of a clause asking what the listener wants the speaker to do for them.
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself; it's the beginning of a subordinate clause introduced by "ce que" used to ask or report what someone wants the speaker to do. Commonly followed by a verb and (optionally) a direct or indirect object: e.g. "ce que tu veux que je te dise" (what you want me to tell you), "ce que tu veux que je te ramène" (what you want me to bring you). Frequently appears in questions: "Qu'est-ce que tu veux que je te... ?"
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que tu veux que je te conseille ?
native_language_example: What do you want me to advise you?

meaning: 'what you just...'/ 'what you have just...'
additional_notes: This is a fragment, not a complete sentence. It combines 'ce que' (what/that which) with 'vous venez' (you come / you have just). In spoken and written French it's often followed by 'de' + infinitive to mean 'what you have just [done]': e.g. 'ce que vous venez de dire' = 'what you have just said'. Without 'de' the phrase could continue with a clause (e.g. 'ce que vous venez me raconter'), but most commonly use is 'ce que vous venez de + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Ce que vous venez de dire est important.
native_language_example: What you have just said is important.

meaning: 'what ... to me' or 'what ... for me' — part of a larger clause (incomplete on its own).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's typically the beginning or middle of a sentence like «ce que ça me coûte», «ce que ça me fait», «ce que ça me plaît», etc. It links 'ce que' (what/that which) plus 'ça' (that/it) and 'me' (to me), so the full meaning depends on the verb or noun that follows. Use it when expressing what something does/means/ costs/feels to you personally.
target_language_example: Regarde ce que ça me fait quand tu dis ça.
native_language_example: Look at what that does to me when you say that.

meaning: what it/that can (do) / how much it can (do); often part of a larger expression (e.g. ce que ça peut coûter = what it can cost).
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete sentence by itself — it appears inside longer phrases. "Ce que" = "what/that which"; "ça" = "that/it"; "peut" = "can/may". Together they introduce a clause about what something is able to do or how much it can be (cost, help, change, etc.). You will commonly see it followed by an infinitive (ce que ça peut coûter) or by a relative clause (ce que ça peut apporter).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce que ça peut coûter.
native_language_example: I don't know what it can cost.

meaning: what
additional_notes: used to mean “what/that which” when it is the subject of the following verb. Compare with ce que, which is used when “what” is the object of the verb.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce qui se passe.
native_language_example: I understand what's happening.

meaning: 'what (happens/is) to him/her' or 'that which is to him/her'.
additional_notes: Combination of 'ce qui' (what/that which, subject) + indirect object pronoun 'lui' (to him/to her) + verb (often omitted in this fragment). Typically introduces a clause about something that happens to or concerns someone: e.g. 'ce qui lui est arrivé' = 'what happened to him/her'. On its own it's incomplete and usually followed by a past participle or verb.
target_language_example: Je vais expliquer ce qui lui est arrivé hier.
native_language_example: I'll explain what happened to him/her yesterday.

meaning: 'what brings you (here)' or 'the reason that brings you (to this place/situation)'.
additional_notes: Polite/formal phrasing used to ask someone the reason for their visit or presence. Often used in professional or service contexts (e.g., at a reception, doctor's office, or meeting). Can be adapted: 'ce qui t'amène' (informal singular) or 'ce qui nous amène' (what brings us).
target_language_example: Bonjour, dites-moi ce qui vous amène aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Hello, tell me what brings you today.

meaning: 'what (has) ... to you' / 'what happened to you' (introduces a clause about something that happened or applies to 'you').
additional_notes: This fragment appears at the start of a relative clause: ce qui vous est arrivé = 'what happened to you' or more literally 'that which to you is happened'. It is used to ask about or refer to an event or situation affecting the person addressed (vous). You will often see it followed by a past participle (arrivé, arrivé(e), arrivé(s)) or other verbs: ce qui vous est arrivé, ce qui vous est arrivé(e)s, ce qui vous est arrivé hier, ce qui vous est arrivé au travail, etc. Use vous for formal singular or plural; for informal singular replace vous with te (ce qui t'est arrivé).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous expliquer ce qui vous est arrivé hier soir ?
native_language_example: Can you explain what happened to you last night?

meaning: 'anything that' (used in subjunctive relative clauses after indefinite/negative expressions).
additional_notes: Forms part of constructions like "quoi que ce soit qui..." or "il n'y a rien qui..." to mean "anything that" or "anything which." It usually appears after indefinite or negative phrases (quoi que ce soit, quelque chose, rien) and the verb in the relative clause often uses the subjunctive (e.g. "vous ait fait"). In everyday speech you may also see simpler alternatives like "quelque chose qui" for affirmative contexts. Use when emphasizing any/something at all, especially after negatives or questions.
target_language_example: Regarde s'il y a quoi que ce soit qui puisse t'aider.
native_language_example: See if there is anything that could help you.

meaning: Not a fixed standalone phrase. This sequence is a fragment combining elements often used in different constructions: 'ce' (this/that/what), 'soit' (subjunctive of être or part of 'que ce soit'), and 'qui se' (relative pronoun + reflexive particle). It can appear inside longer clauses (e.g. 'que ce soit... qui se...') but 'ce soit qui se' by itself is ungrammatical and should not be treated as a set expression.
additional_notes: Use the elements in their correct constructions instead: 'que ce soit...' (meaning 'whether it be...' or 'be it...') and 'ce qui se...' (meaning 'what happens' or 'that which occurs'). A possible correct sequence including these words is 'que ce soit... qui se...' as part of a full sentence: e.g. 'Que ce soit... qui se passe/produise...'. Do not use 'ce soit qui se' alone.
target_language_example: Que ce soit qui se passe demain n'est pas encore certain.
native_language_example: What happens tomorrow is not certain yet.

meaning: that it be a good
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the subordinate clause of expressions like "que ce soit une bonne idée" following verbs of doubt, opinion, or questions (e.g. "je ne pense pas que...", "es-tu sûr que..."). It uses the subjunctive mood (soit). In English you'd usually translate the whole clause as "that it's a good idea" or "that it would be a good idea." The phrase alone is not a complete sentence; keep the surrounding "que" clause.
target_language_example: Je doute que ce soit une bonne décision.
native_language_example: I doubt that it is a good decision.

meaning: Not a correct or grammatical French expression; likely a mistaken fragment of phrases such as 'c'est une bonne...' or 'ce n'est pas une bonne...'.
additional_notes: The sequence 'ce une bonne' is ungrammatical on its own. Common correct forms are 'c'est une bonne...' (it's a good...) or 'ce n'est pas une bonne...' (this/that is not a good...). If you meant to say 'that is a good ...', use 'c'est une bonne'. The fragment 'ce une bonne' should not be used in standard French.
target_language_example: Ce une bonne — (incorrect fragment; does not form a grammatical sentence in French).
native_language_example: 'Ce une bonne' — (incorrect fragment; does not form a grammatical sentence in English).

meaning: what (to/which) — refers to the thing or situation to which something relates (often followed by a verb or clause).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the object or situation that something relates to or is compared with. Commonly appears in phrases like "ce à quoi je m'attendais" (what I expected) or "ce à quoi ma vie ressemble" (what my life looks like). Followed by a verb phrase introduced by relative pronoun "à" + verb (m'attendais, ressemble, crois).
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas ce à quoi il pense.
native_language_example: I don't know what he is thinking about.

meaning: ceci = 'this' (refers to something near or just mentioned); je = 'I'.
additional_notes: The examples show 'ceci' used to point to an object, idea, or action ('this' or 'this thing'). It can appear before a clause or noun and is neutral/formal. The comma plus 'je' in the input isn't a fixed phrase — it's just 'ceci' used in sentences that also include 'je' (I) or polite requests with 'je vous/te prie' ('please'). Use 'ceci' when indicating something specific (often more formal than 'ça').
target_language_example: Regarde ceci, je l'ai fait pour toi.
native_language_example: Look at this; I made it for you.

meaning: that said
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast, clarification, or a qualification after a statement—similar to 'that said' or 'having said that' in English. Often followed by a comma and another clause. Formal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Ceci étant, nous pouvons commencer la réunion.
native_language_example: That said, we can start the meeting.

meaning: seatbelt; safety belt.
additional_notes: Used for cars, airplanes, and other vehicles. Commonly used with verbs like attacher (to fasten) or porter (to wear). In formal instructions (e.g., on planes) you'll often hear Veuillez attacher votre ceinture de sécurité. Plural: ceintures de sécurité.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas d'attacher ta ceinture de sécurité avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don't forget to fasten your seatbelt before leaving.

meaning: that said; however; having said that.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a remark that qualifies or contrasts with what was just said. Often placed at the start of a sentence or clause. Slightly formal/neutral — common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: C'était une bonne idée. Cela dit, il faudra plus de temps pour la réaliser.
native_language_example: It was a good idea. That said, it will take more time to carry out.

meaning: 'how long (has it been)' — asks about the duration of time since something started or happened.
additional_notes: Used to ask for the length of time something has been happening (often followed by 'temps' or a verb phrase with 'que'). Common structure: 'Cela fait combien de temps que... ?' = 'How long have...?' In spoken French you may also hear 'Ça fait combien de temps... ?'.
target_language_example: Cela fait combien de temps que tu habites ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you lived here?

meaning: that said
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting or qualifying remark after a previous statement — similar to 'that said' or 'however'. Often followed by a comma and then the contrasting comment. Formality: neutral; common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je comprends ton point; cela étant, il faut respecter les règles.
native_language_example: I understand your point; that said, we must follow the rules.

meaning: this one
additional_notes: Demonstrative pronoun used to point to something/someone near the speaker or just mentioned. Often contrasted with celui-là (that one). It agrees in gender/number with the noun it replaces (celui, celle, ceux, celles) and can be followed by -ci or -là to indicate proximity (‑ci = near, ‑là = farther).
target_language_example: Je préfère celui-ci plutôt que celui-là.
native_language_example: I prefer this one rather than that one.

meaning: that one
additional_notes: masculine singular demonstrative pronoun. Used to point to or single out a specific person or thing, often in contrast with another option. It can refer to someone with a slightly dismissive tone depending on context. Related forms: celle-là, ceux-là, celles-là.
target_language_example: Je prends celui-là.
native_language_example: I'll take that one.

meaning: 'supposed to (do) it' — indicates expectation, assumption, or obligation that someone will perform an action (the pronoun 'le' = 'it').
additional_notes: Formed from 'être censé' + infinitive; used to say someone is expected or presumed to do something. 'Le' is a direct object pronoun referring to a previously mentioned masculine noun or idea ('it'). Conjugate 'être' for the subject: Je suis censé..., Tu es censé..., Il/elle est censé(e)... Note: agreement of 'censé' with the subject (censée/censés/censées) appears in writing but is often omitted in speech. Common in questions and statements about duties, plans, or assumptions.
target_language_example: Comment je suis censé le savoir ?
native_language_example: How am I supposed to know it?

meaning: completely; totally; one hundred percent.
additional_notes: Used informally and in neutral contexts to express full agreement, certainty, or that something is entirely true. Equivalent to English "100%" or "completely." Can modify verbs or adjectives (e.g., "Je suis cent pour cent d'accord").
target_language_example: Je suis cent pour cent d'accord avec toi.
native_language_example: I am one hundred percent in agreement with you.

meaning: one hundred and seven years (107 years).
additional_notes: A number phrase: 'cent' = 100, 'sept' = 7, 'ans' = years. In French, numbers are read in order (cent + sept) to make 107. Use 'ans' after an age or duration. For ages you can also say "107 ans" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Il a vécu cent sept ans.
native_language_example: He lived one hundred and seven years.

meaning: about a hundred; roughly one hundred (used with a noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an approximate number around one hundred. Always followed by 'de' plus a noun (or a number + noun). Can mean 'hundreds of' in a general sense in some contexts. For exact hundreds use 'une centaine' or a specific number (e.g. 'deux cents').
target_language_example: Il y avait une centaine de livres sur la table.
native_language_example: There were about a hundred books on the table.

meaning: power plant; electricity-generating station
additional_notes: Refers to a facility that produces electrical power (e.g., thermal, hydro, nuclear, wind farms can be called centrales). Commonly used in technical and everyday contexts when talking about where electricity comes from.
target_language_example: La centrale électrique fournit de l'électricité à toute la région.
native_language_example: The power plant supplies electricity to the whole region.

meaning: 'downtown' or 'city center' — the central, usually commercial area of a town or city.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the main central district (shops, offices, transport hub). Can be preceded by prepositions like à, en, dans, or followed by directional verbs (aller, se rendre). 'En centre-ville' and 'au centre-ville' are both common; 'en plein centre-ville' emphasizes 'right in the middle of downtown.'
target_language_example: Le cinéma est en plein centre-ville, à côté de la mairie.
native_language_example: The cinema is right in the downtown area, next to the town hall.

meaning: 'vicious circle' — a harmful situation that keeps repeating and getting worse.
additional_notes: Used to describe a repeating negative cycle where one problem causes another that reinforces the first. Common in discussions of habits, systems, economics, relationships, or personal situations. Equivalent to English "vicious circle" or "vicious cycle."
target_language_example: Nous devons agir maintenant pour ne pas rester dans un cercle vicieux.
native_language_example: We must act now so we don't stay in a vicious circle.

meaning: kite (a toy flown in the sky, made of a frame and a sail with a string).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the flying toy. Always masculine in French: 'un cerf-volant'. Common verbs: 'faire du cerf-volant' (to fly a kite), 'faire voler un cerf-volant', 'attacher la ficelle au cerf-volant'.
target_language_example: Nous avons fait voler le cerf-volant sur la plage.
native_language_example: We flew the kite on the beach.

meaning: the icing on the cake; an extra good (or sometimes bad) detail that makes a situation perfect or complete.
additional_notes: Used idiomatically to describe a final detail that improves (most often) an already good situation. Can be positive ('what makes it even better') or used ironically to emphasize an unexpected final twist. Literal translation is 'cherry on the cake.'
target_language_example: Il a déjà tout réussi, et la cerise sur le gâteau, c'est qu'il a gagné le prix.
