native_language_example: He had already succeeded in everything, and the icing on the cake is that he won the prize.

meaning: these days; nowadays; recently.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current period or recent times. Often placed after the verb or at the start of the sentence. Equivalent to 'these days' or 'lately' in English.
target_language_example: Je suis fatigué ces jours-ci.
native_language_example: I'm tired these days.

meaning: 'this afternoon' (short, informal spoken form)
additional_notes: A colloquial contraction of 'cet après-midi'. Used in casual spoken French to mean 'this afternoon'. Mostly heard in informal conversation; avoid in formal writing. Pronunciation often drops the second part: 'seht ah-pray'.
target_language_example: On peut se voir cet après pour le café ?
native_language_example: Can we meet this afternoon for coffee?

meaning: 'every man for himself' / 'each person looks out for themselves.'
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation where people act selfishly or independently, often in a crisis or competitive context. Can be literal or figurative. Common idiomatic expression; sometimes extended jokingly with 'Dieu pour tous' ('God for all').
target_language_example: Dans cette vente aux enchères, c'est chacun pour soi.
native_language_example: In this auction, it's every man for himself.

meaning: Used before a noun to indicate flesh, skin, or flesh-colour; often conveys 'flesh-colored', 'nude' or literally 'meat/flesh of' depending on context and collocation.
additional_notes: A fragment commonly found in expressions and compounds (e.g. 'chair de poule' = goosebumps; 'couleur chair'/'peau chair' = flesh-coloured/nude). Can be literal when referring to animal or human flesh (e.g. 'chair de bœuf') or figurative/idiomatic when combined with other words. Typically appears as 'chair de + noun' to specify the type of flesh or the flesh-colour.
target_language_example: Elle avait des frissons, la chair de poule lui montait partout.
native_language_example: She shivered; goosebumps (literally 'chicken flesh') rose all over her.

meaning: 'goosebumps' (the feeling/bumps on the skin when you're cold or scared).
additional_notes: Used to describe the physical reaction (raised bumps on the skin) or the feeling of being creeped out or thrilled. Often plural in English ('goosebumps') but in French it's singular 'la chair de poule' when naming the phenomenon; you can also say 'j'ai la chair de poule' to mean 'I have goosebumps.'
target_language_example: Quand j'ai entendu le bruit, j'ai eu la chair de poule.
native_language_example: When I heard the noise, I got goosebumps.

meaning: chair made of (material) — used before a material (e.g., bois, plastique).
additional_notes: The pattern 'chaise en + [material]' indicates the material the chair is made from. In French use 'en' with materials and some materials require agreement in gender/number elsewhere but not for 'en'. Common materials: bois (wood), plastique (plastic), métal (metal), cuir (leather). This is a compositional, literal construction.
target_language_example: J'achète une chaise en métal pour le jardin.
native_language_example: I'm buying a metal chair for the garden.

meaning: the room is (followed by a description).
additional_notes: This is the structure noun + être (La chambre est...) used to describe the room's state or qualities (size, temperature, condition, etc.). Replace 'chambre' with other nouns to describe them similarly. Agreement: adjectives must match the noun in gender and number (e.g. La chambre est petite; Les chambres sont petites).
target_language_example: La chambre est trop petite pour trois personnes.
native_language_example: The room is too small for three people.

meaning: vault; secure room (for storing valuables).
additional_notes: Refers to a reinforced, locked room or safe room in a bank, building, or facility used to protect money, documents, or valuables. Can be translated as 'vault' or 'strongroom.' Used in formal contexts.
target_language_example: La banque a transféré les bijoux dans la chambre forte.
native_language_example: The bank moved the jewels into the vault.

meaning: bedroom (room used for sleeping).
additional_notes: Common French term for the room where people sleep. Used with possessive adjectives (ma/ta/sa/notre/votre) or articles (la/une). You can also say simply "la chambre" in everyday speech. Pronunciation tip: the 'à' links chambre and coucher.
target_language_example: Sa chambre à coucher est au deuxième étage.
native_language_example: His/Her bedroom is on the second floor.

meaning: gas chamber (a room where people are killed with poisonous gas)
additional_notes: Refers to a method of mass killing, historically associated with the Holocaust and also used more generally in contexts meaning 'place of execution' or metaphorically as an extreme punishment. This is a very strong and potentially disturbing term; use with care. Not informal. Literal translation is accurate.
target_language_example: Il a été envoyé dans une chambre à gaz.
native_language_example: He was sent to a gas chamber.

meaning: battlefield; a place where fighting or conflict takes place.
additional_notes: Used literally for a site of military combat (battlefield). Also used figuratively to describe any place of intense conflict, struggle, or chaos (e.g., streets, workplace, debate). Common in both literal and metaphorical contexts.
target_language_example: Les manifestants ont transformé la place en champ de bataille.
native_language_example: The protesters turned the square into a battlefield.

meaning: 'champion of' (masculine singular), used to say someone is the top supporter, defender or winner for something
additional_notes: Literally 'champion of'. Follows a masculine singular noun (du = de + le). Used both for sporting winners (champion du monde = world champion) and figuratively (champion du recyclage = advocate/strong supporter of recycling). For feminine use say 'championne de'.
target_language_example: Il est le champion du recyclage dans notre quartier.
native_language_example: He is the champion of recycling in our neighborhood.

meaning: world champion; the person or title recognized as the best in the world in a sport or competition.
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone who has won a world championship (title) or the status of being the best in the world in a given discipline. Can refer to a single person (le champion du monde / la championne du monde) or multiple-time winners (champion du monde à trois reprises). Often used with articles and verbs: «devenir», «être», «remporter», «défendre le titre».
target_language_example: Il a le potentiel pour devenir un champion du monde.
native_language_example: He has the potential to become a world champion.

meaning: 'lucky to have you' (literally: 'to have the luck to have you')
additional_notes: This is the phrase de la chance de + object pronoun (t' = te) used to say someone is fortunate to have another person. Common variants: « J'ai de la chance de t'avoir » (I'm lucky to have you), « On a de la chance de t'avoir » (We're lucky to have you). The t' is the contraction of te before a vowel sound (t'avoir).
target_language_example: Tu m'aides toujours — j'ai de la chance de t'avoir.
native_language_example: You always help me — I'm lucky to have you.

meaning: 'luck plays a (role)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that luck affects outcomes. Often completed with rôle (la chance joue un rôle important...) but can stand as a shortened idea in conversation. Appears in general statements about life or events. 'La chance' = luck; verb 'jouer' = to play (here: to have an influence).
target_language_example: La chance joue un rôle dans la réussite de ce projet.
native_language_example: Luck plays a role in the success of this project.

meaning: climate change; long-term changes in Earth's climate (warming, weather patterns).
additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about global warming, environmental impact, policies and actions. Can refer to causes (human activity) or effects (rising sea levels, endangered species). Used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Le gouvernement propose des mesures pour lutter contre le changement climatique.
native_language_example: The government is proposing measures to fight climate change.

meaning: 'change is' — a simple subject + verb phrase used to state that change has a certain quality or is necessary/possible/etc.
additional_notes: This pattern pairs the noun 'le changement' (change) with the verb 'être' (to be). In natural French you will more often see 'Le changement est...' with the definite article. Examples show adjectives or complements after 'est'. Use to make statements about change (necessary, beneficial, possible, frightening...).
target_language_example: Le changement est inévitable.
native_language_example: Change is inevitable.

meaning: to change one's mind; to change one's opinion or decision.
additional_notes: Used when someone modifies a previous opinion, decision, or intention. Commonly used with a subject who 'changes mind' (e.g., Il a changé d'avis). Often follows verbs or modal expressions (peut, doit, va) and can be used reflexively in sense but doesn't require a reflexive pronoun in French.
target_language_example: Tu peux encore changer d'avis si tu veux.
native_language_example: You can still change your mind if you want.

meaning: will not change / won't change.
additional_notes: Negative future tense: 'ne ... pas' around the future verb (changera = il/elle/on form of changer). Used to say that someone or something will remain the same or won't change their mind/behavior/outcome. In speech, the 'ne' is often dropped: 'changera pas' or written as 'ne changera pas'.
target_language_example: Il ne changera pas d'avis, même si tu insistes.
native_language_example: He won't change his mind, even if you insist.

meaning: a song in (a particular language or style).
additional_notes: Used before a language or sometimes a musical style to indicate the language/style of the song: chanson en français, chanson en anglais, chanson en espagnol. Typical structure: "chanter/écrire/faire une chanson en + [langue/style]". Not a fixed idiom by itself—it requires the following word (a language or descriptor).
target_language_example: Peux-tu chanter une chanson en espagnol ?
native_language_example: Can you sing a song in Spanish?

meaning: "this song is" (fragment) — 'chanson' = song; 'est' = is
additional_notes: This is a simple noun + verb combination used to describe a song. In natural French you would usually see it as part of a full sentence (e.g. "Cette chanson est belle" = "This song is beautiful"). Note that 'chanson' is a feminine noun: une chanson. Use appropriate adjectives and pronouns that agree in gender and number. The example sentence 4 uses 'chante une chanson' (to sing a song) with a different structure — there 'chanson' is the object of 'chante'.
target_language_example: Cette chanson est très entraînante.
native_language_example: This song is very catchy.

meaning: bounty hunter; someone who captures fugitives or retrieves people for a reward.
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who tracks and arrests or captures criminals or targets in exchange for a monetary reward ('prime' = bounty). Can refer to fictional or real-life figures. Often masculine form; feminine would be 'chasseuse de primes' though 'chasseur de primes' is commonly used generically.
target_language_example: Ils ont engagé un chasseur de primes pour retrouver le voleur.
native_language_example: They hired a bounty hunter to find the thief.

meaning: 'the cat is (in/doing/...)' — a subject + être + en ... construction used to describe a state, condition, or ongoing action of 'the cat'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a combination: chat (the cat) + est (is) + en + following word(s). 'En' can introduce: - a state/condition (en sécurité, en surpoids) meaning 'in/under/with' a condition; - a progressive action with 'en train de' (en train de lire) meaning 'in the process of'. Choose the rest of the phrase to complete the meaning. Word order: 'Le chat est en...' or 'Ton/Votre chat est en...'.
target_language_example: Le chat est en colère.
native_language_example: The cat is angry.

meaning: The noun 'chat' (cat) with the reflexive pronoun 'se' used to form reflexive or pronominal verbs (e.g. se cacher, se porter, se prélasser) — indicates the cat is doing the action to/for itself or is in a certain state.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the word 'chat' followed by the reflexive pronoun 'se' before a verb. In French many verbs use 'se' to become pronominal (se cacher = to hide oneself, se promener = to take a walk, se trouver = to be located/feel). Word order: 'Le chat se [verb]'. Use 'se' with third-person singular subjects (il/elle/on).
target_language_example: Le chat se brosse les pattes après le repas.
native_language_example: The cat grooms its paws after the meal.

meaning: 'cats are (some...)' — a simple subject-verb-article construction used to state a general fact about cats.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the plural noun 'chats' (cats), the verb 'sont' (are, 3rd person plural of être), and the indefinite plural article 'des' (some). It's followed by a noun or noun phrase describing what cats are (e.g., animaux, animaux domestiques). Use for general statements about cats. In French, 'des' is used before plural count nouns and often translates to 'some' or is omitted in English (e.g., 'Cats are pets').
target_language_example: Les chats sont des compagnons indépendants mais affectueux.
native_language_example: Cats are independent but affectionate companions.

meaning: 'shoes before' — but note: this exact order is not a common fixed phrase; 'avant' can mean 'before' (in time) or 'in front (of)'.
additional_notes: The sequence 'chaussures avant' is not a standard French phrase by itself. In the example sentences, 'avant' is used with verbs (e.g. 'avant de sortir', 'avant de rentrer', 'avant de les acheter') meaning 'before (doing something)'. A correct beginner pattern is 'chaussures + avant de + infinitive' to say 'shoes before [doing X]' as in 'enlever/retirer/ôter ses chaussures avant de rentrer' (take off your shoes before entering). Also 'essayer les chaussures avant de les acheter' means 'try the shoes before buying them.' Use 'avant de' + infinitive for 'before (doing)'.
target_language_example: Enlevez vos chaussures avant de monter sur le tatami.
native_language_example: Take off your shoes before stepping on the tatami.

meaning: television channel; TV station.
additional_notes: Refers to a broadcaster or specific TV channel (e.g. 'la première chaîne', 'une chaîne locale'). Often used with articles and adjectives (la chaîne, une chaîne locale, la deuxième chaîne). Can mean the channel itself or the network that transmits programs.
target_language_example: Je regarde les informations sur une chaîne de télévision locale.
native_language_example: I'm watching the news on a local television channel.

meaning: masterpiece; an outstanding work of art, literature, music, etc.
additional_notes: Used to describe a work considered the best or most important in someone's career or the highest-quality example of its kind. Can refer to paintings, films, books, musical compositions, performances, and more. Singular masculine noun (un chef-d'œuvre). Plural: des chefs-d'œuvre.
target_language_example: Ce film est le chef-d'œuvre du réalisateur.
native_language_example: This film is the director's masterpiece.

meaning: a dirt road; an unpaved country lane or track
additional_notes: Used for rural or rough roads, often narrow and unpaved. Can refer to paths for cars, horses, or walking. Common in directions: 'suis le chemin de terre' = follow the dirt road/track.
target_language_example: Prends le chemin de terre à gauche jusqu'à la ferme.
native_language_example: Take the dirt road on the left until the farm.

meaning: 'the way/path of' or 'on the way to' (literally 'path of the...').
additional_notes: Used to talk about a physical path or a figurative route/way to something. Often appears with a place or goal after du (de + le), e.g. 'chemin du lycée' (path to the high school) or 'chemin du trône' (way to the throne). Can be used with 'sur le chemin du...' meaning 'on the way to...' or simply to indicate the route leading to something.
target_language_example: Nous étions sur le chemin du marché quand il a commencé à pleuvoir.
native_language_example: We were on the way to the market when it started to rain.

meaning: "the most ___ way" or "the shortest/fastest/ easiest path" depending on context (part of a superlative phrase).
additional_notes: This fragment is not a complete phrase by itself; it appears in superlative constructions like "le chemin le plus court" (the shortest route) or "le chemin le plus rapide" (the fastest way). In French the adjective and its qualifiers often follow the noun: chemin (noun) + le plus + adjective. Choose the adjective to specify what is being maximized/minimized (court, rapide, sûr, direct, etc.).
target_language_example: Prends le chemin le plus court pour gagner du temps.
native_language_example: Take the shortest route to save time.

meaning: 'to get (some) / to fetch (some)'.
additional_notes: Used when you go to obtain or bring back an unspecified quantity of a non-count or feminine noun (de la + noun). Often followed directly by the thing being fetched (e.g. de la nourriture, de la glace). Common in everyday spoken French. The phrase implies going somewhere to get it and bringing it back for someone. For masculine or plural nouns use 'du' or 'des' (ex. chercher du pain, chercher des pommes).
target_language_example: Je vais te chercher de la soupe.
native_language_example: I'll go get you some soup.

meaning: 'to try to' or 'to seek to' (to attempt to do something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb: chercher à + infinitive. Indicates an effort, intention or attempt to achieve something (similar to 'essayer de', though 'chercher à' can sound slightly more formal).
target_language_example: Il cherche à améliorer son français en parlant tous les jours.
native_language_example: He is trying to improve his French by speaking every day.

meaning: you are trying to / you mean to (do something) — expresses that someone is attempting or intending an action, often with a confrontational or accusatory tone
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: 'tu cherches à + infinitive'. In everyday speech it can point out someone’s action or intention (neutral) but often appears in confrontational contexts to suggest the person is provoking trouble or deliberately doing something (e.g., 'Tu cherches à me punir ?'). English equivalents: 'are you trying to...' / 'do you mean to...'.
target_language_example: Tu cherches à m'embêter ou quoi ?
native_language_example: Are you trying to annoy me or what?

meaning: literally 'horse has' — the noun 'cheval' (horse) followed by the verb 'a' (has).
additional_notes: This phrase shows the structure noun + third-person singular of 'avoir' (il/elle a = he/she/it has). It appears in simple factual sentences (e.g., possessions, states, or events: 'has four legs', 'is thirsty', 'had a heart attack'). For beginners, recognize 'a' as the present tense of 'avoir' for il/elle/on. Word order is subject (le cheval) + verb (a) + complement.
target_language_example: Le cheval a besoin d'eau.
native_language_example: The horse needs water.

meaning: white/grey hair; (literal) white hairs or (idiomatic) worry/causing one to worry
additional_notes: Literally means 'white hairs' or 'grey hair' (sign of aging). Can be used literally to describe someone's hair color (e.g., elderly people). Idiomatically, expressions like 'se faire des cheveux blancs' or 'donner des cheveux blancs (à quelqu'un)' mean 'to worry (oneself) / to cause someone worry' (similar to 'to give someone grey hairs'). Context tells whether it's literal or idiomatic.
target_language_example: Tu te fais des cheveux blancs pour si peu ?
native_language_example: Are you worrying yourself sick over such a small thing?

meaning: at my (male) [place]; at my ... (used before a masculine noun like père, oncle, pote).
additional_notes: chez means 'at the home/place of' or 'with' someone. 'Mon' is the possessive for singular masculine nouns (or before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel sound). Use 'chez ma' for feminine (chez ma mère), 'chez mes' for plural. Common in spoken and written French to say where you are or where you go: 'chez mon père' = at my father's house. Not used with people’s names alone (use chez + name without possessive or with title: chez Huguette or chez le docteur).
target_language_example: Je vais dîner chez mon frère ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm going to have dinner at my brother's tonight.

meaning: at our place
additional_notes: Used to indicate location at the speaker's (or speaker's group's) home or place. Can mean 'at our house' or more generally 'in our household' or 'among us' depending on context. Formality: neutral. Use chez + possessive to refer to someone's home (chez moi, chez toi, chez eux).
target_language_example: On regarde la télé chez nous ce soir.
native_language_example: We're watching TV at our place tonight.

meaning: 'at the home/place of his/her/their' used before a plural noun (possessive).
additional_notes: chez means 'at the home/place of' and is followed by a person or possessive phrase. 'Ses' is the third-person plural/singular possessive (his, her, its, their) used with plural nouns. Together 'chez ses' appears before a plural noun to mean 'at his/her/their [plural noun]'. You will need context to know whether 'ses' means his, her, its, or their. Example: 'chez ses parents' = 'at his/her/their parents' house' (commonly 'at his/her/their parents').
target_language_example: Il dîne ce soir chez ses parents.
native_language_example: He is having dinner tonight at his parents' (house).

meaning: at home; in one's own home; in/from one's own place; in one's own environment or comfort zone.
additional_notes: Used to indicate being at or returning to one's home or personal place. Can be literal (physically at home) or figurative (in one's own sphere or comfort zone). Often used with verbs like être, rentrer, rester; appears in expressions like chacun chez soi (each to their own). Can be combined with possessives (chez moi, chez toi) but the fixed phrase chez soi specifically refers to 'one's own home' in a general sense.
target_language_example: C'est bon d'être chez soi.
native_language_example: It's nice to be at home.

meaning: dog is
additional_notes: This is simply the sequence of the noun chien (dog) followed by the verb est (is). It's not an idiom; it's the basic subject-verb construction 'the dog is...' in French. Depending on context articles or adjectives usually appear (e.g. mon chien est, notre chien est, un chien est). Word order is the same as English (subject + verb).
target_language_example: Mon chien est très joueur.
native_language_example: My dog is very playful.

meaning: Roman numeral (the symbols I, V, X, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the characters of the Roman numeral system. In French, 'chiffre' usually means digit or numeral; 'chiffre romain' specifically contrasts with 'chiffre arabe' (Arabic numeral). Common contexts: chapter headings, monarchs (Louis XIV), centuries (XVIII siècle), clock faces, outlines.
target_language_example: Sur la couverture, les chapitres sont indiqués par un chiffre romain.
native_language_example: On the cover, the chapters are indicated by a Roman numeral.

meaning: white chocolate.
additional_notes: Refers to the sweet confection made mainly from cocoa butter, sugar and milk solids (no cocoa solids). Used like other food nouns in questions and preferences: aimer le chocolat blanc (to like white chocolate). Gender is masculine (le). Plural form: chocolats blancs. Pronounced roughly /ʃɔ.ko.la blɑ̃/.
target_language_example: J'achète du chocolat blanc pour le gâteau.
native_language_example: I'm buying white chocolate for the cake.

meaning: hot chocolate (a warm drink made from chocolate or cocoa and milk/water).
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression. Used to refer to the beverage; can be uncountable (du chocolat chaud) or countable when offering/ordering (un chocolat chaud). Often served in a cup and popular in cold weather or as a treat.
target_language_example: Après la promenade, je prends un chocolat chaud au café.
native_language_example: After the walk, I'll have a hot chocolate at the café.

meaning: something else / another thing
additional_notes: Used to refer to a different thing or something other than what was just mentioned. Often appears in phrases like « quelque chose d'autre » (something else). Alone as « chose d'autre » is less common; beginners will usually see it with a determiner (quelque, rien, autre).
target_language_example: Je voudrais quelque chose d'autre à manger.
native_language_example: I would like something else to eat.

meaning: 'thing in the' (literal phrase fragment used before specifying a place, part, or topic)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a fragment: 'chose' means 'thing' and 'dans le' means 'in the'. It typically appears as part of a longer sentence (e.g. 'une chose dans le jardin' — 'a thing in the garden' or conversationally 'c'est la chose dans le dossier' — 'it's the thing in the file'). Watch gender/number and article agreement: use dans la / dans l' / dans les as needed (dans le for masculine singular).
target_language_example: Il y a une chose dans le sac que tu dois voir.
native_language_example: There is a thing in the bag that you need to see.

meaning: a thing for him / something for him
additional_notes: Literal phrase: chose = 'thing', pour lui = 'for him'. Used to indicate an object, gift, or matter intended for a male person or referring to 'him' in context. Very general and can refer to physical items or abstract matters depending on context. Use 'chose pour elle' for 'for her'.
target_language_example: J'ai acheté une chose pour lui.
native_language_example: I bought something for him.

meaning: 'something for you' or 'a thing for you'.
additional_notes: A simple phrase combining chose (thing) + pour (for) + toi (you). Used to indicate that an object, task, or piece of information is intended for the listener. Can be used in casual or neutral contexts. If speaking formally or to more than one person, use 'pour vous' (formal/plural).
target_language_example: J'ai une chose pour toi.
native_language_example: I have something for you.

meaning: 'the thing that I...' (used to introduce something the speaker did, saw, felt, etc.)
additional_notes: Common phrase structure: 'la/une + chose que j' + [verb]'. Depending on tense/mood, the verb after 'que' is conjugated for 'je' (e.g. j'ai fait, j'ai vue) or in the subjunctive after superlatives/emotion (e.g. que j'aie faite). The past participle agrees in gender with the preceding direct object when required (e.g. 'la chose que j'ai faite' vs 'la chose que j'ai vu[e]').
target_language_example: C'est la chose que j'ai toujours voulu faire.
native_language_example: It's the thing that I've always wanted to do.

meaning: 'thing that I don't...' (start of a clause meaning something I do not ...)
additional_notes: This is a fragment, not a complete phrase. It appears at the start of a subordinate clause: 'la chose que je ne ...' meaning 'the thing that I don't ...' or 'une chose que je ne ...' meaning 'something I don't ...'. You must finish the clause with a verb (e.g. comprends, veux, sais). Word order: 'la/une chose que je ne + verb'. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped in informal speech (je ne comprends → je comprends).
target_language_example: C'est la chose que je ne comprends pas.
native_language_example: That's the thing that I don't understand.

meaning: 'thing that you' or 'something that you' (start of a relative clause referring to something the listener does or has).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a sequence where 'chose' (thing/something) is followed by a relative clause introduced by 'que' and addressed to 'vous' (you formal/plural). It will usually be completed by a verb: e.g. « la chose que vous voulez » = 'the thing that you want'. In spoken French you might also hear 'chose que tu' with the informal 'tu'.
target_language_example: C'est la chose que vous cherchez.
native_language_example: That's the thing that you are looking for.

meaning: 'the thing that matters' or 'what matters'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the most important thing in a situation. Often appears as "la seule chose qui compte" (the only thing that matters) or with adverbs like "vraiment" (really). Can introduce a clause introduced by "est que" or "est si..." to state what matters.
target_language_example: La chose qui compte, c'est que tu sois heureux.
native_language_example: What matters is that you are happy.

meaning: 'the thing that matters' or 'what matters'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the single important thing in a situation. Often appears in the phrase "la seule chose qui importe" (the only thing that matters). Can be followed by a clause introduced by "que" or "si". Formality: neutral — suitable in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: La seule chose qui importe, c'est que tu ailles bien.
native_language_example: The only thing that matters is that you're okay.

meaning: 'thing that has happened to me' (used in relative clauses: 'the best thing that has happened to me')
additional_notes: This phrase appears inside a relative clause using the subjunctive after a superlative or expression of uniqueness: "la meilleure chose qui me soit arrivée" = "the best thing that has happened to me." The full pattern is often "la/une + [adjective] + chose qui me soit (+ jamais) arrivée." In everyday speech the indicative is also common ("qui m'est arrivée"). "Me" is the indirect object meaning 'to me.'
target_language_example: C'est la seule chose qui me soit vraiment utile.
native_language_example: It's the only thing that is really useful to me.

meaning: something for you / something to tell/ask/show you.
additional_notes: Used after a noun like 'une chose' to indicate there is one (or something) the speaker wants the listener to receive, hear, see, or do. Common constructions: 'J'ai une chose à vous demander/dire/montrer' = 'I have something to ask/tell/show you.' Polite/formal because of 'vous'. Replace 'vous' with 'te' for informal singular.
target_language_example: J'ai une chose à vous dire avant de partir.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you before leaving.

meaning: part of reflexive constructions with 'choses' — often appears in phrases meaning 'things happen/turn out' (e.g. 'les choses se sont passées' = 'things happened/turned out').
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself; 'se' is the reflexive pronoun used with verbs to form pronominal verbs (e.g. 'se passer', 'se dérouler', 'se présenter', 'se casser'). Common patterns: 'les choses se sont passées...' (things happened/turned out...), 'les choses se présentent...' (things look/are looking...), 'les choses se sont déroulées...' (things unfolded). Use correct verb agreement and past participle when needed.
target_language_example: Les choses se sont arrangées finalement.
native_language_example: Things worked out in the end.

meaning: things to
additional_notes: Usually seen in patterns like des choses à faire, des choses à apprendre, or des choses à régler, where it means "things to do/learn/sort out." In this very common structure, à is followed by an infinitive. In some sentences, though, à may belong to what comes after instead, so choses just means "things."
target_language_example: J'ai encore des choses à faire ce soir.
native_language_example: I still have things to do tonight.

meaning: sandcastle (a structure made of sand, usually on a beach).
additional_notes: Common, literal phrase used when children (or adults) build a small castle or tower from wet sand. Often used in simple past/future constructions (construire, faire). Can be singular or plural (châteaux de sable).
target_language_example: Les enfants ont construit un château de sable près de l'eau.
native_language_example: The children built a sandcastle near the water.

meaning: 'more expensive than' / 'less expensive than' when used in comparisons (with plus/moins).
additional_notes: Used after a noun with 'plus' or 'moins' to compare prices or cost/expense. Structure: [item] est plus chère que [other item] (is more expensive than) or [item] est moins chère que [other item] (is less expensive than). Agreement: 'chère' agrees in gender and number with the noun it describes (cher, chère, chers, chères). Often shortened to 'que' introducing the second item (than).
target_language_example: Cette voiture est plus chère que la mienne.
native_language_example: This car is more expensive than mine.

meaning: below / under (in the text or page).
additional_notes: Used to refer the reader to information that appears later on the same page, document, or message. Common in instructions and formal writing. Often placed after or before the noun it modifies (e.g., 'le texte ci‑dessous' or 'ci‑dessous, vous trouverez...').
target_language_example: Les instructions ci-dessous expliquent comment créer un compte.
native_language_example: The instructions below explain how to create an account.

meaning: the numbers 'five, six' (used when counting).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom — it's simply two cardinal numbers listed together as part of counting or recitation (e.g., counting aloud, listing numbers, or giving examples). Pronunciation: 'sank, sees'. Useful in sequences like 'un, deux, trois...' and in saying quantities. No special grammar: each is a standalone number.
target_language_example: Un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept.
native_language_example: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.

meaning: five hundred (500).
additional_notes: Used to count 500 of something. Note that 'cinq cents' has an extra 's' on 'cents' when it stands alone or is not followed by another number (e.g., 'cinq cents personnes'). When followed by another number (e.g., 501: 'cinq cent un'), 'cent' is singular (no 's'). In dates/ages like 'cinq cents ans' the plural 's' is kept because it's exactly 500 years.
target_language_example: Cette maison a cinq cents ans.
native_language_example: This house is five hundred years old.

meaning: 'five for' — used to indicate an amount of five (units) allocated to someone or something; can appear in counting/allocation or as part of a percentage (followed by «cent»).
additional_notes: Often used in spoken allocation/counting: 'Cinq pour toi' = 'Five for you.' When followed by 'cent' it forms part of a percentage (e.g. 'quatre virgule cinq pour cent' = 4.5%). Alone, 'cinq pour' without context is incomplete — expect an object or unit after it (toi, moi, cent, etc.).
target_language_example: J'en prends deux, cinq pour toi et trois pour lui.
native_language_example: I'll take two, five for you and three for him.

meaning: All clear; signal received perfectly (radio/phone).
additional_notes: Used in radio/telecom contexts or informally to say you hear/understand someone perfectly. Literally refers to signal strength/clarity (5/5). Common in both formal radio communication and casual speech. Not literal for scoring; don't use for grades.
target_language_example: Oui, je t'entends cinq sur cinq — parle.
native_language_example: Yes, I hear you loud and clear — go ahead.

meaning: fifty-two (the number 52).
additional_notes: Used to say the cardinal number 52. In dates, French often pronounces each group (e.g., mille neuf cent cinquante-deux = 1952). Hyphenation can vary in speech and writing (cinquante-deux or cinquante deux), but the correct written form for compound numbers from 21 to 99 is usually hyphenated. Pronunciation: [sɛ̃.kɑ̃t dø].
target_language_example: Il a cinquante-deux ans.
native_language_example: He is fifty-two years old.

meaning: 'traffic is' (describes the state of traffic)
additional_notes: Used to describe traffic conditions (density, problems, suspensions). Often followed by an adjective (dense, affreuse, fluide) or a past participle (suspendue). Common in news and everyday conversation about roads and urban movement.
target_language_example: La circulation est très lente ce matin sur l'autoroute.
native_language_example: Traffic is very slow this morning on the highway.

meaning: 'moonlight' (the light from the moon); also used in poetic expressions
additional_notes: A common noun phrase meaning the light produced by the moon. Often used in romantic or poetic contexts (e.g., 'bain de clair de lune' = a moonlight bath). Not an idiom here — literal meaning. Can appear in phrases like 'au clair de lune' (by moonlight).
target_language_example: Nous avons marché au clair de lune le long de la plage.
native_language_example: We walked by moonlight along the beach.

meaning: the middle class (social/economic group).
additional_notes: Refers to people or households with moderate incomes, professions, and living standards between working class and upper class. Used in political, social, and demographic contexts. Singular and plural (la classe moyenne / les classes moyennes) are common.
target_language_example: Beaucoup de politiques ciblent la classe moyenne pendant la campagne.
native_language_example: Many politicians target the middle class during the campaign.

meaning: wink; a subtle or playful signal; a small, knowing gesture.
additional_notes: Literally 'blink of an eye.' Used both for the physical action (to wink) and figuratively to mean a hint, nod, or playful/reference (e.g., a wink to the audience). Can be used in expressions like 'faire un clin d'œil' (to give a wink) or 'un clin d'œil à' (a nod to / a reference to).
target_language_example: Elle m'a fait un clin d'œil pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: She winked at me during the meeting.

meaning: USB flash drive; removable USB memory stick.
additional_notes: Common everyday term for a small portable storage device that plugs into a computer's USB port. In French 'clé' literally means 'key', but here it refers to the device. Can be singular 'une clé USB' or plural 'des clés USB'.
target_language_example: J'ai sauvegardé les photos sur ma clé USB.
native_language_example: I saved the photos on my USB flash drive.

meaning: a short prepositional phrase meaning 'code of' or 'code for' (used to link 'code' with what it refers to)
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate a specific code belonging to or governing that noun (e.g. code de la route = highway/traffic code, code de conduite = code of conduct). It is not a complete phrase by itself — you usually need the noun that follows. Word order: 'code de + noun'.
target_language_example: Le code de la route est important pour les conducteurs.
native_language_example: The highway code (traffic rules) is important for drivers.

meaning: the highway code / rules of the road; driving laws and regulations
additional_notes: Refers to the set of laws, signs and rules that govern driving and road behavior in France (similar to 'traffic laws' or 'driving rules' in English). Often used when talking about taking the written driving test (passer le code) or studying traffic signs and rules.
target_language_example: Je révise le code de la route pour l'examen.
native_language_example: I'm studying the highway code for the exam.

meaning: 'the heart is' — literal subject (cœur) + verb (est) used to state a property or condition of the heart, either literal or figurative.
additional_notes: Simple declarative structure: cœur (heart, masculine: le cœur) + est (is). Pronunciation: /kœʁ ɛ/. Commonly appears in phrases like medical descriptions (Le cœur est...), emotional statements (Mon cœur est...), or poetic/metaphorical uses. When used with a possessive, insert the possessive before cœur (e.g., Mon cœur est...).
target_language_example: Le coeur est un organe de feu.
native_language_example: The heart is an organ of fire.

meaning: street corner; the corner where two streets meet.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a specific corner or small area at the intersection of streets. Common in directions and descriptions (e.g., 'the café on the corner'). 'Coin' means 'corner' and 'de rue' specifies it's a street corner. Can be singular or plural ('coins de rue').
target_language_example: Le marché est au coin de rue, près de la boulangerie.
native_language_example: The market is on the street corner, near the bakery.

meaning: "the hill is" (subject + verb: colline = hill, est = is).
additional_notes: This is simply the noun 'la colline' (the hill) followed by the verb 'est' (is). Used to describe the hill's state or location. 'Colline' is feminine: 'la colline'. In sentences you will more often see 'la colline est...' or with a determiner/adjective (e.g. 'la colline est verte').
target_language_example: La colline est couverte d'arbres.
native_language_example: The hill is covered with trees.

meaning: summer camp / holiday camp (organized group stay for children/teenagers).
additional_notes: Refers to an organized camp where children or teenagers stay for several days (often during school holidays) with supervised activities. Can be translated as 'summer camp' when in summer, or more generally 'holiday camp' or 'children's camp'. Often used with partir en / être en / aller en.
target_language_example: Mon neveu part en colonie de vacances cet été.
native_language_example: My nephew is going to summer camp this summer.

meaning: the spine; the backbone (literal anatomy).
additional_notes: Used primarily to refer to the anatomical spine. Can also be used in vivid or figurative expressions (e.g., sensations running along the spine) and in violent contexts. Pronunciation note: the accent on 'vertébrale' influences stress (ver-TÉ-brale).
target_language_example: Un frisson descend le long de ma colonne vertébrale.
native_language_example: A shiver ran down my spine.

meaning: 'how long are' (beginning of a question about duration, addressing 'tu' or 'vous' in inversion contexts)
additional_notes: This looks like the start of a question about duration using the verb 'être' (to be). In French, questions are usually formed as 'combien de temps es-tu...' (How long are you...) or 'combien de temps est-ce que...' for other subjects ('est-ce que tu...'). By itself 'combien de temps es' is incomplete: it needs the subject (tu, il, elle, etc.) or inversion to form a full question. Common uses: asking how long someone/something has been in a state or will stay in a state (e.g. 'Combien de temps es-tu en ville ?' — How long are you in town?).
target_language_example: Combien de temps es-tu en France ?
native_language_example: How long are you in France?

meaning: 'how many' or 'how much' (used in questions with 'il' — full form: 'combien y a-t-il')
additional_notes: This is the common question formula for asking about quantity or existence: 'Combien y a-t-il de + noun ?' The written form often inserts the '-t-' for pronunciation and inversion when followed by 'il'. In speech you may hear 'combien y a-t-il' or the contracted 'combien y a-t'. Use 'de' (not 'des') after the expression before a noun: 'Combien y a-t-il de musées ?'.
target_language_example: Combien y a-t-il de places disponibles ?
native_language_example: How many seats are available?

meaning: 'How many are there?' (asks for the number of things previously mentioned or implied).
additional_notes: Used to ask how many of something exist or remain. The full formal form is "Combien y en a-t-il ?" where "y" refers to a place or situation and "en" replaces a noun introduced earlier (meaning 'of them' / 'of it'). In spoken French you may hear shortened forms like "Combien y en a ?" or "Y en a combien ?". Use when counting items, people, or remaining quantity.
target_language_example: Combien y en a-t-il dans la boîte ?
native_language_example: How many are there in the box?

meaning: 'how much does it cost' / 'how much is it'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about price. Informal to neutral register (ça is casual). Can be used with question intonation or as part of a longer sentence (e.g., Je voulais savoir combien ça coûte). For more formal situations, use "combien cela coûte" or "quel est le prix".
target_language_example: Combien ça coûte pour ce sac ?
native_language_example: How much does this bag cost?

meaning: 'the committee is' — subject (comité) + verb (être) used to describe the committee.
additional_notes: This is simply the phrase 'le comité est' (or 'un comité est') — 'the committee is'. It's followed by adjectives, past participles (e.g. composé, formé) or clauses that describe the committee's composition, actions, or abilities. Remember agreement: 'comité' is masculine singular, so use 'est'. Common continuations: 'composé de.../formé de.../capable de...'.
target_language_example: Le comité est responsable de l'organisation de la foire.
native_language_example: The committee is responsible for organizing the fair.

meaning: short for "comme d'habitude" — "as usual" or "like always".
additional_notes: Informal, conversational contraction of comme d'habitude. Used to say that something happens in the usual way or to comment that nothing has changed. Common in speech and casual writing (texts, social media).
target_language_example: Je vais au travail en retard, comme d'hab.
native_language_example: I'm going to work late, as usual.

meaning: very quickly; in large quantities (sold or gone fast).
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to say something sells or disappears very quickly and easily, like hot buns. Commonly used with vendre/se vendre or partir/être parti(s). Tone: neutral/informal everyday speech. Use to describe popular items or things that sell out fast.
target_language_example: Les places pour le concert se sont vendues comme des petits pains.
native_language_example: The tickets for the concert sold like hotcakes.

meaning: 'as if by magic' / 'like magic' (suddenly or unexpectedly, as if magically).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens suddenly, unexpectedly, or with no visible explanation. Can be literal (in stories about magic) or figurative (everyday situations where something works easily or disappears). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Mon ordinateur a retrouvé tous mes fichiers, comme par magie.
native_language_example: My computer recovered all my files, like magic.

meaning: 'as if for' / 'as with' — used to compare or give an example, often meaning 'in the way you would for' or 'as one would do for'.
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a comparison or an example that illustrates how something is done or treated (e.g., 'comme pour X' = 'as you would for X' or 'as with X'). It often appears before a noun or noun phrase. Not formal only — neutral register.
target_language_example: Il a préparé la salle, comme pour une réunion importante.
native_language_example: He prepared the room, as if for an important meeting.

meaning: very; extremely (informal emphatic expression).
additional_notes: Used after an adjective or phrase to intensify it (like "very" or "so"). Often informal and colloquial. In examples like "comme tout à l'heure" it means "just now/earlier" (set phrase). When used after adjectives (contente comme tout, polie comme tout) it emphasizes the quality: "very happy", "extremely polite."
target_language_example: Il est fier comme tout de son travail.
native_language_example: He's very proud of his work.

meaning: like that
additional_notes: Often means "in that way" or "in that state/appearance." In questions like "Tu vas où comme ça ?", it can sound surprised, critical, or teasing: "Where are you going like that?"
target_language_example: Tu sors comme ça ?
native_language_example: Are you going out like that?

meaning: used to introduce how something happened or how the speaker does/thinks something ("that's how I..." or "that's how I...ed").
additional_notes: This is a colloquial, conversational structure often followed by a verb with the subject 'je' (e.g. j'ai, j'imagine). Full phrase usually appears as 'C'est comme ça que j'ai...' or 'C'est comme ça que j'' + verb. Use to explain manner, cause, or the way something came to be. Can be followed by present or past tense.
target_language_example: C'est comme ça que j'ai appris à cuisiner.
native_language_example: That's how I learned to cook.

meaning: that's how it (or things) work / that's the way it is.
additional_notes: Used to explain or state that something operates or happens in a given way. Often appears in spoken French as part of the phrase "c'est comme ça que ça marche" (that's how it works) or simply "c'est comme ça" (that's how it is). Informal / conversational register. Literal parts are compositional but the whole phrase functions as a fixed expression.
target_language_example: C'est comme ça que ça marche : tu appuies ici et la lumière s'allume.
native_language_example: That's how it works: you press here and the light turns on.

meaning: like that
additional_notes: Used to refer to a manner, appearance, or way of doing something: « comme cela ? » = « like that?/that way? ». It can also introduce a clause in a more formal style with the sense of « as », for example « comme cela avait été prédit » = « as had been predicted ».
target_language_example: Pourquoi tu parles comme cela ?
native_language_example: Why are you speaking like that?

meaning: properly; correctly; respectable (depending on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'properly' or 'the right way' when describing actions (e.g., 'do it properly'). As an adjective phrase (often after a noun) it can describe a respectable, well-behaved or 'proper' person or thing ('a respectable man'). Often used in everyday speech. Tone is neutral; not slang.
target_language_example: Assure-toi que tout est rangé comme il faut.
native_language_example: Make sure everything is tidied properly.

meaning: as they/people say; as the saying goes.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a common saying, proverb, or a widely accepted remark. Often followed by the proverb itself or a summary comment. Neutral register; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Comme on dit, il vaut mieux prévenir que guérir.
native_language_example: As they say, better safe than sorry.

meaning: as planned / as expected
additional_notes: Used to say that something is happening or happened according to a plan or expectation. Can be used as a question (Comme prévu ?) to confirm if things went as expected. Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Tout se passe comme prévu.
native_language_example: Everything is going as planned.

meaning: used to introduce a conclusion or example; roughly 'which shows that' / 'so, ...' / 'meaning that'.
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written French to present a result, a conclusion drawn from what was said, or to introduce an example that supports a point. Can be followed by a clause (comme quoi il faut partir tôt) or used alone as a short comment (— Il a raté le train. — Comme quoi !). Tone can be neutral or slightly colloquial depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a beaucoup travaillé, comme quoi les efforts paient.
native_language_example: He worked a lot, which shows that effort pays off.

meaning: as if
additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical or imagined situation (often contrary to reality). Commonly followed by a clause in the imperfect or pluperfect when referring to unreal/hypothetical past situations (e.g., «comme si rien ne s'était passé»). Can be used in commands/suggestions: «fais/faites comme si…» = pretend / act as if.
target_language_example: Fais comme si tu étais chez toi.
native_language_example: Act as if you were at home.

meaning: as if it were yesterday; used to say you remember something very clearly.
additional_notes: Used to express a vivid, recent-feeling memory of an event that may have happened long ago. Often follows verbs like se souvenir, se rappeler, or stands alone as a comment. Tone is informal to neutral. Literal words translate directly, but the phrase is idiomatic.
target_language_example: Je m'en souviens comme si c'était hier, pourtant ça fait dix ans.
native_language_example: I remember it as if it were yesterday, even though it's been ten years.

meaning: 'as if nothing (had happened)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe behaving or speaking as though an event, problem, or awkwardness did not occur. Often appears in the fuller expression "comme si de rien n'était" but can be shortened in conversation. Tone can be neutral or dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Il est arrivé en retard et a parlé comme si de rien.
native_language_example: He arrived late and spoke as if nothing had happened.

meaning: 'as if nothing had happened' / 'as if nothing were wrong'.
additional_notes: Used to describe behaving normally or pretending nothing unusual/serious occurred. Often used with imperative (Faites...) to tell someone to act naturally, or to describe someone's indifferent behavior. Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il a rangé ses affaires et est parti comme si de rien n'était.
native_language_example: He put away his things and left as if nothing had happened.

meaning: as you want / do as you like (you decide).
additional_notes: Used to give the other person the choice or to concede—can be neutral, permissive, or slightly resigned. Common in spoken French. Can be softened with tone; not strongly formal.
target_language_example: D'accord, fais comme tu veux.
native_language_example: Okay, do as you like.

meaning: 'this/that is how I...' — used to introduce the speaker's way of doing, feeling, or thinking.
additional_notes: Often appears in the fixed phrase 'C'est comme ça que je...' (literally 'It's like that that I...') to explain how the speaker likes, sees, does, or feels about something. Followed by a verb or clause describing the speaker's perspective or behavior. Can be shortened in casual speech to 'c'est comme ça que...' or 'comme ça, je...'.
target_language_example: C'est comme ça que je préfère travailler.
native_language_example: That's how I prefer to work.

meaning: 'starts/does begin' + masculine singular noun (e.g. le concert, le film).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun introduced by 'le' to say when or where something begins. The verb 'commencer' is conjugated (here third person singular 'commence'). For other genders/plural you would use 'commence la', 'commencent les', etc. Common in questions: 'À quelle heure commence le ... ?' Also used in statements: 'Ici commence le ...' (Here begins the ...).
target_language_example: À quelle heure commence le spectacle ?
native_language_example: What time does the show start?

meaning: 'how to go' or 'how to get (to)'.
additional_notes: Used to ask or explain directions or the way to reach a place. Often followed by a destination introduced with à/au/à la/chez/vers (e.g. comment aller à la gare / comment aller au parc). Can be used in questions (Peux-tu me dire comment aller...?) or statements giving instructions.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me dire comment aller au musée ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to get to the museum?

meaning: 'how are you going to' or 'how will you' (beginning of a question about someone's planned action)
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone plans to do something. Often completed by an infinitive (e.g., 'comment allez-vous faire', 'comment allez-vous payer') or by a reflexive construction ('comment allez-vous vous y prendre'). Formal when using 'allez-vous'; in casual speech you might hear 'tu vas' (e.g., 'comment tu vas faire ?').
target_language_example: Comment allez-vous payer ce voyage ?
native_language_example: How are you going to pay for this trip?

meaning: 'how are' (start of the polite question 'Comment allez-vous ?' = How are you?).
additional_notes: Usually completed as 'Comment allez-vous ?' (formal/plural) to ask 'How are you?'. In casual speech people say 'Comment ça va ?' or 'Ça va ?'. 'Comment allez' alone is incomplete — add 'vous' (formal/plural) or 'tu' in informal contexts: 'Comment vas-tu ?'. Used to show politeness when addressing someone (especially strangers, elders, or in formal situations).
target_language_example: Comment allez-vous aujourd'hui, Monsieur Dupont ?
native_language_example: How are you today, Mr. Dupont?

meaning: 'How are you?' (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask about someone's well‑being. Used with people you don't know well, in formal situations, or when addressing more than one person. Informal alternative with one person is 'comment vas‑tu'. Intonation and context can make it a casual greeting or a genuine question about health/feelings.
target_language_example: Bonsoir, comment allez-vous ?
native_language_example: Good evening, how are you?

meaning: 'how are we going to' or 'how will we' (used to ask how a group will do or achieve something).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a verb or infinitive (e.g., 'comment allons-nous faire ?', 'comment allons-nous régler...'). It's a formal/neutral construction using the first-person plural 'nous'. In speech, people often use 'on' instead of 'nous' (e.g., 'comment on va...').
target_language_example: Comment allons-nous résoudre ce problème ensemble ?
native_language_example: How are we going to solve this problem together?

meaning: 'what do you call' (used to ask the name/word for something or someone's name in informal speech)
additional_notes: This is the start of the question 'Comment appelles-tu… ?' meaning 'What do you call…?' or 'What's the name of…?' Often used to ask for the name of a thing (Comment appelles-tu ceci/ça ?) or to ask someone's name (Comment t'appelles ? is the usual short form). In standard written French the full correct forms are 'Comment t'appelles-tu ?' or 'Comment t'appelles-vous ?' for polite/formal. The phrase is compositional and literal. Use 'Comment s'appelle… ?' to ask about a third person (e.g. 'Comment s'appelle ton chien ?').
target_language_example: Comment appelles-tu ce livre ?
native_language_example: What do you call this book?

meaning: how did you
additional_notes: `comment as` is not a standard stand-alone phrase on its own. In correct French, this is usually part of `comment as-tu ... ?`, with inversion in a question. Here `as` is the `tu` form of `avoir`, so the whole expression often means `how did you ... ?` in everyday English, especially with the passé composé.
target_language_example: Comment as-tu fait ça ?
native_language_example: How did you do that?

meaning: how that
additional_notes: Used to ask or explain how something happens or works, with cela referring to a thing or situation already mentioned or understood from context. Cela is more formal than ça, so in everyday speech you will often hear comment ça... instead.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas comment cela s'est passé.
native_language_example: I don't know how that happened.

meaning: how do you plan (to) / how are you going to
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask about someone's plan, method, or intention. Often continues with an infinitive (e.g., 'comment comptes-tu faire?') or a reflexive structure ('comment comptes-tu t'y prendre?'). Can be formal or neutral; dropping 'tu' for 'vous' makes it polite: 'Comment comptez-vous...'. Tone can range from curious to challenging depending on context.
target_language_example: Comment comptes-tu résoudre ce problème ?
native_language_example: How are you going to solve this problem?

meaning: Likely an error or fragment — not a valid French phrase.
additional_notes:
This sequence 'comment en es' does not form a correct or meaningful expression in French. It looks like a mistaken combination of words: 'comment' (how), 'en' (in/of/there), and 'es' (you are, second-person singular of être). Possible intended phrases include:
- 'comment es-tu ?' (How are you?)
- 'comment en est‑il ?' (How is it going / how is he/it?)
- 'comment en êtes‑vous ?' (How are you with that? / what is your status?)
If you meant one of these, use the corrected form above. If this came from spoken French, it may be a transcription error or words run together.
target_language_example: Incorrect: «comment en es» — use «comment es‑tu ?» or «comment en est‑il ?» instead.
native_language_example: Incorrect: "comment en es" — use "comment es-tu ?" (How are you?) or "comment en est-il ?" (How is it going?) instead.

meaning: 'how are' (beginning of the question 'how are you' with the informal 'tu')
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it looks like the start of the informal question 'comment es-tu ?' (how are you?) or a mistaken/informal word order for 'tu es comment ?' In standard French, the common ways to ask 'how are you?' are 'Comment vas-tu ?' (informal), 'Ça va ?' (very common/informal) or 'Comment allez-vous ?' (formal/plural). 'Comment es' followed directly by an adjective can appear in questions like 'Comment es-tu ?' where 'es' is the second-person singular of être (to be).
target_language_example: Comment es-tu aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: How are you today?

meaning: 'how do you explain' (asked when requesting an explanation or cause)
additional_notes: This is the start of a question using the verb expliquer (to explain). Complete forms are usually 'Comment expliquez-vous...?' (formal/plural/inversion) or 'Comment est-ce que vous expliquez...?' or 'Comment vous expliquez...?' (informal). Use to ask someone to give reasons, causes, or an explanation for something. Adjust verb form for subject: explique (tu/il/elle) / expliquez (vous) / expliques (tu).
target_language_example: Comment expliquez-vous ce retard ?
native_language_example: How do you explain this delay?

meaning: 'how' (used before a verb with the clitic pronoun 'me') — asks about the manner or way something was done to/for me.
additional_notes: This is 'comment' + the contracted object pronoun 'm\'' (me). It appears before a verb in questions: e.g. 'Comment m'as-tu appelée ?' = 'How did you call me?' or 'How did you contact me?'. The exact English rendering depends on the verb: 'trouver' can mean 'find' (physically) or 'find'/'think' (opinion) in other contexts, but here it means 'find/locate' or 'reach me'. Pay attention to agreement: past participle may agree with a preceding direct object (e.g. 'retrouvée' when speaker is female).
target_language_example: Comment m'as-tu envoyé ce message ?
native_language_example: How did you send me that message?

meaning: 'how' used when asking how someone did something to/with me (informal written inversion: 'how did you... me?')
additional_notes: This is the start of a question using inversion with the pronoun 'tu' and the verb in the passé composé (m' + as = me + avoir). It appears in questions like 'Comment m'as-tu appelée ?' ('How did you call me?') or 'Comment m'as-tu trouvé ?' ('How did you find me?/How did you come across me?'). The construction is formal/neutral in written French; in speech you'd more often hear 'Comment tu m'as appelée ?' or 'Comment tu m'as trouvée ?'. Remember to agree past participles with a preceding direct object when needed (e.g., 'appelée' if the speaker is feminine).
target_language_example: Comment m'as-tu envoyé ce message ?
native_language_example: How did you send me this message?

meaning: 'how did you (have) me...' — part of a question asking how the speaker was called/found/found out by someone (followed by a past participle).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a formal/inverted question using the passé composé with 'vous' and the clitic 'm'' (me). It always needs a past participle after it (e.g. appelée, retrouvé, trouvée). Word order: 'Comment m'avez-vous + [past participle] ?' equals 'How did you ... me?' in contexts like 'How did you call me?', 'How did you find me?'. The form changes gender of the past participle when the direct object pronoun 'me' refers to a feminine speaker (appelée / trouvée).
target_language_example: Comment m'avez-vous appelée hier soir ?
native_language_example: How did you call me last night?

meaning: how can
additional_notes: Used to introduce a question about possibility or how something can be done. It is usually followed by a subject or pronoun, as in comment peut-il... ? or comment peut-on... ? Note that comment means "how," not the English noun "comment."
target_language_example: Comment peut-on apprendre le français plus vite ?
native_language_example: How can you learn French faster?

meaning: 'how does (someone) know' (used to ask by what means or reason someone knows something).
additional_notes: Used to form questions about the way or reason someone knows something. It is followed by a subject pronoun and often an object (cela/ça/que + clause). In spoken French, 'ça' is common; 'cela' is more formal. The short form 'Comment sait-il ?' can ask 'How does he know?' without repeating the object.
target_language_example: Comment sait-elle que tu es venu ?
native_language_example: How does she know that you came?

meaning: 'how do you know' (start of a question asking how someone knows something).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of questions formed with the verb savoir (to know). In full questions you'll usually see a subject and the rest of the information: e.g. "Comment savez-vous cela ?" or in more familiar register "Comment sais-tu ça ?". Use savoir for factual knowledge or information (not for being familiar with a person/place — use connaître for that). Word order and pronoun change with formality: "Comment savez-vous... ?" (formal/plural) vs "Comment sais-tu... ?" (informal/singular).
target_language_example: Comment savez-vous mon adresse ?
native_language_example: How do you know my address?

meaning: 'how do you find' or 'what do you think of' (used to ask someone's opinion about something)
additional_notes: Often followed by an object (e.g., une idée, ce film, ce restaurant) or by 'vous'/'tu' with an adjective: 'Comment trouvez-vous ce film ?' = 'What do you think of this movie?'. Formal word order in questions can be 'Comment trouvez-vous... ?' In informal speech you might hear 'Tu trouves comment... ?' or 'Comment tu trouves... ?'.
target_language_example: Comment trouvez-vous le nouveau café ?
native_language_example: What do you think of the new café?

meaning: how is ... doing?
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's state or how things are going. It is often followed by a name or noun: Comment va Ben ? / Comment va votre fille ? On its own, Comment va ? is a short, casual way of asking how things are going, similar to Comment ça va ?
target_language_example: Comment va ton frère aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: How is your brother doing today?

meaning: 'how are you' (informal, singular)
additional_notes: A casual way to ask someone how they are doing. Use with friends, family, or people you address with 'tu'. For more formal or plural situations use 'comment allez-vous' or 'comment allez-vous tous'. Can be followed by a time phrase (ce matin, ces temps-ci) or a name/term of endearment.
target_language_example: Comment vas-tu aujourd'hui, Paul ?
native_language_example: How are you today, Paul?

meaning: 'how (did) you ... of/with it' — used to ask how someone managed, coped, recovered, or ensured something (formal/polite).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of polite/formal questions using the passé composé inversion: 'Comment vous en êtes-vous ... ?' The pronoun 'en' refers back to a situation, problem, event, or thing mentioned earlier (e.g. a difficulty, illness, doubt). The verb that completes the phrase (assuré, remis(e), sorti) determines the exact nuance: assuré = made sure/ensured; remis/remise = recovered; sorti = got out/managed to get through. Use with usted-style politeness (vous) or change to 'comment t'en es-tu ... ?' for informal 'tu'.
target_language_example: Comment vous en êtes-vous remis après l'accident ?
native_language_example: How did you recover from it after the accident?

meaning: how (so)
additional_notes: Common spoken phrase. Used in two main ways: 1) to ask how something is done or how it ends (e.g. "How does that end?/How so?"); 2) as a reaction meaning "What do you mean?" or "How so?"—often expressing surprise, confusion or asking for clarification. Tone and context determine which meaning is intended. Informal/conversational.
target_language_example: Comment ça, tu ne viens pas ce soir ?
native_language_example: What do you mean, you're not coming tonight?

meaning: 'How are you?' / 'How's it going?'
additional_notes: A casual, common way to ask about someone's well‑being. Can be used with friends, family, or acquaintances; add a name or term of address after a comma (e.g., « Comment ça va, Paul ? »). For more formal situations use « Comment allez‑vous ? ». Pronunciation often contracts to /kɔmɑ̃ sa va/ or informally /sa va/.
target_language_example: Comment ça va, tu as l'air fatigué ?
native_language_example: How are you? You look tired.

meaning: how did you
additional_notes: Usually part of the formal question pattern « comment êtes-vous + past participle ». In these examples, it asks how someone got somewhere or came to be in a situation. The literal words are closer to "how are," so this fragment is not translated literally here, and on its own it is incomplete.
target_language_example: Comment êtes-vous arrivé ici si tôt ?
native_language_example: How did you get here so early?

commença à faire ses devoirs immédiatement

target_language_multi_word_term: commença à faire ses devoirs immédiatement
meaning: started doing her homework immediately
additional_notes: A full phrase showing action begun right away. 'commença à' = 'began to/start to'; 'faire ses devoirs' = 'do one's homework'; 'immédiatement' = 'immediately/right away'. Commonly used to say someone began an activity at once after something else (e.g., after dinner). Sentence structure: [subject] commença à + infinitive + immédiatement (or immédiatement après ...).
target_language_example: Il commença à faire ses devoirs immédiatement après l'école.
native_language_example: He started doing his homework immediately after school.

meaning: 'I understand what you...'; used to say you understand what someone is saying, feeling, or doing (formal/plural 'vous').
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb comprendre (to understand) with 'ce que' (what/that which) and the formal/plural subject 'vous'. In full sentences the verb agrees with the speaker: Je comprends ce que vous dites = I understand what you are saying. Use 'tu' instead of 'vous' in informal contexts: Je comprends ce que tu dis. Common follow-ups include verbs like dites, faites, traversez, voulez dire.
target_language_example: Je comprends ce que vous ressentez en ce moment.
native_language_example: I understand what you are feeling right now.

meaning: 'do you understand what' / 'you understand what...'
additional_notes: Common phrase used to check that someone understands what was just said. Often appears as a question with tu (informal) — "Tu comprends ce que... ?" followed by an explanation or example. Can be followed by verbs like vouloir dire, signifier, ça fait, or je veux dire. Formal version uses 'comprenez ce que' (vous).
target_language_example: Tu comprends ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you understand what I mean?

meaning: 'do you understand what's (happening)?' — part of the question/statement 'tu comprends ce qui se passe' (you understand what is happening).
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common expression 'tu comprends ce qui se passe ?' or 'je comprends ce qui se passe.' Literally: 'you/ I understand what is happening.' Used to check or state understanding of a situation. In spoken French you may hear it shortened or with rising intonation to make it a question. Replace 'comprends' with other persons ('comprenez', 'comprendons') as needed. Informal registers often use 'tu comprends' or 'vous comprenez'.
target_language_example: Tu comprends ce qui se passe ici ?
native_language_example: Do you understand what's happening here?

meaning: I/you/he/she understand(s) your... (literal: 'understand your').
additional_notes: This is the verb 'comprendre' (to understand) combined with the possessive 'ton' (your, masculine singular noun). In examples it appears as part of a sentence like 'Je comprends ton problème' = 'I understand your problem.' Conjugation and subject matter change: 'Je comprends' (I understand), 'Tu comprends' (you understand), 'Il/Elle comprend' (he/she understands). Use 'ta' before feminine nouns (ta sœur), 'tes' for plural nouns (tes idées).
target_language_example: Je comprends ton point de vue.
native_language_example: I understand your point of view.

meaning: 'I understand your...' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Used to express empathy or understanding toward someone's feelings, situation, or problem. 'Comprends' is the first-person singular present of 'comprendre' (I understand). Always followed by a noun or noun phrase introduced by 'votre' (your, formal or plural). For informal singular, use 'ta' instead of 'votre' (e.g. 'je comprends ta frustration').
target_language_example: Je comprends votre inquiétude concernant le délai.
native_language_example: I understand your concern about the deadline.

meaning: bank account
additional_notes: Common phrase for an account at a bank. Used to ask if someone has one (As-tu un compte bancaire ?) or to refer to actions like checking, closing, or referring to 'your bank account'.
target_language_example: J'ai ouvert un compte bancaire la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: I opened a bank account last week.

meaning: a score to settle; an issue/grievance to resolve (often implies confrontation or revenge).
additional_notes: Used when someone has a grievance or unresolved conflict with another person — literally 'an account to settle.' Can imply they plan to confront or get even. Common in sentences like 'J'ai un compte à régler avec toi' (I have a score to settle with you). Tone can be serious or idiomatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a dit qu'il avait un compte à régler avec son ancien associé.
native_language_example: He said he had a score to settle with his former partner.

meaning: 'what matters is' / 'what counts is'.
additional_notes: Used in the fixed structure 'Ce qui compte, c'est ...' to introduce what is important or what really matters. Followed by a noun, pronoun, or a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' or 'qu' (e.g. 'que je t'aime', 'qu'on soit ensemble'). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Ce qui compte, c'est ta santé.
native_language_example: What matters is your health.

meaning: 'count the' (imperative or present tense of compter + definite plural object 'les')
additional_notes: From the verb compter (to count). Depending on context it can be: 1) an imperative command: 'Compte les...' = 'Count the...'; 2) third-person present: 'Il/Elle compte les...' = 'He/She counts the...' or 'is counting the...'. Used with plural definite nouns (les pommes, les jours, les moutons, les billets, les voitures, les voix). Not idiomatic — literal counting is the usual meaning.
target_language_example: Compte les livres sur la table.
native_language_example: Count the books on the table.

meaning: 'to intend to' or 'to plan to' (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: compter + infinitive = to intend/plan to do that action. Common in spoken and written French. Often interchangeable with 'avoir l'intention de' or 'prévoir de', though 'compter' is more straightforward and frequent in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je compte faire mes devoirs ce soir.
native_language_example: I intend to do my homework tonight.

meaning: 'to count for' / 'to be considered as' / 'to matter (toward something)'
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is taken into account, has weight/value, or contributes toward a total. Common constructions: compter pour + noun/number (e.g. ça compte pour trois), compter pour + dans/chez + noun (e.g. Il compte pour l'équipe), or compter pour + beaucoup/peu. Can be used in negative or reflexive contexts (e.g. ça ne compte pas pour moi).
target_language_example: Ses efforts comptent pour beaucoup dans notre succès.
native_language_example: His efforts count for a lot in our success.

meaning: to count on
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something can be depended on. Followed by a person or thing. Common in everyday speech. Equivalent to English 'count on' (trust/rely).
target_language_example: Tu peux toujours compter sur moi.
native_language_example: You can always count on me.

meaning: self-confidence; confidence in oneself.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a person's belief in their own abilities. Commonly appears with verbs like avoir, manquer de, construire (build), développer (develop). Can be singular and uncountable in French.
target_language_example: Il a beaucoup de confiance en soi quand il parle en public.
native_language_example: He has a lot of self-confidence when he speaks in public.

meaning: press conference (a meeting where officials answer journalists' questions).
additional_notes: Used for formal public announcements or Q&A with the media. Common verbs: 'tenir une conférence de presse' (to hold/give a press conference), 'donner une conférence de presse' (to give a press conference).
target_language_example: Le maire tiendra une conférence de presse cet après-midi.
native_language_example: The mayor will hold a press conference this afternoon.

meaning: 'I don't know this...' (followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the colloquial negative form of 'Je ne connais pas cette ...' used to say you are not familiar with a person, thing, idea or expression. 'Connais' is the verb connaître (to know), and 'cette' is the feminine demonstrative adjective (this/that). Use with feminine nouns (cette dame, cette danse, cette expression, cette fille). In more formal speech you might include the subject pronoun and full negation: 'Je ne connais pas cette...'.
target_language_example: Je ne connais pas cette chanson.
native_language_example: I don't know this song.

meaning: to know nothing about (something); to be clueless about
additional_notes: Informal spoken structure: often appears in the phrase 'je n'y connais rien' or 'je ne connais rien à...' (with the full negative). In casual speech, the 'ne' is frequently dropped: 'je connais rien à la politique'. Use 'connaître' + 'à' + noun to say you don't understand or have no experience with a subject.
target_language_example: Je ne connais rien à l'informatique.
native_language_example: I know nothing about computers.

meaning: I know your ... (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: This is the verb connaître (to know) conjugated for 'je' (je connais) followed directly by the possessive 'ton' (your, masculine singular noun).
