target_language_example: Il y avait une file d'attente de fou devant le concert.
native_language_example: There was a crazy line in front of the concert.

meaning: 'of fruit' or used to indicate a fruit-based (fruit) ingredient or flavor — as in 'jus de fruit' = fruit juice.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to show what something is made of or flavored with (noun + de + fruit). Common in food/drink phrases (un jus de fruit, une salade de fruit). In plural contexts you may see 'jus de fruits' but 'jus de fruit' (singular) is also widely used in everyday speech. Not a standalone phrase — it combines with another noun.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un verre de jus de fruit, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a glass of fruit juice, please.

meaning: on duty; available outside normal hours (e.g. emergency/after-hours).
additional_notes: Used to indicate someone or a service is assigned to be available (often for emergencies) outside usual hours. Common with professions (médecin de garde, pharmacie de garde, infirmier de garde). Can refer to a scheduled shift (être de garde = be on duty).
target_language_example: Le médecin de garde arrive à minuit.
native_language_example: The doctor on duty arrives at midnight.

meaning: to keep the (something) / to keep (it) — part of the infinitive construction 'garder' with a definite article.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the preposition 'de' used after verbs that take an infinitive (e.g., 'essayer de', 'juré de', 'conseillé de') + the verb 'garder' (to keep) + the definite article 'le' (the/it). It often appears before a noun like 'secret' or an abstract noun like 'moral' (mood). Translate depending on context: 'to keep (the secret)', 'to keep up (one's spirits)'. The exact object follows 'le' (or may be 'la', 'les', 'l’' depending on gender/number).
target_language_example: Il a promis de garder le secret.
native_language_example: He promised to keep the secret.

meaning: 'people' (used after expressions of quantity — literally "of people" + 'are')
additional_notes: This sequence appears when talking about how many people (de gens) followed by a verb ('sont' = 'are' or 'were'). Common with quantity expressions (des tas de, pas mal de, une poignée de, personne ne). Note that 'gens' is plural and normally used with 'les/quelques/etc.' or after quantities; the verb agrees with 'gens' (sont/étaient). In spoken/written French you will more often see the quantity phrase plus 'de gens' (e.g. 'beaucoup de gens sont...').
target_language_example: Beaucoup de gens sont arrivés en retard.
native_language_example: Many people arrived late.

meaning: by day; during the daytime.
additional_notes: Used to contrast daytime with nighttime (de nuit). Often appears in expressions like 'de jour comme de nuit' (day and night) or 'de jour ou de nuit' (by day or by night). Can describe when something happens or is visible (e.g., 'visible de jour').
target_language_example: Le parc est calme de jour.
native_language_example: The park is quiet by day.

meaning: day by day; gradually, from one day to the next
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes progressively over successive days (better or worse). Equivalent to "day after day" or "more and more" in English. Often followed by comparative adjectives (plus chaud, plus mal) or verbs like empirer, croître.
target_language_example: Les fleurs semblent se faner de jour en jour.
native_language_example: The flowers seem to be wilting day by day.

meaning: barely; by a narrow margin; just in time.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened with very little room to spare (positive or negative). Often placed after the verb or phrase it modifies: e.g. 'échapper de justesse', 'approuvé de justesse'. Can express narrowly avoiding danger, narrowly succeeding, or a close vote/result.
target_language_example: J'ai attrapé le train de justesse.
native_language_example: I barely caught the train.

meaning: on the other side of / across from
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is located on the opposite side of something else (a street, a river, a wall, etc.). Can be followed by a noun or a place (de l'autre côté de la rue, de l'autre côté du pont). Contracts with le/les (de l'autre côté du, de l'autre côté des).
target_language_example: Le café est de l'autre côté de la rue.
native_language_example: The café is on the other side of the street.

meaning: to ... it
additional_notes: In these examples, l' is the direct object pronoun le/la before a vowel or silent h, meaning 'him,' 'her,' or 'it.' After de, it often appears before an infinitive: de l'entendre, de l'appeler, de l'avoir vu. In English, it may be translated directly ('to call him') or more naturally as 'to hear that' / 'to learn that' depending on context.
target_language_example: Je suis surpris de l'apprendre.
native_language_example: I'm surprised to hear that.

meaning: some / any
additional_notes: Used before feminine singular nouns. It can be the partitive article, meaning "some" or "any" with uncountable things (for example, de la soupe, de la patience), or it can be de + la, meaning "of the" or "from the." In expressions like jouer de la batterie and faire de la randonnée, English often does not translate it word for word.
target_language_example: Je voudrais de la soupe, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like some soup, please.

meaning: of good / some good (feminine) — often 'good' quality; in slang can mean 'good (strong) weed'.
additional_notes: Literally 'of the good' or 'some good' used before a feminine noun: e.g. de la bonne nourriture = some good food. In neutral contexts it simply indicates good quality. In informal/slang contexts (especially with herbe, stuff, or when used alone: 'Tu fumes de la bonne?') it refers to high-quality/strong cannabis.
target_language_example: Tu veux goûter de la bonne nourriture ?
native_language_example: Do you want to try some good food?

meaning: on behalf of; from (someone); as a message from someone.
additional_notes: Used to indicate who is sending something (a message, thanks, greetings) or who is represented. Common in introductions: 'De la part de X?' = 'Who is calling/visiting?' Can mean 'on behalf of' (formal) or 'from' (as a message).
target_language_example: Je téléphone de la part de Marie pour confirmer le rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I'm calling on behalf of Marie to confirm the appointment.

meaning: of the room of / from the room of (part of a phrase indicating possession or location)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone expression; it's a fragment used in longer phrases like "la porte de la salle de classe" (the door of the classroom) or "le bruit de la salle de réunion" (the noise from the meeting room). "De la" is the contraction of preposition + definite article (de + la). Use it before a feminine singular noun. If the following noun begins with a vowel or mute h, use "de l'"; for masculine singular use "du"; for plural use "des."
target_language_example: La porte de la salle de classe est fermée.
native_language_example: The classroom door is closed.

meaning: in that way / like that / of that kind
additional_notes: Used to describe manner or kind—how something is done or the type of thing. Can mean 'in that way' (manner) or 'of that sort/kind' (category). Common in formal and neutral contexts. Often interchangeable with 'comme ça' (informal) or 'de cette façon'. 'Rien de la sorte' = 'nothing of the sort.'
target_language_example: Ne parle pas de la sorte à ton frère.
native_language_example: Don't speak to your brother like that.

meaning: from head to toe; completely, all over.
additional_notes: Used to describe something affecting the whole body (wet, dirty, dressed) or a thorough look/inspection (to look someone over from head to toe). Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Elle était trempée de la tête aux pieds après la pluie.
native_language_example: She was soaked from head to toe after the rain.

meaning: a fragment meaning 'to wash the' (feminine noun follows), not a complete fixed phrase
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase. It's the combination of the preposition 'de' + the infinitive 'laver' + the feminine definite article 'la'. It appears as part of longer sentences like 'arrêter de laver la voiture' (to stop washing the car) or 'le seau de laver la vaisselle' (not idiomatic). In correct French you would usually see either 'de laver' (to wash) after verbs that require 'de' (e.g., 'arrêter de laver') or 'laver la...' directly followed by a feminine noun (e.g., 'laver la voiture'). Do not use 'de laver la' by itself.
target_language_example: Il a arrêté de laver la fenêtre parce qu'il était fatigué.
native_language_example: He stopped washing the window because he was tired.

meaning: of (an) airline / line (used in 'pilote de ligne' = airline pilot); also used in the phrase 'fin de ligne' = end of the line.
additional_notes: Literal meaning depends on context: 'ligne' can mean 'line' or 'route'. In occupations like 'pilote de ligne' it means 'airline' or 'line' (commercial airline pilot). In expressions like 'fin de ligne' it means 'end of the line' (literal or figurative). 'de ligne' is a prepositional phrase used to link a noun to 'ligne'.
target_language_example: Il travaille comme pilote de ligne depuis dix ans.
native_language_example: He has worked as an airline pilot for ten years.

meaning: a sequence meaning 'to read this' (de + infinitive + demonstrative); not a fixed phrase on its own
additional_notes: This is not an idiom but a common grammatical combination: 'de' (of/to) + infinitive verb 'lire' (to read) + demonstrative adjective 'cette' (this, feminine). It appears inside larger sentences, for example when one verb requires 'de' before another infinitive (e.g. 'essayer de lire cette lettre' = 'try to read this letter') or after certain nouns/expressions ('la possibilité de lire cette page' = 'the possibility of reading this page'). You will rarely use 'de lire cette' standing alone; you need the rest of the noun phrase after 'cette' (e.g. 'cette lettre', 'cette page').
target_language_example: J'essaie de lire cette lettre, mais je ne comprends pas tout.
native_language_example: I'm trying to read this letter, but I don't understand everything.

meaning: from afar; by far (when comparing).
additional_notes: Common phrase with two main uses: 1) spatial: 'from a distance' or 'seen from far away' (e.g. De loin, on voit la montagne). 2) emphatic/comparative: 'by far' to stress a superlative (e.g. Il est de loin le meilleur). Context tells which meaning applies. Can also be used alone as a short reply meaning 'from far away' or 'by far.'
target_language_example: Vu de loin, la maison paraît petite, mais de près elle est énorme.
native_language_example: Seen from afar, the house looks small, but up close it is huge.

meaning: by far the (best/most/etc.)
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something or someone is clearly superior or much more so than others. Usually followed by an adjective or noun with a superlative (meilleur, plus grand, etc.). Common structure: « de loin le/la/les + [superlative or noun phrase] ». Tone is neutral and frequently used in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: C'est de loin le film le plus intéressant que j'ai vu cette année.
native_language_example: It's by far the most interesting film I've seen this year.

meaning: luxury; high-end; of superior quality.
additional_notes: Used after a noun (or alone) to indicate something luxurious, expensive, or high-quality. Common with places (hôtel de luxe), goods (voiture de luxe), or tastes (goûts de luxe). Can be used on its own as an adjective phrase meaning "luxurious" or "fancy."
target_language_example: Ils ont réservé une chambre dans un hôtel de luxe.
native_language_example: They booked a room in a luxury hotel.

meaning: 'awesome' / 'amazing' (informal slang expressing strong positive surprise)
additional_notes: Colloquial/slang expression used after a noun or adjective to intensify praise. Equivalent to 'really crazy/great' in English. Often used in spoken French and among young people: e.g. 'C'est beau de malade' or 'Une soirée de malade'. Tone is enthusiastic; not appropriate for formal contexts.
target_language_example: Cette soirée était de malade !
native_language_example: That party was amazing!

meaning: 'of misfortune' / 'unlucky' (expresses bad luck or misfortune)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to emphasize that something is unlucky or brings misfortune (e.g. 'jour de malheur' = unlucky day). Can describe events, people, situations or a portion ('ta part de malheur' = your share of misfortune). Tone is generally neutral/serious, not slang.
target_language_example: C'était un soir de malheur pour toute la famille.
native_language_example: It was an evening of misfortune for the whole family.

meaning: in order to / so that (expresses purpose or intention).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the purpose of an action. Can be followed by an infinitive (de manière à + infinitive) or by 'ce que'/'ce qu'' + subjunctive in some contexts (de manière à ce que + subjunctive). Formal/common in writing and speech. Equivalent to 'afin de', 'pour'.
target_language_example: Il parle doucement de manière à ne pas réveiller le bébé.
native_language_example: He speaks softly so as not to wake the baby.

meaning: a vulgar intensifier meaning 'fucking' or 'damn' (expresses contempt toward the noun it follows).
additional_notes: Informal and vulgar. Placed after a noun to insult it or show strong negative emotion about the person/thing (e.g., 'enflure de merde' = 'fucking bastard' / 'shitty bastard'). Can be added after exclamations for emphasis ('Bon Diable de merde!' — strong curse). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Sale menteur de merde !
native_language_example: You filthy lying bastard!

meaning: 'my balls' used as a vulgar intensifier expressing contempt or dismissal (English equivalents: 'my ass', 'yeah right')
additional_notes: Very vulgar. Attaches after a noun or phrase to mock, belittle, or show disbelief/anger about what was said (e.g. 'X de mes couilles' ≈ 'X my ass'). Common in spoken/informal contexts among people who use strong profanity; avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Tu es un expert, de mes couilles !
native_language_example: You're an expert, my ass!

meaning: an ironic or dismissive interjection like 'yeah, right' / 'as if' / 'my foot' used to express disbelief or contempt.
additional_notes: Colloquial and somewhat rude; used after a noun or phrase to show scorn, sarcasm or to mock what was just said. Not literal — it doesn't mean 'of my two'. Tone and context convey the insult. Avoid in formal situations.
target_language_example: Tu vas devenir médecin, de mes deux !
native_language_example: You’re going to become a doctor, yeah right!

meaning: 'better and better' / 'improving more and more'.
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, person, or thing is progressively improving over time. Can be used alone as a short reaction (like 'even better' or 'getting better'). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Après la pause, tout va de mieux en mieux.
native_language_example: After the break, everything is getting better and better.

meaning: appropriate, fitting, or advisable in a given situation
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say that something is customary, suitable, or expected in the circumstances (often with abstract nouns like 'solidarité', 'remerciements', 'égalité'). Common in formal or neutral registers. Structure: [noun] + est/sont + de mise or quelque chose serait de mise.
target_language_example: Un peu de prudence serait de mise aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: A bit of caution would be appropriate today.

meaning: less and less; gradually decreasing over time.
additional_notes: Used to describe a progressive decline in quantity, frequency, intensity, or degree. Placed after a verb (Il dort de moins en moins) or before an adjective/adverb (de moins en moins nombreux / vite). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je vois mes amis de moins en moins.
native_language_example: I see my friends less and less.

meaning: from memory; by memory; relating to memory (depending on context).
additional_notes:
Common uses:
- 'de mémoire' alone or after a verb means 'from memory' or 'by heart' (e.g. drawing, reciting without looking). 
- In phrases about 'trous de mémoire' or 'perte de mémoire' it relates to memory (memory lapses, memory loss). 
Context decides translation: literal 'from memory' for actions done without reference; when used in medical/psychological contexts it links to 'memory' (e.g. memory loss).
target_language_example: Il a récité le poème de mémoire.
native_language_example: He recited the poem from memory.

meaning: 'in the same way', 'likewise', or 'also'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate similarity or to suggest doing the same action. Can mean 'likewise' when responding (e.g., 'Same to you') or 'in the same manner' when comparing actions. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Si tu m'aides, je ferai de même pour toi.
native_language_example: If you help me, I'll do the same for you.

meaning: 'by birth' / 'from birth' (indicates something present or true since the time of birth)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say that the quality, condition, place, or thing relates to someone's birth (e.g., lieu de naissance = place of birth; aveugle de naissance = blind from birth). Common in descriptions (medical, legal, biographical). Not idiomatic — literal and transparent.
target_language_example: Il est citoyen français de naissance.
native_language_example: He is a French citizen by birth.

meaning: to not say it / to not tell it
additional_notes: This phrase is the infinitive construction with negation: de + ne + le + dire. It appears after verbs like promettre, devoir, or se souvenir (e.g. promettre de ne le dire à personne). 'Le' refers to 'it' (a secret or piece of information). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: promettre de ne le dire → promettre de le dire (with ne omitted) is common but less formal; however dropping 'ne' changes meaning if not careful. The full negative construction is 'ne ... pas/plus/etc.' here only 'ne' plus the object pronoun expresses 'not to tell it'.
target_language_example: Il a juré de ne le dire à personne.
native_language_example: He swore not to tell it to anyone.

meaning: nowadays; these days; in the present time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the present era or current habits/conditions, often to contrast with the past. Common in both formal and neutral registers. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: De nos jours, beaucoup de gens travaillent à distance.
native_language_example: Nowadays, many people work remotely.

meaning: again
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens another time or is restored to a previous state. Slightly more formal/neutral than 'encore' in some contexts; interchangeable with 'à nouveau' in many cases. Follows verb or adjective phrases (e.g., 'être de nouveau', 'arriver de nouveau').
target_language_example: Il est de nouveau heureux.
native_language_example: He is happy again.

meaning: at night / nighttime (used to describe something happening or used during the night).
additional_notes: Used to indicate night-time occurrence or a night-related object. When describing jobs or activities, 'de nuit' means 'night' as in night shift (e.g., 'travaille de nuit' = works at night). In compounds like 'table de nuit' it means an object related to the bedroom/night (a bedside table). Word order: usually follows the noun ('équipe de nuit', 'service de nuit', 'lampe de nuit').
target_language_example: Elle fait des gardes de nuit à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: She does night shifts at the hospital.

meaning: from nowhere; appearing or coming from no recognizable place or origin
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something appears suddenly with no clear origin, or to describe a very remote/isolated place (le centre de nulle part). Common in narratives: 'il est sorti de nulle part' = he appeared out of nowhere. Can be literal (remote location) or figurative (ideas, people).
target_language_example: Une voiture est arrivée de nulle part.
native_language_example: A car came out of nowhere.

meaning: of pairs; used to count or refer to pairs of items (e.g., shoes, socks).
additional_notes: Used after an expression of quantity (combien de, trop de, etc.) to specify 'pairs' as the unit. Common with items that naturally come in pairs (chaussures, chaussettes, gants). Grammar: in questions use 'combien de paires de X' or 'de combien de paires de X' (both are correct).
target_language_example: J'ai trois de paires de chaussettes dans mon tiroir.
native_language_example: I have three pairs of socks in my drawer.

meaning: 'please' (polite/formal request: 'I beg/ask you')
additional_notes: Used to make polite or formal requests or commands. Often follows an imperative or is included in phrases like 'Arrêtez de parler, je vous prie' (Please stop talking). Tone is formal/polite; common in written or polite spoken French. Not used for casual requests with friends—use 's'il te plaît' instead.
target_language_example: Arrêtez de parler, je vous prie.
native_language_example: Please stop talking.

meaning: of (one's) word; trustworthy—keeps promises.
additional_notes: Used after nouns like "homme" or "femme" to say someone keeps their word (reliable, trustworthy). Common fixed expression: "être un homme de parole" = to be a man of one's word / to be trustworthy. Not used literally as 'of speech'.
target_language_example: Elle est une femme de parole : quand elle promet quelque chose, elle le fait.
native_language_example: She is a woman of her word: when she promises something, she does it.

meaning: passing through; just visiting temporarily.
additional_notes: Used to say you are only staying briefly or are temporarily at a place (e.g., traveling, on a short trip, at someone's home or at work for a short time). Common in phrases like 'je suis de passage' (I'm just passing through/visiting). Not formal or slang—neutral everyday expression.
target_language_example: Je suis de passage en ville pour deux jours.
native_language_example: I'm just passing through town for two days.

meaning: by a small margin; barely; narrowly.
additional_notes: Used to say something almost happened or was narrowly avoided. Often follows verbs like 'échapper', 'manquer', or the impersonal expression 'il s'en est fallu de peu'. Translates to 'by a little', 'by a narrow margin', 'barely'.
target_language_example: J'ai raté le bus de peu.
native_language_example: I missed the bus by a little / I barely missed the bus.

meaning: worse and worse; getting progressively worse.
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, condition, or behavior that is deteriorating over time. Equivalent to English 'worse and worse' or 'going from bad to worse.' Common in everyday and formal contexts.
target_language_example: Depuis la panne, tout va de pire en pire.
native_language_example: Since the breakdown, everything is getting worse and worse.

meaning: literally 'of pieces of' — a word sequence that appears when the noun pièces (pieces/coins/parts/rooms) is linked to a following noun introduced by de (e.g. pièces de monnaie, pièces de rechange). It expresses possession or specification (pieces of X).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom but a compositional sequence: 'pièces' followed by 'de' + noun. Meaning of pièces depends on context (coins, spare parts, rooms, plays, etc.). Articles/pluralization follow normal French (une pièce de, des pièces de). In English it often becomes 'pieces/coins/parts of X' or 'X pieces/parts'.
target_language_example: Combien de pièces de monnaie as-tu dans ta collection de pièces de monnaie ?
native_language_example: How many coins do you have in your coin collection?

meaning: voluntarily; of one's own free will
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something willingly, without being forced or obliged. Often appears in formal or neutral registers (legal, administrative, spoken French). Can modify verbs: e.g. 'il a quitté son poste de plein gré' = he left voluntarily.
target_language_example: Elle a accepté l'offre de plein gré.
native_language_example: She accepted the offer voluntarily.

meaning: more
additional_notes: Often used after a quantity, noun, or question word to mean an additional amount: une heure de plus = "one more hour", quelques jours de plus = "a few more days", que dire de plus ? = "what more is there to say?" It does not translate literally word-for-word into natural English.
target_language_example: Je voudrais une minute de plus.
native_language_example: I'd like one more minute.

meaning: more and more
additional_notes: Used to describe a gradual increase over time or becoming more of a quality/degree. Often placed before adjectives, adverbs, verbs (with surrounding context) or noun phrases. Can be repeated with comparatives (e.g., « de plus en plus chaud », « de plus en plus difficile »).
target_language_example: Il devient de plus en plus patient chaque année.
native_language_example: He is becoming more and more patient every year.

meaning: 'pocket' or 'pocket-sized'; also 'pocket money' when used as 'argent de poche'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean small enough to fit in a pocket (édition de poche = paperback/pocket edition; lampe de poche = flashlight/torch). When paired with 'argent' (argent de poche) it means allowance/pocket money. Word order is noun + de poche. Context determines whether it refers to size or to money.
target_language_example: Il a acheté une édition de poche du roman.
native_language_example: He bought a pocket edition of the novel.

meaning: of weight; (figuratively) of importance or influence
additional_notes: Used literally to talk about physical weight (perdre du poids = lose weight; une unité de poids = unit of weight). Used figuratively in expressions like "manquer de poids" or "avoir du poids" to mean lacking or having influence/importance (e.g. "son argument manque de poids" = his argument lacks weight/force). Often appears after a quantity (un peu de poids, beaucoup de poids) or after verbs like perdre, prendre.
target_language_example: Son opinion a beaucoup de poids dans l'entreprise.
native_language_example: His opinion carries a lot of weight in the company.

meaning: 'state-of-the-art' / 'peak' (depending on context)
additional_notes: Used in two main senses: 1) 'de pointe' after a noun = 'state-of-the-art', 'cutting-edge' (e.g. technologie de pointe). 2) In the fixed expression 'heure(s) de pointe' it means 'peak (hour)', 'rush hour' (traffic). Placement: usually follows the noun. Formality: neutral.
target_language_example: La société utilise des équipements de pointe.
native_language_example: The company uses state-of-the-art equipment.

meaning: part of the phrase 'points de suture' meaning 'stitches' (lit. 'of points of'); on its own it's not a complete expression but appears within constructions like 'avoir besoin de points de suture'
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase; appears as the middle of 'avoir besoin de points de suture' or 'avoir X points de suture'. Use with verbs such as 'avoir', 'avoir besoin de', 'recevoir', 'mettre' (mettre des points de suture). Plural 'points de suture' is common. Agreement: number precedes 'points' (e.g. 'trois points de suture').
target_language_example: J'ai besoin de points de suture.
native_language_example: I need stitches.

meaning: 'first-year' (describing someone in their first year) or 'top-quality' in informal exclamation
additional_notes: Most commonly used as part of the phrase 'de première année' (first-year student). Alone, 'de première' often appears in shortened descriptions (e.g. 'un étudiant de première') to mean 'a first-year'. In informal speech or exclamations (e.g. 'Quel/Quand il y a un chien de première !'), it can emphasize something remarkable or top-quality; this usage is colloquial and context-dependent. When used with a field (piano, année, classe), it qualifies the level/grade as first.
target_language_example: Elle est en histoire, étudiante de première année.
native_language_example: She is in history, a first-year student.

meaning: closely; up close; closely watched/followed.
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical proximity (up close) or figurative closeness (closely following, closely monitoring). Common with verbs like voir (voir de près = see up close), suivre (suivre de près = follow closely), surveiller (surveiller de près = monitor closely).
target_language_example: Les médecins ont surveillé le patient de près.
native_language_example: The doctors monitored the patient closely.

meaning: preferably; if possible; rather.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a preference or the preferred option. Can stand alone as an answer (meaning 'preferably' or 'ideally'). Often followed by the preferred item or circumstance (e.g., 'de préférence + noun' or 'de préférence + verb phrase').
target_language_example: Je prendrai du thé, de préférence sans sucre.
native_language_example: I'll have tea, preferably without sugar.

meaning: 'by what right' / 'who do you think you are?'.
additional_notes: Used to challenge someone's authority or behavior — often confrontational. Can be literal (asking on what legal or moral basis) or rhetorical (expressing indignation). Common in formal and informal contexts; tone determines politeness.
target_language_example: De quel droit parlez-vous ainsi à ma sœur ?
native_language_example: By what right do you speak to my sister like that?

meaning: of/from someone (used before an adjective or past participle that begins with a vowel sound)
additional_notes: This is a contracted form used when saying something belongs to or is characteristic of someone, and the next word begins with a vowel or mute 'h'. It appears in constructions like « de quelqu'un d'important » (of someone important) or « de quelqu'un d'heureux » (of someone happy). In English it corresponds to 'of someone' or 'from someone' followed by an adjective or participle. Remember the contraction d' replaces de before a vowel sound.
target_language_example: C'est l'avis de quelqu'un d'intelligent.
native_language_example: It's the opinion of someone intelligent.

meaning: 'who it is about' or 'whom it concerns' (used to ask or say who is meant/being referred to).
additional_notes: Short for 'de qui il s'agit'. Common in questions and statements to ask/confirm the identity of a person previously mentioned or implied. Structure: 'savoir/devoir/être + de qui il s'agit'. In spoken French the full form is 'de qui il s'agit' (often contracted in speech). Use with 'sais-tu', 'savez-vous', 'je sais', etc.
target_language_example: Tu sais de qui il s'agit ?
native_language_example: Do you know who it is about?

meaning: of what
additional_notes: Literally "of what." After verbs or adjectives followed by de, English often says "what ... about/of?" instead: De quoi parlez-vous ? = What are you talking about? Before an infinitive, it often means "something to" or "enough to" do something: de quoi manger, de quoi vivre.
target_language_example: Tu as de quoi écrire ?
native_language_example: Do you have something to write with?

meaning: 'what is it about' / 'what is this concerning'.
additional_notes: Usually appears in the full question form 'De quoi s'agit-il ?' meaning 'What is this about?' or 'What is the matter?' Used to ask for the subject or nature of something. Formal/neutral register. Can be followed by words like 'vraiment', 'au juste', or 'alors' for emphasis.
target_language_example: De quoi s'agit-il exactement dans ce dossier ?
native_language_example: What is this file about exactly?

meaning: 'to watch the' (part of the infinitive phrase 'de regarder la télévision' — 'to watch the television').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the start of an infinitive clause introduced by 'de' followed by the verb 'regarder' and the feminine definite article 'la' (usually before 'télévision' or 'télé'). Commonly appears in constructions like 'avant de regarder la télévision', 'préférer ... que de regarder la télé', or as part of a noun phrase 'un plaisir est de regarder la télé'.
target_language_example: Avant de regarder la télévision, éteins ton téléphone.
native_language_example: Before watching the television, turn off your phone.

meaning: back
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has come back or returned. Commonly follows the subject (e.g., "Il est de retour") or appears after a name. Can be used for people, objects, or services (e.g., "Le site est de retour").
target_language_example: Je suis de retour.
native_language_example: I'm back.

meaning: of retirement; relating to retirement (e.g., 'pension de retraite' = retirement pension)
additional_notes: A prepositional phrase composed of 'de' + 'retraite'. Often appears after a noun to specify that something is related to retirement (e.g., 'pension de retraite', 'âge de retraite', 'fonds de retraite'). Use depends on the noun it modifies. Not used alone as a full noun phrase without context.
target_language_example: Il a pris sa pension de retraite l'année dernière.
native_language_example: He took his retirement pension last year.

meaning: 'you're welcome' (or literally 'of nothing').
additional_notes: Most commonly used as a polite reply to 'merci' to mean 'you're welcome.' It can also appear in negative constructions with verbs like 'se souvenir' or 'douter' to mean 'anything' or 'nothing' (e.g. 'ne ... de rien' = 'not ... anything/remember nothing'). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: — Merci pour ton aide. — De rien !
native_language_example: — Thanks for your help. — You're welcome!

meaning: required, customary, expected (socially or officially).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is customary, considered necessary, or required in a given situation (e.g., a polite behavior, social norm, or official policy). Often appears in expressions like "c'est de rigueur" or "être de rigueur." Not to be confused with "rigueur" alone meaning strictness or rigor.
target_language_example: Dans ce restaurant, une tenue correcte est de rigueur.
native_language_example: In this restaurant, proper dress is required.

meaning: 'as a rule', 'normally', 'usually'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a general rule or usual situation. Often appears in phrases like "en règle générale" or alone after a statement: "De règle, ..." is less common in everyday spoken French than "en général" but is acceptable in written or formal contexts. Can be followed by a clause describing the usual outcome.
target_language_example: De règle, les trains arrivent à l'heure le matin.
native_language_example: As a rule, the trains arrive on time in the morning.

meaning: 'dream' as an adjective: fantastic, perfect, ideal
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as wonderful, ideal, or like a dream (e.g., un corps de rêve = a dream body; un couple de rêve = an ideal couple). Common in informal and neutral registers. Translate depending on context: 'dream', 'dreamlike', 'fantastic', 'ideal'.
target_language_example: Ils ont trouvé une maison de rêve près de la plage.
native_language_example: They found a dream house near the beach.

meaning: backup / emergency (used to describe something kept or used in case of failure or danger).
additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to indicate an emergency or spare version (plan de secours = backup plan; clé de secours = spare key; hélicoptères de secours = rescue helicopters). Can be short as 'secours' in some contexts (aller aux secours = go to help/rescue).
target_language_example: J'ai une copie de secours de tous mes fichiers.
native_language_example: I have a backup copy of all my files.

meaning: 'on duty' / 'service-related' / 'service'
additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something related to work duty, service, or support. Context determines exact sense: 'être de service' = to be on duty; 'porte de service' = service/utility door; 'numéros de service' = service phone numbers (customer service, emergency lines); 'carte de service' could mean an ID or a work/service card. Not a standalone verb phrase — it modifies a noun.
target_language_example: Ce soir, je suis de service à l'hôpital.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm on duty at the hospital.

meaning: 'of (a) situation' — indicates something related to or belonging to a situation.
additional_notes: Commonly used after nouns like 'genre', 'type', 'rapport' to describe the situation being referred to (e.g., 'ce genre de situation' = 'this kind of situation'). Also appears in set phrases like 'rapport de situation' (situation report). Grammar: 'de' links the preceding noun to 'situation' (possession/relationship).
target_language_example: Fais attention pour éviter ce genre de situation.
native_language_example: Be careful to avoid this kind of situation.

meaning: so that / in such a way that (expresses purpose or result)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose or result clause. Followed by an infinitive (de sorte de + infinitive) to express purpose, or followed by que + subjunctive/indicative (de sorte que) to express result. In everyday speech 'pour que' is more common for purpose; 'de sorte de' is slightly more formal and often written.
target_language_example: Il a modifié le texte de sorte de clarifier l'idée.
native_language_example: He modified the text so as to clarify the idea.

meaning: 'so that' / 'in such a way that' (introduces a result or purpose).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a result (so that/as a result) or a purpose (so that/to ensure). Can be followed by indicative (for result/fact) or subjunctive (for purpose/possibility) depending on nuance. Common in formal and neutral registers; interchangeable with 'pour que' for purpose but 'pour que' always takes the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Venez tôt, de sorte que nous puissions en parler tranquillement.
native_language_example: Come early so that we can talk about it calmly.

meaning: 'from a reliable source' or 'reliably/surely sourced'.
additional_notes: Used to say information comes from someone or somewhere trustworthy. Common in news, conversations, and reports. Often follows verbs like savoir, tenir, or apprendre: e.g. « Je sais / On tient de source sûre ». Can be used to signal confidence but not absolute proof.
target_language_example: On tient de source sûre que la réunion est annulée.
native_language_example: We have reliable information that the meeting is canceled.

meaning: right away
additional_notes: Has two common uses: 1) meaning "right away/at once" to ask for immediate action (Je m'en occupe de suite = I'll take care of it right away). 2) meaning "consecutively/in a row" when used with a time expression (cinq jours de suite = five days in a row). Context tells which meaning applies. Informal tone is fine in spoken requests.
target_language_example: Viens ici de suite !
native_language_example: Come here right away!

meaning: 'to stay' (used after verbs like prévoir, compter, espérer — infinitive form with 'de').
additional_notes: This is the infinitive 'séjourner' preceded by the particle 'de' because it follows certain verbs (e.g. prévoir de, décider de, compter de) or expressions that require 'de' before another verb. It means to stay (somewhere) for a period of time. In questions about duration or location it commonly appears after verbs like prévoir/prévoirz/compter. Use without 'de' after other verbs that take a different connector (e.g. 'vouloir séjourner', 'aimer séjourner' — no 'de').
target_language_example: Nous prévoyons de séjourner deux semaines à Paris.
native_language_example: We plan to stay two weeks in Paris.

meaning: of/at the table; used to indicate possession, association, or position related to a table.
additional_notes: Commonly follows a noun to show relation to a table (e.g., 'serviette de table' = table napkin). Also appears in expressions about being at the table or leaving the table ('se lever de table'). Can mean 'of the table' (possession) or 'from the table' (position/association) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ils ont laissé leurs assiettes sur la table, pas de table à débarrasser ?
native_language_example: They left their plates on the table, no table to clear?

meaning: 'of size' / 'big/significant' or idiomatically 'up to the task' (able/able to compete).
additional_notes: Has both literal and idiomatic uses. Literally follows a noun or adjective to describe physical size (e.g., de taille moyenne = of medium size). Idiomatically, used in negative or affirmative constructions to mean 'able' or 'up to the task' (ne pas être de taille = not good/strong enough; être de taille can imply being a worthy opponent or of considerable importance: une surprise de taille = a major surprise). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Il n'est pas de taille pour ce poste.
native_language_example: He is not up to the job.

meaning: 'how long' (used in questions about duration, embedded in inversion with 'il/elle/on').
additional_notes: This sequence appears inside questions formed with inversion and 'combien' to ask about duration: 'Combien de temps a-t-il ... ?' The '-t-' is an inserted liaison consonant used when verb ends with a vowel and followed by 'il' (e.g. 'a' + 'il' → 'a-t-il') for pronunciation and grammar; it doesn't change meaning. You can also ask 'Combien de temps est-ce qu'il...' or 'Depuis combien de temps...' for similar senses. 'Pour combien de temps...' asks 'for how long' (planned or expected duration).
target_language_example: Combien de temps a-t-il étudié au Canada ?
native_language_example: How long did he study in Canada?

meaning: how much time it takes / how long it takes
additional_notes: This looks like a non-standard or slightly mixed phrasing. The usual French expressions are « combien de temps cela prend » or « combien de temps ça prend » (informal) to ask how long something will take. Use « ça » in speech; use « cela » or « cela prend » in more formal contexts. Word order matters: include 'combien' to form a proper question.
target_language_example: Combien de temps cela prend pour finir le projet ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to finish the project?

meaning: from time to time
additional_notes: Used to indicate something happens at irregular, infrequent intervals. Interchangeable with 'parfois' or 'occasionnellement' in many contexts. Can appear at the start, middle or end of a sentence: 'De temps en temps, ...', '... fait ça de temps en temps.'
target_language_example: Je vais au cinéma de temps en temps.
native_language_example: I go to the cinema from time to time.

meaning: '(amount) of time that you' — part of expressions about duration (often appears as "autant de temps que tu veux" or in questions like "ça fait combien de temps que tu...?")
additional_notes: This fragment appears in duration expressions. Common patterns: "autant de temps que tu veux" (as much time as you want) and "Ça fait combien de temps que tu... ?" (How long have you been...?). In spoken French the full phrase often omits 'de' or reorders words (e.g. "combien de temps" + "que tu..."). Use it to talk about how long someone has done or been doing something.
target_language_example: Tu peux rester autant de temps que tu veux.
native_language_example: You can stay as long as you want.

meaning: '(period) of time that you' — part of expressions asking or stating how long (something has lasted) involving 'you'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in common constructions like «Ça fait combien de temps que vous... ?» (How long have you...?) or in statements like «autant de temps que vous pourrez» (as much time as you can). The full phrase often needs surrounding words (Ça fait, autant, etc.). Use with verbs to ask duration: work, live, be together, etc.
target_language_example: Ça fait combien de temps que vous habitez ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been living here?

meaning: part of questions about duration (how long) when addressing 'vous'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears in questions asking about time or duration, usually as part of fixed phrases like "Combien de temps vous a-t-il fallu...?" or "Depuis combien de temps vous... ?" Use the full question forms: "Combien de temps... ?" (How long?) and "Depuis combien de temps... ?" (How long has it been / How long have you been...). The pronoun "vous" makes the question formal or plural. Word order may change in more formal inversion (e.g. "Depuis combien de temps êtes-vous là ?").
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps vous habitez ici ?
native_language_example: How long have you been living here?

meaning: occasionally; from time to time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens now and then, not regularly. Similar to 'parfois' or 'de temps en temps' (very close). Neutral register and common in spoken and written French. Can appear at start, middle or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Je téléphone à mes parents de temps à autre.
native_language_example: I call my parents from time to time.

meaning: 'how long' (asking about duration).
additional_notes: This phrase appears in questions about duration, usually as part of 'combien de temps ça va durer/prendre' — literally 'how much time is it going to last/take'. Common in spoken and written French to ask how long something will continue or require.
target_language_example: Combien de temps ça va durer, selon toi ?
native_language_example: How long will it last, in your opinion?

meaning: part of constructions meaning 'make you a ...' or 'what makes you a ...' (literally 'of you a ...')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence that appears in the structure 'faire de + quelqu'un + (quelque chose)' meaning 'to make someone (something)' or in questions 'Qu'est-ce qui fait de toi...?' meaning 'What makes you...?' Word order in French places the person between 'de' and the noun: faire de toi une star = make you a star. Also watch examples like 'J'ai besoin de toi une seconde' — here 'de toi' is separate: 'I need you for a second.' So context matters: 'de toi une ...' specifically signals 'faire de toi une ...' constructions.
target_language_example: Ils vont faire de toi une meilleure personne.
native_language_example: They are going to make you a better person.

meaning: of/for always; indicating something that lasts forever or is habitual.
additional_notes: Used after nouns or verbs with 'de' + 'toujours' to mean 'of all time' (timeless) or 'always' (habitual). Context determines nuance: with verbs it often means 'always' (Je promets de toujours...), though more common French places 'toujours' after the infinitive (promets de toujours dire → promets de toujours dire is acceptable but 'promets de toujours dire' is less common than 'promets de dire toujours'). With nouns, 'compagnon de toujours' means 'lifelong/everlasting companion.' Can sound slightly literary or emphatic in some uses.
target_language_example: C'est mon ami de toujours.
native_language_example: He's my lifelong friend.

meaning: 'to beat around the bush' — avoid saying something directly.
additional_notes: Used in the phrase 'arrêter de tourner autour du pot' meaning 'stop beating around the bush' / 'stop avoiding the main point'. 'Tourner autour de' literally means 'to turn around', and 'pot' is 'pot' — but the expression as a whole means to dodge the main topic. Common in spoken and written French. You can change 'pot' to refer to a specific thing (e.g., 'tourner autour du sujet'), but 'tourner autour du pot' is the fixed idiom.
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi ce que tu veux vraiment.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what you really want.

meaning: everyday; ordinary; used daily
additional_notes: Used to describe something common, routine, or typical in daily life (e.g., language, objects, habits). Can modify nouns (la vie de tous les jours, le vin de tous les jours) or activities (conversation de tous les jours). Equivalent to 'everyday' or 'day-to-day.'
target_language_example: C'est une tenue de tous les jours, confortable et simple.
native_language_example: It's an everyday outfit, comfortable and simple.

meaning: of all time; ever (used to say someone/something is the best or greatest in history).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to express that someone or something ranks highest across all eras. Common in superlative expressions (le meilleur de tous les temps, le plus grand de tous les temps). Often used in discussions about artists, athletes, works, etc.
target_language_example: C'est le meilleur film de tous les temps.
native_language_example: It's the best film of all time.

meaning: with all my heart; sincerely/wholeheartedly
additional_notes: Used to express strong emotional support, gratitude, or sincerity. Common in phrases like "je suis de tout cœur avec vous" (I'm with you wholeheartedly) or "merci de tout cœur" (thank you from the bottom of my heart). Formal and informal contexts; can be used with je/tu/nous/vous.
target_language_example: Je te souhaite bonne chance de tout cœur.
native_language_example: I wish you good luck with all my heart.

meaning: for all time; since always; throughout history (i.e. for as long as anyone can remember).
additional_notes: Used to say that something has been true for a very long time or forever. Common in formal and neutral registers. Can be synonymous with "depuis toujours" or "toujours" depending on context. Often followed by a verb: « Cela a été vrai de tout temps. »
target_language_example: Les hommes ont raconté des histoires de héros de tout temps.
native_language_example: People have told stories of heroes for all time.

meaning: anyway / in any case / regardless
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that remains true regardless of previous information or to dismiss objections. Common in spoken and written French. Can start a sentence or follow a clause (e.g., «... de toute façon.»). Tone can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: De toute façon, je n'aurais pas pu venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Anyway, I couldn't have come tonight.

meaning: anyway / in any case / regardless
additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement that is true despite other information or to dismiss previous comments. Commonly interchangeable with 'de toute façon' or 'en tout cas'. Can be placed at the start or middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: De toute manière, je viendrai même s'il pleut.
native_language_example: Anyway, I'll come even if it rains.

meaning: obviously; clearly
additional_notes: Used to state that something is evident or obvious from the situation or facts. Can stand alone as an answer (e.g. "De toute évidence.") or modify a sentence before or after the verb. Neutral register — suitable for spoken and written French.
target_language_example: De toute évidence, elle a oublié notre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: Obviously, she forgot our appointment.

meaning: from all sides; from everywhere; on all fronts.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something comes or happens from every direction or from many sources (physical sides, critics, threats, etc.). Common in both literal (surrounded) and figurative (widely criticized) contexts. Can be used with passive constructions (être cerné de toutes parts) or active verbs (se faire critiquer de toutes parts).
target_language_example: Ils ont été attaqués de toutes parts.
native_language_example: They were attacked from all sides.

meaning: with all one's strength; as hard as one can
additional_notes: Used to say someone is using their full physical (or sometimes emotional) effort. Commonly follows verbs like crier, pousser, tirer, se débattre. Equivalent to 'as loud as possible' when used with crier, or 'with all one's might' for physical actions.
target_language_example: Il a soulevé la porte de toutes ses forces.
native_language_example: He lifted the door with all his strength.

meaning: to work more / to work harder (more hours or with more effort).
additional_notes: Appears after verbs like conseiller (to advise) or demander (to ask/request) with the preposition 'de' plus an infinitive. 'Travailler plus' can mean 'work more' (increase hours) or 'work harder' (put in more effort); context (e.g. 'dur' = 'hard') clarifies meaning. Common structure: [verb] + de + infinitive.
target_language_example: Ils m'ont demandé de travailler plus la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: They asked me to work more next week.

meaning: wrong, askew, or not going as planned (depending on context).
additional_notes: Can describe something physically crooked or misaligned (Le tableau est de travers). Used idiomatically to say something went wrong or is going badly (Quelque chose a dû aller de travers; Tout va de travers). In the fixed expression «Pas un cheveu de travers !» it means 'not a single thing out of place' (i.e., perfectly tidy or well-behaved).
target_language_example: Depuis ce matin, tout semble aller de travers.
native_language_example: Since this morning, everything seems to be going wrong.

target_language_multi_word_term: de traverser la rivière à la nage
meaning: to cross the river by swimming
additional_notes: Literal components: 'traverser la rivière' = to cross the river; 'à la nage' = by swimming. Often used after verbs or expressions of ability or possibility (pouvoir, être capable de, être en mesure de) to indicate the method of crossing.
target_language_example: Il a été en mesure de traverser la rivière à la nage.
native_language_example: He was able to cross the river by swimming.

meaning: too many / unnecessary / out of place (depends on context)
additional_notes: Used in different contexts: 1) after verbs to mean 'too much' or 'from doing too much' (often appears as 'trop' or 'de trop' after a past participle: 'malade de trop manger' = sick from overeating). 2) to say someone/something is unnecessary or makes things awkward: 'se sentir de trop' = feel out of place/like a fifth wheel. 3) 'un mot de trop' = one word too many, i.e. an unnecessary or harmful remark. 4) with numbers, 'de trop' = too many (one or more extra). Note: not informal; meaning is compositional in some uses but idiomatic in others.
target_language_example: Il a apporté trois chaises, une était de trop.
native_language_example: He brought three chairs — one was too many.

meaning: 'of the head' or part of fixed expressions; literal meaning 'of the head' but used in several contexts
additional_notes: Literally means 'of the head' and appears in different contexts: 1) literal anatomy (la voiture de tête = lead car; la statue dépourvue de tête = without a head), 2) as part of set phrases (from memory = 'par cœur' rather than 'de tête' in French; note: 'de tête' alone can appear colloquially like 'pas de tête' to mean 'no head' or 'no brains' depending on context), 3) in culinary terms 'fromage de tête' is a head cheese (a terrine made from a pig's head). The meaning depends on the noun that follows or the expression as a whole.
target_language_example: Il a acheté du fromage de tête au marché.
native_language_example: He bought head cheese at the market.

meaning: from one
additional_notes: Usually seen when un is the numeral 1 in a larger expression, especially for counting ranges: de un à dix = 'from one to ten'. It can also appear in counting or score phrases like et de un ! ('and that's one!'). In most other contexts, de + un is normally contracted to d'un.
target_language_example: Les enfants apprennent à compter de un à vingt.
native_language_example: The children are learning to count from one to twenty.

meaning: 'of value' / 'valuable' (used to indicate worth or importance)
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe its worth or value. Can be literal (monetary value) or figurative (importance, usefulness). In some contexts it may be part of a longer phrase (e.g., 'avoir de la valeur' = 'to be valuable'). Word order: 'de valeur' follows the noun it qualifies in the examples.
target_language_example: Cette médaille est un objet de valeur pour moi.
native_language_example: This medal is an object of value to me.

meaning: to lock (the) — infinitive with the definite feminine object after 'de' (e.g., 'to lock the [door]').
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but part of a verb phrase: 'oublier de verrouiller la porte' = 'to forget to lock the door'. 'La' is the feminine definite article referring to a specific feminine noun (e.g., 'la porte'). The structure 'oublier de + infinitive' means 'to forget to [do something]'.
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de verrouiller la porte avant de partir.
native_language_example: Don't forget to lock the door before leaving.

meaning: 'lives are at stake' (part of the phrase used to say lives are at risk)
additional_notes: This is not a complete standalone phrase; it appears inside sentences like "Des milliers/millions de vies sont en jeu." which means "Thousands/millions of lives are at stake." Use with a quantifier before "vies" (des centaines, des milliers, des millions, trop, etc.).
target_language_example: Des milliers de vies sont en jeu.
native_language_example: Thousands of lives are at stake.

meaning: to want to do (something).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the preposition 'de' with the infinitive construction 'vouloir faire' following expressions of certainty/doubt (e.g. 'être sûr de'). It appears in questions like 'Are you sure you want to do that?' The speaker may change gender/number of 'sûr' (sûr/sûre/sûrs/sûres) to match the subject. 'De' is required after certain adjectives and verbs (e.g. 'décider de', 'avoir peur de', 'être sûr de').
target_language_example: Il n'est pas sûr de vouloir faire ce voyage.
native_language_example: He is not sure he wants to make this trip.

meaning: 'to want to (do) it' — part of the phrase used to ask or state whether someone wants to do something (le = it / the action).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but a sequence: 'être sûr de vouloir le faire' = 'to be sure you want to do it'. 'De' follows expressions like 'sûr de' or 'certain de'. 'Le' is a direct object pronoun meaning 'it' (refers to an action or thing already mentioned). Word order: subject + être sûr(e) de + vouloir + le + verb infinitive (faire). Agreement: 'sûr' varies by speaker gender (sûr/sûre) and formality (tu/vous).
target_language_example: Tu es sûr de vouloir le tenter ?
native_language_example: Are you sure you want to try it?

meaning: to want to leave (as part of a larger phrase: 'sure/l'absolutely certain to want to leave')
additional_notes: This construction combines 'vouloir partir' (to want to leave) with the preposition 'de' after adjectives like 'sûr(e)(s)' or verbs expressing certainty/doubt: e.g. 'être sûr de vouloir partir' = 'to be sure that one wants to leave.' Used when asking or stating whether someone really wants to leave. Conjugation/agreement (sûr/sûre/sûrs/sûres) depends on the subject, but 'de vouloir partir' stays the same.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas sûr de vouloir partir si tôt.
native_language_example: I'm not sure I want to leave so early.

meaning: 'of it to you' part of the clitic combination used before entendre/entendre dire: literally 'to hear you say it' (as in 'heureux de vous l'entendre dire' = 'happy to hear you say that').
additional_notes: This fragment appears when the object pronoun 'le/la/les' (here contracted to l') and the indirect object pronoun 'vous' appear before an infinitive verb like 'entendre' or the semi-auxiliary phrase 'entendre dire'. In full order the idea is 'être heureux de + [infinitive phrase]' with the pronouns placed before the infinitive: 'heureux de vous l'entendre dire' = 'happy to hear you say it' (literally 'happy of you it to-hear to-say'). The sequence is formal/neutral and common in written and spoken French. The phrase 'de vous l'' by itself is incomplete — it always attaches to a verb (e.g. l'entendre, l'avoir, etc.).
target_language_example: Je suis content de vous l'entendre dire.
native_language_example: I'm glad to hear you say that.

meaning: of that
additional_notes: Literally combines de + ça. The exact English translation depends on the verb or expression: it can mean of that, about that, from that, or with that. Very common in spoken French; de cela is more formal or written.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus parler de ça.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about that anymore.

meaning: 'about that' (used to refer back to something previously mentioned; literally 'of that of which I...').
additional_notes: This sequence appears when a speaker refers back to a thing or topic already mentioned and then uses a relative construction with 'dont' plus a verb referring to the speaker (je, je veux te, etc.). In natural French you'd usually say 'c'est de ça dont je parle' or more simply 'c'est de ça que je parle' (the latter is more common). 'Dont' replaces 'de + [thing]' and links the noun to the verb; the full phrase emphasizes 'that (thing) is what I'm talking about.' Use with verbs that govern 'de' (parler de, vouloir parler de, rêver de, avoir besoin de, etc.).
target_language_example: C'est de ça dont je voulais te parler hier.
native_language_example: That's what I wanted to talk to you about yesterday.

meaning: 'about that' or 'that's what it's about' (used in questions/confirmations).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the fixed expressions «c'est de ça qu'il s'agit» or «c'est de ça qu'il est question», meaning 'that's what it's about' or 'is that what this is about?'. Often used to confirm or ask if the subject under discussion is that thing. Informal contractions may elide the vowel (qu' + il/est). The phrase relies on the preceding context (ça = that/this).
target_language_example: C'est de ça qu'il s'agit ?
native_language_example: Is that what this is about?

meaning: outside after the (time/event).
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a fixed idiom. 'Dehors' = outside; 'après' = after; 'le' is the definite article that will be followed by a time expression or event (e.g. 'déjeuner', 'film', or a time like 'déjeuner' -> 'le déjeuner'). In a full sentence you might see: 'dehors après le film' (outside after the movie) or 'dehors après le déjeuner' (outside after lunch). Word order: de hors (location) + après le (temporal relation).
target_language_example: On se retrouve dehors après le film.
native_language_example: Let's meet outside after the movie.

meaning: 'I was wondering' (used to introduce a question or curiosity in the past).
additional_notes: This is part of the impersonal reflexive phrase "Je me demandais..." (literally "I was asking myself...") used to politely express wondering about something in the past. It is followed by a subordinate question introduced by "ce que" (what/that which) or "ce qui" (what/which when the clause is subject). Common in spoken and written French to soften questions.
target_language_example: Je me demandais ce que tu ferais demain.
native_language_example: I was wondering what you would do tomorrow.

meaning: 'was wondering why' (I was wondering why...)
additional_notes: Used with 'je me' as part of the imperfect reflexive phrase 'je me demandais pourquoi' to politely express wondering about a past situation. Followed by a clause explaining what was wondered (often with 'tu/es arrivé', 'vous êtes arrivé(s)'). Can be used to soften questions or introduce a reason request. In spoken French, many speakers might use the present tense in the subordinate clause (e.g. 'tu es arrivé') even though the main clause is imperfect.
target_language_example: Je me demandais pourquoi tu as choisi ce livre.
native_language_example: I was wondering why you chose that book.

meaning: I was wondering when…
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the imperfect tense with 'je me' (je me demandais) to politely express curiosity or expectation about the timing of something. Followed by a clause introduced by 'tu', 'vous', or a verb in conditional/conditional-past: e.g. 'tu allais', 'tu viendrais'. Can be used to soften questions or express that you had been thinking about something for a while.
target_language_example: Je me demandais quand tu rentrerais à la maison.
native_language_example: I was wondering when you would come home.

meaning: asked if
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of demander + si. Used to report a past request/question about whether something was true or would happen. Common in reported speech: «Je demandais si...» = 'I asked if/whether...'. Can also mean 'I was asking whether' (ongoing/polite). 'Si' here means 'if/whether', not 'yes'.
target_language_example: Je demandais si vous pouviez m'aider.
native_language_example: I asked if you could help me.

meaning: 'the request has' (part of the passive construction 'demande a été ...' = 'the request was ...')
additional_notes: This appears as part of the passive perfect form 'la demande a été + past participle' meaning 'the request was ...' (accepted/rejected/etc.). 'Demande' = request; 'a' is the third-person singular of 'avoir' used to form compound tenses. Not a complete phrase by itself — you will commonly see 'la demande a été acceptée/rejetée'.
target_language_example: La demande a été acceptée hier.
native_language_example: The request was accepted yesterday.

meaning: a marriage proposal; the act of asking someone to marry you.
additional_notes: Used for the formal proposal or request to marry. Can refer to the moment, the offer itself, or the request letter/gesture. Commonly used with verbs like accepter (accept), refuser (refuse), faire (make/perform) or recevoir (receive).
target_language_example: Il a fait sa demande en mariage au bord de la mer.
native_language_example: He proposed to her by the sea.

meaning: 'wonder(s) what' or 'ask(s) what' (used in expressions like je me demande ce qu')
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the impersonal/reflexive phrase je me demande (I wonder) followed by ce qu' + clause. Ce qu' is the contraction of ce que before a vowel/ mute h. Used to introduce a subordinate question (what ...). Translate as "what" or "what ... like/has/did" depending on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Je me demande ce qu'il fait demain.
native_language_example: I wonder what he is doing tomorrow.

meaning: '(one) wonders/how many' — used to ask or wonder about the number of something.
additional_notes: Often appears in the structure 'Je me demande combien de ...' (I wonder how many ...). Followed by a plural noun or plural verb construction. Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about a quantity. For direct questions you can use 'Combien de ... ?' without 'Je me demande'.
target_language_example: Je me demande combien de livres elle a lus.
native_language_example: I wonder how many books she has read.

meaning: 'asks/wonders whether' or 'ask/wonder if'
additional_notes: This is a contracted form used after verbs like demander (to ask) or se demander (to wonder). The s' is the start of s'il/s'elle/s'ils, short for si + il/elle/ils (if/whether + he/she/they). Use 'Demande s'il...' to tell someone to ask whether; use 'Je me demande s'il...' to say 'I wonder if...'. Pronunciation often links the words: 'dəmɑ̃d sil...'.
target_language_example: Je me demande s'il viendra demain.
native_language_example: I wonder if he will come tomorrow.

meaning: 'wonder (to myself) whether I should...'
additional_notes: This phrase is the first-person singular impersonal expression 'je me demande' + 'si je/devrais...' used to express doubt or consideration about doing something. Use it to say you are wondering whether you ought to do a specific action. It can be followed by an infinitive (e.g. 'faire confiance', 'y aller', 'parler') and is common in everyday speech and writing.
target_language_example: Je me demande si je devrais accepter cette offre.
native_language_example: I wonder if I should accept that offer.

meaning: 'I wonder if you...' or 'I ask whether you...'.
additional_notes: This phrase appears as part of Je me demande si vous... meaning 'I wonder if you...'. It's used to introduce a question about someone else's ability, opinion, feelings, actions, or possession — often politely or reflectively. In spoken French the full set phrase is Je me demande si vous (avez, comprenez, pourriez, êtes, etc.).
target_language_example: Je me demande si vous pouvez m'aider demain.
native_language_example: I wonder if you can help me tomorrow.

meaning: to ask for advice; to seek someone's guidance or opinion.
additional_notes: Used when someone requests guidance, opinion, or professional advice. Often followed by à + person (demander conseil à quelqu'un). Common in everyday and formal contexts (e.g., demander conseil à un médecin, à un avocat).
target_language_example: Tu devrais demander conseil à un médecin avant de prendre ce médicament.
native_language_example: You should ask a doctor for advice before taking this medication.

meaning: to ask someone to marry (someone); to propose marriage.
additional_notes: Used when one person asks for another's hand in marriage (to propose). Often used with a direct object: demander (quelqu'un) en mariage or demander en mariage (les mains de) quelqu'un. Formal phrasing can include 'demander la main de...'.
target_language_example: Je vais la demander en mariage ce week-end.
native_language_example: I'm going to propose to her this weekend.

meaning: to apologize (to ask for forgiveness).
additional_notes: Used to say you ask someone to forgive you. Common in both spoken and written French. Can be followed by a person (demander pardon à quelqu'un) or a reason (pour ...).
target_language_example: Il est allé la voir pour demander pardon.
native_language_example: He went to see her to apologize.

meaning: used to say 'after so long' or 'it's been a long time' (about something that has been happening or talked about for a long time).
additional_notes: Often used colloquially to express that something has been ongoing for a long time or that one has waited/expected something for a long time. Can be followed by a clause (Depuis le temps que...) or used alone as an exclamation (Depuis le temps ! / Super, depuis le temps !). In questions like "Ça va, depuis le temps ?" it means "How have you been after all this time?" or "It's been a while — how are you?"
target_language_example: Depuis le temps que tu me disais de venir, je suis enfin là.
native_language_example: After all the time you told me to come, I'm finally here.

meaning: for a long time
additional_notes: Used to indicate an action or state that has lasted for a long period up to now (present perfect sense) or — in counterfactual/hypothetical past contexts — to mean 'long ago' (e.g. 'would have disappeared long ago'). Often used with present tense (je connais) or perfect/past contexts depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Je t'attends depuis longtemps.
native_language_example: I've been waiting for you for a long time.

meaning: for a short time / recently
additional_notes: Used to say that something started a short time ago. Similar to 'recently' or 'not long ago'. Often placed after verb or at sentence start. Can be used alone as a short answer ('Depuis peu.').
target_language_example: Je travaille ici depuis peu, mais j'apprends vite.
native_language_example: I've been working here for a short time, but I'm learning quickly.

meaning: since when
additional_notes: Used to ask when something started or how long something has been true. Can be followed by a verb in the present (to ask about a situation that started in the past and continues) or by a past reference. In informal speech you may hear "ça fait combien de temps" or simply "tu fais ça depuis quand ?"
target_language_example: Depuis quand étudies-tu le français ?
native_language_example: Since when have you been studying French?

meaning: 'Since when are/ have you been...?' — asks how long someone has been in a state or place.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the starting point in time of a current situation: residence, membership, a relationship, presence, etc. Followed by a location (à/in), group (des nôtres), or adjective/noun phrase. Formal register (uses êtes). Informal spoken French often uses 'Vous êtes' → 'tu es' or different word order: 'Tu es là depuis quand ?' or 'Depuis quand est-ce que vous êtes... ?'.
target_language_example: Depuis quand êtes-vous ici ?
native_language_example: Since when have you been here?

meaning: 'since always' → for as long as one can remember; forever / forever up to now (i.e. for a very long time)
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time — often translated as "for as long as I/you/we/they can remember" or simply "forever" in casual speech. Can be used as an emphatic question ("Depuis toujours ?") to express surprise. Followed by a subject and verb introduced by 'depuis'.
target_language_example: Je vis dans ce quartier depuis toujours.
native_language_example: I've lived in this neighborhood for as long as I can remember.

meaning: 'since' (introduces a point in time from which something has been true)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the starting point of an action or situation that continues to the present (or to another reference time). Followed by a clause (subject + verb). Can translate as 'since' or 'ever since'. For past reference, English often uses 'since' + past tense or 'ever since'.
target_language_example: Depuis que je travaille ici, j'ai appris beaucoup.
native_language_example: Since I started working here, I've learned a lot.

meaning: the final word; the last decision or concluding remark
additional_notes: Used both literally (the final spoken comment) and figuratively to mean having the final say or decision in an argument/situation. Common in expressions like "avoir le dernier mot" (to have the last word). Can be used in questions to ask if someone wants to say anything last.
target_language_example: Tu as le dernier mot dans cette décision ?
native_language_example: Do you have the final say in this decision?

meaning: 'the last thing I...' or 'the last thing that I...'
additional_notes: This phrase begins a clause where the speaker refers to the last (most recent or final) thing they did, thought, said, want, etc. It is usually completed by a verb and the rest of the sentence (e.g. 'dernière chose que j'ai faite', 'dernière chose que je voulais dire'). Watch the contraction: 'je' becomes 'j'' before a vowel sound (dernière chose que j'ai...).
target_language_example: La dernière chose que je veux, c'est te déranger.
native_language_example: The last thing I want is to bother you.

meaning: the final stretch; the last phase before the end.
additional_notes: Literally 'last straight line'. Used metaphorically for the final part of a process, project, race, exam period, etc., when the end is near and final efforts are made. Can be used in many contexts (work, school, events).
target_language_example: Nous sommes dans la dernière ligne droite avant la présentation.
native_language_example: We're in the final stretch before the presentation.

meaning: last-minute; happening or decided very shortly before an event.
additional_notes: Used to describe something done or arranged at the last moment (e.g., a last-minute change, booking, or news). Often appears in phrases like "une annonce de dernière minute", "un achat de dernière minute" or "une réservation de dernière minute". Agreement: when used as an adjective before a feminine noun write "dernière minute" (invariable as a fixed phrase), e.g., "une décision de dernière minute". Can be used as a noun phrase meaning "breaking news" (les dernières minutes) in journalistic contexts.
target_language_example: J'ai dû faire une réservation de dernière minute pour le train.
native_language_example: I had to make a last-minute reservation for the train.

meaning: behind bars; in prison.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is imprisoned or will be imprisoned. Often follows verbs like 'être', 'passer (X années)', or 'mettre (quelqu'un)'. Informal/neutral phrase — common in spoken and written French. Literal image: behind the metal bars of a cell.
target_language_example: Après le procès, il s'est retrouvé derrière les barreaux pour cinq ans.
native_language_example: After the trial, he ended up behind bars for five years.

meaning: things to tell you / things to say to you
additional_notes: Used when someone has information, opinions, or remarks they need to say to (vous). Often implies multiple points or matters. Context determines tone — can be neutral (news, details) or suggestive/critical. You can replace 'vous' with another indirect object (me, lui, etc.).
target_language_example: J'ai des choses à vous dire ce soir.
native_language_example: I have things to tell you tonight.

meaning: some families / families (plural, indefinite)
additional_notes: Des is the plural form of the indefinite article (un/une → des) and also the contraction of de + les in some contexts. Here it means 'some' or simply the plural 'families'. Use before a plural noun to indicate an unspecified number. In negative sentences des becomes de (e.g. «Il n'y a pas de familles»).
target_language_example: Il y a des familles qui ont besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: There are some families who need help.

meaning: sometimes; occasionally.
additional_notes: Informal/common spoken expression meaning 'from time to time'. Used at start or middle of a sentence; can stand alone. Close alternative: 'parfois' (slightly more formal). Often followed by a comma when at the beginning.
target_language_example: Des fois, je prends le bus au lieu de marcher.
native_language_example: Sometimes I take the bus instead of walking.

meaning: 'ups and downs' — periods of good and bad times.
additional_notes: Used to describe fluctuating situations (life, relationships, projects). Can be used in past, present, or general statements. Often preceded by verbs like avoir (avoir des hauts et des bas) or il y a.
target_language_example: Dans notre relation, il y a eu des hauts et des bas.
native_language_example: In our relationship, there have been ups and downs.

meaning: 'got off' or 'got down from' (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with être (Il est descendu / Je suis descendu(e)) to indicate someone dismounted or got down from a vehicle or object (moto, vélo, cheval, bus, etc.). Followed by de + noun. Past participle agrees with subject in compound tenses with être (descendu(e)(s)).
target_language_example: Il est descendu de sa moto.
native_language_example: He got off his motorcycle.

meaning: animated cartoon; cartoon (animated film or TV show).
additional_notes: Refers to animation for children or general audiences (TV series or short/feature films). Plural is dessins animés. Used with definite/indefinite articles (le dessin animé, un dessin animé).
target_language_example: On regarde un dessin animé ce soir.
native_language_example: We're watching a cartoon tonight.
