meaning: used to address two people together: 'you two' (telling both of you to do/stop something).
additional_notes: Placed after the verb phrase (often set off by commas) to emphasize that the instruction applies to both people. Agreement with gender/number: tous deux (masculine or mixed), toutes deux / toutes les deux (feminine). Common verbs: arrêter, cesser, etc. Equivalent in informal speech: 'vous deux'.
target_language_example: Arrêtez, toutes les deux, de vous disputer.
native_language_example: Stop, both of you, arguing.

meaning: 'two hundred' (200).
additional_notes: Used as the numeral 200. Note the plural form: 'cent' takes an -s (cents) when it is multiplied and not followed by another number (e.g., 'deux cents' = 200). If another number follows (e.g., 201), 'cent' stays singular: 'deux cent un'. Often used in exclamations (e.g., 'Deux cents !') to emphasize a large quantity.
target_language_example: Ils ont vendu deux cents billets.
native_language_example: They sold two hundred tickets.

meaning: a few; two or three (used to indicate a small, approximate number).
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate an approximate small quantity (literally 'two or three'). Can mean 'a couple of' or 'a few times' depending on context. Informal to neutral register and very frequent in speech. Count noun or frequency: 'deux ou trois personnes' (people), 'deux ou trois fois' (times).
target_language_example: Je lis deux ou trois livres par mois.
native_language_example: I read two or three books per month.

meaning: two pairs (of something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the quantity 'two' applied to items that come in pairs (socks, shoes, pairs in cards, etc.). The noun following 'deux paires' is usually in the plural and introduced by 'de' (or changed for definite/partitive articles). Can be used standalone in context (e.g., at a shop or in card games) when the item is understood from context.
target_language_example: Elle a besoin de deux paires de chaussures pour la semaine.
native_language_example: She needs two pairs of shoes for the week.

meaning: in pairs; two at a time.
additional_notes: Used to indicate grouping in pairs (e.g., people in a line) or doing something two items/steps at a time (e.g., climbing stairs two steps at once). Common in commands (e.g., teachers, drill instructors).
target_language_example: Mettez-vous deux par deux pour la sortie.
native_language_example: Line up in pairs for the outing.

meaning: two dots; can mean 'two points' (literal) — also the punctuation mark ':' in French (les deux-points).
additional_notes: Literally 'two points'. In everyday French, 'les deux-points' (always plural) is the name for the colon punctuation mark (:). In other contexts it simply describes two points or spots (e.g., markings on an animal). Capitalization and presence of 'les' often indicate the punctuation meaning.
target_language_example: La coccinelle a deux points rouges sur le dos.
native_language_example: The ladybug has two red spots on its back.

meaning: a second chance; another opportunity to try or to be forgiven.
additional_notes: Used to say someone should be given another opportunity after a mistake or failure. Common in everyday speech. Can refer to relationships, jobs, exams, etc. Often preceded by verbs like 'donner', 'avoir', 'mériter' or phrases like 'droit à'.
target_language_example: Elle a demandé une deuxième chance pour finir le travail.
native_language_example: She asked for a second chance to finish the job.

meaning: 'second most' (used to say something ranks second in a superlative: second largest, second longest, etc.)
additional_notes: Placed before an adjective (usually with adjective in feminine/masculine as needed). Often followed by the adjective and the noun: « le/deuxième plus grand pays », « la deuxième plus longue rivière ». In speech/writing, you may also see « deuxième plus + adjectif » with the definite article agreeing with the noun: « la deuxième plus longue rivière ». Use when something is #2 in a category.
target_language_example: C'est la deuxième plus haute montagne du pays.
native_language_example: This is the second-tallest mountain in the country.

meaning: 'I had to [do] it' (imperfect tense: obligation or necessity in the past).
additional_notes: Combines the imperfect of devoir (devais = I/you/he/she/we/they depending on subject) with the direct object pronoun le (it/him). Used to express a past obligation, intention, or something one was supposed to do. The subject is not included here; the form devais is first- and second-person singular (je/tu) or third-person singular with context—most often seen with je: Je devais le... For other subjects use devions, deviez, devaient, etc. Word order: subject + devoir (imperfect) + object pronoun + verb infinitive or past participle (e.g., Je devais le faire / Je devais le dire).
target_language_example: Je devais le finir avant demain.
native_language_example: I had to finish it before tomorrow.

meaning: in front of her; before her (figurative: ahead of her, with her entire future ahead).
additional_notes: Can be literal (physically in front of a female person) or figurative. In sentence 1 it means 'ahead of her' (time/future). In sentences 2–4 it’s literal or idiomatic: admiration 'in front of her', 'flat on their stomachs before her' (showing submission), and 'certainly not in front of her' (expressing refusal to do something when she is present). Word order: devant + pronoun (elle).
target_language_example: Elle a encore toute sa carrière devant elle.
native_language_example: She still has her whole career ahead of her.

meaning: in front of everyone; publicly, with all people present
additional_notes: Used to say an action or event happens where everyone present can see or hear it. Often appears as "devant tout le monde" (in front of everyone). Can be used to warn against doing something publicly or to express embarrassment. Formal/informal contexts both possible depending on vocabulary around it.
target_language_example: Ne dis pas ça devant tout le monde.
native_language_example: Don't say that in front of everyone.

meaning: you must (to) him/her — expresses obligation directed toward a third person (formal/plural you).
additional_notes: Devez = 2nd-person plural (vous) present of devoir meaning 'must/ought to/should'. Lui is an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him' or 'to her'. Together they appear before an infinitive or a verb: 'Vous devez lui dire' = 'You must tell him/her'. In spoken French 'vous' can be formal singular or plural. For informal singular use 'dois lui' with 'tu' (tu dois lui...).
target_language_example: Vous devez lui expliquer la situation demain.
native_language_example: You must explain the situation to him/her tomorrow.

meaning: you must (to) me
additional_notes: Combination of the verb devoir (vous devez = you must / you have to) + object pronoun me (me / to me). Used when telling someone they are obliged to do something in relation to the speaker (e.g. believe me, trust me, tell me, let me). The pronoun me follows the conjugated verb in affirmative statements. In spoken or familiar language, vous can be replaced by tu (tu dois me...).
target_language_example: Vous devez me dire la vérité.
native_language_example: You must tell me the truth.

meaning: 'you must find' or 'you have to find' (formal/plural or polite 'you').
additional_notes: Combined verb phrase: devez (2nd person plural of devoir = must/have to) + trouver (to find). Used to tell or advise someone (vous) that they need to locate, discover, or come up with something (a solution, a job, an answer, etc.). Can be polite (vous) or plural. For informal singular 'you' use 'tu dois trouver'.
target_language_example: Vous devez trouver une solution rapidement.
native_language_example: You must find a solution quickly.

meaning: 'you must take care (of)' or 'you need to look after'.
additional_notes: Form is the polite/plural imperative/obligation using devoir + pronominal verb s'occuper de. Commonly used to tell someone they have a responsibility to care for someone or something. In normal word order you'd usually say "vous devez vous occuper de...". The verb s'occuper de means "to take care of" or "to look after" and is followed by de + noun. Can address one person formally or a group.
target_language_example: Vous devez vous occuper de votre frère cet après-midi.
native_language_example: You must take care of your brother this afternoon.

meaning: must be more / need to be more
additional_notes: A polite or neutral instruction using the verb devoir (vous devez = you must/should) followed by être plus + adjective to say someone needs to be more [adjective]. Agreement of the adjective depends on the subject (masculine/feminine, singular/plural). Can be softened as 'vous devriez être plus...' for 'you should be more.'
target_language_example: Vous devez être plus attentifs la prochaine fois.
native_language_example: You must be more attentive next time.

meaning: 'guess what' (used to introduce surprising news or get attention).
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase used at the start of a sentence to announce surprising, interesting, or unexpected information. Can stand alone as a prompt for someone to ask for the news. Tone can be playful, excited, or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Devine quoi, j'ai obtenu le poste !
native_language_example: Guess what, I got the job!

meaning: a supervised written test or in-class exam (shorter than a full exam).
additional_notes: Common in schools and universities in French-speaking countries. It usually refers to a timed, proctored classroom exercise or quiz that counts toward a grade. Not the same as 'examen' (which can be longer or more formal) or 'devoir à la maison' (homework).
target_language_example: Nous avons un devoir surveillé de mathématiques vendredi matin.
native_language_example: We have a supervised math test on Friday morning.

meaning: 'we must/should (do something) to her/it' — 'devons' = we must/should; 'la' = her/it (direct object).
additional_notes: This is the verb devoir (nous devons = we must/ought to) followed by the direct object pronoun la (feminine singular). In sentences the pronoun comes before the main verb in simple tenses (nous la devons is incorrect) but in affirmative infinitive constructions it attaches to the infinitive (ex.: devoir la persuader → we must persuade her). Context determines the exact English translation: 'la' can mean 'her' (a person/female) or 'it' (a feminine noun). Watch word order: nous devons la + [infinitive] = we must + [verb] her/it.
target_language_example: Nous devons la convaincre de rester.
native_language_example: We must convince her to stay.

meaning: 'we must/we have to (do) it' or 'we must him/it' depending on context.
additional_notes: Combines the verb devoir (to have to/must) in the first-person plural (nous devons = we must) with the direct object pronoun le (him/it). The pronoun le can refer to a masculine singular person or thing and usually comes before the infinitive (nous devons le faire) or before a conjugated verb (nous le devons — less common). Word order: subject (nous) + devons + le (before an infinitive or after in some constructions). Use le for masculine singular objects; use la for feminine, les for plural, or l' before a vowel.
target_language_example: Nous devons le dire tout de suite.
native_language_example: We must tell him/it right away.

meaning: 'we must/should (do something to) them' — 'devoir' (we must) + object pronoun 'les' (them).
additional_notes: This is the first-person plural present of devoir (nous devons = we must/have to) followed by the direct-object pronoun les (them). The pronoun usually refers to people or things already mentioned. Word order: in simple present tense the pronoun follows the verb in written examples here (nous devons les aider), but in spoken/neutral French it's more common to place the pronoun before the conjugated verb (nous les devons is incorrect — correct is nous devons les + verb infinitive or when using a direct object with an infinitive: nous devons les aider). With another verb (infinitive) the pronoun can either attach to that infinitive (les aider) or refer to a preceding noun. Use 'les' for plural direct objects (masculine or mixed; for feminine plural use 'les' as well).
target_language_example: Nous devons les prévenir avant qu'ils partent.
native_language_example: We must warn them before they leave.

meaning: 'we must/should always' or 'we always have to'.
additional_notes: Combines the first-person plural of devoir (nous devons) with toujours (always). Used to express obligation or strong recommendation that applies at all times. Can be followed by an infinitive (nous devons toujours respecter...) or by a clause. Tone can be strong (must) or softer (should), depending on context.
target_language_example: Nous devons toujours écouter les consignes de sécurité.
native_language_example: We must always follow the safety instructions.

meaning: 'we must/need to find a' (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Combination of the verb devoir (nous devons = we must/should/have to) + trouver (to find) + the indefinite article un. Use when saying that 'we' need to find something (e.g. a plan, a solution). The noun following 'un' agrees in gender/number as usual (une for feminine).
target_language_example: Nous devons trouver un autre endroit.
native_language_example: We need to find another place.

meaning: 'we must find a' / 'we need to find a'.
additional_notes: Combination of the modal verb devoir (nous devons = we must/need to) + trouver (to find) + the indefinite article une. Used to express that 'we' have to find something (a way, a solution, a person, etc.). Replace the noun after 'une' as needed (une solution, une façon, une baby-sitter). Common in everyday speech and neutral register.
target_language_example: Nous devons trouver une solution rapidement.
native_language_example: We need to find a solution quickly.

meaning: 'you should go and [do something to yourself]' — used to give advice telling someone to go do a reflexive action (e.g., wash yourself, go to bed, rest).
additional_notes: Formed from the conditional of devoir (tu devrais = you should), followed by aller + reflexive pronoun te and an infinitive (se laver → te laver). Common for advising someone to go do a personal action: te coucher (go to bed), te laver (wash up), te reposer (rest). Polite/soft advice rather than a command. Use 'tu' form here; for other subjects change pronouns (je devrais, il/elle devrait, nous devrions) and reflexive pronouns (me/te/se/nous/vous).
target_language_example: Tu devrais aller te détendre après le travail.
native_language_example: You should go and relax after work.

meaning: should it / him
additional_notes: Not a fixed standalone expression. devrais is a form of devoir meaning 'should' (with je or tu: 'I should' or 'you should'), and le is a direct object pronoun meaning 'it' or 'him'. In French, le comes before the infinitive: je devrais le faire = 'I should do it'.
target_language_example: Tu devrais le lire ce soir.
native_language_example: You should read it tonight.

meaning: 'you/one should them' — the conditional form of devoir + object pronoun 'les' (them).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the verb devoir (to have to / should) in the conditional (devrais = I/you/one should) followed by the direct object pronoun les (them). Meaning depends on subject and context: tu devrais les... = you should [do something to them]; je devrais les... = I should [do something to them]. In spoken French object pronouns usually come before the verb (les voir, les servir, les jeter). Use devrais for the conditional/soft advice or hypothetical.
target_language_example: Tu devrais les appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: You should call them tonight.

meaning: 'should not' (contraction/informal negative of 'devrais ne pas')
additional_notes: Colloquial/informal way to say "tu ne devrais pas" or "je ne devrais pas" (shouldn't). Often used in speech by dropping the 'ne'. Expresses advice, warning, or moral judgement. Use full form "ne devrais pas" in careful/formal writing, though in spoken French the 'ne' is frequently omitted.
target_language_example: Tu devrais pas y aller seule.
native_language_example: You shouldn't go there alone.

meaning: 'you should take a' / 'you should have a' (suggesting someone ought to take/bring/have one of something)
additional_notes: Polite/soft advice using the conditional of devoir (tu devrais...). Followed by a noun: prendre un parapluie (take/bring an umbrella), prendre un jour de repos (take a day off), prendre un petit-déjeuner (have breakfast). Use with 'tu' (informal you) here; for formal/plural use 'vous devriez prendre un'.
target_language_example: Tu devrais prendre un manteau, il fait froid dehors.
native_language_example: You should take a coat; it's cold outside.

meaning: 'should really do' — expresses a strong recommendation or obligation to do something.
additional_notes: Used to give advice or urge action; combines the conditional of devoir (devrais = 'you/I/he/she should') with vraiment ('really') and faire ('do'). Tone can be gentle or insistent depending on context. Commonly followed by an infinitive or 'ça' (that/it).
target_language_example: Tu devrais vraiment faire tes devoirs ce soir.
native_language_example: You should really do your homework tonight.

meaning: should (there)
additional_notes: Combination of the conditional of devoir (devrais = 'should/ought to' for je/tu) plus the pronoun y ('there' or 'to it'). 'Y' refers to a place, situation, or previously mentioned thing introduced by à. Use changes with subject (je devrais, tu devrais, il/elle devrait, nous devrions, etc.). Commonly followed by a verb: 'devrais y + infinitive' = 'should [do something] there' or 'should [do something] about it.'
target_language_example: Tu devrais y penser avant de décider.
native_language_example: You should think about it before deciding.

meaning: 'should to him/her' — the conditional of devoir combined with the indirect object pronoun 'lui', used to express a recommendation, suggestion or obligation directed toward someone (to/for him or her).
additional_notes: 'Devrait' is the 3rd-person singular conditional of devoir (or used with tu in polite inversion: 'vous devriez'); 'lui' functions as an indirect object pronoun meaning 'to him' or 'to her'. Typically followed by an infinitive or a past participle with an auxiliary (e.g. 'devrait lui dire', 'devrait lui avoir dit'). The referent of 'lui' is determined by context and can be male or female. Word order: subject + devrait + lui + verb.
target_language_example: Tom devrait lui dire la vérité.
native_language_example: Tom should tell him/her the truth.

meaning: 'should (do) it' — polite suggestion or advice directed to 'you' (formal/plural).
additional_notes: Formed from the conditional of 'devoir' (devriez = vous devriez) plus the direct object pronoun 'le' (it/him). Used to give polite advice or recommendation. Word order: in simple tenses, the pronoun comes before the verb (vous le devriez is incorrect); with an infinitive it attaches differently (vous devriez le faire). For informal singular 'tu', use 'tu devrais le'.
target_language_example: Vous devriez le laisser ici.
native_language_example: You should leave it here.

meaning: shouldn't go (you shouldn't go).
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial contraction of 'ne devriez pas y aller' (the 'ne' omitted in casual speech). Used to advise someone not to go somewhere. 'Vous devriez pas y aller' addresses one or more people (formal or plural). Agreement in example sentences (seul/sole/soles/seuls) shows gender/number of the person(s) who would go alone. For polite or written French, use the full negative: 'Vous ne devriez pas y aller.'
target_language_example: Vous devriez pas y aller ce soir, il y a une tempête.
native_language_example: You shouldn't go tonight, there's a storm.

meaning: you should be more (…)
additional_notes: Polite recommendation using conditional of 'devoir' + infinitive 'être' + 'plus' + adjective/phrase. 'Vous devriez être plus prudente/prudents/attentifs…' Tailor adjective to gender/number: prudente (fem. sing.), prudentes (fem. pl.), prudent (masc. sing.), prudents (masc. pl.). Often followed by an adjective or an expression indicating what to increase (careful, careful next time, patient, vigilant, etc.). Formal/polite (vous).
target_language_example: Vous devriez être plus attentif en traversant la rue.
native_language_example: You should be more careful when crossing the street.

meaning: 'we should (about it/of it)'.
additional_notes: Combines the conditional form of devoir (nous devrions = 'we should' / 'we ought to') with the pronoun en, which replaces a noun introduced by de (about it, of it, some of it). Use when suggesting an action concerning something already mentioned. Word order: subject + devrions + en + verb (e.g., «Nous devrions en parler» = 'We should talk about it').
target_language_example: Nous devrions en discuter ce soir.
native_language_example: We should discuss it tonight.

meaning: 'thank God' or 'thank goodness' (expression of relief).
additional_notes: Used to express relief or gratitude that something good happened or a bad outcome was avoided. Often starts a sentence and is followed by a comma. Can be said sincerely or more casually; not typically a literal religious statement in everyday use.
target_language_example: Dieu merci, tout le monde va bien.
native_language_example: Thank God, everyone is fine.

meaning: God knows / only God knows (used to say something is unknown or uncertain).
additional_notes: Used to express that something is unknown, uncertain, or beyond anyone's knowledge — sometimes emphatic. Often followed by a subordinate clause introduced by ce que, de quoi, si, etc. Can also stand alone as an interjection: "Dieu sait." (meaning "Who knows?" or "Only God knows"). Not necessarily religious — can be idiomatic.
target_language_example: Dieu sait pourquoi il est parti si vite.
native_language_example: God knows why he left so quickly.

meaning: 'thank God' or 'God be praised' (expression of relief or gratitude).
additional_notes: Used to express relief, gratitude, or thankfulness when something good happens or a danger is avoided. Often said spontaneously; can be religious or idiomatic. Capitalization may vary (Dieu soit loué). Equivalent to English 'thank God' or 'praise God.'
target_language_example: Dieu soit loué, tout le monde est sain et sauf.
native_language_example: Thank God, everyone is safe and sound.

meaning: 'make a difference to' / 'matter to (someone)' (used in negative sentences to say something does not matter)
additional_notes: Usually appears in negative phrases: "ne fait pas de différence pour moi" or "ne fait aucune différence pour moi" = "it doesn't matter to me". It follows verbs like "faire" (faire une différence) and is followed by the person affected (pour moi, pour toi, pour lui/elle). Can be used with clauses introduced by "que" or with infinitive/nominal phrases.
target_language_example: Que tu viennes ou pas, ça ne fait aucune différence pour moi.
native_language_example: Whether you come or not, it makes no difference to me.

meaning: 'I will tell you everything that...' (start of a clause promising to reveal all relevant information).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a common construction: Je te/vous dirai tout ce que + clause. Use te (informal you) or vous (formal/plural). It introduces that the speaker will tell everything that meets the condition expressed by the following clause (e.g. que je sais / que tu veux savoir). Often followed by a verb clause starting with que + subject + verb.
target_language_example: Je te dirai tout ce que je sais demain.
native_language_example: I will tell you everything that I know tomorrow.

meaning: would you like to
additional_notes: Usually appears in the pattern « ça te dirait de... ? » or « ça vous dirait de... ? » to make a suggestion or invitation. It is followed by an infinitive: « Ça te dirait de venir ? » = « Would you like to come? » The meaning is idiomatic, not a literal use of « dire ».
target_language_example: Ça te dirait de regarder un film ce soir ?
native_language_example: Would you like to watch a movie tonight?

meaning: 'looks like' or 'seems like' (followed by a feminine noun with partitive article 'de la')
additional_notes: This is the conditional/impersonal form of 'sembler'/'ressembler' using 'on dirait (que)' + noun introduced by 'de la' (partitive). It expresses that something appears to be or resembles the thing named (e.g., On dirait de la neige = It looks like snow). Often used in spoken French: 'On dirait...' = 'It looks like...' or 'You would say...'. If the noun is masculine singular use 'du' (On dirait du cuir), and for plural use 'des' or rephrase (On dirait des fleurs).
target_language_example: On dirait de la peinture fraîche sur le cadre.
native_language_example: It looks like fresh paint on the frame.

meaning: wouldn't say
additional_notes: Contraction of 'ne dirait pas' (conditional of dire). Used in impersonal constructions like 'on dirait (que)...' meaning 'it looks/seems (like)...'. With 'pas' it negates: 'it wouldn't seem/you wouldn't say/it doesn't look like'. Can be followed by a clause ('que...') or stand alone as a brief comment. Informal speech often drops the 'ne'.
target_language_example: On dirait pas que c'est dangereux.
native_language_example: It wouldn't seem like it's dangerous.

meaning: 'it looks like' / 'one would say that he' (used to express an impression or guess about someone/something).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the impersonal phrase 'On dirait qu'il...' or simply 'dirait qu'il...' to give an impression, guess, or appearance about a person or situation (e.g. looks like he's sleeping, seems like he's gone, etc.). Tense is conditional 'dirait' used to soften the statement (like 'seems' or 'it looks like'); can be replaced by 'on dirait que' + clause about any subject.
target_language_example: On dirait qu'il a froid.
native_language_example: It looks like he's cold.

meaning: 'it seems (that) they' / 'one would say that they'
additional_notes: From the impersonal verb 'on dirait' (literally 'one would say' or 'it looks like') followed by 'qu'ils' introduces a guess or impression about what 'they' did or how they are. Common in spoken French to soften statements (like 'it looks like' or 'seems that'). Can be used with present, past, or infinitive constructions in the clause that follows.
target_language_example: On dirait qu'ils ont oublié la réunion.
native_language_example: It seems like they forgot the meeting.

meaning: it seems like / it looks like (that).
additional_notes: Used to express an impression, observation, or tentative conclusion based on what you see or hear. 'On dirait que...' is a common impersonal phrase (literally 'one would say that...') and 'ça' refers to the situation or thing being commented on. Can be followed by verbs in various tenses. Polite/neutral spoken register.
target_language_example: On dirait que ça va mieux maintenant.
native_language_example: It looks like it's better now.

meaning: Used as a filler or discourse marker to introduce, clarify, emphasize, or soften what you are about to say (like 'I mean,' 'let me tell you,' or 'you know').
additional_notes: Common spoken French. Placement varies: often at the start of a sentence ('Je veux dire, ...' = 'I mean, ...') or in constructions like 'Laisse-moi te dire' ('Let me tell you'). Can introduce an explanation, a clarification, a surprise, or emphasis about the person addressed (tu). Informal but widely used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je veux dire, tu devrais vraiment essayer ce plat.
native_language_example: I mean, you should really try this dish.

meaning: to say goodbye (often with a sense of finality).
additional_notes: Used to mean saying farewell; can imply a permanent or emotional parting (not just a casual 'see you later'). Often followed by 'à' + person or place (dire adieu à quelqu'un/à quelque chose). Can be used reflexively (se dire adieu) for mutual farewells.
target_language_example: Je suis venue pour te dire adieu.
native_language_example: I came to say goodbye to you.

meaning: to say goodbye
additional_notes: Common expression used when leaving or parting from someone or something. Often followed by à + person (dire au revoir à quelqu'un) or can be used alone. Not formal slang.
target_language_example: Je dois dire au revoir à mes collègues avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to say goodbye to my colleagues before leaving.

meaning: to say the same (about oneself) / to be able to say the same (about one's situation).
additional_notes: Used with 'en' (en dire autant) to compare one's situation or opinion to someone else's. Often follows a statement about someone else, meaning 'I (or someone) can say the same' or 'I cannot say the same.' Common in spoken and written French to express agreement or contrast. Typical patterns: 'J'aimerais en dire autant' (I wish I could say the same) and 'Je ne peux pas en dire autant' (I can't say the same).
target_language_example: Il a réussi son examen, mais je ne peux pas en dire autant.
native_language_example: He passed his exam, but I can't say the same.

meaning: say what
additional_notes: Used before clauses introduced by 'que' or relative pronouns (qui/que) to mean 'to say what/that...'. Often appears in expressions like 'dire ce qui est' (say what is true) or 'dire ce qu'il faut' (say what is necessary). The exact translation depends on the following clause (e.g. 'dire ce qu'il veut' = 'say what he wants').
target_language_example: Dis-moi de dire ce que tu penses.
native_language_example: Tell me to say what you think.

meaning: to say what (something) is / to state what ... is
additional_notes: This is a contracted beginning of phrases like « dire ce que c'est » (to say what it is) or « dire ce que c'était » (to say what it was). You will typically see the full forms (c'est, c'était, ça) in speech and writing. Used when asking or reporting someone stating the identity, nature, or content of something. The contraction c' appears before vowel sounds.
target_language_example: Peux-tu dire ce que c'est ?
native_language_example: Can you say what it is?

meaning: start of a phrase meaning 'to say what happens' or 'to say what is being done/said', usually continued with a verb (e.g. 'dire ce qui se passe').
additional_notes: This fragment is incomplete on its own and normally appears before a reflexive verb: 'dire ce qui se passe' (to say what is happening), 'dire ce qui se dit' (to say what people are saying). Use it only as part of a full clause. Word-for-word: 'to say what oneself/itself ...' (se is a reflexive pronoun).
target_language_example: Il est difficile de dire ce qui se passe en ce moment.
native_language_example: It's hard to say what is happening right now.

meaning: 'to speak ill (of someone)'; to say negative or bad things about someone.
additional_notes: Used with de + person/people (dire du mal de quelqu'un). Common expression meaning to criticize, gossip negatively, or slander. Can be general (complain about) or stronger (badmouth). Often appears in negative constructions (ne ... jamais) or warnings.
target_language_example: Ne dis pas dire du mal de tes collègues sans les connaître.
native_language_example: Don't speak ill of your colleagues without knowing them.

meaning: to say the same (thing).
additional_notes: Used when two or more people express the same idea or comment. Often appears in phrases like «dire la même chose» (say the same thing) or in shorter forms where «chose» is implied. Common in responses like «J'allais vous dire la même chose» (I was going to tell you the same thing).
target_language_example: Tu penses qu'il a tort ? — Je pourrais dire la même.
native_language_example: You think he's wrong? — I could say the same.

meaning: to ask someone to tell you where you are or where you should go (literally: 'tell me where I...').
additional_notes: Used when asking someone for location or directions. Usually followed by a verb or clause (e.g., 'dois changer', 'me situe', 'suis', 'peux prendre'). Common in polite questions: 'Pouvez-vous me dire où je ... ?' or 'Peux-tu me dire où je ... ?'.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me dire où je dois descendre pour aller au musée ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where I should get off to go to the museum?

meaning: 'to tell (someone) when' — ask or refer to the time/date of something.
additional_notes: Commonly used with an object (me, nous, etc.) or a question word to ask for the time or moment of an event. In casual speech negative or surprised rhetorical questions like "Tu comptais me le dire quand ?" mean "When were you planning to tell me that?" — expressing surprise or annoyance at a late disclosure. Can appear with different subjects and polite/formal forms (tu, vous).
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me dire quand commence la réunion ?
native_language_example: Can you tell me when the meeting starts?

meaning: say that
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause after dire. Most often it means "say/tell that" (often as dire à quelqu’un que = "tell someone that"), but after verbs like vouloir it can mean "mean that". Very common for reporting information, opinions, or messages.
target_language_example: Je voulais te dire que je pars demain.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you that I'm leaving tomorrow.

meaning: to say something
additional_notes: A common verb phrase used when someone speaks or expresses an idea. Can mean a brief remark ('say something') or to convey information ('tell something'). Often used with indirect objects (dire quelque chose à quelqu'un) to mean 'tell someone something'.
target_language_example: Je veux dire quelque chose au sujet de ce projet.
native_language_example: I want to say something about this project.

meaning: 'to say who' (to tell who someone is or who did something)
additional_notes: A common short phrase combining the verb dire (to say/tell) + qui (who). Used when asking or instructing someone to identify a person or indicate who performed an action: e.g. «Tu peux dire qui a fait ça?» = 'Can you say who did that?'. Often appears inside longer sentences (dire + interrogative or clause).
target_language_example: Peux-tu dire qui a appelé ?
native_language_example: Can you say who called?

meaning: what (to say)
additional_notes: Colloquial phrase used to ask or refer to what was said or what should be said. Often appears in questions like "Dire quoi?" meaning "What did you say?/Say what?" or in indirect contexts: "J'aurais dû dire quoi?" = "What was I supposed to say?" Can be used alone as a surprised/clarifying reaction. "Tu veux dire quoi ?" = "What do you mean?"
target_language_example: Tu veux dire quoi par ça ?
native_language_example: What do you mean by that?

meaning: to always say; to repeatedly state (habitually say something).
additional_notes: Literal composition: verb dire + adverb toujours. Not a fixed idiom — used to indicate habitual or repeated speech. Can be followed by a noun phrase or a clause (e.g. dire toujours la même chose / dire toujours que...). Contexts: neutral descriptive, can be slightly critical if emphasizing repetition.
target_language_example: Il a tendance à dire toujours la même chose.
native_language_example: He tends to always say the same thing.

meaning: an interjection meaning roughly 'well, hey' or 'wow/you know' used to express surprise, emphasis, mild reproach, or to get attention.
additional_notes: Very common spoken phrase. Tone and meaning depend on context and intonation: can show surprise (Wow!), mild reproach or teasing (Come on/Now then), draw attention (Hey!), or add emphasis to a comment. Informal but widely used in everyday speech. Not literally 'say then' despite the words.
target_language_example: Dis donc, tu as fini si vite !
native_language_example: Well, you finished so quickly!

meaning: 'never say' (imperative/negative expression with the verb dire).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the verb dire (to say/tell) with jamais (never). In examples it appears both in imperatives (Ne dis jamais = Never say) and in present tense negatives (Je ne dis jamais = I never say; Tu ne me dis jamais rien = You never tell me anything). Remember: in standard French the negative structure places ne before the verb and jamais after it (or ne...jamais around the verb). In spoken informal French speakers sometimes drop the 'ne'.
target_language_example: Ne dis jamais ça à personne.
native_language_example: Never say that to anyone.

meaning: you were saying that
additional_notes: Imperfect tense + que + subject pronoun tu. Used to report what someone was repeatedly saying or what they said in the past (ongoing or habitual past). Can translate as 'you were saying that...' or in many contexts simply 'you said that...'. Followed by a clause describing what was said.
target_language_example: Tu disais que tu viendrais ce week-end.
native_language_example: You were saying that you would come this weekend.

meaning: say the
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Disent is the ils/elles form of dire ("to say"), and les means "the." You often see this word order when a plural subject comes after the verb, especially in formal questions or in phrases like ce que disent les gens = "what people say."
target_language_example: Je me demande ce que disent les experts.
native_language_example: I wonder what the experts say.

meaning: used in questions to ask how far something is (lit. 'at what distance is [it] located').
additional_notes: Common construction: 'À quelle distance se trouve ... ?' = 'How far is ...?' Use with places or things. You can replace 'se trouve' with 'est' in casual speech ('À quelle distance est la bibliothèque ?'). 'À quelle distance' asks for a measurement (kilometers, meters).
target_language_example: À quelle distance se trouve la gare la plus proche ?
native_language_example: How far is the nearest train station?

meaning: vendor of / distributor of / machine that dispenses (something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate someone or something that distributes or sells that item. Often refers to vending machines (distributeur de boissons = drink vending machine) or companies/people who distribute products (distributeur de pièces détachées). Grammar: 'de' contracts with le/la/les when followed by definite article (du, de la, des).
target_language_example: Il y a un distributeur de billets près de la gare.
native_language_example: There is an ATM near the station.

meaning: ATM; cash machine (machine that dispenses banknotes).
additional_notes: Commonly used in France to refer to an automated teller machine where you withdraw cash or use bank cards. Often shortened in speech to «distributeur» or «DAB» (distributeur automatique de billets). Useful when asking for nearby machines or describing problems (card retained, machine out of service, card rejected).
target_language_example: Le distributeur de billets est en panne, pouvons-nous aller à un autre ?
native_language_example: The ATM is out of order; can we go to another one?

meaning: uses of the verb 'dire' (to say) in short sequences where 'dit' and 'je' appear near each other in phrases like 'Après ce que tu as dit, je…', 'Je me suis dit…' or 'Ceci dit, je…' — idiomatic ways to report speech, thoughts, or introduce a contrast.
additional_notes: This entry groups common patterns where 'dit' (past participle or third-person present) appears in constructions with 'je' (first-person pronoun). Typical uses: reporting what someone said ('Après ce que tu as dit, je…'), expressing an internal thought ('Je me suis dit…'), or making a transition/contrast ('Ceci dit, je…'). Verb form and punctuation vary: 'dit' can be part of a compound tense (tu as dit), a past participle (après ce que tu avais dit), or a fixed phrase (ceci dit).
target_language_example: Après ce que tu avais dit, je pouvais venir vers toi ?
native_language_example: After what you had said, could I come to you?

meaning: ‘said what I…’ — the start of a clause meaning 'I said what I [did/was going to do/etc.]'.
additional_notes: This fragment appears when reporting what the speaker said; it's usually completed by a verb (e.g., ai vu, avais à dire, allais faire). Common construction: «J'ai dit ce que j'ai vu» = I said what I saw. The pronoun and verb following the apostrophe depend on tense/person: j'ai, j'avais, j'allais, etc. Useful for reported-information phrases like 'I told you what...'.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit ce que j'allais faire.
native_language_example: I told you what I was going to do.

meaning: 'told (me/you/etc.) not to (do) it'.
additional_notes: Part of a larger reported-speech construction with the verb dire (to tell). Common pattern: [person] + a + dit + de + ne + pas + [infinitive] (and sometimes a direct object pronoun like le). Example shows le referring to an action or thing previously mentioned. Pronouns (me, lui, te, on) indicate the indirect object who was told. The exact subject and pronoun can change (e.g. 'm'a dit de ne pas le faire' = 'told me not to do it').
target_language_example: Il m'a dit de ne pas le toucher.
native_language_example: He told me not to touch it.

meaning: 'told (someone) not to' (colloquial omission of standard negation)
additional_notes: This construction is informal and commonly heard in spoken French. It replaces the standard 'dire de ne pas + infinitive' (e.g. 'je t'ai dit de ne pas venir'). Grammatically, it's a contraction where the 'ne' is dropped: 'je t'ai dit de pas venir'. Use in casual conversation; avoid in formal writing or speech. The subject is the person who said it (je, je t'avais, je vous ai...), followed by 'dire de pas' + verb infinitive.
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de pas le faire.
native_language_example: I told you not to do it.

meaning: short for 'dit de te...' used before a reflexive or pronominal verb: 'told you to (do something)'.
additional_notes: This is a contracted sequence found when someone reports an order or instruction: Je t'ai dit de t' + verb (e.g. t'asseoir, t'habiller, t'en débarrasser). The first 't'' is the indirect object 'te' (to you) after 'dire' (to tell). The second 't'' is the reflexive or pronominal pronoun attached to the verb (te + verb). In spoken and written French the pronouns often contract: 'Je t'ai dit de t'asseoir' = 'I told you to sit down.'
target_language_example: Je t'ai dit de t'occuper de la valise.
native_language_example: I told you to take care of the suitcase.

meaning: says the same (thing) / expresses the same opinion
additional_notes: A short phrase built from the verb dire (to say) in the third person singular (dit) plus la même (the same). It usually appears in contexts like «il/elle dit la même chose» or «tu dis la même» to mean someone repeats or holds the same statement or opinion as another. On its own ('dit la même') is informal and elliptical — speakers often omit words (e.g. 'chose') in casual speech.
target_language_example: Elle dit la même que lui, donc ils sont d'accord.
native_language_example: She says the same as him, so they agree.

meaning: said where he (would/were) — introduces reported information about a man's location or plans
additional_notes: Used in reported speech or questions to ask whether someone (he) told another person about his location, destination, or plans. Tense of the verb after 'où il' (allait, était, etc.) shows time (future/intent vs past/state). In English it's often rendered as "said where he was/was going/would go."
target_language_example: Elle m'a dit où il partait demain ?
native_language_example: Did she tell me where he was leaving tomorrow?

meaning: said that I (it/her/him/…)
additional_notes: This is a truncated clip of reported speech: 'dit que' = 'said that', 'je' = 'I', and 'l'' is a contracted object pronoun (le/la/les or l' before a vowel). The full phrase depends on the next word: e.g. 'dit que je l'aimais' = 'said that I loved/liked him/her/it'. Often appears in past tenses (j'ai dit que...). Context determines whether l' = him, her, it. Can also be used with adjectives: 'dit que je l'étais' = 'said that I was (it/that)'.
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit que je l'aimais.
native_language_example: I told him/her that I loved him/her/it.

meaning: '(he/she) said that I would do it' (literal fragment: 'said that I it')
additional_notes: This is a fragment built from the verb dire (to say) in the past (dit) plus a subordinate clause introduced by que. In examples it appears as part of sentences like "J'ai dit que je le ferais" (I said that I would do it). The pronoun le refers to a masculine object or action already mentioned. Word order: subject + ai/ai/ai etc. + dit + que + je + le + verb. Tense inside the clause can be conditional (ferais) or future (ferai) depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Je lui ai dit que je le ferais demain.
native_language_example: I told him/her that I would do it tomorrow.

meaning: 'says that I/you...' (beginning of a reported speech phrase; often followed by a verb or object)
additional_notes: This is a fragment used when reporting what someone says about the speaker or the listener (je/te). In French spoken/colloquial style, contractions like "je t'" appear before a vowel (e.g. "je t'aime", "je t'appelle"). Alone it is incomplete — expect a verb or rest of phrase after the apostrophe. Often appears in longer sentences: "Il dit que je t'aime" (He says that I love you).
target_language_example: Il dit que je t'aime.
native_language_example: He says that I love you.

meaning: an exclamation meaning roughly 'well, well' / 'wow' / 'say, now' used to express surprise, emphasis, or to call attention.
additional_notes: Polite/formal second-person plural imperative of dire + 'donc' used conversationally as an interjection. Tone depends on context: can show surprise (Mais dites donc !), mild admiration (Dites donc, il est très classe), incredulity (Enfin, dites donc !), or to draw attention before addressing someone (Dites donc, Doinel). Not strongly informal, but familiar in speech.
target_language_example: Dites donc, tu as changé de coupe de cheveux !
native_language_example: Well, you've changed your haircut!

meaning: 'eighteen' (the number 18).
additional_notes: Used to name the number 18 in counting, dates, ages, math, phone numbers, prices, etc. Hyphenated in French numbers from 17–99 (with some variations). Pronunciation: /dis‿ɥit/.
target_language_example: Elle a dix-huit ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: She is eighteen years old today.

meaning: 'nineteen' (the number 19).
additional_notes: Used as the cardinal number 19. Can appear alone, before nouns (e.g., 'dix-neuf ans' = nineteen years old), or in time expressions: 'pour dix-neuf heures' means 'by 7 p.m.' (24-hour clock). Pronounced /di.nəf/.
target_language_example: Il a dix-neuf ans.
native_language_example: He is nineteen years old.

meaning: seventeen (the number 17).
additional_notes: Used to give an age, a quantity, a time (minutes), or to count. Written with a hyphen in French numerals (dix-sept). Pronounced [dees-set]. Common in everyday speech and formal writing.
target_language_example: Elle a dix-sept ans aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: She is seventeen years old today.

meaning: I must / I have to buy (some)...
additional_notes: Combines devoir (conjugated «je dois» = I must/have to) + acheter (to buy) + des (partitive/plural indefinite article = some). Used to say you need to purchase unspecified items. Change 'des' to a specific article or quantity when needed (e.g. 'acheter le', 'acheter des tomates', 'acheter cinq pommes'). For other subjects, conjugate devoir (tu dois, il/elle doit, nous devons...).
target_language_example: Je dois acheter des fruits pour la semaine.
native_language_example: I have to buy some fruit for the week.

meaning: 'I must/need to buy a (masculine singular item)'.
additional_notes: Combines: devoir (conjugated: je dois = I must/need to) + acheter (to buy) + un (masculine indefinite article). Use for expressing obligation/need to purchase one masculine singular noun. Change 'un' to 'une' for feminine nouns, plural 'des' for plural. If you want softer necessity, use 'je dois' or 'il faut que'.
target_language_example: Je dois acheter un nouveau livre pour le cours.
native_language_example: I need to buy a new book for the class.

meaning: 'I must say that I...' or 'I have to say that I...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal comment, often an opinion, reaction, or feeling. Conveys a mild admission or emphasis (e.g., surprise, admiration, curiosity). Commonly followed by an adjective, feeling, or clause about the speaker. Formality: neutral — suitable in spoken and written contexts.
target_language_example: Je dois dire que je suis agréablement surpris par le résultat.
native_language_example: I must say that I am pleasantly surprised by the result.

meaning: 'must do' or 'have to do' followed by a clause introduced by 'ce' (what/that).
additional_notes: This construction pairs a conjugated form of devoir (here 'dois') + faire + 'ce' + a relative clause (que/qui/qu'il faut, etc.). It expresses obligation: 'you/I must do what...'. The exact translation depends on the clause that follows (ce que = what; ce qui = what/that which). Common in advice, commands, or moral statements.
target_language_example: Tu dois faire ce qui te rend heureux.
native_language_example: You must do what makes you happy.

meaning: 'must do' or 'have to do' (part of phrases meaning to perform or give effort toward something).
additional_notes: This sequence combines the modal verb devoir (dois = you/I/one must) + faire de. Meaning depends on what follows: often followed by un/ton/mon + noun or expressions like 'mon mieux' (my best). Can also appear in questions 'Que dois-je faire de...?' meaning 'What should I do with...?' Not a fixed idiom by itself; interpret according to the full phrase.
target_language_example: Tu dois faire de ton mieux pour l'examen.
native_language_example: You must do your best for the exam.

meaning: 'I/you must + him/her/it' (contraction of 'dois le' or 'dois la').
additional_notes: Combination of the verb devoir (conjugated: je dois = I must / I have to; tu dois = you must) with the direct object pronoun 'le' or 'la' contracted before a vowel: l' + verb that follows (e.g. l'appeler = call him/her/it). Used to say you must do something to someone or something. Word order: subject + devoir + object pronoun + infinitive (Je dois l'appeler = I must call him/her/it).
target_language_example: Je dois l'écouter avant de décider.
native_language_example: I must listen to him/her/it before deciding.

meaning: 'I must/I've got to (do) it' — first-person singular of devoir + direct object pronoun 'la' (feminine 'it').
additional_notes: Combines the verb devoir (to have to/must) in the present (je dois = I must) with the feminine direct object pronoun la (it/her). Used when the speaker refers to a feminine noun previously mentioned (la clé, la lettre, la voiture, etc.). Word order: subject + devoir + object pronoun (je dois la + infinitive) or je dois la + verb (je dois la saisir). In spoken French the pronoun stays before the infinitive (je dois la retrouver).
target_language_example: Je dois la réparer avant ce soir.
native_language_example: I must fix it before tonight.

meaning: 'I must/need to (do something) to them' or 'I have to (do something) them' — combines the verb devoir (first/second/third person forms vary) with the direct object pronoun les (them).
additional_notes: dois = first-person singular present of devoir (je dois = I must/have to) or second-person singular (tu dois). Here it's je dois = I must. les is the plural direct object pronoun meaning 'them' (people or things). In French the pronoun comes before the main verb: Je dois les avertir = I must warn them. With infinitive verbs, the pronoun stays before the infinitive (les avertir, les rejoindre, les trouver).
target_language_example: Je dois les appeler ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to call them tonight.

meaning: 'I must / I have to' + reflexive pronoun (short form).
additional_notes: Dois is the 1st or 2nd person singular present of devoir (je dois = I must, tu dois = you must). The m' is the elided reflexive pronoun (me) used before a vowel or muted h (m'excuser, m'habiller, m'occuper, m'y remettre). Together they start reflexive or pronominal verbs: Je dois m'excuser = I must excuse myself / I have to apologize. In spoken French the pronoun stays attached to the verb that follows. Use m' for je/tu with verbs beginning with a vowel or h muet.
target_language_example: Je dois m'excuser pour être en retard.
native_language_example: I must apologize for being late.

meaning: 'I must (do something) about it' / 'I have to (do something) with/about it' (first-person singular obligation + 'en' referring to something).
additional_notes: Combines the verb devoir (dois = I must / you must in informal tu) with the pronominal sequence m' + en. m' = me (to/for me or reflexive pronoun), en = 'of it', 'about it', 'from it', or 'about them' depending on context. Common patterns: 'm'en débarrasser' (get rid of it), 'm'en occuper' (take care of it), 'm'en souvenir' (remember it), 'm'en dire' (tell me about it). Word order: the pronouns come before the infinitive (dois m'en + infinitive).
target_language_example: Je dois m'en occuper demain.
native_language_example: I have to take care of it tomorrow.

meaning: 'I must / I have to get ready' (first-person singular, informal spoken word order).
additional_notes: Combination of devoir (must/have to) in the present (je dois) + reflexive verb se préparer (to get ready). Used to say you need to prepare or get yourself ready for something (school, work, an event, prayer, etc.). In full grammatically complete form you might say "je dois me préparer"; in casual speech the subject pronoun (je) is often dropped when context is clear. You can change the object of preparation by adding "pour" + noun or an infinitive (e.g. "pour l'école", "pour partir").
target_language_example: Je dois me préparer pour la soirée de ce soir.
native_language_example: I have to get ready for tonight's party.

meaning: 'I must/should speak' (first person singular of devoir + infinitive parler).
additional_notes: Combines the present tense of the modal verb devoir (je dois = I must/should/have to) with the infinitive parler (to speak). Used to express obligation, necessity, or strong recommendation that the speaker needs to speak. Context determines force (must vs. should). Contraction: in speech, je dois often sounds like /ʒə dwa/ or /ʒə dwa/ and may be followed directly by the infinitive.
target_language_example: Je dois parler au professeur demain.
native_language_example: I must speak to the teacher tomorrow.

meaning: 'must not say' / 'should not say' (negative obligation; you mustn't say)
additional_notes: Informal spoken structure: standard written form is 'ne dois pas dire' (often contracted to 'dois pas dire' in speech). Use with 'je/tu/il/etc.' and an object (de mensonge, ça, du mal de...). Conveys prohibition or advice not to say something. For formal/written French include the 'ne' before the verb: 'tu ne dois pas dire...'.
target_language_example: Tu ne dois pas dire ça devant les enfants.
native_language_example: You mustn't say that in front of the children.

meaning: 'you must not' (informal negative with 'tu') — used to tell someone (tu) not to do something.
additional_notes: This is the negative form of devoir with the informal singular pronoun 'tu' plus a reflexive or other verb: 'tu ne dois pas te...' (you must not ... yourself). Common in commands or strong advice. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: 'tu dois pas te...'. Replace 'te' with another object pronoun if needed (me, nous, vous, se).
target_language_example: Tu ne dois pas te moquer d'eux.
native_language_example: You must not make fun of them.

meaning: 'I/you must know what' — part of phrases meaning someone needs to know something specific.
additional_notes: This is composed of the modal verb devoir (conjugated: je dois, tu dois, etc.) + savoir (to know) + ce (introducing a clause: ce que / ce qui). It appears before clauses like ce que (what + direct object) or ce qui (what + subject). Use it to express obligation or necessity to find out information: "I must know what happened," "You must know what you're doing." Conjugate devoir to match the subject (je dois, tu dois, il/elle doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils/elles doivent).
target_language_example: Je dois savoir ce que tu as dit.
native_language_example: I must know what you said.

meaning: I must tell you (it) / I have to tell you (it).
additional_notes: This combination is part of a larger verb phrase: from devoir (to have to) + indirect object pronoun te (to you) + direct object pronoun le (it/him). Used when the speaker says they need to tell someone something (or repeat it). Word order: subject + devoir conjugated + te + le + (dire/répéter/etc.). Informal/register: neutral; common in speech. Pronunciation note: the pronouns link to the verb (dois-te-le pronounced quickly).
target_language_example: Je dois te le dire maintenant.
native_language_example: I have to tell you (it) now.

meaning: must not
additional_notes: informal spoken form of "ne doit pas", with the "ne" dropped. It uses doit, the 3rd-person singular present of devoir, so you hear it with il/elle/on/ça. It expresses prohibition, advice, or what is not supposed to happen; with être, it can also mean "can't be" in the sense of what is probably not the case ("ça doit pas être facile").
target_language_example: On doit pas faire ça ici.
native_language_example: You shouldn't do that here.

meaning: 'must not' / 'do not have to' (negation of obligation) — context determines whether it's prohibition or lack of obligation
additional_notes: Formed from devoir (to have to / must) in third-person plural (ils/elles doivent) plus ne ... pas for negation. In most of the example sentences it expresses prohibition: 'they must not' / 'you must not'. In some contexts devoir can also mean 'to have to' (obligation) and with negation it can mean 'do not have to' (no obligation), but that reading is less common with devoir; context and intonation decide the sense. For informal spoken French the ne is often dropped (ils doivent pas).
target_language_example: Ils ne doivent pas entrer dans cette salle.
native_language_example: They must not enter this room.

meaning: to give a right to; to entitle (someone) to something.
additional_notes: Used with indirect objects or a de/à + noun to indicate that an action, decision or status grants someone a legal or official right or entitlement (e.g., a document, a vote, a décision). Common constructions: 'donner droit à [quelqu'un] de + infinitif' or 'donner droit à [quelque chose]'. Formal/legal register.
target_language_example: La nouvelle loi peut donner droit aux travailleurs à des congés supplémentaires.
native_language_example: The new law may give workers the right to additional leave.

meaning: 'to make someone want (to do something)' or 'to create the desire (for something)'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone gives another person the desire or motivation to do or have something. Often followed by an infinitive (donner envie de + infinitive) or a noun (donner envie de + noun). Common in everyday French: e.g. "Ça me donne envie de voyager."
target_language_example: Ce film sait donner envie de lire le livre.
native_language_example: That movie manages to make you want to read the book.

meaning: to give one's hand (literally); to offer help, support, or accompaniment; to lead someone by the hand (physically or ceremonially).
additional_notes: Literally "to give the hand." Common uses: donner la main à quelqu'un = take or offer someone's hand (holding hands), help or support someone, or escort/lead someone (e.g., in a formal context). Context determines whether the sense is physical or figurative. Not an idiom with a completely unrelated meaning.
target_language_example: Elle a décidé de lui donner la main pour l'accompagner jusqu'à la sortie.
native_language_example: She decided to give him her hand to accompany him to the exit.

meaning: 'to give birth' or 'to deliver' (to cause a child or offspring to be born).
additional_notes: Used for people and animals. Can be literal (a woman/animal giving birth) or figurative (to give birth to an idea/project = to originate/create). Commonly used in formal and neutral contexts. The subject is the one who gives birth (e.g. Elle a donné naissance à un garçon).
target_language_example: Elle va donner naissance demain.
native_language_example: She is going to give birth tomorrow.

meaning: 'to agree with (someone)' or 'to admit someone is right'.
additional_notes: Used when you acknowledge another person's opinion, argument, or point as correct. Often used with a person as indirect object: donner raison à quelqu'un. Can be followed by a clause introduced by que (e.g., je lui ai donné raison que...). Not literal (donner = give, raison = reason); idiomatically means to concede that someone is right.
target_language_example: Je lui ai donné raison dans cette discussion.
native_language_example: I agreed with him/her in that discussion / I admitted he/she was right in that discussion.

meaning: 'to open onto', 'to face' (used for windows/doors/views)
additional_notes: Used to describe what a window, door, balcony, or room faces or overlooks (e.g., une rue, un jardin, une cour). Common in real estate and everyday descriptions of apartments/houses. Often conjugated according to the subject (e.g., donne, donnent) and followed by a noun introduced by sur or à (e.g., donner sur la rue, donner sur le jardin).
target_language_example: La fenêtre donne sur le jardin. / Le balcon donne sur la rue. / Les chambres donnent sur la cour.
native_language_example: The window opens onto/faces the garden. / The balcony faces the street. / The bedrooms face the courtyard.

meaning: to teach someone a lesson / to reprimand or punish someone so they learn not to repeat a mistake.
additional_notes: Can be literal (to give a lesson, i.e. teach) but in these examples it means to reprimand, scold, or punish someone so they learn a lesson. Tone can be threatening or corrective depending on context. Use with indirect object: donner une leçon à quelqu'un.
target_language_example: Si tu continues, je vais lui donner une leçon.
native_language_example: If you keep going, I'm going to teach him a lesson.

meaning: 'I will give everything that...' (start of a clause meaning you'll give all that someone has or wants).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a relative clause using the future tense (donnerai = I will give) + 'tout ce que' ('everything that/what'). It normally continues with a verb phrase: e.g. 'donnerai tout ce que j'ai' (I will give everything I have) or 'donnerai tout ce que tu veux' (I will give you everything you want). Commonly used to express strong willingness or promise. Word order: 'donnerai (je) + tout ce que + subject + verb'.
target_language_example: Je te donnerai tout ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: I will give you everything that you want.

meaning: 'you give (some)'.
additional_notes: This is the second-person singular present form of the verb donner + the partitive/indefinite article des (some). It appears in informal contexts when speaking to one person (tu). In English you'd usually translate it as 'you give (some)' or 'you are giving (some)'. The article des makes the object plural/indefinite (e.g., donnes des conseils = you give some advice; donnes des bonbons = you give some candies). Contraction or placement with pronouns follows normal French grammar (tu me donnes des → you give me some).
target_language_example: Tu donnes des livres aux enfants.
native_language_example: You give some books to the children.

meaning: 'given this' or 'given that' (used to introduce a fact or premise)
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the phrase 'donné ce que...' or 'donné ce/que' to mean 'given that' or 'considering that'. It is used to introduce a premise or fact that affects what follows. In French you will frequently see the full connector 'donné que' or the phrase 'eu donné' in other constructions; 'donné ce' by itself is usually followed by a demonstrative (ce/cet) or by 'que' plus a clause.
target_language_example: Donné ce problème, nous devons changer de méthode.
native_language_example: Given this problem, we must change our method.

meaning: gave the
additional_notes: Literal past participle of donner combined with the definite article le. Appears in past-tense constructions (il a donné le = he gave the / has given the) or passive-like phrases (qui a donné le = who gave/has given the). Use depends on verb tense and subject; must agree in compound tenses when using direct object pronouns (e.g. il l'a donné).
target_language_example: Elle m'a donné le numéro de téléphone.
native_language_example: She gave me the phone number.

meaning: gave everything that (I/you/he/she/etc.) had or that was asked for.
additional_notes: Used as part of the phrase 'donner tout ce que...' meaning to give all of something or everything one possesses/has available (or everything someone wants). Commonly appears with past tenses (j'ai donné, je t'ai donné). The structure is: donner + tout ce que + clause. It implies completeness — nothing left to give.
target_language_example: Je leur ai donné tout ce que j'avais.
native_language_example: I gave them everything I had.

meaning: gave a (single) blow/knock; hit or struck (once) or gave a quick action (e.g., a push, a tap).
additional_notes: Literal phrase: past participle of 'donner' + 'un coup' (a blow/knock). Used to say someone gave a hit, knock, push, tap, or other quick action once. Context determines exact translation: 'donner un coup de pied' = kick, 'donner un coup de téléphone' = make a (quick) phone call, but shortened 'donné un coup' usually needs the object or is understood from context (e.g., donné un coup sur la table = knocked on the table).
target_language_example: Il m'a donné un coup sur l'épaule pour attirer mon attention.
native_language_example: He gave me a tap on the shoulder to get my attention.

donné un coup de pied dans

target_language_multi_word_term: donné un coup de pied dans
meaning: kicked (someone) in (a body part); gave a kick to.
additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning 'to give a kick into/in' followed by the body part. Often used with informal or vulgar words for genitalia (e.g. «les couilles», «les burnes», «les parties»). Common construction: [Person] a donné un coup de pied dans + [noun]. Can describe a physical act (actual kicking) or be used figuratively (less common).
target_language_example: Il lui a donné un coup de pied dans la jambe.
native_language_example: He kicked him in the leg.

meaning: 'of which/whose he has' or 'that he has' (used to link a noun to a verb with the preposition de)
additional_notes: This is part of a relative clause using 'dont' (which replaces 'de + noun') followed by the subject 'il' and verb 'a' (has). It links back to a noun mentioned earlier: e.g. 'le livre dont il a parlé' = 'the book he talked about'. Here 'parlé' would follow 'a' in compound tenses ('dont il a parlé' = 'that he has spoken about'). 'Dont il a' alone is incomplete; you need a past participle or object after 'a' for a full clause.
target_language_example: La voiture dont il a parlé est rouge.
native_language_example: The car that he talked about is red.

meaning: to sleep very well or very deeply (like a baby).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who sleeps soundly, without disturbance. Can be used literally (about an actual baby) or figuratively (about an adult who slept well). Common, informal expression.
target_language_example: J'ai dormi comme un bébé après la longue journée.
native_language_example: I slept like a baby after the long day.

meaning: 'to sleep the whole...' (e.g. the whole night/day).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a common combination: dormir + toute + time period (toute la nuit, toute la journée). Use definite article to match gender/number of the time noun (toute la nuit, toute la journée). It expresses sleeping for the entire duration. Can be followed by 'la' (toute la nuit), 'la' (toute la journée) or plural/time phrases when appropriate.
target_language_example: Je veux dormir toute la nuit.
native_language_example: I want to sleep the whole night.

meaning: 'to sleep a little' or 'to sleep a bit longer'
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'un peu' (a little) or 'un peu plus longtemps' (a bit longer). Appears in questions and requests (Aimerais-tu dormir un peu ?) and statements (Je veux dormir un peu plus longtemps.). Use dormir seul to mean 'to sleep'. Word order: dormir + un peu (+ plus longtemps).
target_language_example: Je vais dormir un peu avant de partir.
native_language_example: I'm going to sleep a little before leaving.

meaning: 'to sleep very deeply' or 'to sleep like a log'.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning to sleep soundly with no disturbance. Literally: 'to sleep with fists closed' (image of a very deep, tight sleep). Used in everyday speech. Not literal — you don't need to clench your fists.
target_language_example: Il a dormi à poings fermés après la longue randonnée.
native_language_example: He slept like a log after the long hike.

meaning: 'sleep on' (followed by a position or surface) — e.g. sleep on one's back/side/stomach or sleep on the sofa.
additional_notes: Used with dormir (conjugated) + sur + noun/pronoun to indicate the sleeping position or the surface/place where someone sleeps. Examples: dormir sur le dos (sleep on one's back), dormir sur le canapé (sleep on the couch). For subjects other than 'tu' use the appropriate conjugation (je dors, tu dors, il/elle dort, nous dormons...).
target_language_example: Je dors sur le côté quand j'ai mal au dos.
native_language_example: I sleep on my side when my back hurts.

meaning: doesn't sleep / is not sleeping.
additional_notes: This is the negative form of the verb dormir (to sleep) in spoken or informal French where the 'ne' is kept but 'pas' follows the verb; in standard written French you would say 'ne dort pas' or often omit 'ne' in informal speech: 'il dort pas' or 'il ne dort pas'. Used to state that someone or something is not sleeping (literal) or metaphorically 'is always alert/active' (e.g., 'Dieu ne dort pas').
target_language_example: Il ne dort pas cette nuit.
native_language_example: He isn't sleeping tonight.

meaning: 'with (one's) back to' — used figuratively: 'backed against' or 'cornered'.
additional_notes: Literally 'back to'. Often appears in the expression 'le dos au mur' meaning 'with one's back to the wall' → trapped, cornered, or forced to fight/act. Can be used both literally (physically facing a wall) and figuratively (in a difficult situation). Usually followed by a noun (e.g. 'le mur') or used in passive constructions ('avoir le dos au mur').
target_language_example: Avec tous les dettes, il a le dos au mur.
native_language_example: With all the debts, he is backed against the wall.

meaning: 'cold shower' — literal cold-water shower; also used metaphorically for a shock, disappointment, or reality check.
additional_notes: Can be used literally (taking a shower with cold water) or figuratively to mean a sudden unpleasant surprise or discouraging event (e.g., 'that was a cold shower' = that was a letdown). Common in both everyday and literary contexts. Context usually makes the sense clear.
target_language_example: Cette nouvelle a été une vraie douche froide pour toute l'équipe.
native_language_example: That news was a real cold shower for the whole team.

meaning: "the pain is" or "the pain has" (used to describe when/where/how pain appeared or is felt).
additional_notes: This phrase combines douleur (pain) with the verb être (is) and appears in descriptions of symptoms: when pain appeared (est apparue), where it is, how it started (suddenly, progressively), or to ask about timing (Quand ... est‑elle apparue?). In many cases the full verb phrase is est apparue (has appeared/appeared).
target_language_example: La douleur est très forte depuis hier soir.
native_language_example: The pain has been very strong since last night.

meaning: 'the pain was' — simple past description (imperfect) of pain/state.
additional_notes: Combines douleur (pain) + était (imperfect of être = was). Used to describe the intensity or quality of pain in the past. Often followed by adjectives (atroce, insupportable, intense, etc.). Grammatically, était is the 3rd person singular imparfait used to set a past-state; you can replace était with est for present (la douleur est).
target_language_example: La douleur était réelle, mais elle a fini par diminuer.
native_language_example: The pain was real, but it eventually decreased.

meaning: an exclamation like 'good Lord' or 'oh my God' expressing surprise, shock, frustration, or emphasis.
additional_notes: Informal, often used emphatically by speakers to react to something surprising, shocking, upsetting or remarkable. Can be used alone or with other words (e.g., 'Oh, doux Jésus'). It's a mild religious expression — some may find it blasphemous depending on context or personal beliefs.
target_language_example: Doux Jésus, tu as vu la taille de cette file d'attente ?
native_language_example: Good Lord, did you see the length of that line?

meaning: 'red flag' — a red flag or signal (literal); also used to mean a warning or stop signal in contexts like racing.
additional_notes: Usually literal: a red-colored flag. Common in contexts like motorsport where a 'drapeau rouge' means the race is stopped or neutralized. Can be shouted briefly (e.g. 'Drapeau rouge !') or used in descriptions. Not slang. In everyday French 'drapeau rouge' can also be understood metaphorically as a warning sign, similar to English 'red flag'.
target_language_example: Après l'accident, les commissaires ont agité le drapeau rouge.
native_language_example: After the accident, the marshals waved the red flag.

meaning: direct; straight to the point (literally: 'straight to the goal').
additional_notes: Used to describe speech or action that is concise and goes straight to the essential point, without detours. Can modify verbs or describe someone's manner (e.g. aller droit au but = get straight to the point). Literally from sports: going straight toward the goal.
target_language_example: Va droit au but et dis-lui ce que tu veux.
native_language_example: Get straight to the point and tell them what you want.

meaning: 'the right to' (used before a verb or verb phrase)
additional_notes: Used to express that someone has a legal, moral or personal right to do something; followed by an infinitive verb (d' + vowel or de + consonant). In speech and writing you may also see "le droit de" before a noun or when the next word starts with a consonant. Common in phrases like "avoir le droit de + infinitive" or negative forms like "nul n'a le droit de..."
target_language_example: Tu as le droit d'accepter ou de refuser.
native_language_example: You have the right to accept or refuse.

meaning: the right to vote; suffrage.
additional_notes: Refers to the legal/political right to participate in elections. Used with verbs like exercer (exercise), retirer (remove), avoir (have), donner (give). Often preceded by possessive (son droit de vote) or qualified by conditions (à vingt ans).
target_language_example: Tous les citoyens ont le droit de vote.
native_language_example: All citizens have the right to vote.

meaning: 'strange' / 'odd' / 'funny' (in the sense of unusual), used before a noun or expression.
additional_notes: Used to describe something unusual, unexpected, or a bit odd. Often placed directly before a noun or noun phrase: drôle de + noun. Can be neutral, amused, or mildly critical depending on tone and context. Not the same as drôle (alone) meaning "funny" (humorous) when used after a verb or as an adjective: il est drôle = he is funny. With "de" it modifies the following noun (drôle de situation = odd situation).
target_language_example: C'est une drôle de journée pour partir en vacances.
native_language_example: It's an odd day to go on vacation.

meaning: the local/nearby (something); 'the ... around here' or 'the neighborhood ...'.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean the local or nearby one (e.g. 'le café du coin' = the local café/nearby café). Common in everyday speech to refer to a familiar nearby shop, bar, etc.
target_language_example: Le boulanger du coin fait de très bonnes baguettes.
native_language_example: The local baker makes very good baguettes.

meaning: 'so' / 'therefore' / 'as a result' (spoken filler linking cause and consequence)
additional_notes: Very common spoken connector used to show a consequence, result, or change of plan. In informal French it often appears at the start of a sentence as a discourse marker and can be used repeatedly; it can be closer to English fillers like "so" or "then" than a formal "therefore." Not typically used in formal writing.
target_language_example: Du coup, on est partis plus tôt.
native_language_example: So, we left earlier.

meaning: on the side of; with; regarding (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate alignment, support, or reference to a particular person, group, opinion, family, or topic. Common in contexts like 'on someone's side' (support), 'as far as X is concerned' (regarding), or 'from X's side' (family background). Can be followed by a person, group, idea, or noun phrase. Negative form 'je ne suis du côté de personne' = 'I'm not on anyone's side.'
target_language_example: Je suis du côté de mes amis sur cette décision.
native_language_example: I'm on my friends' side about this decision.

meaning: from the beginning to (the)... — used to say 'from start to finish' when completed by a final word like "la fin".
additional_notes: This is a fixed chunk meaning 'from the beginning to...' and normally appears as 'du début à la fin' (from start to finish). You can use it literally (reading/doing something entirely) or figuratively (someone lied the whole time). It needs a final noun (usually 'fin'), so by itself it feels incomplete but is commonly heard in that full phrase.
target_language_example: Il a regardé le film du début à la fin.
native_language_example: He watched the movie from beginning to end.

meaning: because of; due to; as a result of
additional_notes: Used to introduce a cause or reason. Slightly formal; common in written and spoken French. Can be followed by a noun phrase (du fait de + noun) or a clause. Synonyms: 'à cause de' (neutral/colloquial), 'en raison de' (formal).
target_language_example: La route est fermée du fait de la neige.
native_language_example: The road is closed due to the snow.

meaning: from the bottom of (one's) heart; sincerely, deeply thankful.
