additional_notes: Used to express deep, heartfelt gratitude or emotion. Often follows remercier (to thank) but can be used with other verbs expressing feelings. Formality: neutral to slightly formal — appropriate in both personal and polite contexts.
target_language_example: Je te remercie du fond du cœur pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

meaning: overnight; very suddenly, from one day to the next.
additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens abruptly with little or no warning. Can be positive or negative (e.g., a sudden change in life, mood, health, or value). Often used in negative constructions to say something won't happen 'overnight' (Rien ne se passera du jour au lendemain).
target_language_example: Il a perdu son travail du jour au lendemain.
native_language_example: He lost his job overnight.

meaning: all day / from morning to night (continuously or very often).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something throughout the day or constantly. Often carries a sense of 'non-stop' or 'all the time' (can be neutral: long working hours, or negative: complaining, being drunk). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il est au travail du matin au soir.
native_language_example: He is at work from morning to night.

meaning: at least; or rather / anyway (used to qualify or soften a previous statement).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to limit or correct what was just said. Often placed after the idea it modifies: e.g. "Il est sympa, du moins, avec moi." It can mean "at least" (minimum) or be a soft correction like "or rather" / "anyway". Tone is neutral and suitable in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas fini, du moins pas complètement.
native_language_example: I haven't finished, at least not completely.

meaning: 'provided that' / 'as long as' / 'since' (depending on context) — introduces a condition or time-related clause.
additional_notes: Commonly used to introduce a condition: 'as long as' or 'provided that' (e.g. Tu peux rester, du moment que ...). In some contexts it can mean 'since' or 'now that' when giving a reason (less common). Equivalent to 'à condition que' (more formal/subjunctive) or 'tant que' for ongoing conditions. Often followed by an indicative verb.
target_language_example: Tu peux venir, du moment que tu me préviens à l'avance.
native_language_example: You can come, provided that you let me know in advance.

meaning: 'on the first try' or 'at first attempt'.
additional_notes: Used to say something succeeded immediately or that someone understood something immediately. Can describe actions (réussir du premier coup) or perceptions (comprendre du premier coup). Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il a réussi le test du premier coup.
native_language_example: He passed the test on the first try.

meaning: of the century; used to emphasize greatness, notoriety, or trendiness (e.g., 'the ... of the century').
additional_notes: Literally 'of the century'. Frequently used in French to exaggerate — positive or negative — something remarkable, historic, or notable (e.g., 'le procès du siècle' = 'the trial of the century'). Can be used ironically. Also appears in expressions like 'le mal du siècle' (the malaise of the century).
target_language_example: C'est la découverte du siècle, selon les scientifiques.
native_language_example: It's the discovery of the century, according to the scientists.

meaning: feels good to / it's good to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say that doing something feels good, is soothing or beneficial. Common fixed structure: (Ça) fait du bien + d' + infinitive. The apostrophe d' appears before a verb beginning with a vowel or mute h (d'en parler, d'entendre, d'être). Can be used with 'Ça' or other subjects (Me fait du bien de... / Lui fait du bien de...).
target_language_example: Ça fait du bien d'être chez soi.
native_language_example: It feels good to be at home.

meaning: good (quality)
additional_notes: Used to describe something of good quality; often appears before a noun (du bon + noun) to mean "good [noun]" or more loosely "some good [noun]." Can be used informally. Context determines whether it means objectively high quality (du bon café) or colloquially/ironically (du bon porno). In the phrase "du bon et du moins bon" it contrasts good and less good items. When followed by people (du bon monde) it means "good people" or "respectable company."
target_language_example: Il faut acheter du bon pain pour ce repas.
native_language_example: You need to buy good bread for this meal.

meaning: on the bright/good side; from the positive side
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to look at the positive side of a situation (English: 'look on the bright side'). Can also mean 'on the good/right side' in some contexts; context determines whether it refers to attitude or physical side. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Regarde toujours du bon côté de la vie.
native_language_example: Always look on the bright side of life.

meaning: 'a good time' / 'having fun'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone enjoyed themselves or is enjoying themselves. Often appears with verbs like passer (passer du bon temps = to have a good time) or in casual speech (se payer du bon temps = to treat oneself to some fun). Neutral to informal register depending on context; common everyday phrase.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé du bon temps au parc hier.
native_language_example: We had a good time at the park yesterday.

meaning: 'calm down' or 'take it easy' (a short command/request to be quiet or calmer).
additional_notes: Informal, used to tell one person or a group to calm down, quiet down, or stop getting excited/angry. Often said alone or before addressing someone (e.g., "Du calme, mec!"). Tone can be firm or soothing depending on context. Not a literal construction to translate word-for-word in many contexts; functions as an interjection/command.
target_language_example: Du calme, on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Calm down, we'll find a solution.

meaning: 'of the devil' — used figuratively to mean 'very', 'extremely', or 'terribly' (often to emphasize a quality, sometimes with a playful or negative tone).
additional_notes: This phrase attaches to a noun to intensify it (e.g., "un sac du diable" = a terribly big/remarkable bag) or appears in expressions like "c'est du diable" to indicate something impressive or alarming. It's somewhat literary or idiomatic — you'll more often hear other intensifiers in everyday speech, but it's useful for colorful emphasis. The literal meaning is 'of the devil' and can convey danger, difficulty, or exceptional degree depending on context.
target_language_example: Il a une énergie du diable aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He has devilish energy today. / He has an incredible amount of energy today.

meaning: of/from Sunday; used to mean 'Sunday' in fixed expressions (e.g., weekly or habitual Sunday event).
additional_notes: Literally 'of Sunday' or 'Sunday's'. Often used in expressions to describe something that happens on Sundays (promenade du dimanche = Sunday walk) or a habitual/traditional Sunday thing (dîner du dimanche = Sunday dinner). Can also imply a special, sometimes relaxed or typical quality associated with Sundays (la paix du dimanche).
target_language_example: Nous avons la soupe du dimanche après-midi.
native_language_example: We have the Sunday afternoon soup.

meaning: a hard time; something/someone that causes difficulty or trouble
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone or something is difficult to deal with or gives trouble. Often used in contexts like 'donner du fil à retordre' (to give a hard time / cause problems for someone). Not literal (threads/winding).
target_language_example: Le nouveau projet nous a donné du fil à retordre.
native_language_example: The new project gave us a hard time.

meaning: speaking ill of the dead; saying bad things about someone who has died.
additional_notes: Used to express the moral or social rule that one should not criticize or insult people after their death. Often appears in negative constructions like «Il ne faut pas dire du mal des morts» (One must not speak ill of the dead). It is an idiomatic phrase; literal words mean "bad of the dead," but the intended sense is "bad things said about deceased people."
target_language_example: Même s'il avait ses défauts, on ne dit pas du mal des morts.
native_language_example: Even though he had flaws, you don't speak ill of the dead.

meaning: people
additional_notes: Used idiomatically to indicate that there are many people present. Often appears in phrases like 'il y a du monde' (there are people/it's crowded) or as a short question 'Du monde ?' meaning 'Is anyone there?' or 'Are there many people?'. Not a literal partitive + 'world' here; it refers to 'people' or 'a crowd'.
target_language_example: Il y a du monde au marché ce matin.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people at the market this morning.

meaning: 'Show some energy / get a move on / put some pep into it.'
additional_notes: Informal exhortation used to urge people to be more energetic, brisk, determined or to hurry up. Often said to a group or to encourage someone (like 'Come on, get a move on!' or 'Let's have some energy!'). Tone can be encouraging or mildly impatient depending on context.
target_language_example: Allez, du nerf — on doit finir avant midi !
native_language_example: Come on, some energy — we have to finish before noon!

meaning: the rest / the remaining part; or 'otherwise' / 'besides' depending on context.
additional_notes: Commonly used after verbs like s'occuper de to mean 'take care of the rest' (s'occuper du reste). Can also appear in formal nouns (évacuation du reste du personnel = evacuation of the remaining staff). In other contexts, du reste can mean 'besides' or 'moreover' (similar to 'en outre').
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, nous nous occupons du reste.
native_language_example: Don't worry, we'll take care of the rest.

meaning: during the time of; in the days of (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past period associated with a person, era, institution, or event (e.g. du temps de Napoléon, du temps de mon enfance). Often followed by a proper noun or a noun phrase. Equivalent to 'during' or 'in the time of' in English.
target_language_example: Du temps de mes grands-parents, on écrivait beaucoup de lettres.
native_language_example: In my grandparents' time, people wrote a lot of letters.

meaning: literally 'thunder'; idiomatically 'amazing' or 'fantastic' (colloquial).
additional_notes: Primary literal meaning: 'du tonnerre' describes actual thunder (weather). Idiomatic/colloquial use: used to praise something as impressive, powerful, or very successful (e.g., a great performance, a strong punch). Context determines meaning—weather vs. compliment. Informal register when used idiomatically.
target_language_example: Le spectacle était du tonnerre, tout le monde a adoré.
native_language_example: The show was amazing, everyone loved it.

meaning: at all
additional_notes: Used to intensify a negation or to mean 'at all' after negative expressions (e.g. pas, ne ... plus). Can also appear after adjectives to stress 'completely' in informal speech (context determines exact nuance). Often follows the negative word: 'pas du tout' = 'not at all'.
target_language_example: Je n'aime pas du tout ce film.
native_language_example: I don't like this movie at all.

meaning: some wind / there is wind; indicates windy conditions. Can also mean "nonsense" figuratively depending on context.
additional_notes: Literally the partitive article + noun (du = de + le) used with the uncountable noun "vent." Commonly used in weather statements (e.g. "Il y a du vent"). In exclamations like "Du vent !" it can express annoyance about wind. Figuratively, "du vent" can mean "nonsense" or "hot air" (e.g. « Ce qu'il raconte, c'est du vent »).
target_language_example: Il faisait froid, et en plus il y avait du vent.
native_language_example: It was cold, and on top of that there was wind.

meaning: a tough person; hard-boiled; someone who is strong, tough, or not easily intimidated.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used to describe someone physically or mentally tough, experienced, or uncompromising. Can be used as a noun (un dur à cuire — a tough guy) or adjectivally (il est dur à cuire). Often informal; can be playful or admiring, sometimes implies roughness.
target_language_example: Ne te moque pas de lui, c'est un dur à cuire.
native_language_example: Don't make fun of him, he's a tough guy.

meaning: for (a) — used to say how long something lasted (followed by a feminine singular time period).
additional_notes: Durant = 'during' or 'for' and is interchangeable with 'pendant' in most contexts. 'Une' is the feminine indefinite article, so 'durant une' is followed by a feminine time unit (semaine, journée, heure, nuit, etc.). Used to state duration: 'durant une semaine' = 'for a week'. Formality: neutral; slightly more formal/literary than 'pendant' but common in speech.
target_language_example: Il a voyagé durant une journée complète.
native_language_example: He traveled for a whole day.

meaning: lifespan; lifetime; useful life (how long something or someone lives or lasts).
additional_notes: Used for people, animals, devices, products, or components to indicate how long they live or remain functional. Can mean 'life expectancy' (average human lifespan) or 'service life' (battery life, lifespan of a window). Often followed by de + noun (durée de vie de la batterie, de la fenêtre, etc.).
target_language_example: La durée de vie moyenne d'un téléphone est d'environ trois ans.
native_language_example: The average lifespan of a phone is about three years.

meaning: as soon as possible; at the earliest opportunity.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to indicate doing something without unnecessary delay. Often shortened in speech/writing to 'dès que possible' or 'dès que je peux/peux' (with pronoun change). Equivalent to English ASAP. Use with future or conditional verbs: 'Je le ferai dès que possible.'
target_language_example: Je vous enverrai les documents dès que possible.
native_language_example: I will send you the documents as soon as possible.

meaning: as soon as
additional_notes: Used to link two actions: the second happens immediately when the first occurs. Can be followed by indicative mood for real/expected events. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je t'appelle dès que j'arrive.
native_language_example: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.

meaning: decided to (do something).
additional_notes: Past tense (il/elle se décida à ...) of the pronominal verb se décider à: to make up one's mind or finally decide to do something. Followed by an infinitive (à + infinitive) or sometimes à + verb/place (y aller). Commonly used in written/narrative French; spoken French often uses 'décider de' or 'se décider à' in present/passé composé (elle s'est décidée à...).
target_language_example: Elle se décida à parler au directeur.
native_language_example: She decided to speak to the manager.

meaning: part of a passive construction meaning 'the decision was...' (followed by a past participle).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but the start of a passive sentence: 'la décision a été + past participle' = 'the decision was + verb(ed)'. Common verbs: prise (taken/made), reportée (postponed). Use to describe actions done to the decision. Note word order: definite article (la), noun (décision), auxiliary avoir in present (a) + été (past participle of être) + past participle of main verb.
target_language_example: La décision a été annulée hier.
native_language_example: The decision was canceled yesterday.

meaning: 'decorations for' (used with a noun to indicate what the decorations are for, e.g. Noël = Christmas decorations).
additional_notes: Followed by a noun (often a holiday, event or place). Common collocation: 'décorations de Noël' = Christmas decorations. Can be used in different tenses with verbs like 'installer', 'monter', 'mettre', 'décorer'.
target_language_example: Nous avons rangé les décorations de Noël après la fête.
native_language_example: We put away the Christmas decorations after the party.

target_language_multi_word_term: le petit déjeuner est / le déjeuner est
meaning: ‘breakfast/lunch is ...’ — used to say that breakfast or lunch is (ready/served/etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the structure noun + est (is). 'Le petit déjeuner est prêt' = 'breakfast is ready.' 'Le déjeuner est servi' = 'lunch is served.' Use 'petit déjeuner' for breakfast and 'déjeuner' for lunch. Common verbs after 'est': prêt (ready), servi (served), inclus (included), prêté (rare).
target_language_example: Le petit déjeuner est prêt, vous pouvez venir.
native_language_example: Breakfast is ready, you can come.

meaning: already seen
additional_notes: Literally 'already seen'. Used both for the psychological phenomenon (a strong sense that a current situation has happened before) and more simply to say you've seen someone or something before. Informal spoken forms may drop the 'je' (e.g. "T'as déjà vu ça ?").
target_language_example: J'ai l'impression de l'avoir déjà vu.
native_language_example: I feel like I've already seen him/it.

meaning: 'hit-and-run' (the crime of leaving the scene after causing an accident).
additional_notes: Refers to leaving an accident scene without stopping to help or exchange information; used in police/reports and everyday speech. Often appears with verbs like 'commettre', 'signaler', 'être victime de'.
target_language_example: La voiture a pris la fuite — c'était clairement un délit de fuite.
native_language_example: The car fled the scene — it was clearly a hit-and-run.

meaning: common denominator; something shared by different things (literal: math denominator).
additional_notes: Used both in math (lowest common denominator) and figuratively to mean a shared characteristic or cause among different items or problems. In math: "plus petit dénominateur commun" = least common denominator. Can be singular or plural depending on context.
target_language_example: Le dénominateur commun entre ces deux projets est le manque de budget.
native_language_example: The common denominator between these two projects is a lack of budget.

meaning: to go too far; to cross the line (behave in an unacceptable or excessive way).
additional_notes: Used when someone's words or actions are beyond what is acceptable. Often used in spoken French to express that a limit of politeness or propriety has been crossed. Can apply to insults, rude behaviour, excessive demands, etc.
target_language_example: Il a vraiment dépassé les bornes en parlant ainsi à sa collègue.
native_language_example: He really went too far by speaking to his colleague like that.

meaning: asks whether an action would bother or inconvenience someone ("does it bother you if...").
additional_notes: Commonly used to politely request permission or check for objection. Often appears as "Ça te/vous dérange si je... ?" with informal "te" or formal/plural "vous". Can be followed by verbs in the present or subjunctive (colloquially present). Equivalent to "Est-ce que ça vous dérange si... ?"
target_language_example: Ça vous dérange si j'ouvre la fenêtre ?
native_language_example: Does it bother you if I open the window?

meaning: private detective; private investigator.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a person hired to investigate private matters (infidelity, missing persons, fraud, etc.). Agreement: 'détective' is masculine; used without article in short IDs ("Arbogast, détective privé"). Can be used with verbs like engager (to hire) or être (to be).
target_language_example: Elle a engagé un détective privé pour retrouver son frère.
native_language_example: She hired a private detective to find her brother.

meaning: 'I hate my...' (first-person singular + 'my')
additional_notes: Déteste = 'hate' (verb, je déteste = I hate). 'Mon' is the masculine singular possessive used before masculine nouns and before feminine nouns that begin with a vowel sound (e.g. mon amie). Together they start phrases like 'Je déteste mon ...' to express dislike or strong negative feeling about something you own or are related to (job, body, father, country in example 4). Use 'ma' for feminine nouns without a vowel (ma voiture), 'mes' for plural (mes amis). Tone can be strong — in polite contexts consider milder verbs like 'n'aime pas'.
target_language_example: Je déteste mon travail en ce moment.
native_language_example: I hate my job at the moment.

meaning: 'hate to see' or 'really dislike seeing' (followed by noun / clause).
additional_notes: Common construction: détester + voir + [noun/infinitive/that-clause implied]. Expresses strong emotional dislike at witnessing something (people, images, situations). Often followed by direct object (des animaux, des enfants, sa photo) or a verb phrase (voir quelqu'un + infinitive/participle). Tone is neutral to strong; not slang.
target_language_example: Je déteste voir des animaux blessés.
native_language_example: I hate to see injured animals.

meaning: 'I hate to be' / 'I hate being'.
additional_notes: Combines the verb détester (to hate) with the infinitive être (to be). Used to state dislike of a state or situation. In English you can translate as 'I hate being ...' or 'I hate to be ...'. Conjugate détester to match the subject (e.g., Je déteste, Tu détestes, Il/Elle déteste).
target_language_example: Je déteste être en retard au travail.
native_language_example: I hate being late for work.

meaning: 'destroyed the' (past/past-participle form of détruire used with a masculine singular noun)
additional_notes: Détruit is the past participle of détruire (to destroy). In sentences like the examples it functions as the passé composé (e.g. a détruit = has/—destroyed) or as an adjective/past participle agreeing when necessary. Here 'le' is the masculine singular definite article before the noun (le château, le canapé, le jardin, le bâtiment). For feminine nouns use 'la' (a détruit la maison). To form the passé composé: avoir + détruit (elle a détruit, ils ont détruit).
target_language_example: Le vent a détruit le toit.
native_language_example: The wind destroyed the roof.

meaning: 'should have told me (it)'.
additional_notes: This is the perfect conditional of devoir + object pronouns: 'aurais dû' (you should have) + 'me' (to me) + 'le' (it/that). Used to express that someone ought to have told the speaker something in the past. In natural speech you will usually see the full form 'tu aurais dû me le dire' or 'vous auriez dû me le dire.'
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû me le dire plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have told me that earlier.

meaning: 'owed/should have to us' or part of compound verbs meaning 'had to us' / 'should have (done) to us' (past participle + indirect object pronoun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the past participle dû (from devoir) followed by the indirect object pronoun nous. Devoir in the past tense (avoir dû) can mean 'had to' / 'must have' or, in conditional past (aurait dû / aurait dû), 'should have (done)'. The pronoun nous means 'to us' or 'us' and refers to the indirect object. Word order: past participle + pronoun often appears when the pronoun follows the verb (as in compound tenses with infinitives or in some constructions). Examples above show meanings like 'he should have returned it to us', 'they must have spotted us', 'you should have told us'.
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû nous prévenir plus tôt.
native_language_example: You should have warned us earlier.

meaning: should have (to) you
additional_notes: This is the past participle dû (from devoir) followed by the clitic pronoun t' (te) attached to a verb that follows: e.g. J'aurais dû t'appeler = I should have called you. In English you use 'should have' + past participle. The construction expresses regret or obligation not met. The literal sense 'owed you' can appear in other contexts (e.g. quelqu'un a dû t'apporter = someone must have brought you), so pay attention to context: in conditional perfect (j'aurais dû) it means 'should have'.
target_language_example: J'aurais dû t'aider hier.
native_language_example: I should have helped you yesterday.

meaning: email; an electronic message sent or received via the internet.
additional_notes: Commonly used in French as both a noun and verb (envoyer un e-mail). Pronunciation often like English. Alternative French words: courriel (more formal/Canadian) or mél. Used with articles: un e-mail, l'e-mail. Plural can be e-mails.
target_language_example: Je t'ai envoyé un e-mail avec les informations.
native_language_example: I sent you an email with the information.

meaning: fresh water (not salt water).
additional_notes: Used to describe bodies of water (rivers, lakes) or animals that live in non-salty water. Opposite: eau salée or eau de mer (sea water). Common in biological and geographic contexts.
target_language_example: Ces poissons ne supportent pas l'eau douce.
native_language_example: These fish cannot tolerate fresh water.

meaning: 'personal effect' or 'personal possession' (an item belonging to a person).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's belongings or possessions (often in contexts like travel, luggage, police reports, estates). Can be pluralized as "effets personnels" to mean "personal belongings." Not commonly used to describe emotions—it's about physical items.
target_language_example: Un policier a retrouvé un effet personnel près du lieu de l'accident.
native_language_example: A police officer found a personal effect near the scene of the accident.

meaning: 'the effect that' or 'the impression that' (what something causes or how it makes someone feel).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the effect, impression or feeling produced by something. Often follows verbs like 'savoir', 'faire' or expressions like 'ça me fait' (it makes me feel). Common in everyday speech to describe emotional or physical reactions and social impressions.
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas l'effet que ça lui fera.
native_language_example: I don't know the effect that will have on him/her.

meaning: side effect (an unintended effect, especially of a drug or action).
additional_notes: Commonly used in medical contexts to describe unwanted or secondary consequences of a treatment or medication. Can also be used figuratively for indirect, unintended results of actions or policies.
target_language_example: Un effet secondaire fréquent de ce médicament est la somnolence.
native_language_example: A common side effect of this medicine is drowsiness.

meaning: well
additional_notes: A filler or discourse marker used to start a response, show hesitation, introduce a conclusion, or move the conversation forward. Tone and context change the nuance (surprise, resignation, reflection). Very common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Eh bien, d'accord — commençons tout de suite.
native_language_example: Well, all right — let's start right away.

meaning: herself (emphatic/reflexive).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize 'she' (contrast or focus) or as a reflexive pronoun meaning 'she did it herself'. Can appear alone for emphasis ('Elle-même.' = 'She herself.'). Agreement: 'elle-même' (singular feminine); plural would be 'elles-mêmes'. Often follows the verb or subject.
target_language_example: Elle a réparé la porte elle-même.
native_language_example: She repaired the door herself.

meaning: Used in questions to ask whether something (feminine) is correct or right.
additional_notes: The phrase appears in the structure '... est-elle correcte ?' where 'elle' is the subject pronoun referring back to a feminine noun (la réponse, la traduction, la phrase, la montre, etc.). In spoken and written French, you can also ask 'Est-ce que c'est correct ?' or 'C'est correct ?' For a masculine noun use 'est-il correct ?' or simply 'correcte' agrees in gender (correcte for feminine, correct for masculine).
target_language_example: Cette phrase est-elle correcte ?
native_language_example: Is this sentence correct?

meaning: she is on the (masculine singular noun follows)
additional_notes: A simple phrase meaning 'she is on the…' used before a masculine singular noun (le). It is just the subject pronoun + être + preposition + definite article. Common in literal contexts (e.g. elle est sur le canapé) or in descriptive phrases. Make sure the noun after 'le' is masculine and singular; if feminine use 'elle est sur la', if plural 'elle est sur les'.
target_language_example: Elle est sur le canapé.
native_language_example: She is on the sofa.

meaning: she demanded (formal/literary past tense).
additional_notes: Elle exigea is the passé simple (literary past) of exiger used with 'elle' — means 'she demanded' or 'she insisted on'. Commonly followed by de + infinitive (e.g. de voir...). In spoken and informal written French, the passé composé (elle a exigé) is used instead. Used in formal, narrative or written contexts.
target_language_example: Elle exigea une explication immédiate.
native_language_example: She demanded an immediate explanation.

meaning: literally 'she/it at night' — combination of pronoun (elle) + time expression (la nuit).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it's the pronoun 'elle' (she or it) followed by the time expression 'la nuit' (at night). Depending on context, 'elle' can mean 'she' (a person) or 'it' (a feminine noun, e.g. la lune). Word order matters: 'elle la nuit' appears in sentences like questions with inversion (Pourquoi la lune brille-t-elle la nuit ?) or statements indicating presence/actions at night (avec elle la nuit dernière = with her last night). For beginners: recognize 'la nuit' = 'at night' and 'elle' = 'she/it'.
target_language_example: La lampe s'allume toute seule, on la voit bien elle la nuit.
native_language_example: The lamp lights up by itself, you can see it well at night.

meaning: 'she' + past participle 'passed' (from verb passer) appearing when 'elle' is subject and passer is in a compound tense or construction, e.g. in questions or statements meaning 'where did she go?', 'how did she go/turn out?', or 'she went/was passed'.
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom by itself; it's the sequence of subject pronoun 'elle' followed by the past participle 'passée' (agreeing in gender) when used with the auxiliary être (e.g. Où est‑elle passée ?). Common uses: asking where someone went (Où est‑elle passée ? / Par où est‑elle passée ? / Où est‑elle passée alors ?), asking how an event went when reflexive (Comment s'est‑elle passée ?), or noting that she went unnoticed (elle est passée inaperçue). Word order and auxiliary (être) are required in compound tenses; the past participle agrees in gender with 'elle'.
target_language_example: Mais où est-elle passée ?
native_language_example: But where did she go?

meaning: she (is the one) who has / who did (used to emphasize that she is the person who performed an action).
additional_notes: Used in cleft sentences (C'est... qui/que) to emphasize the subject: 'C'est elle qui a...' = 'She is the one who...'. Follows with a past participle or verb phrase (often passé composé). Common in spoken and written French to point out or confirm who did something.
target_language_example: C'est elle qui a envoyé la lettre.
native_language_example: She is the one who sent the letter.

meaning: contraction of 'elle t'' used before a verb: 'she (to) you...' — 'she [verb] you' or 'did she [verb] you?'.
additional_notes: This is 'elle' (she) + the clitic object pronoun 'te' reduced to 't'' before a vowel or mute h, followed by a past participle or verb (e.g. a dit, a aimé, attend, adore). It represents 'she' as the subject and 'you' as the direct or indirect object depending on the verb. In spoken and informal written French the apostrophe appears (t') when the verb begins with a vowel: elle t'a (she told you), elle t'aime (she loves you). Word order and meaning depend on the verb: elle t'a quitté = 'she left you'; elle t'en a parlé = 'she talked to you about it'.
target_language_example: Elle t'a envoyé un message hier.
native_language_example: She sent you a message yesterday.

meaning: themselves (feminine plural reflexive/emphatic pronoun).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action is done by the women/them (feminine group) or reflexively. Can follow a verb or preposition: 'elles l'ont fait elles-mêmes' (they did it themselves). Contracts with pronouns in object position (e.g., 'parler d'elles-mêmes' = 'talk about themselves').
target_language_example: Elles l'ont préparé elles-mêmes.
native_language_example: They prepared it themselves.

meaning: ‘all of them’ referring to a group of females (they all).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that every member of a female group shares a quality or status. Often appears after a verb in questions or statements: 'Sont-elles toutes...' = 'Are they all...'. 'Elles toutes' can be reordered as 'toutes elles' (more emphatic) or 'toutes' placed before a noun (toutes les filles). Pronoun 'elles' makes it feminine plural.
target_language_example: Sont-elles toutes prêtes pour le départ ?
native_language_example: Are they all ready to leave?

meaning: take (someone) to (a place).
additional_notes: From the verb emmener (to take someone). Used when someone is bringing another person to a destination. The object is a person (often expressed with a pronoun: le, la, l', vous, etc.). Common with places: à l'hôpital, à l'école, à la gare. If talking about taking oneself, use emmener vs. amener (regional/nuance) — both mean to bring/take someone; conduire is used for driving. Followed by à + place or a person.
target_language_example: Je l'emmène à la gare demain matin.
native_language_example: I'm taking him/her to the station tomorrow morning.

meaning: fingerprint (the unique pattern on a fingertip); also used for biometric fingerprint
additional_notes: Commonly used in contexts of identification, security, police, or unlocking devices (e.g., téléphone à empreinte digitale). 'Empreinte' alone can mean 'imprint' or 'footprint'; 'empreinte digitale' specifically refers to fingerprints. Plural: empreintes digitales.
target_language_example: Le policier a relevé une empreinte digitale sur la porte.
native_language_example: The police officer lifted a fingerprint from the door.

meaning: to borrow (some amount of something, often money) — used with 'de' + noun (e.g. 'emprunter de l'argent').
additional_notes: Used when you take something temporarily. With a specific lender, French more commonly uses 'emprunter quelque chose à quelqu'un' or 'de' + noun for the thing borrowed. Examples: 'Hé, je peux t'emprunter de l'argent ?' (Can I borrow some money from you?), 'J'ai besoin d'emprunter de l'argent.' When asking informally, 'Je peux t'emprunter de l'argent ?' is common.
target_language_example: Hé, je peux t'emprunter de l'argent ?
native_language_example: Hey, can I borrow some money from you?

meaning: to borrow (a ...).
additional_notes: Used when asking to take something temporarily from someone. Conjugate the verb (emprunter) as needed and change the noun after 'un' to the item: e.g. 'emprunter un stylo' = borrow a pen. When the item is specified with a pronoun use forms like 't'emprunter' (borrow from you) or 'vous l'emprunter' (borrow it from you).
target_language_example: Est-ce que je peux emprunter un chargeur, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can I borrow a charger, please?

meaning: 'a snack' (small bite between meals).
additional_notes: Common noun meaning a light food taken between meals. Often used in spoken and written French. Can be singular or plural (des en-cas). Usually unstressed; may appear with verbs like prendre, préparer. Hyphenated: en-cas.
target_language_example: Je te prépare un petit en-cas pour la route.
native_language_example: I'll make you a little snack for the road.

meaning: as a friend; in a friendly way (offering advice or help rather than hostility)
additional_notes: Used to indicate the speaker's friendly intentions or that a comment is meant kindly — often said before giving criticism or advice. Common in phrases like "Je te parle en ami" (I'm speaking to you as a friend). Not idiomatic to use literally with an article (not "en un ami").
target_language_example: Je te parle en ami : écoute ce que je dis.
native_language_example: I'm speaking to you as a friend: listen to what I say.

meaning: back; backwards; back (movement) or back (to a previous state).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical movement toward the back (Mets ta tête en arrière = tilt your head back) or figuratively to go back to a previous point/state (revenir en arrière = go back/undo). Can appear in commands (En arrière toute! = Reverse! / All back!) or in phrases like revenir en arrière (to go back).
target_language_example: Si tu veux annuler, tu peux revenir en arrière.
native_language_example: If you want to cancel, you can go back.

meaning: 'meanwhile' or 'for the time being' (while waiting).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens during a wait or as a temporary measure. Often followed by a clause or comma + phrase. Can be used alone as a discourse marker ('In the meantime').
target_language_example: En attendant la réparation, prenez le bus.
native_language_example: In the meantime, take the bus while the repair is done.

meaning: 'while waiting for' or 'until (something happens)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause with the subjunctive when referring to an event or action that is expected or anticipated. Equivalent to 'while waiting for' or 'until' in English. Commonly followed by a verb (e.g. 'en attendant que + subjunctive'). Can also be used without 'que' as 'en attendant + noun' (e.g. 'en attendant le bus').
target_language_example: En attendant que le train arrive, nous lisons.
native_language_example: While waiting for the train to arrive, we are reading.

meaning: 'waiting' or 'on hold' (in a state of waiting)
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is waiting or put on hold. Common in phone contexts (être mis en attente = put on hold) and in formal contexts (a request, application or process pending). Can be used alone as a brief status: "En attente."
target_language_example: Votre commande est en attente de vérification.
native_language_example: Your order is waiting for verification.

meaning: 'under no circumstances' or 'in no case'.
additional_notes: Used to strongly forbid or rule out something. Often placed at the start of a sentence (En aucun cas, ...), after a verb with 'ne' (tu ne dois en aucun cas ...), or alone for emphasis. It's formal/neutral — common in both spoken and written French to give a firm prohibition.
target_language_example: Tu ne dois en aucun cas partager ton mot de passe.
native_language_example: You must under no circumstances share your password.

meaning: in no way; not at all; in no manner
additional_notes: Used to deny any connection, possibility, or manner. Often appears in negative constructions (similar to 'en aucune façon' or 'd'aucune manière'). Formal or emphatic; in spoken French you might hear 'en aucune façon' or simply 'pas du tout'. Can be used alone as a short emphatic response.
target_language_example: Je ne suis impliqué en aucune manière dans cette affaire.
native_language_example: I am not involved in this matter in any way.

meaning: early; ahead of time.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something arrives or happens before the expected time. Commonly follows a time expression (e.g. 'dix minutes en avance'). Can refer to people, trains, events. Opposite: 'en retard' (late).
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé en avance pour la réunion.
native_language_example: I arrived early for the meeting.

meaning: forward; ahead; in front (movement or position).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement toward the front or the position ahead. Can be used literally (physically leaning or moving forward) or figuratively/idiomatically as an encouragement (e.g., "En avant, cow-boy!" = "Go ahead, cowboy!/Move forward!"). Common in commands and directions. Pair with verbs like aller, avancer, regarder, or se pencher.
target_language_example: Penche-toi un peu en avant pour que je voie.
native_language_example: Lean forward a little so I can see.

meaning: 'full speed ahead' or 'forward at full power' (command to move forward at maximum speed)
additional_notes: A nautical/military-style command used to order all engines or units to go forward at full power. Often appears as an imperative exclamation. Literal words: en (in), avant (forward), toute (all), so it is compositional. Not common in casual conversation; more formal or technical (ships, machinery, vehicles).
target_language_example: En avant toute ! On met toutes les machines en marche.
native_language_example: Full speed ahead! Start all the engines.

meaning: downstairs
additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower location or level (physically downstairs or below a reference point). Commonly used alone (Je suis en bas) or with verbs (aller en bas, porter en bas). Can also mean 'down' in a general sense (Là, en bas = down there).
target_language_example: Je descends, je te retrouve en bas.
native_language_example: I'm coming down, I'll meet you downstairs.

meaning: down/downwards at the bottom of; below (location).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is located lower down, at the bottom of a slope, street, building, etc. Commonly followed by a place (la rue, la colline, l'escalier). Can mean 'down the street' or 'at the bottom of the street' in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il y a un café en bas de la rue.
native_language_example: There is a cafe down the street / at the bottom of the street.

meaning: in style; in a grand/good way; spectacularly (often used about endings or departures).
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a striking, impressive, or stylish manner — especially 'partir en beauté' (to leave/finish on a high note). Can be exclamatory on its own. Not slang; idiomatic but fairly transparent.
target_language_example: Il veut partir en beauté en faisant un dernier discours.
native_language_example: He wants to leave on a high note by giving one last speech.

meaning: for the better; in a good way
additional_notes: Used to indicate improvement or a positive direction/result. Can stand alone (En bien.) or appear in phrases like 'en bien pire' (= by far worse, ironically using 'bien' as intensifier) and 'aller/changer en bien' (= to change for the better). Also appears in 'en bien des' meaning 'many' (literally 'in many'), which is a different fixed expression — be careful: 'en bien des théories' means 'in many theories' not 'many good theories'.
target_language_example: J'espère que la situation évoluera en bien.
native_language_example: I hope the situation will change for the better.

meaning: made of concrete; (figurative) rock-solid, very strong or reliable
additional_notes: Literally describes something constructed from concrete (e.g., a floor, wall). Commonly used figuratively to mean 'foolproof', 'undeniable' or 'hard/unchanging' (an alibi en béton = a rock‑solid alibi; un cœur en béton = a hard/stone heart). Context determines literal vs. figurative meaning.
target_language_example: Son explication était en béton, personne n'a pu la contredire.
native_language_example: His explanation was rock-solid; no one could contradict it.

meaning: 'secretly' or 'on the sly'.
additional_notes: Used to describe actions done in secret, hidden from others. Can imply secrecy because of disapproval, surprise, or privacy. Common with people (rencontrer quelqu'un en cachette), actions (partir en cachette), or observations (regarder en cachette).
target_language_example: Ils se sont rencontrés en cachette pendant des semaines.
native_language_example: They met secretly for weeks.

meaning: 'in case of' or 'in the event of' (used to introduce a possible situation, contingency, or condition, typically followed by a noun).
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase used before a noun to warn about, prepare for, or state responsibility regarding a specific situation. Often followed by a noun: en cas de pluie, en cas d'urgence, en cas de problème. Not normally used to introduce a full clause—use 'si' for clauses. Can appear in formal and informal contexts depending on register and sentence.
target_language_example: En cas de pluie, la fête sera déplacée à l'intérieur.
native_language_example: In case of rain, the party will be moved indoors.

meaning: in question; being accused, challenged, or implicated.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like mettre/remettre/mettre en cause to mean 'to call into question,' 'to challenge,' 'to accuse,' or 'to involve/implicate' someone or something. Context decides nuance: can mean 'to doubt someone's ability/authority' (challenge) or 'to implicate/accuse' (legal). Common in formal and neutral registers.
target_language_example: On ne doit pas mettre en cause sa réputation sans preuves.
native_language_example: We must not call his reputation into question without proof.

meaning: on the run; fleeing (usually from the police or authorities).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who has escaped custody or is avoiding arrest. Common in news and everyday speech. Often followed by agent (ex.: 'un tueur en cavale') or used as 'être en cavale' = to be on the run. Slightly dramatic but neutral; not slang.
target_language_example: Ils ont dit qu'il était en cavale depuis trois jours.
native_language_example: They said he has been on the run for three days.

meaning: right now
additional_notes: Used to indicate the present time or current situation. Can describe something happening now (temporary) or a current trend/period. Equivalent to 'en ce moment-même' (emphatic).
target_language_example: Je suis un peu débordé en ce moment.
native_language_example: I'm a bit overwhelmed at the moment.

meaning: at that time; in those days.
additional_notes: Refers to a past period being described or remembered. Often used to contrast past and present (nostalgic or descriptive). Can be placed at the start or end of a sentence. Equivalent to 'à cette époque-là'.
target_language_example: En ce temps-là, on vivait sans téléphone portable.
native_language_example: In those days, we lived without mobile phones.

meaning: regarding; as for; concerning
additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or aspect being talked about. Formal/neutral register and very common in spoken and written French. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'en ce qui concerne toi/lui/ce projet'). Can be replaced in more informal contexts by 'pour ce qui est de' or simply 'pour' or 'quant à'.
target_language_example: En ce qui concerne le délai, nous avons besoin de deux semaines.
native_language_example: Regarding the deadline, we need two weeks.

meaning: 'as far as I'm concerned' / 'regarding me'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal opinion, position, or feelings about a topic. Complete phrase in examples is 'en ce qui me concerne' (formal). Often shortened in speech to 'pour moi' or 'en ce qui me regarde', but 'en ce qui me concerne' is common in both spoken and written French. Followed by a comma and a clause stating your view.
target_language_example: En ce qui me concerne, je préfère rester ici.
native_language_example: As far as I'm concerned, I'd rather stay here.

meaning: in person; physically present (literally 'in flesh and bone').
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is physically present rather than only known by voice, photo, message, or online. Often used after meeting someone you've previously known only remotely or from descriptions. Formality: neutral; can be used in both polite and casual contexts. Gender agreement affects verbs/adjectives (e.g., rencontré / rencontrée) but the phrase itself is fixed.
target_language_example: Je suis si heureux de te voir en chair et en os !
native_language_example: I'm so happy to see you in person!

meaning: 'in charge of' / 'responsible for'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has responsibility or oversight for a person, group, task, place, or project. Followed by a noun (e.g., en charge de la classe, en charge du secteur). Formal and neutral; common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je suis en charge de l'organisation de la réunion.
native_language_example: I am in charge of organizing the meeting.

meaning: on the way / en route / along the way.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently traveling toward a destination (Il est en chemin = he's on the way). It can also mean 'along the way' for something that happened during a trip (quelque chose en chemin). Common in short replies: 'En chemin.' = 'On my/our way.'
target_language_example: Je suis en chemin, j'arrive dans dix minutes.
native_language_example: I'm on my way; I'll arrive in ten minutes.

meaning: angry
additional_notes: Used to describe someone feeling anger. Typically used with être (être en colère) or with reflexive se mettre en colère (to get angry). Can be followed by a preposition + object (en colère contre/avec quelqu'un or en colère à propos de quelque chose).
target_language_example: Il est en colère contre son frère.
native_language_example: He is angry with his brother.

meaning: 'in how much (time)' — asks about the duration needed for something.
additional_notes: Used to ask how long something will take. Always followed by a time expression (e.g., temps, semaines, jours, minutes) or a verb phrase implying arrival/completion. Common constructions: "En combien de temps... ?" (How long does it take / will it take?) or shortened to "En combien de temps ?" as a follow-up question.
target_language_example: En combien de temps peux-tu finir ce rapport ?
native_language_example: How long will it take you to finish this report?

meaning: in common; shared (between people or groups).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is shared or mutual (e.g., interests, traits, decisions). Common constructions: 'avoir quelque chose en commun' (to have something in common) and 'pris en commun' (made jointly). Can follow nouns (des intérêts en commun) or appear after 'avoir'.
target_language_example: Nous avons beaucoup d'amis en commun.
native_language_example: We have many friends in common.

meaning: in the company of; with (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say you are with someone or accompanied by someone. Formal/neutral tone. Can refer to people or animals. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., en compagnie de mes amis, en compagnie de lui).
target_language_example: Je suis en compagnie de mes collègues ce soir.
native_language_example: I am in the company of my colleagues tonight.

meaning: with full knowledge / knowingly / being fully informed
additional_notes: Used to say someone acted with awareness of the facts or consequences. Often translates as “knowingly,” “with full knowledge,” or “informedly.” Common in formal and neutral registers. Can be used alone as a short reply (meaning “I know” or “I did it knowingly”).
target_language_example: Il a signé le contrat en connaissance de cause.
native_language_example: He signed the contract with full knowledge (knowingly).

meaning: in a romantic relationship; as a couple.
additional_notes: Used to say two people are romantically together. Can describe a relationship status (être en couple = to be in a relationship). Often contrasts with 'célibataire' (single). Not necessarily married. Common in everyday French.
target_language_example: Ils sont en couple depuis deux ans.
native_language_example: They have been a couple for two years.

meaning: in progress; ongoing; currently happening.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is happening now or underway (a process, project, investigation, transmission, etc.). Common in formal and everyday contexts. Often follows the noun (l'enquête est en cours) or appears alone as a short status message (En cours.).
target_language_example: Le dépannage est en cours, ça devrait être réglé bientôt.
native_language_example: The repair is in progress; it should be fixed soon.

meaning: in the process of; during (an action or event).
additional_notes: Used to say something is currently happening or ongoing (en cours de + noun/verb infinitive) or to indicate 'during' when referring to a class or session (en cours de français = during French class). Common with verbs: en cours de construction / en cours de réparation. Not used for finished actions.
target_language_example: Le rapport est en cours de rédaction.
native_language_example: The report is being written / is in the process of being written.

meaning: 'in danger' or 'at risk'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is threatened, unsafe, or at risk of harm. Common in both literal (physical danger) and figurative (financial, legal, etc.) contexts. Usually follows the verb être (être en danger) or verbs implying a state (se retrouver en danger, mettre quelqu'un en danger).
target_language_example: Les voyageurs sont en danger à cause de la tempête.
native_language_example: The travelers are in danger because of the storm.

meaning: outside of; away from; not involved in.
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical location outside something (en dehors de la maison = outside the house) or figurative exclusion (stay out of my business). It is followed by de + noun. Can mean 'except' in some contexts when used as 'en dehors de'.
target_language_example: Restez en dehors de cette affaire.
native_language_example: Stay out of this matter.

meaning: outside of; apart from; not involved in.
additional_notes: Common prepositional phrase. Can mean physically outside (outside of a place), figuratively apart from or except for (apart from), or to say someone is not involved in something (leave someone out). Context determines translation: 'outside of' (physical), 'apart from/except' (exclusion), or 'not involved in' (avoid involvement). Often followed by a noun or pronoun.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi en dehors de cette dispute.
native_language_example: Leave me out of this argument.

meaning: under; below; beneath (physically or figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both for physical position (under/beneath) and for comparative measures (below a value, below average). Followed by a noun, number, or article + noun. Can be interchangeable with 'sous' in many contexts (e.g. 'sous zéro' vs 'en dessous de zéro'), but 'en dessous de' is common before a specific value or phrase.
target_language_example: Le chat dort en dessous de la table.
native_language_example: The cat sleeps under the table.

meaning: 'in trouble' or 'having difficulties' (can be general or specific, e.g. financial, practical, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is experiencing problems or struggling. Can refer to short-term trouble (e.g. in danger, needing help) or ongoing difficulties (e.g. financial hardship). Context clarifies the type of difficulty. Common in everyday and formal registers.
target_language_example: Elle est en difficulté avec ses paiements ce mois-ci.
native_language_example: She is having difficulties with her payments this month.

meaning: 'live' (as in live broadcast: happening now, not recorded).
additional_notes: Used to say something is being broadcast or shown in real time (TV, radio, streaming). Commonly placed before a noun (en direct à la télé) or alone to indicate current live coverage. Can also be 'en direct de' + location or person.
target_language_example: La conférence est diffusée en direct sur Internet.
native_language_example: The conference is being broadcast live on the Internet.

meaning: quietly; secretly; on the sly.
additional_notes: Informal expression used to describe doing something discreetly or leaving without being noticed. Often used with verbs like 'filer', 'partir', 'sortir' or 'se tirer'. Conveys mild secrecy or stealth rather than malicious intent.
target_language_example: Il est parti en douce avant que personne ne le voie.
native_language_example: He left quietly before anyone saw him.

meaning: gently; softly; smoothly.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do something gently, slowly, or carefully. Can describe actions (do it gently), processes (happen smoothly), or manners (in a gentle way). Common in spoken French: Allez-y en douceur = Go gently / take it easy. Not slang.
target_language_example: Parle-lui en douceur, il est encore fragile.
native_language_example: Speak to him gently; he is still fragile.

meaning: in the end; ultimately; all in all.
additional_notes: Used to summarize or draw a final conclusion after considering facts or a story. Similar to 'finalement' or 'en fin de compte' but slightly more formal. Often placed at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: En définitive, il a décidé de refuser l'offre.
native_language_example: In the end, he decided to turn down the offer.

meaning: despite; in spite of (followed by a noun or noun phrase).
additional_notes: Formal connective used to introduce a contrast: it means that something happens although there is an obstacle or contrary fact. It is followed by a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase (e.g., en dépit de la pluie, en dépit de ses efforts). Synonyms: malgré, malgré que + subjunctive (different structure).
target_language_example: En dépit de la fatigue, elle continua à travailler.
native_language_example: Despite the fatigue, she kept working.

meaning: in detail; thoroughly; with all the specifics.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is described, explained, or examined thoroughly. Can follow verbs like décrire, expliquer, discuter, raconter. Often used with un peu (un peu plus en détail) to ask for a bit more explanation.
target_language_example: Peux-tu me l'expliquer en détail, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me in detail, please?

meaning: indeed / in fact (used to confirm, agree, or introduce support/explanation).
additional_notes: Used to confirm or reinforce a statement, agree with someone, or introduce an explanation. Can appear at the start of a sentence (En effet, ...) or after the verb/phrase (..., en effet.). Tone is neutral and common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: En effet, c'est exactement ce que je voulais dire.
native_language_example: Indeed, that's exactly what I meant.

meaning: completely; in full; whole (with emphasis on completeness).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is done or applies to the whole/entire thing, from start to finish. Common with verbs like lire, remplir, manger, détruire. Can be used alone as a short question ("En entier ?") to ask if something is complete. Equivalent to "complètement" or "tout entier" in many contexts.
target_language_example: J'ai regardé la série en entier ce week-end.
native_language_example: I watched the whole series over the weekend.

meaning: opposite; across (from).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something or someone located directly opposite or across from another place or person. Commonly followed by 'de' + noun (en face de la maison) or used alone when context makes the reference clear. Can also be used in expressions meaning 'right in front of' or 'in the presence of' (informal/emphatic).
target_language_example: Le café est en face de la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: The café is opposite the library.

meaning: across from; opposite (facing something)
additional_notes: Used to indicate location directly opposite something (often with buildings, people, streets). Commonly followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., 'en face de la gare', 'en face de chez moi'). You can also say 'en face' alone if context is clear. Not formal/slang; literal and compositional.
target_language_example: Le café est en face de l'école.
native_language_example: The café is across from the school.

meaning: actually
additional_notes: Used to correct, clarify, emphasize or add new information; often appears at the start of a sentence or clause. Can soften or contrast what was said before ("actually/in fact"). Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: En fait, je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
native_language_example: Actually, I can't come tonight.

meaning: with family; as a family (doing something together).
additional_notes: Used to indicate an activity done together with family members. Common with verbs of going or spending time (aller, passer, camper, dîner, voyager). Neutral register. Gender/number of speaker affects other words but not this phrase.
target_language_example: Nous partons en famille ce week-end.
native_language_example: We're going as a family this weekend.

meaning: in favor of; supporting or for (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to express support, approval, or agreement with a proposal, person, plan, or idea. Followed by a noun or pronoun (en faveur de + X). Common in both formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Nous sommes en faveur de cette réforme.
native_language_example: We are in favor of this reform.

meaning: 'on fire' (burning).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is burning. Can describe buildings, vehicles, or places. Not idiomatic here — literal fire. Also used figuratively in informal contexts (e.g., someone 'on fire' meaning performing very well), but examples show literal use.
target_language_example: La voiture est en feu, appelle les pompiers !
native_language_example: The car is on fire, call the firefighters!

meaning: 'in the end' / 'ultimately' / 'all things considered'.
additional_notes: Used to summarize or give the final outcome or conclusion after considering everything. Common in spoken and written French to introduce a conclusion or final judgment.
target_language_example: En fin de compte, tout s'est bien passé.
native_language_example: In the end, everything went well.

meaning: 'sharply' or 'skyrocketing' (very quickly and steeply upward)
additional_notes: Used adverbially to describe something that rises very quickly or steeply (prices, figures, emotions, movement). Often translated as "skyrocketing," "soaring," or "shooting up." Can apply to physical movement (someone rising quickly) or abstract increases (prices, rates, flows).
target_language_example: Les ventes ont monté en flèche après la publicité.
native_language_example: Sales shot up after the advertisement.

meaning: depending on; based on; according to
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something varies or is determined by another factor. Followed by a noun or pronoun (en fonction de + quelque chose). Common in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Les horaires sont adaptés en fonction de la demande.
native_language_example: The schedules are adapted depending on demand.

meaning: in shape / in good shape; (also) in the shape of (when describing form).
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) As an adjective phrase meaning physically fit, well, or energetic: Je suis en forme = I'm in good shape/feeling well. 2) As part of a construction en forme de + noun to describe the shape of an object: un gâteau en forme de cœur = a cake in the shape of a heart. Context tells which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Après le jogging, je me sens en forme.
native_language_example: After the jog, I feel in shape / I feel great.

meaning: 'to warn' (to caution someone) or an imperative 'watch out/guard!' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used two main ways: as a verb phrase 'mettre en garde (contre)' meaning 'to warn/caution (against)'; and as an interjection 'En garde !' meaning 'Watch out!' or the fencing command 'On guard!'. Context decides sense. Commonly followed by 'contre' when warning about something. Literal components ('in guard') don't directly explain the idiom in all uses.
target_language_example: Il m'a mis en garde contre les vols dans le quartier.
native_language_example: He warned me about thefts in the neighborhood.

meaning: 'basically' / 'roughly' or 'in large pieces/large (when describing items)' depending on context.
additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase with two main uses: 1) colloquial discourse marker meaning 'basically', 'roughly speaking', or 'in short' to summarize or simplify an idea (very frequent in conversation). 2) literal descriptive use meaning 'large' or 'in large chunks' (e.g., 'en gros flocons' = large flakes). Context determines which sense is meant. Informal but widely used. Can be translated literally as 'in large'.
target_language_example: En gros, il faut trois heures pour y aller.
native_language_example: Basically, it takes three hours to get there.

meaning: 'as' or 'in the form of; used as' (to indicate something used to serve the role of something else).
additional_notes: Used to say that one thing is being used or presented as something else (often temporarily or symbolically). Common with nouns: en guise de + noun. Can be translated as "as," "as a," "in lieu of," or "by way of." Formal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Il a posé une caisse en guise de siège.
native_language_example: He used a crate as a seat.

meaning: 'in general' / 'generally' (to speak about what is usually true)
additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement or common tendency. Often placed at the start of a sentence and followed by a comma in written French. Can be interchangeable with 'généralement'.
target_language_example: En général, je prends du thé le matin.
native_language_example: Generally, I have tea in the morning.

meaning: 'rising' or 'on the rise' (prices, rates, value going up).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that is increasing (prices, currency, rates, etc.). Often follows the noun (Le prix est en hausse). Opposite: «en baisse» (falling). Can be used in present, past (étaient en hausse) and with articles as needed.
target_language_example: Les loyers sont en hausse cette année.
native_language_example: Rents are on the rise this year.

meaning: up; upstairs; above (indicating a higher place).
additional_notes: Used to indicate location at a higher position or floor. Can be alone ('en haut') or with modifiers like 'tout en haut' (at the very top). Common with verbs of movement (monter, grimper) and with être to say someone is upstairs or up somewhere.
target_language_example: Elle est en haut, dans sa chambre.
native_language_example: She is upstairs, in her room.

meaning: 'at the top of' or 'above' (location on or above something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position at the upper part of something (a building, page, list, etc.). Often followed by a noun: en haut de la page, en haut de la montagne. Can also be used without 'de' as 'en haut' meaning 'upstairs' or 'above'.
target_language_example: Il y a un drapeau en haut de la tour.
native_language_example: There is a flag at the top of the tower.

meaning: at stake; involved; in play.
additional_notes: Used to say what is at risk or what is involved in a situation. Often follows a noun (e.g. "beaucoup de choses en jeu") or appears in fixed expressions like "la vie est en jeu". Also used in phrases meaning 'to come into play' with verbs like "entrer en jeu" (you come into the situation).
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup d'enjeu(s) en jeu dans ce projet.
native_language_example: There is a lot at stake in this project.

meaning: 'in the air' / 'up in the air' — literal; idiomatic uses include 'up' (arms raised), 'ruined/thrown away', and sexual slang 'have sex'.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: physically in the air or raised (e.g., bras en l'air = arms up). Idiomatic meanings depend on context: 1) sexual slang: s'envoyer en l'air = have casual sex; 2) spoil/ruin: foutre/mettre en l'air = mess up or destroy something; 3) informal expression for being flustered or awkward (la queue en l'air = disordered/embarrassed in context). Register varies: literal uses are neutral; the sexual meaning is informal/slang and can be crude; verbs with en l'air (foutre en l'air, mettre en l'air) are informal and can be strong.
target_language_example: Ils ont les bras en l'air pendant la photo.
native_language_example: They have their arms in the air during the photo.

meaning: 'at large' / 'free' / 'free-range' depending on context.
additional_notes: Can mean physically free (not confined) or legally free (not imprisoned). In agriculture, used to describe animals raised free-range: 'poulets élevés en liberté' = free-range chickens. In legal contexts, 'en liberté conditionnelle' = on parole / released on condition. Often followed by 'conditionnelle' for 'on parole'.
target_language_example: Après sa peine, il est sorti et est resté en liberté.
native_language_example: After his sentence, he got out and remained free.

meaning: in a safe place; somewhere safe
additional_notes: Used to say that a person or object is kept somewhere safe or protected. Often appears with verbs like être (to be) or mettre (to put). Formal/neutral phrasing; more common spoken alternatives: en sécurité, en lieu sûr (slightly formal) or en lieu sûr can be shortened to 'en sécurité' for everyday use.
target_language_example: J'ai mis les documents importants en lieu sûr.
native_language_example: I put the important documents in a safe place.

meaning: 'online' or 'in a line/queue' depending on context.
additional_notes: Two main uses: 1) digital/connected: 'online' (connected to the internet, using a website/service, or in a call). Example: "Je suis en ligne" = I'm online / I'm on the line. 2) physical arrangement: 'in a line' or 'in a queue' (people standing one after another). Context and verbs tell you which meaning. Common collocations: 'être en ligne' (be online / be on the phone), 'faire une demande en ligne' (apply online), 'rester en ligne' (stay on the line).
target_language_example: Je fais mes courses en ligne ce soir.
native_language_example: I'm doing my shopping online tonight.

meaning: in a bad way; speaking ill (of someone).
additional_notes: Used mainly in the fixed expression 'parler (de quelqu'un) en mal' meaning 'to speak ill of someone' or 'talk negatively about someone'. Often appears in negative imperatives or moral advice (e.g. 'Ne parle jamais des autres en mal'). Not commonly used alone except in short responses like 'En mal ?' (meaning 'Badly? / In what way?').
target_language_example: Ne parle jamais des autres en mal.
native_language_example: Never speak ill of others.

meaning: to be suffering from / to have a longing or ache for (often followed by a noun)
additional_notes: Used to express a lack, longing, craving or physical/psychological suffering for something. Common constructions: 'en mal de' + noun (en mal d'amour, en mal de vivre, en mal de compagnie). Tone can be literary or slightly formal; often describes an ongoing state (not a one-time desire).
target_language_example: Depuis son départ, elle est en mal de compagnie.
native_language_example: Since he left, she has been longing for company.

meaning: 'running' / 'in operation' / 'in motion' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Used for machines or devices to mean 'turned on' or 'operating' (e.g. 'La machine est en marche' = the machine is on). For vehicles or people it can mean 'in motion' / 'walking' / 'on the move' (e.g. 'train en marche' = moving train; 'Ils sont en marche' = they are on the move). Not idiomatic for planned actions (use 'en marche' can also imply something has started).
target_language_example: La télévision est en marche, tu peux mettre le film.
native_language_example: The TV is on, you can put on the movie.

meaning: with regard to; in the field of; concerning
additional_notes: Used to specify a topic, domain, or subject area. Often followed by a noun phrase (en matière de + [nom]). Formal/neutral register; common in written and spoken French to point to expertise, rules, or aspects of a subject.
target_language_example: En matière de santé, il faut écouter les médecins.
native_language_example: With regard to health, you should listen to doctors.

meaning: able to; in a position to; capable of (doing something).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say someone is (or will be) able or in a position to do something. Common with pouvoir/être (e.g., 'être en mesure de', 'pouvoir être en mesure de'). Slightly more formal than just 'pouvoir'.
target_language_example: Je serai bientôt en mesure de signer le contrat.
native_language_example: I will soon be able to sign the contract.

meaning: very quickly; in no time
additional_notes: Informal idiomatic expression meaning something will happen extremely fast. Literally 'in less than two' (understood as 'two moments/instants'). Commonly used in spoken French to reassure that an action will be done quickly.
target_language_example: Je reviens en moins de deux.
native_language_example: I'll be back in no time.

meaning: 'in motion' or 'moving'.
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone that is moving or not stationary. Can be literal (a moving object) or figurative (busy, constantly on the move). Common in short phrases: 'Cible en mouvement' = 'moving target'.
target_language_example: La voiture est en mouvement, reste à distance.
native_language_example: The car is in motion, keep your distance.

meaning: on average; typically, on the whole.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an average value or typical amount across time or people. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence (e.g., 'En moyenne, ...' or '... en moyenne'). Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: En moyenne, je marche trente minutes par jour.
native_language_example: On average, I walk thirty minutes a day.

meaning: at the same time; meanwhile; also (to add a remark).
additional_notes: Common phrase with several close uses: 1) to say two or more actions happen simultaneously (equivalent to 'at the same time'), 2) as a short reaction or hesitation in conversation ('En même temps ?' ≈ 'Well, at the same time.../I mean...'), and 3) to introduce a contrasting or qualifying remark (similar to 'that said' or 'mind you'). Very frequent in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il a étudié et travaillé en même temps pendant deux ans.
native_language_example: He studied and worked at the same time for two years.

meaning: made of gold; (figuratively) excellent or ideal.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to say something is made of gold (literal: jewelry, objects). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., un boulot en or = a great/ideal job). In literal uses, it describes material (comme « en argent », « en acier »).
target_language_example: Elle porte un collier en or pour la fête.
native_language_example: She is wearing a gold necklace for the party.

meaning: in order; everything OK/arranged properly.
additional_notes: Used to say that things are correct, organized, functioning, or acceptable. Common in everyday and formal contexts. Can mean 'in order' (tidy/organized), 'all set', or 'everything is fine.' Often appears in phrases like 'tout est en ordre' (everything is in order).
target_language_example: Avant de partir, vérifie que tout est en ordre.
native_language_example: Before leaving, check that everything is in order.

meaning: besides; moreover; in addition
additional_notes: Used to add another point or piece of information. Formal to neutral register; common in written and spoken French. Often placed at the start of a sentence or clause and followed by a comma.
target_language_example: En outre, il faudra réparer la porte.
native_language_example: Moreover, the door will need to be repaired.

meaning: broken down; not working (for machines, vehicles, appliances).
additional_notes: Used to say a device or vehicle has stopped functioning. Commonly used with verbs like tomber (tomber en panne) or être (être en panne). Can refer to temporary failures; context indicates whether repair is needed. Not informal.
target_language_example: La photocopieuse est en panne, on doit appeler le technicien.
native_language_example: The photocopier is broken down; we must call the technician.

meaning: 'in perfect (condition)' or 'as a perfect...'
additional_notes: Commonly used before a noun like 'état' (en parfait état) to mean 'in perfect condition'. Can also appear in phrases like 'transformé en parfait soldat' meaning 'turned into a perfect/complete [soldier]' — there it means 'as a perfect/example of'. Usually followed by a noun; adjective agrees with the noun in gender/number (e.g. en parfait état, en parfaite condition).
target_language_example: La voiture est en parfait état après la réparation.
native_language_example: The car is in perfect condition after the repair.

meaning: 'particularly' or 'specifically'.
additional_notes: Used to single out one thing, person, place or detail among others. Can start a phrase or be inserted mid-sentence. Often followed by de/à/chez or a noun/pronoun to specify what is meant.
target_language_example: Je m'intéresse aux films, en particulier aux documentaires.
native_language_example: I'm interested in films, particularly documentaries.

meaning: partly; in part; to some extent.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is true only to a certain degree or not completely. Often appears in short answers (e.g., “Oui, en partie”) and before verbs/nouns (e.g., “en partie responsable”). Formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: C'est en partie à cause du mauvais temps.
native_language_example: It's partly because of the bad weather.

meaning: 'in passing' / 'by the way' / 'while passing through' (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common multi-use phrase. Can mean: 1) 'in passing' or 'incidentally' when mentioning something briefly (e.g. En passant, ... = By the way); 2) 'while passing by/through' when describing movement (en passant par = via / by way of); 3) 'as one passes' for a short action done on the way. Context determines nuance.
target_language_example: En passant, j'ai acheté du pain au marché.
native_language_example: By the way / While passing, I bought bread at the market.

meaning: 'about to' or 'on the verge of' (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone/something is very close to doing something or a situation is about to happen. Often followed by "de" + infinitive: en passe de + infinitive. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Il est en passe de réussir l'examen.
native_language_example: He is about to pass the exam.

meaning: continuously; all the time; permanently.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens without interruption or very frequently. Can mean 'constantly' (temporary ongoing action) or 'permanently' (long-term state) depending on context. Common in both formal and everyday speech.
target_language_example: Elle travaille en permanence sur ce projet.
native_language_example: She works on this project all the time.

meaning: in person; personally (physically present).
