additional_notes: Very informal and offensive. Literally 'big pile' or 'big lump', but used as an insult similar to 'you big oaf' or stronger 'you piece of shit' depending on context. Often combined with 'de merde' to be more insulting. Use only in strong informal contexts (angry speech) — avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Ne m'appelle pas gros tas de merde !
native_language_example: Don't call me you big piece of shit!

meaning: headline (a big, prominent title on a page or article).
additional_notes: Used for the main, attention-grabbing title of a newspaper article, web article, poster, etc. Can also mean a large-font title in design/layout. Not idiomatic — literal use of gros (big) + titre (title).
target_language_example: Le gros titre du journal parlait de la grève.
native_language_example: The newspaper's headline was about the strike.

meaning: insult: 'big cow' used to call someone stupid, mean, or nasty.
additional_notes: A rude, offensive expression in French. Literally means "big/ fat cow," but used as an insult toward a person (often implying cruelty, clumsiness, or unpleasantness). Can be shouted or said angrily. Avoid using in polite company; it can be strong, especially toward women. Tone and context determine severity; in casual teasing among friends it may be less harsh, but generally not appropriate for formal situations or with strangers.
target_language_example: Ne l'appelle pas une grosse vache, ce n'est pas gentil.
native_language_example: Don't call her a 'big cow,' that's not nice.

meaning: blood type (blood group).
additional_notes: Refers to a person's blood classification (A, B, AB, O and Rh factor: positif/négatif). Commonly used in medical contexts and when donating/receiving blood. You can answer with e.g. "A positif" / "O négatif" or ask "Quel est votre groupe sanguin ?"
target_language_example: Mon groupe sanguin est O négatif.
native_language_example: My blood type is O negative.

meaning: because of; thanks to (used to indicate cause or positive reason).
additional_notes: Used to attribute a cause or reason, often with a positive connotation (something good happened). Followed by a noun or pronoun. Can be used neutrally but usually implies gratitude or a beneficial cause. For negative causes, French prefers 'à cause de'.
target_language_example: J'ai réussi l'examen grâce à mes révisions.
native_language_example: I passed the exam thanks to my studying.

meaning: civil war — an armed conflict within a single country between organized groups or factions.
additional_notes: Used to describe internal wars (historical or fictional) inside a state, region, organization, or even metaphorically in smaller groups. Can refer to well-known events (e.g., la guerre civile américaine) or imagined/conflictual situations (e.g., within a community, section, or 'empire' in fiction).
target_language_example: La guerre civile a duré plusieurs années et a dévasté le pays.
native_language_example: The civil war lasted several years and devastated the country.

meaning: the Vietnam War (the armed conflict in Vietnam, mainly 1955–1975).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the historical war in Vietnam. Capitalization: in French it's usually written 'guerre du Vietnam' (only 'Vietnam' capitalized). Common in contexts about history, politics, veterans, protests. Can be used with verbs like 'être opposé à', 'mourir pendant', 'manifester contre'.
target_language_example: Il a étudié la guerre du Vietnam en cours d'histoire.
native_language_example: He studied the Vietnam War in history class.

meaning: 'hangover' (after drinking too much alcohol).
additional_notes: Informal idiom. Literally 'mouth of wood' but means the physical symptoms (headache, nausea, fatigue) after excessive drinking. Common in spoken French: J'ai la gueule de bois = I'm hungover. Use in casual contexts; avoid in very formal writing.
target_language_example: Après la fête, il avait la gueule de bois toute la journée.
native_language_example: After the party, he was hungover all day.

meaning: tour guide; a person who leads and informs tourists.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone (job/profession) who shows visitors around sights and provides information. Can be used with articles and job titles: 'être guide touristique' (to be a tour guide) or 'un/une guide touristique'.
target_language_example: Il travaille comme guide touristique à Paris.
native_language_example: He works as a tour guide in Paris.

meaning: 'cake with' (used before a flavor or ingredient, e.g. gâteau au chocolat = chocolate cake).
additional_notes: Used to describe the main flavor or ingredient of a cake. Follows gâteau (masculine) so au = à + le. For plural or feminine ingredients the form changes (gâteau à la, gâteau aux). Common collocations: gâteau au chocolat, gâteau au citron, gâteau aux pommes.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un gâteau au citron pour l'anniversaire.
native_language_example: I would like a lemon cake for the birthday.

meaning: kind/generous of (someone) to do something — used to comment on someone's generosity.
additional_notes: Typically appears in the fixed expression "C'est [très] généreux de + (pronoun/noun) + part" or "de votre/sa part." It literally points out that an action or offer is generous coming from that person. Common in polite responses to offers or compliments. Use the appropriate pronoun (ma part, ta part, sa part, votre part) to indicate whose generosity you mean.
target_language_example: C'est vraiment généreux de votre part de m'aider.
native_language_example: It's really generous of you to help me.

meaning: to shrug (one's shoulders); indicate indifference, uncertainty, or lack of an answer.
additional_notes: Used to describe the gesture of raising the shoulders. Often used literally (Il a haussé les épaules) or figuratively to indicate not knowing or not caring. Common in descriptions and spoken replies. The reflexive form se hausser les épaules is uncommon; typically use hauser les épaules with a subject.
target_language_example: Il a haussé les épaules quand je lui ai demandé, en haussant les épaules.
native_language_example: When I asked him, he shrugged his shoulders.

meaning: high-end; top quality; premium.
additional_notes: Used to describe products, services or places that are of superior quality or luxury (hotels, restaurants, goods). Often placed after the noun (un hôtel haut de gamme) but can appear alone as a label. Not slang.
target_language_example: Nous avons choisi un restaurant haut de gamme pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: We chose a high-end restaurant for his birthday.

meaning: high-ranking; well-placed (influence or position).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who holds a high position or has strong influence (e.g., a senior official, executive, or someone with connections). Often appears after a noun: un fonctionnaire haut placé, une source haut placée. Agreement: when used as an adjective before a noun it follows normal gender/number rules (haut placé → haute placée, hauts placés, hautes placées).
target_language_example: Il a obtenu des informations auprès d'une source haut placée.
native_language_example: He obtained information from a high-ranking source.

meaning: 'what time did you' (used in questions with 'à quelle' — 'À quelle heure as-tu ... ?')
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the question pattern 'À quelle heure as-tu ... ?' meaning 'At what time did you ...?' It's used with the passé composé (as-tu + past participle) to ask when an action happened. Informal spoken questions may drop inversion and use 'tu as ... à quelle heure ?' instead.
target_language_example: À quelle heure as-tu acheté le billet ?
native_language_example: What time did you buy the ticket?

meaning: '(at) what time did you...?' (part of the question 'À quelle heure avez-vous...')
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common question pattern 'À quelle heure avez-vous + past participle' (passé composé) to ask when someone did something in the past. Full form is 'À quelle heure avez-vous [fait X] ?' You can replace 'avez-vous' with 'as-tu' (informal singular) or 'avez-vous' stays for formal/plural. The phrase requires a verb in the past participle after it (e.g. fermé, quitté, entendu).
target_language_example: À quelle heure avez-vous mangé hier soir ?
native_language_example: What time did you eat last night?

meaning: 'time to' (do something) / 'hour of' (a period of time)
additional_notes: Used in two common patterns: 1) C'est l'heure de + infinitive/noun = 'it's time to ...' or 'it's time for ...' (e.g., C'est l'heure de partir = It's time to leave). 2) [une] heure de + noun or retard = 'one hour of ...' or 'one hour late' (e.g., une heure de retard = one hour delay/one hour late). Context determines whether it means 'time to' or 'an hour of'.
target_language_example: C'est l'heure de manger; nous avons une heure de trajet.
native_language_example: It's time to eat; we have an hour of travel.

meaning: 'moment of glory' — a brief time when someone is praised, successful or in the spotlight.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a short, often celebratory or triumphant period when someone receives attention or admiration. Common in informal and formal contexts. Comparable to English 'moment of glory' or 'time to shine.'
target_language_example: Allez, montre ce que tu sais — c'est ton heure de gloire !
native_language_example: Come on, show what you can do — it's your moment of glory!

meaning: rush hour; peak traffic time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the times of day when roads, public transport, or services are busiest (typically morning and evening commutes). Can be singular or plural: heures de pointe. Often used with aller, éviter, prendre, or être coincé dans (être coincé dans les bouchons).
target_language_example: Évite l'heure de pointe si tu peux, les trains sont toujours pleins.
native_language_example: Avoid rush hour if you can; the trains are always full.

meaning: 'what time should I' or 'at what time must I'.
additional_notes: Combines the question phrase 'À quelle heure' (at what time) with 'dois-je' (should I / must I). Used to ask when the speaker is expected to do something (arrive, be picked up, check in, etc.). In full questions include the verb or action (e.g., 'À quelle heure dois-je venir ?'). Polite and neutral register.
target_language_example: À quelle heure dois-je arriver à l'aéroport ?
native_language_example: What time should I arrive at the airport?

meaning: the time for (something); it's time to (do/eat) [masculine noun follows].
additional_notes: Used to say it's the time for a particular activity or meal. 'Heure' (feminine) + 'du' = de + le, so 'du' is used before masculine nouns (le dîner, le déjeuner, le thé, le dodo, le dessert). For feminine nouns use 'de la' (e.g. l'heure de la sieste) and for plural use 'des'. Often appears in expressions like 'C'est l'heure du + noun' or 'C'est bientôt l'heure du...'.
target_language_example: C'est l'heure du goûter.
native_language_example: It's snack time.

meaning: 'what time ... leaves/departs' (literally: 'what time leaves')
additional_notes: Used in questions with 'À quelle' to ask the departure time of a vehicle (train, plane, bus). The full phrase is 'À quelle heure part ... ?'. 'Part' is from the verb partir (to leave). Common in travel contexts.
target_language_example: À quelle heure part le bus pour la gare ?
native_language_example: What time does the bus to the station leave?

meaning: 'at what time did you (yourself) ...' — used to ask what time someone did something (formal/plural or polite).
additional_notes: This is part of the inversion question form with 'à quelle heure' + 'vous êtes-vous' + past participle (e.g. couché, levé, réveillé). It’s formal or plural (vous). Use with reflexive verbs in the passé composé. Word order: À quelle heure + vous êtes-vous + past participle. Spoken French often uses 'vous vous êtes' or 'à quelle heure est-ce que vous ...' instead.
target_language_example: À quelle heure vous êtes-vous levés hier ?
native_language_example: At what time did you get up yesterday?

meaning: 'what time are you' or 'at what time are you' (formal/inverted question form)
additional_notes: This is part of the formal/inverted question structure 'À quelle heure êtes-vous ... ?' used to ask about the time something happened (arrival, leaving, going to bed, etc.). 'Êtes-vous' is the formal second-person singular or plural inversion of 'vous êtes' (you are / you were in passé composé with past participle). For informal speech, French speakers often use 'Tu es allé(e) à quelle heure ?' or 'À quelle heure t'es allé(e) ?'.
target_language_example: À quelle heure êtes-vous parti hier soir ?
native_language_example: What time did you leave last night?

meaning: overtime hours (work done beyond normal working time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about working extra hours beyond the usual schedule; can refer to the hours themselves or the act of doing overtime. Often shortened in speech to "heures sup". May be paid at a higher rate or compensated with time off, depending on contract/law.
target_language_example: Je vais devoir faire des heures supplémentaires cette semaine.
native_language_example: I'll have to work overtime this week.

meaning: 'every ... hours' (used to say how often something happens, e.g. every 2 hours)
additional_notes: This phrase is part of a time-frequency expression. Structure: 'tous les + [number] + heures' = 'every [number] hours'. In speech you may see 'toutes les' when referring to feminine nouns (e.g. 'toutes les semaines'). With 'heures' the standard form is 'tous les'. Commonly used for schedules, medication timing, or repeating events. Note: the exact ordering in French is normally 'tous les [nombre] heures' rather than 'heures tous les' — the entry shows the sequence of words but real sentences place the number between 'tous les' and 'heures'.
target_language_example: Nous devons administrer le médicament toutes les 6 heures; vérifiez les heures tous les jours.
native_language_example: We must give the medicine every 6 hours; check the times every day.

meaning: 'happy that you' (feminine speaker) — used to express being glad about something the listener did or is/has done.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the adjective heureuse (feminine) + que + the subject pronoun tu. A speaker who is masculine would say "heureux que tu...". It is followed by a verb in the appropriate tense (subjunctive after expressions of feeling: e.g. "que tu sois", "que tu te sois souvenu(e)"). Common in sentences like "Je suis heureuse que tu sois là" (I'm happy that you are here).
target_language_example: Je suis heureuse que tu aies pu venir.
native_language_example: I'm happy that you were able to come.

meaning: 'old news' or 'something in the past / no longer relevant'.
additional_notes: Used idiomatically to say that something is past, settled, or no longer worth discussing. Often appears as the fixed phrase "c'est de l'histoire ancienne" (it's old news / ancient history). Not about the academic field of 'ancient history' unless context makes that clear.
target_language_example: Ce qui s'est passé l'année dernière, c'est de l'histoire ancienne.
native_language_example: What happened last year is old news / ancient history.

meaning: 'to' or 'in order to' (used to express purpose) OR 'story of/about' depending on context.
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) As a preposition phrase meaning 'story of/about' when referring to an event, person, or subject (C'est l'histoire de ma famille = the story of my family). In this sense it is literal/compositional and a cognate.
2) Informal/familiar use: 'histoire de' + infinitive = 'just to / in order to / so as to' to explain a short purpose or reason (Histoire de te dépanner, je vais t'aider = Just to help you, I'll help). This use is very frequent in spoken French. It can also introduce a brief comment like 'just' or 'so as to' and is often followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase. Pay attention to tone: in some contexts (e.g. Quelle histoire de chiottes?) it appears in idiomatic or colloquial expressions.
target_language_example: Je l'ai appelé, histoire de lui demander conseil.
native_language_example: I called him, just to ask for his advice.

meaning: businessman; a man who works in or runs business.
additional_notes: Common French term for a male businessperson. The plural is hommes d'affaires. To refer to a female businessperson, use femme d'affaires or the gender-neutral dirigeant(e) / personne d'affaires. Used in formal and neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Mon oncle est un homme d'affaires et voyage beaucoup.
native_language_example: My uncle is a businessman and travels a lot.

meaning: the right person for the situation; someone capable or suitable.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the appropriate person to handle a task or problem. Often used about a man (homme) but can be used more generally or jokingly for anyone. Common in spoken and written French. Can be affirmative (Il est l'homme de la situation) or self-referential (Je suis l'homme de la situation).
target_language_example: Il faut quelqu'un de calme pour ce travail — c'est l'homme de la situation.
native_language_example: We need someone calm for this job — he's the right man for the job.

meaning: caveman; (figurative) a very old-fashioned, brutish, or uncivilized man
additional_notes: Literally 'man of the caves'. Used literally for prehistoric humans or figuratively as an insult to describe someone rude, sexist, or old-fashioned in behaviour. Tone can be playful or offensive depending on context. Plural: hommes des cavernes.
target_language_example: Arrête de te comporter comme un homme des cavernes.
native_language_example: Stop behaving like a caveman.

meaning: the man was
additional_notes: A simple past / descriptive phrase: homme = man, était = was (imperfect of être). In English you'd normally say "the man was" or "that man was" depending on context; French word order is the same as English (le/ cet/ ce + homme + était). This phrase appears in continuous or descriptive contexts (e.g. "the old man was sitting...").
target_language_example: Cet homme était très gentil.
native_language_example: That man was very kind.

meaning: 'an honest man' or 'a respectable/upright person' (a man of integrity).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man who is morally upright, honorable, respectable or trustworthy. Can be literal (truthful) or more generally about good character. In modern French it's somewhat formal or old-fashioned; context may simply mean 'a decent person'. The phrase refers specifically to a man (homme).
target_language_example: Pour être promu, il faut être un honnête homme aux yeux de ses collègues.
native_language_example: To be promoted, you must be an honest/respectable man in the eyes of your colleagues.

meaning: out of danger; safe (after an accident, illness, or problem).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is no longer in danger or that a problem is resolved. Common in contexts about health, accidents, or urgent situations. Often used with être: «être hors d'affaire».
target_language_example: Après l'opération, le médecin a dit qu'il était hors d'affaire.
native_language_example: After the surgery, the doctor said he was out of danger.

meaning: very old; beyond the usual age (often used for wines or brandies to mean of exceptional, very old vintage)
additional_notes: Literally 'outside/of age'. Commonly used in wine, cognac, armagnac, and cheeses to indicate something is exceptionally old or aged beyond standard categories. Can be used figuratively for people or things to mean 'antique' or 'very old', but most natural in tasting/descriptive contexts. Not slang.
target_language_example: Ce cognac est hors d'âge et mérite une dégustation spéciale.
native_language_example: This cognac is hors d'âge and deserves a special tasting.

meaning: out of; outside of; (figuratively) beyond (a state or control).
additional_notes: Used both literally (physical position: out of/ outside of something) and figuratively (emotional/state: 'hors de moi' = extremely angry, 'hors de service' = out of order). Often followed by a noun: hors de + (noun). Context determines translation.
target_language_example: Il a sauté hors de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: He jumped out of the window.

meaning: 'out of action' or 'unable to fight/participate' (physically incapacitated or neutralized).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person who is temporarily or permanently unable to fight, act, or take part (due to injury, unconsciousness, capture, etc.). Common in formal, military, or medical contexts but can be used figuratively (e.g., exhausted, out of commission).
target_language_example: Après l'accident, il était hors de combat pendant plusieurs jours.
native_language_example: After the accident, he was out of action for several days.

meaning: 'out of control' — not manageable or under control.
additional_notes: Used to describe people, machines, or situations that have become unmanageable, chaotic, or uncontrollable. Common in everyday speech. Can describe temporary states (e.g., after drinking) or ongoing situations (e.g., life or events).
target_language_example: La fête est devenue hors de contrôle.
native_language_example: The party got out of control.

meaning: 'out of danger' or 'no longer in danger' (safe, out of immediate risk).
additional_notes: Used to say a person or situation is no longer in danger—often after an accident, illness, or threat. Common in both formal and everyday speech. Can be used with je/tu/on/nous/il/elle. Literal words mean 'outside of danger.'
target_language_example: Les blessés sont hors de danger après l'opération.
native_language_example: The injured are out of danger after the operation.

meaning: out of reach; beyond reach or beyond one's means/ability
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically out of reach) and figuratively (unaffordable, unattainable, or beyond someone's ability). Common with être: 'être hors de portée' = 'to be out of reach' or 'to be beyond one's means'.
target_language_example: Ce livre est hors de portée sur l'étagère du haut.
native_language_example: That book is out of reach on the top shelf.

meaning: out of (someone's) reach; out of (someone's) way — usually used to say keep something where someone (often children) cannot reach it.
additional_notes: Common phrase used with children (des enfants) or pets. Structure: hors de portée de + noun (usually plural with article: des enfants). Can be used with objects: médicaments, allumettes, produits chimiques. Often appears in safety instructions: Gardez X hors de portée des enfants.
target_language_example: Range les médicaments hors de portée des enfants.
native_language_example: Put the medicines out of the children's reach.

meaning: extremely expensive; priceless (depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly used to say something costs far too much: 'Cet objet est hors de prix' = 'This is way too expensive.' Can also mean 'priceless' (very valuable) in a positive sense, but that use is less common. Often used in everyday speech about prices and costs.
target_language_example: Ce restaurant est hors de prix pour nous.
native_language_example: That restaurant is way too expensive for us.

meaning: irrelevant / not appropriate to the subject or moment.
additional_notes: Used to say that a comment, question, or person’s remarks are off-topic, inappropriate, or untimely. Can be polite or mildly critical depending on tone. Often used after or about a remark: « Cette remarque est hors de propos. »
target_language_example: Ta question est hors de propos pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: Your question is irrelevant during the meeting.

meaning: absolutely not; out of the question.
additional_notes: Used to firmly refuse or rule something out. Strong, emphatic phrase — often followed by an infinitive or a noun phrase (e.g. "Il est hors de question de + infinitive"). Common in spoken and written French; can sound blunt.
target_language_example: Il est hors de question que je prête ma voiture.
native_language_example: There's no way I'm lending my car.

meaning: out of order; not working.
additional_notes: Used to say a machine, device, or facility is not functioning or temporarily unavailable. Common on signs and spoken notices. Can apply to technical breakdowns or to items turned off for maintenance.
target_language_example: L'ascenseur est hors service aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The elevator is out of order today.

meaning: hot dog (a sausage in a bun).
additional_notes: Borrowed from English; used in spoken and written French to mean the same food item. Pronounced roughly like /ɔt.dɔɡ/ or /hot-dog/; plural is usually 'hot-dogs'. Common in casual contexts (restaurants, street food).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un hot-dog, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a hot dog, please.

meaning: eight hundred.
additional_notes: Used to say the number 800. 'Cents' takes an -s when it is an exact multiple of 100 and not followed by another number (e.g. huit cents = 800). If followed by another number (e.g. huit cent cinq = 805) the plural -s is dropped. Pronunciation: [ɥit sɑ̃].
target_language_example: Il me doit huit cents euros.
native_language_example: He owes me eight hundred euros.

meaning: inherited (from); received something by inheritance from someone.
additional_notes: Used to say someone received property, money, or possessions after another person's death. Often follows the verb 'hériter' conjugated (e.g., il a hérité de = he inherited from). Can be used with concrete items (maison, château) or abstract (fortune).
target_language_example: Elle a hérité de la maison de sa grand‑mère.
native_language_example: She inherited her grandmother's house.

meaning: here for as long (as)...; staying here for the same/any length of time (used with a clause).
additional_notes: Usually followed by a clause introduced by que (e.g. que possible, que tu veux, que vous le désirez, que tu restes tranquille) to express duration: 'as long as possible' or 'as long as you want/are quiet.' Common in polite permission or statements about staying. Literal: 'here also long'.
target_language_example: Tu peux rester ici aussi longtemps que tu veux.
native_language_example: You can stay here for as long as you want.

meaning: here and there; in various places; scattered around.
additional_notes: Used to indicate things or actions occurring in different places or spread out. Common in spoken and written French. Can be used literally (physical locations) or figuratively (occurring occasionally). Often interchangeable with 'par-ci, par-là'.
target_language_example: Ils ont cherché ici et là jusqu'à trouver la clé.
native_language_example: They searched here and there until they found the key.

meaning: he has his / he has (something belonging to him)
additional_notes: This is the start of a possessive phrase: 'il a sa' must be followed by a noun (feminine singular) to mean 'he has his [something]'. Example: 'Il a sa voiture' = 'He has his car.' Note that depending on context, 'sa' can refer to something belonging to a female person ('her') when the subject is third person singular feminine, but with 'il' as subject it means possession by a male ('his').
target_language_example: Il a sa valise avec lui.
native_language_example: He has his suitcase with him.

meaning: used to indicate that someone has something to (do/have) — often followed by an infinitive or noun (he has to / he has at/with).
additional_notes: This sequence appears in constructions like « il a à + infinitive » meaning 'he has (something) to [do]' (e.g. « il a à parler » = he has something to say / he must speak) or « il a à + noun » meaning he has something (with him or in store). It is not a fixed idiom by itself; meaning depends on the words that follow. More common alternatives for obligation are « il doit » or « il a quelque chose à ». Use context to determine whether it's obligation, possession, or purpose.
target_language_example: Il a à expliquer pourquoi il est en retard.
native_language_example: He has something to explain about why he's late.

meaning: 'he was five' (referring to age)
additional_notes: Common way to state someone's age in the past using imparfait: il avait cinq ans = he was five years old. The full phrase normally includes 'ans' (years), but in context 'il avait cinq' clearly implies 'ans'. Use imparfait (avait) for past background or ongoing states.
target_language_example: Il avait cinq ans quand il a commencé l'école.
native_language_example: He was five when he started school.

meaning: 'what time is it?' (informal/question form)
additional_notes: A casual way to ask for the time. More standard/formal order is "quelle heure est-il ?" Both are understood; "il est quelle heure" is slightly more colloquial and often used in spoken French. Can be followed by a question mark or rising intonation.
target_language_example: Il est quelle heure, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: What time is it, please?

meaning: 'he does what' (used to start a clause meaning 'he does what/... he did what').
additional_notes: This construction combines 'il fait' (he does/makes) with 'ce' + a relative clause introduced by 'que' (qu'il, qu'il a, etc.). It appears in phrases like 'Il fait ce qu'il peut' = 'He does what he can.' The pattern is: il fait ce + que + [clause]. In questions about past actions you may see 'Pourquoi a‑t‑il fait ce qu'il a fait ?' ('Why did he do what he did?').
target_language_example: Il fait ce qu'il doit pour sa famille.
native_language_example: He does what he must for his family.

meaning: must
additional_notes: An impersonal expression used to talk about necessity or obligation. Literally it means something like "it is necessary," but in everyday English it is usually translated as "must" or "have to." It is often followed by an infinitive: il faut partir = we/you have to leave.
target_language_example: Il faut partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We have to leave now.

meaning: It must be done / You have to do it.
additional_notes: Il faut + infinitive expresses necessity or obligation (impersonal: 'il faut'). Here 'le' refers to 'it' (a task or thing). Can be used generally ('it must be done') or as instruction/advice ('you have to do it'). Tone can be neutral; context determines who should do it. The phrase can be emphatic with an exclamation mark.
target_language_example: Il faut le faire avant la réunion.
native_language_example: It must be done before the meeting.

meaning: 'if/when it's necessary' or 'when needed'.
additional_notes: Common fixed phrase used to indicate that something should be done when required. Often appears in conditional structures (s'il le faut = if it is necessary) or statements like "quand il le faut" (when necessary). "Il" is impersonal here (refers to the situation/need), not a specific person.
target_language_example: Je parlerai seulement quand il le faut.
native_language_example: I will speak only when it's necessary.

meaning: he ... it
additional_notes: l’ is the shortened form of le or la before a vowel or silent h. It usually stands for him, her, or it, and in French it comes before the verb: il l’a vu = he saw him/her/it. Before être, l’ can also refer back to a quality or identity already mentioned: il l’était = he was.
target_language_example: Il l’a mis sur la table.
native_language_example: He put it on the table.

meaning: you/one/it shouldn't have (done that) / it wasn't necessary (polite refusal).
additional_notes: Used to express that something should not have happened, was unnecessary, or was not required. Can be a comment about past obligation (shouldn't have) or a polite way to refuse thanks/offers (like 'you shouldn't have' / 'that's not necessary'). Context determines whether it's moral/incorrect action (Il ne fallait pas voler = You shouldn't have stolen) or polite modesty (Merci, il ne fallait pas = Thanks, you didn't have to).
target_language_example: Oh non, il ne fallait pas emmener un gâteau pour moi !
native_language_example: Oh no, you shouldn't have brought a cake for me!

meaning: 'he' + negative + 'me' (object pronoun) — contracted start of sentences meaning 'he ... me' in a negative form (he did not me...)
additional_notes: This is the beginning of negative past-tense or present-tense sentences where 'm'' is the contracted form of 'me' (direct or indirect object). It appears before the past participle or verb: e.g. 'Il ne m'a jamais aimé' = 'He never loved me.' The full negative structure often uses 'ne ... pas/jamais/même pas' around the verb. The contraction 'm'' is used before a vowel sound (m'a, m'aime, m'a regardé).
target_language_example: Il ne m'a pas dit la vérité.
native_language_example: He did not tell me the truth.

meaning: 'he/it is not' (used to say someone or something is not well or not okay) — part of the negation 'il ne va pas'.
additional_notes: Commonly appears as 'il ne va pas' to mean 'he/it is not well' or 'it's not working.' Context determines subject: usually 'il' refers to a male person ('he') or an inanimate thing/situation ('it'). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: 'il va pas'.
target_language_example: Il ne va pas bien depuis hier.
native_language_example: He hasn't been well since yesterday.

meaning: 'he spends his' (time) — used with 'temps' + infinitive to say someone spends their time doing something
additional_notes: Common construction: 'il/elle passe son temps à + infinitive' = 'he/she spends his/her time (doing ...)'. Often implies frequency or habit; can be neutral or slightly critical depending on context (e.g. 'il passe son temps à ne rien faire' = he wastes his time doing nothing). Replace 'son' with 'son/sa/ses' to agree with the possessed noun (usually 'temps' — 'son temps').
target_language_example: Il passe son temps à lire avant de dormir.
native_language_example: He spends his time reading before bed.

meaning: 'is it possible to' / 'would it be possible to' (used to ask politely if something can be done)
additional_notes: Used in questions (often inverted: Est-il possible de... or Serait-il possible de...) to make polite requests or ask if an action can be done. Follows with an infinitive verb (de + infinitive). Common in formal or polite situations.
target_language_example: Serait-il possible de repousser la réunion d'une heure ?
native_language_example: Would it be possible to postpone the meeting by an hour?

meaning: 'how could he... (have) ...' — part of a question form expressing surprise or seeking explanation about something someone did or that happened to them.
additional_notes: This sequence is not a standalone phrase: it appears in inverted question forms with passé composé or conditional perfect verbs (e.g. 'a-t-il pu se...','aurait-il pu se...'). 'Pouvoir' here expresses possibility or ability (could/can), and 'se' is the reflexive pronoun for reflexive verbs (se suicider, se casser, se réfugier, se produire — note 'se produire' is not reflexive for a person but 'se produire' means 'to occur'). Common in questions starting with 'Comment' or 'Dans quel...' to ask how something could have happened. Literal parts are compositional but the whole construction functions grammatically rather than as an idiom.
target_language_example: Comment a-t-il pu se blesser sans que personne ne voie ?
native_language_example: How could he have hurt himself without anyone seeing?

meaning: portion of inverted-question constructions where 'il' (from inversion like 'y a-t-il', 'avait-il', 'figure-t-il') appears near the prepositional phrase 'sur la' ('on the'). Used to form questions about existence, presence, appearance or placement (e.g. 'is there ... on the ...', 'did he/it have ... on the ...', 'does ... appear on the ...').
additional_notes: 'il sur la' is not a standalone fixed phrase but a sequence that can occur when an inverted interrogative clause includes 'il' and is immediately followed by a 'sur la' prepositional phrase. Common in questions such as 'Combien de livres y a-t-il sur la table ?' or 'Votre nom figure-t-il sur la liste ?'. Formal/neutral register; found in both spoken and written French. The literal words translate directly (il = he/it; sur la = on the), but the full meaning depends on the surrounding verb (y a-t-il = is/are there; avait-il = did he/it have/was there; figure-t-il = does ... appear).
target_language_example: Combien de livres y a-t-il sur la table ?
native_language_example: How many books are there on the table?

meaning: 'it goes without' or 'it is without' (usually part of the expression 'il va sans dire' meaning 'it goes without saying')
additional_notes: On its own 'il va sans' is incomplete in French; you will commonly see it in the fixed phrase 'il va sans dire' or 'il va sans dire que...' meaning 'it goes without saying (that...)'. Use that full expression to indicate something is obvious and doesn't need to be stated. Not used alone in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il va sans dire que ta sécurité est la priorité.
native_language_example: It goes without saying that your safety is the priority.

meaning: 'he means' or 'he wants to say'.
additional_notes: Used to report someone's intended meaning or to ask what someone means. Often appears in questions (Qu'est-ce qu'il veut dire ?) and in sentences like Je sais ce qu'il veut dire (I know what he means). In French, 'vouloir dire' = 'to mean'.
target_language_example: Quand il parle vite, ce qu'il veut dire n'est pas toujours clair.
native_language_example: When he speaks quickly, what he means is not always clear.

meaning: there is / there are
additional_notes: Very common fixed expression. Most often it introduces something that exists or is present: il y a un livre sur la table = there is a book on the table. It is used for both singular and plural. Before a length of time, it means 'ago': il y a deux ans = two years ago.
target_language_example: Il y a beaucoup de monde ici.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people here.

meaning: a long time ago; long ago; for a long time (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common phrase used to talk about something that happened far in the past or that should have been done earlier. In passé context it means "a long time ago" (Il y a longtemps que... or Il y a longtemps, ...). In conditional or perfect constructions it often translates as "should have done it a long time ago." Literal components (il y a = there is/are) help but the full phrase functions as a time expression.
target_language_example: Tu aurais dû commencer il y a longtemps.
native_language_example: You should have started a long time ago.

meaning: there was something
additional_notes: This fragment comes from the full phrase "il y avait quelque chose" meaning "there was something" or "something was going on." In the provided sentences, "quelque" is an incomplete citation of "quelque chose." Use the complete phrase "il y avait quelque chose" in normal speech. It expresses that an unspecified thing, feeling, or problem existed or happened.
target_language_example: Il y avait quelque chose dans sa valise.
native_language_example: There was something in his suitcase.

meaning: there is/are (of them/of it)
additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is available, often referring back to a quantity of something previously mentioned. The en replaces a noun introduced earlier (meaning 'of it' / 'of them'). The phrase changes with number in English ('there is' vs 'there are') but in French it stays the same. Common in answers: "Il y en a cinq." = "There are five (of them)."
target_language_example: Tu as des tomates ? — Oui, il y en a.
native_language_example: Do you have tomatoes? — Yes, there are some (of them).

meaning: 'there are some of' (used before a feminine/plural noun starting with a vowel or mute h), often shortened in speech/writing as part of a longer phrase
additional_notes: This is a partial phrase: il y en a (de) + noun/phrase. 'Il y en a' means 'there are some' or 'there is/are of them', and when followed by de + a noun that begins with a vowel or mute h, the de contracts with the article or pronoun that follows (e.g. "d'" before a vowel). You'll usually see it as part of sentences like "Il y en a d'autres" (There are others) or "Il y en a d'intéressantes" (There are some interesting ones). Common in spoken and written French. Note that grammar and agreement depend on the noun referred to.
target_language_example: Il y en a d'autres qui aiment ce genre de musique.
native_language_example: There are others who like that kind of music.

meaning: he was (of/from) — used to describe someone's nature, opinion, origin, membership or association.
additional_notes: This construction combines the impersonal subject pronoun 'il' with 'être de'. Depending on context it can mean: 'he was of a certain nature' (Il était de nature passive), 'he shared an opinion' (Il était de notre avis = he agreed with us), 'he belonged to/was from' (J'ai dit qu'il était de toi = I said he was yours/connected to you), or 'he attended/was part of' (il était de toutes les fêtes = he was at every party). Translation varies by context; literal word-for-word translation ('he was of') is possible but often sounds unnatural in English. Commonly followed by a noun, possessive, or phrase indicating membership/character/attendance.
target_language_example: Il était de bonne humeur ce jour-là.
native_language_example: He was in a good mood that day.

meaning: 'once upon a time' (storytelling opening for fairy tales or past narratives).
additional_notes: A set phrase used to begin traditional stories or to introduce a narrative set in the past. Formality: neutral; mostly used in storytelling, not in everyday factual statements. Literal word-for-word translation is possible, but it's an idiomatic formula in French like in English.
target_language_example: Il était une fois une petite fille qui habitait près de la forêt.
native_language_example: Once upon a time there was a little girl who lived near the forest.

meaning: 'the important thing is' / 'what matters is'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce what matters in a situation. Common structure: "L'important, c'est que + [subjunctive or indicative clause]". Often followed by a clause explaining the main point or priority. Tone is neutral; suitable for everyday and formal use.
target_language_example: L'important, c'est que tu sois en sécurité.
native_language_example: The important thing is that you are safe.

meaning: 'more interesting than' (used to compare)
additional_notes: Used in comparative structures with 'plus' (plus intéressant que) or in constructions like 'plus intéressant que je ne le pensais'. Often appears as 'plus intéressant que' to compare two things or express that something exceeds expectations. If used alone as 'intéressant que' it may begin a clause (e.g. 'C'est intéressant que...') meaning 'it's interesting that...'; here examples show the comparative use.
target_language_example: Ce musée est plus intéressant que je l'imaginais.
native_language_example: This museum is more interesting than I imagined.

meaning: invited to the (feminine singular noun that follows).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase — it's the start of a construction meaning someone is invited to attend or take part in something. It uses 'invité' (invited) plus the preposition 'à' and the feminine definite article 'la' before a feminine noun: e.g. 'invité à la réunion' (invited to the meeting). For a masculine noun use 'invité au' (à + le), for a plural use 'invités aux' (à + les). If the invited person is female, you may see 'invitée à la'.
target_language_example: Il est invité à la conférence demain.
native_language_example: He is invited to the conference tomorrow.

meaning: 'will be all right for' / 'will turn out well for'.
additional_notes: Used in the future tense (il/elle/on ira) with 'tout' often preceding: 'Tout ira bien pour [quelqu'un]'. It's a reassuring phrase meaning that a situation will be okay or will work out in someone's favor. Common in spoken and written French. Can be followed by a pronoun or noun indicating who it will go well for.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout ira bien pour nous.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything will be all right for us.

meaning: I had (some/any/of) — part of a past expression meaning 'I experienced/received/had' followed by 'de' and a noun or expression.
additional_notes: This is the first part of a passé composé phrase: j'ai (avoir in present) + eu (past participle) + de + noun/phrase. It often introduces what someone had, received, or experienced (e.g. j'ai eu de la chance, j'ai eu de bons retours). The exact sense depends on the noun that follows. In speech, context decides whether 'de' means 'some', 'any', 'of', or is part of a fixed phrase. Not a complete sentence on its own.
target_language_example: J'ai eu de la chance pendant le voyage.
native_language_example: I was lucky during the trip.

meaning: 'I'm hungry'.
additional_notes: Common, everyday way to say you are hungry. Literal components: j' (je) = I, ai = have, faim = hunger — French uses 'avoir' (to have) to express physical states like hunger and thirst (e.g. j'ai soif = I'm thirsty). Can be used alone or in short responses.
target_language_example: J'ai faim, on mange maintenant ?
native_language_example: I'm hungry, shall we eat now?

meaning: I'm afraid / I'm scared.
additional_notes: Used to express fear, worry, or concern about something. Commonly followed by de + infinitive (J'ai peur de tomber) or que + clause (J'ai peur que ce soit vrai). Can also be used alone as a short answer.
target_language_example: J'ai peur de parler en public.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of speaking in public.

meaning: 'I have a question.'
additional_notes: Common, polite phrase used to indicate you want to ask something. Can be used to get attention before asking a question (formal or informal). Contraction 'j'' is short for 'je'. You can add specifics after it (e.g. 'pour toi', 'importante', or 'à poser').
target_language_example: J'ai une question sur le devoir.
native_language_example: I have a question about the homework.

meaning: I have things to do / I'm busy (I have work/errands to do).
additional_notes: Used to say you are occupied or have tasks to complete. Can be followed by a noun or an infinitive: 'j'ai à faire' alone means 'I have things to do'. More specifically, 'j'ai à + infinitive' means 'I need to / I have to (do something)' (e.g. 'j'ai à parler' is uncommon; prefer 'je dois parler'). Common everyday way to decline an invitation or explain you're busy. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne peux pas sortir ce soir, j'ai à faire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go out tonight, I have things to do.

meaning: literally 'I like in/about (someone)'; used to say what you like about a person.
additional_notes: This construction is followed by a pronoun or noun indicating the person (elle, lui, toi, vous). It highlights a quality, habit or trait of that person: 'C'est ce que j'aime chez toi' = 'That's what I like about you.' 'Chez' here doesn't mean 'at someone's home' but 'in/regarding someone.' Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Ce sens de l'humour, c'est ce que j'aime chez toi.
native_language_example: That sense of humour is what I like about you.

meaning: I don't know
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of "je ne sais pas". Common in casual conversation and often written in informal texts (messages, dialogue). It drops the "ne" and contracts "je" + "sais" to "j'sais". Use in informal contexts only.
target_language_example: J'sais pas si on y va ce soir.
native_language_example: I don't know if we're going tonight.

meaning: 'I don't know what' / 'something-or-other' (colloquial)
additional_notes: Informal spoken contraction of "je ne sais pas quoi" or "je sais pas quoi" used when the speaker can't recall a word or wants to be vague — similar to English "I don't know what" or "something-or-other." Common in casual conversation and often appears in expressions like "un truc, j'sais pas quoi." The dropped "ne" and the contraction "j'sais" reflect relaxed spoken French.
target_language_example: Il m'a parlé d'un projet, j'sais pas quoi, mais ça avait l'air intéressant.
native_language_example: He told me about a project, something-or-other, but it sounded interesting.

meaning: 'I was on the' (literal) — used to start a sentence saying you were about to do or were on the point of doing something, or describing being physically on something.
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a longer phrase. Literally means 'I was on the...' and can be followed by a noun (e.g., 'j'étais sur le toit' = I was on the roof) or used in more idiomatic expressions like 'j'étais sur le point de...' (I was about to...). By itself it is incomplete; listen for the words that follow to know the full meaning. Pronunciation tip: the final 'le' is pronounced /lə/.
target_language_example: J'étais sur le point de partir quand tu as appelé.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when you called.

meaning: 'never' + 'like' — used to say something will never be the same / never in that way
additional_notes: Combines 'jamais' (never) with 'comme' (like/as). Common in phrases expressing that something will never be as it was or will never happen in a certain way. Often appears in sentences like 'plus jamais comme avant' (never like before again) or 'ça ne marchera jamais comme ça' (that will never work like that). Tone can be neutral or emotional depending on context.
target_language_example: Rien ne sera jamais comme avant.
native_language_example: Nothing will ever be like it was before.

meaning: No way; never in my life; absolutely not.
additional_notes: A strong, emphatic refusal or denial. Used to reject a suggestion or express that something will never happen. Can stand alone or be combined with non (e.g. "Non, jamais de la vie"). Informal to neutral — common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Tu accepterais de sauter en parachute ? — Jamais de la vie !
native_language_example: Would you accept to skydive? — No way!

meaning: 'never played' (past participle construction)
additional_notes: Used with negation (ne... jamais) to say you have never done something involving 'jouer' (to play, perform, or play a role). Context determines meaning: jouer de + instrument (play an instrument), jouer à + sport/game (play a game), jouer un rôle (play a role), jouer quelque chose/à quelque part (play somewhere or play something). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: 'J'ai jamais joué.'
target_language_example: Je n'ai jamais joué de piano devant un public.
native_language_example: I have never played piano in front of an audience.

meaning: never (her/it) again; 'jamais' + object pronoun 'la' meaning 'never her/it'.
additional_notes: This is 'jamais' (never) followed by the feminine direct-object pronoun 'la' (her/it). Common in negatives: 'ne ... jamais la revoir' = 'to never see her/it again.' In contexts without a preceding 'ne', 'jamais la' can appear in emphatic contrasts (e.g. 'jamais la sienne' = 'never his/hers'). Word order matters: pronoun comes after 'jamais' when both appear together in infinitive constructions or certain emphatic phrases.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus jamais la revoir.
native_language_example: I never want to see her/it again.

meaning: 'never (you)' — used with a verb to say 'never (to) you' or 'never see/leave you again'.
additional_notes: This sequence combines 'jamais' (never) with the object pronoun 'te' (you, familiar). It appears in negative constructions (often with ne... jamais or with modifiers like plus jamais meaning 'never again') and goes before the verb in normal word order: e.g. Je ne veux jamais te revoir (I never want to see you again). The pronoun 'te' is informal (used with tu). In spoken French, ne is often dropped: Je veux jamais te revoir → commonly Je ne veux jamais te revoir or Je ne veux plus jamais te revoir for 'never again'.
target_language_example: Je ne veux plus jamais te perdre.
native_language_example: I never want to lose you again.

meaning: 'the garden was' — simple past/state description (imparfait) used to describe how the garden was or what it contained.
additional_notes: This is the noun jardin (garden) + était (imparfait of être = 'was'). Use to describe ongoing or background states in the past (e.g., its surroundings, what's in it, or how it looked). Replace jardin with other nouns to form similar descriptions (e.g., la maison était...).
target_language_example: Le jardin était calme au coucher du soleil.
native_language_example: The garden was calm at sunset.

meaning: May I have a glass? (polite request for a drink)
additional_notes: Used to politely ask for a drink (water, milk, wine, etc.). «Puis-je» is slightly more formal; «Pourrais-je» is very polite/conditional. In casual spoken French you can also say «Je peux avoir un verre ?», «Est-ce que je peux avoir un verre ?» or simply «Un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît.» Add the type of drink after «un verre de…» (eau, lait, vin, etc.).
target_language_example: Pourrais-je avoir un verre d'eau, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: May I have a glass of water, please?

meaning: I'm getting by / I'll manage (informal, modest way to say you'll cope).
additional_notes: Colloquial French expression used to downplay difficulties or say you're managing despite problems. Often used in response to 'Ça va?' or to describe how things are going. Tends to sound casual and sometimes resigned. More standard alternatives: 'Je m'en sors', 'Ça va', 'Je me débrouille'.
target_language_example: Tu vas bien ? — Bof, je fais aller.
native_language_example: Are you OK? — Meh, I'm getting by.

meaning: 'I'm doing my best' or 'I try my best'.
additional_notes: Used to say you are putting in as much effort as you can. Common in spoken and written French. Can be used defensively or to reassure someone. Literal parts ('je fais' = I do/make, 'de mon mieux' = of my best) help understand it: compositional. Not informal — polite and neutral.
target_language_example: Je fais de mon mieux pour finir le projet à temps.
native_language_example: I'm doing my best to finish the project on time.

meaning: 'that I make/do a' or 'that I take a' (used with subjunctive after expressions like il faut que / que + verb)
additional_notes: This phrase combines the subjunctive form je fasse (from faire) with the indefinite article un. It appears after expressions requiring the subjunctive (e.g., il faut que, que) and is completed by a noun to indicate doing/making/taking something (faire un garrot = make a tourniquet; faire un somme = take a nap; faire un scandale = make a scene). For beginners: focus on recognizing je fasse as the present subjunctive of faire, used after verbs/phrases that express necessity, desire, doubt, or emotion.
target_language_example: Il faut que je fasse un appel avant de partir.
native_language_example: I need to make a call before leaving.

meaning: I'll do my (best) / I'll do what I can (phrase typically begins a longer expression).
additional_notes: This fragment is the start of a sentence: je ferai de mon + (mieux/possible/mieux que...) — e.g. 'je ferai de mon mieux' = I'll do my best, 'je ferai de mon mieux pour...' = I'll do my best to.... 'Je ferai de mon mieux' is the complete, common phrase. Alone, 'je ferai de mon' is incomplete and needs a noun like 'mieux' (best) or 'possible'.
target_language_example: Je ferai de mon mieux pour t'aider demain.
native_language_example: I'll do my best to help you tomorrow.

meaning: 'I earn my' (as in 'I earn my living').
additional_notes: This is the beginning of the common expression 'je gagne ma vie' meaning 'I earn my living' or 'I make a living'. It is used to talk about how one earns money, often followed by 'vie' (life) or a noun describing what's earned. In everyday speech you will most often see the full phrase 'je gagne ma vie'.
target_language_example: Je gagne ma vie en donnant des cours le soir.
native_language_example: I earn my living by giving lessons in the evenings.

meaning: 'to tell him/her' (infinitive with first-person subject; literal pieces: je = I, lui = to him/her, dire = to tell).
additional_notes: This string mixes a conjugated subject pronoun (je) with an infinitive (dire) and is not grammatically correct as written. In the example sentences the intended phrase is actually a conjugated form like «que devrais-je lui dire ?», «que vais‑je lui dire ?», or «que dois‑je lui dire ?» — all mean 'what should/shall/must I tell him/her?'. Use 'lui' for 'to him' or 'to her' (indirect object). Correct full forms: je lui dis (I tell him/her), je vais lui dire (I'm going to tell him/her), je lui ai dit (I told him/her).
target_language_example: Que vais‑je lui dire si je le vois demain ?
native_language_example: What am I going to tell him if I see him tomorrow?

meaning: I am called / My name is (I call myself).
additional_notes: Use this to give your name. It's the common, polite way to introduce yourself. Structure: Je m'appelle + [name]. The literal translation is 'I call myself.' For asking someone's name in return, use 'Comment vous appelez-vous ?' (formal) or 'Tu t'appelles comment ?' (informal). Note: contraction m' is from 'me' (reflexive pronoun).
target_language_example: Je m'appelle Sophie et toi ?
native_language_example: My name is Sophie — and you?

meaning: 'I brush my (plural body part) ...' as the beginning of phrases like 'I brush my teeth.'
additional_notes: This is the reflexive verb construction 'se brosser' used with a plural body part introduced by 'les' (e.g. les dents, les cheveux). In French you say 'je me brosse les dents' rather than 'je brosse mes dents'. The full phrase will usually include the body part (les dents = teeth, les cheveux = hair) or end simply with 'les' implied in speech. Commonly used for daily routines and hygiene.
target_language_example: Je me brosse les cheveux avant de sortir.
native_language_example: I brush my hair before going out.

meaning: This combination is incorrect in French; it is not a valid conjugation. Likely a mistaken form of either "je me rends" (from the reflexive verb se rendre: to go/surrender) or "je me rends compte" (I realize), or a confusion with the infinitive construction "aller se rendre" or similar.
additional_notes:
"Je me rendre" mixes the subject "je" with the infinitive "rendre" and the reflexive pronoun "me"; French requires the verb to be conjugated to match the subject: e.g. "je me rends" (present), "je vais me rendre" (near future), or a periphrasis with an infinitive after a conjugated auxiliary. There is no correct sentence where "je me rendre" stands alone. Possible intended forms:
- "je me rends" — I go / I surrender / I turn myself (context dependent).
- "je vais me rendre" — I am going to go / I will surrender.
- "je me rends compte" — I realize.
If you see "je me rendre" in writing or speech, it is an error or a transcription of a larger structure (e.g., "je vais me rendre").
target_language_example: Je vais me rendre demain à la mairie, mais on ne dirait pas *je me rendre* tout seul.
native_language_example: I am going to go to the town hall tomorrow, but one would not say *je me rendre* by itself.

meaning: 'I don't understand' (I do not understand).
additional_notes: Use to say you don't understand something someone said or a situation. Commonly used alone as a short response (Je ne comprends pas) or followed by que/quoi/comment/why + clause. Informal spoken French often drops the 'ne' (Je comprends pas).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas pourquoi il est en retard.
native_language_example: I don't understand why he is late.

meaning: I am not saying / I'm not saying that...
additional_notes: Used to deny, soften, or qualify a statement. Often followed by a noun, adjective, clause, or opposing phrase (e.g., 'mot', 'non', 'oui', 'que...'). Can introduce a contrast ('I'm not saying the opposite') or a reluctant acceptance ('I'm not saying no'). Common in spoken and written French; the full negative construction may be shortened in casual speech ('je dis pas').
target_language_example: Je ne dis pas que c'était une bonne idée, mais ça a marché.
native_language_example: I'm not saying it was a good idea, but it worked.

meaning: I don't remember (something) / I don't recall.
additional_notes: This is the negative form of "je me souviens de" (I remember). In standard negative construction in French you usually include "pas" (je ne me souviens pas de) or add "rien" (je ne me souviens de rien) to mean "I don't remember anything." In spoken French the negation is often reduced (e.g. «je me souviens pas de…»). Use "de" before a noun, pronoun, or clause introduced by "que" when appropriate (e.g. «je ne me souviens pas de son nom», «je ne me souviens pas de ce qui s'est passé»).
target_language_example: Je ne me souviens de rien.
native_language_example: I don't remember anything.

meaning: 'I don't think' or 'I don't believe'.
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or a negative opinion. Followed by que + clause. In formal French, when the clause expresses uncertainty about the action of someone else, the subjunctive is often used (e.g. 'je ne pense pas qu'il revienne'), though in everyday speech the indicative appears frequently. Can be softened with 'je ne pense pas vraiment' or made stronger with 'je ne pense pas du tout'.
target_language_example: Je ne pense pas qu'elle viendra demain.
native_language_example: I don't think she'll come tomorrow.

meaning: I don't know
additional_notes: A very common phrase used to say you do not know something. It is often followed by an indirect question, such as ce que, pourquoi, qui, or où. In everyday spoken French, the ne is often dropped: je sais pas.
target_language_example: Désolé, je ne sais pas où il habite.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know where he lives.

meaning: I thought that everyone/everything (followed by rest of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a past assumption or belief. Often followed by « le monde », « était », or another clause that completes the idea. Conveys that the speaker's prior belief turned out to be incorrect or is being reconsidered. Can be shortened in speech to « je pensais que » + clause.
target_language_example: Je pensais que tout le monde savait la réponse, mais apparemment non.
native_language_example: I thought that everyone knew the answer, but apparently not.

meaning: I think so; I believe so.
additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or tentative agreement. Slightly formal/neutral; context can make it more or less certain. Often used alone as a short reply (Je pense bien.) or followed by a clause (Je pense bien que...).
target_language_example: Je pense bien que c'est la bonne solution.
native_language_example: I think so that it's the right solution.

meaning: I really think / I truly believe
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the speaker's opinion or belief. Often followed by 'que' + clause. Polite when combined with conditional (e.g., 'je pense vraiment que vous devriez...') to give advice or express concern. 'Je pense' alone is weaker; 'vraiment' adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Je pense vraiment que tu devrais en parler à un médecin.
native_language_example: I really think you should talk to a doctor.

meaning: Not a correct or standard French multi-word expression. 'Je peux' means 'I can'; the preposition 'à' does not normally follow 'je peux' directly. This sequence likely results from an error, a typo, or mis-segmentation in a sentence.
additional_notes: If you mean ability or permission followed by a verb, use 'je peux' + infinitive (e.g. 'je peux venir'). If 'à' appears after 'peux' in a sentence, check for missing words or that 'à' belongs to a following noun phrase (e.g. 'Je peux à peine...' is incorrect; use 'Je n'en peux plus' or 'Je peux à peine respirer' should be 'Je peux à peine respirer' — note that 'peux' can be followed by adverbs like 'à peine' but not by 'à' alone). It may also be a typo for constructions like 'je peux t'aider' or 'je peux y aller'. Provide the full sentence to get a correct fix.
target_language_example: Je peux à peine suivre la conversation.
native_language_example: I can barely follow the conversation.

meaning: 'I watch the' (used with feminine nouns like "la télé" = the TV).
additional_notes: This is the subject + verb + definite article pattern: je (I) regarde (watch) la (the, feminine). Commonly followed by nouns such as "télé" or "télévision". In spoken French, "télé" is casual for "télévision." You can also say "je regarde la télé" or the more formal "je regarde la télévision." To say you watch something regularly use adverbs: «je regarde la télé tous les jours» (I watch TV every day).
target_language_example: Je regarde la télé ce soir avec des amis.
native_language_example: I'm watching TV tonight with friends.

meaning: 'I know who you (are)'.
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a sentence meaning 'I know who you are.' It is normally completed with 'es' (je sais qui tu es). Used to assert knowledge of someone's identity or true nature; can be neutral or confrontational depending on tone and context (e.g., 'vraiment' or an insult after it).
target_language_example: Je sais qui tu es vraiment.
native_language_example: I know who you really are.

meaning: I am pregnant.
additional_notes: Used to announce or state that someone is pregnant. Formality: neutral — can be used in both casual and formal contexts. Note gender: only said by someone who is female (or someone who identifies as pregnant). Pronunciation tip: 'enceinte' pronounced /ɑ̃.sɛ̃t/. Can be used with question or emphasis (Je suis enceinte ? / Parce que je suis enceinte.).
target_language_example: Je suis enceinte et nous sommes très heureux.
native_language_example: I am pregnant and we are very happy.

meaning: I am a
additional_notes: A sentence fragment meaning "I am" with the masculine singular article un. Before a noun, it means "I am a ..."; when followed by de + plural noun, it often means "I am one of ..." as in the examples.
target_language_example: Je suis un de tes voisins.
native_language_example: I am one of your neighbors.

meaning: am I supposed to
additional_notes: Used to ask or say what is expected of someone. In questions the inversion 'suis-je supposé' appears (formal); more commonly spoken as 'je suis supposé' with intonation or 'est-ce que je suis supposé'. Often followed by an infinitive (faire, manger, etc.). Can express annoyance or disbelief ("How am I supposed to...?").
target_language_example: Comment suis-je supposé le finir aujourd'hui ?
native_language_example: How am I supposed to finish it today?

meaning: 'I supposed' or fragment of 'je suis supposée' — used to express what a feminine speaker is expected to do; often appears in constructions meaning 'I am supposed to...'. Alone, 'je supposée' is ungrammatical in standard French and should be 'je suis supposée' or 'suis-je supposée' in questions.
additional_notes: This entry targets the multi-word sequence 'je supposée' as requested, but note that in correct French the auxiliary 'suis' (from 'être') is required: 'je suis supposée' (feminine speaker) or 'je suis supposé' (masculine). In questions inversion is common: 'Suis-je supposée...?' Informal alternatives: 'je suis censée.' Use with an infinitive: 'je suis supposée + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Avec qui je supposée y aller ? (non standard; correct: Avec qui suis-je supposée y aller ?)
native_language_example: With whom am I supposed to go?

meaning: I love you
additional_notes: A direct, common way to say "I love you" in French. Used for romantic love, strong affection for family or close friends depending on context. The contraction 't'' stands for 'te' (object pronoun). Can be intensified (e.g. "je t'aime beaucoup") or altered in tense/person (e.g. "je l'aime" = I love him/her/it).
target_language_example: Je t'aime plus que tout.
native_language_example: I love you more than anything.

meaning: 'please' or 'you're welcome' depending on context; used to politely insist, beg, ask someone to do/stop something, or to respond to thanks.
additional_notes: Very common polite phrase. With an imperative (e.g. "Je t'en prie, laisse-moi passer") it means 'please' or 'I beg you' — asking or pleading. As a response to 'merci', it means 'you're welcome.' Tone and context determine meaning (can be formal or familiar). Contraction: 'je vous en prie' is the formal/plural version.
target_language_example: Je t'en prie, attends une minute.
native_language_example: Please, wait a minute.

meaning: I'll bring/drive you back to the (feminine place).
additional_notes: Commonly used when offering to give someone a ride back to a specific feminine noun introduced by 'la' (e.g. la maison, la gare). Informal, conversational register. Context determines the place; often shortened in speech (e.g. « je te ramène » if the destination is already clear). If the destination is masculine, you'd say « je te ramène au ». If plural, « je te ramène aux ».
target_language_example: Je te ramène à la maison après la fête.
native_language_example: I'll bring you back to the house after the party.

meaning: 'I find a' (literal) — used to say you find/think of something; often followed by a noun or an opinion.
additional_notes: Je trouve (que) + phrase = I find/think (that)... — when expressing an opinion, French often uses "je trouve que...". Without "que", "je trouve" + noun means "I find a/one...". In spoken French you may hear shortened forms. Make sure the noun that follows agrees in gender/number with the article (une = feminine singular).
target_language_example: Je trouve une solution au problème.
native_language_example: I find a solution to the problem.

meaning: I'm going to go / I will go (near-future plan to go somewhere or do something).
additional_notes: A near-future construction using aller + infinitive where 'je vais' = 'I am going' and 'aller' repeats the verb 'to go' when the action is literally going somewhere (je vais aller = I'll go). Often in spoken French speakers say 'je vais' + infinitive (je vais me coucher) instead of 'je vais aller me coucher'; both are common. Use 'je vais aller' when emphasizing the act of going or when planning to go somewhere.
target_language_example: Je vais aller au marché demain matin.
native_language_example: I'm going to go to the market tomorrow morning.

meaning: 'I just want a little (bit)' — expresses a small, simple desire.
additional_notes: Used to soften a request or express modest wants. Followed by nouns (un peu de sommeil), phrases (un peu plus de temps) or pronouns (un peu plus de ça). 'Juste' here means 'just/only' and 'un peu' means 'a little'. Tone is informal to neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Je veux juste un peu de paix ce soir.
native_language_example: I just want a little peace tonight.

meaning: 'I want to switch from' or 'I want to move from' (followed by a noun/pronoun indicating what you're leaving).
additional_notes: This phrase is the start of a sentence: 'je veux passer du/ de la/ des/ de l'' + noun (or 'au/à' + new thing) to say you want to change, switch, or move from one thing to another. Use du (de + le) for masculine singular nouns. Common continuations: 'au' (to the) or 'à' + new option (e.g. 'je veux passer du café au thé' = I want to switch from coffee to tea). If the next word begins with a vowel, use 'de l''.
target_language_example: Je veux passer du jus d'orange au thé.
native_language_example: I want to switch from orange juice to tea.

meaning: 'I want ... for' (used to say what you want someone to have or what you want for an occasion).
additional_notes: This phrase is typically part of a larger clause introduced by ce/ce que/ce que je, e.g. C'est ce que je veux pour toi (That's what I want for you). It can mean either: 1) what I want you to have or receive, or 2) what I want for an event (for my birthday/Christmas). The full structure is often ce que je veux pour + [person/occasion].
target_language_example: Je sais ce que je veux pour mon anniversaire.
native_language_example: I know what I want for my birthday.

meaning: I want everyone to... / I want everything to... (depends on continuation).
additional_notes: This is the start of a subordinate clause introduced by 'que'. In most examples it continues as 'je veux que tout le monde...' meaning 'I want everyone...' followed by a verb (e.g. 'sache', 'reste', 'soit'). Alone, 'je veux que tout' is incomplete — you must finish the sentence (e.g. 'je veux que tout le monde' or 'je veux que tout soit prêt'). Use with subjunctive after 'que' when expressing desire about someone/something doing/being something.
target_language_example: Je veux que tout le monde comprenne la situation.
native_language_example: I want everyone to understand the situation.

target_language_multi_word_term: je veux te montrer quelque chose
meaning: 'I want to show you something.'
additional_notes: Common phrase used to tell someone you will show them an object, place, or surprise. Quelque chose = 'something'. The full phrase includes 'quelque chose' (two words). Use 'te' for informal 'you' (singular). For formal/polite use 'vous' → 'je veux vous montrer quelque chose' or softer 'je voudrais vous montrer quelque chose.'
target_language_example: Je veux te montrer quelque chose dans la cuisine.
native_language_example: I want to show you something in the kitchen.

meaning: 'I just want' or 'I simply want' (used to introduce a modest, straightforward desire).
additional_notes: In these examples 'tout simplement' is an adverbial phrase meaning 'quite simply' or 'just'. When speakers say 'Je veux tout simplement...' they emphasize that their wish is plain, reasonable or modest. The literal words 'je veux tout' alone would mean 'I want everything', but here the full phrase is 'je veux tout simplement'. Watch word order: 'tout simplement' usually follows 'veux'.
target_language_example: Je veux tout simplement savoir la vérité.
native_language_example: I just want to know the truth.

meaning: that I live
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular present-subjunctive form of vivre (to live). Used after verbs or expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., que, il faut que, souhaiter que) to express doubt, wish, necessity, possibility, or emotion. In simple statements you'd use je vis (indicative). Can often be translated as "that I live" or "I may live" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il faut que je vive pleinement chaque jour.
native_language_example: I must live fully every day.

meaning: i see
additional_notes: Literally means seeing with your eyes, but very often also means understanding or realizing something from context. With "que" or "ce que," it often means "i see that..." or "i see what...".
target_language_example: Ah, je vois ce que tu veux dire.
native_language_example: Ah, I see what you mean.

meaning: 'I see (what...)' — used to say you understand something.
additional_notes: Common spoken expression followed by que + clause (e.g. 'je vois ce que...') meaning 'I understand what...'. Often used to acknowledge explanation or realization. In full sentences you usually hear 'je vois ce que tu veux dire' or 'je vois ce que c'est'.
target_language_example: Je vois ce que tu veux dire maintenant.
native_language_example: I see what you mean now.

meaning: 'I love you' (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Used to express love. 'Vous' can be plural (to more than one person) or formal singular (to someone you address respectfully). For informal singular with a friend/partner/family member, use 'je t'aime'. Tone depends on context; can be romantic, familial, or friendly when plural.
target_language_example: Je vous aime et je serai toujours là pour vous.
native_language_example: I love you and I will always be there for you.

meaning: 'should I call you...?' or 'do I call you...?' (polite question using 'vous')
additional_notes: This construction is actually the infinitive verb 'appeler' used after 'dois-je' (must/should I) to ask whether you should call someone or call something (e.g. a taxi). In natural French you usually say 'Dois-je vous appeler... ?' or more commonly 'Je dois vous appeler... ?' or 'Est-ce que je dois vous appeler... ?'. 'Vous' is the polite or plural 'you'. Use 't'appeler' (informal) for friends/family.
target_language_example: Dois-je vous appeler ce soir pour confirmer ?
native_language_example: Should I call you tonight to confirm?

meaning: 'I owe you some' (used before a noun like 'apologies' — e.g. 'I owe you some apologies' → 'I owe you an apology').
additional_notes: A polite/formal way to admit obligation or responsibility toward someone (vous = formal or plural 'you'). Usually followed by a plural noun (des excuses, des explications). Common in apologies: 'je vous dois des excuses' = 'I owe you an apology' or more literally 'I owe you some apologies.' Use 'te' instead of 'vous' in informal singular contexts: 'je te dois des...'.
target_language_example: Je vous dois des explications pour ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: I owe you some explanations for what happened.

meaning: please
additional_notes: Polite/formal phrase. Depending on context it can mean 'please' (as a polite request or invitation), 'you're welcome' (in response to thanks), or 'do come in/go ahead' (encouraging someone). Use 'je t'en prie' for informal singular. Often used to soften commands or invitations.
target_language_example: Entrez, je vous en prie.
native_language_example: Please come in.

meaning: 'I wish you good...' (used to start phrases like 'I wish you good luck')
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a polite formula often completed by a noun such as 'chance' (luck), 'journée' (day), or 'réussite' (success). 'Je vous souhaite bonne chance' = 'I wish you good luck.' Use 'je vous souhaite' for formal/plural 'you' (vous). For informal singular use 'je te souhaite bonne...'.
target_language_example: Je vous souhaite bonne chance pour votre entretien.
native_language_example: I wish you good luck for your interview.

meaning: to take a quick look; to glance.
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning to look briefly at something. Used in casual and neutral contexts to suggest checking or inspecting quickly. Often followed by à (jeter un coup d'œil à quelque chose) when specifying what to look at.
target_language_example: Peux-tu jeter un coup d'œil à ce document ?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at this document?

meaning: to take a quick look; to glance (informal).
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to look briefly at something. Common in spoken French. Can be followed by 'à' + noun (jeter un œil à la porte) or used alone. Tone is casual but appropriate in many situations.
target_language_example: Je vais jeter un œil au rapport et je reviens.
native_language_example: I'll take a quick look at the report and I'll be back.

meaning: very easy; child's play.
