additional_notes: Used to say something is simple to do — equivalent to English 'child's play' or 'a piece of cake'. Can be used with different tenses: C'est un jeu d'enfant (It's easy), Ça va être un jeu d'enfant (It will be easy).
target_language_example: Réparer cette lampe? Ce sera un jeu d'enfant.
native_language_example: Fixing this lamp? It will be child's play.

meaning: a deck or pack of playing cards.
additional_notes: Refers to the full set of playing cards used for card games (usually 52 cards in many contexts). Can mean 'a deck' or 'a pack' in English. Used when talking about the physical set of cards or offering/asking for one.
target_language_example: Joue une partie avec mon jeu de cartes ce soir.
native_language_example: Play a game with my deck of cards tonight.

meaning: a pun; a play on words.
additional_notes: Used to refer to wordplay where words with multiple meanings or similar sounds create a humorous or clever effect. Common phrases: "sans jeu de mots" (without a pun) and "sans mauvais jeu de mots" (no offense intended, literally 'no bad pun'). Can be used neutrally or to note a deliberate pun.
target_language_example: Il a fait un jeu de mots et tout le monde a ri.
native_language_example: He made a pun and everyone laughed.

meaning: 'video game' — an electronic game played on a console, computer, or mobile device.
additional_notes: Common, neutral term. Singular 'jeu vidéo', plural 'jeux vidéo'. Used for both the medium (a game) and the activity (playing games). Can be preceded by qualifiers (jeu vidéo en ligne, jeu vidéo mobile). Pronunciation: [ʒø ve.de.o].
target_language_example: Fortnite est un célèbre jeu vidéo en ligne.
native_language_example: Fortnite is a famous online video game.

meaning: young woman
additional_notes: A neutral, common description for an adult female who is relatively young (late teens to thirties, context-dependent). Can refer to age, appearance, or simply be used in descriptions. Used in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: La jeune femme a accepté le poste hier.
native_language_example: The young woman accepted the job yesterday.

meaning: young girl; young woman (teenage or unmarried female).
additional_notes: Refers to a female who is young — often a teenager or young adult. Can be used neutrally (Qui est cette jeune fille ?) or politely/formally to address a young woman (Merci, jeune fille). In contexts like "ma plus jeune fille" it means "my youngest daughter." Not necessarily exact age; tone depends on context.
target_language_example: Qui est cette jeune fille près de la porte ?
native_language_example: Who is that young girl by the door?

meaning: young man; a young male (man, gentleman).
additional_notes: Used to describe a male who is young (late teens to early adulthood). Can be neutral or polite when addressing someone (e.g., 'jeune homme?' as 'young man?'). In speech, context determines formality—when addressing someone directly it can sound slightly old-fashioned or patronizing depending on tone.
target_language_example: C'est un jeune homme très sérieux.
native_language_example: He is a very serious young man.

meaning: newlywed (a person who has recently married)
additional_notes: Literally 'young married [person]'; used to refer to someone who has just gotten married (can be masculine or, with agreement, feminine: 'jeune mariée'). Often used in contexts talking about honeymoon, newlywed life, or describing a couple as newly married.
target_language_example: Le jeune marié porte un costume élégant pour la réception.
native_language_example: The newlywed is wearing a smart suit for the reception.

meaning: young people; youths (young men and women).
additional_notes: Plural noun phrase meaning ‘young people’ or ‘youths’. Neutral to slightly formal — common in writing and speech. Can refer to both young men and women (context may imply gender). Often used where English would use 'young people' or 'the youth'.
target_language_example: Les jeunes gens du quartier se retrouvent au parc le week-end.
native_language_example: The young people from the neighborhood meet in the park on weekends.

meaning: to make ends meet; to have just enough money to cover expenses.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used when someone struggles financially to cover basic costs (rent, bills, food). Not literal — it doesn't refer to tying or joining physical ends. Common in everyday speech about tight budgets.
target_language_example: Avec un petit salaire, il essaie de joindre les deux bouts chaque mois.
native_language_example: With a small salary, he tries to make ends meet each month.

meaning: 'pretty' ... 'than' — used to compare (more/less/as) pretty than someone or something.
additional_notes: This is the adjective 'jolie' (pretty, feminine form) followed by the conjunction 'que' used in comparisons: 'plus jolie que' (prettier than), 'moins jolie que' (less pretty than), 'aussi jolie que' (as pretty as). The adjective agrees in gender and number with the noun it describes (jolie/jolies for feminine, joli/jolis for masculine/plural). In spoken/familiar French 'que' is also used after 'plus/moins/aussi' in comparisons.
target_language_example: Elle est plus jolie que moi.
native_language_example: She is prettier than me.

meaning: to play tricks on someone; to prank, tease, or deceive someone (can be playful or malicious).
additional_notes: Often used with à/aux + person: jouer des tours à quelqu'un. Can describe one-time pranks or habitual mischief. Tone ranges from light-hearted to more harmful depending on context.
target_language_example: Il aime jouer des tours.
native_language_example: He likes to play tricks on people.

meaning: 'to play along' or 'to go along with it' (cooperate, act as expected).
additional_notes: Used when someone agrees to cooperate, follow the rules, or pretend for the sake of a situation. Can be literal (take part in a game) but more often figurative: accept the situation and behave accordingly. Tone is neutral; context determines formality.
target_language_example: Si tu veux que ça marche, il faut jouer le jeu.
native_language_example: If you want it to work, you have to play along.

meaning: day after day; every day, continuously over time.
additional_notes: Used to express something that happens repeatedly or changes gradually over a period of days. Can be neutral, positive or negative depending on context (e.g., improving, getting worse, continuing). Often placed before or after the verb or clause: 'Jour après jour, ...' or '... jour après jour.'
target_language_example: Jour après jour, il devient plus confiant.
native_language_example: Day after day, he becomes more confident.

meaning: literally 'day of my' — used before a noun to say 'my [special] day' (e.g. my wedding day, my birthday).
additional_notes: This is a fragment that appears before a noun (jour de mon mariage, jour de mon anniversaire). It literally translates word‑for‑word into English. In some sentences it names an event (le jour de mon mariage = my wedding day) or is used idiomatically to mean 'on my day' when asking for a favor or exception. Make sure the noun that follows agrees (mon for masculine or before a vowel; use ma for feminine nouns: le jour de ma naissance, le jour de mes quinze ans).
target_language_example: Je veux profiter du jour de mon anniversaire.
native_language_example: I want to enjoy my birthday.

meaning: on the day of his/her/its (followed by a noun like anniversaire, mariage, retour).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'le jour de' (the day of) with a possessive ('son' = his/her/its) to indicate a specific day tied to someone. The gender of 'son' depends on the possessed noun (son anniversaire, son mariage) not the owner. Commonly used with anniversaries, weddings, returns, deaths, etc.
target_language_example: Elle a reçu la lettre le jour de son anniversaire.
native_language_example: She received the letter on her birthday.

meaning: day and night; continuously; all the time.
additional_notes: Used idiomatically to mean continuously or without stopping. Can describe actions, work, surveillance, etc. Equivalent to 'around the clock' in English. Not informal; literal words are 'day and night' and the phrase is compositional.
target_language_example: Ils surveillent la caméra jour et nuit.
native_language_example: They monitor the camera day and night.

meaning: logbook; record of events, activities or observations (often for a ship, aircraft, or project).
additional_notes: Used for official or personal records kept regularly to document actions, decisions, observations or progress. Common in nautical and aviation contexts (ship's log, flight log) but also used more broadly (project log, travel diary). Formal register.
target_language_example: Le pilote a noté l'incident dans le journal de bord.
native_language_example: The pilot recorded the incident in the logbook.

meaning: diary; a personal/private journal for recording thoughts and events.
additional_notes: Used for a private notebook where someone writes daily thoughts, feelings, or events. Can refer to a physical notebook or a digital/private diary. 'Tenir un journal intime' = to keep a diary. Often implies privacy (e.g., 'mon journal intime').
target_language_example: Elle écrit chaque soir dans son journal intime.
native_language_example: She writes in her diary every evening.

meaning: appears to be a mistaken word order for 'tous les matins' used with 'journal'—intended meaning: 'the newspaper every (morning) / every day'.
additional_notes: In French the correct order is usually 'tous les matins' (every morning) or 'tous les jours' (every day). Sentences 1–4 show reading the newspaper as a habitual action: 'Elle lit un journal tous les matins.' = 'She reads a newspaper every morning.' Don't say 'journal tous' alone; put the frequency expression after the verb or after the object: 'lire le journal tous les matins' or 'tous les matins, il lit le journal.'
target_language_example: Il lit le journal tous les matins.
native_language_example: He reads the newspaper every morning.

meaning: 'days in' — used to indicate a number of days spent inside or within a period/place.
additional_notes: Combines jours (days) with dans (in/inside). Often follows a number to say how many days something lasts or is spent in a place (e.g., 'six jours dans cette grotte' = six days in that cave). Can also appear in fixed expressions like 'sept jours dans une semaine' (seven days in a week). Word order: number + jours + dans + place/time unit.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé trois jours dans la maison de campagne.
native_language_example: We spent three days in the country house.

meaning: literally 'days in'; used to indicate duration (number of days) spent in or during something (a place, a mode of travel, imprisonment, etc.).
additional_notes: Usually appears after a numeral or expression of quantity (e.g. 'dix jours en Europe', 'deux jours en train', 'trente jours en prison'). It marks how many days are spent inside/using/experiencing the thing that follows. In many cases French uses 'passer X jours en/à' or 'faire X jours en' to say 'spend X days in/ travelling by/etc.'.
target_language_example: Ils ont passé quinze jours en Italie cet été.
native_language_example: They spent fifteen days in Italy this summer.

meaning: every day except (on) — used to indicate that something happens daily with one specific day excluded
additional_notes: Commonly used in schedules or timetables. Followed by a day of the week (e.g., lundi). Word order often appears in contexts like « ouvert tous les jours sauf le lundi » or « service disponible tous les jours, sauf le dimanche ». You can also see the variant without the article: « tous les jours sauf dimanche », but the article « le » before the day is very common in French.
target_language_example: Le magasin est ouvert tous les jours sauf le dimanche.
native_language_example: The store is open every day except Sunday.

meaning: Merry Christmas.
additional_notes: A common seasonal greeting used to wish someone a happy Christmas. Can be said formally or informally; context and tone (e.g., adding a name or term of endearment) make it personal. Note the capital N in Noël. Often used alone with an exclamation mark.
target_language_example: Joyeux Noël à toi et à toute la famille !
native_language_example: Merry Christmas to you and the whole family!

meaning: 'happy birthday'.
additional_notes: Standard way to wish someone a happy birthday in French. Can be followed by a name (Joyeux anniversaire, Marie !) or by 'à toi'/'à vous' or 'à [person]'. Formal and informal contexts; you can also say 'Bon anniversaire' which is equally common.
target_language_example: Joyeux anniversaire à toi — profite bien de ta journée !
native_language_example: Happy birthday to you — enjoy your day!

meaning: 'I swear that I' (used to strongly assert or promise something).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize the speaker's certainty or promise. Common forms: 'Je jure que je…' (I swear that I…), 'Je te jure que je…' (I swear to you that I…). Often followed by a statement of fact ('je l'ai vu') or a promise ('je ne le ferai jamais', 'je vais le faire'). Tone can be serious or colloquial depending on context.
target_language_example: Je te jure que je reviendrai demain.
native_language_example: I swear that I will come back tomorrow.

meaning: until the end; all the way; to see something through to completion.
additional_notes: Used to say you will continue something to its conclusion or not give up. Can be literal (go to the far end) or figurative (finish a task, persist). Common in commands, promises, and statements of determination.
target_language_example: Nous devons aller jusqu'au bout de ce projet.
native_language_example: We must see this project through to the end.

meaning: 'until' (introduces a clause; followed by a subjunctive verb).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that one action or state continues up to the point when another action/state occurs. It is followed by the subjunctive mood (e.g. 'jusqu'à ce que tu viennes'). Common in instructions and descriptions of time. Not literal word-for-word translation (contains the conjunction 'ce que').
target_language_example: Reste ici jusqu'à ce que je revienne.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back.

meaning: until then / up to that point / that far
additional_notes: Used to refer to a point in time or extent previously mentioned or understood. Can mean 'until then' (temporal) or 'that far'/'to that extent' (degree/place). Often appears at clause start for 'until now' or after a verb for 'up to that point'.
target_language_example: Jusque-là, tout se passait bien.
native_language_example: Until then, everything was going well.

meaning: until that point / up to then
additional_notes: Used to indicate up to a specific moment, place, or degree previously mentioned or understood from context. Can refer to time (until then) or extent/limit (up to that length/point). Often written 'jusque-là' with a hyphen in formal writing when meaning 'until then'.
target_language_example: Il a vécu ici jusque là.
native_language_example: He lived here until then.

meaning: 'just need to' or 'just need (something)'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to downplay urgency or emphasize a small/simple need. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "d'envoyer") or a noun introduced by "un/une/un peu de" (note the elision with d' before a vowel). "Juste" here means "only"/"just". Can be used in many everyday contexts to request a short time, an item, or to state a simple requirement.
target_language_example: J'ai juste besoin d'un verre d'eau.
native_language_example: I just need a glass of water.

meaning: just now; a moment ago; right now (emphatic).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something happened a very short time ago (just now) or to emphasize timing (right now/at this exact moment). Tone can be neutral or slightly irritated depending on context: e.g. "Elle a appelé juste maintenant" = she called a moment ago; "Pourquoi tu me déranges juste maintenant ?" = why are you bothering me right now? Often interchangeable with "à l'instant" or "tout à l'heure" depending on nuance.
target_language_example: Je n'avais pas fini, et il est arrivé juste maintenant.
native_language_example: I hadn't finished, and he arrived just now.

meaning: to just stop by / to just pass by (brief, casual visit or quick stop).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a brief or casual visit, or that one only intended to stop by briefly. 'Juste' = 'just/only'; 'passer' = 'to pass/stop by'. Common constructions: 'je voulais juste passer (pour ...)', 'je viens juste passer'. Tone: neutral; suitable for everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Je voulais juste passer pour dire bonjour.
native_language_example: I just wanted to stop by to say hello.

meaning: just that you be / I (we) just want you to be (something).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like vouloir or expressions of desire/worry to introduce a simple wish about someone’s state or action. 'Juste' here means 'only' or 'just', softening the request. The verb after 'que' is in the subjunctive (sois). Can be used with different subjects (je veux juste que tu sois..., nous voulons juste que tu sois...).
target_language_example: Je veux juste que tu sois honnête avec moi.
native_language_example: I just want you to be honest with me.

meaning: 'just that you' — used to introduce a simple wish, request, or clarification directed at 'you' (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Often appears after verbs like vouloir, penser, falloir, or expressions meaning 'I just want/think/need...' It softens or limits the statement (just/only) and is followed by a verb in the subjunctive or indicative depending on the main verb (e.g. 'que vous regardiez' — subjunctive after 'il faut'; 'que vous savez' — indicative). 'Vous' can be formal singular or plural.
target_language_example: Je veux juste que vous sachiez la vérité.
native_language_example: I just want you to know the truth.

meaning: just you / only you
additional_notes: Used to emphasize exclusivity: that someone alone is involved or remains (often in contrast with others). Common in phrases like "juste toi et moi" (just you and me). "Juste" here means "only" or "just". Tone is neutral and appropriate in casual and formal contexts depending on surrounding words.
target_language_example: C'est juste toi et moi ce soir.
native_language_example: It's just you and me tonight.

meaning: the ...'s birthday (female possessor: my ...'s birthday)
additional_notes: Used before a feminine family member or female person: ma femme (my wife), ma fille (my daughter), ma mère/maman (my mother), ma puce (affectionate for a child/partner). Structure: C'est l'anniversaire de ma + [noun]. In English you say "It's my [noun]'s birthday" or more naturally "It's my wife's/daughter's/mother's birthday."
target_language_example: C'est l'anniversaire de ma sœur aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It's my sister's birthday today.

meaning: the other day; a few days ago (refers to a recent past occasion).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a past event or occasion that both speakers likely remember. Can mean 'the other day' or 'recently' without specifying an exact date. Common in apologies and casual references to something that happened previously.
target_language_example: Je voulais m'excuser pour l'autre jour.
native_language_example: I wanted to apologize for the other day.

meaning: 'time to' (followed by a reflexive verb) — indicates it's time to do something (yourself).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it's the start of expressions like "l'heure de se coucher" (time to go to bed) or "l'heure de se préparer" (time to get ready). It is always followed by a reflexive verb (se + infinitive). Use to say it's the appropriate or scheduled time to perform a personal action.
target_language_example: C'est l'heure de se coucher.
native_language_example: It's time to go to bed.

meaning: short for "l'heure qu'il est" — "what time it is" (asking or stating the time).
additional_notes: This is a clipped form used before a verb starting with a vowel (qu'il, qu'elle, qu'on). Common in questions and exclamations: "Sais-tu l'heure qu'il est ?" = "Do you know what time it is?" Can be used in statements: "Je sais l'heure qu'il est." — though more natural is "Je sais quelle heure il est." Informal spoken French often uses the shortened form.
target_language_example: Sais-tu l'heure qu'il est ?
native_language_example: Do you know what time it is?

meaning: didn't (do something)
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of (ne) l' + a + pas used in spoken French to form the negation of passé composé when the object pronoun l' is present (e.g. elle l'a pas dit = elle ne l'a pas dit). The full negative form is "ne ... pas"; in informal speech the "ne" is often dropped. Can mean either "didn't" or "hasn't" depending on context and tense (passé composé).
target_language_example: Elle me l'a pas dit.
native_language_example: She didn't tell me (it).

meaning: 'I have it in' (used in phrases like 'I have it in mind / in view / online')
additional_notes: This is part of constructions with the direct object pronoun 'le/la' (here contracted to 'l'') + avoir + en + noun. It expresses that you 'have' something in a certain state or context (en tête = in mind, en ligne = online/connected, en vue = in sight/visible, en visuel = visually). English translations vary by context; translate the whole phrase rather than word-for-word. Typical structure: Je l'ai en + noun.
target_language_example: Je l'ai en réserve.
native_language_example: I have it in reserve.

meaning: have it
additional_notes: Contraction of le or la + avons. It is used with nous and means that the object ('him,' 'her,' or 'it') comes before the verb: nous l'avons vu = 'we saw him/it.' In writing, the past participle can agree with that earlier direct object: trouvée shows a feminine object.
target_language_example: Nous l'avons déjà fait.
native_language_example: We've already done it.

meaning: 'one after the other' or 'one by one'.
additional_notes: Used to describe actions or events happening sequentially, with each item/person following the previous in order. Can be used for both people and objects. For a mixed-gender or plural group of people, you might also see 'les uns après les autres' or 'les unes après les autres'.
target_language_example: Les invités sont entrés l'un après l'autre.
native_language_example: The guests came in one after the other.

meaning: each other / one another (mutual action or relation between two or more people or things).
additional_notes: Used to express mutual actions or feelings between two or more subjects. Agreement in gender/number: if subjects are feminine, form becomes "l'une l'autre" (two) or "les unes les autres" etc.; with plural masculine or mixed groups use "les uns les autres" or simply "les uns les autres" is less common — more typical forms: "l'un(e) l'autre", "les uns les autres", "les unes les autres". Often appears with reflexive or reciprocal verbs (se voir, s'aimer) or as object: "Ils se regardent l'un l'autre."
target_language_example: Ils s'aident l'un l'autre quand ils en ont besoin.
native_language_example: They help each other when they need it.

meaning: 'for each other' (used in the expression "être fait l'un pour l'autre" = to be made for each other / to be perfect for each other)
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the fixed expression "être fait l'un pour l'autre" or "faits l'un pour l'autre." It describes two people (or things) who are ideally suited to one another. The full phrase is usually "l'un pour l'autre"; here the final vowel of "l'" links to the next word when spoken (e.g. "l'un pour l'autre"). Use with plural/subject agreement: "Nous sommes faits l'un pour l'autre."
target_language_example: Ils sont faits l'un pour l'autre.
native_language_example: They are made for each other.

meaning: porridge; a soft, often mushy food made by boiling cereals or other ingredients.
additional_notes: Used for soft, easily swallowed foods (rice porridge, oatmeal, baby food). Can be savory or sweet. Often implies a smooth, mushy texture. In informal contexts, can also mean something ruined or turned into a mess (e.g., 'faire de la bouillie' = to mess up or make mush of something).
target_language_example: Chaque matin, je prépare de la bouillie d'avoine avec du miel.
native_language_example: Every morning I make oatmeal porridge with honey.

meaning: the chance/opportunity to (do something); the likelihood of
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or a noun to express having the possibility/opportunity to do something or the probability of something happening. Context determines whether it means 'opportunity' ('a chance to...') or 'probability' ('the chance of...'). Common structure: 'avoir la chance de + infinitive' (to be lucky to / have the opportunity to).
target_language_example: J'ai la chance de voyager cet été.
native_language_example: I have the chance/opportunity to travel this summer.

meaning: 'the way' or 'the manner' (how something is done).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the manner, method or style of doing something. Often followed by 'dont', 'de', 'de faire', or a clause: la façon dont/ la façon de + infinitive. Can be used in formal and informal contexts. Plural: les façons.
target_language_example: J'aime la façon dont tu expliques les choses.
native_language_example: I like the way you explain things.

meaning: to the party with (someone).
additional_notes: Used to say going/being present at a party accompanied by someone. 'Avec' means 'with' and is followed by the person (moi, toi, lui, Tom...). The phrase itself is not idiomatic—it's just the noun 'la fête' + preposition 'avec'. You can change 'la fête' to other events (le concert, la réunion) the same way.
target_language_example: Je voudrais aller à la fête avec mes amis.
native_language_example: I would like to go to the party with my friends.

meaning: A polite phrase used when asking to be let off/left at the train station (literally: 'drop me at the station, please').
additional_notes: This construction appears in requests like "Descendez-moi à la gare, je vous prie" or informal "Descends-moi à la gare, je te prie." "Je vous prie/je te prie" is a polite way to say "please." "Largue-moi à la gare" is informal/slang (larguer = drop/leave someone). Also used literally in narration: "En sortant de la gare, je vis…" where "la gare" simply means "the station." Context decides whether it's a request (imperative + me) or a location in a sentence.
target_language_example: Descends-moi à la gare, je te prie — je dois attraper le train de 18h.
native_language_example: Drop me off at the station, please — I need to catch the 6 pm train.

meaning: to (be) at the station / to arrive at the station (with a time expression).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the noun la gare (the station) with the preposition à when indicating arrival or presence at a place and often used with a time: arriver à la gare à 7 heures = arrive at the station at 7. For beginners: use 'être à la gare' (to be at the station) or 'arriver à la gare' (to arrive at the station). The second 'à' before a time marks when (à cinq heures).
target_language_example: Je serai à la gare à six heures.
native_language_example: I will be at the station at six o'clock.

meaning: 'food and' — the phrase 'la nourriture' (food) followed by 'et' (and).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the noun 'la nourriture' plus the conjunction 'et' to join another item (e.g. 'la nourriture et des couvertures'). Use 'de la nourriture' for unspecified quantity (some food). Watch agreement: 'nourriture' is feminine singular. Common in lists of supplies or donations.
target_language_example: Ils ont apporté de la nourriture et des vêtements.
native_language_example: They brought food and clothes.

meaning: witchcraft; sorcery; the practice of magic.
additional_notes: Used to describe supernatural magic, occult practices, or figuratively to express that something seems mysterious or inexplicable (e.g., "It's like witchcraft"). Often uncountable in French when speaking generally: "de la sorcellerie."
target_language_example: Ce mécanisme fonctionne sans explication — on dirait de la sorcellerie.
native_language_example: This mechanism works without explanation — it looks like witchcraft.

meaning: Bring/let her in (object pronoun + infinitive).
additional_notes: This appears to be the combination of the feminine direct object pronoun 'la' (her/it) placed before an infinitive 'entrer' (to enter). In standard written French the pronoun comes before the infinitive only when another verb governs it: e.g. 'Fais-la entrer' = 'Make/bring her enter' or more naturally 'Let her in' / 'Bring her in'. In polite/formal commands use 'Faites-la entrer, s'il vous plaît.' For negative commands with an infinitive, the pronoun still precedes the infinitive: 'Ne la faites pas entrer.' Note: 'la entrer' by itself is not a standalone phrase — it always appears as part of a verb phrase (imperative or with another conjugated verb).
target_language_example: Faites-la entrer, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Please let her in.

meaning: to make her (do something) / to get her to (do something).
additional_notes: A construction using the causative verb 'faire' + object pronoun 'la' (her). 'Faire' + infinitive means 'to cause/make/get someone to do something'. Word order: subject + faire + object pronoun + infinitive (e.g. Nous l'avons fait partir). In the example, 'la faire aller dormir' = 'get her to go to sleep'. Pronoun 'la' stands for a feminine singular person or noun. Replace with le, les, etc. as needed.
target_language_example: Je vais la faire parler au téléphone.
native_language_example: I'll get her to speak on the phone.

meaning: 'shut up' (tell someone to be quiet).
additional_notes: Colloquial and somewhat rude. Literally 'to close it' (la = it, referring to the mouth). Commonly used in spoken French to tell someone to stop talking. Use with caution; can be offensive in formal situations.
target_language_example: Il ferait mieux de la fermer pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: He'd better shut up during the meeting.

meaning: 'to play it' / 'to act/handle a situation in a certain way' (informal conversational use)
additional_notes: Used with a direct object pronoun (la, le) to mean 'to play it' literally or figuratively: how to approach, perform, present, or handle something. Common in expressions like « la jouer serrée » (play it tight/keep things guarded) or « la jouer clean » (play it clean/ play fair). Tone can be neutral or blunt; in informal contexts it may be used with slang/insults. The verb jouer keeps its normal meanings (play, act), so the phrase is compositional.
target_language_example: On va la jouer tranquille et éviter les risques.
native_language_example: We'll play it safe and avoid risks.

meaning: to bring her back / to take her home (bring someone back to a place).
additional_notes: La ramener is the colloquial use of ramener + object pronoun la (her/it). Depending on context it can mean 'bring her back' (return someone to a location) or 'take her home'. It's common in spoken French. If the object is masculine use le (le ramener); plural use les. Ramener comes from ramener (to bring back).
target_language_example: Tu peux la ramener chez elle ce soir ?
native_language_example: Can you bring her back to her place tonight?

meaning: There she is / here she is (feminine), or 'there it is' for a feminine noun; used to point someone or something out.
additional_notes: Common spoken expression used when someone or something (usually feminine) appears or is pointed out. Can be used literally (spotting a woman, girl, or a feminine noun like 'voiture') or playfully/ironically (e.g. calling someone 'la belle' or 'Cendrillon'). Often accompanied by surprise, relief, or mild reproach. Tone and context determine nuance.
target_language_example: La voilà qui sort de la voiture.
native_language_example: There she is getting out of the car.

meaning: the Cavalry; (also) the cavalry unit or a place name (La Cavalerie).
additional_notes: Capitalized 'La Cavalerie' is often a proper noun — the name of a town in southern France (in Aveyron) — or the name of a military unit. Lowercase 'la cavalerie' refers to cavalry (soldiers on horseback). Context (capitalization, article, geography or military) tells you which meaning applies.
target_language_example: Nous visiterons La Cavalerie pendant notre voyage en Aveyron.
native_language_example: We will visit La Cavalerie during our trip to Aveyron.

meaning: the conception; the idea or the moment of conception (also a proper name: place/Marian title).
additional_notes: Capitalized as 'La Conception' can be a proper noun (e.g., name of a town, church, or the Marian title 'Immaculate Conception'). In lowercase 'la conception' commonly means 'the act of conceiving' (pregnancy) or 'the design/creation of an idea or project'. Context tells whether it's biological, creative, or a place/name.
target_language_example: La conception du projet a pris plusieurs mois.
native_language_example: The conception/design of the project took several months.

meaning: The La Défense district in Paris (major business/commercial district); can also mean 'defense' in general depending on context.
additional_notes: When capitalized and preceded by 'la', La Défense refers to the large business district west of Paris (offices, métro/RER station, landmarks). In spoken French, 'la Défense' can be used in phone or travel contexts to mean the La Défense station or area (e.g., 'Passez-moi la Défense' = put someone through to a line/office at La Défense). Lowercase 'défense' without 'La' means defense (military/protection).
target_language_example: Je travaille dans un cabinet à La Défense.
native_language_example: I work at a firm in La Défense.

meaning: the barn (feminine singular) — 'la Grange' can also be a proper name (e.g., a place, restaurant, or surname).
additional_notes: As a common noun, 'la grange' means 'the barn' (a building for farm animals or hay). Capitalized as 'La Grange' it often appears as a place name, business name, or family name; in that case treat it as a proper noun and translate according to context. Feminine noun: une grange / la grange. Pronunciation note: the 'g' is hard (like in 'go').
target_language_example: Ils ont réparé la grange avant l'hiver.
native_language_example: They repaired the barn before winter.

meaning: 'fishing' (the activity) OR 'peach' (the fruit) depending on context; informally can mean 'energy' or 'pep'.
additional_notes: Primary meanings: 1) la pêche = fishing (activity). 2) la pêche = the peach (fruit). Colloquially, avoir la pêche / être en pleine pêche means to be energetic, in high spirits (similar to 'to be full of energy'). Context (capitalization not significant in French) and articles help: parler de la pêche (talking about fishing) vs. manger une pêche (eat a peach).
target_language_example: Ce week-end, je vais à la pêche; j'espère revenir avec du poisson.
native_language_example: This weekend I'm going fishing; I hope to come back with some fish.

meaning: 'the Queen' (the female monarch or a queen as a figurehead).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a reigning female monarch or to the queen consort in contexts like formal speech, chants, toasts, or exclamations (e.g., 'Vive la Reine!'). Capitalization (La Reine) is common when referring to a specific sovereign. Can also be used more generally to speak about 'a queen' in a story or conversation.
target_language_example: Vive la Reine et son règne !
native_language_example: Long live the Queen and her reign!

meaning: the farm; can also be used colloquially to tell someone to 'shut up' (short for «ta ferme» / «la ferme» as an interjection).
additional_notes: Primary meaning: 'la ferme' = 'the farm' (a place where animals/plants are raised). Context determines meaning. As an interjection, 'La ferme !' is informal and rude — equivalent to 'Shut up!' or 'Be quiet!' Can appear in sentences like 'Vous venez de la ferme ?' (Are you from the farm?) or 'Les chevaux sont dans la ferme.' (The horses are in the farm).
target_language_example: Arrête de parler et la ferme, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop talking and shut up, please.

meaning: shame; embarrassment; disgrace.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a feeling of personal embarrassment (avoir honte), an action that brings disgrace on someone or a group (être la honte de...), or an exclamation to express strong embarrassment ('La honte!' or 'Rien que la honte!'). Can be used as a noun (la honte) or in expressions (me fous pas la honte = don't embarrass me).
target_language_example: Ne me fous pas la honte devant mes amis.
native_language_example: Don't embarrass me in front of my friends.

meaning: 'the day has' (used as the start of a past-tense comment about how the day was).
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the structure 'La journée a été...' followed by an adjective (longue, rude, épuisante, belle, bonne) to describe how the day went. 'La journée a' by itself is incomplete — it needs a past participle (été) and a complement. Useful for asking or stating how someone's day was: 'La journée a été bonne ?' = 'Was the day good?'.
target_language_example: La journée a été stressante, mais maintenant je me détends.
native_language_example: The day was stressful, but now I'm relaxing.

meaning: 'the ... language' used in superlative/questions (part of the construction: « quelle/quel est la langue la plus ... »).
additional_notes: This appears as part of superlative questions about languages: «Quelle est la langue la plus + adjective?» (Which language is the most ...?). Grammatically, use quelle (feminine) with langue (f.), or quel with masculine nouns. The second «la» is the definite article used in the superlative construction «la plus» (the most). In correct phrasing, you usually see: «Quelle est la langue la plus difficile au monde?» or shortened focus: «Quelle langue est la plus difficile?» Both are natural. Remember agreement: adjective after plus must agree with langue.
target_language_example: Quelle est la langue la plus parlée au monde?
native_language_example: Which language is the most spoken in the world?

meaning: to raise one's hand to ask (a question).
additional_notes: Used to describe the action of raising a hand (in class, a meeting, etc.) with the purpose of asking a question. In examples given the full verb phrase is usually 'lever la main pour poser (une question)'. 'Lever la main' is the core expression; 'pour poser' specifies the intention. Common in classroom contexts.
target_language_example: Il a levé la main pour poser une question pendant le cours.
native_language_example: He raised his hand to ask a question during class.

meaning: This exact form is incorrect in standard French; likely a mistaken mix of 'la majeure' (feminine) or 'le majeur' (masculine).
additional_notes:
There is no common French phrase 'la majeur'. Possible intended forms:
- 'la majeure' (feminine adjective or noun): e.g. 'la majeure partie' = 'the majority' or in music 'la majeure' (major, as in interval/third) when agreeing with a feminine noun.
- 'le majeur' (masculine noun): can mean 'the thumb' (in anatomy) or 'the major' in rank, or 'majeur' as adjective 'adult' => 'le majeur' (the adult male). Spellings and agreement matter: 'majeure/majeur'.
For beginners: learn 'la majeure partie' = 'the majority' and 'majeur/majeure' as adjective meaning 'adult' or 'major'.
target_language_example: La majeure partie des étudiants a réussi l'examen.
native_language_example: The majority of the students passed the exam.

meaning: 'the majority' or 'the greater part' (of something).
additional_notes: Often used in the fixed expression 'la majeure partie (de)' meaning 'the majority of' or 'most of'. Followed by a noun introduced by 'de' (la majeure partie de + noun). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: La majeure partie de la journée, il a travaillé dehors.
native_language_example: Most of the day, he worked outside.

meaning: 'the piece of' or 'the room of' depending on context; used as part of a longer phrase.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase — "la pièce de" needs a noun or name after it. It can mean "the piece of (something)" (e.g., la pièce de monnaie = the coin) or start a possessive construction with 'de' (e.g., la pièce de théâtre = the play/literary piece). It can also be used when talking about a room owned or used by someone if followed by a person (less common: la pièce de la maison = the room of the house). Choose the meaning based on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: La pièce de monnaie que j'ai trouvée est vieille.
native_language_example: The coin that I found is old.

meaning: most
additional_notes: Used to indicate the majority of a group or amount. Frequently appears as "la plupart de" or "la plupart d'" followed by a noun or pronoun (la plupart d'entre vous = most of you). Can be followed by a verb when referring to most of someone's time/life (la plupart de sa vie).
target_language_example: La plupart des étudiants ont réussi l'examen.
native_language_example: Most of the students passed the exam.

meaning: most people
additional_notes: Used to talk about the majority of people in general. Can be followed by verbs or adjectives. Tone depends on the rest of the sentence (neutral, positive, or negative). Often contracted in speech to "la plupart" when context is clear.
target_language_example: La plupart des gens aiment les jours ensoleillés.
native_language_example: Most people like sunny days.

meaning: 'most of' (used in the expression 'la plupart du temps' = 'most of the time')
additional_notes: Literally 'the majority of'. Commonly appears in the fixed phrase 'la plupart du temps' meaning 'most of the time' or 'usually'. Can be followed by different nouns (la plupart des gens = most people), but with 'temps' the partitive 'du' (de + le) is used: 'la plupart du temps'.
target_language_example: La plupart du temps, je prends le bus pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Most of the time, I take the bus to go to work.

meaning: most of the time; usually
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens frequently or generally. Can appear at the start or within a sentence. Equivalent to 'usually' or 'generally' in English.
target_language_example: La plupart du temps, je prends le bus pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: Most of the time, I take the bus to get to work.

meaning: 'the apple into' (used with a verb of cutting or dividing to mean splitting the apple into parts)
additional_notes: This phrase fragment appears before a measure or number (e.g. "en deux" = into two). In the examples the full expression is "couper la pomme en deux" = to cut/split the apple into two pieces. The preposition "en" + number/measure indicates the resulting number/size (en deux, en quatre, en morceaux, en tranches). You will normally see the complete phrase (la pomme en deux / en morceaux).
target_language_example: Elle veut couper la pomme en quartiers.
native_language_example: She wants to cut the apple into quarters.

meaning: 'please' (polite request added after an imperative or question; literally 'I beg you').
additional_notes: This is a polite formula often added after a command or question to soften it. Full phrase is "je vous prie" (formal). In spoken French you may hear just "je vous en prie" in replies, but after imperatives/questions it's usually "je vous prie" or simply "s'il vous plaît". Use with verbs: "Fermez la porte, je vous prie." It's formal/polite and suitable in respectful situations.
target_language_example: Fermez la porte, je vous prie.
native_language_example: Please close the door.

meaning: the door left open at night / leaving the door open during the night
additional_notes: Used to refer to the state of a door being left open during the night (often implying a security or comfort issue). Commonly appears in questions about who left the door open. You can replace «la nuit» with a specific night (e.g. «la nuit dernière», «la nuit passée») to indicate which night.
target_language_example: Tu as laissé la porte ouverte la nuit dernière?
native_language_example: Did you leave the door open last night?

la première fois que nous nous

target_language_multi_word_term: la première fois que nous nous
meaning: 'the first time that we (verb... )' — introduces a memory of a first occasion involving both speakers.
additional_notes: Used to start a clause recalling a first shared experience (commonly followed by a reflexive verb like 'sommes rencontrés', 'nous sommes vus', etc.). Agreement (rencontrés/rencontrées) matches the group's gender(s). Often appears with verbs of remembering: 'se rappeler', 'se souvenir de'.
target_language_example: Je me souviens de la première fois que nous nous sommes parlés.
native_language_example: I remember the first time that we spoke.

meaning: the falling of / the onset of (used with times or things that 'fall' or begin, e.g. la tombée de la nuit = the onset of night).
additional_notes: Often used in fixed expressions like "la tombée de la nuit" (dusk/nightfall) or "la tombée du jour" (dusk). It conveys the idea of something descending or beginning (light, night, silence). It is followed by a noun and translated as "the onset/coming/fall of" in English. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Nous partirons à la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We will leave at nightfall.

meaning: with head held high; confidently, proudly
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to act confidently or to describe doing something without shame or embarrassment. Common in commands (Garde la tête haute) and statements (rentrer la tête haute). Literal components are understandable (tête = head, haute = high), so it's compositional and can be translated literally.
target_language_example: Après l'entretien, elle est repartie la tête haute.
native_language_example: After the interview, she left with her head held high.

meaning: 'the cow' (literal) — also an exclamation like 'wow'/'oh my!'
additional_notes: Literally means the female cow. Commonly used in spoken French as an informal interjection (Oh la vache !) to express surprise, astonishment, annoyance or admiration — similar to 'wow', 'jeez', or 'oh my goodness' in English. In a literal context it refers to the animal (e.g. donner du lait, traire). Tone and context tell you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: La vache donne du lait chaque matin.
native_language_example: The cow gives milk every morning.

meaning: the city where I (was/was born, live, etc.).
additional_notes: A relative expression combining 'la ville' (the city) + 'où' (where) + a verb with 'je'. Use it to point to a specific city connected to the speaker (birthplace, residence, memories). 'Où' introduces a clause of place and is followed by a verb (e.g. 'suis né', 'vis', 'ai grandi'). Agreement (né/née) depends on the speaker's gender when using past participles.
target_language_example: La ville où je vis est tranquille.
native_language_example: The city where I live is peaceful.

meaning: 'to let go' / 'to let oneself go' / 'to allow to go' (depends on context).
additional_notes: This phrase has several related uses: 1) reflexive (se laisser aller) means 'to let yourself go' — relax, stop controlling emotions or appearance; 2) transitive or intransitive (laisser aller quelqu'un/quelque chose) can mean 'allow someone/something to go/leave' or 'let something get out of control' (e.g. laisser aller plus loin); 3) polite/formal permission (Veuillez me laisser aller...) = 'please allow me to go'. Context determines whether it's about permitting movement, emotional release, or neglect.
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas se laisser aller.
native_language_example: You must not let yourself go.

meaning: 'to let (someone) do (something)' or 'allow (something) to happen' (often with a sense of permitting or tolerating).
additional_notes: Commonly used with a direct object or an infinitive: laisser + faire/infinitive. Can mean 'allow' in a neutral way or 'let get away with' when expressing disapproval (e.g. I can't let you do that). Context and tone determine whether it's permissive or critical.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas vous laisser faire ça.
native_language_example: I can't let you do that.

meaning: to let speak; to allow someone or something to express itself (often used figuratively: let feelings, silence, or facts 'speak for themselves')
additional_notes: Literally 'to let speak.' Used to mean permitting someone to speak, or figuratively to let something reveal itself (e.g., 'laissez parler votre cœur' = 'let your heart speak' meaning follow your feelings). Common constructions: 'laisser parler quelqu'un' (allow someone to speak) and 'laisser parler + noun' (let X show/reveal itself). Can be used in imperative ('laisse' or 'laissez') and infinitive forms.
target_language_example: Il faut parfois laisser parler les émotions pour guérir.
native_language_example: Sometimes you need to let emotions speak in order to heal.

meaning: to let (someone/something) pass; to allow through; to miss/let slip (an opportunity or mistake).
additional_notes: Can be used literally (allow physical passage: 'let someone/something through') or figuratively (fail to act, 'let something slip' or 'miss something'). In questions it is common as a request: "Vous pouvez me laisser passer ?" = "Can you let me through?" Verb construction: laisser + infinitive (laisser + passer).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, pouvez-vous me laisser passer ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you let me through?

meaning: to drop; to give up; to let go (literally and figuratively)
additional_notes: Used both literally (to let an object fall) and figuratively (to give up on something, stop pursuing or stop worrying). Very common in spoken French and informal registers. Context and conjugation determine whether it's literal or figurative (e.g. "laisser tomber la boisson" = give up drinking; "Laisse tomber" = drop it/forget it).
target_language_example: Je ne vais pas laisser tomber !
native_language_example: I'm not going to give up!

meaning: 'to leave (someone) alone' — to stop bothering, disturbing, or interfering with someone.
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to ask or tell someone not to disturb or bother. Can be used imperatively (Laisse-moi tranquille !) or politely (Pouvez-vous me laisser tranquille ?). The subject of laisser is the person doing the leaving; the object is the person being left alone. Frequently used in spoken French and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Il nous a demandé de le laisser tranquille.
native_language_example: He asked us to leave him alone.

meaning: to let (something/someone) come; to allow to approach or occur
additional_notes: Commonly used when allowing someone or something to come closer or to allow an event/situation to develop. Can be literal (physically letting someone come) or figurative (letting things happen). Construction: laisser + venir (infinitive) or imperative plural/formal laissez venir. Often followed by the person/thing allowed (e.g. laisser quelqu'un venir).
target_language_example: Il faut laisser venir l'occasion plutôt que de forcer les choses.
native_language_example: You should let the opportunity come rather than force things.

meaning: to let (someone) see; to allow to be seen
additional_notes: A combination of laisser (to let/allow) + voir (to see). Used when allowing someone to look at, inspect, or discover something (physically or metaphorically). Appears in different conjugated forms (e.g. «laissez voir», «laisse voir», «laisser voir») and can be used in both infinitive and imperative contexts (e.g. «laisse-moi voir» = “let me see”).
target_language_example: Il va me laisser voir le rapport demain.
native_language_example: He will let me see the report tomorrow.

meaning: to be lacking; to leave something to be desired (i.e., not be good enough).
additional_notes: Used to criticize quality or performance. Commonly appears in constructions like 'Ça laisse à désirer' (= That leaves something to be desired). Neutral to slightly formal register; often followed by a noun or an implied subject.
target_language_example: La manière dont il a décoré la chambre laisse à désirer.
native_language_example: The way he decorated the room leaves something to be desired.

meaning: 'let (someone or something) do' — allow to act or leave alone.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to allow a person or situation to proceed without intervening. Can be an instruction (Laissez faire = Let it be / Leave him alone) or part of a sentence (e.g., si vous le laissez faire = if you let him do it). Related to the economic term 'laissez-faire' but here it functions as an imperative phrase or verbal construction meaning 'let act'.
target_language_example: Laissez faire, il saura se débrouiller.
native_language_example: Let him do it, he'll manage on his own.

meaning: left the window (open).
additional_notes: From the verb laisser (to leave/allow) + direct object la fenêtre. Commonly used with an adjective like 'ouverte' (open). It appears in past tenses (passé composé) with different subjects: J'ai laissé la fenêtre ouverte = I left the window open. Can also mean 'allowed the window' in some contexts, but usually 'left (as it was)'.
target_language_example: Tu as laissé la fenêtre ouverte toute la nuit ?
native_language_example: Did you leave the window open all night?

meaning: 'the milk is' (subject + verb — simple statement about milk).
additional_notes: This is just the noun 'lait' (milk) followed by the verb 'est' (is). Use it to describe the state or quality of milk (fresh, good, bad, etc.). In normal French you would usually include the definite article 'le' before 'lait' (Le lait est...) unless context has already made the article unnecessary. Match adjectives' gender/number if present (lait is masculine singular).
target_language_example: Le lait est encore bon.
native_language_example: The milk is still good.

meaning: 'milk for' — indicates milk intended for someone or something.
additional_notes: A simple combination: lait (milk) + pour (for). Used to say who the milk is for or to request/serve milk to someone (e.g., 'Un verre de lait pour Léon' = 'A glass of milk for Léon'). Can appear without a determiner in casual speech ('Un lait pour moi' = 'A milk for me' / 'One milk for me').
target_language_example: Un verre de lait pour moi, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A glass of milk for me, please.

meaning: Not a standard fixed phrase in French; appears to be the sequence of the noun 'lait' (milk) followed by 'tous' used as part of a larger time expression (e.g. 'lait tous les matins' meaning 'milk every morning'). On its own 'lait tous' is incomplete and non-idiomatic.
additional_notes: You will normally see 'lait' followed by a time expression introduced by 'tous' plus an article: e.g. 'du lait tous les matins' or 'une bouteille de lait tous les matins'. Use 'tous' with a plural time unit: 'tous les matins', 'tous les dimanches', 'tous les mois'. The sequence 'lait tous' should be kept within a larger phrase; by itself it sounds unfinished. Informal speech may drop articles: 'il boit du lait tous les matins' is common.
target_language_example: Elle boit du lait tous les matins.
native_language_example: She drinks milk every morning.

meaning: flashlight; a portable handheld light.
additional_notes: Common everyday noun. Used to refer to a small, battery-powered handheld light. In Canadian French you may also hear 'flambeau' in some contexts, but 'lampe de poche' is standard in France. Plural: lampes de poche.
target_language_example: J'ai mis une lampe de poche dans mon sac au cas où il ferait sombre.
native_language_example: I put a flashlight in my bag in case it gets dark.

meaning: flashlight; a hand-held electric torch.
additional_notes: Common everyday noun in French for a portable light you hold in your hand. Used in questions and requests (Donne-moi ta lampe torche / Peux-tu me prêter une lampe torche?). In Canadian French, 'lampe de poche' is also used. Pronunciation tip: the final 'e' in 'lampe' is silent, so sounds like 'lahmp torsh'.
target_language_example: J'ai pris une lampe torche pour la randonnée.
native_language_example: I took a flashlight for the hike.

meaning: sign language (a visual language using hand signs and gestures).
additional_notes: Refers to any natural sign language used by Deaf communities (e.g. Langue des Signes Française = LSF). Used like other language names (apprendre la langue des signes, interprète en langue des signes).
target_language_example: Elle apprend la langue des signes pour aider des amis sourds.
native_language_example: She is learning sign language to help deaf friends.

meaning: mother tongue; native language (the first language learned from childhood).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the language someone grew up speaking or learned first. Can refer to one’s primary language even if the person now speaks other languages. Commonly used in questions about nationality, background, or language ability.
target_language_example: Le français est ma langue maternelle.
native_language_example: French is my mother tongue.

meaning: 'which language (is spoken)'.
additional_notes: Used in questions asking what language is spoken in a place or by someone. Full forms in examples: «Quelle langue parle-t-il ?» (Which language does he speak?/Which language is spoken by him?) and the impersonal/plural/singular general form «Quelle langue parle-t-on… ?» meaning 'which language do people speak…?' The '-t-' is an insertion for pronunciation when the subject pronoun il/elle/on follows a verb that ends with a vowel (parle + il → parle-t-il).
target_language_example: Quelle langue parle-t-on au Canada ?
native_language_example: Which language is spoken in Canada?

meaning: foreign language
additional_notes: Used to refer to any language that is not the speaker's native language. Common in contexts about learning languages (apprendre une langue étrangère), teaching, or describing skills (parler une langue étrangère). Étrangère agrees in gender/number with langue (feminine singular).
target_language_example: J'apprends une langue étrangère à l'école.
native_language_example: I am learning a foreign language at school.

meaning: Which languages are spoken (in/on)...?
additional_notes: Common question pattern: 'Quelles/Combien de + langues + parle-t-on + [location] ?' uses impersonal construction 'on' with inversion 'parle-t-on' for questions. Use 'Quelles langues...' for 'which languages' and 'Combien de langues...' for 'how many languages'. Replace location after the verb phrase (en France, au Canada, etc.).
target_language_example: Quelles langues parle-t-on en Suisse ?
native_language_example: Which languages are spoken in Switzerland?

meaning: 'which I' or 'for which I' (relative phrase starting a clause referring back to a feminine singular antecedent).
additional_notes: Laquelle is a feminine singular relative or interrogative pronoun meaning 'which' or 'which one'. When combined with a relative preposition (à laquelle, pour laquelle, dans laquelle, etc.) it introduces a clause that describes the antecedent. 'Laquelle je...' on its own is incomplete in French — you will almost always see a preposition before 'laquelle' (à laquelle, pour laquelle, dans laquelle) or more context after the clause (e.g. 'laquelle je pensais', 'laquelle je suis né' would be ungrammatical; use 'dans laquelle je suis né'). Make sure the gender and number of 'laquelle' agree with the noun it replaces (feminine singular).
target_language_example: C'est la maison dans laquelle je vivais.
native_language_example: This is the house in which I used to live.

meaning: do you wash (the) — used to ask someone if/when/how they wash a body part (les mains, les cheveux, etc.).
additional_notes: This is the inversion question form: verb (laves) + subject pronoun (tu) + definite article + plural noun (les). Common with reflexive verb se laver: te laves-tu les mains? = 'Do you wash your hands?'. In everyday spoken French, people often use est-ce que or rising intonation instead: Tu te laves les mains? Also adjust the body part (les mains, les cheveux, les dents).
target_language_example: Te laves-tu les mains avant de préparer le repas ?
native_language_example: Do you wash your hands before preparing the meal?

meaning: The Cape (name of a place); often refers to Cape Town (Le Cap) in French.
additional_notes: Capitalized and preceded by the definite article 'le'. In French, 'Le Cap' is the standard name for the city of Cape Town (South Africa). It can also mean any cape (geographical headland) when used with 'le' plus a specific name (e.g., 'le Cap-Vert'), but without further context 'Le Cap' usually means Cape Town. Pronounce the 'p' in 'Cap' as in French.
target_language_example: Nous partons pour Le Cap la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: We are leaving for Cape Town next week.

meaning: 'the bath is' (used to say that the bath is ready or to ask if it is ready).
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: le bain (the bath) + est (is). Commonly used with 'prêt' (ready) as in 'Le bain est prêt.' Also appears in questions with inversion or 'est-ce que' (Est‑ce que le bain est prêt? / Le bain est‑il prêt?). Useful for everyday family contexts (telling someone the bath is ready).
target_language_example: Le bain est prêt, je vais le remplir.
native_language_example: The bath is ready, I'll fill it.

meaning: This exact sequence is not a fixed French phrase; 'le bien' means 'the good' and 'et' means 'and'.
additional_notes: These words are simply a noun phrase ('le bien' = the good, benefit, or well-being) followed by the conjunction 'et' ('and'). Alone, 'le bien et' is incomplete and needs another element after 'et' to form a full expression (e.g. 'le bien et le mal' = 'good and evil', or 'le bien-être et la santé' = 'well-being and health'). 'Le bien' can also mean 'property' or 'possession' in some contexts (un bien immobilier = a property).
target_language_example: Nous devons choisir entre le bien et le mal.
native_language_example: We must choose between good and evil.

meaning: 'the good and the' — fragmental phrase that typically begins a larger expression (e.g., le bien et le mal); by itself it is incomplete and usually part of a contrast or compound noun phrase.
additional_notes: This is a multi-word fragment rather than a standalone idiom. It commonly appears as the beginning of paired contrasts (for example, "le bien et le mal") or in constructions where "le" that follows is completed by another noun (e.g., "le bien et le juste"). Because it's incomplete, its exact meaning depends on the word that follows the second "le." Usage is formal-to-neutral; not a sentence by itself.
target_language_example: Il faut combattre le bien et le mal dans nos consciences.
native_language_example: We must fight the good and the evil in our consciences.

meaning: 'the dog is' — simple present description of the dog.
additional_notes: A subject (le chien = the dog) + conjugated verb être (est = is). Used to state a condition, quality, location with prepositions, possession with 'à', or describe appearance/state. For beginners, remember agreement: to describe with an adjective the adjective may change gender/number (un chien vert, une chienne verte).
target_language_example: Le chien est content aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: The dog is happy today.

meaning: 'the (sun)set of' or 'the time of (the) setting (of)'.
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'soleil' (le coucher du soleil) to mean 'sunset' or 'the time after sunset' when combined with verbs like 'après' or expressions like 'avant le coucher du soleil' (before sunset). 'Le coucher du' is a fragment that needs a noun (typically 'soleil').
target_language_example: Nous partons demain matin, mais rentrons avant le coucher du soleil.
native_language_example: We're leaving tomorrow morning, but returning before sunset.

meaning: 'worth (the) effort' or 'worth doing' (used in expressions like "ça vaut le coup d'..." meaning it's worth trying/seeing/etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the fixed expression "ça vaut le coup d'..." (short for "ça vaut le coup de + infinitive"). It means that doing something is worthwhile or worth the effort/time. Followed by an infinitive (essayer, aller voir, etc.). Informal to neutral register; very frequent in spoken French.
target_language_example: Ça vaut le coup d'essayer ce restaurant ce soir.
native_language_example: It's worth trying that restaurant tonight.

meaning: 'the fact that' — introduces a clause stating a fact, a reason, or something asserted/considered true.
additional_notes: Common connective used to present or emphasize a statement, cause, or reported fact. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive when the speaker expresses doubt, emotion, necessity, or subjectivity (e.g., 'le fait que Tom ait...'), but indicative is used when stating an objective fact. Can also appear in fixed expressions (e.g., 'malgré le fait que' = 'despite the fact that').
target_language_example: Le fait que tu sois venu m'a rendu heureux.
native_language_example: The fact that you came made me happy.

meaning: ‘French is…’ — a way to make statements about the French language (followed by an adjective, noun phrase, or passive clause).
additional_notes: Use 'le français' to mean the French language. 'Est' is the 3rd‑person singular of 'être' (to be). Common continuations: an adjective (complicated), a noun phrase (my favorite language), or a passive construction with 'parlé' + location (is spoken in/at...).
target_language_example: Le français est difficile à prononcer pour certains anglophones.
native_language_example: French is difficult to pronounce for some English speakers.

meaning: along, alongside (follow a line or length of something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or position following the length or edge of something (a street, a beach, a cheek, a leg). Common in spatial descriptions: marcher le long de la rivière = walk along the river. Can be used with physical surfaces or abstract paths. Requires the definite article and a noun after it (le long de + noun).
target_language_example: Nous avons marché le long de la rivière au coucher du soleil.
native_language_example: We walked along the river at sunset.

meaning: The damage is done; what's done is done.
additional_notes: Used to say that something bad (a mistake or harm) has already happened and cannot be changed now. Often expresses resignation or that it's pointless to complain or try to undo it.
target_language_example: Le mal est fait, il faut maintenant trouver une solution.
native_language_example: The damage is done; now we must find a solution.

meaning: when the time comes; at the appropriate time.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a future moment when something should be done or will happen. Often appears in phrases like «on verra le moment venu» (we'll see when the time comes) or «être prêts le moment venu» (be ready when the time comes). Neutral register.
target_language_example: On prendra une décision le moment venu.
native_language_example: We'll make a decision when the time comes.

meaning: everyone has the right (to ...)
additional_notes: Usually appears as 'Tout le monde a le droit de/à ...' meaning 'everyone has the right to/for ...'. Use 'de' before a verb (de + infinitive) and 'à' before a noun ('le droit à une deuxième chance'). Formal register; common in legal, moral, or general statements about rights.
target_language_example: Tout le monde a le droit d'accéder aux soins de santé.
native_language_example: Everyone has the right to access healthcare.

meaning: people are afraid / everyone is afraid
additional_notes: Often appears as 'tout le monde a peur' meaning 'everyone is afraid'. Used to talk about general fear felt by many people. Can be followed by 'de' + noun or verb infinitive (e.g. 'de la mort', 'de faire quelque chose').
target_language_example: Tout le monde a peur de changer de travail.
native_language_example: Everyone is afraid to change jobs.

meaning: 'everyone at' or 'everybody in/at' (used to specify a location or group)
additional_notes: This construction is actually the phrase 'tout le monde' (everyone) followed by a preposition + noun to indicate location or group (e.g. 'au bureau', 'au village', 'au pas' in the idiom 'mettre au pas'). In natural French you will usually see 'tout le monde au...' rather than 'le monde au'. Use it to mean 'everyone at/in [place]' or 'everyone to [place]' depending on the verb (context matters).
target_language_example: Ils ont dit : « Tout le monde au travail ! »
native_language_example: They said, "Everyone to work!"

meaning: people should / the world should (expresses what people or society ought to do)
additional_notes: Le monde = 'people' or 'the world' (in a general sense). Devoir (devrait = conditional of devoir) expresses advice, obligation or expectation translated as 'should' or 'ought to'. Commonly used to state what people in general ought to do: e.g. «Le monde devrait être plus tolérant.»
target_language_example: Le monde devrait écouter davantage les scientifiques.
native_language_example: People should listen to scientists more.

meaning: 'what a small world' — used when you meet someone unexpectedly or discover a surprising connection.
additional_notes: An exclamation expressing surprise at an unexpected coincidence or familiar connection. Common in spoken French; can be used alone or followed by the person's name. Tone ranges from neutral to amused. Literal translation is 'the world is small', but meaning is idiomatic.
target_language_example: Le monde est petit — tu connais aussi Marc ?
native_language_example: What a small world — you know Marc too?

meaning: literally 'the world makes/does' — not a common fixed phrase in French; likely part of a larger sentence (e.g. « le monde fait X » = 'people/the world do X' or 'the world makes X').
additional_notes: This is not an independent idiom in French. More likely it's the start of a clause like « le monde fait la queue » (people/the crowd are queuing) or « le monde fait semblant » (people pretend). In spoken French, "le monde" often means "people" or "everyone." The verb that follows (here "fait") will determine the full meaning. Do not use "le monde fait" alone unless completing the sentence.
target_language_example: Le monde fait la queue devant le cinéma.
native_language_example: People are queuing in front of the cinema.

meaning: 'people can't' / 'the world cannot' — used to say that people (in general) are unable to do something or that something is impossible for people.
additional_notes: Le monde = 'people' or 'the world' depending on context; here it usually means 'people' in general. Peut pas is the spoken/informal contraction of 'ne peut pas' (cannot). Often followed by an infinitive or a clause explaining what people can't do. In formal writing you might keep the full 'ne...pas' or use 'on ne peut pas'.
target_language_example: Le monde ne peut pas tout savoir.
native_language_example: People can't know everything.

meaning: 'everyone knew' or 'the world knew' (past tense)
additional_notes: Le monde = 'people/everyone' (informal generalization). Savait is the imparfait of savoir (to know) and gives a past, ongoing or background sense: 'everyone already knew' or 'it was known by everyone.' Common in narratives or to say something was common knowledge. Not literal 'the world' but 'people in general.'
target_language_example: Quand il est parti, le monde savait déjà la vérité.
native_language_example: When he left, everyone already knew the truth.

meaning: the price for (per) — used to indicate the price associated with an item or unit
additional_notes: This is part of a larger expression like "le prix à l'unité" (the price per unit) or "le prix à la bouteille" (the price per bottle). On its own "le prix à" is incomplete and expects a noun or measure after "à" (e.g., "le prix à la personne", "le prix à l'heure"). Common translations: "the price for...", "the price per...".
target_language_example: Quel est le prix à la bouteille ?
native_language_example: What is the price per bottle?

meaning: 'the connection/relevance to' or 'what does ... have to do with'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the relationship, relevance, or connection between something and someone/another thing. Common in questions: "Quel est le rapport avec X ?" = "What does that have to do with X?" Can be used neutrally or to challenge relevance.
target_language_example: Quel est le rapport avec cette histoire ?
native_language_example: What does that have to do with this story?

meaning: time to (have time to do something)
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone has (or doesn't have) enough time to do an action. Common patterns: 'avoir le temps de + infinitive' (to have time to ...). Can be used in questions and future/negative forms: 'Tu as le temps de...?', 'Je n'ai pas le temps de...'.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas le temps de finir ce rapport.
native_language_example: I don't have time to finish this report.

meaning: 'while' / 'by the time' (depending on tense) — indicates a period during which something happens or the time until something occurs.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause about duration or timing. With the present/future it often means 'while' or 'during the time that' (Je fais X le temps que tu fais Y). With the imperfect or pluperfect it can mean 'by the time' (Le temps que nous arrivions, il était déjà parti = by the time we arrived...). Context and verb tense determine whether it emphasizes simultaneous action (during) or that one event is already completed when another happens (by the time).
target_language_example: Je lirai pendant le temps que tu ranges la maison.
native_language_example: I'll read while you tidy the house.

meaning: appears in constructions where 'le temps' is followed by 'à' to indicate time required, time given or time allowed for someone or something (e.g. mettre du temps à, donner le temps à quelqu'un de, prendre le temps à...).
additional_notes:
Not a fixed standalone idiom; used inside verb phrases. Common patterns:
- donner le temps à quelqu'un de + infinitive = give someone time to ...
- prendre le temps de + infinitive = take the time to ... (note: souvent sans 'à')
- mettre du temps à + infinitive = take time to ...
When using literally include the determiner (le/du) and appropriate verb. For learners, memorize full verb+phrase constructions rather than 'le temps à' alone.
target_language_example: Il ne lui a pas donné le temps à réfléchir; il l'a interrompu.
native_language_example: He didn't give him the time to think; he interrupted him.

meaning: to go get him/it; to fetch him/it.
additional_notes: Construction = pronoun (le = him/it) + chercher (to look for/fetch). Usually means to go somewhere to pick up or fetch a person or object. Verb requires appropriate subject and often a destination: aller le chercher = go fetch him. Replace le with la/les/me/te/nous/vous as needed. Formality: neutral, common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je vais le chercher à la gare.
native_language_example: I'll go get him at the station.

meaning: don't even know him/it (colloquial negative construction)
additional_notes: Informal spoken French where 'même' adds emphasis after negation: 'Je ne le connais même pas' = 'I don't even know him/it.' In casual speech the 'ne' is often dropped: 'Je le connais même pas.' Position: 'le' (object pronoun) before the verb; 'même' after the verb + object. Use for emphasizing lack of familiarity.
target_language_example: Je ne le connais même pas, comment pourrais-tu l'inviter ?
native_language_example: I don't even know him, how could you invite him?

meaning: to ask him/her for one (feminine noun) or to ask someone for one
additional_notes: This is a fragment rather than a complete fixed phrase. It combines: le (direct object pronoun 'him' or 'it' when masculine) + demander (to ask/request) + une (the feminine indefinite article 'a/one') and would appear in sentences like « Je vais le lui demander une fois de plus » (though that exact ordering may change). In normal French you'd more commonly see pronouns arranged as le demander + à + quelqu'un or with indirect object pronouns (lui, leur). Be careful: word order and pronoun choices depend on whether 'le' refers to a person (him) or a thing (it) and whether the thing asked for is feminine (une).
target_language_example: Je vais le demander une fois de plus à Marie.
native_language_example: I'll ask him/it one more time from Marie.

meaning: to say more about it; to add further information or elaborate
additional_notes: Contains the definite article/pronoun 'le' referring to the thing being discussed (it). Commonly used in expressions like « je n’ai rien à le dire plus » is incorrect — correct phrasing usually places 'de' as in « dire de + » constructions; however 'le dire plus' can appear in contexts such as « si je peux le dire plus clairement… » where 'le' refers to a prior statement. Register: neutral; can be used in both spoken and written French when referring back to something previously mentioned.
target_language_example: Si je peux le dire plus clairement, il faut respecter les délais.
native_language_example: If I can say it more clearly, we must respect the deadlines.

meaning: to say it once / to say it one more time (used with modifiers like 'fois', 'dernière', 'de plus', 'autre').
additional_notes: This fragment alone is incomplete; in French you normally say « le dire une fois », « le dire une dernière fois », « le dire une fois de plus », or « le dire une autre fois ». It means to say something one time (again, one more time, or one last time) and requires a word like 'fois' (time) or a qualifier. Use with pronouns (le, la) to refer to what is being said.
target_language_example: Laisse-moi le dire une fois de plus.
native_language_example: Let me say it one more time.

meaning: leave him/it
additional_notes: A combination of the direct object pronoun 'le' (him/it) + the verb 'laisser' in the imperative or infinitive context. Commonly appears as part of commands or requests (Ne le laissez pas = Don't let him/it) or questions offering permission (Vous le laissez ... ? = Will/Do you let him/it ...?). The exact English auxiliary ('leave' vs 'let') depends on context. Subject and tense must be inferred from the sentence.
target_language_example: Ne le laissez pas entrer.
native_language_example: Don't let him come in.

meaning: theirs (masculine singular object pronoun) / to them (with direct object pronoun + indirect 'leur')
additional_notes: Used as a possessive pronoun meaning "theirs" when referring to a masculine singular noun (Ce livre est le leur = That book is theirs). It also appears in constructions with a direct object pronoun + indirect object 'leur' (e.g. Dis-lui de le leur donner = Tell him/her to give it to them).
