native_language_example: He didn't know what to do after the bad news.

meaning: 'I will not' (first-person future negative of être).
additional_notes: Ne + serai is the negative form of the verb être in the simple future (je serai = I will be → je ne serai = I will not be). Often appears with jamais (never), pas (not), or other negatives. In spoken French, the 'ne' is frequently dropped: "je serai pas".
target_language_example: Je ne serai pas disponible demain.
native_language_example: I will not be available tomorrow.

meaning: 'would not be' (conditional form of 'être' with negation)
additional_notes: This is the negated conditional of 'être' (je/tu/on/etc. ne serais...), used to express hypothetical or polite statements: refusal, lack of objection (Je ne serais pas contre = I wouldn't be opposed to), expectation about someone's reaction (Je ne serais pas fâché = I wouldn't be angry), prediction of disagreement, or polite guesses/questions (Tu ne serais pas... des fois?). The full form usually includes the subject and may contract in speech (e.g., 'je serais pas').
target_language_example: Je ne serais pas contre un café.
native_language_example: I wouldn't be opposed to a coffee.

meaning: 'will not be' (2nd person singular future of 'être' with negation).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone (tu) that they will not be something in the future. Formed by placing 'ne' before the verb (sometimes with 'pas', 'jamais', 'ni', or other negative words after the verb): ne seras pas (will not be), ne seras jamais (will never be), ne seras ni...ni... (will be neither...nor...). In spoken French the final 'ne' is often dropped: tu seras pas/tu seras jamais.
target_language_example: Tu ne seras pas prête demain.
native_language_example: You will not be ready tomorrow.

meaning: will no longer be
additional_notes: Future tense with negation: 'seras' is the 2nd-person singular (tu) future of 'être' (to be). 'Ne ... plus' means 'no longer' or 'no more'. Often used with 'jamais' (never) or words like 'seul' (alone). In spoken French the 'ne' is sometimes dropped: 'tu seras plus...' (informal), but written French keeps 'ne'.
target_language_example: Tu ne seras plus inquiet quand tout sera réglé.
native_language_example: You will no longer be worried when everything is sorted out.

meaning: the negative future tense form of 'être' for 'vous' — 'you will not' (be).
additional_notes: Used with 'vous' (formal you or plural) in the simple future. 'Ne' + verb (here 'serez') makes the negative; often paired with words like 'jamais' (never), 'plus' (no longer), or adverbs. In spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped: 'Vous serez jamais...' (informal).
target_language_example: Vous ne serez pas prêts avant demain matin.
native_language_example: You will not be ready before tomorrow morning.

meaning: "are not" (first-person plural negative: we are not)
additional_notes: Used with 'nous' (we) to form negative statements in the present tense. French negatives commonly use 'ne ... pas' (or other negative words) around the verb: 'nous ne sommes pas' = 'we are not'. In spoken French, the 'ne' is often dropped: 'nous sommes pas' or more commonly 'on n'est pas' for informal speech. Combine with adjectives, nouns, or past participles: 'nous ne sommes pas prêts' (we are not ready), 'nous ne sommes pas responsables' (we are not responsible).
target_language_example: Nous ne sommes pas d'accord.
native_language_example: We do not agree.

meaning: am not
additional_notes: Usually follows je, as in je ne suis.... With ne ... pas, it means "I am not"; with ne ... que, it means "I am only." Here suis is the je form of être.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas prêt.
native_language_example: I'm not ready.

meaning: 'I am not the kind/type of' (used in expressions like "je ne suis pas du genre..." or "je ne suis pas du même avis")
additional_notes: Common construction: "je ne suis pas du genre + (à + verb / noun)" means 'I'm not the sort of person who...'. "Je ne suis pas du même avis" means 'I don't share the same opinion'. The negative "ne ... pas" surrounds the verb; context determines whether it refers to character/behaviour (du genre) or opinion (du même avis).
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas du genre à mentir.
native_language_example: I'm not the sort of person who lies.

meaning: 'am not in' (part of a negated present-tense statement saying you are not in a particular state, place, mood, or situation)
additional_notes: This is a fragment of a full sentence using the negation 'ne ... pas' with the verb 'être' in first person singular (je suis). It needs a complement to finish the idea, for example a place (ne suis pas en ville), a mood/condition (ne suis pas en forme), or a situation (ne suis pas en mesure de...). In spoken French, the 'ne' is often dropped: 'je suis pas en...'.
target_language_example: Je ne suis pas en forme aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I am not in good shape today.

meaning: I don't believe you / I don't think you are (something).
additional_notes: This is the negative form of croire (to believe) with the informal singular object pronoun te (you). It can mean 'I don't believe you' (disbelieving what someone says) or 'I don't believe you are ...' when followed by an adjective (e.g. coupable = guilty). For polite/formal use, use 'ne vous crois' (rare) or more commonly 'je ne vous crois pas'. Common variants: drop 'ne' in spoken French: 'Je te crois pas.' 'Je ne te crois plus.' means 'I no longer believe you.'
target_language_example: Je ne te crois pas quand tu dis ça.
native_language_example: I don't believe you when you say that.

meaning: 'do not touch' (used in negative imperative with 'rien' = do not touch anything / don't touch).
additional_notes: This phrase is the negative imperative of the verb toucher + the preposition à, commonly used with rien (ne touche à rien) to warn someone not to touch anything. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: 'touche à rien' (informal). Use with a direct object is possible (ne touche pas à mon téléphone = don't touch my phone).
target_language_example: Ne touche à rien avant que j'arrive.
native_language_example: Don't touch anything before I arrive.

meaning: 'doesn't go anywhere' / 'isn't going anywhere' or 'goes nowhere'.
additional_notes: This is the negative construction using ne ... nulle(part) to mean 'nowhere' or 'not going anywhere'. In standard French, you'd usually see the full form 'ne ... nulle part'. In spoken French the 'part' may be dropped in hurried speech, but beginners should learn 'ne ... nulle part' as the normal form. Used with a verb (aller) to say someone/something doesn't go anywhere, or more generally with verbs to mean 'nowhere'.
target_language_example: Il ne va nulle part aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: He isn't going anywhere today.

meaning: you don't want me to (do something).
additional_notes: This is the negative second-person singular form used to say someone doesn't want the speaker to do something. It's followed by a verb in the subjunctive or (in spoken/colloquial French) the infinitive or indicative depending on structure: after 'que' standard written French uses the subjunctive (e.g. 'que je vienne'), but in everyday speech you may hear indicative or simplified forms. Context: used to express another person's desire about the speaker's actions.
target_language_example: Tu ne veux pas que je t'appelle ce soir ?
native_language_example: You don't want me to call you tonight?

meaning: 'I do not want you' (part of a negative sentence meaning 'I don't want to... you')
additional_notes: This phrase is the combination of the subject implied (je) + ne ... pas (negation) + veux (want) + vous (you). It appears in sentences where the speaker expresses they do not want to do something to or to bother 'you' (formal you or plural). In everyday speech, the spoken 'ne' is often dropped: "je veux pas vous...". Remember the full form is "je ne veux pas vous..." followed by a verb or infinitive (e.g. déranger, interrompre).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas vous déranger maintenant.
native_language_example: I don't want to bother you now.

meaning: would not come
additional_notes: Conditional form of venir (to come) in the first or second person singular (je/tu) used with negation. Common in hypothetical or reported contexts: "I/you would not come" or in past contexts with verbs of thinking/belief (reported speech). In spoken French the negative particle ne is often dropped (e.g. je ne viendrais pas → je viendrais pas).
target_language_example: Si j'étais occupé, je ne viendrais pas demain.
native_language_example: If I were busy, I wouldn't come tomorrow.

meaning: do not want
additional_notes: Used with nous to mean "we do not want," usually as part of a full negation like nous ne voulons pas.... In standard French, ne normally goes with another negative word such as pas, plus, or jamais. In ne...que, it means "only": nous ne voulons que toi = "we only want you."
target_language_example: Nous ne voulons pas partir maintenant.
native_language_example: We don't want to leave now.

meaning: 'it's none of your business' / 'doesn't concern you'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something does not concern them. Common in formal (vous) and informal (tu) forms: e.g. "Ça ne te regarde pas." Can be softened with polite phrases, but by itself it can sound blunt or rude depending on context and tone. Variants: "Ça ne vous regarde pas", "Cela ne vous regarde pas", "Ne te mêle pas de ce qui ne te regarde pas."
target_language_example: Ce qui se passe chez moi ne vous regarde pas.
native_language_example: What happens in my home is none of your business.

meaning: don't you see
additional_notes: A negative question or statement using the formal/plural 'vous' with the verb 'voir' (to see). Common in spoken French to ask if someone notices or understands something. Often appears in questions: 'Vous ne voyez pas ?' = 'Don't you see?'. Word order may include 'pas' or other negatives (aucun, rien).
target_language_example: Vous ne voyez pas ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Don't you see what I mean?

meaning: 'noir' = black; 'est' = is. (Together they form the phrase 'noir est' meaning 'black is' as part of a sentence, not a fixed expression.)
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase. 'Noir' is an adjective meaning 'black' and must agree in gender/number with the noun (noir, noire, noirs, noires). 'Est' is the third-person singular of the verb être (to be). You will see 'noir est' inside sentences like 'Le ciel noir est menaçant' (The black sky is threatening) or in poetic constructions. Make sure to adjust the adjective or verb as needed (e.g., 'La robe est noire').
target_language_example: Le chat noir est sur le canapé.
native_language_example: The black cat is on the sofa.

meaning: black and white (literally); used for black-and-white photos, images, or things that are black and white in color.
additional_notes: Can describe photographs or films (monochrome) and also the color pattern of objects or animals (e.g., a black-and-white dog). Often used without articles: «photos noir et blanc». Pronunciation: the 's' on 'noir' is silent; 'et' = and.
target_language_example: J'aime regarder les films noir et blanc classiques.
native_language_example: I like watching classic black-and-white films.

meaning: 'full name' (first name(s) + family name)
additional_notes: Used on forms or when asking for someone's complete name (given name(s) plus surname). Can be formal or neutral. For children or informal speech you might hear 'ton nom complet' (your full name) or simply 'nom' when context is clear.
target_language_example: Inscris ton nom complet sur le formulaire.
native_language_example: Write your full name on the form.

meaning: an exclamation: 'for God's sake' or 'good God' (used to show anger, shock, impatience).
additional_notes: A strong, sometimes profane exclamation invoking God. Used to express surprise, annoyance, anger or urgency. Can be offensive to some listeners (religious people). In milder contexts speakers may use softened forms like 'bon sang' or 'pour l'amour de Dieu'.
target_language_example: Nom de Dieu, ferme la porte !
native_language_example: For God's sake, shut the door!

meaning: family name; last name; surname.
additional_notes: Used to ask or state someone's last name. Common in forms and questions. 'Nom' = name, 'de famille' = of family. In everyday speech you may also hear 'nom' alone in contexts where it's clear you mean the last name. Feminine: 'son nom de famille' can refer to a woman's family name; for married women some speakers use 'nom d'épouse' for married name.
target_language_example: Quel est ton nom de famille ?
native_language_example: What is your last name?

meaning: maiden name (a woman's family name before marriage).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state the surname a woman had before marriage. Common in forms, questions about family, or when referring to a mother's original surname. Literally 'name of young/maiden (girl)'. Typically applied to women who changed their surname upon marriage.
target_language_example: Son nom de jeune fille est Dupont.
native_language_example: Her maiden name is Dupont.

meaning: 'the name of my' (feminine possessor) — used before a feminine family member or female person.
additional_notes: This phrase combines nom (name) + de (of) + ma (my, feminine). Use 'ma' when the possessed noun is feminine (ma mère, ma femme, ma grand-mère). The full noun follows: e.g. 'le nom de ma mère' = the name of my mother. In spoken French, possessive agrees with the thing owned (ma mère), not the speaker. If the possessed noun is masculine, use 'nom de mon' (e.g. 'le nom de mon père').
target_language_example: C'est le nom de ma sœur.
native_language_example: That's my sister's name.

meaning: 'name that' or 'the name which'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the name given to someone or something; 'que' is a relative pronoun linking to the clause with the name. Common in sentences like 'C'est le nom que j'ai donné' (It's the name that I gave). Word order and agreement follow normal French relative clause rules.
target_language_example: C'est le nom que nous avons choisi pour le projet.
native_language_example: That's the name that we chose for the project.

meaning: 'a number of' / 'many' / 'several' (quantity expression).
additional_notes: Used to indicate quantity. Can be followed by a noun to mean 'a number of' (several/many). In formal/old usage 'nombre de' can also appear before a plural noun as a subject (e.g. 'Nombre de passagers...') meaning 'many passengers...'. Context determines whether it's specific (an exact count) or vague (several/many).
target_language_example: Nombre de livres ont été prêtés à la bibliothèque.
native_language_example: A number of books were lent to the library.

meaning: Used to express surprise, disbelief, annoyance, or to reinforce what follows (like 'no, but...' / 'come on' / 'seriously').
additional_notes: Informal spoken phrase often placed at the start of a sentence. Can soften a contradiction ('no, but...') or show incredulity/annoyance ('come on', 'seriously'). Tone and context determine exact nuance. Common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Non mais, tu plaisantes ?
native_language_example: Come on, are you kidding?

meaning: 'no, thank you' — a polite refusal.
additional_notes: Used to decline offers, invitations, help, or unwanted items. Can stand alone or be followed by a brief explanation (e.g., "je ne fume pas"). Tone depends on context and intonation: with a smile it's polite; with a sharp tone it can sound curt. Common in both formal and informal situations.
target_language_example: Non merci, j'ai déjà mangé.
native_language_example: No, thank you, I already ate.

meaning: either
additional_notes: Used to add a negative or similar negative idea, often after another negative statement. In English it corresponds to "either" (in negative contexts) or sometimes "as well" in informal negation. Placement: follows the verb or phrase it refers to (e.g. "je ne... pas non plus", or after a clause).
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas faim non plus.
native_language_example: I'm not hungry either.

meaning: not only
additional_notes: Used to introduce the first element in a contrast, often paired with 'mais (aussi)' or 'mais encore' to add the second element (e.g. 'non seulement... mais aussi...'). Can be followed by a verb, noun, clause, or phrase. Formal to neutral register.
target_language_example: Elle est non seulement intelligente, mais aussi très gentille.
native_language_example: She is not only intelligent, but also very kind.

meaning: to feed one's (masculine singular noun); 'nourrir' = to feed, 'son' = his/her/one's (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to indicate feeding that person/animal/thing (e.g., 'nourrir son chien' = to feed one's dog). Remember 'son/sa/ses' agree with the gender/number of the noun being possessed, not the possessor. The phrase is compositional and can be translated literally. In speech and writing you'll normally see it followed by the noun ('nourrir son chien', 'nourrir son bébé').
target_language_example: Après la partie, il se rendit directement chez lui pour nourrir son chien.
native_language_example: After the game, he went straight home to feed his dog.

meaning: ourselves (emphatic reflexive: we, by ourselves).
additional_notes: Used for emphasis or reflexive actions involving 'nous' (we). Often follows or accompanies a verb or object to stress that the action is done by us, without help, or to blame/credit ourselves. In contractions with pronouns it appears as 'nous-mêmes' (not changed).
target_language_example: Nous devons réparer la voiture nous-mêmes.
native_language_example: We must fix the car ourselves.

meaning: to sing (to) us a (…); request someone to sing one (song) for us.
additional_notes: Common in requests: verb 'chanter' plus indirect object 'nous' (to us) and an indefinite article 'une' followed by a noun (usually 'chanson'). Structure: 'Peux-tu/Voudriez-vous nous chanter une (chanson)?' Polite forms use 'vous'/'pourriez'/'voudriez'. Replace 'une chanson' with another noun if asking for a different item to be sung.
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous nous chanter une chanson en français ?
native_language_example: Could you sing us a song in French?

meaning: This phrase as written is ungrammatical in French; likely intended to be 'nous devons faire quelque chose' meaning 'we must do something'.
additional_notes:
In French you cannot end a clause with 'quelque' alone. Use 'quelque chose' (something) or 'quelques' + plural noun (some + noun). Correct forms:
- Nous devons faire quelque chose. (We must do something.)
- Nous devons faire quelques changements. (We must make some changes.)
Also note 'devoir' expresses obligation or strong probability depending on context: 'nous devons' = 'we must' / 'we have to' (obligation) or 'we should' / 'we must be' (logical deduction).
target_language_example: Nous devons faire quelque chose pour résoudre ce problème.
native_language_example: We must do something to solve this problem.

meaning: 'we need to take' or 'we must take' (lit. 'it is necessary for us to take')
additional_notes: This is part of the impersonal construction 'Il nous faut + infinitive' meaning 'we need to... / it is necessary for us to...'. Use with an infinitive verb (prendre + noun/phrase here). Common in spoken and formal French. Equivalent: 'Nous devons prendre'.
target_language_example: Il nous faut prendre une décision rapidement.
native_language_example: We need to make a decision quickly.

meaning: 'we all know the' or 'we all know that the...'
additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact or commonly known information. It is often followed by a noun (e.g. 'faits') or a subordinate clause introduced by 'que' (e.g. 'nous savons tous que...'). In everyday speech, speakers more commonly say 'nous savons tous que...' or simply 'on sait tous que...'.
target_language_example: Nous savons tous les risques, mais nous devons avancer.
native_language_example: We all know the risks, but we must move forward.

meaning: we were in / we found ourselves in (past, descriptive)
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of 'se trouver' + location preposition. Used to describe a past ongoing or background situation: 'we were in (a place)' or 'we found ourselves in (a situation)'. Often appears as 'nous nous trouvions dans...' (reflexive pronoun included). Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Nous nous trouvions dans la cuisine quand la lumière a clignoté.
native_language_example: We were in the kitchen when the light flickered.

meaning: tell/ give us a little (of)… / make us a little space / talk to us a bit about…
additional_notes: This sequence combines a verb (imperative or infinitive) + nous (object 'to us') + un peu de ('a little of' or 'a bit of'). It's not a fixed idiom by itself — meaning depends on the verb: e.g. 'fais-nous un peu de place' = 'give us a little space', 'parle-nous un peu de...' = 'tell us a bit about...'. Used in polite requests or commands. Word order: verb + nous + un peu de + noun/topic.
target_language_example: Parle-nous un peu de ton expérience.
native_language_example: Tell us a bit about your experience.

meaning: 'a fresh start' or 'a new beginning'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is starting again or beginning a new phase (life, job, relationship, place). Literal components: 'nouveau' = new, 'départ' = departure/start. Common in personal contexts: 'Je veux un nouveau départ' = I want a fresh start.
target_language_example: Après la séparation, elle cherche un nouveau départ.
native_language_example: After the breakup, she is looking for a fresh start.

meaning: 'new to' or 'new for' (indicates something is unfamiliar or recent for someone)
additional_notes: Used to say that something is recent, unfamiliar, or surprising from the perspective of a person. Can describe information (J'ai du nouveau pour toi = I have news for you) or an experience/state (C'est nouveau pour moi = That's new to me). When used with 'du nouveau' it means 'news' or 'something new'.
target_language_example: Ce métier est encore nouveau pour moi.
native_language_example: This job is still new to me.

meaning: 'news of' or 'the news that... (about)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce information received about an event or person. 'Nouvelle' here means 'news' (a piece of information); 'de' links the news to its content (e.g. 'la nouvelle de sa mort' = 'the news of his/her death'). Often appears in contexts conveying announcement, shock, or reaction. Can be used with verbs like recevoir, apprendre, être choqué par/à, arriver.
target_language_example: J'ai appris la nouvelle de ton déménagement hier.
native_language_example: I heard the news of your move yesterday.

meaning: 'news' or 'information for (someone)'; used to say you have news or an update for someone.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in phrases like "J'ai des/ de bonnes nouvelles pour toi/vous" (I have news/ good news for you). "Nouvelles" here means 'news' or 'updates' (feminine plural). Use "pour" to indicate the recipient. Formality depends on tu (informal) vs vous (formal/plural).
target_language_example: J'ai de bonnes nouvelles pour toi : tu as obtenu le poste.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: you got the job.

meaning: 'black cloud' — literally a dark cloud; can be used literally or metaphorically to mean trouble, gloom, or a bad omen.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a dark or storm cloud. Metaphorically, it can describe a gloomy mood, a looming problem, or misfortune (e.g., 'un nuage noir au-dessus de la ville' or 'un nuage noir planait sur la réunion'). Common and understandable to beginners; translation into English is literal.
target_language_example: Un nuage noir arrive, il va sûrement pleuvoir.
native_language_example: A black cloud is coming; it's surely going to rain.

meaning: an all-nighter; staying awake all night (often for work, study, or social events).
additional_notes: Literally 'white night'. Used to describe spending the entire night awake. Can refer to working/studying through the night or attending an all-night cultural event (e.g., 'La Nuit Blanche' festivals). Neutral register.
target_language_example: J'ai fait une nuit blanche pour finir ce projet.
native_language_example: I pulled an all-nighter to finish this project.

meaning: ‘night in/at’ — indicates spending or being in a place during the night.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like passer (passer la nuit), faire (faire la nuit), or venir (venir la nuit) + preposition dans + place. Shows location where someone spent the night (hotel, chambre, désert, couloir, foyer, etc.). Common in everyday speech. Word order: « passer la nuit dans + [lieu] ». Can be literal (physically spending the night) or figurative/idiomatic (e.g. being stuck overnight).
target_language_example: Nous avons passé la nuit dans une petite auberge.
native_language_example: We spent the night in a small inn.

meaning: 'wedding night' — the first night after a wedding when the newlyweds sleep together.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the night immediately following a wedding (often implying privacy/intimacy). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., 'a second wedding night' to mean another intimate or special night). Common in formal and everyday French.
target_language_example: Ils ont passé leur nuit de noces à parler jusqu'au matin.
native_language_example: They spent their wedding night talking until morning.

meaning: day and night; continuously, without stopping
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens all the time or very continuously (often to emphasize hard work, constant care, or continual effort). Can be interchangeable with "jour et nuit". Common in both literal (round-the-clock) and figurative (constantly thinking/praying) contexts.
target_language_example: Ils travaillent nuit et jour pour finir le projet.
native_language_example: They work day and night to finish the project.

meaning: the night here / (to) spend the night here.
additional_notes: Used to indicate spending the night at the current location. Commonly appears with verbs like passer (passer la nuit = to spend the night). Can be used in statements, suggestions (Passons la nuit ici), or questions. Word order in French is 'passer la nuit ici' = 'spend the night here.'
target_language_example: Nous allons passer la nuit ici ce soir.
native_language_example: We are going to spend the night here tonight.

meaning: complete darkness; pitch black (night).
additional_notes: Used to describe a very dark night or total darkness. Common in expressions like 'Il fait nuit noire' (it's pitch dark). Can be used literally (no moon/streetlights) or figuratively for very dark situations. Usually feminine noun phrase (la nuit).
target_language_example: Il fait nuit noire, on ne voit rien dans la rue.
native_language_example: It's pitch dark; you can't see anything in the street.

meaning: 'nowhere' or 'no place'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something or someone is not in any place or that a situation leads to no result. Often follows verbs (e.g., aller, mener) or follows 'de' in expressions like 'de nulle part' ('from nowhere'). Negative sense; pairs with verbs in affirmative sentences (no besoin for ne...pas around it).
target_language_example: Tout ce que je cherche est nulle part.
native_language_example: Everything I'm looking for is nowhere.

meaning: telephone number
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone's phone number. Can be used in formal and informal contexts (e.g., asking for, giving, or writing down a contact). In French, 'numéro' is masculine: le numéro de téléphone. Often preceded by possessive (votre, mon) or determiners (un, ce).
target_language_example: Donnez-moi votre numéro de téléphone, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Give me your telephone number, please.

meaning: haven't
additional_notes: Contracted form of ne + as, used with tu. It usually appears with another negative word such as pas, plus, or jamais: tu n’as pas = “you don’t have / you haven’t.” In sentences like tu n’as pas vu, it is the auxiliary in the passé composé.
target_language_example: Tu n’as pas compris la question ?
native_language_example: Didn't you understand the question?

meaning: 'n’as' is the contracted form of 'ne' + 'as' used for negation with the 2nd person singular of avoir (tu). It appears in negative constructions meaning 'you don't have' or as part of perfect-tense negation ('you haven't' when followed by a past participle with 'tu n'as ...').
additional_notes: Always appears with a following negative particle or phrase (commonly 'pas', but also 'rien', 'personne', etc.) or before a past participle. In speech, 'ne' is often dropped (tu n’as → t'as), but in writing the contraction with the apostrophe is standard when 'ne' is kept. Examples show common contexts: obligation/need, possession, or forming the negative perfect.
target_language_example: Regarde-moi droit dans les yeux, si tu n’as rien à te reprocher.
native_language_example: Look me straight in the eye, if you have nothing to reproach yourself for.

meaning: would never
additional_notes: This is the negative conditional form: ne + conditional of avoir (aurais) + jamais (never). Used in hypothetical statements about the past or present (e.g. 'I would never have...' or 'I would never...') depending on context and surrounding verbs. In speech the 'ne' is often dropped: 'j'aurais jamais'.
target_language_example: Je n’aurais jamais fait ça si j’avais su.
native_language_example: I would never have done that if I had known.

meaning: 'is not necessary' / 'doesn't need to (be/done)'.
additional_notes: Used to say something is not required. Often followed by 'que' + subjunctive when introducing an action or state (e.g. 'Il n’est pas nécessaire que tu sois...'). Can precede an infinitive to mean 'there's no need to...': 'Il n’est pas nécessaire de + infinitive.' Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Il n’est pas nécessaire que tu viennes si tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: It's not necessary for you to come if you are tired.

meaning: objects of / items belonging to (used before a noun to show purpose, type, or possession).
additional_notes: A short phrase combining the plural noun 'objets' (objects/items) with the preposition 'de'. It typically appears before a noun or noun phrase to indicate the type, purpose, source, or possession (e.g. objets de valeur = valuable objects; objets de décoration = decorative items; objets de la maison = household items). Because it's not a fixed idiom, the exact translation depends on the noun that follows. Remember to agree and use 'objets' for plural; singular is 'objet de'.
target_language_example: J'ai vendu des objets de décoration.
native_language_example: I sold some decorative items.

meaning: to take care of you / to look after you (someone is handling your needs).
additional_notes: Usually appears with a reflexive verb (s'occuper de) meaning 'to take care of' or 'to deal with' someone or something. In these examples it's used in the passive/agent sense ('someone is/I'll take care of you'). Common in service, medical, or helpful contexts. Conjugate according to subject: Je m'occupe de vous, On s'occupe de vous, Ils s'occupent de vous. Can be polite/offering help.
target_language_example: Ne vous inquiétez pas, je m'occupe de vous.
native_language_example: Don't worry, I'll take care of you.

meaning: will take care of / will look after / will deal with
additional_notes: Future form of the pronominal verb s'occuper de (used with a reflexive pronoun: il/elle/on s'occupera de...). Commonly used to say someone will handle, deal with, or look after a person or thing. Often followed by pronouns or nouns (toi, ça, tout).
target_language_example: Il s'occupera de toi demain.
native_language_example: He will take care of you tomorrow.

meaning: This sequence is not a correct French phrase; likely a mistake. 'occupé' means 'busy' or 'occupied', and 'ces' means 'these' (plural demonstrative).
additional_notes: The two words do not form a natural phrase together in French. Possible intended phrases: 'occupé(e) ces jours-ci' (busy these days), 'occupé ces places' (occupied these seats — more natural: 'ces places sont occupées'), or 'je suis occupé ces jours-ci' (I am busy these days). Remember agreement: 'occupé' must agree in gender/number with subject or with a preceding noun when used as adjective (occupée, occupés, occupées).
target_language_example: Je suis occupé ces jours-ci.
native_language_example: I am busy these days.

meaning: to offer (something) to someone; 'make an offer to'.
additional_notes: Used with faire une offre or avoir une offre + à + person (indirect object). Common structures: 'faire une offre à [person]' = 'to make an offer to [person]'; 'avoir une offre à [pronoun]' = 'to have an offer to make to [someone]'. The indirect object (à + name/pronoun) indicates the recipient. Formal or neutral register.
target_language_example: Ils ont fait une offre à Marie pour acheter sa voiture.
native_language_example: They made an offer to Marie to buy her car.

meaning: an exclamation expressing surprise, dismay, admiration, annoyance, or emphasis (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Very common informal interjection in French. Tone and context determine meaning: can be positive (wow, lovely), negative (oh no, what a pity), or neutral (expressing emphasis). Often repeated or followed by punctuation to show stronger feeling. Not literal—don't translate word-for-word.
target_language_example: Oh là là, quel désastre !
native_language_example: Oh no, what a disaster!

meaning: Oh my God; an exclamation expressing surprise, shock, delight, frustration, etc.
additional_notes: Very common spoken expression. Tone and context determine emotion (shock, amazement, annoyance, joy). Can be used alone or before a name or comment. Religious speakers may prefer milder forms (e.g. « oh mon Dieu » is informal to neutral; some may avoid for religious reasons). Written form often without punctuation: « oh mon dieu ». Variants: « mon Dieu ! », « Oh là là » (different nuance).
target_language_example: Oh mon Dieu, je n'arrive pas à y croire !
native_language_example: Oh my God, I can't believe it!

meaning: 'oh no' — an exclamation of disappointment, dismay, surprise or concern.
additional_notes: Informal, used like English 'oh no'. Can express mild regret ('Oh no, désolé') or alarm ('Oh non, une grosse vague arrive'). Repeated for emphasis ('Oh non, oh non'). Tone and context determine whether it's regretful, worried, or startled.
target_language_example: Oh non, j'ai oublié mes clés !
native_language_example: Oh no, I forgot my keys!

meaning: we go
additional_notes: "on aille" is the present subjunctive of aller with on, which often means "we." It usually appears after que in phrases expressing necessity, desire, suggestion, or possibility, such as il faut qu'on aille, tu veux qu'on aille, or où veux-tu qu'on aille. In English, it is often translated simply as "we go" or more naturally as "we should go," depending on context.
target_language_example: Je préfère qu'on aille à pied.
native_language_example: I'd rather we go on foot.

meaning: 'we are a' or 'one is a' (used to describe identity or role of a group or general people).
additional_notes: On is an impersonal/pronoun often used like 'we' or 'one' in spoken French. When followed by est un + noun, it describes what group or type someone belongs to (e.g. 'we are a couple', 'we are a group'). Context determines whether 'on' means 'we' (informal) or the generic 'one/people'. The phrase is compositional and literal: 'on' + 'est' (is/are) + 'un' (a).
target_language_example: On est un petit groupe de voisins.
native_language_example: We are a small group of neighbors.

meaning: 'no longer' / 'anymore' (used to say something is no longer possible or true)
additional_notes: Common fixed negative expression. Often followed by a verb: on ne peut plus + infinitive (e.g. on ne peut plus fumer = we can no longer smoke). Can also be used emphatically in affirmative contexts as an adverbial phrase meaning 'extremely' (colloquial: « c'est bon, on ne peut plus délicieux »), but that use is informal and less common. If you want the simple negative of 'we can't' use 'on ne peut pas'.
target_language_example: On ne peut plus sortir sans masque.
native_language_example: We can no longer go out without a mask.

meaning: 'you never know' / 'one never knows' (used to express uncertainty or that something might happen).
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression used to remind someone that unexpected things can occur. Can be used alone as a short comment (e.g., On ne sait jamais.) or followed by a clause (e.g., On ne sait jamais quand...). Equivalent to English 'you never know.' Neutral register—appropriate in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Prends un parapluie, on ne sait jamais.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella, you never know.

meaning: Let's have/take a ... (suggestion using 'on' for 'we').
additional_notes: A casual way to make a suggestion. 'On' is used colloquially for 'we'. 'Prenait' is the imperfect used in a polite, tentative suggestion often introduced by 'Et si...' or 'Si...'. Complete the phrase with a noun (un apéritif, un café, un verre, etc.).
target_language_example: Et si on prenait un chocolat chaud ?
native_language_example: How about we have a hot chocolate?

meaning: 'see you later' / 'we'll see each other later'.
additional_notes: Casual farewell used when arranging to meet again or ending a conversation. 'On' is an informal/we/us/they subject often used for 'we' in spoken French. 'On se voit plus' here omits 'tard' (later) that appears in examples; in examples shown the full phrase is 'on se voit plus tard' meaning 'see you later'. Without 'tard', 'plus' can be ambiguous in other contexts (meaning 'no longer'), so learners should use the full 'on se voit plus tard' for 'see you later.'
target_language_example: D'accord, on se voit plus tard au café.
native_language_example: Okay, we'll see each other later at the café.

meaning: we be
additional_notes: Usually appears as qu'on soit. Here on commonly means "we" in everyday French, even though the verb stays in the 3rd-person singular form. soit is the subjunctive of être, used after expressions like je veux que..., j'aimerais que..., content que..., or c'est important que.... In natural English, this is often translated as "we are" or "us to be," depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Je veux qu'on soit ensemble ce soir.
native_language_example: I want us to be together tonight.

meaning: 'we're going in circles' or 'we're stuck, making no progress'.
additional_notes: Usually appears as the full phrase 'on tourne en rond'. 'On' is an impersonal/we/they form often meaning 'we' in conversation. Used to describe a situation where people repeat the same actions or discussions without solving the problem. Can be said with frustration. Pronunciation: [ɔ̃ tuʁn ɑ̃ ʁɔ̃].
target_language_example: On tourne en rond et il faut changer d'approche.
native_language_example: We're going in circles and we need to change our approach.

meaning: ‘my/your/his/her/their uncle has’ — the noun oncle (uncle) followed by the verb avoir (to have) in the 3rd person singular.
additional_notes: This sequence shows possession or age when talking about an uncle: 'oncle a' is usually followed by a noun (e.g. une maison, trois enfants) or an expression of age (la quarantaine). In full sentences you will normally include a possessive before oncle (mon oncle, son oncle) or a subject pronoun if context requires (Il a un oncle…). The verb a is the present tense of avoir (il/elle/on a).
target_language_example: Mon oncle a deux voitures.
native_language_example: My uncle has two cars.

meaning: 'they said that you...' (reporting what others said about 'you')
additional_notes: A common reported-speech structure: 'ils/elles ont dit que vous...' = 'they said that you...'. 'Ont dit' is passé composé of 'dire' (they said). Use 'ils' for mixed/male groups and 'elles' for all-female groups; adjective/participe passé agreement (e.g. 'viré/virée') agrees with the subject (here 'vous' can be singular/formal or plural) and with the past participle when necessary in other constructions. The phrase is neutral/formal and used to relay information someone else said.
target_language_example: Ils ont dit que vous pouvez venir demain.
native_language_example: They said that you can come tomorrow.

meaning: laptop; portable computer.
additional_notes: Common French phrase for a laptop. 'Ordinateur' = computer, 'portable' = portable (can be moved). Used like English: un ordinateur portable / cet ordinateur portable. Plural: ordinateurs portables.
target_language_example: Je travaille sur mon ordinateur portable aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm working on my laptop today.

meaning: 'How dare you (to) me' — used to express shock or offense at what someone said or did to the speaker.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in questions like «Comment osez-vous me...?» followed by a verb or phrase (dire ça, parler ainsi, etc.). Formal/plural register because of 'vous'. Conveys strong disapproval or indignation. Tone can be outraged, offended, or scolding. Not literal — 'osez' = 'dare', but the whole phrase functions as an idiomatic challenge.
target_language_example: Comment osez-vous me mentir ?
native_language_example: How dare you lie to me?

meaning: or else / alternatively / otherwise
additional_notes: Used to offer an alternative, a different possibility, or a contrasting idea. Can introduce a second suggestion, a consequence, or a doubt. Tone depends on context—can be neutral (alternatively) or skeptical ('or else...'). Often followed by a clause or an interjection.
target_language_example: Je n'entends rien, ou alors le son est coupé.
native_language_example: I can't hear anything, or else the sound is off.

meaning: or / or else (used to offer an alternative or to introduce a second possibility).
additional_notes: Common coordinating phrase used to present alternatives, choices or contrasts. Can appear between clauses or at the start of a question. In questions it often emphasizes the alternative (e.g. "Are you X or else Y?"). Can be followed by inversion in formal questions (Êtes-vous... ou bien travaillez-vous?). Synonymous with simple "ou" but slightly more emphatic or formal.
target_language_example: Tu veux du café ou bien du thé ?
native_language_example: Do you want coffee or else tea?

meaning: or four (used to mean 'or so' / 'or about' after a number, e.g. 'three or four').
additional_notes: Commonly follows a specific small number (e.g. 'trois ou quatre') to indicate an approximate quantity or frequency ('about three or four'). Can be used with time expressions (ans), counts (fois), or sizes. Tone is neutral and suitable for everyday speech.
target_language_example: Il est resté ici trois ou quatre jours.
native_language_example: He stayed here for three or four days.

meaning: or what
additional_notes: Informal tag question used after a statement to challenge, criticize, or express disbelief about someone's behavior or a situation. Often adds annoyance, sarcasm, or incredulity (e.g. "T'es sourd, ou quoi ?" = "Are you deaf or what?" meaning "How can you not hear that?"). Can be used with a full sentence or a short phrase. Avoid in very polite/formal contexts.
target_language_example: Tu regardes encore ton téléphone, ou quoi ?
native_language_example: Are you still looking at your phone, or what?

meaning: or a woman (used to offer 'woman' as the alternative in a choice).
additional_notes: Used after a noun or question to present 'a woman' as the alternative to 'a man' (often following 'un homme'). Common in questions about gender or when listing possibilities. Word order and article match the noun's gender/number (e.g. "ou une femme", "ou des femmes").
target_language_example: C'est un garçon ou une femme ?
native_language_example: Is it a boy or a woman?

meaning: 'forgot to (tell/give) you' — part of the phrase meaning you failed to do something for someone because you forgot.
additional_notes: This is the past participle oublié (forgot) with the infinitive construction oublié de + verb, followed by the indirect object te (to you). Common uses: oublié de te dire (forgot to tell you), oublié de te donner (forgot to give you). Te goes before the verb or attached as a pronoun (e.g. oublié de te le dire / je t'ai oublié de... is incorrect). Often appears in spoken French as J'ai oublié de te dire or J'avais oublié de te le dire.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié de te montrer la photo hier.
native_language_example: I forgot to show you the photo yesterday.

meaning: forgot (the) — 'oublié' = forgot; 'les' = the (plural).
additional_notes: This is 'oublier' (to forget) in the past participle used with 'avoir' (J'ai oublié = I forgot). 'Les' is the definite article for plural direct objects (the). Use with other articles/pronouns as needed: J'ai oublié la clé (singular), Je les ai oubliées (if you replace 'les clés' with a pronoun, note agreement in writing/speech: past participle may agree in gender/number when preceded by the direct object pronoun). Commonly used to say you left/forgot things: J'ai oublié mes clés / Tom a oublié les clés sur la table.
target_language_example: J'ai oublié les lunettes à la maison.
native_language_example: I forgot the glasses at home.

meaning: teddy bear; a soft stuffed toy bear.
additional_notes: Refers to a stuffed (plush) toy in the shape of a bear, often a child's comfort object. Used like other possession phrases: 'son ours en peluche' = 'his/her teddy bear.' Plural: 'ours en peluche'.
target_language_example: Elle a offert un nouvel ours en peluche à la petite.
native_language_example: She gave the little girl a new teddy bear.

meaning: open on (a specific day).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether a business or place operates on a particular day: ouvert le dimanche = open on Sundays. In questions the article 'le' + weekday is common (le lundi, le dimanche). Not used for continuous sense like 'eyes open' (that would be 'les yeux ouverts').
target_language_example: Le musée est-il ouvert le mercredi ?
native_language_example: Is the museum open on Wednesday?

meaning: open the
additional_notes: Imperative of ouvrir, used to tell one person informally to open something. It is usually followed by a masculine singular noun: ouvre le livre, ouvre le coffre. If you mean "open it," French normally writes the pronoun with a hyphen: ouvre-le.
target_language_example: Ouvre le frigo, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Open the fridge, please.

meaning: opens to / opens at (depending on context).
additional_notes: Can mean 'to open the door to someone' (ouvrir à quelqu'un) or 'to open at [a certain time]' (ouvrir à [heure]). In sentence 1–2 it means 'opens the door to' or 'lets in'. In sentence 3 it asks 'What time does it open?'. Use context to choose translation.
target_language_example: Le magasin ouvre à 9 heures et il ouvre à tous les clients.
native_language_example: The store opens at 9 o'clock and it opens to all customers.

meaning: to open wide (fully); to open wide one's mouth/eyes; to open something wide.
additional_notes: A verb phrase used with a direct object (e.g., ouvrir grand la porte, ouvrir grand la bouche). Often used with body parts (bouche, yeux) or containers/doors to mean open fully. Conjugate ouvrir normally; 'grand' follows the verb. Common in commands: «Ouvre grand la bouche.» Can be used literally and figuratively (e.g., ouvrir grand les yeux = to be very surprised).
target_language_example: Il a dû ouvrir grand la fenêtre pour aérer la pièce.
native_language_example: He had to open the window wide to air out the room.

meaning: to open the door (literally).
additional_notes: A common literal phrase used to ask or tell someone to open a door, offer to open a door for someone, or describe having someone open it. Use impératif (Ouvre / Ouvrez) or polite forms (veuillez, s'il vous plaît) for requests. Can be used literally or politely as a gesture (letting someone in).
target_language_example: Peux-tu ouvrir la porte, s'il te plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you open the door, please?

meaning: to open one's eyes; literally 'open the eyes' — used literally and sometimes figuratively (become aware).
additional_notes: Commonly used literally (asking someone to open their eyes). Can also be used figuratively to mean 'wake up to' or 'become aware of' (e.g. ouvrir les yeux sur une réalité). In imperative or polite requests, use tu/vous according to formality and number.
target_language_example: Tu peux ouvrir les yeux maintenant ?
native_language_example: Can you open your eyes now?

meaning: 'where would (you) like' — beginning of a polite question about someone's preferred place.
additional_notes: Où = where. Aimeriez is the conditional form of aimer (vous aimeriez = you would like). Together they start polite questions asking someone's preference (e.g., where they'd like to go, live, work). In full questions you usually include a subject pronoun (vous, tu) and an infinitive verb after (aller, vivre, travailler). Useful for making polite requests about preferences.
target_language_example: Où aimeriez-vous vivre à l'avenir ?
native_language_example: Where would you like to live in the future?

meaning: Where were we (in the conversation / what were we discussing)?
additional_notes: Used to return to or resume a conversation, meeting, or topic after a pause or interruption. Often appears as "Où en étions-nous ?" or informally "Où en était-on ?". It asks to recall the point reached previously and is common in meetings, stories, or phone calls.
target_language_example: Bon, où en étions-nous avant la coupure ?
native_language_example: Right, where were we before the interruption?

meaning: 'where are' or 'where did (you) go' when followed by a past participle; literally 'where are/where did you'.
additional_notes: Où = where. Es is the second-person singular present of être (tu es). Common in questions with inversion (Où es-tu...?) or with past participle (Où es-tu allé? = Where did you go?). With passé composé, être is the auxiliary for many verbs of motion (aller, partir, arriver), so 'Où es-tu allé(e)?' means 'Where did you go?' In casual speech you may hear 't'es où?' or 'où t'es allé?'.
target_language_example: Où es-tu allé hier soir ?
native_language_example: Where did you go last night?

meaning: 'where can' — used to ask about possible location or possibility (where something/someone can be or where one can do something).
additional_notes: Always followed by a verb (often être, aller, trouver, se trouver). Forms vary with subject: 'où peut-il' (where can he be), 'où peut-on' (where can one/we), 'où pouvez-vous' (where can you). Use to ask about location or where an action/place is possible. Pronunciation: 'oo puh' (approx.).
target_language_example: Où peut-on acheter des billets ce soir ?
native_language_example: Where can one buy tickets tonight?

meaning: 'where can (we)...' — used to ask where something is possible for 'we'.
additional_notes: It's the beginning of a question with the first-person plural (nous) and the modal verb 'pouvoir' (to be able to / can). Usually completed by an infinitive (aller, trouver, s'asseoir, etc.). In spoken French, 'où pouvons-nous' may be replaced by 'où est-ce qu'on peut...' which is more informal and more common in conversation.
target_language_example: Où pouvons-nous acheter des billets ?
native_language_example: Where can we buy tickets?

meaning: wherever; in whatever place (introduces a subordinate clause).
additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive to mean 'no matter where' or 'wherever (someone/something) is'. Often appears in questions or commands (e.g., asking if there's pain 'anywhere') and in statements like 'I never stay anywhere long'. The structure is 'où que' + subject + subjunctive (e.g., 'où que tu sois'). Can be followed by 'ce soit' in more general expressions ('où que ce soit' = 'anywhere').
target_language_example: Où que tu ailles, je te suivrai.
native_language_example: Wherever you go, I'll follow you.

meaning: A reduced form used in colloquial or emphatic contexts as part of the expression 'où que ce soit' meaning 'wherever' or 'no matter where'. On its own 'où que ce' is incomplete and normally requires following elements (e.g. 'soit', a pronoun + verb) to form a grammatical clause.
additional_notes: 'Où que ce' appears in spoken French as the beginning of the fixed phrase 'où que ce soit'. It must be completed (typically by 'soit' or by a subjunctive clause such as 'où que ce soit que tu ailles'). Use in formal writing should use the complete form 'où que ce soit' or 'où que' + subjunctive. The phrase conveys 'wherever' or 'no matter where'.
target_language_example: Où que ce soit, tu trouveras toujours des gens prêts à aider.
native_language_example: Wherever it may be, you will always find people willing to help.

meaning: 'where are' (question asking location of plural noun(s) or multiple items).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the location of more than one person or thing. 'Où' = where; 'sont' = (they) are (3rd person plural of être). For singular use 'où est' (where is). Can appear in embedded questions (...me dire où sont...).
target_language_example: Où sont mes clés ?
native_language_example: Where are my keys?

meaning: 'where you come from' (informal spoken French)
additional_notes: Often used in the question form 'D'où tu viens ?' meaning 'Where are you from?' or 'Where did you come from?'. The word order is informal/colloquial (standard written: 'D'où viens-tu ?' or 'D'où est-ce que tu viens ?'). Can also appear in statements: 'Je sais d'où tu viens' = 'I know where you're from.' In the command 'Retourne d'où tu viens' it means 'Go back to where you came from' and can be rude or confrontational depending on context.
target_language_example: D'où tu viens, on t'accueillera toujours.
native_language_example: Where you come from, you'll always be welcomed.

meaning: 'what's the world coming to?' — an expression of shock, disbelief, or dismay at how things are going.
additional_notes: Used to complain about or react to something seen as absurd, upsetting, or declining in society. Often rhetorical and informal; may be followed by an expletive for emphasis. Not literal — you're not asking for the world's location.
target_language_example: Où va le monde, ils ont fermé la bibliothèque du quartier ?
native_language_example: What's the world coming to — they closed the neighborhood library?

meaning: 'where do (you) live' (asks about someone's place of residence).
additional_notes: Usually part of the question 'Où vivez-vous ?' (formal/plural 'you') or 'Où vis-tu ?' (informal singular). 'Vivez' is the present tense of 'vivre' for 'vous'. Can be followed by modifiers: 'exactement', 'désormais' (nowadays), or 'tous' (asking a group).
target_language_example: Où vivez-vous exactement en ville ?
native_language_example: Where do you live exactly in the city?

meaning: where were
additional_notes: Used to ask where someone was in the past. In the examples it appears as où étiez-vous, which is the formal or plural way to say "where were you?". Étiez is the imperfect form of être with vous.
target_language_example: Où étiez-vous hier soir ?
native_language_example: Where were you yesterday evening?

meaning: 'where he goes' or 'wherever he goes'
additional_notes: Used to indicate places someone goes — often appears with 'partout' (everywhere) as 'partout où il va' meaning 'everywhere he goes' or 'wherever he goes'. Pronoun 'il' can change (elle, on, je, tu, nous, vous) to match the subject: 'où elle va', 'où je vais', etc. Can introduce a clause: 'Partout où il va, ...' or follow a noun: 'les endroits où il va'.
target_language_example: Il emporte son appareil photo partout où il va.
native_language_example: He takes his camera everywhere he goes.

meaning: where there is / where there are
additional_notes: Used to point to a place or situation that contains something. Common in fixed expressions like "là où il y a..." (where there is...). Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Can refer to physical location or abstract situation.
target_language_example: Pose-le là où il y a de la place.
native_language_example: Put it where there is space.

meaning: 'where you (yourself) ...' — used to introduce a clause about the place or point at which the listener did something or was in a certain state.
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase 'là où vous vous êtes ...' meaning 'where you left off' or 'where you were ...'. The double 'vous' is the subject pronoun plus the reflexive pronoun for pronominal verbs (e.g. s'arrêter, s'évanouir). Verb agreement (participle) matches the subject in gender/number when using être in compound tenses (e.g. 'arrêté', 'arrêtée', 'arrêtés', 'arrêtées').
target_language_example: Racontez-moi le moment où vous vous êtes senti(e) seul(e).
native_language_example: Tell me the moment when you felt alone.

meaning: toasted bread; toast.
additional_notes: Commonly used for slices of bread that have been toasted until crisp. Can refer to a single slice (une tranche de pain grillé) or toast in general. Used in everyday situations (breakfast, offering food).
target_language_example: Le petit-déjeuner comprend du pain grillé et de la confiture.
native_language_example: Breakfast includes toast and jam.

meaning: part of the idiom "avoir du pain sur la planche" — to have a lot of work or tasks to do.
additional_notes: This is not used alone in French; it appears in the full idiom "avoir du pain sur la planche" (literally: "to have bread on the board"). It means to have a lot to do or many tasks ahead. Used in everyday speech; can be used in formal and informal contexts. Conjugate "avoir" as needed (J'ai du pain sur la planche, Nous avons...).
target_language_example: J'ai encore du pain sur la planche cette semaine.
native_language_example: I still have a lot on my plate this week.

meaning: May peace be with (you/them). A blessing or wish for peace.
additional_notes: Used as a short blessing or greeting, often religious or formal; commonly appears as 'Que la paix soit avec toi/vous' or shortened to 'La paix soit avec toi'. Use 'toi' for informal singular, 'vous' for formal or plural. Equivalent to 'peace be with you.'
target_language_example: Que la paix soit avec toi en ces temps difficiles.
native_language_example: May peace be with you in these difficult times.

meaning: 'the basket was' (simple past description of the basket's state).
additional_notes: This is the phrase panier (basket) + était (imperfect of être: was). Used to describe what a basket contained or its condition in the past. Common follow-ups: plein de / rempli de / plein à ras bord de = full of / filled to the brim with. É tait is a past tense (imperfect) used for descriptions or ongoing past states.
target_language_example: Le panier était plein de pain.
native_language_example: The basket was full of bread.

meaning: toilet paper; bathroom tissue.
additional_notes: Common everyday noun. Used both in singular (du papier toilette) for an unspecified amount and with articles (le papier toilette) when referring to the item in general or a specific roll. Can be shortened in speech to 'papier' in some contexts, but 'papier toilette' is standard. Plural 'des papiers toilettes' is rare — usually stays uncountable or 'rouleaux de papier toilette' for rolls.
target_language_example: Il n'y a plus de papier toilette dans les toilettes.
native_language_example: There is no toilet paper left in the bathroom.

meaning: over, above, or on top of; can also mean 'from above' or used idiomatically in phrases like 'look over/above'.
additional_notes: Used as a preposition or adverb meaning physically over/on top of (par-dessus la barrière = over the fence) or metaphorically (regarder par-dessus son épaule = look over one's shoulder). Can appear alone as a short reply ('Par-dessus.' = Over it/On top) or in imperatives like 'Venez, par-dessus!' meaning 'Come over (on top/from above)!' Context determines whether it implies movement across/over or position above. Not informal.
target_language_example: Il a sauté par-dessus la clôture.
native_language_example: He jumped over the fence.

meaning: overboard; (onto/over) the side of a boat or ship.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something goes over the side of a boat or is thrown off a vessel. Can be literal (falling into the water) or used emphatically (throw away). Often appears with verbs like tomber (to fall) or jeter (to throw).
target_language_example: Ne pousse pas le sac par-dessus bord !
native_language_example: Don't push the bag overboard!

meaning: by accident; unintentionally
additional_notes: Used to say something happened without intention. Common in everyday speech. Can be used alone as a short answer ("Par accident."). Note: with informal/sexual contexts in examples, meaning stays the same. Equivalent to "accidentellement."
target_language_example: J'ai renversé le café par accident.
native_language_example: I spilled the coffee by accident.

meaning: 'out of love' or 'for love's sake' (doing something because of love).
additional_notes: Used to say that an action is motivated by love. Can describe past, present, or hypothetical actions (Je l'ai fait par amour / Je le fais par amour). Common in everyday and literary French. Not idiomatic beyond the literal sense.
target_language_example: Elle a accepté ce voyage par amour.
native_language_example: She accepted that trip out of love.

meaning: in advance; beforehand
additional_notes: Used to say something is done or felt before an event happens (e.g., payment, anticipation, thanks). Often appears in formal and neutral contexts (e.g., "Je vous remercie par avance"). Can be placed after a verb or phrase. Synonyms: "à l'avance."
target_language_example: Je vous remercie par avance pour votre aide.
native_language_example: I thank you in advance for your help.

meaning: 'fortunately' or 'luckily'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a positive, relieving fact or circumstance. It is a formal/neutral adverbial phrase placed at the start or in the middle of a sentence (often set off by commas).
target_language_example: Par bonheur, j'ai trouvé mes clés avant de partir.
native_language_example: Fortunately, I found my keys before leaving.

meaning: 'by luck' or 'fortunately'
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened thanks to luck or good fortune. Often appears at the start of a sentence (with a comma) but can also be placed inline. Registers as neutral — suitable in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Par chance, j'ai trouvé mes clés sous le canapé.
native_language_example: Fortunately, I found my keys under the sofa.

meaning: 'on the other hand' / 'however' (to contrast two ideas).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or opposition to what was just said. More neutral than 'mais' and often used to present an alternative point or drawback. Common in spoken and written French. Can appear at the start of a sentence or clause: 'Il est bon en maths. Par contre, il est moins bon en français.'
target_language_example: J'aime bien ce film. Par contre, la fin était décevante.
native_language_example: I like this movie. On the other hand, the ending was disappointing.

meaning: by heart; from memory (learned or known without needing to read).
additional_notes: Used to say you know or have learned something memorically (words, texts, facts). Common with verbs like apprendre, savoir, réciter. Not literal (not about the heart).
target_language_example: Elle sait le poème par cœur.
native_language_example: She knows the poem by heart.

meaning: by e-mail / via email.
additional_notes: Used to indicate the means of sending or contacting via electronic mail. Often appears as 'par e‑mail', 'par email', or 'par courriel' (Canada). Common in requests or statements about sending documents or messages.
target_language_example: Peux-tu m'envoyer le fichier par e‑mail ?
native_language_example: Can you send me the file by e‑mail?

meaning: by mistake; accidentally.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened unintentionally or in error. Common in both spoken and written French. Can appear at start, middle, or end of a sentence: 'Par erreur, j'ai...' / 'Il l'a fait par erreur.' Often interchangeable with 'par mégarde' or 'accidentellement.'
target_language_example: J'ai effacé le fichier par erreur.
native_language_example: I deleted the file by mistake.

meaning: for example; e.g.
additional_notes: Used to introduce an example or illustration. Can start a sentence or appear mid-sentence with commas. Very common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Nous pourrions visiter un musée, par exemple.
native_language_example: We could visit a museum, for example.

meaning: by chance; accidentally; unexpectedly.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened without planning or intentionally. Common in questions to soften a request or ask if someone knows something by chance (e.g., "Tu ne saurais pas... par hasard ?"). Can be placed after a verb or phrase. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Je l'ai trouvé par hasard en feuilletant un livre.
native_language_example: I found it by chance while flipping through a book.

meaning: around here
additional_notes: Used to indicate location near the speaker or in this area. Can be standalone (Oui, par ici) or in questions (Il y a un bureau de poste par ici ?) and idiomatic expressions (Que fais-tu par ici ? = What are you doing around here?). Tone can be neutral; in contexts like 'Par ici, état critique !' it can introduce a location in a brief announcement.
target_language_example: Il y a un bon café par ici ?
native_language_example: Is there a good café around here?

meaning: in the past; previously; formerly.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened at an earlier time. Often interchangeable with auparavant, autrefois or dans le passé. Common in both formal and informal contexts to indicate prior occurrences or past habits.
target_language_example: J'ai travaillé dans ce secteur par le passé.
native_language_example: I worked in that industry in the past.

meaning: that/there (in that sense)
additional_notes:
Has several uses depending on context:
- To refer to a vague location: "par là" ≈ "around there/over there" (example: Elle a toujours une pelle par là = She always has a shovel around there). 
- To indicate passing through or having been in a place: "passer par là" ≈ "to pass through/been there". 
- To ask for clarification about what someone means: "Que veux-tu dire par là ?" ≈ "What do you mean by that/that remark?". 
Choose the sense from context. Can be informal in spoken language but is common in neutral speech.
target_language_example: Quand j'étais petit, je suis souvent passé par là.
native_language_example: When I was little, I often passed through there / I was often there.

meaning: 'by a miracle' / 'miraculously' — indicates something happened in an extraordinary or unexpected way.
additional_notes: Used to say that an outcome was surprising, unlikely, or seemed caused by luck/divine intervention. Common in both spoken and written French. Can be placed before the verb (Par miracle, ...) or after (il est arrivé par miracle). Tone is neutral; not informal.
target_language_example: Par miracle, nous avons trouvé de l'eau dans le désert.
native_language_example: Miraculously, we found water in the desert.

meaning: at times; sometimes; occasionally.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens intermittently or from time to time. Often appears at the start or end of a sentence. Similar to «par moment» (less common) and «parfois». Useful for describing feelings, memories, habits, or occurrences that are not constant.
target_language_example: Par moments, je me sens dépassé.
native_language_example: At times, I feel overwhelmed.

meaning: 'per person' or 'each person'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a rate, portion, or distribution relative to each individual. Common with prices (par personne = price per person) and with quantities (une par personne = one each). Can appear alone as a short answer.
target_language_example: Le billet coûte 15 euros par personne.
native_language_example: The ticket costs 15 euros per person.

meaning: 'please' or 'for pity's sake' — a plea asking someone to stop or do something, often urgent or emotional.
additional_notes: Used to make a strong request or beg; can express desperation, exasperation, or pleading. Tone depends on context and intonation — can be polite ('please') or urgent/dramatic ('for pity's sake'). Common in spoken French and in urgent written appeals.
target_language_example: Par pitié, ne me laissez pas seul.
native_language_example: Please, don't leave me alone.

meaning: in relation to; compared to; with respect to.
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or indicate a reference point (location, time, quantity, opinion). Can mean 'compared with' (Par rapport à Tokyo...), 'with respect to' (par rapport à la situation), or 'relative to/compared to' (tu as du retard par rapport à l'équipe). Often followed by a noun or pronoun. Very common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Par rapport à ce plan, nous devons changer la porte.
native_language_example: Compared to this plan, we must change the door.

meaning: because of; as a result of; due to
additional_notes: Formal/written expression used to indicate cause or consequence. Common in reports, official documents, or formal speech. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase (par suite de + [nom]). Can be replaced in everyday speech by à cause de or en raison de.
target_language_example: Par suite de travaux, la route sera fermée demain.
native_language_example: Due to construction, the road will be closed tomorrow.

meaning: by surprise; unexpectedly.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened unexpectedly or that someone was caught off guard. Follows verbs like 'prendre' (prendre quelqu'un par surprise) or can modify a passive construction (être pris par surprise). Can be used with people or groups (attendus par surprise / attaqués par surprise).
target_language_example: Ils nous ont attaqués par surprise.
native_language_example: They attacked us by surprise.

meaning: on the ground / on the floor
additional_notes: Used to say something is lying on the ground or floor, or to indicate position (on the ground). Common in everyday French. Can describe indoor (le sol) or outdoor (la terre, ground) locations and is used with people (tomber par terre) or objects (être par terre).
target_language_example: J'ai laissé mon sac par terre près de la porte.
native_language_example: I left my bag on the floor near the door.

meaning: by phone; via a phone call.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is done using the telephone (calling or receiving information). Common in formal and informal contexts. Can appear alone as a short answer (e.g., "Par téléphone.") or inside sentences to explain how you contacted someone or how to place an order.
target_language_example: Je te confirmerai l'heure par téléphone.
native_language_example: I'll confirm the time by phone.

meaning: in writing; written (rather than spoken).
additional_notes: Used to say that something should be written down or submitted as a written document (letter, email, form). Common in formal contexts (applications, complaints) and everyday advice (take notes). Often follows verbs like mettre, poser (une candidature), faire (une réclamation).
target_language_example: Envoyez votre demande par écrit.
native_language_example: Send your request in writing.

meaning: take/bring an umbrella with (you).
additional_notes: Used in phrases like 'prendre un parapluie avec (toi/vous)' meaning 'bring/take an umbrella with you.' Commonly followed by a pronoun (toi, vous) or omitted in informal speech where context implies 'with you.' Useful for weather advice: 'Prends un parapluie avec toi.'
target_language_example: N'oublie pas de prendre un parapluie avec toi aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: Don't forget to take an umbrella with you today.

meaning: “umbrella in/inside” — used to say an umbrella is located in or left inside something (train, bus, car, holder).
additional_notes: A simple preposition phrase: parapluie (umbrella) + dans (in/inside). Common in statements about forgetting or placing an umbrella. Use dans + definite/indefinite article or possessive (dans le train, dans sa voiture, dans le porte-parapluie). Word order: parapluie dans + location (often reversed in full sentences: Elle a laissé son parapluie dans le train).
target_language_example: J'ai mis mon parapluie dans le coffre de la voiture.
native_language_example: I put my umbrella in the car trunk.

meaning: because
additional_notes: Introduces a reason or explanation. It is the standard way to say why something happens or is true, and it can also be used at the start of a sentence or as a short answer: « Parce que... »
target_language_example: Je reste à la maison parce que ma voiture est en panne.
native_language_example: I'm staying home because my car has broken down.

meaning: 'parents' (the word 'parents') often appears with 'ne' as part of negation or in subjunctive negative clauses; here the pair shows typical contexts for 'parents' + negation.
additional_notes: This entry highlights two things: 1) 'parents' = 'parents' (mother and father). 2) The particle 'ne' is the common negation marker used with verbs (usually paired with 'pas', 'plus', 'jamais', etc.) or appears in negative subjunctive constructions after conjunctions like 'avant que', 'sans que'. Beginners should note that in spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped (e.g. 'mes parents viennent' with context), but in written or formal French 'ne' marks negation or negative subjunctive. Examples 1–2 show 'ne' in subjunctive negatives after 'sans que' and 'avant que'; examples 3–6 show standard negation (mes parents ne ... pas / ne ... plus / ne ... jamais).
target_language_example: Je suis allé les voir avant que mes parents ne sachent.
native_language_example: I went to see them before my parents knew.

meaning: parents (subject) + reflexive pronoun 'se' used with pronominal verbs (e.g., se rencontrer, se séparer, se disputer) — indicates actions between the parents (they met, separated, argued, etc.).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the combination of the noun 'parents' with a reflexive verb form using 'se' (often appearing as 'se sont' in past tense). Common verbs: se rencontrer (to meet each other), se séparer (to split up), se disputer (to argue). In questions and formal inversion you may see 'se sont-ils' or 'se sont-ils rencontrés'. The past participle agrees when the reflexive pronoun is the direct object (check grammar separately).
target_language_example: Mes parents se sont mariés en 1990.
native_language_example: My parents got married in 1990.

meaning: 'perfectly' or 'completely' used before a masculine singular noun or noun phrase (le + noun).
additional_notes: Parfaitement is an adverb meaning 'perfectly' or 'completely'. When followed by the definite article le and a noun, it describes doing something perfectly in that language/role or that something fits/complements something exactly. Examples show it with languages (parler parfaitement le grec) and with objects/rights (parfaitement le droit). Use the appropriate article/gender: parfaitement la, parfaitement les, or just parfaitement before verbs/adjectives (parfaitement compris).
target_language_example: Il comprend parfaitement le problème.
native_language_example: He understands the problem perfectly.

meaning: I bet (that) you ...; I'm sure/probably you ...
additional_notes: Informal spoken way to express a strong guess or assumption about the listener. Often used with present or past tense (e.g., 'tu as', 'tu es', 'tu l'as pas appelée'). Can be followed by 'que' + a full clause. Tone can be playful, teasing, or confident.
target_language_example: Je parie que tu vas adorer ce film.
native_language_example: I bet that you will love this movie.

meaning: I bet (that) you ... / I wager you ...
additional_notes: Used to express a confident guess or assumption about the listener's actions, knowledge, or qualities. Often followed by a clause introduced with que + subject (vous). Can be used jokingly or rhetorically. In spoken French you may also hear Je parie (que) t'as... or Je parie que tu... with tu for informal situations.
target_language_example: Je parie que vous avez déjà vu ce film.
native_language_example: I bet you have already seen this movie.

meaning: 'speak to' or 'talk to' (imperative or present: speak/talk to + masculine singular person/role).
additional_notes: Parle au = conjugated verb parler (tu or je/il forms in examples) + preposition à + definite article le contracted to au. Used before a masculine singular person or role (le maire, le juge, le chauffeur, le conseiller). For feminine nouns use 'parle à la' or before a name just 'parle à'. Can be imperative (Parle au juge = Talk to the judge) or present tense (Je parle au chat = I am talking to the cat).
target_language_example: Parle au professeur si tu as des questions.
native_language_example: Talk to the teacher if you have questions.

meaning: talks about; is talking about
additional_notes: A present-tense form of parler de, used when the topic of conversation follows: parler de quelque chose / de quelqu’un = to talk about something / someone. It can also appear in sentences like parler à quelqu’un de quelque chose, meaning to talk to someone about something. Don't confuse it with parler à, which means to talk to someone.
target_language_example: Tout le monde parle de toi.
native_language_example: Everyone is talking about you.

meaning: 'does not speak ... nor ...' (used in negative sentences to link two languages or items)
additional_notes: Used with ne ... ni ... ni to express 'neither ... nor ...'. The verb (parle) appears between ne and the first ni in these examples. In English word order you usually translate as 'doesn't speak X or Y' or 'speaks neither X nor Y.' Replace the languages with other nouns as needed. Common structure: Subject + ne + verb + ni + item1 + ni + item2. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: Il parle ni anglais ni français (colloquial).
target_language_example: Elle ne parle ni russe ni italien.
native_language_example: She speaks neither Russian nor Italian.

meaning: 'speak' (they speak + language article), used with a language: they speak the/— (language).
additional_notes: Third-person plural form of parler (ils/elles parlent). In French you often use the definite article with languages (parler le français, parler l'anglais, parler le kabyle), though in English we usually omit the article (they speak French). Use 'parlent' for they (ils/elles).
target_language_example: Elles parlent le français et l'anglais.
native_language_example: They speak French and English.

meaning: to speak alone with someone; to speak privately (one-on-one).
