additional_notes: Used when you want a private, one-to-one conversation. The phrase must agree in gender/number when used as an adjective phrase after verbs: seule (feminine singular), seul (masculine singular), seules (feminine plural), seuls (masculine plural). More natural phrasing: "parler en tête-à-tête" or "parler en privé." With indirect object pronouns: "te/vous parler seul(e)(s)" (Je dois te parler seul = I must speak to you alone).
target_language_example: Je dois te parler seule à seule.
native_language_example: I need to speak with you alone (private, one-on-one).

meaning: 'to speak too quickly' or 'to talk too fast'.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone talking faster than is easy to understand. Can refer to rate of speech (articulation) or figuratively to rushing through ideas. Commonly used in everyday speech. Can be conjugated or used in infinitive constructions: Il parle trop vite; Tu parlais trop vite; Elle va parler trop vite; Ne parle pas trop vite.
target_language_example: Il a tendance à parler trop vite quand il est nerveux.
native_language_example: He tends to speak too quickly when he's nervous.

meaning: to speak to
additional_notes: Used before the person or group you are addressing. To say what the conversation is about, French usually uses parler de (“to talk about”).
target_language_example: Je dois parler à mon professeur demain.
native_language_example: I need to talk to my teacher tomorrow.

meaning: Do you speak French? (formal or plural)
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask whether someone speaks French. Used with vous (formal singular or plural). To ask informally to one person, use « Tu parles français ? ». Can be followed by adverbs (e.g. « couramment », « aussi », « tous les jours »). Pronunciation tip: [par-lay voo frahn-say].
target_language_example: Parlez-vous français couramment ?
native_language_example: Do you speak French fluently?

meaning: 'you speak well' (formal/plural 'vous' form)
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone's skill in speaking a language or to ask if they speak a language well. Usually appears with a language after it (parlez bien français/anglais/allemand). With just 'Vous parlez bien.' it means 'You speak well' (general compliment). 'Parlez' is the vous form of 'parler' (formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Vous parlez bien espagnol.
native_language_example: You speak Spanish well.

meaning: 'you speak like' / 'you talk like' (used to compare someone's way of speaking to someone/something else).
additional_notes: Directs a comparison of how someone speaks to another person, group, profession, or stereotype. Typically used with vous (formal/plural) for the imperative/statement form, but the structure can appear with other subjects (parles comme, parle comme). Structure: parlez comme + noun/pronoun or parlez comme + clause (parlez comme si...). Tone can be neutral, complimentary, or critical depending on context, intonation, and additional words.
target_language_example: Vous parlez comme un psychologue quand vous analysez les autres.
native_language_example: You speak like a psychologist when you analyze others.

meaning: let's not talk (about it)
additional_notes: Context decides meaning. With 'n'en parlons pas' it means 'let's not talk about that (now)' — a suggestion to stop discussing a topic. In 'ne parlons pas de moi' it means 'let's not talk about me'. Without the imperative/let's implication (e.g. 'nous ne parlons pas la même langue') it simply states 'we do not speak (the same language)'. The full negative forms are 'ne... pas' or colloquial 'n'... pas'.
target_language_example: N'en parlons pas tout de suite, revenons-y plus tard.
native_language_example: Let's not talk about it right now; we'll come back to it later.

meaning: 'part des' itself is not a fixed standalone expression; it appears in two related constructions: 1) 'la part de/sa part des ...' meaning someone's share/portion of something (e.g. 'sa part des bénéfices' = his share of the profits). 2) within the fixed phrase 'de la part de/des ...' meaning 'from' or 'on behalf of' when indicating who sent something ('de la part des Powell' = from the Powells). Context determines whether it refers to a share or is part of the 'de la part de/des' sender construction.
additional_notes: The sequence 'part des' can occur when the definite article 'les' contracts with 'de' (de + les = des) after 'part' in plural contexts (e.g. 'sa part des bénéfices'). More commonly you'll see 'la part de' (singular) or the fixed phrase 'de la part de/du/des' for 'from'. Make sure to keep surrounding words to disambiguate meaning.
target_language_example: Il a réclamé sa part des bénéfices.
native_language_example: He claimed his share of the profits.

meaning: 'doesn't leave' / 'doesn't go' (negative form of partir with il/elle/on/ça or with subject implied)
additional_notes: This is the negative short form of partir (to leave/go) used with various subjects: e.g. 'ça ne part pas' (it doesn't come off / won't come off), 'on ne part pas' (we/one don't leave). In spoken French the subject may be explicit (on, nous, il/elle/qui) or implied from context. Watch for different senses of partir: physical leaving, departing, or something stopping/removing (e.g. a stain 'ne part pas'). In informal speech you may hear 'on ne part pas' or 'je ne pars pas' contracted to 'je pars pas'.
target_language_example: On ne part pas avant midi.
native_language_example: We don't leave before noon.

meaning: political party
additional_notes: Refers to an organized group sharing political goals and seeking to influence government (e.g., through elections). Commonly used in formal and everyday contexts when talking about membership, founding, joining, or criticizing a party.
target_language_example: Elle a adhéré à un parti politique l'année dernière.
native_language_example: She joined a political party last year.

meaning: 'left with' or 'went off with' (she departed accompanied by someone or took someone along).
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle partie (from partir, used with être: elle est partie) + avec. Used to indicate that a (usually feminine) subject left accompanied by one or more people or took someone along. Can be neutral (simply left together) or imply elopement, running away, or abandonment depending on context. Agreement: participe passé partie agrees in gender/number with the subject when used with être (elle est partie, elles sont parties).
target_language_example: Elle est partie avec ses amis.
native_language_example: She left with her friends.

meaning: (someone) has gone out to do (something) — commonly used with errands or shopping (e.g. courses, emplettes). Indicates the person left to perform that activity.
additional_notes: Structure: [être] parti(e) + faire + noun (often "des courses" or "des emplettes"). Use past-participle agreement with être when appropriate (elle est partie). Can be used in spoken and written French. Literal translation is possible ("has gone to do some ___").
target_language_example: Elle est partie faire des courses.
native_language_example: She has gone out to do some shopping.

meaning: 'to start from' or 'to leave from' (indicates origin or starting point)
additional_notes: Used before a noun or pronoun indicating the place or point of departure or the basis/starting point of an idea. Contraction: partir de + vowel becomes partir d'. Can mean physically leaving (Je pars d'ici = I'm leaving from here) or figuratively (Partir d'une hypothèse = to start from a hypothesis). If followed by an infinitive (partir + de + infinitive) it can mean 'to begin by' doing something.
target_language_example: Nous devons partir d'une hypothèse simple pour avancer.
native_language_example: We must start from a simple hypothesis to move forward.

meaning: 'left for' or 'departed for' (plural subjects).
additional_notes: Participe passé 'partis' (masculine plural) of partir followed by 'à' + destination (e.g. 'partis à Paris') means that a group left for a place. Use 'parties à' for feminine groups; singulars are 'parti à' (m.) / 'partie à' (f.). Often appears in past contexts (passé composé or plus-que-parfait) or as adjective after être.
target_language_example: Ils sont partis à Lyon ce matin.
native_language_example: They left for Lyon this morning.

meaning: manage to / succeed in (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say you are able to achieve or accomplish something (often despite difficulty). Conjugated form of parvenir + à. Common with verbs like voir, ressentir, prouver, etc.
target_language_example: Je parviens à finir ce projet aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I manage to finish this project today.

meaning: not allowed / not admitted (permission denied to enter or participate).
additional_notes: Used on signs and rules to indicate that people, animals, objects or behaviors are not permitted. Often follows the noun: 'Les animaux de compagnie ne sont pas admis.' Formal/register neutral. Can refer to entry, participation, or presence.
target_language_example: Les sacs volumineux ne sont pas admis dans la salle.
native_language_example: Large bags are not allowed in the room.

meaning: 'not to catch' — a negative construction meaning to fail to catch or to miss catching something or someone; can also mean 'not to understand' in informal contexts when used with comprendre or saisir.
additional_notes: Formed by pas (not) + infinitive attraper (to catch). In standard French the negative is ne ... pas + infinitive (ne pas attraper), but in speech ne is often omitted (pas attraper). Can refer to missing an object (a ball), missing transportation (a train), failing to catch someone physically, or colloquially failing to understand ('je n'ai pas attrapé' → 'j'ai pas attrapé' meaning 'I didn't get it').
target_language_example: Je vais pas attraper le train si je pars maintenant.
native_language_example: I won't catch the train if I leave now.

meaning: 'not to have been' (the negative perfect infinitive of 'être')
additional_notes: Used after verbs that require an infinitive (often after expressions like 'désolé de', 'regretter de') to say you regret or apologize for not having been/been present or not having behaved in a certain way. It's the negative form of 'avoir été' and refers to a past state or action. Common in set phrases: 'désolé de ne pas avoir été là' = 'sorry for not being there.'
target_language_example: Je suis désolé de ne pas avoir été présent hier.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for not having been present yesterday.

meaning: 'not doing well' / 'not well at all' (used to say someone feels unwell or is not okay).
additional_notes: Colloquial negative phrase used to describe physical or emotional state. Often appears as 'ne ... pas bien du tout' or in spoken/informal French dropped 'ne' as in 'pas bien du tout'. The '(tout)' can be omitted or added for emphasis ('du tout' = 'at all'). Use with subjects and forms of 'aller' (aller bien / ne pas aller bien).
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui, je ne vais pas bien du tout.
native_language_example: Today I'm really not doing well.

meaning: "(don't tell me) what I should / must (do)" — used in negative commands or statements telling someone not to say/instruct what one must do.
additional_notes: This phrase appears inside negative imperatives or statements like "Ne me dis pas ce que je dois faire" = "Don't tell me what I should do." Often followed by an infinitive (faire). The examples show familiar (tu) and formal/plural (vous) forms: "Ne me dis pas..." (tu), "Ne me dites pas..." (vous). In spoken French the initial "ne" is often dropped: "Me dis pas ce que je dois."
target_language_example: Ne me dis pas ce que je dois faire, je gère la situation.
native_language_example: Don't tell me what I should do, I can handle it.

meaning: a fragment used in negative questions or statements meaning 'not what I...' or 'don't know what I...'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a common word order fragment appearing in informal spoken French where pas negates a verb (je ne sais pas) and ce que je introduces a clause ('what I...'). Often the ne is dropped in speech (Je sais pas ce que je... / Tu me demandes pas ce que je...). Use it to say you don't know what you do/feel/will do, or to form negative questions.
target_language_example: Je sais pas ce que je ferais sans toi.
native_language_example: I don't know what I would do without you.

meaning: 'not the one' (masculine singular) — used to say someone/something is not the person or thing referred to.
additional_notes: Pas celui combines the negation pas with the demonstrative pronoun celui (masculine singular). It refers back to a specific person or object already mentioned or implied. For feminine use say pas celle; plural: pas ceux / pas celles. Common in sentences like "Je ne suis pas celui que vous pensez" (I am not the one you think).
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas celui que j'attendais.
native_language_example: That is not the one I was expecting.

meaning: 'not changed' (used before a noun or phrase beginning with a vowel or elided form), often in expressions like "pas changé d'avis" = 'haven't changed your mind'.
additional_notes: This is the negative form of "changer de" (+ noun): "ne... pas changé d'..." means someone/something has not changed in that respect. Common collocations: "changer d'avis" (change one's mind), "ne pas changer d'un poil/pouce" (not change at all — idiomatic, meaning 'not change even a bit'). Contraction: the final d' is the elided form of "de" before a vowel (e.g. d'avis). Informal spoken French often drops the "ne" (T'as pas... / Tu n'as pas...).
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas changé d'avis ?
native_language_example: Haven't you changed your mind?

meaning: 'not continue' or 'cannot continue' (negation of continuer).
additional_notes: Combines the negation particle 'pas' with the verb 'continuer' to say that something does not or cannot go on. Word order: in simple present or imperfect negation, 'ne ... pas continuer' surrounds the verb (often contracted in speech to 'pas continuer' when shown alone). Commonly appears with modal verbs (pouvoir) to mean 'cannot continue'. Used for actions, situations, or processes that should stop or cannot proceed.
target_language_example: Ça ne peut pas continuer comme ça.
native_language_example: This cannot continue like this.

meaning: no
additional_notes: Used before a noun to show absence or non-existence: pas de guerre = 'no war'. Very common in negative sentences such as il n'y a pas de... ('there is/are no...'). After pas, French usually uses de before the noun instead of un/une/des.
target_language_example: Il n'y a pas de problème.
native_language_example: There is no problem.

meaning: 'not (of) the' or the negative part of expressions like 'pas de + noun' when followed by a feminine definite article 'la'.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the negation 'pas' + the partitive/possessive construction 'de' followed by the feminine singular definite article 'la'. It appears in sentences like 'pas de la mienne' (not mine) or 'pas de la tienne' (not yours). Context determines the exact translation: it can negate ownership ('not mine'), negate an action with an object introduced by 'de' ('not to throw it'), or form part of expressions after verbs that take 'de' (e.g. 'se lasser de'). In speech, word order and pronouns matter — sometimes a pronoun (la) refers back to a feminine noun mentioned earlier.
target_language_example: Ce livre n'est pas de la mienne, il est à Claire.
native_language_example: This book is not mine, it's Claire's.

meaning: 'not worth mentioning' (you're welcome) OR 'nothing to' / 'not enough to'.
additional_notes: Has two common uses: 1) As a short reply to 'merci' meaning 'you're welcome' or 'no problem' (informal/polite). 2) Literally inside sentences with 'ne ... pas de quoi' meaning 'not enough to' or 'no reason to' (e.g. 'pas de quoi rire' = 'nothing to laugh about'). Intonation and context determine which meaning is intended. Can stand alone as 'Pas de quoi.' in conversation.
target_language_example:
— Merci pour ton aide.
— Pas de quoi.
native_language_example:
— Thanks for your help.
— You're welcome.

meaning: 'not of yours' / 'not your' (used to refuse or disagree; literally 'not of your')
additional_notes: A negative construction combining pas + de + votre. Often appears in expressions of disagreement, refusal, or to exclude something as belonging to someone (opinion, help, vote, family, etc.). Context determines the noun omitted after 'votre' (e.g. 'avis', 'famille', 'vote'). In spoken French the noun can be omitted when it's clear from context. Tone can be blunt or rude depending on context.
target_language_example: Non merci, je ne veux pas de votre aide.
native_language_example: No thanks, I don't want your help.

meaning: not about that / don't do that / none of that (used to reject a topic or behavior)
additional_notes: Informal phrase used to refuse, reject or tell someone not to involve you in something or not to talk about a subject. Often appears in contractions (On n'en parle pas / On parle pas) and in imperatives (Pas de ça avec moi = Don't do that with me). Tone can be firm or annoyed depending on context.
target_language_example: Pas de ça entre nous, d'accord ?
native_language_example: None of that between us, okay?

meaning: 'not standing' or (idiomatic) 'doesn't hold up / makes no sense' depending on context
additional_notes: Literally relates to standing (debout). In sentences with tenir (tenir debout), the negative phrase "ne ... pas debout" or colloquial "pas debout" means "doesn't hold up" or "isn't coherent/credible" (e.g., an argument or story). With a person, "je ne tiens pas debout" means "I can't stand up" (physically unsteady/tired/drunk). Informal speech often drops "ne": "ça tient pas debout". Can be used for physical inability or to say something is nonsensical.
target_language_example: Son excuse ne tient pas debout, je n'y crois pas.
native_language_example: His excuse doesn't hold up, I don't believe it.

meaning: 'didn't ask (someone) to...'; used to say you did not request or tell someone to do something.
additional_notes: Appears after a negated perfect or simple verb (ne ... pas + demander) when followed by an infinitive (de + infinitive or directly infinitive depending on pronouns). Common in speech with subject + pronoun: Je ne lui ai pas demandé de venir = I didn't ask him/her to come. Informal spoken French often drops the 'ne' (Je t'ai pas demandé...).
target_language_example: Je ne t'ai pas demandé de m'attendre.
native_language_example: I didn't ask you to wait for me.

meaning: not say
additional_notes: Used with negation (ne ... pas) to indicate not saying something or inability/prohibition to say something. Depending on context it can mean 'do not say' (imperative/advice), 'you must not say' (prohibition), or 'cannot say' (unable/unwilling to say). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped (e.g. « Peut pas dire ! »).
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas dire la vérité maintenant.
native_language_example: I cannot say the truth right now.

meaning: not to say that / doesn't mean that
additional_notes: Used to negate or qualify a previous statement: 'Je ne dis pas que...' or in spoken French often shortened to 'pas dit que' after a negation (e.g. 'C'est pas dit que...') meaning 'it's not certain/it's not guaranteed that...'. Common in conversation to express doubt or to avoid a strong assertion.
target_language_example: C'est pas dit que nous partions demain.
native_language_example: It's not certain that we'll leave tomorrow.

meaning: not at all
additional_notes: Common negative intensifier used to strongly negate a statement or to reassure someone. Often follows 'ne' in full negation (e.g., 'ça ne me gêne pas du tout') but in spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped (e.g., 'Ça me gêne pas du tout'). Can be used alone as a short reply to mean 'no, not at all.'
target_language_example: Merci pour l'aide — pas du tout, c'était un plaisir.
native_language_example: Thanks for the help — not at all, it was a pleasure.

meaning: not yet
additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened up to now but is expected or possible in the future. Often appears in negative constructions with ne ... pas encore (spoken French may drop ne). Can be used in questions and statements.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas encore mangé.
native_language_example: I haven't eaten yet.

meaning: 'not finish' or 'not end' (negation of finir)
additional_notes: Used with an auxiliary (ne... pas) or informal 'pas' after a verb to negate finishing/ending something or to express a fear/wish that a situation will not end a certain way. In speech the 'ne' is often dropped (e.g. 'Je veux pas...'). Can mean 'not finish' (complete) or 'not end up' (result/ending).
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas finir comme ça.
native_language_example: I don't want to end up like that.

meaning: not it
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: pas makes the verb negative, and le is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" or "him." In standard French, this usually appears as part of ne ... pas le + verb, as in ne pas le faire ("not do it"). In everyday speech, ne is often dropped: je veux pas le savoir.
target_language_example: Je ne peux pas le croire.
native_language_example: I can't believe it.

meaning: 'not read' (negation of 'lu', the past participle of 'lire').
additional_notes: Used in spoken and written French to say someone did not read something. Often appears in contracted spoken forms: 't'as pas lu' (tu as pas lu) instead of the standard negation 'tu n'as pas lu'. It requires an auxiliary (avoir) in passé composé: 'tu n'as pas lu le journal'. 'Pas lu' by itself is not a complete verb phrase — include the subject and auxiliary or an object to be clear.
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas lu ce message ?
native_language_example: You haven't read this message?

meaning: quite a lot / not bad (depends on context).
additional_notes: Common, versatile phrase. Literally 'not bad'. Used praiseably to mean 'not bad' or 'pretty good' (e.g., C'est pas mal = That's not bad). Can also mean 'quite a lot' or 'a fair amount' in questions or statements (e.g., Ça fait pas mal ? = Does that make quite a difference?/Is that a lot?). In casual speech the 'ne' is dropped: 'pas mal' instead of 'ne ... pas mal'.
target_language_example: C'est pas mal, ton dessin.
native_language_example: Your drawing is not bad.

meaning: quite a lot of / many / a fair amount of
additional_notes: Informal-to-neutral expression used to indicate a considerable quantity or number. Often used before a noun (pas mal de + noun). Can be used with countable or uncountable nouns. Tone is conversational but acceptable in writing; not very formal. Equivalent to 'beaucoup de' but slightly less emphatic or more colloquial.
target_language_example: Il y a pas mal de gens au marché aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: There are quite a lot of people at the market today.

meaning: quite a lot of things / many things
additional_notes: Informal-to-neutral expression meaning 'a good number of things' or 'many things'. Used both in positive sentences (we talked about many interesting things) and to say something explains a lot. Can modify nouns: 'pas mal de + noun'. Tone is casual but common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Il y avait pas mal de choses à voir au musée.
native_language_example: There were quite a lot of things to see at the museum.

meaning: 'not necessary that' / 'it's not necessary that...'
additional_notes: Used to say that something is not required or doesn't need to happen. Often appears in constructions with il n'est pas nécessaire que + subjunctive (e.g. il n'est pas nécessaire que tu viennes). In spoken or shortened contexts you may see just pas nécessaire (informal). When a subject follows, French typically uses a full phrase (il n'est) before pas nécessaire que.
target_language_example: Il n'est pas nécessaire que tu m'attendes.
native_language_example: It's not necessary that you wait for me.

meaning: not open the (feminine noun) — a negative construction used when saying someone cannot or will not open something (la + feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but the negative pattern "ne ... pas + ouvrir + la" (or colloquially without "ne"). The feminine article "la" indicates the object is feminine (e.g. la boîte, la fenêtre). Use "ne...pas" for formal negatives; in spoken French people often drop "ne": "Tu peux pas ouvrir la fenêtre ?" Conjugate the verb (peux, peut, pouvons) and place object after the verb.
target_language_example: Elle ne veut pas ouvrir la porte.
native_language_example: She doesn't want to open the door.

meaning: 'don't cry' (a short, direct negative command or comment).
additional_notes: A concise negative phrase combining 'pas' (not) with the infinitive 'pleurer' (to cry). It can be used as a command (spoken to someone) or as a remark (e.g., telling someone not to complain or to stop crying). Tone depends on context — can be gentle, firm, or dismissive. For a polite command use 'ne pleure pas' (tu) or 'ne pleurez pas' (vous).
target_language_example: Allez, pas pleurer — on va trouver une solution.
native_language_example: Come on, don't cry — we'll find a solution.

meaning: 'not ready' (plural, masculine or mixed groups).
additional_notes: Used after a conjugated être (ils ne sont pas prêts, nous ne sommes pas prêts, etc.). For feminine plural use pas prêtes. Can refer to people or things (e.g., plans) when plural. Common negative construction: ne ... pas + adjective; in informal speech the 'ne' is often dropped (Ils sont pas prêts).
target_language_example: Ils ne sont pas prêts.
native_language_example: They are not ready.

meaning: 'could not' (negation of 'pouvoir' in the passé composé).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was unable to do something in the past. Formed with ne ... pas + avoir (a) + past participle 'pu' (from pouvoir). In speech, the 'ne' is often dropped: Elle n'a pas pu → Elle a pas pu or Elle n'a pas pu (formal). Followed by an infinitive or action: pas pu venir, pas pu faire, pas pu marcher.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas pu venir hier soir.
native_language_example: I couldn't come last night.

meaning: 'not that' or the negation part of 'not that' in subordinate clauses (short for "ne ... pas que" or used in spoken negation before 'que')
additional_notes: In French spoken and written negative sentences, 'pas qu'' appears when negating verbs that introduce a subordinate clause with 'que' (or when 'ne' is dropped in informal speech). Often you see full forms like "je ne crois pas que..." or the spoken contraction "je crois pas qu'...". It does not stand alone; it must be followed by a clause starting with 'que' (or 'qu'' before a vowel). Used to express doubt, denial, or to negate a fact. Remember that subjunctive is often required after 'je ne crois pas que' in formal writing/speaking.
target_language_example: Je crois pas qu'elle vienne ce soir.
native_language_example: I don't think that she'll come tonight.

meaning: not that
additional_notes: This sequence is usually part of a larger negative structure rather than a fixed expression by itself. After a verb, *ne ... pas que* introduces a clause: *je ne savais pas que...* = 'I didn't know that...'. In *il n'y a pas que...*, it means 'not only' or 'not just'.
target_language_example: Je ne pensais pas que ce serait si difficile.
native_language_example: I didn't think it would be so difficult.

meaning: No way / absolutely not (used to refuse something strongly).
additional_notes: Used in informal and neutral contexts to refuse or forbid an action. Often appears as 'Pas question de + infinitive' (No way of + verb) or 'Il n'est pas question que + subjunctive' (It is out of the question that...). In spoken French 'Il n'est pas' is frequently shortened to 'Il est pas' or omitted entirely: 'Pas question...'.
target_language_example: Pas question d'ouvrir la porte ce soir.
native_language_example: No way I'm opening the door tonight.

meaning: Not a standard fixed French phrase; a sequence of words that can appear in larger grammatical contexts. Literally 'step/negation who/that is' (depending on sense of 'pas'). Often a fragment or result of word order in a clause, e.g. part of 'qui n'est pas' if words are reordered or in elliptical speech.
additional_notes: This sequence by itself is uncommon as a set phrase. 'Pas' is primarily the negation particle ('not') but can also mean 'step'. 'Qui est' means 'who/which is'. If you encounter 'pas qui est' it is likely a fragment, typo, or part of a clause where words have been split for emphasis or in poetry. For standard negation with a relative clause use 'qui n'est pas' ('which is not'). Literal translation of the sequence is possible but context-dependent.
target_language_example: Ce n'est pas qui est responsable ; c'est plutôt le système.
native_language_example: It is not who is responsible; it is rather the system.

meaning: didn't answer (to); did not reply to
additional_notes: Negative past participle construction: 'pas' negates the verb 'répondu' (past participle of répondre). Usually appears with a subject and an indirect object introduced by 'à' (e.g. 'Je n'ai pas répondu à son message' = I didn't reply to his message). Word order often: subject + ne/n' + auxiliary (avoir) + pas + répondu + à + object. In spoken French, 'ne' is often dropped: 'J'ai pas répondu à...'
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas répondu à ton e‑mail hier.
native_language_example: I didn't reply to your email yesterday.

meaning: haven't answered my (…)
additional_notes: This is a fragment used to say someone did not reply to the speaker's question or message. It combines negation (ne ... pas) + past participle (répondu) + indirect object introduced by à and a possessive (ma = my, feminine noun follows). In full: «Tu n'as pas répondu à ma question.» Informal spoken forms often drop 'ne' (T'as pas répondu à ma...). Use 'mon' before masculine nouns (pas répondu à mon...), 'mes' for plural, 'vos'/'votre' for formal/plural.
target_language_example: Tu n'as pas répondu à ma question hier.
native_language_example: You didn't answer my question yesterday.

meaning: 'not trust' or 'not rely on' (used with à: ne pas se fier à ...).
additional_notes: Negative form of the reflexive verb se fier (à) meaning 'to trust' or 'to rely on'. Typically appears as "ne pas se fier à" + noun/pronoun. Common in warnings or advice: "Il ne faut pas se fier à..." = "Don't trust/...". Use à before the person/thing you don't trust (se fier à quelqu'un/quelque chose).
target_language_example: Il ne faut pas se fier aux apparences.
native_language_example: Don't trust appearances.

meaning: Not so fast; slow down; hold on.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to slow down, stop, or take things one at a time. Can be literal (walking/running) or figurative (rushing through actions or conclusions). Common in spoken French and can be followed by a name or phrase: "Pas si vite, [name]!"
target_language_example: Pas si vite — attends, vérifie d'abord.
native_language_example: Not so fast — wait, check first.

meaning: Don't touch (it) / Hands off.
additional_notes: Informal, strong command used to tell someone not to touch or interfere with something or someone. Often followed by the object (à + noun) or used alone as an interjection. Tone can be protective or angry.
target_language_example: Pas touche à mon téléphone !
native_language_example: Don't touch my phone!

meaning: 'not too early' or more commonly 'about time' / 'it's about time' (used to say something happened later than expected).
additional_notes: Literally 'not too early'. Often used informally to comment that something finally happened after a delay (similar to 'it's about time' or 'finally'). Can also be used more literally to say something shouldn't be done too early. Tone depends on context; often mildly impatient or relieved.
target_language_example: Ah, tu arrives enfin — pas trop tôt !
native_language_example: Ah, you're finally here — it's about time!

meaning: not to kill / can't kill (negation with the verb tuer)
additional_notes: pas is the negation particle used with verbs (ne ... pas). In spoken French, the 'ne' is often dropped, so you hear 'tu peux pas' instead of 'tu ne peux pas'. 'Pas tuer' by itself isn't a fixed phrase — it's just the verb 'tuer' (to kill) negated. Can be used literally (kill a person or animal) or figuratively (e.g. 'you can't kill an idea').
target_language_example: Tu ne peux pas tuer une idée.
native_language_example: You can't kill an idea.

meaning: not a good (one); indicates someone/something is not good at/for something
additional_notes: Used to negate that someone or something is 'a good' [noun/role/thing]. Appears before a noun (un/une) and an adjective or noun like 'danseur', 'nageur', 'amant', 'moment'. In English: 'not a good [X]'. Can modify people, activities or objects. Word order: ne ... pas un bon + noun (or pas un bon + noun phrase).
target_language_example: Il n'est pas un bon professeur.
native_language_example: He is not a good teacher.

meaning: 'not travel' or 'cannot travel' (negation of voyager).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the verb voyager (to travel) with negation. In French negation is often formed with ne ... pas around the verb: je ne peux pas voyager = I cannot travel / I can't travel. Spoken French sometimes drops the 'ne' (e.g. je peux pas voyager). Use appropriate conjugation for different subjects (je ne peux pas, tu ne peux pas, il/elle/on ne peut pas, nous ne pouvons pas, vous ne pouvez pas, ils/elles ne peuvent pas).
target_language_example: Nous ne pouvons pas voyager cet été à cause des restrictions.
native_language_example: We cannot travel this summer because of the restrictions.

meaning: 'step by step' or 'gradually'.
additional_notes: Used to describe doing something slowly, carefully, or progressively. Can appear at the start, middle, or end of a sentence. Common in instructions, encouragement, or reflections about progress.
target_language_example: On va résoudre ce problème pas à pas.
native_language_example: We'll solve this problem step by step.

meaning: 'no problem' / 'no worries' / 'it's fine'.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to say that something is not an issue. Common in spoken and informal contexts but also acceptable in neutral situations. Can respond to a request, confirm agreement, or say you can handle something.
target_language_example: Tu peux m'aider cet après‑midi ? — Pas de problème.
native_language_example: Can you help me this afternoon? — No problem.

meaning: no problem; don't worry; it's okay.
additional_notes: Informal, friendly phrase used to reassure someone or to say that something is not an issue. Equivalent to "no worries" or "no problem" in English. Commonly used alone or after a statement (e.g., "Pas de souci, je m'en occupe.").
target_language_example: Pas de souci, je peux t'aider ce soir.
native_language_example: No problem, I can help you tonight.

meaning: 'what is happening in' (used in questions: Que se passe-t-il dans ... ? = What's happening in ...?)
additional_notes: This appears inside the common question formula "Que se passe-t-il dans + [place/thing] ?". Literally: "What happens it in...", but in natural English: "What's happening in..." or "What's going on in...". Use to ask about events, situations, or someone's thoughts (e.g. "dans sa tête"). Formality: neutral; common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Que se passe-t-il dans la rue ?
native_language_example: What's happening in the street?

meaning: 'happen with' or 'be going on with' (used in questions/statements about what is occurring concerning someone or something).
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase "Qu'est-ce qui se passe avec... ?" meaning "What's going on with... ?" Used to ask about someone's situation, condition, or events involving a person or thing. Passe is from the verb se passer (to happen); avec means with. The verb agrees with qu' (impersonal construction: "Qu'est-ce qui se passe...").
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce qui se passe avec ton ordinateur ?
native_language_example: What's going on with your computer?

meaning: have a
additional_notes: Commonly appears in different constructions: 'il se passe un ...' = 'there is/there is happening a ...' (something is happening); 'passer un bon moment/bon week-end' = 'to spend/have a good time, to have a good weekend'; 'Passe un ...' used as an imperative (informal) = 'Have a ...' (e.g. Passe un agréable Noël = Have a pleasant Christmas). The exact English verb (have, spend, happen) depends on context.
target_language_example: Passe un bon voyage !
native_language_example: Have a good trip!

meaning: to place an order (for goods or services).
additional_notes: Commonly used when ordering in shops, restaurants, online, or by phone. Conjugate passer as needed (e.g., je passe commande, nous avons passé commande). Often followed by what is being ordered (passer commande de + item) or by a direct object.
target_language_example: Je vais passer commande d'une nouvelle imprimante aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I'm going to place an order for a new printer today.

meaning: to go past or pass in front of (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used when moving so that you go by the front of a place or person. Can refer to walking, driving, or being located in front of something briefly. Also used figuratively (e.g., 'to pass someone' in a race or ranking) depending on context.
target_language_example: Nous allons passer devant le musée en revenant.
native_language_example: We'll pass in front of the museum on the way back.

meaning: to go from (something) — used when indicating a change from one state/thing to another (followed by a noun or noun phrase).
additional_notes: A contraction of 'passer de' + definite article 'le' (du = de + le). Often appears before a masculine singular noun: 'passer du froid au chaud' (to go from cold to warm). It can express physical movement, a transition in time, change of state, or switching topics. Requires an object (what you're moving from). For feminine nouns you'd see 'passer de la' (or 'de l'' before a vowel).
target_language_example: Il a dû passer du chômage à un emploi stable pour subvenir aux besoins de sa famille.
native_language_example: He had to go from unemployment to a steady job to provide for his family.

meaning: to spread the word; to tell people / pass on a message.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to inform others or pass along a short message. Commonly used in commands or reports (Fais/Faites passer le mot = 'Spread the word'). Can be followed by a recipient (Je lui ai fait passer le mot = I passed the message to him). Neutral register.
target_language_example: Fais passer le mot à tout le monde.
native_language_example: Spread the word to everyone.

meaning: to pass the time; to kill time (do something to make time go by).
additional_notes: Used to describe activities done to occupy oneself while waiting or to make time feel shorter. Neutral register; can mean harmless, casual activities (reading, watching TV, chatting). Often appears in questions (Que fais-tu pour passer le temps ?) or short phrases (Pour passer le temps).
target_language_example: Je regarde des vidéos pour passer le temps.
native_language_example: I watch videos to pass the time.

meaning: to come to mind; to occur to (someone).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say that a thought, idea or possibility briefly appears in someone's mind. Often used impersonally with constructions like 'il m'est/te/leur/etc. passé par la tête' or in colloquial speech 'ça m'a/te/etc. passé par la tête'. Can describe fleeting or sudden thoughts.
target_language_example: Il m'est passé par la tête de passer par la tête cette idée.
native_language_example: The idea of passing through my mind came to me.

meaning: to make a few (phone) calls; to call a few people.
additional_notes: Short for "passer quelques coups de fil". Used when you want to say you'll place a few telephone calls. Common in spoken French. Can take "de fil" (singular) or colloquial plural "de fils", but "de fil" is standard. Often followed by "de fil" explicitly, but understood from context if omitted.
target_language_example: Je vais passer quelques coups de fil cet après-midi.
native_language_example: I'll make a few phone calls this afternoon.

meaning: to spend or go through (a period of time or an event); to experience or have (something).
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (une + noun). Common constructions: passer une nuit/soirée/journée/bonne journée/bonne soirée = to spend/have a (night/evening/day). Can also mean to let something go by (J'ai vu passer une souris = I saw a mouse run by) or to undergo an event (passer une audition = to take/attend an audition). Context determines whether it means 'spend', 'have', 'go by', or 'take'.
target_language_example: Nous allons passer une semaine tranquille à la campagne.
native_language_example: We are going to spend a quiet week in the countryside.

meaning: to move on; to get past something and focus on something else.
additional_notes: Used when telling someone (or oneself) to stop dwelling on a situation, problem, relationship, or emotion and start focusing on something new. Common in everyday speech. Often followed by context or nothing: e.g. 'passer à autre chose' (move on) or 'passer à autre chose dans la vie'.
target_language_example: Après cette dispute, il vaut mieux passer à autre chose.
native_language_example: After that argument, it's better to move on.

meaning: 'to miss' or 'to fail to take advantage of' (an opportunity); can also mean 'to pass by' something without noticing it.
additional_notes: Common idiom. Often used with chance/opportunity/occasion (une occasion, une chance, l'amour, etc.) to say you missed it. Can be literal (pass by something) but most often idiomatic: passer à côté de quelque chose = ne pas profiter de, rater. Typical constructions: passer à côté de + noun. Context tells whether it's literal or figurative.
target_language_example: Il a passé à côté d'une grande opportunité en refusant le poste.
native_language_example: He missed a great opportunity by refusing the job.

meaning: would happen (in questions) — literally 'would happen it' (formal inversion).
additional_notes: Used in hypothetical questions with the impersonal verb se passer (to happen). Formed by conditional tense + subject-verb inversion for questions (Que se passerait-il ? = What would happen?). Common in hypothetical or speculative situations. Equivalent informal word order: Qu'est-ce qui se passerait ?
target_language_example: Que se passerait-il si on supprimait les voitures du centre-ville ?
native_language_example: What would happen if we removed cars from the city center?

meaning: pass (something) to
additional_notes: Used as an imperative or polite request (vous form) meaning to hand something to someone or to convey/send something (a greeting, a message, news). Followed by the direct object: a physical object (le journal), a greeting (le bonjour), a message (le mot) or a phrase (le secteur au peigne fin = sweep the area thoroughly). In spoken requests you may also hear 'passe-moi' (tu form) for informal situations.
target_language_example: Passez le sel, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Pass me the salt, please.

meaning: 'to spend' (time) + definite article (feminine noun), as in 'spent the (day/night)'.
additional_notes: Passer (quelque chose) + la + [période] = to spend (that period). In examples, 'passé la journée', 'passé la nuit' mean 'spent the day/night'. The verb agrees with subject (J'ai passé, Il a passé). The article 'la' matches a feminine time-word (la journée, la nuit). For other periods you may see 'le' (le matin), 'la' (l'après-midi sometimes 'l'après-midi'), or no article with plurals.
target_language_example: Nous avons passé la soirée au restaurant.
native_language_example: We spent the evening at the restaurant.

meaning: 'spent' or 'took' (used with a noun to say someone spent time doing something, took an exam, celebrated an event, or physically moved a body part).
additional_notes: A construction using the past participle passé + a possessive (son/sa/ses) + noun. Meaning depends on the noun: e.g. passé son permis = took (and passed) his/her driving test; passé son enfance = spent his/her childhood; passé son bras = put/placed his/her arm; passé son tour = skipped his/her turn; passé son anniversaire = spent his/her birthday. Context and the following noun determine translation. Gender/number of the possessive changes with the noun (son/sa/ses).
target_language_example: Il a passé son diplôme l'année dernière.
native_language_example: He took his diploma (completed his degree) last year.

meaning: spent/ended up spending three (units of time).
additional_notes: Used with a time period (jours, semaines, mois, heures, ans) to say someone spent three of those units doing something. Common structure: passé + number + time unit (here 'trois'). In these examples 'passé' is the past participle of 'passer' and indicates duration experienced. Often followed by a prepositional phrase: en/à/derrière + noun (e.g. en mer, à Islamabad, en plein air, derrière les barreaux).
target_language_example: Elle a passé trois semaines à apprendre le français.
native_language_example: She spent three weeks learning French.

meaning: 'happen/occur at the (place)' — used in past tense to ask or say what happened at a specific location.
additional_notes: This is a contracted part of expressions like «s'est passé à l'hôpital/à l'école/à l'hôtel». It appears in past-tense questions and statements (e.g. «Comment ça s'est passé à l'école ?», «Que s'est-il passé à l'hôtel ?», «Ça s'est bien passé à l'école ?»). The full structure is usually «(Ça/)Que s'est-il passé à + definite article + lieu» or «(Ça) s'est bien passé à + lieu». The contraction "à l'" happens before a vowel (l'école, l'hôpital, l'hôtel).
target_language_example: Comment ça s'est passé à l'hôpital hier ?
native_language_example: How did it go / What happened at the hospital yesterday?

meaning: "the past and" — used to link 'past' with another noun (e.g., the present) or in expressions like 'forget the past and...'.
additional_notes: Directly combines passé (the past) with et (and). Common in phrases that contrast or connect the past with something else (le présent, demain, etc.) and in imperatives telling someone to 'forget the past and ...' — e.g., "Oublie le passé et concentre-toi sur demain." Grammatically straightforward and widely used in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Oublie le passé et regarde vers l'avenir.
native_language_example: Forget the past and look toward the future.

meaning: 'patron a' — likely 'the boss has' or 'boss at' depending on context; 'patron' = boss/employer, 'a' = has or at.
additional_notes:
This appears to be two words: 'patron' (masculine noun meaning boss, employer, owner, or regular customer in other contexts) and 'a' (third-person singular present of avoir = 'has', or the preposition 'à' meaning 'at/to'). Without context it's ambiguous. Common uses:
- patron a (with 'a' = has): e.g. 'Le patron a dit...' = 'The boss has said...' or 'The boss said...'
- patron à (with accent) as part of a phrase: e.g. 'un patron à l'écoute' = 'a boss who listens'.
For learners: remember the pronunciation differs between 'a' (has) and 'à' (at), though both are pronounced the same. Pay attention to articles and agreement: 'le patron', 'la patronne' (female boss).
target_language_example: Le patron a signé le contrat.
native_language_example: The boss has signed the contract.

meaning: insult meaning 'poor idiot' or 'stupid fool'.
additional_notes: Vulgar and offensive. 'Con' is a strong insult (roughly 'idiot'/'asshole' depending on tone) and 'pauvre' here is sarcastic or contemptuous — not expressing pity. Used to insult or mock someone. Avoid in polite company.
target_language_example: Arrête de parler comme ça, pauvre con !
native_language_example: Stop talking like that, you stupid fool!

meaning: to pay a lot (for something); to be expensive.
additional_notes: Used to say that something costs a high price or that someone has to spend a lot of money. Often appears as payer cher + (quelque chose) or on its own with context (Il a payé cher = He paid dearly/paid a lot). Can also be used figuratively (payer cher pour = suffer consequences).
target_language_example: J'ai dû payer cher ce livre rare.
native_language_example: I had to pay a lot for that rare book.

meaning: 'the most' + country (used to say a country is the most ... of/in ...)
additional_notes: Used to form superlative descriptions of countries (e.g. le pays le plus riche = the richest country). Usually followed by an adjective and optionally 'du monde', 'd'Europe', 'en matière de...', etc. Agreement: adjective that follows must agree in gender/number with 'pays' (masculine singular).
target_language_example: La France est le pays le plus visité d'Europe.
native_language_example: France is the most visited country in Europe.

meaning: 'paid it' or 'paid the (feminine noun)'.
additional_notes: Combination of the past participle payé and the feminine definite article la. In examples it refers to paying a specific feminine noun (e.g. la facture). When using a direct object pronoun (e.g. l' for la), French often places it before the verb: je l'ai payé (not *je payé la). In spoken or informal written French you may see 'je l'ai payé' pronounced/typed like 'je l'ai payé' (written correctly) — avoid separating the pronoun and auxiliary incorrectly. Agreement: with avoir, past participle agrees with a preceding direct object pronoun (Elle l'a payée if 'la' refers to a feminine noun and the pronoun l' precedes the verb).
target_language_example: Tu as payé la facture ?
native_language_example: Did you pay the bill?

meaning: death penalty; capital punishment.
additional_notes: Refers to the legal sentence of execution for certain crimes. Commonly used in debates (être pour/contre la peine de mort = to be for/against the death penalty). Formal term.
target_language_example: Je suis contre la peine de mort.
native_language_example: I am against the death penalty.

meaning: while; during the time that (introduces an action happening at the same time as another).
additional_notes: Used to link two simultaneous actions. Can introduce an ongoing action in the past, present or imperative contexts. Often interchangeable with 'alors que' or 'tandis que' in some contexts, but 'pendant que' emphasizes duration. Not used for single time points (use 'lorsque' or 'quand' for some cases).
target_language_example: Je cuis le dîner pendant que tu ranges la table.
native_language_example: I'll cook dinner while you clear the table.

meaning: to hang on (to) someone — figuratively: to cling to or fawn over someone
additional_notes: Used reflexively in examples (se pendent à) to mean people cling to or hang on someone's neck; commonly used figuratively to say fans or admirers constantly surround or fawn over a person. Can be literal (something hanging on) but here is figurative. Often appears as 'se pendre à' + 'le cou' (hang on someone's neck) or 'se pendre à quelqu'un' (cling to someone).
target_language_example: Les fans se pendent à ses lèvres pendant l'interview.
native_language_example: The fans hang on his every word during the interview.

meaning: 'wasn't thinking of' / 'didn't think about'
additional_notes: Colloquial contraction of 'ne pensais pas à' (first- or second-person imperfect). Used to say you weren't thinking about someone/something at a moment in the past or didn't remember to do something. In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped. Add an object after 'à' (e.g. 'pensais pas à toi', 'pensais pas à ça').
target_language_example: Je ne pensais pas à toi hier.
native_language_example: I wasn't thinking of you yesterday.

meaning: 'I thought that the (feminine noun) ...' — expresses a past belief about something feminine.
additional_notes: This is the imperfect form of penser (je pensais) + que + the feminine definite article la. Use it to say you believed or assumed something in the past about a feminine noun (la guerre, la réunion, la salle, la partie). For masculine nouns you'd see 'je pensais que le' or 'je pensais que l'' before a vowel. Common in explanations and apologies.
target_language_example: Je pensais que la porte était fermée.
native_language_example: I thought that the door was closed.

meaning: I thought I had told you...
additional_notes: Used to express that the speaker believed they had already told the listener to do (or not do) something. Structure: "Je pensais (que) + je vous avais dit" but here uses infinitive construction "pensais vous avoir dit de + infinitive". Common in direct addresses: polite/formal due to "vous". Often followed by an instruction or prohibition (de + verb).
target_language_example: Je pensais vous avoir dit de verrouiller la porte.
native_language_example: I thought I had told you to lock the door.

meaning: 'still think' or 'think about (someone) still'.
additional_notes: Used with a subject (je, tu, etc.) and often followed by 'à' + person/place/thing. Indicates continuing or repeated thought about someone or something (e.g. 'I still think about him/her'). Common in everyday speech. Can be combined with time phrases like 'tout le temps' (all the time) or 'de temps en temps' (from time to time).
target_language_example: Je pense encore à mes amis d'université.
native_language_example: I still think about my university friends.

meaning: don't think
additional_notes: A negated form of penser (to think). Often appears with ne ... pas around the verb: je ne pense pas (I don't think). In casual speech the 'ne' is frequently dropped, leaving pense pas (e.g. 'N'y pense pas' = 'Don't think about it'). Use appropriate subject or object pronouns when needed (e.g. 'Je ne le pense pas' = 'I don't think that').
target_language_example: N'y pense pas, ça ira mieux demain.
native_language_example: Don't think about it, it'll be better tomorrow.

meaning: I think that it's
additional_notes: Shortened form of the clause "je pense que c'..." where c' is the contracted form of "ce" before a vowel (c'est, ce sera, etc.). Used to introduce your opinion about something. In full sentence you usually say "Je pense que c'est..." — here the entry shows the part up to the contracted pronoun. Common in speech and writing.
target_language_example: Je pense que c'est une bonne idée.
native_language_example: I think it's a good idea.

meaning: I think I
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a clause meaning 'I think that I...'. In French you often drop the 'e' in 'je' before a vowel (j') and follow with a verb: pense que j'ai (I think I have), pense que j'ai compris (I think I understood). Use 'je pense que' to express an opinion or belief. The full phrase is 'je pense que j'' when the next word begins with a vowel or silent h.
target_language_example: Je pense que j'ai besoin de repos.
native_language_example: I think I need some rest.

meaning: 'I think that we have' (used to express the speaker's opinion about something involving 'we have' + past/participial phrase).
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular of penser (je pense) followed by a clause with nous avons. Commonly used to give an opinion about something that concerns 'we' (e.g., we had, we lost, we found). The following words complete the idea (e.g., eu = had, perdu = lost, trouvé = found). In spoken French, je is sometimes dropped: pense que nous avons → (Je) pense que nous avons...
target_language_example: Je pense que nous avons besoin d'aide.
native_language_example: I think that we have/need help.

meaning: 'I think that we need' or 'I think we have need of'.
additional_notes: Common phrase used to express the speaker's opinion about a need for something. Usually followed by de + noun (de celles-là, de plus de glace) or by an infinitive (de faire une pause). In spoken French the full subject 'je' and verb 'pense' can be contracted into 'je pense' or shortened in speech, but the structure remains: pense que + nous avons besoin + de + [thing/infinitive].
target_language_example: Je pense que nous avons besoin de plus de temps pour finir.
native_language_example: I think that we need more time to finish.

meaning: 'I think that everyone' or 'I think that everything' depending on context (here: 'everyone').
additional_notes: The phrase begins with 'Je pense que...' (I think that...) followed by 'tout le monde' (everyone). In the examples, 'tout' is part of 'tout le monde' meaning 'everyone'. Use 'Je pense que tout le monde...' to give an opinion about people in general. If 'tout' stands alone it can also mean 'everything'—context matters.
target_language_example: Je pense que tout le monde devrait écouter avant de juger.
native_language_example: I think that everyone should listen before judging.

meaning: think that you need (someone/something); expresses belief about someone's need
additional_notes: This is part of a larger clause introduced by verbs like penser. Grammatically it combines penser que (to think that) + tu as besoin (you need). In full sentences you usually specify what is needed: pense que tu as besoin de + noun/infinitive (e.g. pense que tu as besoin de repos / pense que tu as besoin d'aide). Use tu for informal 'you' (singular). For polite/formal or plural use vous: pense que vous avez besoin.
target_language_example: Je pense que tu as besoin de repos.
native_language_example: I think that you need rest.

meaning: 'to think of/about' (used to ask for or refer to someone's opinion about a person, thing, situation, idea, etc.).
additional_notes: Used when asking or expressing opinions (often in questions or uncertain/negative contexts). Distinct from penser à (to think about/remember) and penser + infinitive (to intend to). Common constructions: Qu'est-ce que tu penses de... / Je ne sais pas quoi penser de....
target_language_example: Je ne sais pas trop quoi penser de tout ça.
native_language_example: I don't really know what to think of all this.

meaning: 'to plan/intend to do' or 'to think of doing' (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb: penser + faire quelque chose. It expresses intention or a tentative idea (e.g. Je pense faire = I'm thinking of doing / I intend to do). Can be more or less certain depending on context and tone. For stronger intention use 'prévoir de' or 'avoir l'intention de'.
target_language_example: Je pense faire un voyage en Espagne cet été.
native_language_example: I'm thinking of taking a trip to Spain this summer.

meaning: to think about; to have in mind
additional_notes: Used with a person, thing, or idea you have in mind: penser à quelqu’un / à quelque chose. It can also be used before an infinitive to mean thinking of doing something or remembering to do something, depending on context. Compare with penser de, which usually asks for an opinion about something.
target_language_example: Vous devriez penser à votre avenir.
native_language_example: You should think about your future.

meaning: 'you think that he/it...' (second person singular, informal)
additional_notes: This is the informal present-tense form of penser (tu penses) followed by 'qu'il' (that he/it). Use when speaking to one person you know well (tu). In writing or formal speech, use 'pensez qu'il' for vous. The clause that follows expresses what you believe about a male person or a masculine noun (il).
target_language_example: Tu penses qu'il viendra demain ?
native_language_example: Do you think that he/it will come tomorrow?

meaning: you think that... / do you think that...? (informal 'tu' form, followed by c'… = c'est)
additional_notes: This is the familiar 2nd-person singular (tu) form of penser + que + c' (short for c'est). Used to state or question someone's opinion about something. In spoken French c'est is often reduced to c' before a vowel or in casual speech. Common in questions: "Tu penses que c'est... ?"
target_language_example: Tu penses que c'est une bonne idée ?
native_language_example: Do you think that's a good idea?

meaning: 'do you think that.../you think that...'
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used to ask or state someone's opinion about a situation or what something means. 'Tu penses que...' = 'Do you think that...?' or 'You think that...'. 'Ça' refers to 'that' or 'it' (something just mentioned or obvious from context). Can appear with different subjects (Tu penses que, Est-ce que tu penses que, Je pense que...).
target_language_example: Tu penses que ça va être difficile ?
native_language_example: Do you think that it's going to be difficult?

meaning: 'what do you think of this' (formal/plural).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask someone's opinion about a specific feminine noun (cette + noun). Often appears as part of the full question 'Que pensez-vous de cette ... ?' Formal or polite (using vous). For informal/singular use say 'Que penses-tu de cette ... ?'. You can replace 'cette' with 'ce' or 'ces' depending on the gender/number of the noun.
target_language_example: Que pensez-vous de cette peinture ?
native_language_example: What do you think of this painting?

meaning: 'you (formal/plural) think that it/this is...' or 'do you think that...?'
additional_notes: Common informal/conversational fragment used to introduce someone's opinion or a question about something previously mentioned. 'Pensez' is the second-person plural (vous) form of 'penser'. The full phrase is usually 'vous pensez que c'est...' or 'si vous pensez que c'est...'. Can be used as a statement or a question (intonation or inversion/est-ce que).
target_language_example: Vous pensez que c'est dangereux ?
native_language_example: Do you think it's dangerous?

meaning: 'to lose consciousness; to faint (become unconscious)'.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone becoming unconscious suddenly (fainting, passing out) or losing awareness (e.g., after an injury or shock). Common synonym: "s'évanouir". Often used with a subject: Il/Elle a perdu connaissance; past infinitive: avoir perdu connaissance. Can be followed by 'à cause de' or 'après' to give a reason/time (e.g., 'perdre connaissance à cause de la chaleur').
target_language_example: Après avoir appris la nouvelle, elle a commencé à se sentir mal et a perdu connaissance.
native_language_example: After hearing the news, she began to feel ill and lost consciousness.

meaning: 'to lose sight of' or 'to lose contact with' (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used both literally (physically losing sight of someone or something) and figuratively (losing contact or losing track of someone, an idea, or progress). Commonly followed by a person or thing (e.g., 'perdre de vue quelqu'un/quelque chose').
target_language_example: Après le déménagement, j'ai un peu perdu de vue mes voisins.
native_language_example: After the move, I lost touch with my neighbors a bit.

meaning: 'to waste time' or 'to lose time' (doing something that is not a good use of time).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is spending time inefficiently or doing something pointless. Can be reflexive in context (e.g., 'Je perds mon temps' = I'm wasting my time). Often used with an infinitive: 'perdre du temps à + infinitive' (e.g., 'Il perd du temps à attendre'). Also appears in negative imperatives and advice: 'Ne perds pas ton temps...'.
target_language_example: Je ne veux pas perdre du temps à expliquer encore une fois.
native_language_example: I don't want to waste time explaining it again.

meaning: 'to lose hope' or 'to give up hope'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to stop believing that a good outcome is possible. Common in advice and encouragement. Often appears in negative imperatives (Ne ... pas perdre espoir) meaning 'don't lose hope.'
target_language_example: Il ne faut jamais perdre espoir.
native_language_example: You must never lose hope.

meaning: 'to lose face' — to be humiliated or lose respect/reputation.
additional_notes: Used when someone is embarrassed, publicly shamed, or their social standing is damaged. Often about reputation, honor, or dignity. Common in contexts of failure, scandal, or public exposure. Equivalent to English idiom 'lose face'.
target_language_example: Il a menti pour ne pas perdre la face devant ses collègues.
native_language_example: He lied so he wouldn't lose face in front of his colleagues.

meaning: 'to lose one's mind' / 'to go crazy' or 'to lose control/forget caution'.
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression. Used both for temporary strong emotion (acting irrationally because of love, anger, fear, excitement) and for more extreme 'go mad' senses. Context determines intensity: can be playful (Je perds la tête pour elle = I'm crazy about her) or serious (Il a perdu la tête = he lost his mind / went mad). Not typically literal (not about physically losing one's head).
target_language_example: Si tu commences à perdre la tête, rappelle-toi pourquoi tu fais cela.
native_language_example: If you start to lose your head, remember why you're doing this.

meaning: 'to lose one's life' — a polite or neutral way to say 'to die' (usually used for someone who has died, often in an accident, war, crime, etc.).
additional_notes: Used in formal or written contexts (news reports, official statements) to report a death. Often refers to an accidental, violent, or otherwise notable death. It's more formal/neutral than mourir and less blunt than 'être tué' when death is caused by someone else. Can be used with a subject: «Il a perdu la vie», with a noun: «Plusieurs personnes ont perdu la vie», or in passive-like constructions in reports.
target_language_example: Plusieurs personnes ont perdu la vie lors de l'accident.
native_language_example: Several people lost their lives during the accident.

meaning: to lose control emotionally or become overwhelmed; to panic or be unable to think clearly
additional_notes: Informal idiom literally meaning 'to lose the pedals' (from bicycle imagery). Used when someone becomes confused, panicked, or loses composure in a situation; often temporary. Register: colloquial/informal.
target_language_example: En voyant autant de monde, il a perdu les pédales et n'a plus su quoi dire.
native_language_example: Seeing so many people, he lost it and didn't know what to say anymore.

meaning: to lose patience; to stop being patient
additional_notes: Used when someone becomes impatient or irritated after waiting or dealing with something for too long. Often appears with a subject (je/tu/il/elle/on/nous/etc.) and sometimes with 'avec' to indicate who you're losing patience with: perdre patience avec quelqu'un. Can be used in both literal waiting contexts and figurative situations (e.g., with someone's behavior).
target_language_example: J'ai commencé à perdre patience après une heure d'attente.
native_language_example: I began to lose patience after an hour of waiting.

meaning: 'to lose one's way' (both literally and figuratively).
additional_notes: Commonly used for physically getting lost (not knowing the route) and figuratively (losing direction in life, a project, or a conversation). Verb phrase: perdre (to lose) + son chemin (one's way). Conjugate perdre; for past you can say j'ai perdu mon chemin or je me suis perdu(e). Use with subject pronouns: Il perd son chemin, Nous avons perdu notre chemin.
target_language_example: Nous avons perdu son chemin en sortant du village, il faut demander ; on a perdu son chemin.
native_language_example: We lost our way when leaving the village; we need to ask — we've lost our way.

meaning: 'to waste one's time'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is spending time on something useless or unproductive. Can be inflected for different subjects (perdre mon/ton/son temps). Common in everyday speech; tone can be neutral or mildly critical depending on context.
target_language_example: Marie lui a dit de ne pas lui faire perdre son temps.
native_language_example: Marie told him not to waste his time.

meaning: lost in his/her/their (thoughts); deeply absorbed in one's thoughts
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun like pensées (thoughts). Used to describe someone who is distracted or mentally elsewhere. The possessive 'ses' matches the person’s belongings/thoughts (plural). Often appears with être or participles (est, semblait, était, perdu) and can start a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Il est perdu dans ses pensées.
native_language_example: He is lost in his thoughts.

meaning: 'lost' (used with uncountable nouns introduced by 'du' = some/of the)
additional_notes: This is the past participle 'perdu' (lost) used with the partitive article 'du' before an uncountable noun (e.g. du poids = some weight, du temps = some time). Commonly appears as "avoir perdu du + [noun]" to mean "to have lost some [noun]" (lost weight, lost time). The exact English translation depends on the noun: "perdre du poids" = "lose weight", "perdre du temps" = "lose time/waste time."
target_language_example: Il a perdu du temps à attendre le bus.
native_language_example: He lost some time waiting for the bus.

meaning: driver's license; official permit to drive a vehicle.
additional_notes: Refers to the official document/qualification that allows someone to drive. Often shortened to "permis" in spoken French. Used with verbs like "avoir" (to have), "obtenir" (to obtain), or "passer" (to take the driving test). Can refer to different vehicle categories (car, motorcycle) depending on context.
target_language_example: Elle a enfin eu son permis de conduire hier.
native_language_example: She finally got her driver's license yesterday.

meaning: 'person' used with a preposition/part of a phrase — depends on context (e.g. 'a person about/about whom', 'a person in/visible on', or part of a ratio 'one person in/among')
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed idiom by itself. 'Personne' means 'person' and 'sur' means 'on/about/among' — together their meaning changes with the rest of the sentence:
- judging someone by something: "juger une personne sur sa tenue" = judge a person by their outfit.
- identifying someone in an image: "la personne sur cette photo" = the person in/on this photo.
- part of a ratio/ statistic: "une personne sur trois" = one person out of three / one in three.
Use surrounding words to determine the exact translation.
target_language_example: Une personne sur cinq préfère travailler de chez elle.
native_language_example: One person in five prefers to work from home.

meaning: an elderly person / older adult.
additional_notes: Polite, neutral term used to refer to someone who is old. Common in everyday speech and formal contexts (e.g., public signs, announcements). 'Âgée' agrees in gender/number (une personne âgée, des personnes âgées).
target_language_example: Il a aidé une personne âgée à traverser la rue.
native_language_example: He helped an elderly person cross the street.

meaning: used in questions to ask 'how many people do/have you…' (lit. 'people have you').
additional_notes: This phrase appears in questions with Combien de personnes + as-tu + past participle or infinitive. It asks for a number of people involved (invited, seen, killed, etc.). Remember past participles agree in gender/number with preceding direct object (e.g., «Combien de personnes as-tu invitées ?»). Word order: Combien de personnes + as-tu + verb.
target_language_example: Combien de personnes as-tu invitées à la réunion ?
native_language_example: How many people did you invite to the meeting?

meaning: a waste of time
additional_notes: Used to say that something is pointless or not worth the time spent. Can be used neutrally or with irritation. Common in spoken and written French. Often preceded by adjectives or exclamations (Quelle perte de temps !, une vraie perte de temps).
target_language_example: Faire ces démarches maintenant serait une perte de temps.
native_language_example: Doing these steps now would be a waste of time.

meaning: grandchild (child of one's son or daughter).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a grandchild. Singular: petit-enfant (m or f). Plural: petits-enfants. Can be used for both grandsons and granddaughters; to specify gender use petit-fils (grandson) or petite-fille (granddaughter). Informal/affectionate alternatives in speech include « petitou », « p'tit », or simply « mon petit » in context.
target_language_example: Le premier petit-enfant de la famille est né en avril.
native_language_example: The family's first grandchild was born in April.

meaning: grandson.
additional_notes: Family term for the male child of one's son or daughter. Used in possessive phrases (mon petit-fils, votre petit-fils). Plural = petits-fils. Hyphenated in French.
target_language_example: Mon petit-fils va à l'école primaire.
native_language_example: My grandson goes to elementary school.

meaning: boyfriend (romantic male partner).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a woman's or a person's male romantic partner. Feminine equivalent: petite amie. Can be used in informal and neutral contexts. Often preceded by possessive (mon/son) or by an article (un/le).
target_language_example: Elle présente son petit ami à ses amis.
native_language_example: She introduces her boyfriend to her friends.

meaning: euphemism for 'toilet' or 'a small place/spot' (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a polite/euphemistic way to say 'toilet' (e.g. Je vais au petit coin = I'm going to the loo). In other contexts, especially with descriptions of places (e.g. 'ce petit coin'), it means 'a small corner/spot' (a cozy little place). Listen to context to choose the right translation.
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je vais au petit coin.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I'm going to the restroom.

meaning: boyfriend (informal)
additional_notes: Common, casual way to say 'boyfriend' in French. Used for a romantic male partner; feminine equivalent is 'petite copine' or more commonly 'petite amie' / 'copine'. Can be used for young people or adults in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Elle a présenté son petit copain à ses amis.
native_language_example: She introduced her boyfriend to her friends.

meaning: 'a little (something)', used before a noun to mean a small amount or brief action (e.g. a little drink, a quick boost, a short fix).
additional_notes: Informal expression often followed by a noun to indicate a small quantity or brief action: e.g. 'petit coup de fil' (a quick phone call), 'petit coup de main' (a little help), 'petit coup de fatigue' (a short bout of tiredness), 'petit coup de blanc' isn't standard — use context. 'Coup' here means a sudden action or blow; combined with 'petit' it softens to a minor or brief occurrence.
target_language_example: Je vais faire un petit coup de fil à Marie.
native_language_example: I'm going to make a quick phone call to Marie.

meaning: 'little finger' (literally) — used idiomatically in several expressions (see notes).
additional_notes: Literally means the smallest finger on the hand (pinky). Idiomatically appears in phrases: "Mon petit doigt me l'a dit" (an informal way to say 'I have a hunch' or 'rumor has it'); "Mon petit doigt" alone can imply 'I have a feeling' or be a teasing shorthand; "faire quelque chose de son petit doigt" can mean 'to be able to do something easily' or be a boast (often informal); "montrer le petit doigt" (show the little finger) is used in expressions meaning to give a little and then be taken advantage of — here it suggests that if you show weakness or give a small thing, others will laugh or exploit you. Context matters: many uses are idiomatic and informal.
target_language_example: Mon petit doigt me dit qu'il va pleuvoir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: My little finger tells me it's going to rain today. (i.e. I have a hunch)

meaning: breakfast (the morning meal).
additional_notes: Common French term for the first meal of the day. Often used with verbs like prendre (prendre son petit déjeuner = have breakfast) or préparer (préparer le petit déjeuner). 'Petit' here is part of the fixed expression; not literally 'small breakfast'.
target_language_example: Nous prenons notre petit déjeuner à 8 heures.
native_language_example: We have our breakfast at 8 o'clock.

meaning: the early morning (just after dawn; very early hours)
additional_notes: Used to describe the very early hours of the day, often before or around sunrise. Common in expressions like 'partir au petit matin' (leave very early) or 'faire la fête jusqu'au petit matin' (party until the early morning). Not formal or slang—neutral everyday French.
target_language_example: Ils sont rentrés au petit matin après la soirée.
native_language_example: They came back in the early morning after the party.

meaning: a small bread roll; a bun
additional_notes: Commonly used in France to mean a single small loaf or roll eaten at breakfast or with a meal. More often you will hear "un petit pain" or simply "pain"; regional terms include "petit pain" and "petit pain au lait" (milk roll). Plural: "petits pains". Use with an article: "un petit pain", "des petits pains".
target_language_example: Je voudrais un petit pain, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I would like a bread roll, please.

meaning: part of the expression "petit à petit" meaning 'little by little' or 'gradually' (when used alone, incomplete).
additional_notes: Alone, "petit à" is incomplete; the full common phrase is "petit à petit" or "petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid" meaning gradually/step by step. You may also see "petit à petit" followed by a verb (e.g. "petit à petit, il comprend"). Use the full repeated form for correct, natural French.
target_language_example: Petit à petit, elle apprend le français.
native_language_example: Little by little, she is learning French.

meaning: granddaughter.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the daughter of one's child. Feminine noun; singular form is 'petite-fille', plural 'petites-filles'. With possessives: ma petite-fille, sa petite-fille, votre petite-fille. Can also mean a young girl in some contexts but most commonly 'granddaughter'.
target_language_example: Ma petite-fille vient ce week-end.
native_language_example: My granddaughter is coming this weekend.

meaning: girlfriend
additional_notes: Used to refer to a female romantic partner. Can be used in informal and neutral contexts. The literal components mean 'small/young' (petite) + 'female friend' (amie) but together they mean 'girlfriend'. For a male partner, use 'petit ami'.
target_language_example: Il présente sa petite amie à ses parents.
native_language_example: He introduces his girlfriend to his parents.

meaning: girlfriend (informal).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for a female romantic partner. 'Petite' here is diminutive/affectionate and doesn't necessarily refer to size or age. Used in casual speech; for formal contexts you can say 'ma compagne' or 'ma petite amie' (both also common). Masculine equivalent: 'petit copain' or 'petit ami'.
target_language_example: Ma petite copine est venue me voir ce week-end.
