additional_notes: Often used for events or situations. With subjects like ça, quelque chose, or qu'est-ce qui, it usually means "to happen" or "to occur." It can also describe how something goes or unfolds, depending on context.
target_language_example: Quelque chose vient de se passer.
native_language_example: Something just happened.

meaning: to do without; to be able (or not) to go without something or someone.
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun introduced by de (se passer de quelque chose / de quelqu'un). Can express necessity (cannot do without: ne pas pouvoir se passer de) or dismissiveness (can easily do without). Common in both formal and informal contexts. Example contexts: personal needs, services, habits. Conjugates reflexively (je me passe de, tu te passes de, il/elle se passe de, nous nous passons de, vous vous passez de, ils/elles se passent de).
target_language_example: Les gens modernes ne peuvent se passer de voitures.
native_language_example: Modern people cannot do without cars.

meaning: to complain (about something or someone).
additional_notes: Pronominal verb: always appears with a reflexive pronoun (je me plains, tu te plains, il/elle se plaint, nous nous plaignons, vous vous plaignez, ils/elles se plaignent). Can be followed by de + noun or que + clause to indicate what one complains about (se plaindre de quelque chose / se plaindre que ...). Common in everyday and formal contexts (e.g., customer service).
target_language_example: Il ne fait que se plaindre de son travail.
native_language_example: He does nothing but complain about his job.

meaning: 'to be' or 'to feel' (used to describe someone's state or condition); can also mean 'to fare' or 'to do' (how someone is doing).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb used to talk about health, mood, or general condition. Common constructions: "se porter bien/mal" (to be well/ill), "se porter mieux" (to get better). Often appears with an adverb or adjective. Conjugate with the subject (e.g., "je me porte", "il se porte"). Not used for carrying objects (use "porter" without se). Can be used in formal and informal contexts depending on phrasing.
target_language_example: Se porter bien est important après une maladie ; je veux me porter mieux.
native_language_example: Being well is important after an illness; I want to get better.

meaning: to be possible (rare, formal/literary; reflexive construction used to indicate that something can or cannot happen)
additional_notes: Very uncommon in modern spoken French. More typical alternatives: pouvoir (il peut), cela se peut, être possible. 'Se pouvoir' occurs in fixed or archaic phrases (e.g. « ça ne se peut pas ») and in literary/registered contexts. Use with caution—learners will rarely need it.
target_language_example: Il ne se peut pas que cela se pouvoir ainsi.
native_language_example: It cannot be that this can be so.

meaning: 'to take' (reflexive) — part of many idiomatic constructions with varied meanings depending on context (e.g. to consider oneself, to get/hit oneself, to be fooled, to get carried away, to end up).
additional_notes: A flexible reflexive form of prendre used only within larger expressions or constructions. Meaning depends on what follows or context: se prendre pour (to consider oneself/pretend to be), se prendre une claque (to get slapped), se prendre au jeu (to get carried away), se prendre (quelque chose) (to get/receive something). Conjugates like prendre but with reflexive pronouns: je me prends, tu te prends, il/elle se prend, nous nous prenons, vous vous prenez, ils/elles se prennent. Alone it is often incomplete; check the rest of the phrase to determine sense.
target_language_example: Il va se prendre une surprise s'il pense que tout est facile.
native_language_example: He will get a surprise if he thinks everything is easy.

meaning: 'to remember' or 'to recall' (reflexive form).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object or with 'de' + noun/pronoun (both are common in speech: se rappeler quelque chose or se rappeler de quelque chose). Indicates the act of bringing something back to mind. Conjugates like a reflexive verb (je me rappelle, il se rappelle). Context and preposition use can vary by region and register.
target_language_example: Il a des difficultés à se rappeler les noms.
native_language_example: He has difficulty remembering names.

meaning: 'to go' or 'to get to' (to travel/arrive somewhere); also 'to surrender' or 'to give oneself up' in another sense.
additional_notes: Common pronominal verb with two main uses: 1) movement: se rendre (à/au/à la/chez) + place = to go/ travel/ get to a place (e.g., se rendre au travail, se rendre à Boston). 2) surrender: se rendre = to give oneself up/surrender (used in military, police or informal contexts). The presence of a destination preposition (à/au/à la/chez) usually indicates the movement meaning; context and tone determine the surrender meaning. Conjugates with reflexive pronouns (je me rends, tu te rends, il/elle se rend, nous nous rendons, vous vous rendez, ils/elles se rendent) and past participle agrees when used pronominally with être (elle s'est rendue).
target_language_example: Combien de temps faut-il pour se rendre à Boston ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to get to Boston?

meaning: to stick together, support one another (especially in difficult times).
additional_notes: Idiomatic reflexive expression meaning to unite and help each other. Used for friends, family, coworkers, or communities facing challenges. Not literal (you don't actually squeeze elbows). Often appears with phrases like il faut / c'est le moment de / on doit.
target_language_example: C'est le moment de se serrer les coudes.
native_language_example: It's time to stick together.

meaning: 'to use' (something) or 'to make use of' (also 'to help oneself to' in certain contexts).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb construction: se servir de + noun. Use de before the thing being used (je me sers de mon téléphone). Can also mean 'to help oneself to' (e.g. «Servez‑vous» = 'Help yourself'). Conjugates like servir but reflexive: je me sers, tu te sers, il/elle se sert, nous nous servons, vous vous servez, ils/elles se servent.
target_language_example: Elle aime se servir de son téléphone pour prendre des notes.
native_language_example: She likes to use her phone to take notes.

meaning: to remember; to recall (something).
additional_notes: Reflexive verb: used with de when followed by a noun or pronoun (se souvenir de quelque chose / de quelqu'un). Conjugated with être in compound tenses (e.g., je me suis souvenu(e)). Commonly followed by an object introduced by de (je me souviens de toi). Can be followed by an infinitive to mean 'remember to' in negative or certain contexts (e.g., souviens‑toi de fermer la porte).
target_language_example: Il éprouve des difficultés à se souvenir des noms.
native_language_example: He has difficulty remembering names.

meaning: 'where is my...?' (used to ask the location of something you own)
additional_notes: This is the combination of the reflexive verb se trouver (to be located) and a possessive mon (my). In questions you can invert or use 'Où est mon...' instead; both are natural. Use mon before masculine singular nouns (or before any singular noun starting with a vowel sound). To ask about someone, word order is the same: 'Où se trouve mon ami ?' Formal/neutral register.
target_language_example: Où se trouve mon portefeuille ?
native_language_example: Where is my wallet?

meaning: to be located; to be found
additional_notes: Commonly used to say where someone or something is: se trouver quelque part = to be / be found somewhere. With a noun object, it can also mean to find or get something for oneself, as in se trouver un travail or se trouver un appartement. In the location sense, it is usually not translated literally as 'to find oneself'.
target_language_example: Mon livre doit se trouver quelque part dans la chambre.
native_language_example: My book must be somewhere in the room.

meaning: 'see each other at' or 'meet at' (used to say where you'll meet someone).
additional_notes: Common informal way to say you'll meet someone at a place or time. Often used in the impersonal/plural form "On se voit à..." meaning "We'll see each other/See you at..." Can be followed by a location (l'école, la réunion) or a time expression (mon retour). Verb is reflexive (se voir = to see each other).
target_language_example: On se voit à la gare à 18 heures.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the station at 6 PM.

meaning: to shake one's head (usually to say 'no' or show disapproval).
additional_notes: Common physical gesture: moving the head from side to side. Can indicate refusal, disagreement, disbelief, or disapproval. Use with subject: je secoue la tête, il a secoué la tête. For nodding 'yes' use 'hocher la tête'.
target_language_example: Elle secoue la tête quand elle n'est pas d'accord.
native_language_example: She shakes her head when she disagrees.

meaning: 'it seemed that' or 'seemed like'.
additional_notes: Used to express an impression, appearance, or belief about something (often with impersonal il + semblait que). Can be followed by a clause introduced by que. When referring to the speaker's impression use 'Il me semblait que...' ('It seemed to me that...'). The verb 'sembler' is regular and here in the imperfect tense ('semblait').
target_language_example: Il me semblait que tu étais déjà parti.
native_language_example: It seemed to me that you had already left.

meaning: 'it seems that all the / it seems like the whole...'
additional_notes: This looks like an incomplete fragment rather than a fixed phrase. It combines the verb 'sembler' (to seem) + 'que' (that) + 'tout le...' (all the / the whole...). You will usually see a complete sentence like 'Il semble que tout le monde...' (It seems that everyone...) or 'Il semble que tout le projet...' (It seems that the whole project...). Remember to include a subject (e.g. 'il' or a noun) and finish 'tout le...' with an appropriate noun (monde, projet, monde, personnel, etc.).
target_language_example: Il semble que tout le monde soit déjà parti.
native_language_example: It seems that everyone has already left.

meaning: 'seems a' / 'appears a' (used before an adjective or noun phrase meaning someone/something appears to be ...)
additional_notes: Formed from the verb sembler (to seem/appear) plus the indefinite article un. In many examples the article is followed by an adjective (e.g., 'un peu fatigué' = 'a little tired') or a noun phrase. More commonly you will see 'semble' used with adjectives without 'un' (e.g., 'Il semble fatigué'), but 'semble un peu ...' is a frequent pattern to soften a judgement ('seems a little ...'). Use with subject pronouns: 'Il semble un peu ...', 'Ça me semble ...'.
target_language_example: Cette décision me semble un peu risquée.
native_language_example: This decision seems a little risky to me.

meaning: 'common sense' (basic practical judgment or good sense).
additional_notes: Used to refer to practical, everyday judgment that most people are expected to have. Often appears in negative constructions (manquer de sens commun / être dépourvu de sens commun) to criticize someone's poor judgment. Can be used generally (Le sens commun) or about a person.
target_language_example: Il lui manque du sens commun quand il traverse sans regarder.
native_language_example: He lacks common sense when he crosses without looking.

meaning: the meaning of this/that (thing); 'sens' = meaning, 'de ce' = of this/that
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the meaning or sense of something mentioned (a word, gesture, paragraph, etc.). 'Ce' agrees with a masculine demonstrative noun (le mot, le geste, le paragraphe). For feminine nouns you'd say 'sens de cette…'. Common in questions: 'Quel est le sens de ce… ?' or statements: 'Je ne crois pas que tu comprennes le sens de ce mot.'
target_language_example: Quel est le sens de ce geste ?
native_language_example: What is the meaning of this gesture?

meaning: the meaning of this/that (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state what something (a feminine noun) means or signifies. 'Sens' = meaning, direction, or sense depending on context; here it refers to 'meaning'. 'Cette' agrees with a feminine noun (cette image, cette phrase, cette lettre). Use 'le sens de ce' before masculine nouns (ce livre).
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas le sens de cette phrase.
native_language_example: I don't understand the meaning of this sentence.

meaning: a sense of humor; the ability to appreciate or express humor.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone's capacity to find things funny or to make others laugh. Can be positive (Il a un grand sens de l'humour) or ironic/critical (Vous avez un curieux sens de l'humour). Often used with verbs like avoir (avoir le sens de l'humour) or in questions (Où est ton sens de l'humour ?) to suggest someone is not being funny.
target_language_example: Elle n'a pas le sens de l'humour quand on plaisante.
native_language_example: She doesn't have a sense of humor when we joke.

meaning: 'feel now' or 'I now feel' (indicates a change to the current feeling/state)
additional_notes: Used to say that one's feelings or state have changed compared with before. 'Sens' is from the verb 'se sentir' (to feel) in the first person singular ('je me sens'). 'Désormais' means 'from now on' or 'now/anymore' and emphasizes the new situation. Common in sentences like 'Je me sens désormais...' followed by an adjective (en sécurité, en confiance, sûr(e) de moi, etc.).
target_language_example: Je me sens désormais plus calme.
native_language_example: I now feel calmer.

target_language_multi_word_term: se sentir en / me sens en
meaning: 'to feel (in a certain state)'. Used with adjectives/nouns introduced by en (e.g. en sécurité, en forme).
additional_notes: This is the reflexive verb se sentir followed by en + noun/adjective phrase to describe how someone feels: physical or emotional states (en sécurité, en forme, en confiance...). Use the appropriate reflexive pronoun (je me sens, tu te sens, il se sent...). Not all adjectives require en (e.g. je me sens heureux), but many common states use en + noun/adjective. In the example 'Comment tu te sens en toi-même ?' the meaning is 'How do you feel about yourself/inside?'.
target_language_example: Je me sens en confiance quand je parle en public.
native_language_example: I feel confident when I speak in public.

meaning: 'I feel that we/people will...' (expression of a present feeling or intuition about a future event involving 'on' = we/people/one).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like s'entendre, s'amuser, se marrer to express a gut feeling or expectation about how things will go. 'Je sens' = 'I feel/I have a sense'; 'qu'on' contracts 'que' + 'on' (we/people/one). Often followed by 'va' + infinitive to talk about a future occurrence (e.g., 'je sens qu'on va s'entendre' = I feel we'll get along). Informal to neutral register depending on the verb (e.g., 'se marrer' is more informal).
target_language_example: Je sens qu'on va bien s'amuser ce week-end.
native_language_example: I have a feeling we'll have a great time this weekend.

meaning: 'feel so' — used to intensify how someone feels (e.g. 'I feel so good').
additional_notes: Used after a reflexive verb se + sentir (je me sens) to strengthen the adjective that follows (bien, seul, stupide, etc.). In correct French the order is usually 'je me sens si + adjective'. Be careful: 'tu sens si bon' is incorrect — for smelling good you'd say 'tu sens si bon' is colloquial/awkward; better: 'tu sens tellement bon' or 'tu sens si bon' is uncommon; for 'you smell good' use 'tu sens bon' or 'tu sens très bon'. 'Si' here means 'so' (degree), not 'if'.
target_language_example: Je me sens si heureux aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I feel so happy today.

meaning: 'feel so' or 'feel very' (used after 'je me sens')
additional_notes: Typically appears as 'je me sens tellement ...' where 'tellement' intensifies an adjective or adverb describing how someone feels (bien, mal, mieux, jolie, stupide, etc.). Use with reflexive verb 'se sentir' (je me sens, tu te sens…). 'Tellement' = 'so/very' and emphasizes degree or emotion.
target_language_example: Je me sens tellement fatigué aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I feel so tired today.

meaning: 'feel always' — used with 'je/tu/il se' etc. to say you always feel a certain way (e.g. 'I always feel...').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but the combination of the verb se sentir (me sens = I feel) plus toujours (always). Use with an adjective: Je me sens toujours fatigué(e). Remember to agree the adjective in gender and number (fatigué for masculine, fatiguée for feminine). For other subjects change the reflexive pronoun: Tu te sens toujours..., Il/Elle se sent toujours..., Nous nous sentons toujours..., Ils/Elles se sentent toujours....
target_language_example: Je me sens toujours content après une promenade.
native_language_example: I always feel happy after a walk.

meaning: 'will feel better' (informal future, 2nd person singular)
additional_notes: This is the future tense of 'se sentir' (to feel) used with 'tu' (you). It expresses reassurance or expectation that someone's physical or emotional state will improve. Often appears with time words (demain, après) or conditions (si...). In spoken French the subject pronoun 'tu' is usually included: 'tu te sentiras mieux.'
target_language_example: Tu te sentiras mieux si tu te reposes.
native_language_example: You will feel better if you rest.

meaning: 'will be a' (future tense + indefinite article)
additional_notes: Combines the future tense of être (sera = he/she/it/one will be) with the indefinite article un (a). Used to say that someone or something will become or be regarded as a particular thing or quality in the future (Ce sera un honneur = It will be an honor). Agreement: 'un' changes to 'une' for feminine nouns (ce sera une bonne idée).
target_language_example: Ce sera un bon souvenir.
native_language_example: It will be a good memory.

meaning: 'When I grow up, I want...' (used to introduce what someone wants to be/do in the future).
additional_notes: Literally built from 'Quand/Lorsque je serai grand' ('when I will be big') + 'je veux' ('I want'). Commonly used by children to state future ambitions. In natural French you usually say 'Quand je serai grand, je voudrai' less often; however 'je veux' is frequently used in spoken or simple sentences. You can replace 'grand' with 'âgé' or use 'être' + profession/role.
target_language_example: Quand je serai grand, je veux devenir médecin.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to become a doctor.

meaning: I'll be there in (a) ... — used to tell someone when you'll arrive, followed by a time unit.
additional_notes: This phrase uses the future tense (je serai = I will be) + 'là' (there) + 'dans' (in) + 'une' (a/an) before a time expression (minute, heure, demi-heure, seconde, etc.). Replace 'une' with the correct article/number when needed (e.g. 'dans 10 minutes', 'dans une heure', 'dans une demi-heure'). Common for short waiting times.
target_language_example: Je serai là dans une demi-heure.
native_language_example: I'll be there in half an hour.

meaning: when you are grown up
additional_notes: Second-person singular future of être + grand; used to talk about something that will happen or be allowed once the person is an adult (or older). Common in questions about future plans (Que feras-tu quand tu seras grand ?) or in conditional/permission contexts (Tu pourras... quand tu seras grand). Can be used figuratively for 'older/mature'.
target_language_example: Quand tu seras grand, tu pourras choisir ta carrière.
native_language_example: When you are grown up, you will be able to choose your career.

meaning: 'will be (in)'. (Future tense of 'être' + preposition 'en' meaning 'in' or part of a phrase like 'en sécurité' = 'will be safe')
additional_notes: This is the second-person plural (vous) future form of être (vous serez) followed by en. Often appears in set phrases such as 'en sécurité' (safe) or 'en retard' (late). Alone 'serez en' needs a following noun or adjective phrase (e.g. 'serez en sécurité', 'serez en mesure de...'). Use with vous (formal you or plural you).
target_language_example: Vous serez en sécurité pendant votre voyage.
native_language_example: You will be safe during your trip.

meaning: will be released (passive future tense)
additional_notes: Passive construction: être (au futur simple) + participe passé 'libérés' (agreeing in gender/number with the subject). Used to say that people or things will be freed or set free in the future. Subject usually plural (e.g., 'les otages'). You can change tense/person by conjugating 'être' (je serai libéré, il sera libéré, nous serons libérés).
target_language_example: Les prisonniers seront libérés la semaine prochaine.
native_language_example: The prisoners will be released next week.

meaning: 'will not be' (negative future tense of être or other verbs in third-person plural)
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial contraction of the future negative construction 'ne ... pas' with a third-person plural verb (ils/elles seront pas). In written or formal French, the full form is 'ne seront pas'. Used to say that 'they' or 'things' will not be something in the future. Can appear with other verbs in the future (e.g. 'ne seront pas' or colloquially 'seront pas').
target_language_example: Ils seront pas prêts demain.
native_language_example: They will not be ready tomorrow.

meaning: Not a standard French phrase; literally 'snake is'.
additional_notes: This exact two-word string is not a fixed expression in French. If you meant 'le serpent est...' it would simply be the start of a sentence meaning 'the snake is...'. Check whether you intended: • 'serpent' (snake) on its own, • 'serpent est' as part of a longer sentence (e.g. 'Le serpent est venimeux' = 'The snake is venomous'), or • a different phrase like 'serpent à sonnettes' (rattlesnake) or an idiom such as 'être une serpente' (rare/dated). For beginners: use 'le serpent' for 'the snake' and conjugate être (est) to describe it: 'Le serpent est grand.'
target_language_example: Le serpent est dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The snake is in the garden.

meaning: to shake someone's hand; to give a handshake.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression for greeting, agreement, or formality. Used with indirect object (serrer la main de quelqu'un) or with reflexive/reciprocal forms (se serrer la main = to shake each other's hands). Can be polite or formal (Veuillez vous serrer la main = Please shake hands).
target_language_example: Il a refusé de leur serrer la main.
native_language_example: He refused to shake their hands.

meaning: to grit one's teeth; to endure something painful or difficult without complaining.
additional_notes: Literally 'to tighten the teeth.' Used when someone suppresses pain, frustration, or discomfort and keeps going. Can be used for physical pain or for tolerating unpleasant situations. Common in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Elle a dû serrer les dents pendant toute la réunion.
native_language_example: She had to grit her teeth throughout the meeting.

meaning: Not a fixed phrase. Appears to be the adjective/past participle 'serré' followed immediately by the feminine direct-object pronoun 'la' (her/it), which in correct French would normally be contracted or reordered (see notes). On its own it suggests 'tight/held/squeezed her/it' but is not standard surface word order.
additional_notes: This sequence is typically ungrammatical in standard French as written: object pronouns normally precede the verb (e.g. 'je l'ai serrée') or attach to an imperative (e.g. 'serre-la' written with a hyphen). If intended as adjective + noun, agreement and order differ ('la robe est serrée'). If intended as verb + pronoun in affirmative imperative, write 'serre-la' (with hyphen). If intended after a past participle, the pronoun precedes the auxiliary: 'Je l'ai serrée.'
target_language_example: Serre-la vite, elle est serrée.
native_language_example: Hold her/it quickly, it's tight.

meaning: 'secret service' or 'intelligence service/agency' (a government organization that gathers intelligence and conducts covert operations).
additional_notes: Used to refer to secret/intelligence services (e.g., domestic security, foreign intelligence, spy agency). Often used in plural (les services secrets) when speaking generally, but can be singular to refer to a specific service. Not necessarily the proper name of an organization (e.g., la CIA).
target_language_example: Le service secret a intercepté des communications suspectes pendant l'enquête.
native_language_example: The secret service intercepted suspicious communications during the investigation.

meaning: completely alone; feeling utterly isolated (emotionally or physically).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is totally alone or feels isolated — often emotional. Can be literal (no one else present) or figurative (feeling nobody understands you). Common in expressions like « je me sens seul au monde » (I feel completely alone).
target_language_example: Après la dispute, je me sentais seul au monde.
native_language_example: After the argument, I felt completely alone.

meaning: alone together; one-on-one (private, between two people).
additional_notes: Used to say that two people will speak privately, without others present. Similar to English 'one-on-one' or 'alone together'. Often used before or during a request to speak privately: Je veux parler seul à seul avec toi. Can be used as a short command/statement: 'Seul à seul.'
target_language_example: Peux-tu rester dehors ? Je dois parler à Marc seul à seul.
native_language_example: Can you stay outside? I need to speak to Marc one-on-one.

meaning: 'only' or 'just' + 'you' (object pronoun) — used to say the action is limited to the person 'you'.
additional_notes: seulement = 'only/just'. te is the unstressed direct or indirect object pronoun for 'you' (singular, familiar). Together they often appear after a verb (e.g. Je veux seulement te parler = I just want to talk to you). Word order: verb + (seulement) + te. The tense of the verb can change (veux, voulais, etc.).
target_language_example: Je veux seulement te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I just want to tell you the truth.

meaning: so/so much that; to the extent that; (in negative context) 'that much' or 'that well'.
additional_notes: Has two main uses: 1) as a conjunction meaning 'so... that' to introduce a result (Il faisait chaud, si bien que nous sommes partis). 2) in conversational/negative contexts as a comment about degree, often in shortened questions or negatives meaning 'that much/that well' (Je ne le connais pas si bien que ça = I don't know him that well). Tone can be neutral or informal depending on context.
target_language_example: Je l'apprécie, mais pas si bien que ça.
native_language_example: I like him, but not that much / not that well.

meaning: 'so happy' or 'very happy'.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize strong happiness. 'Si' here means 'so' (intensifier). Commonly followed by 'de' + infinitive/nom (content de vous voir), 'pour' + quelqu'un (happy for someone), or 'que' + subjunctive (content que tu sois venu). Can be used alone as an exclamation: 'Je suis si content.'
target_language_example: Je suis si content pour toi, tu as réussi l'examen !
native_language_example: I'm so happy for you, you passed the exam!

meaning: 'so happy to' (used by a female speaker)
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb or clause to say you are very happy about something. 'Si' intensifies 'heureuse' (very). Because 'heureuse' is the feminine form, the speaker is female (male speakers would say 'si heureux de'). Followed by 'de' plus an infinitive or 'de' + clause (e.g., 'de te voir', 'de savoir que…').
target_language_example: Je suis si heureuse de te voir aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: I am so happy to see you today.

meaning: so little / so few (to a small extent).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a small amount, degree, or extent. Placed before nouns (si peu de ...) or before adjectives/adverbs (si peu photogénique / si peu sûrs) to mean 'so little' or 'so hardly'. Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Nous savons si peu de choses sur ce sujet.
native_language_example: We know so little about this subject.

meaning: if only (expressing a wish or regret).
additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish, regret, or longing for something that is not (or may not be) true. Often followed by a clause in the imperfect, conditional, or past conditional depending on time and likelihood. Can be used alone as a short exclamation: «Si seulement!»
target_language_example: Si seulement je pouvais partir demain.
native_language_example: If only I could leave tomorrow.

meaning: if it is not / unless / except if
additional_notes: Commonly used in conditional phrases. Can introduce a negative condition (if it is not the case) or make an exception (except if). Often followed by pas (not) or que (only). Equivalent to English 'if it isn't', 'unless', or 'except that'.
target_language_example: Je viendrai, si ce n'est que je suis malade.
native_language_example: I'll come, unless I am sick.

meaning: so/that being the case; if that's the case.
additional_notes: Formal/literary expression used to introduce a conclusion or consequence based on what was just stated. Equivalent to 'dans ce cas' or 'si c'est le cas'. You may see it in written or formal spoken French; less common in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Si fait, nous devrons organiser une réunion urgente.
native_language_example: If that's the case, we will need to organize an urgent meeting.

meaning: 'if ever' / 'in case (that)'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conditional or hypothetical situation; often adds emphasis or a sense of precaution (English: 'if ever', 'if by any chance', 'in case'). Common in spoken and written French. Can appear alone at the start of a sentence or inside one. Not formal/slang—neutral.
target_language_example: Si jamais tu as besoin d'aide, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If ever you need help, call me. (In case you need help, call me.)

meaning: a polite hedge: 'if I may say (so)' or 'so to speak'.
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a remark, show modesty, or indicate the speaker is aware the phrasing may be imperfect. Common in formal or polite contexts but also in everyday speech. Equivalent to 'if you will' or 'so to speak'.
target_language_example: C'est, si je puis dire, une solution élégante.
native_language_example: It is, if I may say so, an elegant solution.

meaning: a polite formula meaning 'if I may' or 'if I may be allowed to (say)'.
additional_notes: Used to politely introduce an opinion, suggestion, or question. Often followed by permettre (e.g. 'si je puis me permettre') and usually appears at the start of a sentence. Formal/polite register; can be omitted in casual speech. English equivalents: 'if I may', 'if I may say so', or 'with your permission'.
target_language_example: Si je puis me permettre, je vous conseillerais de relire ce paragraphe.
native_language_example: If I may, I would advise you to reread this paragraph.

meaning: 'if necessary' / 'if needed'.
additional_notes: Used to indicate something will be done only if required. Can appear at start of a sentence (Si nécessaire, ...), inline (faire X si nécessaire), or alone as a short response meaning 'if needed' or 'if necessary.' Formality: neutral — suitable for both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je t'appellerai si nécessaire.
native_language_example: I'll call you if necessary.

meaning: if possible; preferably
additional_notes: Used to add a polite preference or wish — softens a request or condition. Often follows a time, quantity, or description (e.g., "dès demain, si possible" = "tomorrow, if possible" or "preferably tomorrow"). Common in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me rappeler ce soir, si possible ?
native_language_example: Can you call me back tonight, if possible?

si tu as besoin de quoi

target_language_multi_word_term: si tu as besoin de quoi
meaning: 'if you need anything' (informal, short for 'si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit')
additional_notes: Used to offer help or availability. Informal and conversational; often followed by an instruction (e.g. 'appelle', 'viens me voir'). Full formal version: 'si tu as besoin de quoi que ce soit'. Can be used alone as a reassurance: 'Si tu as besoin de quoi, dis-le.'
target_language_example: Si tu as besoin de quoi, appelle-moi.
native_language_example: If you need anything, call me.

meaning: used to show doubt, mild disagreement, or to accept someone's statement reluctantly ('if you say so').
additional_notes: A common conversational phrase. Can be neutral acceptance, polite doubt, or ironic/skeptical depending on tone and context. Often short and dismissive. Use with friends or in informal situations; tone conveys meaning more than grammar.
target_language_example: D'accord, si tu le dis, mais je ne suis pas convaincu.
native_language_example: Alright, if you say so, but I'm not convinced.

si vous avez besoin de quoi que

target_language_multi_word_term: si vous avez besoin de quoi que
meaning: if you need anything (at all).
additional_notes: Commonly completed as "si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit" — a polite offer of help. Used in formal and neutral contexts (vous form). Often followed by suggested contact methods (appeler, envoyer un courriel, etc.). Literal elements: 'si' = if, 'vous avez besoin de' = you need, 'quoi que ce soit' = anything at all.
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quoi que ce soit, appelez le bureau.
native_language_example: If you need anything at all, call the office.

meaning: means 'means the' or 'signifies the' (to indicate the meaning of a specific noun).
additional_notes: Used when asking or stating what something (usually a noun introduced by the feminine definite article 'la') means or signifies. Often appears in questions with 'Que signifie la ... ?' = 'What does the ... mean?' Also used in exclamations: 'Ça signifie la ...' (That means the ...). The verb 'signifier' is formal/neutral; the article 'la' agrees with a feminine noun that follows.
target_language_example: Que signifie la liberté pour toi ?
native_language_example: What does freedom mean to you?

meaning: 'otherwise' or 'if not' (followed by a clause introduced by 'le' in these examples)
additional_notes: sinon = 'otherwise' / 'if not'. In the example sentences it appears before a clause that starts with 'le' (e.g. 'le magasin sera fermé', 'le bébé va se réveiller'). Use sinon to warn about a negative consequence if something isn't done. Can appear alone (sinon + clause) without 'le' depending on sentence; here 'le' is just the definite article starting the following noun phrase.
target_language_example: Dépêche-toi, sinon le train partira sans toi.
native_language_example: Hurry up, otherwise the train will leave without you.

meaning: website (an address or location on the web).
additional_notes: Common French term for an online website. 'Internet' is often capitalized in French; you may also see 'site web' (less formal) or 'site internet' in lowercase. Used for both the site itself and sometimes its URL. Plural: 'sites Internet'.
target_language_example: J'ai trouvé l'information sur un site Internet fiable.
native_language_example: I found the information on a reliable website.

meaning: 'the site is' — a short way to describe a website (site) using the verb être (is).
additional_notes: Common structure: 'Ce site est + adjective' to give an opinion about a website (useful, horrible, great, etc.). 'Site' here means 'website'. 'Ce' (this/that) plus 'site est' = 'This site is...'. Useful for simple descriptions and reviews.
target_language_example: Ce site est très intéressant pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: This site is very interesting for learning French.

meaning: website (a collection of web pages accessible on the internet).
additional_notes: Common French term for 'website'. Often used interchangeably with 'site internet' or simply 'site'. Plural is 'sites web' or 'sites internet'. Used in formal and informal contexts; you can say 'un site web' or drop 'web' and say 'un site' when context is clear.
target_language_example: J'ai créé un site web pour mon entreprise.
native_language_example: I created a website for my business.

meaning: 'situation en' taken as a contiguous fragment is not a fixed, standalone idiom in French; it typically appears where the noun 'situation' is followed by the preposition 'en' introducing a phrase (e.g. 'situation en un clin d'œil', 'situation en main'). 'Situation' = situation/state of affairs; 'en' meaning varies by expression.
additional_notes: The input is a fragment that needs a following phrase to convey a specific meaning. Example usages: 'prendre la mesure de la situation en un clin d'œil' = quickly grasp the situation; 'avoir la situation en main' = have the situation under control. Learners should treat 'situation' as a feminine noun (la situation). 'En' is a very common preposition whose meaning depends on context and cannot be translated on its own here.
target_language_example: Elle a pris la mesure de la situation en un clin d’œil.
native_language_example: She grasped the situation in the blink of an eye.

meaning: at six o'clock every (followed by a time period, e.g. matin/soir).
additional_notes: This phrase is used with a time period (matin, soir, jours, semaines, etc.) to mean 'every morning/evening...' or 'every ... at 6:00'. In English word order it's 'at six o'clock every morning/evening.' Common structure: 'se lever à six heures tous les matins' = 'get up at 6 every morning.'
target_language_example: Il prend son café à six heures tous les matins.
native_language_example: He has his coffee at six every morning.

meaning: 'the seat is' (literal: 'seat is') — used to state something about a seat (e.g. taken, free, reserved, free of charge).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it's simply the noun siège ('seat') followed by the verb est ('is'). You'll commonly hear it in short sentences like «Ce siège est pris» (This seat is taken) or in questions with est-ce que: «Est-ce que ce siège est libre?» (Is this seat free?). Use it to describe the state or condition of a seat.
target_language_example: Est-ce que ce siège est occupé ?
native_language_example: Is this seat occupied?

meaning: 'so-called' (used to express doubt or sarcasm about a label or claim).
additional_notes: Placed before a noun or adjective to indicate that the name or description is claimed by someone but is questionable, ironic, or not accepted by the speaker. Often conveys skepticism: 'the so-called X' = 'what they call X (but I doubt/deny it)'.
target_language_example: Il est le soi-disant expert en nutrition, mais il donne de mauvaises informations.
native_language_example: He is the so-called nutrition expert, but he gives bad information.

meaning: 'oneself' (reflexive emphasis: himself/herself/oneself/themselves depending on subject).
additional_notes: Used as a reflexive pronoun for emphasis or to refer back to the subject. Appears after verbs or prepositions (faire soi-même = do oneself). Agrees in meaning with subject but form is invariable. Common in expressions like se connaître soi-même (to know oneself) or tout faire soi-même (do everything by oneself).
target_language_example: Elle a réparé la chaise soi-même.
native_language_example: She repaired the chair herself.

meaning: 'care of my' or 'take care of my' (part of expressions like prendre soin de ma ...).
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the phrase prendre soin de (quelqu'un/quelque chose) = to take care of/look after someone or something. 'Ma' is the feminine singular possessive (my). Use prendre soin de + [noun] (no preposition). For masculine singular use 'mon', plural 'mes'. Common with people (ma santé, ma fille, ma nièce) or objects (ma cravate).
target_language_example: Prends soin de ma plante pendant mon absence.
native_language_example: Take care of my plant while I'm away.

meaning: 'take care of your...' (used before a feminine noun)
additional_notes: This is part of the phrase 'Prends/Prend soin de ta ...' meaning 'take care of your ...'. Use 'Prends' (imperative tu) when addressing someone informally: 'Prends soin de ta santé' = 'Take care of your health.' The word after 'ta' must be feminine singular (ta = your, informal). For masculine nouns use 'ton' (Prends soin de ton père). For plural use 'tes'.
target_language_example: Prends soin de ta santé et repose-toi.
native_language_example: Take care of your health and rest.

meaning: intensive care (hospital unit for very sick patients).
additional_notes: Refers to the hospital department and level of medical care for critically ill or unstable patients (ICU). Often used with être: 'être en soins intensifs' = 'to be in intensive care'. Plural in French even when referring to the unit ('les soins intensifs' or simply 'soins intensifs').
target_language_example: Elle est en soins intensifs après l'accident.
native_language_example: She is in intensive care after the accident.

meaning: seventy (70).
additional_notes: French numeral for 70. Used in counting, ages, percentages, quantities, addresses, etc. Note: In standard French (France), 70 is formed as soixante-dix (literally 'sixty-ten'). In some regional varieties (e.g., Swiss, Belgian French), 70 is expressed as septante instead. Pronunciation: /swasɑ̃t dis/.
target_language_example: Il y a soixante-dix chaises dans la salle.
native_language_example: There are seventy chairs in the room.

meaning: sixty-seven (67).
additional_notes: A compound number formed from soixante (60) + sept (7). Used when stating someone's age, years, counts, or any quantity. Pronunciation note: the hyphen is often written; spoken as [swa-sɑ̃t sɛt].
target_language_example: Il a fêté ses soixante-sept ans la semaine dernière.
native_language_example: He celebrated his sixty-seventh birthday last week.

meaning: 'rising sun' or 'sunrise'; also used to refer to Japan (the Land of the Rising Sun).
additional_notes: Literally 'rising sun'. Used both for the physical sunrise (le soleil qui se lève) and figuratively as a poetic name for Japan: «le pays du soleil levant». Can appear in descriptive or poetic contexts.
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes levés tôt pour voir le soleil levant.
native_language_example: We got up early to see the rising sun.

meaning: the sun was (doing something) — past description of the sun or its state.
additional_notes: Combines soleil (the sun) with était (imperfect of être) to describe past ongoing or background states (e.g., hidden, about to set, already high). Use était for descriptions or actions in progress in the past; you will usually find another verb or adjective after it (caché, sur le point de se coucher, déjà haut).
target_language_example: Le soleil était brillant quand nous sommes partis.
native_language_example: The sun was bright when we left.

meaning: deep sleep
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is sleeping very deeply or soundly. Commonly used in everyday and literary contexts. Can follow verbs like 'être', 'être plongé dans', or 'tomber' (tomber dans un sommeil profond).
target_language_example: Après la randonnée, il est tombé dans un sommeil profond.
native_language_example: After the hike, he fell into a deep sleep.

meaning: 'we sat' or 'we are seated' (past participle construction: nous nous sommes assis = we sat down / we sat).
additional_notes: This is the first-person plural passé composé of the reflexive verb s'asseoir (nous nous sommes assis). It describes that 'we' sat down or were seated. Commonly followed by location or position (devant la cheminée, en cercle, sur un banc, là-bas). Use gender agreement when the group is all-female: nous nous sommes assises. For present tense use nous sommes assis(e)s (less common) or nous nous asseyons / nous nous sommes assis (past).
target_language_example: Après la promenade, nous nous sommes assis sur le banc du parc.
native_language_example: After the walk, we sat on the park bench.

meaning: we are lost / we got lost (we have become lost).
additional_notes: This is the past participle construction with the auxiliary être (nous sommes perdus) or the reflexive past (nous nous sommes perdus) meaning 'we got lost' or 'we are lost' depending on context. Use 'nous nous sommes perdus' to say 'we got lost' (past). Without the extra 'nous' it can be present: 'nous sommes perdus' = 'we are lost'. Can be used for being physically lost (in streets, forest) or metaphorically (lost sight of each other: 'nous nous sommes perdus de vue'). Agreement: with nous (plural) the past participle 'perdus' takes plural masculine/feminine form as needed (perdues if all female).
target_language_example: Nous nous sommes perdus en ville après le concert.
native_language_example: We got lost in the city after the concert.

meaning: we met / we encountered (past participle agreement with a feminine plural noun when used in compound past passive or with 'être').
additional_notes: This sequence combines the conjugated auxiliary verb 'sommes' (nous form of être) with the past participle 'rencontrés'. It appears in compound tenses (e.g. passé composé or in passive constructions) and requires agreement in gender/number with the subject or the preceding direct object when applicable. Example: 'Nous sommes rencontrés' = 'We met' (used when the speakers are the people who met each other; common in French to use être with certain pronominal or reciprocal verbs). If the subject is feminine plural, you might see 'sommes rencontrées'.
target_language_example: Nous sommes rencontrés au café hier.
native_language_example: We met at the café yesterday.

meaning: we are separated / we separated (we have broken up).
additional_notes: This is the past participle form used with the auxiliary être (nous sommes séparés) to say 'we are separated' or 'we broke up'. In context with reflexive se (nous nous sommes séparés) it usually means 'we separated' or 'we split up' (relationship ended). Can be used to state current status ('we are separated') or to report a past event ('we separated'). Agreement: séparés agrees in gender/number with the subject (nous sommes séparés / séparées).
target_language_example: Après des disputes constantes, nous nous sommes séparés l'année dernière.
native_language_example: After constant arguments, we separated last year.

meaning: 'we are what we' — part of the structure used to say 'we are what we (do/eat/think/etc.)'.
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase; it's the beginning of comparative sentences built as "Nous sommes ce que nous + verb" (e.g. faisons, mangeons, pensons). Literal translation is possible. Used to state identity defined by actions, habits, thoughts, etc. You'll often see the full sentence "Nous sommes ce que nous faisons/ mangeons/ pensons."
target_language_example: Nous sommes ce que nous faisons chaque jour.
native_language_example: We are what we do every day.

meaning: we are sorry
additional_notes: Plural first-person form of être + désolé(e). Used to express apology or sympathy on behalf of a group (we). In spoken English contraction "we're sorry" is common. In French you may see "nous sommes désolés" or the shorter "désolés" in informal contexts; add a gendered -e if speakers are all female (nous sommes désolées). Can be followed by de/pour + clause or by a direct address (e.g., "Nous sommes désolés, madame").
target_language_example: Nous sommes désolés pour le retard.
native_language_example: We are sorry for the delay.

meaning: are just
additional_notes: Usually appears as nous sommes juste... = 'we are just/only...'. It is used to limit or downplay what follows, as in 'just friends' or 'just farmers'. Here juste means 'only/simply', not 'fair' or 'exact'.
target_language_example: Nous sommes juste ici pour aider.
native_language_example: We're just here to help.

meaning: 'we are the' (used to describe a group as something specific)
additional_notes: This is the present-tense verb 'être' (nous sommes = we are) followed by the definite article 'les' and a noun or adjective. Use it to state a quality or identity of the group 'we' (e.g., we are the best, we are the only ones). Word order: nous sommes les + [noun/adjective]. The phrase itself isn't idiomatic — it's simply the combination of 'we are' + 'the'.
target_language_example: Nous sommes les champions de la classe.
native_language_example: We are the champions of the class.

meaning: we are here / we exist / we are present.
additional_notes: From the verb être (nous sommes) + là (here). Used literally to say 'we are present' or more figuratively to mean 'we're still here' or 'we remain' (emphasizing existence, presence, or support). Common in statements of reassurance or persistence.
target_language_example: Après toutes ces années, nous sommes là.
native_language_example: After all these years, we are still here.

meaning: we are not (plural) + noun (informal spoken form of 'nous ne sommes pas des')
additional_notes: Colloquial omission of the ne in spoken French: 'nous ne sommes pas des...' becomes 'nous sommes pas des...' or just 'sommes pas des' in fragments. Used to deny identity or membership in a group (e.g. 'we are not Americans', 'we are not samurai'). Followed by a noun or noun phrase. In writing, use the full negative 'nous ne sommes pas des...'.
target_language_example: Nous sommes pas des touristes, nous vivons ici.
native_language_example: We are not tourists, we live here.

meaning: 'we are all (some category)'.
additional_notes: Used with nous (we) to state that all members of the group belong to a category (animals, humans, sinners, etc.). Followed by a noun or noun phrase. Literal word order: nous (we) + sommes (are) + tous (all) + des (some/of the) + noun. In English the 'des' is usually not translated directly: 'we are all X' or 'we are all [a type of]'.
target_language_example: Nous sommes tous des voyageurs sur cette route.
native_language_example: We are all travelers on this road.

meaning: are really
additional_notes: Usually appears after nous: nous sommes vraiment... = "we are really...". It adds emphasis to a description, feeling, or identity, as in who we really are or we are really sorry.
target_language_example: Nous sommes vraiment contents d'être ici.
native_language_example: We are really happy to be here.

meaning: the top of the (feminine) — e.g. the top of the mountain/hill.
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (la montagne, la colline). Commonly appears as "au sommet de la" (at the top of the ...) or "le sommet de la" (the top of the ...). Can describe a physical peak or a figurative high point.
target_language_example: Nous avons vu la vallée depuis le sommet de la montagne.
native_language_example: We saw the valley from the top of the mountain.

meaning: literally 'his/her son in' — used as part of a larger phrase indicating where or how someone's son was (e.g. 'lost his/her son in [an accident/place]').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom by itself but a sequence of words: 'son fils' (his/her son) followed by 'dans' (in/into). It requires a noun phrase or clause after 'dans' (e.g. 'dans un accident', 'dans un pensionnat'). Common in sentences about where the son was or what happened to him. Gender of 'son' agrees with the possessor, not the child's gender (son = his/her son).
target_language_example: Elle a envoyé son fils dans un internat pour ses études.
native_language_example: She sent her son to a boarding school for his studies.

meaning: 'do one's best to' or 'try as hard as possible to (do something)'.
additional_notes: Appears in the fixed expression 'faire de son mieux pour + infinitive' (to do one's best to ...). Use to describe someone making their greatest effort. Common in everyday and written French. Subject agrees with 'son' (refers back to the person doing the action).
target_language_example: Elle fait de son mieux pour apprendre le français.
native_language_example: She is doing her best to learn French.

meaning: his/her [followed by a type of name]; literally 'his/her name of' — used before a noun that specifies which name (e.g. nom de naissance, nom de jeune fille, nom de plume).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it needs a following noun (nom de + X). Common uses: son nom de naissance (his/her birth name), son nom de famille (family name), son nom de scène (stage name), son nom de cadre (corporate name). In some examples, verbs like 'enlever/rayer' use 'son nom' alone: 'enlevez son nom de la liste' = remove his/her name from the list. Word order: 'son nom de X' or 'enlevez son nom de la liste'.
target_language_example: Elle a changé son nom de scène l'année dernière.
native_language_example: She changed her stage name last year.

meaning: his/her reflection in (a surface, usually a mirror).
additional_notes: Used to describe looking at or interacting with one's reflection in something (most often 'le miroir'). 'Son' agrees with the possessor (his/her). Commonly followed by the object where the reflection appears: 'le miroir', 'la vitrine', 'l'eau', etc.
target_language_example: Elle regarda son reflet dans la vitrine du magasin.
native_language_example: She looked at her reflection in the shop window.

meaning: 'the sound/volume of the' (used with a feminine noun like 'radio').
additional_notes: son means 'sound' or 'volume'. 'de la' is the partitive/article or 'of the' before a feminine noun (here 'la radio'). Together 'le son de la radio' = 'the sound of the radio' or 'the radio's sound/volume'. In commands about volume, French often uses 'baisse le son' (lower the volume) or 'mets le son plus bas.'
target_language_example: Baisse le son de la télévision, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Turn down the TV's volume, please.

meaning: 'the sound is' (used to describe the quality or level of sound).
additional_notes: son = sound; est = (he/she/it) is — used to state characteristics of sound (e.g., good/bad/too low/too weak). Common in sentences about audio quality or volume. Use with adjectives (beau, mauvais, trop bas, faible, bon).
target_language_example: Le son est trop fort dans cette salle.
native_language_example: The sound is too loud in this room.

meaning: they arrived there / they got there (past, plural).
additional_notes: Third-person plural passé composé of arriver + locative 'là' (there). Used to say a group reached a place or ended up in a situation. Context determines whether 'là' means a physical location ('there') or a figurative state ('to that point'). Pronounced [sɔ̃ aʁiˈve la].
target_language_example: Ils sont arrivés là hier soir après le concert.
native_language_example: They arrived there last night after the concert.

meaning: they met (each other) — past tense (passé composé) of 'se rencontrer'.
additional_notes: Used for plural feminine subjects (elles) with the reflexive verb 'se rencontrer' in passé composé. The auxiliary is être, so the past participle 'rencontré' agrees in gender and number (rencontrées for feminine plural). Means 'met' as in 'met each other' or 'were introduced/encountered'.
target_language_example: Elles se sont rencontrées à Paris l'année dernière.
native_language_example: They met each other in Paris last year.

meaning: 'have passed' or 'have gone by' (about time).
additional_notes: Used with a time expression and the reflexive verb s'écouler to say that a certain amount of time has passed. Common structure: [time period] + se sont écoulés (plural agrees with the time period). Often appears as 'X se sont écoulés' or 'X se sont écoulés depuis...' in past reference.
target_language_example: Cinq ans se sont écoulés depuis notre rencontre.
native_language_example: Five years have passed since we met.

meaning: are off / have gone out (feminine plural).
additional_notes: Passive/compound form of éteindre used with être in the passé composé or as a present-state description: agrees in gender/number with the noun (here 'les lumières' → éteintes). Used to say lights or other feminine plural things are switched off or have gone out suddenly.
target_language_example: Toutes les bougies sont éteintes après la pluie.
native_language_example: All the candles are out after the rain.

meaning: are in
additional_notes: Compositional phrase: sont is the 3rd-person plural of être ("are"), used with plural subjects, and dans means "in/inside." It is used for location (Ils sont dans la voiture), and sometimes more figuratively, as in dans le même bateau ("in the same boat"). With a time expression, it can mean something will happen after that amount of time, as in Les élections sont dans un an ("The elections are in a year").
target_language_example: Les clés sont dans mon sac.
native_language_example: The keys are in my bag.

meaning: are in
additional_notes: "sont" means "are" (for ils/elles), and "en" is usually followed by a place or state. So this chunk is often incomplete on its own: the full meaning depends on what comes after it. In the examples, "sont en bas" means "are downstairs".
target_language_example: Les enfants sont en classe.
native_language_example: The children are in class.

meaning: are out of / are outside of (something)
additional_notes: Hors de means 'outside of' or 'out of.' 'Sont hors de' is the present plural form (ils/elles sont hors de). Often followed by a noun or phrase: hors de la maison, hors de danger, hors de portée. Can also be used figuratively (hors de prix = exorbitant, hors de question = out of the question) but those are fixed expressions where 'hors de' combines with another word.
target_language_example: Ils sont hors de la maison maintenant.
native_language_example: They are outside the house now.

meaning: 'are the foods that you...' (part of a longer sentence)
additional_notes: This is a fragment, not a complete sentence. It combines the verb 'être' (sont = are) with a noun phrase 'les aliments' (the foods) and the relative clause introducer 'que tu' (that you...). You would finish it with another verb or description, for example: 'sont les aliments que tu manges' (are the foods that you eat). Useful when describing or asking about which foods someone eats, likes, avoids, etc.
target_language_example: Voici sont les aliments que tu manges souvent.
native_language_example: Here are the foods that you eat often.

meaning: 'are the foods that you...' (part of a sentence introducing foods someone consumes or prefers).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a fragment: 'sont' (are) + 'les aliments' (the foods) + 'que vous' (that you / which you). It will usually continue with a verb (e.g. 'mangez' = you eat, 'préférez' = you prefer). Use it to describe or ask about foods someone eats, avoids, or prefers. Order can change depending on full sentence (e.g. 'Quels sont les aliments que vous aimez ?').
target_language_example: Quels sont les aliments que vous mangez régulièrement ?
native_language_example: What are the foods that you eat regularly?

meaning: 'are not like' (used to say someone/something is different from others).
additional_notes: This is part of the negative construction 'ne ... pas comme' (often spoken without 'ne': 'sont pas comme'). Used to compare people or things and say they are different. You will commonly see it with subject pronouns (ils/elles, nous, vous, tu) and adjectives or noun phrases after 'comme' (e.g., 'comme nous', 'comme toi').
target_language_example: Ils ne sont pas comme nous.
native_language_example: They are not like us.

meaning: 'are not the' (used in negative sentences with plural nouns or pronouns)
additional_notes: This sequence appears when negating a plural noun with être: Ce ne sont pas les... (These/They are not the...). In spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: Ce sont pas les... or Ce sont pas mes... The phrase must agree in number with the noun (les, mes, tes, etc.). Commonly followed by an adjective, a noun phrase, or a possessive pronoun.
target_language_example: Ce ne sont pas les miennes.
native_language_example: They are not mine.

meaning: are on
additional_notes: Plural form of être + sur. It often shows physical location ('are on the path', 'are on the table'), but can also be used more figuratively, like being on a trail, on a flight, or under consideration.
target_language_example: Mes lunettes sont sur le canapé.
native_language_example: My glasses are on the couch.

meaning: 'are yours' (they belong to you).
additional_notes: Used to say that multiple items or people belong to someone. 'Sont' is the plural form of 'être' (to be); 'à toi' means 'to you' or 'yours' (informal singular). For formal/plural 'you', use 'sont à vous'. Can refer to things or, in casual contexts, people (e.g., responsibility).
target_language_example: Ces clés sont à toi, prends-les.
native_language_example: These keys are yours, take them.

meaning: 'took out' or 'pulled out' (something belonging to him/her).
additional_notes: Literal past participle + possessive: sortir (pp. sorti) + son/sa/ses + noun. Commonly used to say someone took or produced an object (weapon, phone, handkerchief) from a pocket, bag, etc. Context determines register: can be neutral (took out a phone) or dramatic (pulled out a gun). Use the correct gender/number for the possession (ex. a sorti sa clé, ont sorti leurs livres).
target_language_example: Elle a sorti son portefeuille pour payer.
native_language_example: She took out her wallet to pay.

meaning: emergency exit; an exit used in case of danger.
additional_notes: Commonly seen on signs in buildings. Used both in instructions (Prends la sortie de secours !) and to ask for location (Où est la sortie de secours ?). Always feminine singular: la sortie de secours. Literal components: sortie (exit) + de secours (of rescue/aid).
target_language_example: En cas d'incendie, suivez la sortie de secours la plus proche.
native_language_example: In case of fire, follow the nearest emergency exit.

meaning: to go out with; to date (someone) — also can be literal 'to take out with' in context
additional_notes: Commonly used idiomatically to mean 'to date' or 'to be in a romantic relationship' (sortir avec quelqu'un). Can also be literal when followed by a thing, but that use is less common and depends on context. Often used in everyday speech. Use present tense forms (e.g., Je sors, Il/Elle sort) when conjugated.
target_language_example: Je sais que des tas de garçons veulent sortir avec toi.
native_language_example: I know lots of boys want to go out with you.

meaning: to come out of; to get out of
additional_notes: Used for leaving a place, container, situation, or state: sortir de la maison = come/go out of the house. With a direct object, it can mean taking someone or something out of something: sortir quelqu’un de l’eau = take someone out of the water. It is also used figuratively, as in sortir de sa retraite = come out of retirement.
target_language_example: Je dois sortir de ma retraite et retourner à la vie publique.
native_language_example: I have to come out of retirement and return to public life.

meaning: 'to date' or 'to go out together' (to be in a romantic relationship or to go on dates).
additional_notes: Commonly used to indicate being a couple or dating. Can also mean simply going out together for social outings depending on context. Frequently appears with verbs like commencer (Quand avez-vous commencé à sortir ensemble ?) or in suggestions (On devrait sortir ensemble). Tone is neutral; can be used in both formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Quand avez-vous commencé à sortir ensemble ?
native_language_example: When did you start dating each other?

meaning: 'worry about' or 'be concerned about' (someone or something).
additional_notes: Used with se faire du souci à/au/aux + subject of concern (often 'à ton sujet', 'à son sujet', 'à propos de...'). Common construction: 'se faire du souci (pour/à) ...' — in spoken and written French you may also see 'se faire du souci pour'. It expresses emotional concern; the verb form changes with the subject (Je me fais, Il se fait, Nous nous faisons).
target_language_example: Je me fais du souci à propos de ton examen.
native_language_example: I'm worried about your exam.

meaning: wishes (someone) the (something); used to say you hope someone has something (e.g., happiness, the best).
additional_notes: Form of souhaiter + definite article + noun. Often followed by what is wished (le bonheur, le meilleur, le bonjour). The subject (je/tu/il) and indirect object (te/vous/lui) indicate who is wishing and to whom. Common uses: Je te souhaite le meilleur (I wish you the best), Je vous souhaite le bonjour (a formal/fixed greeting meaning 'I send my regards' or 'good day').
target_language_example: Je te souhaite le bonheur.
native_language_example: I wish you happiness.

meaning: I/you/he/she wish (someone) a [something]; used to express wishes (e.g., happy birthday, good trip).
additional_notes: Souhaite is the verb souhaiter (to wish) conjugated (je/il/elle souhaite). 'Souhaite un/une' + noun expresses giving a wish to someone: Je te souhaite un joyeux Noël = I wish you a merry Christmas. Use je te/vous souhaite depending on familiar/formal or plural. Common in set phrases: souhaite un bon séjour, souhaite un prompt rétablissement. The direct object is the wish (un bon voyage), and the person receiving the wish is introduced by à or by object pronouns (te, vous).
target_language_example: Je vous souhaite un excellent week-end.
native_language_example: I wish you an excellent weekend.

meaning: wish someone a (good) ... (used before words like journée, soirée, nuit).
additional_notes: This is part of the phrase 'je (te/vous) souhaite une bonne + [journée/soirée/nuit/...]' meaning 'I wish you a good ...'. Use 'je te souhaite' for informal singular 'you' and 'je vous souhaite' for formal or plural 'you'. Common completions: journée (day), soirée (evening), nuit (night), et belle journée (a nice day).
target_language_example: Je te souhaite une bonne soirée.
native_language_example: I wish you a good evening.

meaning: wishes (something) to (someone).
additional_notes: Souhaite à is the verb souhaiter (to wish) followed by the preposition à to indicate the person who receives the wish. You will often see it in constructions like "souhaite à quelqu'un [quelque chose]" (wishes someone something) or with an infinitive/phrase after: "je lui souhaite bonne chance" (I wish him/her good luck). Use indirect object pronouns (lui, leur) or a noun after à. Formal and neutral register.
target_language_example: Je souhaite à Marie beaucoup de succès dans son nouveau travail.
native_language_example: I wish Marie lots of success in her new job.

meaning: I would really wish / I would really like (to)...
additional_notes: Polite or tentative way to express a strong wish or desire; uses the conditional form of souhaiter (je souhaiterais). Often followed by an infinitive (pouvoir + infinitive) or que + subjunctive. More formal/soft than je veux; can be used with tu/vous forms (je souhaiterais vraiment pouvoir te/vous croire).
target_language_example: Je souhaiterais vraiment pouvoir venir demain.
native_language_example: I would really like to be able to come tomorrow.

meaning: 'suspect that' or 'have a suspicion that'.
additional_notes: Used to express a belief or suspicion about something, often without full proof. Follows the subject (je soupçonne que...) and is typically followed by a clause with a verb. Neutral register — not strongly formal or informal.
target_language_example: Je soupçonne que Pierre a oublié notre rendez-vous.
native_language_example: I suspect that Pierre forgot our appointment.

meaning: underwear; an item of clothing worn under outer clothes.
additional_notes: Used as a general term for underwear (singular). The plural is "sous-vêtements" (underwear, undergarments). Can refer to bras, panties, briefs, undershirts, etc. Formal/neutral word; common in everyday speech. When talking about a specific piece use an article: "un sous-vêtement" or "des sous-vêtements".
target_language_example: J'ai acheté de nouveaux sous-vêtements hier.
native_language_example: I bought new underwear yesterday.

meaning: 'under penalty of' / 'subject to' (used to warn that an action will lead to a specified punishment or consequence).
additional_notes: Formal/legal expression used to introduce the negative consequence (punishment, fine, legal sanction, or other penalty) if a stated requirement is not followed. Often followed by an infinitive or a noun (e.g. 'amende', 'emprisonnement'). Common in laws, official notices, and formal warnings: 'sous peine de ...'.
target_language_example: Interdiction de stationner, sous peine de suspension de permis.
native_language_example: No parking, under penalty of suspension of license.

meaning: 'shortly', 'soon'.
additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen in a short time. Formal or neutral register; common in news, announcements, and spoken French. Often appears with verbs like arriver, revenir, annoncer, se rétablir.
target_language_example: Le spectacle commencera sous peu.
native_language_example: The show will begin shortly.

meaning: with subtitles; subtitled (e.g. a film is shown with written translation or transcription on screen).
additional_notes: Used to describe movies, videos or programs that include subtitles (sous-titres). Often followed by the language (e.g. «sous-titré en anglais»). Can be used in questions and negatives: «est-il sous-titré?» / «n'est pas sous-titré».
target_language_example: Le film est sous-titré en anglais.
native_language_example: The movie is subtitled in English.

meaning: to underestimate; to judge something or someone as less important, capable, or large than they really are.
additional_notes: Commonly used with a direct object (e.g., 'sous-estimer quelqu'un/quelque chose'). Can refer to abilities, risks, costs, time needed, quantities, etc. Conjugated like a regular -er verb. Opposite: 'surestimer' (to overestimate).
target_language_example: Tu ne dois pas sous-estimer la charge de travail.
native_language_example: You must not underestimate the workload.

meaning: 'basement' or 'cellar' (the space under a building).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the floor or area below ground level. Can be described with adjectives (humide, fermé à clé, infesté) or with être + noun/phrase. Common in contexts about buildings, storage, or restricted areas. Not informal.
target_language_example: Le sous-sol est plein de cartons anciens.
native_language_example: The basement is full of old boxes.

meaning: will remember (about/of)
additional_notes: Future tense of se souvenir de (to remember). Used with a subject (je, tu, il...) and followed by the thing or person remembered introduced by de. English translations often use 'will remember' + direct object or 'remember' + preposition 'of'/'about'. Can express remembering people, moments, feelings, etc.
target_language_example: Je me souviendrai de cette soirée toute ma vie.
native_language_example: I will remember that evening my whole life.

meaning: 'remember (something/someone)'.
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb se souvenir de (je me souviens de, tu te souviens de, etc.). In speech the de often contracts before a vowel or is written d'. Use 'tu te souviens de...' to ask 'do you remember...?' and follow with a noun, pronoun, or clause (e.g. d'elle, d'autre chose, de ce jour).
target_language_example: Tu te souviens d'où nous étions allés?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we went?

meaning: remember my/remember that relates to my (someone or something).
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb se souvenir de (to remember). In full sentences you say Je me souviens de mon père (I remember my father) or Tu te souviens de mon frère ? (Do you remember my brother?). Use the correct reflexive pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous) to match the subject and adjust the noun that follows (mon/ma/mes) for possession. Often followed by a person, name, or thing. Common in questions and statements.
target_language_example: Tu te souviens de mon professeur de français ?
native_language_example: Do you remember my French teacher?

meaning: 'remember his/her/its' (used to say you recall something belonging to or about someone)
additional_notes: Form comes from the reflexive verb se souvenir de + possessive (son). Use with je/tu/il etc. plus the appropriate possessive: 'son' = his/her/its (masculine or general). The English subject (I/you) is explicit in French (je me souviens, tu te souviens). Commonly followed by a noun (visage, nom, anniversaire, numéro) or a clause introduced by que.
target_language_example: Je me souviens de son nom.
native_language_example: I remember his/her name.

meaning: 'don't remember (of/about)'.
additional_notes: Informal/colloquial negative form of se souvenir de (to remember). In full formal form you'd say "ne me/te/se/etc. souviens pas de" or with ne...pas around the verb: "je ne me souviens pas de..." The phrase is followed by a person or thing introduced by de (de lui, de ça, de cet endroit). Use reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nous, vous) depending on the subject.
target_language_example: Je ne me souviens pas de ton visage.
native_language_example: I don't remember your face.

meaning: no longer remember; don't remember anymore
additional_notes: This is part of the reflexive verb se souvenir (to remember) plus 'plus' meaning 'no longer' or 'anymore' after a negative construction (often with ne). In spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped, so 'Je (ne) me souviens plus' means 'I don't remember anymore.' Can be used with or without an object: 'de l'air' / 'de toi', or alone ('Tu ne te souviens plus ?').
target_language_example: Je ne me souviens plus de son nom.
native_language_example: I don't remember his/her name anymore.

meaning: gas station; petrol station.
additional_notes: Common term for a place where you buy fuel for vehicles and often find a convenience store, pumps, and sometimes a service bay. Used in everyday speech and on signs. In Canada you may also hear 'station-service'.
target_language_example: Je vais à la station essence pour faire le plein.
native_language_example: I'm going to the gas station to fill up.

meaning: ballpoint pen; a pen that uses a small rotating ball to dispense ink.
additional_notes: Common, neutral term for a ballpoint pen in French. Used when specifying the pen type (as opposed to fountain pen = "stylo plume" or felt-tip = "feutre"/"stylos marqueur"). "À" here indicates the pen has a ball (bille).
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un stylo à bille pour signer ce document.
native_language_example: I need a ballpoint pen to sign this document.

meaning: 'knew that I...' (past participle 'su' + conjunction 'que' + subject 'j'' as in 'j'étais') — used in questions like 'How did you know that I...?'
additional_notes: This fragment appears in spoken/written questions: Comment (as-/t-)as-tu su que j'... / Comment avez-vous su que j'... / Comment tu as su que j'... It combines the past participle su (from savoir = to know) with que + the start of a subordinate clause about the speaker (j'), e.g. j'étais. English equivalent: 'How did you know that I...?' Contractions like t'as (tu as) and the drop of vowels (j') are common in speech. Use 'su que je...' in full when not eliding the vowel.
target_language_example: Comment as-tu su que j'étais venu ?
native_language_example: How did you know that I had come?

meaning: southwest (direction or region).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the compass direction or a region located to the southwest. Can be used with articles and prepositions (au sud-ouest de..., dans le sud-ouest de...) or alone as a label/direction. Hyphenated in French. Pronounced like 'soo-dwɛst'.
target_language_example: Le vent vient du sud-ouest.
native_language_example: The wind is coming from the southwest.

meaning: I went (to) — used with a reflexive infinitive: 'I went to [do something for myself]'.
additional_notes: This is the first-person singular passé composé of 'aller' + a reflexive pronoun and an infinitive (aller + se + infinitive). It expresses that the speaker went somewhere in order to do an action for themselves (e.g., se promener = go for a walk, se faire vacciner = get vaccinated). In English you usually say 'I went to [do something]' or 'I went and [did something]'. The reflexive 'me' agrees with the subject 'je'.
target_language_example: Je suis allé me coucher tôt hier soir.
native_language_example: I went to bed early last night.

meaning: 'I had fun' or 'I enjoyed myself' (past tense, first person singular with reflexive verb se amuser).
additional_notes: This is part of the passé composé of the reflexive verb se amuser: Je me suis amusé(e). Use me/te/se/nous/vous + être (suis/es/est/sommes/êtes/sont) + amusé. The past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject when the reflexive pronoun is a direct object: Je me suis amusé (m) / Je me suis amusée (f). Also used in exclamations (Que je me suis amusé !) to emphasize how much fun you had.
target_language_example: Je me suis amusée à la fête hier soir.
native_language_example: I had fun at the party last night.

meaning: I arrived at the (feminine place).
additional_notes: First-person singular past tense of arriver (être arrivé): 'je suis arrivé(e)'. 'À la' is the feminine singular form of 'at the' used before feminine place nouns (la gare, la maison, la fête). If the speaker is female, write 'je suis arrivée'. Can be followed by a specific place or time expression.
target_language_example: Je suis arrivé à la gare hier soir.
native_language_example: I arrived at the train station last night.

meaning: am sitting
additional_notes: This phrase is the first-person singular past (passé composé) of se asseoir used in examples where the speaker says they sat down or are seated. In French you usually say "je me suis assis(e)" (with reflexive pronoun and agreement with gender: add -e for feminine). In casual present descriptions someone might also say "je suis assis(e)" to mean "I am sitting". Context determines whether it's a completed action (I sat down) or a state (I am seated).
target_language_example: Je me suis assis près de la fenêtre.
native_language_example: I sat down near the window.

meaning: 'am/is/was sitting on' or part of 'to sit (oneself) on'—from the reflexive verb s'asseoir + preposition sur.
additional_notes: Derived from the reflexive verb s'asseoir (to sit down). In context you will usually see it with a reflexive pronoun (je me suis assis(e) sur, il s'est assis sur) or following a subject (je suis assis(e) sur for state). Use sur to indicate the surface or object being sat on (canapé, sol, banc, rocher). Be mindful of past-participle agreement when using passé composé with a preceding reflexive pronoun: je me suis assis (masc) / je me suis assise (fem).
target_language_example: Je me suis assis sur le canapé à côté de lui.
