additional_notes: Common phrase structure: subject + (aller/venir/vouloir) + te dire ce que + clause. It introduces the content of what will be told to 'te' (you, informal). 'Te' is the informal singular object pronoun; use 'vous dire ce que' for formal or plural. The following clause can be in any tense (present, past, future).
target_language_example: Je vais te dire ce que j'ai vu hier.
native_language_example: I'll tell you what I saw yesterday.

meaning: the beginning of a clause meaning 'to tell you what I...' (incomplete fragment)
additional_notes: This is a partial phrase — you need to finish the sentence with a verb or clause (e.g. 'te dire ce que je pense', 'te dire ce que je veux'). 'Te' is the informal singular 'you' (object), 'dire' = 'to tell', and 'ce que je' starts a relative clause 'what I...'. Common in spoken and written French when addressing someone directly. To be polite or formal, use 'vous' instead of 'te'.
target_language_example: Je veux te dire ce que je pense.
native_language_example: I want to tell you what I think.

meaning: 'to tell you the' (part of the phrase 'te dire la vérité' = 'to tell you the truth')
additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase; it's the sequence 'te dire' (to tell you) followed by a definite noun (here 'la vérité'). 'Te' is the informal singular object pronoun (you). You'll most often see it in sentences like 'te dire la vérité' (to tell you the truth). In formal situations use 'vous' instead of 'te' (e.g. 'vous dire la vérité').
target_language_example: Je dois te dire la vérité maintenant.
native_language_example: I must tell you the truth now.

meaning: to tell you a (something) — the start of a phrase meaning 'to tell you a [thing/comment]' (informal/colloquial spoken French).
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; it's the beginning of expressions like «te dire une chose» or casual constructions «je vais te dire une/te dire un truc» meaning 'I'll tell you something'. Often used in speech before giving news, a comment, or a secret. In many contexts speakers shorten it to «te dire un truc» or «te dire quelque chose». When using, finish with a noun (une chose, un truc, une vérité, etc.) or add the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Je vais te dire une chose : arrête de t'inquiéter.
native_language_example: I'll tell you one thing: stop worrying.

meaning: I give you a (masculine singular) ... / I'll give you a ...
additional_notes: Informal spoken order: subject (je) + te (you, informal object) + donne (give) + un + noun. 'Te' is the familiar singular indirect/direct object pronoun. The noun following 'un' must be masculine singular (un livre, un indice, un coup). Use 'je vous donne un' for formal or plural 'you'.
target_language_example: Je te donne un exemple pour t'aider.
native_language_example: I'll give you an example to help you.

meaning: 'hurry' or 'hurry up' (reflexive: you hurry yourself).
additional_notes: Second-person singular informal form of the reflexive verb se dépêcher. Used to tell someone to be quick or to say that if they hurry they can catch or do something. Common in questions and conditional clauses (Si tu te dépêches...). Tone can be neutral or slightly urgent depending on context.
target_language_example: Dépêche‑toi, tu vas manquer le train si tu ne te dépêches pas.
native_language_example: Hurry up, you'll miss the train if you don't hurry.

meaning: to have (something) cut for you / to get yourself cut (e.g., hair, clothes altered)
additional_notes: This is a reflexive/causative construction using 'faire' + infinitive: someone arranges for an action to be done to you or for you. With 'te' it means the action is arranged for 'you' (informal singular). Commonly used for haircuts (te faire couper les cheveux) or having clothing altered (te faire couper un pantalon). Use the appropriate direct object after the infinitive ('les cheveux', 'le pantalon', etc.).
target_language_example: Tu devrais te faire couper les cheveux avant la fête.
native_language_example: You should get your hair cut before the party.

meaning: part of a colloquial construction meaning 'to make you (feel/think/etc.)' or 'to get you (to do something)' depending on context
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed phrase by itself; te faire de appears as part of larger colloquial verbs or expressions (e.g. te faire de la peine, te faire croire, te faire rire, te faire avoir). The pronoun te is the object 'you' (informal singular). Faire is 'to make' or 'to do'. The meaning depends on the noun or infinitive that follows. Often used in spoken French. Watch agreement and word order: pronoun (te) + faire + noun/infinitive. Alone 'te faire de' is incomplete and requires what follows (noun or verb).
target_language_example: Il a essayé de te faire de la peine en racontant cette histoire.
native_language_example: He tried to make you feel hurt by telling that story.

meaning: 'are you kidding (me)?' / 'are you making fun of (me)?'
additional_notes: Informal expression used when someone thinks another person is joking, teasing, or not serious. Often appears in questions: "Tu te fous de moi ?" (= "Are you kidding me?"). Literally comes from "se foutre de" meaning 'to make fun of' or 'not care about' depending on context. Stronger/emotional than neutral phrases like "tu plaisantes ?"
target_language_example: Tu te fous de moi, sérieux ?
native_language_example: Are you kidding me, seriously?

meaning: to hear you say it (to hear you say that).
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the pronouns 'te' (to you) and 'l'' (it) with the verb entendre in an infinitive construction (entendre + infinitive implied). It appears in expressions like 'Heureux de te l'entendre dire' meaning 'Glad to hear you say that.' The full idea is 'to hear you say it' or 'to hear you say so.' Common in spoken and written French. Pronunciation often links words (te l'entendre ≈ 'tuh-lahn-tahndruh').
target_language_example: Ça me rassure de te l'entendre dire.
native_language_example: It reassures me to hear you say that.

meaning: to show you a (something).
additional_notes: Informal, everyday phrase used to say you'll show the listener one item/example/thing. 'Te' is the familiar 'you' (object pronoun). After 'te montrer un' you normally add a noun (truc, exemple, document, etc.). In formal situations use 'vous montrer un' instead.
target_language_example: Je vais te montrer un exemple.
native_language_example: I'll show you an example.

target_language_multi_word_term: te parler un (instant/un moment/un petit moment)
meaning: 'to speak to you for' (a short time) — used to ask/request a brief conversation
additional_notes: This is a common way to request or offer a short one-on-one conversation. Forms vary: 'te parler un instant', 'te parler un moment', 'te parler un petit moment'. Often appears in questions with 'Je peux…' or 'Puis-je…' and is followed by 's'il te plaît' or context. Use 'te' for informal/familiar 'you' (tu). For formal 'you' (vous) say 'vous parler un instant' or better 'vous parler un instant ?' or 'vous parler un moment ?'.
target_language_example: Excuse-moi, je peux te parler un instant ?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I speak to you for a moment?

meaning: to speak to you for a short moment / 'talk to you for a second'.
additional_notes: Common, casual way to ask someone for a brief conversation. Usually appears in phrases like «Je peux te parler une seconde ?», «Est-ce que je peux te parler une seconde ?», or «Puis-je te parler une seconde ?». The word 'une' (short for 'une seconde' or 'une minute') implies a very short time. Use with tu/te (informal). For a more formal request use «vous» (e.g. «Puis-je vous parler un instant ?»).
target_language_example: Je peux te parler une seconde pour te demander un service ?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a second to ask a favor?

meaning: 'ask you a' (as in 'ask you a question')
additional_notes: This is the informal 1st person singular present tense form of poser + object: je te pose une... It appears before a noun (e.g. question). te = 'you' (object). Used in conversation to say 'I ask you a...' or 'May I ask you a...'. For polite requests use 'Puis-je vous poser une question ?' or 'Je peux te poser une question ?' in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je te pose une question : tu veux venir ce soir ?
native_language_example: I'm asking you a question: do you want to come tonight?

meaning: 'do you remember this' or 'you remember this' (informal, spoken)
additional_notes: Colloquial clipped form using the familiar pronoun te and the verb se rappeler. Not grammatically complete in standard written French on its own — speakers usually say "tu te rappelles ce truc ?" or more commonly "tu te rappelles ça ?" but the fragment "te rappelles ce" can appear in rapid, informal speech or as part of a larger sentence (e.g. "Te rappelles ce qu'on a fait ?"). Use with people you know well (tu). For a neutral or polite phrasing, use "vous vous rappelez ceci/ça ?"
target_language_example: Te rappelles ce qu'on a fait l'été dernier ?
native_language_example: Do you remember what we did last summer?

meaning: to hold you tightly in (someone's arms) / to hug you tightly into
additional_notes: Usually followed by a noun like les bras (te serrer dans les bras) meaning 'to hug you'. Often used to express affection or comfort. The construction is: te (object pronoun) + serrer (to squeeze/hold tight) + dans + noun. For beginners, remember the full common phrase is 'te serrer dans les bras'.
target_language_example: J'ai juste envie de te serrer dans les bras.
native_language_example: I just want to hold you tightly in my arms (hug you).

meaning: to see you in my (place) — used to ask or tell someone to come to the speaker's room/office.
additional_notes: This phrase is a fragment used in invitations or requests meaning "see you in my [office/room]". The noun (e.g., bureau, appartement, labo) usually follows: "te voir dans mon bureau" = "see you in my office." Common in formal and informal contexts; verbs at start can be questions (Je peux/Puis-je te voir...?) or statements (Je veux te voir...).
target_language_example: Puis-je te voir dans mon bureau cet après-midi ?
native_language_example: May I see you in my office this afternoon?

meaning: 'dye (one's) + plural noun' — used in reflexive constructions meaning 'to dye one's (hair, etc.)'.
additional_notes: Appears as part of the reflexive verb se teindre (past participle teint) used with a plural body-part noun (e.g. les cheveux). In your examples the structure is usually: (subject) se/s' + teindre → past participle teint used in compound tenses (e.g. vous êtes-vous teint les cheveux ?) or in questions (me suis teint les cheveux). English: 'Did you dye your hair?' or 'He dyes his hair.' Note: teindre is irregular; common phrase is se teindre les cheveux. The literal words 'teint les' alone are not a standalone phrase — they occur with a reflexive pronoun and a noun.
target_language_example: Je me suis teint les cheveux en rouge.
native_language_example: I dyed my hair red.

meaning: ‘such as’, ‘as’, or ‘just as’ (used to introduce an example, a manner, or to mean ‘as…’).
additional_notes: Used to introduce examples (tel que = such as) or to say ‘as’ / ‘just as’ when comparing or describing manner (tel que + clause or tel que + pronoun). Can appear alone in spoken French as a brief question (Tel que ? = Like what?). Agreement: 'tel' can change (tel que, tels que, telle que, telles que) to match gender/number of the noun it refers to.
target_language_example: Montre-moi comment tu joues, tel que tu le fais en concert.
native_language_example: Show me how you play, just as you do in concert.

meaning: so happy (feminine speaker).
additional_notes: Tellement = 'so' / 'so much' (intensifier). Contente is the feminine form of content (happy). Use tellement + adjective to express strong feeling. Change contente to content for a male speaker (e.g. tellement content). Can be followed by de + infinitive/verb or que + subjunctive/indicative depending on the clause.
target_language_example: Je suis tellement contente de te voir aujourd'hui !
native_language_example: I'm so happy to see you today!

meaning: 'the weather' or 'time' (depending on context); here primarily 'the weather'.
additional_notes: Le mot 'temps' peut signifier soit 'le temps' (la durée) soit 'le temps' (la météo) selon le contexte. Dans des phrases comme «le mauvais temps», il signifie 'bad weather'. L'article 'le' est souvent utilisé ; l'ordre donné ici suit la convention de fiches lexicographiques («temps, le»). Faites attention au contexte pour distinguer 'time' et 'weather'.
target_language_example: À cause du mauvais temps, le match a été annulé.
native_language_example: Because of the bad weather, the match was cancelled.

meaning: 'How much longer are we going to...' or 'How long are we going to...'
additional_notes: Used to ask how much time will be spent on, or how much longer an action or situation will continue. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., attendre, discuter, rester) or a phrase describing the situation. Common in everyday speech and can express impatience.
target_language_example: Combien de temps allons-nous attendre avant de partir ?
native_language_example: How much longer are we going to wait before leaving?

meaning: 'how long have you' / 'how long did you' (used to ask about duration)
additional_notes: This fragment comes from questions formed with 'Combien de temps as-tu...' (informal singular 'you') to ask the duration of an action or state. It can be used with different tenses (passé composé, imparfait, etc.) depending on whether you ask about completed actions or ongoing states. For formal or plural 'you' use 'Combien de temps avez-vous...'.
target_language_example: Combien de temps as-tu vécu à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long did you live in Paris?

meaning: 'how long' (asking duration)
additional_notes: Used in questions asking about duration. Often appears in full phrases like "Combien de temps as-tu... ?" (How much time do you have/How long have you had...). With "Depuis combien de temps... ?" it asks how long something has been the case (since when). "As-tu" is the inversion form of "tu as" used in formal or neutral questions.
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps as-tu ton nouveau travail ?
native_language_example: How long have you had your new job?

meaning: "how long do you have" or "how long have you" (used to ask about duration or amount of time)
additional_notes: This phrase appears in questions about duration. Often used with Combien (Combien de temps avez-vous ?) to ask "How long do you have?" or "How much time do you have?" With Depuis (Depuis combien de temps avez-vous...) it asks "How long have you had...?/Since when have you had...?." Can be followed by a noun (congé, besoin) or a clause (ce problème).
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps avez-vous ce rendez‑vous confirmé ?
native_language_example: How long have you had this appointment confirmed?

meaning: 'how long will this/that take?' (used in questions about duration)
additional_notes: This phrase appears in questions asking about the duration of an event or action. It's usually part of the fixed question phrase Combien de temps cela va-t-il (prendre/durer) ? — formal or neutral register. In spoken French, people often say Combien de temps ça va durer ? or Combien de temps ça va prendre ? (more informal). The verb that follows is commonly prendre (to take) or durer (to last).
target_language_example: Combien de temps cela va-t-il prendre pour finir le projet ?
native_language_example: How long will this take to finish the project?

meaning: time each day; (some) time every day
additional_notes: Used to say you spend or should spend a certain amount of time every day on an activity. Often appears with verbs like passer (to spend) or consacrer (to devote). Can be followed by an infinitive (e.g. 'à lire') or a noun phrase. Implies a regular, daily habit or recommendation.
target_language_example: Je passe vingt minutes de temps chaque jour à pratiquer le piano.
native_language_example: I spend twenty minutes each day practicing the piano.

meaning: 'How long do you plan to ...?' (asks about the length of time someone intends to do or stay)
additional_notes: Polite/formal way to ask how long someone intends to do something or to stay somewhere. Uses the verb compter (comptez-vous) meaning 'to intend/plan' + a duration expression. In everyday speech you may also hear the informal inversion 'vous comptez rester combien ?' or 'Combien de temps allez-vous rester ?'. Replace the verb or ending as needed: 'partir', 'rester', etc.
target_language_example: Combien de temps comptez-vous rester en France ?
native_language_example: How long do you plan to stay in France?

meaning: time to take/have (to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say someone has (or needs) time to do an action (e.g., prendre une douche, prendre un café). Common in questions and statements about having enough time. Often preceded by expressions like 'avoir le temps de', 'laisser le temps de', or 'à peine le temps de'.
target_language_example: J'ai le temps de prendre un sandwich avant la réunion.
native_language_example: I have time to grab a sandwich before the meeting.

meaning: 'time to' (followed by a reflexive or indirect object pronoun meaning 'you') — used to say it's time for you to do something.
additional_notes: This phrase appears in the construction 'Il est temps de + (pronoun) + infinitive'. 'Te' is the informal singular 'you' (reflexive/indirect object). Use 'vous' for formal/plural: 'Il est temps de vous...'. Common for telling someone it's time to start/stop an action (go to bed, wake up, change behaviour, etc.).
target_language_example: Il est temps de te reposer après cette longue journée.
native_language_example: It's time for you to rest after this long day.

meaning: 'how long do we (have to) —' used to ask about the duration someone (we) must wait or stay
additional_notes: This fragment appears in questions about duration, usually after 'Combien de' (Combien de temps devons-nous...?). It literally combines 'temps' (time) and the inverted question 'devons-nous' (must/do we have to). Use to ask how long we must wait, stay, or continue an action. You will usually hear: 'Combien de temps devons-nous...?' or variants with 'encore' for 'how much longer'.
target_language_example: Combien de temps devons-nous attendre ici ?
native_language_example: How long do we have to wait here?

meaning: 'how long (something) lasts' — used to ask about duration.
additional_notes: This phrase comes from the question pattern Combien de temps dure + [event/thing]. Use it to ask how long an event, action or period lasts. You can replace the noun with a verb in the infinitive: Combien de temps dure + le film / le vol / l'exposition / la réunion. For short units you might also hear Combien de temps ça dure (more informal).
target_language_example: Combien de temps dure le spectacle?
native_language_example: How long does the show last?

meaning: 'How long did you stay?' (literally: 'time did you stay')
additional_notes: This is the middle part of the question Combien de temps es-tu resté...? used to ask about the duration of someone's stay or how long they stayed somewhere. Combien de temps = 'how long'; es-tu resté is the passé composé question form of rester (to stay). For feminine speaker: es-tu restée. Can be used with places or events (au Canada, à la fête, dans la ville...).
target_language_example: Combien de temps es-tu resté en France l'année dernière ?
native_language_example: How long did you stay in France last year?

meaning: 'how long did you stay' (asking duration, feminine subject)
additional_notes: This phrase is part of the question formula 'Combien de temps es-tu restée ... ?' used to ask how long someone stayed somewhere. The verb is in passé composé (être + past participle) and the past participle 'restée' agrees in gender and number with the subject: 'resté' (m., sing.), 'restée' (f., sing.), 'restés' (m. pl.), 'restées' (f. pl.). For a masculine subject use 'es-tu resté' (tu being singular familiar). Formal or written inversion ('es-tu') is common in examples; in spoken French you may hear 'tu es restée combien de temps ?' or 'Combien de temps es-tu restée ?'.
target_language_example: Combien de temps es-tu restée à Paris l'année dernière ?
native_language_example: How long did you stay in Paris last year?

meaning: 'How long have you been ...?' (asks duration up to now)
additional_notes: Use this question to ask how long an action or state has been true up to the present moment. It is formed with 'Depuis combien de temps' + verb in present (here 'es-tu' for 'you are'). In spoken French you can also say 'Ça fait combien de temps que tu ... ?' or use inversion less often in casual speech: 'Depuis combien de temps tu es ... ?'.
target_language_example: Depuis combien de temps es-tu en France ?
native_language_example: How long have you been in France?

meaning: time is
additional_notes: This phrase combines temps (which can mean 'time' or 'weather') with the verb est ('is'). Meaning depends on context: when talking about météo it means 'the weather is...', e.g. 'Le temps est changeant' = 'The weather is changeable.' When talking about abstract concepts it means 'time is...' as in sayings or descriptions (e.g. 'Le temps est précieux' = 'Time is precious').
target_language_example: Le temps est important pour ce projet.
native_language_example: Time is important for this project.

meaning: used in questions to ask 'how long does it take to...?'
additional_notes: This phrase appears in the fixed question form 'Combien de temps faut-il pour + infinitive' meaning 'How long does it take to [do something / go somewhere]?'. 'Faut-il' is the impersonal form of 'falloir' (to be necessary). You can also ask 'Ça prend combien de temps pour...' (informal) or invert word order: 'Pour aller à X, combien de temps faut-il ?'.
target_language_example: Combien de temps faut-il pour visiter le musée ?
native_language_example: How long does it take to visit the museum?

meaning: free time; leisure time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about time available outside work, school, or obligations. Often used with verbs like avoir (avoir du temps libre), passer (passer son temps libre), faire (faire quelque chose pendant son temps libre).
target_language_example: Pendant mon temps libre, je lis des romans.
native_language_example: In my free time, I read novels.

meaning: literally 'time that he/it' — used in phrases meaning 'the time it takes' or 'as long as (is) needed'.
additional_notes: Appears in constructions like «le temps qu'il faut» or «le temps qu'il faudra» to indicate duration required: 'the time it takes' / 'as long as necessary'. Often used with verbs like prendre/prenez (Prends le temps qu'il te faut = take as much time as you need). Not to be confused with weather phrase «le temps qu'il fait» (the weather).
target_language_example: Prends le temps qu'il te faut pour finir ton travail.
native_language_example: Take the time you need to finish your work.

meaning: 'the time that' or 'the time when' (refers to a period/duration related to an action or event).
additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount or period of time connected to an action (e.g., the time something takes, the time someone was gone). Can introduce a relative clause with a verb: "le temps que + clause". Note: Do not confuse with conjunction "tant que" (as long as).
target_language_example: Le temps que tu es parti, j'ai tout rangé.
native_language_example: While/for the time you were gone, I tidied everything up.

meaning: 'how long will you stay?' (literally: 'time will-you-stay')
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of someone's stay. Often appears with Où/au/à (place) or alone. Formal due to inversion (resterez-vous). Informal alternatives: « Combien de temps tu restes ? » or « Vous restez combien de temps ? ». Can be answered with a duration (e.g. 'une semaine', 'trois jours').
target_language_example: Combien de temps resterez-vous à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long will you stay in Paris?

meaning: 'how long' (literally 'time + will it') used in questions about duration
additional_notes: This phrase appears inside questions like "Combien de temps va-t-il/elle... ?" to ask how long someone or something will do or remain. The "-t-" is an insertion used for pronunciation in formal inversion when the subject pronoun il/elle follows a verb that ends with a vowel (va + t + il). Do not use "va-t" alone — it's always part of a larger question (e.g. Combien de temps va-t-il rester ?).
target_language_example: Combien de temps va-t-elle rester ici ?
native_language_example: How long will she stay here?

meaning: how long (something) will last / how long will (it) last
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of an event, situation, weather, meeting, flight, etc. Commonly appears in the question pattern "Combien de temps va durer + [noun] ?" — note that "temps" here means 'duration' or 'time' and is pronounced /tɑ̃/. You can also use "Combien de temps cela va durer ?" or the simpler "Ça va durer combien de temps ?"
target_language_example: Combien de temps va durer la panne d'électricité ?
native_language_example: How long will the power outage last?

meaning: 'how long' (asking about duration of an action or stay).
additional_notes: Used in questions with Combien de (temps) + vas-tu ... to ask how long someone will do something in the future (near future with aller + infinitive) or how long they will stay somewhere. Common structure: Combien de temps vas-tu + infinitive / rester / habiter / garder + ...
target_language_example: Combien de temps vas-tu rester en France ?
native_language_example: How long will you stay in France?

meaning: 'how long' (literally: 'time are you') — used in questions about duration (with Combien de).
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the question Combien de temps êtes-vous ...? meaning 'How long were you...?' or 'How long did you...?' It pairs with past participles (parti, resté, restée, restés) and agrees in gender/number with the subject when using être as the auxiliary. Use Combien de temps (not just Combien temps) to ask about duration. Formal register (vous).
target_language_example: Combien de temps êtes-vous restée à Paris ?
native_language_example: How long were you in Paris?

meaning: snowstorm; heavy snowfall with strong winds and poor visibility.
additional_notes: Used to describe a severe winter storm with heavy snow and often strong winds. Can be used in everyday and formal contexts. Plural: tempêtes de neige. Gender: 'une tempête' (feminine). Example sentences show agreement differences for past participles with être (pris/prises) but the phrase itself is invariable.
target_language_example: La tempête de neige a bloqué la route toute la nuit.
native_language_example: The snowstorm blocked the road all night.

meaning: wanted/insisted on (doing or that something happen); attached importance to.
additional_notes: Used to express that the speaker cared about or insisted on something. Often followed by an infinitive (tenais à + infinitive) meaning 'I wanted to...' or by 'ce que' + clause to mean 'I wanted that.../I made a point of...'. Polite and common in spoken and written French. Tense here is imparfait (je tenais à = I wanted/was keen to).
target_language_example: Je tenais à te remercier pour ton aide.
native_language_example: I wanted to thank you for your help.

meaning: to reach out (physically or figuratively); to offer help or make contact
additional_notes: Used both literally (to stretch out one's hand) and figuratively (to offer help, support, or to initiate contact). Common phrases: tendre la main à quelqu'un (offer help to someone) or tendre la main pour se saluer (reach out to shake hands).
target_language_example: Il a décidé de tendre la main à son voisin après l'incendie.
native_language_example: He decided to reach out to his neighbor after the fire.

meaning: to stretch out one's arms; to hold one's arms out (toward someone or something).
additional_notes: Used physically (to reach for, embrace, or offer help). Can also be used figuratively (e.g., to welcome someone or seek comfort). Often followed by à + personne/infinitive or vers + lieu/personne (tendre les bras à quelqu'un, tendre les bras vers la porte).
target_language_example: Elle a tendance à tendre les bras quand elle voit son fils.
native_language_example: She tends to stretch out her arms when she sees her son.

meaning: Hold it / Hold the (something).
additional_notes: Imperative form of tenir (vous form) + feminine article la. Used to tell someone to hold or keep hold of a specific feminine noun (la barre, la bouteille, la porte, la position, la rampe). Can also appear in reflexive constructions (vous vous tenez la main = you hold each other's hand). Context determines which feminine noun is referenced; often followed by the noun or said with gesture while handing an object.
target_language_example: Tenez la porte, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: Hold the door, please.

meaning: to keep (someone) informed; to stay informed (when used reflexively)
additional_notes: Used transitively as tenir quelqu'un au courant (to keep someone updated) and reflexively as se tenir au courant (to keep oneself up to date). Common in both everyday and formal contexts; applies to news, progress on tasks, trends, etc.
target_language_example: Je voulais vous tenir au courant de l'avancement du projet.
native_language_example: I wanted to keep you informed about the progress of the project.

meaning: to hold on; to persevere; to keep going (not give up).
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to stay resilient during difficulty or to describe something that endures or resists. Can apply to people, groups, projects, or objects. Common in spoken and written French. Equivalents: «hang in there», «hold firm», «stay strong».
target_language_example: Il faut tenir bon jusqu'à la fin du projet.
native_language_example: You have to hang in there until the end of the project.

meaning: to keep (someone) company; to stay with someone so they aren't alone.
additional_notes: Used when one person stays with or accompanies another to provide company or comfort. Commonly followed by an indirect object (lui, me, nous, etc.). Neutral register; suitable in formal and informal contexts.
target_language_example: Je peux te tenir compagnie ce soir si tu veux.
native_language_example: I can keep you company tonight if you want.

meaning: to take into account; to consider; to bear in mind.
additional_notes: Used with de or with 'en' to mean 'consider/ take into account something'. Commonly appears in impersonal or obligation phrases (Il faut en tenir compte). Formal/neutral register. Structure: tenir compte de + noun (tenir compte de sa situation) or tenir compte de + pronoun 'en' (Il faut en tenir compte).
target_language_example: Nous devons tenir compte de ses contraintes.
native_language_example: We must take his constraints into account.

meaning: to take into account; to consider (when making a decision)
additional_notes: Common formal expression used when you want to say that something is being considered or factored in. Often followed by a noun or pronoun (tenir compte de quelque chose / de quelqu'un). Can be used in instructions, reports, or everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Il faut tenir compte de la météo avant de partir.
native_language_example: We must take the weather into account before leaving.

meaning: 'to resemble' or 'to come from / be derived from' (someone or something); can also mean 'to owe to' in the sense of origin.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something looks like, has qualities of, or originates from another person/thing. Common construction: tenir de + noun (Elle tient de sa mère = She takes after her mother / She gets it from her mother). Context determines nuance: physical/character trait resemblance or origin/heritage. Not the same as tenir à (to care about) or tenir (to hold).
target_language_example: Il tient de son grand-père pour le sens de l'humour.
native_language_example: He takes after his grandfather for his sense of humour.

meaning: to stand up; to remain standing; to be able to stand.
additional_notes: Used literally to say someone is standing or can remain standing (physically). Often appears with reflexive construction (se tenir debout) or without reflexive when describing ability (tenir debout). Can also be used figuratively to mean 'to hold up' (an argument or story), but primary beginner use is physical standing. Commonly used with modal verbs (pouvoir, arriver) and negatives.
target_language_example: Après la longue marche, je ne pouvais plus me tenir debout.
native_language_example: After the long walk, I couldn't stand up anymore.

meaning: to hold up; to cope; to hang on — to endure a difficult situation or keep going despite hardship
additional_notes: Used to say someone endures hardship, fatigue, stress or manages temporarily until conditions improve. Common in everyday French. Can refer to emotional endurance (getting through a breakup), physical stamina (staying awake), or short-term resilience (waiting for help). Often appears with il faut, tu dois, peux-tu, etc.
target_language_example: Il faut tenir le coup jusqu'à la fin de la semaine.
native_language_example: We have to hang on until the end of the week.

meaning: to keep one's word; to keep a promise.
additional_notes: Used when someone honors a promise or commitment. Commonly used in constructions like «tenir sa parole» (to keep one's word) or «je tiens parole» (I keep my promise). The subject is the person who promised; the thing kept is a promise or agreement. Can be followed by an infinitive or a clause describing what was promised.
target_language_example: Je vais tenir parole et vous aider demain.
native_language_example: I will keep my word and help you tomorrow.

meaning: to keep one's mouth shut; to stay silent (not reveal something).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning to refrain from speaking or to keep a secret. Used with a person as subject: garder le silence or literally 'hold one's tongue'. Often used to criticize someone who speaks too much or reveals things they shouldn't.
target_language_example: Il a su tenir sa langue pendant la réunion.
native_language_example: He knew how to keep his mouth shut during the meeting.

meaning: 'to care about', 'to be attached to', or 'to insist on' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun to express emotional attachment or importance (Il tient à sa famille = He cares about his family). Used with an infinitive to express that someone insists on or is keen to do something (Je tiens à venir = I insist on/very much want to come). Common in everyday and formal French.
target_language_example: Je tiens à te remercier pour ton aide — je tiens à exprimer ma gratitude.
native_language_example: I want to thank you for your help — I am keen/insist on expressing my gratitude.

meaning: to be important to someone; to care deeply about something
additional_notes: Used to express that something matters a lot to a person or that they care about it. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., tenir à cœur + noun / tenir à cœur de + infinitive). Common in both spoken and written French to show personal commitment or emotional importance.
target_language_example: Il tient à cœur la protection de l'environnement.
native_language_example: He cares deeply about protecting the environment.

meaning: indicates playing tennis on a regular repeated day (e.g., every Monday/Sunday).
additional_notes: This phrase combines the sport 'tennis' with 'tous les' + day of week to mean 'tennis every (day)'. In French the full expression is usually 'jouer au tennis tous les [jours de la semaine]' or 'tous les dimanches/lundis/etc.' Use 'au tennis' for playing the sport. 'Tous les' means 'every' or 'every (plural day)'.
target_language_example: Nous jouons au tennis tous les samedis.
native_language_example: We play tennis every Saturday.

meaning: blood pressure
additional_notes: Refers to the pressure of blood in the arteries. Commonly used in medical contexts and routine health checks. You can talk about measuring it (prendre/mesurer la tension artérielle) or saying it's high/low/normal (tension élevée/basse/normale).
target_language_example: Votre tension artérielle est normale.
native_language_example: Your blood pressure is normal.

meaning: 'green tea'.
additional_notes: Refers to the type of tea made from unoxidized leaves; commonly used in drinks and menus. Used with partitive/indefinite articles (du thé vert, un thé vert) and in questions (Tu bois du thé vert?).
target_language_example: Je préfère le thé vert le matin.
native_language_example: I prefer green tea in the morning.

meaning: I care to / I want to / I am keen to (expressing that the speaker considers something important to do for you).
additional_notes: Used with a verb or infinitive to emphasize that the speaker feels it is important, necessary, or personally significant to do that action toward 'te' (you). Common constructions: 'je tiens à te dire', 'je tiens à te remercier', 'je tiens à te voir'. Polite and often slightly formal; expresses intention or strong desire rather than obligation.
target_language_example: Je tiens à te dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I want to tell you the truth (I feel it is important to tell you).

meaning: to care about you / to be attached to you (to value someone)
additional_notes: Used to say someone cares about or values another person. Often appears as part of a sentence with a subject (e.g. Je tiens à vous, Il tient à vous) or followed by an infinitive (je tiens à vous aider = I want/need to help you). It can be polite or emotional depending on context. Not reflexive.
target_language_example: Je tiens à vous dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I want to tell you the truth / I feel it is important to tell you the truth.

meaning: too shy to (do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say someone is too shy to perform an action (e.g., parler, ouvrir son cœur). Common in spoken and written French. 'Timide' describes a personality trait; 'pour' introduces the action they're too shy to do.
target_language_example: Elle est trop timide pour demander de l'aide.
native_language_example: She is too shy to ask for help.

meaning: to stick out one's tongue (literally: to pull the tongue).
additional_notes: Used to describe the physical action of protruding the tongue, often playfully, in disgust, or as a childish gesture. Can be literal (someone sticks out their tongue) or figurative in descriptions. Not an idiom meaning something else.
target_language_example: Il a tiré la langue à son frère pour le taquiner.
native_language_example: He stuck his tongue out at his brother to tease him.

meaning: to get/make the best of (something); to draw/close (a curtain) depending on context.
additional_notes: Commonly appears in the expression "tirer le meilleur parti (de)" meaning "to make the most of" or "to get the best out of" a situation or thing. "Tirer le" alone can also combine with nouns like "rideau" (tirer le rideau = draw/close the curtain). Context determines whether it means "make the most of" (figurative) or a physical action like pulling/drawing (literal).
target_language_example: Elle a su tirer le meilleur parti de son séjour à l'étranger.
native_language_example: She knew how to make the most of her stay abroad.

meaning: 'to take advantage (of)', 'to make the most of', or 'to benefit from'.
additional_notes: Used with de + noun or pronoun: tirer parti de quelque chose = to profit from or make good use of something. Neutral register; can be used in many contexts (work, opportunities, situations). Not necessarily negative (unlike 'to take advantage of someone' which can be exploitative) — context matters. Commonly followed by 'de'.
target_language_example: Il faut tirer parti de cette occasion pour apprendre.
native_language_example: You should make the most of this opportunity to learn.

meaning: adds emphasis or affection to 'toi' (you); similar to 'you, then' or 'you, you know' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is a colloquial spoken feature where 'la' (often pronounced [la] or [là]) follows a pronoun to add emphasis, familiarity, or a slight emotional tone. It can stress the person addressed ('you!') or add a rhythmic/poetic touch in narration. Not a separate grammatical unit—more a discourse particle. Usage and nuance depend on intonation and context.
target_language_example: Regarde-toi, la, comme tu as changé !
native_language_example: Look at you, you — how you've changed!

meaning: yourself
additional_notes: Used for emphasis or reflexively to indicate the person addressed performs the action or is the focus. Can be placed after a verb (Dis-lui toi-même = tell him yourself) or after a prepositional/pronominal phrase (compte sur toi-même). Often used for encouragement (Reste toi-même) or to insist someone do something personally (Répare-le toi-même).
target_language_example: Fais-le toi-même si tu préfères.
native_language_example: Do it yourself if you prefer.

meaning: used to say that it is your turn/responsibility to do or say something ("it's up to you to ...").
additional_notes: This construction appears in phrases like «c'est à toi de le faire/ dire/ découvrir» or shortened «à toi de le dire». It expresses obligation, responsibility, or that the next action is the other person's. In French you often see «à toi de + infinitive» or «c'est à toi de + infinitive». The pronoun order can vary in full sentences (e.g. «C'est facile pour toi de le dire» uses 'pour toi de ...').
target_language_example: C'est à toi de le terminer aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: It's up to you to finish it today.

meaning: 'toi' (you — used in emphatic/disjunctive positions or as attached reflexive '-toi' in imperatives) adjacent to 'de lui' (of/about him) — appears in phrases where 'toi' (or attached '-toi') and 'de lui' occur close together, e.g. responsibility/turn (à toi de lui...) or reflexive imperatives (débarrasse-toi de lui).
additional_notes: The exact sequence 'toi de lui' can appear inside larger constructions but is not a standalone fixed idiom. Two common patterns: 1) 'C'est à toi de lui dire' where 'à toi de' indicates it's your turn/responsibility to do something to/about him. 2) Imperative reflexive verbs: the clitic '-toi' attaches to the verb in affirmative imperatives (débarrasse-toi de lui) meaning 'get rid of him.' Word-order/note: in affirmative imperatives the reflexive pronoun follows the verb with a hyphen; 'lui' after 'de' is a disjunctive/indirect pronoun meaning 'him'/'to him' depending on the verb. Register: informal (imperative reflexive uses informal singular '-toi').
target_language_example: C'est à toi de lui dire.
native_language_example: It's up to you to tell him.

meaning: 'yourself' + 'your' used in familiar imperative/reflexive commands (e.g. 'Occupe-toi de ta...')
additional_notes: This sequence appears when a reflexive verb in the imperative or infinitive is followed by 'de' + a noun with the possessive 'ta' (your). Common in commands and reminders: Occupe-toi de ta ... (Take care of your ...), Souviens-toi de ta ... / Rappelle-toi de ta ... (Remember your ...). The imperative is familiar (tu form). Use 'toi' because the verb is reflexive (s'occuper, se souvenir, se servir, se rappeler).
target_language_example: Occupe-toi de ta chambre.
native_language_example: Take care of your room.

meaning: the reflexive imperative part of 'brush your teeth' (used with 'brosse-toi les dents').
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common command 'Brosse-toi les dents' (Brush your teeth). 'Toi' is the reflexive pronoun for 'tu' placed after the verb with a hyphen in the affirmative imperative. The full phrase is 'Brosse-toi les dents.' In negative commands you would say 'Ne te brosse pas les dents.' 'Lave-toi les dents' is a less common alternative meaning the same.
target_language_example: Brosse-toi les dents avant d'aller te coucher.
native_language_example: Brush your teeth before going to bed.

meaning: the reflexive construction used to tell someone to wash/dry their hands (as in 'wash your hands' or 'dry your hands').
additional_notes: This appears in imperatives with a reflexive verb: 'lave-toi les mains' (wash your hands) or 'essuie-toi les mains' (dry your hands). The pronoun 'toi' is the stressed form used after the verb with a hyphen in the affirmative imperative (lave-toi). In negative commands you would say 'ne te lave pas les mains'. Use 'les mains' (the hands) — French uses the definite article where English uses a possessive.
target_language_example: Lave-toi les mains avant de manger.
native_language_example: Wash your hands before eating.

meaning: 'fell to' or 'fell onto' (past tense of tomber + contraction 'au' = à + le).
additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone falling onto a surface (here 'le sol' = the ground). 'Tomba' is the passé simple of 'tomber' (literary/formal past); in spoken French you'd more often hear 'est tombé(e)'. 'Au' is the contraction of 'à le' and links the verb to a masculine singular noun (e.g. 'au sol').
target_language_example: Il tomba au sol après avoir glissé.
native_language_example: He fell to the ground after slipping.

meaning: to fall in love (with someone).
additional_notes: A common French expression used to say someone begins to feel romantic love. It often appears with a preposition (tomber amoureux de quelqu'un). Can be used reflexively/gendered: tomber amoureux (masc.), tomber amoureuse (fem.). Present progressive is expressed with 'être en train de tomber amoureux'.
target_language_example: Je crois que je commence à tomber amoureux de toi.
native_language_example: I think I'm starting to fall in love with you.

meaning: 'to fall into' (literally) or 'to get into' (a situation or state)
additional_notes: Used both literally (fall into a hole, water, etc.) and figuratively (fall into a habit, mistake, trap, or a state such as depression). Followed by a noun or noun phrase (tomber dans la rue, tomber dans le piège, tomber dans la dépression). If you want to say 'fall into + verb-ing' in English, French often uses 'tomber dans' + noun (tomber dans l'oubli) or 'se mettre à' / 'se retrouver à' + infinitive for actions. Conjugate 'tomber' according to subject.
target_language_example: Il a failli tomber dans le trou.
native_language_example: He almost fell into the hole.

meaning: to faint; to pass out.
additional_notes: Informal idiom meaning to lose consciousness. Used in everyday speech. Literal translation ('to fall into the apples') is nonsensical in English. Can be used in past or future (e.g. « Elle est tombée dans les pommes », « Il va tomber dans les pommes »).
target_language_example: Quand elle a vu le sang, elle est tombée dans les pommes.
native_language_example: When she saw the blood, she fainted.

meaning: to come out of nowhere; to appear unexpectedly (literally: 'to fall from the sky').
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say that something or someone arrived or appeared unexpectedly, often as a pleasant surprise or as an unearned benefit. Can be used for events, help, money, opportunities, or people. Literal sense (objects falling from the sky) is possible but less common in everyday idiomatic use.
target_language_example: Une aide financière ne va pas tomber du ciel; il faut en faire la demande.
native_language_example: Financial help won't fall from the sky; you have to apply for it.

meaning: to break down; to stop working (for machines, vehicles, devices).
additional_notes: Used for mechanical or technical failures (car, machine, appliance, generator, etc.). Often conjugated with être in compound tenses: "il est tombé en panne". Can be used for temporary stoppages (e.g., "la voiture est tombée en panne sur l'autoroute").
target_language_example: La voiture peut tomber en panne à tout moment si on ne l'entretient pas.
native_language_example: The car can break down at any time if you don't maintain it.

meaning: to become pregnant
additional_notes: Common French expression meaning to get pregnant. Literally 'to fall pregnant' (tomber = to fall). Used for women becoming pregnant; typically followed by verbs or time expressions (e.g. 'tomber enceinte de six semaines', 'tomber enceinte rapidement'). Neutral, standard usage.
target_language_example: Elle espère tomber enceinte cette année.
native_language_example: She hopes to become pregnant this year.

meaning: to get sick / fall ill.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone becomes ill (suddenly or unexpectedly). 'Tomber' (to fall) + 'malade' (sick) — literal image of 'falling into illness'. Can be used in warnings, complaints, or descriptions (e.g. Tu vas tomber malade = You'll get sick / You're going to get sick).
target_language_example: Si tu sors sans manteau, tu vas tomber malade.
native_language_example: If you go out without a coat, you'll get sick.

meaning: to come across / to encounter; also to fall onto (physically) or to befall someone (events).
additional_notes: A versatile multi-word verb. Common uses: 1) 'tomber sur quelqu'un/quelque chose' = to encounter or find by chance (e.g., meet someone unexpectedly, discover something). 2) Can mean 'to fall onto' in a physical sense (e.g., fall onto a couch). 3) Used idiomatically to mean something befalls someone (often negative) as in responsibilities or troubles 'falling on' someone. Context and the object determine the sense.
target_language_example: Même là-bas on peut tomber sur de mauvais professeurs.
native_language_example: Even over there you can come across bad teachers.

meaning: 'fallen from' (feminine singular form of 'tombé(e) de')
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (tombé/tombée) plus 'de'/'du' to say someone or something fell from a place. 'Tombée' here is feminine singular; for a male speaker or subject use 'tombé'. 'Du' is the contraction of 'de le' (from the). Can be used literally (fell from the roof) or figuratively/idiomatically (e.g. 'tombée du ciel' = 'fell from the sky' / 'appeared as if from nowhere'). Agreement: subject gender and number change the past participle (tombé, tombée, tombés, tombées).
target_language_example: Elle est tombée du toit ce matin.
native_language_example: She fell from the roof this morning.

meaning: to have broken down while (doing something) / to have a breakdown on the way
additional_notes: Used to say a vehicle (or machine) stopped working during a trip or while doing something. The full verb is 'tomber en panne' (to break down). The preposition 'en' here introduces a time/circumstance like 'en chemin', 'en route', 'en allant au travail' (while/on the way). Conjugate 'tomber' to match the subject (e.g. 'ma voiture est tombée en panne').
target_language_example: Notre voiture est tombée en panne en route pour la gare.
native_language_example: Our car broke down on the way to the station.

meaning: at nightfall; when night falls (dusk/early night).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the time around dusk or the moment when daylight ends and night begins. Common in schedules/plans (arrive/leave by nightfall). Can be preceded by 'à' (à la tombée de la nuit) to mean 'at nightfall' or used without a verb in short statements.
target_language_example: Nous partirons à la tombée de la nuit.
native_language_example: We will leave at nightfall.

meaning: bare-chested; without a shirt
additional_notes: Describes someone whose upper body is uncovered (no shirt). Used for men/boys typically. Can be used literally (physically without a shirt) and sometimes figuratively in descriptions. Adjective phrase: placed after the noun (e.g., 'il était torse nu').
target_language_example: Il était torse nu sur la plage.
native_language_example: He was bare-chested on the beach.

meaning: to knock on wood (to avoid jinxing something); to express a hope that good luck will continue.
additional_notes: Used when mentioning a positive outcome and wanting to prevent bad luck. Often accompanied by physically touching or knocking on wood, or said aloud without action. Equivalent to English 'knock on wood.' Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Jusqu'à présent tout va bien, toucher du bois.
native_language_example: So far everything is fine, knock on wood.

meaning: 'to hit rock bottom' — to reach the lowest point (emotionally, financially, morally, etc.).
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say someone or something has reached a very low point. Can describe feelings, situations (e.g., addiction, depression, finances) or events. Often used with être or avoir: il a touché le fond / il a l'impression d'avoir touché le fond. Not literal unless speaking of physically touching the bottom.
target_language_example: Après des mois sans travail, il a dit qu'il avait touché le fond.
native_language_example: After months without work, he said he had hit rock bottom.

meaning: to come to an end; to be drawing to a close.
additional_notes: Used to describe something (an event, period, project, life, etc.) that is reaching its conclusion. Often found in formal or neutral contexts. Commonly used with nouns like "la journée", "le film", "la période" or abstract things like "sa carrière".
target_language_example: La réunion touche à sa fin, nous allons bientôt présenter les conclusions.
native_language_example: The meeting is coming to an end; we will soon present the conclusions.

meaning: still as / just as (used to compare and say someone/something remains the same in a quality or state)
additional_notes: Placed before an adjective or adverb to emphasize that a quality or condition remains unchanged (positive or negative). Can be used in statements or questions: "toujours aussi + adjective/adverb". Often conveys surprise, admiration, criticism, or continuity (e.g., "still as beautiful", "still as cold").
target_language_example: Il est toujours aussi gentil avec tout le monde.
native_language_example: He is still as kind to everyone.

meaning: 'always need' or 'still need' (dependence or ongoing necessity)
additional_notes: Combines toujours (always/still) + besoin (need). Depending on context, it can mean a continuous/recurring need ('always need') or that someone 'still needs' something now. Often followed by de + infinitive or de + noun (e.g., besoin de se nourrir, besoin de toi, besoin de fric).
target_language_example: Tu as toujours besoin de parler de ça ?
native_language_example: Do you still always need to talk about that?

meaning: magic trick; a trick performed by a magician.
additional_notes: Common phrase to ask or offer to show a simple magic trick. Used both literally (sleight-of-hand, illusions) and sometimes metaphorically to mean a clever trick or stunt. 'Tour' here means 'trick' or 'act'; 'de magie' specifies it's magical. Can be singular or plural (des tours de magie).
target_language_example: Tu veux voir un tour de magie ?
native_language_example: Do you want to see a magic trick?

meaning: a trick, sleight of hand; a clever or deceptive maneuver
additional_notes: Literally refers to a magician's sleight of hand. Used for physical magic tricks and figuratively for any clever, tricky, or deceptive action (e.g., a cunning maneuver, political trick, or clever solution). Often implies deception or showmanship.
target_language_example: Il a fait un tour de passe-passe pour éviter la question.
native_language_example: He pulled a trick to avoid the question.

meaning: to turn/rotate around something (literal); to concern or be about a topic; figuratively, to avoid addressing something directly (to beat around the bush)
additional_notes: Structure: 'tourner autour de' + noun (with article: du/de la/des or de l'). Literal use: physical rotation around an object. Figurative uses: 1) indicate that something concerns a topic (Le débat tourne autour du climat). 2) indicate evasive speech when combined with 'le pot' (tourner autour du pot). Commonly followed by a definite article ('du', 'de la', 'des') or 'de' + noun.
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-nous la vérité.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell us the truth.

meaning: to beat around the bush; to avoid getting to the point.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used when someone is avoiding a direct answer or delaying the main point. Often used in imperatives: "Arrête de tourner autour du pot" = "Stop beating around the bush." Use in conversation when urging clarity or directness.
target_language_example: Arrête de tourner autour du pot et dis-moi ce que tu veux vraiment.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what you really want.

meaning: 'to go around in circles' — to make no progress, to keep repeating the same actions or thoughts.
additional_notes: Used both literally (walking around in a confined space) and figuratively (not making progress on a problem, repeating the same ideas). Common in everyday speech. Can be used with impersonal subject (On tourne en rond), personal subject (Il/Elle tourne en rond), or with an agent (Nous tournons en rond avec ce projet).
target_language_example: Nous continuons de tourner en rond et rien n'avance.
native_language_example: We keep going around in circles and nothing is moving forward.

meaning: to move on; to put the past behind you (literally: 'turn the page').
additional_notes: Common idiom used when talking about leaving a past event, relationship, or situation behind and starting anew. Used both literally (turn a page in a book) and figuratively (emotionally or in life). Can be used with infinitive (tourner la page) or conjugated (il faut tourner la page, j'ai tourné la page).
target_language_example: Après la rupture, elle a décidé de tourner la page.
native_language_example: After the breakup, she decided to move on.

meaning: to turn one's back (literally) / to turn away from or abandon someone (idiomatic)
additional_notes: Can be literal (physically turning so your back faces someone) or idiomatic (to abandon, ignore, refuse support). Usually used with a person or group: tourner le dos à quelqu'un. Context and verbs/tense indicate literal vs. figurative use. Common in both spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Comment oses-tu me tourner le dos ?
native_language_example: How dare you turn your back on me?

meaning: every day
additional_notes: Usually means something happens daily. It is sometimes also used more loosely in expressions like ce n'est pas facile tous les jours, meaning something is not easy day after day or all the time.
target_language_example: Je vais à l'école à pied tous les jours.
native_language_example: I walk to school every day.

meaning: both
additional_notes: Used to refer to two people/things together (both of them). Often follows a subject or object (e.g., "vous tous deux", "nous tous deux"). Can be used with verbs or with nouns. Agreeing in number is handled by the verb or adjective, not by "tous deux" itself.
target_language_example: Ils ont tous deux aimé le film.
native_language_example: They both liked the movie.

meaning: both
additional_notes: Means both of two people or things. It often comes after a pronoun or noun: nous tous les deux = both of us, vous tous les deux = both of you. With two females, French usually uses toutes les deux.
target_language_example: On va y aller tous les deux.
native_language_example: We'll both go there.

meaning: at most; no more than; (indicates an upper limit)
additional_notes: Used to give a maximum estimate or limit (time, quantity, price, size, etc.). Equivalent to 'au plus' or English 'at most' / 'no more than'. Common in both spoken and written French. Can follow the quantity/time it limits (e.g., 'une semaine tout au plus') or precede a verb phrase ('Il peut tout au plus...').
target_language_example: Je réserverai une heure, tout au plus.
native_language_example: I'll book one hour, at most.

meaning: after careful thought; on second thought
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion reached after considering something. Often placed at the start or end of a sentence to indicate the speaker has reconsidered or weighed options. Equivalent to 'all things considered' or 'when I think about it' in English.
target_language_example: Tout bien réfléchi, je préfère accepter l'offre.
native_language_example: After thinking it over, I prefer to accept the offer.

meaning: all right; OK; fine (used to agree or say something is good)
additional_notes: Informal expression used to show agreement, approval, or that something is acceptable. Can be used alone (Tout bon !) or before a noun/adjective to mean 'completely' or 'really' in some contexts (less common). Tone and context determine if it means 'okay', 'good', or 'that's fine.'
target_language_example: Tu veux qu'on parte maintenant? — Tout bon.
native_language_example: You want us to leave now? — All right.

meaning: just like; exactly like; as well as
additional_notes: Used to compare similarity or to add someone/something in the same situation. Can introduce a comparison ('just like X') or indicate inclusion ('X, as well as Y'). Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause. Neutral register.
target_language_example: Elle veut réussir tout comme sa sœur.
native_language_example: She wants to succeed just like her sister.

meaning: exactly like someone; the spitting image of; just like (used after a noun/pronoun).
additional_notes: Informal expression used after a noun or name to say someone looks or behaves exactly like another person (often a parent). Literally 'all spat' — idiomatic. Common in spoken French: «C'est toi tout craché» = 'You're just like it/you'.
target_language_example: Il est son frère tout craché.
native_language_example: He's the spitting image of his brother.

meaning: still / all the same / nevertheless (adds contrast, surprise, or emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to soften a contradiction, express mild surprise or emphasis, or to say 'nevertheless' or 'anyway.' Tone depends on context: can show disbelief (Je dois tout de même demander pourquoi?), refusal/objection (Je ne vais tout de même pas payer...), admiration despite reservations (tout de même impressionnant), or emphasize annoyance (il a du culot, tout de même!).
target_language_example: Il pleuvait, mais nous sommes sortis tout de même.
native_language_example: It was raining, but we went out all the same.

meaning: right away
additional_notes: A very common adverb phrase for doing something without delay. In some contexts, especially when speaking to customers or guests, it can also mean 'in just a moment' or 'I'll be right with you.'
target_language_example: Je reviens tout de suite.
native_language_example: I'll be right back.

meaning: straight ahead; go straight/onward.
additional_notes: Used for giving directions or describing movement in a straight line. Can mean 'straight on' (keep going without turning) or 'straight down' depending on context. Common in both spoken and written French for navigation.
target_language_example: Continuez tout droit jusqu'au rond-point.
native_language_example: Keep going straight until the roundabout.

meaning: out loud; aloud (spoken so others can hear).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is said or thought audibly. Common with verbs like dire, parler, penser, lire. Can be swapped with 'à haute voix' (more formal). Not to be confused with 'tout haut' meaning 'very high' — in this phrase it means 'completely/entirely' + 'high' (spoken loud), but functionally translates to 'out loud'.
target_language_example: Ne dis pas ça tout haut ici.
native_language_example: Don't say that out loud here.

meaning: all the
additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun. It often means "the whole" or "all the." In your examples, it appears in the fixed expression "tout le temps," which means "all the time" or "constantly."
target_language_example: J'ai regardé tout le film.
native_language_example: I watched the whole movie.

meaning: fully attentive; all ears.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is listening very carefully. Literally 'all ear(s)'; often used after 'être' (je suis tout ouïe). Can be used for singular people or groups (ton public est tout ouïe). Slightly literary but common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je suis tout ouïe — raconte-moi ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: I'm all ears — tell me what happened.

meaning: very small; (when said of a person) make oneself very small or inconspicuous.
additional_notes: Can describe size (very tiny) or, with a person, the idea of shrinking back or making oneself unnoticeable (Je me ferai tout petit = I'll make myself very small / I'll keep a low profile). Often used before a noun (un tout petit appartement) or after a verb/pronoun for the figurative sense.
target_language_example: Elle a acheté un tout petit gâteau pour la fête.
native_language_example: She bought a very small cake for the party.

meaning: all alone
additional_notes: Used for being alone or doing something without help. It often translates as "alone," "by yourself," or "on your own." The form changes to match the person: toute seule, tout seuls, toutes seules.
target_language_example: Je peux le faire tout seul.
native_language_example: I can do it on my own.

meaning: be all smiles; with a big smile
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is smiling broadly or looking very pleased/happy. Often placed after être (être tout sourire) or used adjectivally: 'Il est tout sourire.' Informal/neutral tone. Not literal—'tout' here intensifies 'sourire' (compositional to some degree).
target_language_example: Elle est tout sourire après la bonne nouvelle.
native_language_example: She is all smiles after the good news.

meaning: suddenly; all of a sudden.
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens abruptly or unexpectedly. Can appear at beginning, middle, or end of a sentence. Synonyms: soudain, tout d'un coup. Neutral register (not slang).
target_language_example: Tout à coup, la musique a cessé.
native_language_example: Suddenly, the music stopped.

meaning: completely
additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase to emphasize degree or to agree strongly. Common translations include "completely/absolutely" (strong emphasis) and "quite" or "entirely" (softer). Often used alone as a short, polite agreement like "Absolutely" or "Exactly." Can appear before adjectives or after verbs (e.g., "pas tout à fait" = "not quite").
target_language_example: Ce projet est tout à fait faisable.
native_language_example: This project is completely feasible.

meaning: in a little while / shortly; a short time ago (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Can refer to a near future ('see/speak you shortly') or a recent past ('earlier a little while ago') depending on context and intonation. Common in everyday speech. Use present/future verbs for future sense (Je te rappelle tout à l'heure = I'll call you soon) and past/reference verbs for past sense (La fille qui était là tout à l'heure = the girl who was here a little while ago). Alone, it can mean 'See you soon' or 'A moment ago.'
target_language_example: Je passe chez toi tout à l'heure pour déposer le livre.
native_language_example: I'll stop by your place in a little while to drop off the book.

meaning: all the time
additional_notes: Used to say something happens very often or continuously. It can be neutral, or it can suggest annoyance depending on context.
target_language_example: Il est tout le temps en retard.
native_language_example: He's late all the time.

meaning: everything that / all that (which).
additional_notes: Used to refer broadly to all things of a certain type or whatever fits a description. Often followed by a relative clause (est + adjective, or a verb clause). Can be followed by subjunctive after expressions like 'tout ce qui te plaît / te chante' but indicative is common.
target_language_example: J'aime tout ce qui brille.
native_language_example: I like everything that shines.

meaning: 'everything that' (used before a verb starting with 'est' in examples: 'everything that happened').
additional_notes: This is the beginning of the phrase 'tout ce qui s'est ...' meaning 'everything that ...' or 'all that ...' followed by a past participle (e.g. 's'est passé' = 'happened'). The contraction s' comes from the reflexive pronoun 'se' before a vowel (s'est). Common in sentences referring to events or things that occurred. Can be shortened in speech: 'tout ce qui s'est passé' → 'tout ce qui s'est'.
target_language_example: Je n'oublierai jamais tout ce qui s'est passé.
native_language_example: I will never forget everything that happened.

meaning: 'everything' or 'all things' — note: 'tout chose' is nonstandard in modern French; forms and usage depend on gender/number.
additional_notes: 'Tout chose' as written is uncommon or archaic. Modern French normally uses 'toute chose' (rare, formal), 'toutes les choses' (all the things), or simply 'tout'/'tout le monde' depending on context. Pay attention to agreement: tout/toute/tous/toutes. Use of 'tout chose' may be found in older texts or poetic contexts; avoid in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Tout chose considérée, il faut agir avec prudence.
native_language_example: All things considered, one must act with caution.

meaning: all things considered; when you think it over
additional_notes: Used to express a conclusion or change of mind after weighing factors. Common in spoken and written French. Often placed at the start of a sentence, or alone as a short comment (with or without punctuation).
target_language_example: Tout compte fait, je vais accepter l'offre.
native_language_example: All things considered, I'm going to accept the offer.

meaning: 'everything is under' — used as the start of phrases meaning 'everything is under control' or 'everything is secured'.
additional_notes: This fragment is typically completed by a noun: most common is 'contrôle' (tout est sous contrôle = everything is under control). It can also be followed by 'clé' (sous clé = locked up) or other nouns. In everyday speech you will often hear the full phrase 'Tout est sous contrôle.' Useful for assuring someone that a situation is handled or that items are secured.
target_language_example: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout est sous contrôle.
native_language_example: Don't worry, everything is under control.

meaning: 'everything' or 'did everything' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: 1) as a phrase meaning 'everything' (Il a tout fait = He did everything / he did it all) or 'they did everything' (Ils ont tout fait). 2) in expressions like 'tout fait à la main' = 'everything made by hand'. Context tells whether it's a noun phrase ('tout' = everything) or part of a verb phrase ('a tout fait' = did everything). 'Tout' is variable in agreement in other constructions but here is invariable.
target_language_example: Elle a tout fait pour réussir l'examen.
native_language_example: She did everything to pass the exam.

meaning: everyone
additional_notes: Refers to all people in a group or people in general. Even though it means more than one person, it normally takes a singular verb in French: tout le monde est..., not sont.... Literally it is "all the world," but the usual English translation is "everyone" or "everybody."
target_language_example: Tout le monde est prêt ?
native_language_example: Is everyone ready?

meaning: 'anything but a' / 'far from being a'.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to strongly deny that someone is that kind of person — equivalent to 'far from being a...' or 'anything but a...'. Often followed by a noun (sometimes with an article). Tone can be emphatic and sometimes ironic. Can be used with professions, character traits, or labels.
target_language_example: Il est tout sauf un ami.
native_language_example: He is anything but a friend.

meaning: all that
additional_notes: Refers to a group of things, information, or a situation that is visible or already understood from context. Very common in everyday French; more casual than tout cela.
target_language_example: Je ne comprends pas tout ça.
native_language_example: I don't understand all that.

meaning: toxic at higher doses / can become toxic if taken in larger amounts.
additional_notes: Used to warn that a substance is safe or harmless at low doses but becomes harmful or toxic when the dose increases. Common in medical, pharmacological or food-safety contexts. Literal components: 'toxique' (toxic), 'à plus forte dose' (at a stronger/larger dose).
target_language_example: Ce médicament est généralement sans danger, mais il devient toxique à plus forte dose.
native_language_example: This medicine is generally safe, but it becomes toxic at higher doses.

meaning: train from
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. After train, de often gives the place the train comes from (train de Paris = train from Paris) or its scheduled time (train de huit heures = the eight o'clock train). In sentences like empêcher le train de rouler, de belongs to the verb pattern empêcher ... de + infinitive, not to train itself.
target_language_example: Le train de Marseille arrive à 18 heures.
native_language_example: The train from Marseille arrives at 6 p.m.

meaning: used to indicate something one is about to say or to signal the act of saying (literally: 'in the process of saying').
additional_notes: Très informel et peu utilisé seul; 'être en train de dire' means 'to be in the process of saying'. Without 'être', 'train de dire' by itself is incomplete in standard French. You will commonly see the structure 'je suis en train de dire...' or 'j'étais en train de dire...' to emphasize a continuous action (I am/was saying...). Works with other verbs: 'il est en train de manger'.
target_language_example: Je suis en train de dire la vérité.
native_language_example: I am in the process of saying the truth. / I am telling the truth.

meaning: 'train de' + verb indicates an action in progress; here it would mean 'is reading a...' (i.e. 'is in the process of reading a...')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself; 'être/train de + infinitive' (more commonly 'être en train de + infinitive') expresses that someone is currently doing something. 'Train de lire un' would appear before a noun or phrase (e.g. 'Je suis en train de lire un livre' = 'I am reading a book'). Beginners should learn the full, common form 'être en train de + infinitive'.
target_language_example: Je suis en train de lire un roman intéressant.
native_language_example: I am reading an interesting novel.

meaning: literally 'train was'; likely part of a sentence describing a train's state or location (past tense of être with 'train').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself — it's the noun 'train' (train) followed by the imperfect or past tense of 'être' (was/were). You will usually see it inside a larger sentence, e.g. 'Le train était en retard' (The train was late) or 'Le train était plein' (The train was full). Choose the tense (imparfait, passé composé, etc.) depending on context.
target_language_example: Le train était en retard ce matin.
native_language_example: The train was late this morning.

meaning: the train had already (left).
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'le train' (the train) with 'était déjà' (was already) and is used to say the train had already gone/left by the time something happened. In English you usually translate it with the past perfect ('had already left') or simple past depending on context. You can replace 'le train' with other subjects (e.g. 'le bus était déjà', 'la réunion était déjà').
target_language_example: Quand je suis arrivé, le train était déjà parti.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the train had already left.

meaning: word processing (software or the act of editing text on a computer).
additional_notes: Refers typically to software used to create, edit and format written documents (e.g., Microsoft Word, Google Docs). Can mean the program itself or the activity of using such a program. Common in contexts asking about which program someone uses or whether they know how to use one.
target_language_example: J'ai besoin d'un logiciel de traitement de texte pour rédiger mon rapport.
native_language_example: I need a word processing program to write my report.

meaning: turned into; transformed into; became (something else).
additional_notes: Past tense of 'se transformer en' (to transform into). Used for physical or figurative changes (objects, people, feelings, voice, etc.). Often appears with the reflexive pronoun 'se' (se transforma en) but can appear without it in transitive constructions depending on context. Common in narratives, fairy tales, and descriptive language.
target_language_example: Par degrés, leur amitié se transforma en amour.
native_language_example: Gradually, their friendship transformed into love.

meaning: 'to pass on' or 'to convey' (usually followed by 'message' or similar: 'to pass on a...').
additional_notes: Commonly used with 'message' (transmettre un message) meaning to give someone a message for another person. Can also mean to transmit/send information or an object. Polite requests: 'Pouvez-vous lui transmettre un message ?' = 'Can you pass a message on to him/her?'.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous lui transmettre un message de ma part ?
native_language_example: Can you pass a message on to him/her for me?

meaning: teamwork; work done by a group together.
additional_notes: Used to describe activities or tasks performed collaboratively by a group. Can be used as a noun phrase ('Le travail d'équipe est important') or as a short label ('Travail d'équipe'). Emphasizes cooperation and coordination.
target_language_example: Le succès du projet vient du bon travail d'équipe.
native_language_example: The project's success comes from good teamwork.

meaning: work here; (often) tasks or job to do in this place or context.
additional_notes: Used to refer to work or tasks located 'here' (this place or situation). Can mean ongoing duties ('J'ai encore du travail ici' = I still have work to do here) or completion ('Mon travail ici est terminé' = my work here is finished). 'Travail' can be uncountable (du travail) or countable (le travail) depending on context. 'Ici' can be literal (a physical place) or figurative (in this role/situation).
target_language_example: Il reste encore du travail ici avant la réunion.
native_language_example: There is still work to do here before the meeting.

meaning: 'work all' — used with a following feminine time period to indicate working for the entire duration (e.g. 'travailler toute la journée' = 'to work all day').
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom on its own; 'travailler' + 'toute' requires a feminine time noun after ('la journée', 'la nuit', 'la matinée'). For masculine time nouns use 'tout le' (e.g. 'travailler tout le matin'). Agreement: 'toute' is feminine singular. Common constructions: 'travailler toute la journée', 'travailler toute la nuit', 'travailler toute la matinée'.
target_language_example: Elles nous ont fait travailler toute la journée.
