meaning: real life; everyday, actual life (as opposed to fiction, imagination, or online life).
additional_notes: Used to contrast what happens in books, films, virtual/online worlds, dreams, or performances with everyday reality. Can refer to someone's real-life situation or the real world in general.
target_language_example: Dans la vie réelle, il faut souvent travailler dur pour réussir.
native_language_example: In real life, you often have to work hard to succeed.

meaning: "life devoted to" or "life spent (doing)" — used in phrases where someone's life is given to or spent on something, or in fixed expressions like wishes (e.g., "Longue vie à...").
additional_notes: Typically appears in contexts such as "passer sa vie à...", "consacrer sa vie à...", "dédier sa vie à..." or in exclamations like "Longue vie à...". After "à" you may find an infinitive (for actions) or a noun/definite phrase (for a person, cause, or thing). The exact phrase "vie à la" occurs when the article "la" precedes a feminine noun or part of a fixed expression.
target_language_example: Il a consacré toute sa vie à la science.
native_language_example: He devoted his whole life to science.

meaning: life in/of (a particular setting) — 'life in the ...' or 'life of the ...'.
additional_notes: Used to describe a way of life tied to a location or condition: e.g. la vie à la campagne (life in the countryside), la vie à la mer (life by the sea). Often followed by a noun with the definite article la. Not a fixed idiom by itself; it combines with a place or state. Can also appear in poetic or contrasting expressions (e.g. la vie à la mort).
target_language_example: La vie à la campagne lui convient parfaitement.
native_language_example: Life in the countryside suits her perfectly.

meaning: life was
additional_notes: A combination of the noun vie (life) + the imperfect of être (was). Literally 'life was'. In context it often appears with a possessive (ma/sa) or subject (la/sa) — e.g. "ma vie était..." = "my life was..." Use to describe past states or situations. Not an idiom; meaning is compositional and literal.
target_language_example: Ma vie était plus simple avant.
native_language_example: My life was simpler before.

meaning: an old/longtime friend of mine (used before a possessive expression).
additional_notes: Used in the construction 'un vieil ami à moi' (or 'une vieille amie à moi') to mean 'an old/longtime friend of mine'. The phrase literally mixes 'vieil ami' (old friend) with 'à moi' (of mine). It's colloquial but common in spoken and written French. You can replace 'à moi' with another possessor (e.g. 'à lui', 'à elle'). Use 'vieil' before masculine nouns starting with a vowel sound (vieil ami) and 'vieux ami' elsewhere (e.g. 'un vieux ami' before consonant).
target_language_example: Elle a rencontré un vieil ami à elle au marché.
native_language_example: She met an old friend of hers at the market.

meaning: 'spinster' or 'unmarried woman (old-fashioned, often pejorative)'
additional_notes: Literally 'old girl'. Used to describe a woman who has never married, usually older — the term is dated and can be derogatory. In modern usage it's often avoided; use célibataire (single) or femme non mariée for neutral terms. Can be used jokingly in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Elle est restée vieille fille toute sa vie.
native_language_example: She remained a spinster her whole life.

meaning: old town; the historic part of a town or city.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the older, often historic district of a city (narrow streets, old buildings). In French, 'vieille' agrees in gender with 'ville' (feminine). Can mean 'an old city' when used without the article (e.g. 'une vieille ville').
target_language_example: Nous avons visité la vieille ville cet après-midi.
native_language_example: We visited the old town this afternoon.

meaning: old-fashioned; from the old school (traditional, conservative).
additional_notes: Used to describe a person, idea, style or method that follows older traditions or conservative ways. Can be neutral, affectionate, or mildly critical depending on tone and context. Often used as «être de la vieille école» (to be old-school).
target_language_example: Il est de la vieille école : il préfère les méthodes classiques.
native_language_example: He's old-school: he prefers classical methods.

meaning: spoken negative form of venir: "(I/you) don't come" or "(I/you) am/are not coming".
additional_notes: Informal, colloquial contraction of "ne ... pas" around the verb venir. Often used in speech and casual writing; standard form is "ne viens pas" (tu) or "je ne viens pas" (je). Context decides subject: with no subject shown, it can be part of a sentence addressing someone (tu) or reporting about oneself (je) when combined with a subject pronoun. Used for commands (Ne viens pas !) and statements (Je viens pas / Tu ne viens pas ?).
target_language_example: Je viens pas ce soir, désolé.
native_language_example: I'm not coming tonight, sorry.

meaning: 'come (here) more' or part of commands with 'plus' meaning 'no more' / 'closer' / 'earlier' depending on context
additional_notes: This phrase appears in two different uses because 'plus' has multiple meanings in commands: 1) 'ne ... plus' = 'no longer / don't (do something) anymore' (negative imperative): e.g. 'Ne viens plus me voir' = 'Don't come see me anymore.' 2) In positive imperatives, 'plus' can mean 'more' or 'closer' or 'earlier' when combined with verbs: 'Viens plus près' = 'Come closer.' or 'Viens plus tôt' = 'Come earlier.' Pay attention to negation: 'Ne viens plus...' = stop doing it; 'Viens plus...' = come more/closer/earlier.
target_language_example: Ne viens plus m'embêter, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Don't bother me anymore, please.

meaning: come to (a place or event); an invitation or question asking someone to attend or come over.
additional_notes: Used to invite or ask if someone will attend an event or go to a location. 'Viens' is the informal singular imperative or present tense (tu) of venir. The preposition 'à' + definite article + place/event follows (à la fête, à la réunion, à la cuisine). For formal or plural address use 'venez à la'. Often shortened in speech to 'tu viens à...' meaning 'are you coming to...'.
target_language_example: Tu viens à la fête ce soir ?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party tonight?

meaning: '(he/she/it) comes to (see) us' or 'comes to visit us'.
additional_notes: Vient is the 3rd-person singular present of venir (to come). 'Nous' is the object pronoun 'us' and follows the verb in standard word order. Often used with verbs of seeing/visiting (voir, rendre visite) or simply venir + infinitive. Context determines whether it's 'comes to see us', 'comes to visit us', or 'comes by'.
target_language_example: Il vient nous aider ce week-end.
native_language_example: He is coming to help us this weekend.

meaning: 'lives are in' (literal sequence of words); incomplete fragment — not a standalone phrase
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression. It's a sequence of words that could appear inside a sentence (e.g. "nos vies sont en danger" = "our lives are in danger"). You can't use "vies sont en" alone; it needs a complement (a noun or adjective) after "en". "Vies" is the plural of "vie" (life), "sont" is the 3rd-person plural of "être" (are), and "en" is a preposition/pronoun with various uses (here meaning "in" or part of a phrase like "en danger").
target_language_example: Leurs vies sont en danger à cause de la tempête.
native_language_example: Their lives are in danger because of the storm.

meaning: old-fashioned; traditional (often with a mildly critical tone)
additional_notes: Used to describe a person, their ideas, or behavior as out of date, conservative, or not modern. Can be mildly teasing or critical depending on tone. Agreement: when describing a feminine plural noun, use form 'vieilles jeux' is incorrect — correct adjective agreement is 'vieux' stays unchanged before masculine plural nouns, but for feminine use 'vieille(s)' (however the fixed expression is most often used with people/ideas as 'vieux jeu' for men or 'vieux jeu' applied generally). Commonly used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ses vêtements sont un peu vieux jeu, mais il s'en fiche.
native_language_example: His clothes are a bit old-fashioned, but he doesn't care.

meaning: ‘the town/city where I...’ — beginning of a relative clause locating where the speaker does something or is from.
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own; it starts a clause that must be finished (e.g. ville où je suis né / ville où je vis). 'Ville' = city/town. 'Où' = where (relative pronoun: place or time). Use it to give the place connected to the subject 'je'. Word order: 'ville où je' + verb or past participle. Common completions: 'je vis' (I live), 'je suis né(e)' (I was born), 'j'ai grandi' (I grew up).
target_language_example: C'est la ville où je suis né.
native_language_example: This is the town where I was born.

meaning: 'the city was' (simple past/state description).
additional_notes: Combines ville (city/town) with était (imperfect of être = 'was'). Used to describe a past or ongoing state or background condition. In English you'd usually translate as 'the city was...' followed by an adjective or past participle. Étaient would be plural for 'les villes étaient'.
target_language_example: La ville était vivante la nuit.
native_language_example: The city was lively at night.

meaning: white wine.
additional_notes: Commonly used to refer to wine made from white grapes or light-colored wine. Used in drinking/restaurant contexts (e.g., ordering a glass) and comparing preferences (vin blanc vs. vin rouge = white wine vs. red wine). Pronunciation: 'van blahn'.
target_language_example: Un verre de vin blanc, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: A glass of white wine, please.

meaning: 'the wine is' (subject + verb 'être')
additional_notes: This is the phrase 'vin est' where 'vin' (wine) is the subject and 'est' is the third-person singular of 'être' (to be). It appears in sentences that describe how wine is made (e.g., 'Le vin est fabriqué...' — 'The wine is made...'). In natural French you usually include the definite article: 'Le vin est...'.
target_language_example: Le vin est vieilli en fûts de chêne.
native_language_example: The wine is aged in oak barrels.

meaning: red wine.
additional_notes: Common phrase for wine made from red grapes. Used when ordering or talking about wine preferences. Plural form is vins rouges (but often stays as vin rouge when talking in general). Can be preceded by partitive/article (du vin rouge, un verre de vin rouge).
target_language_example: Je vais prendre un verre de vin rouge, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'll have a glass of red wine, please.

meaning: 'wine on' (the combination of the noun vin + the preposition sur: indicates wine located on or spilled onto something)
additional_notes: This is not an idiom—it's simply the noun vin ('wine') followed by the preposition sur ('on', 'onto', 'upon'). Used to say that wine is resting on a surface (e.g. 'une bouteille de vin sur la table') or that wine has been spilled onto something (e.g. 'du vin sur sa chemise'). Word order is noun + sur; articles and determiners (du, une, le) still apply.
target_language_example: Il y a du vin sur la nappe.
native_language_example: There is wine on the tablecloth.

meaning: twenty-five (25).
additional_notes: A cardinal number. Used for quantities, ages, dates (e.g., le vingt-cinq décembre = December 25th), money, etc. Pronounced [vɛ̃t siŋ]. In dates spoken with day + month, the article le is used: le vingt-cinq décembre. Written with a hyphen.
target_language_example: Il a vingt-cinq ans.
native_language_example: He is twenty-five years old.

meaning: the number twenty-two (22); used for time, age, dates, or counting.
additional_notes: Pronounced [vɛ̃.dø]. Used like the English 'twenty-two' for hours (e.g. vingt-deux heures = 10 p.m.), ages, calendar dates (le vingt-deux janvier = the 22nd of January), and simple counting or lists. In spoken French, numbers are often linked to the context (time, âge, date) so include the unit (heures, ans, janvier) when needed.
target_language_example: La réunion commence à vingt-deux heures.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at ten p.m. (22:00).

meaning: 'twenty-six' (the number 26).
additional_notes: Used as a cardinal number for counting, dates, ages, quantities, etc. In dates you may hear both 'le vingt-six octobre' (the 26th of October) and simply 'le vingt-six' when the month is understood. Hyphenated in modern French spelling: vingt-six.
target_language_example: Aujourd'hui nous sommes le vingt-six mars.
native_language_example: Today is the twenty-sixth of March.

meaning: twenty-three (the number 23).
additional_notes: Used as a numeral for age, time (hours), measurement, counting, or standalone answers. In spoken French, hyphenated numbers from 21 to 99 use hyphens (vingt-trois). Pronunciation: [vɛ̃ twa].
target_language_example: Il a vingt-trois ans et habite à Paris.
native_language_example: He is twenty-three years old and lives in Paris.

meaning: the number 'twenty-one'.
additional_notes: Used to say the number 21. Appears in counts, ages, scores, or when calling out a number (e.g., in a game or taking a turn). In compound numbers like 81 it appears as part of 'quatre‑vingt‑un' (literally 'four‑twenty‑one' = 81). Pronunciation and liaison rules can affect sounds in connected speech.
target_language_example: J'ai vingt‑un ans.
native_language_example: I am twenty-one years old.

meaning: 'twenty-one' (the number 21).
additional_notes: Used whenever referring to the number 21. In French numbers, 'et' is used between tens and 'un' for 21, 31, 41, 51, and 61 (e.g., vingt et un, trente et un). Pronunciation: the 't' in 'et' is pronounced; the final 't' of 'vingt' is usually silent unless followed by a vowel in liaison.
target_language_example: Il y a vingt et un étudiants dans la classe.
native_language_example: There are twenty-one students in the class.

meaning: 'visited and how long' — used when asking which place someone visited and the duration of their stay.
additional_notes: This phrase combines the past participle 'visité' (visited) with a question about duration 'combien de (temps)'. Often followed by 'temps' (time) and a subject-verb (e.g., 'es-tu resté(e)?', 'êtes-vous resté(e)(s)?'). Gender and number affect past participle agreement (resté vs restée, restés, restées). Common in informal and formal questions about travel.
target_language_example: Quel pays as-tu visité et combien de temps es-tu restée ?
native_language_example: Which country did you visit and how long did you stay?

meaning: 'vitamin A' (a fat‑soluble vitamin important for vision, skin and immune system).
additional_notes: Used like in English to talk about the specific vitamin. Often appears with verbs like contenir (contain), être riche en (be rich in), or être toxique (be toxic) at high doses. In French the article and gender: 'la vitamine A' (feminine).
target_language_example: Les carottes sont une bonne source de vitamine A.
native_language_example: Carrots are a good source of vitamin A.

meaning: vitamin C (the nutrient).
additional_notes: Refers to the essential nutrient (ascorbic acid) found in fruits and vegetables and in supplements. Used just like in English: can talk about foods that contain it or taking it for health. In French the measure is feminine: 'la vitamine C' and you can say 'contient de la vitamine C' or 'riche en vitamine C'.
target_language_example: Je prends de la vitamine C quand je sens un rhume arriver.
native_language_example: I take vitamin C when I feel a cold coming on.

meaning: quickly; in a quick, informal way.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done fast, often informally. Can modify verbs (faire quelque chose vite fait) or be used alone as a short reply meaning "quickly" or "briefly." Tone can be casual; context may imply a quick, possibly rough job rather than thorough.
target_language_example: Je vais préparer le repas vite fait.
native_language_example: I'll prepare the meal quickly.

meaning: 'live longer' (they live longer)
additional_notes: Literal: 'vivent' = they live (from vivre), 'plus' = more/longer. Used to compare lifespans or duration: 'vivre plus longtemps' is the full phrase. Here 'vivent plus' is followed by 'longtemps' or the comparison context (e.g. 'que les hommes' = than men).
target_language_example: Les femmes vivent plus longtemps que les hommes.
native_language_example: Women live longer than men.

meaning: we live in a (…)
additional_notes: A common phrase used to describe the environment, situation or place where 'we' live. Combine with a noun (monde, pays, quartier, etc.) and often followed by an adjective: "vivons dans un monde/ un pays + adjective." Conjugation note: 'vivons' is the first-person plural (nous) form of 'vivre' (to live). To talk about 'I live in a...', use 'je vis dans un/une'.
target_language_example: Nous vivons dans un monde plein d'espoir.
native_language_example: We live in a world full of hope.

meaning: we live in a (…)
additional_notes: First-person plural present tense of vivre + preposition dans + indefinite article une. Used to say where a group including the speaker lives (a city, house, farm, etc.). Followed by a noun or noun phrase describing the place. Change article/gender/number as needed (ex: nous vivons dans un appartement; nous vivons dans le sud).
target_language_example: Nous vivons dans une petite maison près de la mer.
native_language_example: We live in a small house near the sea.

meaning: to live a (life/experience) — used before a noun like vie (life) or expérience (experience).
additional_notes: Common construction: vivre + une + [noun]. Often followed by vie (une vie) or expérience (une expérience). Means to experience or spend one's life in a certain way (to have/lead a life, or to go through an experience). Use vivre (infinitive) with appropriate subject and tense: Je veux vivre une vie heureuse = I want to live a happy life.
target_language_example: Elle espère vivre une vie pleine de voyages.
native_language_example: She hopes to live a life full of travel.

meaning: railway; railroad track(s).
additional_notes: Refers to the tracks or the railway line used by trains. Can mean the physical tracks (the line you cross) or the railway route (a railway service). Often used with traverser (to cross) or long de (along).
target_language_example: Il traverse la voie ferrée pour aller au travail.
native_language_example: He crosses the railway track to go to work.

meaning: See this / you should see this (informal imperative/suggestion).
additional_notes: From the verb voir (to see) in subjunctive or familiar imperative-like constructions: phrases like «Il faut que tu voies ça» or «Faut que tu voies ça» mean 'you need to see this' or 'you should see this' — used to urge someone to look at or watch something (a photo, video, situation, etc.). In casual speech, subject pronouns and 'il' can be dropped: «Faut que tu voies ça.» Not a literal idiom; it's a direct request/suggestion.
target_language_example: Tu dois venir, faut que tu voies ça.
native_language_example: You have to come, you need to see this.

meaning: this is how / that's how (used to introduce an explanation or the way something is done or seen).
additional_notes: Common phrase to present a method, explanation, or opinion. Often placed at the start of a sentence to summarize or conclude: 'Voilà comment...' + clause. Tone is neutral; can be used in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Voilà comment on a résolu le problème.
native_language_example: That's how we solved the problem.

meaning: that's all; that's it; nothing more to say.
additional_notes: Used to conclude a statement or to downplay/finish an explanation. Can sound dismissive or final. Often follows a clause to indicate there's no deeper reason or nothing else to add (English equivalents: "that's all", "that's it"). Common in spoken French.
target_language_example: Je n'ai pas menti, voilà tout.
native_language_example: I didn't lie, that's all.

meaning: to have to do with; to be related to; to discuss/arrange with (depending on context).
additional_notes: Commonly used in two senses: 1) Être/avoir quelque chose à voir avec = 'to be related to' or 'to have something to do with' (cause or relation). Example: "rien à voir avec" = 'nothing to do with.' 2) Voir avec quelqu'un = 'check with' or 'arrange with' (ask or coordinate with someone). Context determines meaning.
target_language_example: Je dois voir avec mon collègue avant de confirmer.
native_language_example: I need to check with my colleague before confirming.

meaning: 'see what I' — start of phrases meaning to look at or check what I (am doing/see/can do/just did).
additional_notes: This is a fragment used to introduce what the speaker is doing, has done, can do, or is seeing. It typically continues with a verb (e.g. vois, fais, peux faire, viens de faire) and is followed by an object or clause. Common uses: inviter someone to look (Viens voir ce que je fais), offer to check (Laisse-moi voir ce que je peux faire), or report perception (Vous devriez voir ce que je vois).
target_language_example: Regarde, viens voir ce que je viens de découvrir.
native_language_example: Look, come see what I just discovered.

meaning: 'to see clearly' — both literally (visually) and figuratively (to understand a situation).
additional_notes: Can be used for physical sight (e.g., after cleaning glasses) or for understanding/confusion resolution (to 'see the truth' or 'get a clear picture'). Common constructions: 'voir clair dans (quelque chose)' = understand something clearly, or 'ne pas voir clair' = not understand / be suspicious. Often followed by a direct object or an explanation clause.
target_language_example: Je commence à voir clair dans cette affaire.
native_language_example: I'm beginning to see clearly in/understand this matter.

meaning: to check on how you are / to see how you are doing
additional_notes: Common conversational phrase used when someone wants to find out another person's state, progress, or reaction. Often appears in past or present (je suis venu voir comment tu allais / je viens voir comment tu vas). Can be followed by different verbs (vas, allais, vas te mettre) depending on tense and context. Polite and neutral; not slang. Use with tu for informal singular 'you'. For formal or plural use 'voir comment vous...'.
target_language_example: Je viens voir comment tu vas après ton opération.
native_language_example: I'm coming to see how you're doing after your surgery.

meaning: to see in/into; depending on context, either 'to perceive inside/within' (visual perception) or part of the verb phrase 'voir' plus a prepositional complement indicating location (to visit or meet someone in/at a place).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom — compositional: 'voir' (to see/visit) + 'dans' (in/inside/within). Common uses: 1) literal perception with 'dans' indicating environment or medium (voir dans le noir = see in the dark), 2) encountering or visiting someone located in a place (te voir dans cet hôtel = to see you at/in that hotel), 3) appears in larger expressions or quotations (voir dans le monde). Context determines whether it means visual perception or meeting/visiting.
target_language_example: Est‑ce que les chats peuvent vraiment voir dans le noir ?
native_language_example: Can cats really see in the dark?

meaning: 'see (me/it) when you...' — used to invite someone to visit or check something at a time that suits them
additional_notes: Common in informal and neutral contexts. Usually followed by a verb like veux, peux, voudras, souhaites, auras du temps. Can mean 'come see me when you want' or 'look/check it when you have time.' Tone depends on the verb used: veux/woudras = more casual offer; auras du temps = when you have time. The phrase is compositional (literal meaning clear) and not a false cognate.
target_language_example: Passe me voir quand tu veux.
native_language_example: Drop by to see me whenever you want.

meaning: to anticipate or foresee; (informal) to have enough resources/room to cope with the future
additional_notes: Primary sense: 'voir venir' means to see something coming / anticipate an event (J'aurais dû le voir venir = I should have seen it coming). Informal uses: can mean 'to leave margin/cover for the future' or 'to wait and see' depending on context (Je te passe quelques dollars, pour voir venir = I'll give you some dollars to tide you over / to have some buffer). Also appears in expressions like 'avoir de quoi voir venir' meaning 'to have enough to get by/plan ahead.'
target_language_example: Garde un peu d'argent de côté pour voir venir.
native_language_example: Keep some money aside to be prepared for what's coming.

meaning: 'to see your' (followed by a noun: e.g. see your shoes, papers, etc.)
additional_notes: Common construction using the verb voir + possessive adjective vos (plural or formal 'your'). Used when asking or stating that someone wants to look at something belonging to the other person(s). In polite requests, être + pouvoir or pourrions/ pourrions-je is often added: "Puis-je voir vos papiers ?" Vos is the formal or plural 'your'.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous me laisser voir vos documents, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Can you let me see your documents, please?

meaning: 'do you see' (informal/neutral question form with inversion)
additional_notes: Second-person singular of voir (to see) used in inversion questions. Common in spoken and written French to ask if someone perceives, understands, or meets someone/something. Can be literal (visually seeing) or figurative (seeing/understanding). Often appears with negatives (ne ... pas) or question words (que).
target_language_example: Vois-tu ce que je veux dire ?
native_language_example: Do you see/understand what I mean?

meaning: 'see no' or 'don't see any' (negative phrase used with 'je/tu/il/elle/on' forms of voir plus 'aucune' to mean not seeing any)
additional_notes: 'Vois aucune' appears as part of a negative construction: subject + vois + aucune + noun (often spoken as 'je ne vois aucune...'). In everyday French the full negative often includes 'ne' (je ne vois aucune raison), but in informal speech the 'ne' is frequently dropped (je vois aucune raison). 'Aucune' agrees in gender with the noun it modifies (aucun for masculine). Use to mean 'not any' or 'no ... at all.'
target_language_example: Je ne vois aucune solution au problème.
native_language_example: I don't see any solution to the problem.

meaning: 'see what I mean' (used to check if someone understands your point).
additional_notes: Informal everyday phrase used after explaining something to ask if the listener understands or agrees. Often appears as 'tu vois ce que je veux dire?' or shortened to 'vois ce que je veux' in casual speech; context may drop 'tu' and 'dire'. Can be used alone or at the end of a sentence.
target_language_example: J'ai expliqué le problème deux fois, vois ce que je veux ?
native_language_example: I explained the problem twice, see what I mean?

meaning: 'do you see this' or 'do you see that' (informal spoken phrase used to draw attention to something nearby).
additional_notes: A combination of the verb 'voir' (to see) in the 2nd-person singular imperative/question form 'tu vois' plus the demonstrative 'cette' (this/that). Common in spoken French to point out or ask if someone notices a person or object. Can also be used with 'tu vois ce' (masculine singular) or 'tu vois ces' (plural). Tone and context tell whether it's a question or a prompt (e.g. 'Do you see that?').
target_language_example: Tu vois cette maison au bout de la rue ?
native_language_example: Do you see that house at the end of the street?

meaning: ‘see (someone/something) as’ — to perceive or consider someone/something in a certain way.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object (me, le, la, etc.) + comme + description (un étranger, comme ça, dans la réalité). Common for expressing someone’s perception or self-image: Je le vois comme un ami / Je me vois comme ça. Often appears in spoken and written French.
target_language_example: Je te vois comme une personne honnête.
native_language_example: I see you as an honest person.

meaning: see (something) in (someone/something) — notice a quality, sign, or presence inside or through someone/something; or 'see you in' when arranging time/place.
additional_notes: Formed from the verb voir + preposition dans. Common uses: 1) to say you perceive or recognize a trait, emotion, or sign in someone's eyes, face, behavior, etc. (Je le vois dans ses yeux = I can see it in his eyes). 2) to indicate seeing someone in a film or medium (Tu la vois dans le film = You see her in the movie). 3) to indicate time for a meeting or appointment (Je te vois dans une heure = I'll see you in an hour). Context (pronouns, nouns following dans) determines whether 'dans' expresses location, medium, or time.
target_language_example: Je le vois dans ses yeux.
native_language_example: I can see it in his eyes.

meaning: 'don't you see (that)...' — used to ask if someone understands or notices something
additional_notes: This is a colloquial/conversational fragment from the question 'Tu ne vois pas ce qui... ?' or 'Tu vois pas ce qui... ?' It literally uses 'voir' (to see) but means 'to notice/understand' in context. Often followed by a clause introduced by 'qui' (what/that) describing the situation. In spoken French the 'ne' is frequently dropped: 'Tu vois pas... ?'.
target_language_example: Tu ne vois pas ce qui se passe dehors ?
native_language_example: Don't you see what's happening outside?

meaning: 'don't see' or 'don't understand (what/who)' in negative expressions like "je ne vois pas de..."
additional_notes: Used in negative sentences to indicate you don't understand or can't identify the person/thing being referred to. Often appears as part of "je ne vois pas de qui/quoi..." meaning "I don't see/know who/what (you are talking about)". In everyday speech the spoken form may drop the 'ne' (Je vois pas de...).
target_language_example: Je ne vois pas de quoi tu parles.
native_language_example: I don't see/understand what you're talking about.

meaning: 'see' or 'notice' that / 'only see' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Two common uses: 1) As part of 'je vois que...' it means 'I see that...' or 'I notice that...'. 2) In negative constructions like 'je ne vois que...' it can mean 'I only see...' (limited to). Be careful: informal/colloquial uses include 'je vois que dalle' meaning 'I don't see anything' (dalle = slang for 'nothing'). Context (negation, emphasis, or exclamation) determines the sense.
target_language_example: Je vois que tu es fatigué.
native_language_example: I see that you're tired.

meaning: 'I see that you...' / 'I notice that you...'.
additional_notes: A phrase used by the speaker to comment on or point out something they observe about the listener(s). It often begins a sentence: 'Je vois que vous…' followed by a clause (verb or adjective). Can be used politely or neutrally to state an observation. Conjugation depends on subject (here 'je vois' = I see).
target_language_example: Je vois que vous avez fini le travail.
native_language_example: I see that you have finished the work.

meaning: Phrase showing the noun 'voiture' (car) followed by the verb 'avoir' (to have) or 'a' as third-person singular of 'avoir' or part of other constructions (e.g. 'a l’air').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase — it's simply the word 'voiture' (feminine noun meaning 'car') followed by the verb form 'a' (il/elle a = he/she/it has) or part of expressions like 'a l’air' (seems). Useful patterns: 'La voiture a...' (The car has...), 'Sa voiture a deux ans' (His/her car is two years old), 'Cette voiture a l’air...' (This car seems...). Remember agreement: 'voiture' is singular, so use 'a'.
target_language_example: La voiture a un pneu crevé.
native_language_example: The car has a flat tire.

meaning: rental car; a car rented for temporary use.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a car borrowed from a rental company. Common in travel contexts (airport, agency). Can appear with determiners: une voiture de location (a rental car), la voiture de location (the rental car). In signs or documents you may see shortened forms like "voiture de location exclue" (rental car excluded).
target_language_example: Nous avons pris une voiture de location pour visiter la région.
native_language_example: We rented a car to visit the area.

meaning: sports car
additional_notes: Refers to a car designed for performance, speed, and handling. Used like any noun phrase; plural is voitures de sport. Common in everyday speech and formal contexts. You can use adjectives normally: une petite voiture de sport, une nouvelle voiture de sport.
target_language_example: Il a acheté une voiture de sport rouge.
native_language_example: He bought a red sports car.

meaning: the car is
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb phrase: voiture (car) + est (is). Used to state something about a car (condition, location, readiness, etc.). In natural French you would often include a possessive before voiture (ma/ta/sa/notre/votre) or an adjective/complement after est. Word order: [possessive] voiture est + complement. Can be used in questions with Est-ce que or inversion: Est-ce que ta voiture est neuve ?
target_language_example: Ma voiture est en panne.
native_language_example: My car is broken down.

meaning: literally 'car here' — used to refer to a car and its location (e.g., asking to stop or park the car here).
additional_notes: Common in imperatives and questions about stopping or parking: 'Arrête la voiture ici' (Stop the car here) or 'Je peux garer ma voiture ici ?' (Can I park my car here?). Use with verbs like arrêter (stop) or garer (park). Word order is normal: determiner + voiture + adverb/place (ici).
target_language_example: Arrête la voiture ici, s'il te plaît.
native_language_example: Stop the car here, please.

meaning: 'car' + time/condition word 'when' — not a fixed phrase; shows examples where voiture (car) appears with quand (when).
additional_notes: This is not an idiom: it's the noun voiture (car) used in sentences that also include quand (when). Useful patterns shown: 1) quand introduces a clause of time or condition (Quand il passe la prendre = when he comes to pick her up). 2) Quand can mean 'when' or 'if' in conditional sense (Pourquoi acheter... quand la vieille fonctionne = Why buy... when/if the old one still works). 3) Quand bon te semble / quand tu veux / quand vous voulez = 'whenever you like' / 'whenever you want' — polite offers. Word order: voiture stays as a noun; quand starts the temporal/conditional phrase.
target_language_example: Tu peux emprunter ma voiture quand tu veux.
native_language_example: You can borrow my car whenever you want.

meaning: electric car; a car powered by electricity rather than gasoline.
additional_notes: Common everyday term. 'Voiture' = car, 'électrique' = electric — so the phrase is compositional and can be translated literally. Used like any noun phrase: une voiture électrique, la voiture électrique, acheter une voiture électrique. Pronunciation tip: électrique (é-lec-trique).
target_language_example: Ils vendent une voiture électrique dans ce magasin.
native_language_example: They sell an electric car in that store.

meaning: 'voice of' (the voice belonging to or representing someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone or something expresses opinions, authority or representation for a person, group, institution or abstract idea. Often followed by a noun (le peuple, le gouvernement, le Seigneur). Common in proverbs and formal statements (e.g. "La voix du peuple..."). Not idiomatic — literal possession.
target_language_example: La voix du professeur compte dans la décision.
native_language_example: The voice of the teacher matters in the decision.

meaning: 'are flying in' or 'fly in' (they fly in/are flying in a place).
additional_notes: Third-person plural of the verb 'voler' (ils/elles volent) followed by the preposition 'dans' meaning 'in' or 'inside'. Commonly used to say that birds or objects are flying in/through a space (e.g. 'volent dans le ciel' = 'are flying in the sky'). Use a different preposition for other nuances (e.g. 'volent au-dessus de' = fly above).
target_language_example: Les papillons volent dans le jardin.
native_language_example: The butterflies are flying in the garden.

meaning: thief who steals by (a certain method or in a certain place); used before a noun to describe the type of thief (e.g. voleur à la tire = pickpocket).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own: 'voleur' means 'thief' and 'à' is followed by a noun indicating the method or location (à la tire, à la roulotte, à l'étalage). Common fixed expressions include 'voleur à la tire' (pickpocket) and 'voleur à l'étalage' (shoplifter). Use with definite/indefinite articles as needed: un voleur à la tire, le voleur à l'étalage.
target_language_example: La police recherche un voleur à la tire dans le métro.
native_language_example: The police are looking for a pickpocket in the subway.

meaning: 'pickpockets' (literally: 'thieves at the pull'), i.e., thieves who steal from pockets/bags in public.
additional_notes: Used to warn about or describe people who steal wallets, phones, or other items by stealth in crowded places (on buses, trains, markets). Often appears in signs or spoken warnings: «Attention aux voleurs à la tire» = Watch out for pickpockets. The phrase is fixed; 'à la tire' specifies the method. Gender/number agreement applies to surrounding words (e.g., 'Soyez attentif/attentive(s) aux voleurs à la tire').
target_language_example: Attention aux voleurs à la tire dans le métro.
native_language_example: Watch out for pickpockets on the subway.

meaning: stole the / has stolen the (feminine singular noun follows).
additional_notes: From the verb voler (to steal). 'La' is the feminine singular definite article, so 'volé la' appears before a feminine noun (la cassette, la pomme, la vedette, la bière). Context determines tense/person (e.g. 'Elle a volé la...' = she stole the...). Can also be used idiomatically (e.g. 'voler la vedette' = to steal the show).
target_language_example: Il a volé la montre de son frère.
native_language_example: He stole his brother's watch.

meaning: they are going to (do) it / they will (do) it.
additional_notes: Formed from the third-person plural of aller (vont = they go/are going) + direct object pronoun le (it/him). Used to express a near-future action or to ask if someone will do something. Gender/number of the object may change the pronoun (la, les, l'). In spoken French, future with aller is very common: Ils vont le faire = They are going to do it. Word order: subject + vont + object pronoun + verb.
target_language_example: Ils vont le finir demain.
native_language_example: They are going to finish it tomorrow.

meaning: 'shut up' (very rude, plural).
additional_notes: Extremely vulgar and insulting way to tell a group to be quiet; 'vos' is the plural possessive 'your', and 'gueules' literally means 'mugs' or 'faces' (slang for mouths). Use only in strong, confrontational contexts (or when quoting/understanding profanity). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Fermez vos gueules et partez d'ici.
native_language_example: Shut up and get out of here.

meaning: Your Highness (formal address to a prince/princess or royal person).
additional_notes: Used as a very formal, respectful form of address to royalty or nobility. Always capitalized for the title in French (Altesse). Often followed by a verb or polite phrase (e.g., «je vous conseille», «je vous en prie»). Not used in casual situations.
target_language_example: Votre Altesse, permettez-moi de vous présenter notre invité.
native_language_example: Your Highness, allow me to introduce our guest.

meaning: a formal way to address someone with the title 'Excellency' (used for high officials, diplomats, bishops).
additional_notes: Very formal and honorific. Used when speaking to or about people who hold certain high-ranking positions (e.g., ambassadors, heads of state, some ecclesiastical figures). In France it is less common in everyday speech; expect it in diplomatic, ceremonial, or historical contexts. Use in spoken French only in very formal situations.
target_language_example: Votre Excellence, puis-je vous poser une question ?
native_language_example: Your Excellency, may I ask you a question?

meaning: 'Your Majesty' — a formal address for a king, queen, emperor, or empress.
additional_notes: Very formal and respectful. Used when directly addressing a monarch (royal title). Capitalize 'Majesté' when used as a title. Not used for ordinary people; in modern everyday French it's rare except in historical, ceremonial, or fictional contexts (books, films, role-play).
target_language_example: Votre Majesté, permettez-moi de vous présenter le rapport.
native_language_example: Your Majesty, allow me to present the report to you.

meaning: Please (may) I have your attention? / Attention, please.
additional_notes: A polite phrase used to ask a group or person to listen or look. Common in announcements, formal settings, meetings, or when addressing an audience. Full form is « Votre attention, s'il vous plaît. » Variations: « Je peux avoir votre attention, s'il vous plaît ? », « Pourrais‑je avoir votre attention ? »
target_language_example: Votre attention, s'il vous plaît : le train partira dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Attention please: the train will depart in five minutes.

meaning: your room too / your room as well (often in comparisons like 'as ... as you can').
additional_notes: This phrase combines 'votre chambre' (your room) with 'aussi' (also/as). In the example sentences 'aussi' is used in comparisons: 'aussi ... que vous pouvez' = 'as ... as you can' (e.g., 'aussi propre que vous pouvez' = 'as clean as you can'). Alone, 'votre chambre aussi' can mean 'your room too' (adding your room to a list) or be part of a comparative structure. Word order and meaning depend on context.
target_language_example: Gardez votre chambre aussi propre que possible.
native_language_example: Keep your room as clean as possible.

meaning: would like ... to
additional_notes: Usually seen as je voudrais que... to express a wish or polite request about what someone else does or what happens. It is followed by que + another clause, typically with the subjunctive: je voudrais que tu viennes = "I'd like you to come." English often translates this with "would like someone to..." rather than a literal "would like that..."
target_language_example: Je voudrais que tu viennes avec nous.
native_language_example: I'd like you to come with us.

meaning: would like a
additional_notes: Used to ask for or say you want one masculine singular thing in a polite way. It comes from the conditional of vouloir. Use une with feminine nouns instead: je voudrais une table.
target_language_example: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee, please.

meaning: would like to ... you
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a longer pattern such as je voudrais vous parler / vous montrer / vous dire. Voudrais means 'would like' (a polite form of vouloir), and vous means 'you' (formal singular or plural). In French, object pronouns like vous come before the infinitive: je voudrais vous parler = 'I would like to speak to you.'
target_language_example: Je voudrais vous aider.
native_language_example: I would like to help you.

meaning: I just wanted (that)... / I only wanted (that)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce a simple, often explanatory wish or intention about something someone wanted to happen or for someone to know. Commonly followed by a subordinate clause with subjunctive (e.g., 'que ce soit...') or indicative (especially in spoken French: 'que tu le saches'). 'Juste' softens or minimizes the request/intent ('only', 'just').
target_language_example: Je voulais juste que tu comprennes la situation.
native_language_example: I just wanted you to understand the situation.

meaning: I just wanted to see (what)...
additional_notes: Used to introduce curiosity or intention to observe an outcome. Commonly followed by a clause like 'qui...' (what/who) plus a verb in various tenses (se passait, se passerait, arriverait). Polite/neutral; often expresses that the action was only to watch or check, not to intervene.
target_language_example: Je voulais juste voir ce qui allait se passer.
native_language_example: I just wanted to see what would happen.

meaning: 'wanted to (her/it)'.
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect tense of vouloir (voulais = I/he/she/you(you-singular informal) wanted / was wanting) followed by the direct object pronoun la (her/it). In English this expresses a past desire or intention directed at a feminine singular person or a feminine/neutral noun (la = her/it). Context determines whether it means 'wanted to see her', 'wanted to get it (feminine)', etc. The verb that follows may be omitted in casual speech when understood from context: e.g. 'Je voulais la' plus an understood verb becomes 'Je voulais la voir' or 'Je voulais la récupérer'.
target_language_example: Je voulais la voir hier, mais elle n'était pas là.
native_language_example: I wanted to see her yesterday, but she wasn't there.

meaning: 'wanted to (do something) to/for him/her'.
additional_notes: Combination of the imperfect tense of vouloir (je voulais = I wanted / I was wanting) plus the indirect object pronoun lui (to him / to her). Used before an infinitive verb: Je voulais lui dire = I wanted to tell him/her. The imperfect here expresses a past desire or intention (often incomplete or background action). Pronoun lui does not show gender.
target_language_example: Je voulais lui offrir un cadeau pour son anniversaire.
native_language_example: I wanted to give him/her a gift for his/her birthday.

meaning: wanted to ... me
additional_notes: A combination of voulais (“wanted” / “was wanting”) and me (“me”). Before an infinitive, me can be the object of the verb (tu voulais me dire = “you wanted to tell me”) or part of a reflexive verb (je voulais me rendre = “I wanted to go/get myself to”). French puts me before the infinitive, unlike English.
target_language_example: Je voulais me reposer un peu.
native_language_example: I wanted to rest a little.

meaning: didn't want (someone/something) to...; expresses a past desire that something not happen.
additional_notes: Informal negative past construction of vouloir + que + subjunctive (often shortened in speech: "je voulais pas que..."). Used to say you didn't want someone to do/see/be somewhere. The verb after "que" usually takes the subjunctive in full written French (e.g. "je ne voulais pas que tu sois").
target_language_example: Je ne voulais pas que tu saches la vérité comme ça.
native_language_example: I didn't want you to find out the truth like that.

meaning: wanted you to
additional_notes: A sentence fragment rather than a fixed expression. It most often appears as je voulais que tu..., meaning 'I wanted you to...'. French often uses vouloir que + subjunctive where English uses 'want someone to + verb', for example: je voulais que tu viennes = 'I wanted you to come'.
target_language_example: Je voulais que tu viennes avec nous.
native_language_example: I wanted you to come with us.

meaning: 'I just wanted to' (polite, followed by an action directed at 'you').
additional_notes: This is the imperfect form vouloir (je voulais) used to make a polite or less direct request or statement: 'I just wanted to [do something to/for you].' Commonly followed by an infinitive verb (parler, poser, regarder, etc.). Can be used to soften interruptions or requests. In spoken French you may also hear 'je voulais juste vous...' (juste ~ seulement).
target_language_example: Je voulais seulement vous aider.
native_language_example: I just wanted to help you.

meaning: 'I wanted to (to) you it' → part of 'Je voulais te le dire' = 'I wanted to tell you (it)'.
additional_notes: This is a fragment combining the verb 'voulais' (imperfect of vouloir = wanted) with the object pronouns 'te' (to you / you) and 'le' (it / him). In full sentences you'll usually see 'Je voulais te le dire' (I wanted to tell you it / I wanted to tell you) or 'Je voulais te le montrer' (I wanted to show it to you). The imperfect 'voulais' expresses a past desire or intention. Word order: subject + voulais + indirect object pronoun (te) + direct object pronoun (le) + verb (dire/montrer).
target_language_example: Je voulais te le dire avant que tu partes.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you before you left.

meaning: 'wanted a car' (imperfect past tense — she/he wanted a car).
additional_notes: Voulait is the imperfect (imparfait) form of vouloir (to want) used to describe a past, ongoing, habitual, or background desire. "Une voiture" = a car. Context and subject determine gender/number (here examples use different female/male names; verb agrees with subject). Use when describing what someone wanted in the past: e.g., childhood wishes, ongoing past desires, or polite indirect speech.
target_language_example: Quand il était jeune, il voulait une voiture rouge.
native_language_example: When he was young, he wanted a red car.

meaning: 'would you kindly' or 'would you please (for me)' (used to form a polite request with a clitic pronoun 'me').
additional_notes: This phrase fragment combines the polite imperative/question form 'voulez bien' with the clitic 'm'' (short for 'me') and is completed by an infinitive or verb phrase (e.g. 'voulez bien m'aider', 'voulez bien m'apporter'). It is formal/polite and used to ask someone to do something for the speaker. Written usage often appears as 'Voulez-vous bien m'...' when addressing 'vous'.
target_language_example: Voulez bien m'aider à porter ces sacs ?
native_language_example: Would you please help me carry these bags?

meaning: polite way to ask someone to allow or excuse us (literally: 'would you kindly/please allow us' or 'please excuse us').
additional_notes: Used in polite requests where the speaker asks others to excuse, allow, or give space/time to the speaker and their group. Often appears as 'Vous voulez bien nous ... ?' + verb (excuser, laisser, accorder un instant, etc.). Formal/polite register; common in spoken and written French when being courteous.
target_language_example: Vous voulez bien nous excuser un instant ?
native_language_example: Would you please excuse us for a moment?

meaning: want to do
additional_notes: Combines the verb vouloir (to want) with an infinitive (faire — to do/make). Used to ask or state what someone wants to do. In polite or plural/formal speech use vous voulez faire; in informal singular use tu veux faire. Word order in questions can change (Qu'est-ce que vous voulez faire? / Vous voulez faire quoi?).
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que vous voulez faire ce weekend ?
native_language_example: What do you want to do this weekend?

meaning: 'do you want to see a...' (polite/plural or formal you)
additional_notes: A common spoken phrase used to offer to show something. 'Vous' is formal or plural; structure = vous (voulez) voir (infinitive) + un/une + noun. Can be used with nouns (film, truc, bon combat). For informal singular use 'tu veux voir un...'.
target_language_example: Vous voulez voir un endroit sympa ?
native_language_example: Do you want to see a nice place?

meaning: to be willing to
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to do something or to express willingness/consent. Often appears in requests or commands to soften them (e.g. « voulez-vous bien ... ? » = 'would you kindly ...?'). Can be followed by an infinitive (vouloir bien faire quelque chose) or used with vouloir + bien + que + subjunctive for willingness about someone else. Formal/polite register.
target_language_example: Pourriez-vous vouloir bien signer ce formulaire ?
native_language_example: Could you be so kind as to sign this form?

meaning: to mean
additional_notes: Usually used to talk about the meaning of words, signs, actions, or situations. Although the words literally look like 'to want to say,' the common meaning is 'to mean.' Often appears in questions like Qu'est-ce que ça peut vouloir dire ? ('What could that mean?').
target_language_example: Qu'est-ce que ça peut vouloir dire ?
native_language_example: What could that mean?

meaning: A polite or familiar way to address someone directly: 'you, my…' (e.g. 'you, my son', 'you, my friend').
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase but a common pattern: vous + comma + mon + noun (mon fils, mon ami, mon Père, mon colonel, mon pays). It can be affectionate (mon ami, mon fils), formal/respectful (mon Père in religious contexts, mon colonel), or rhetorical (addressing an entity like mon pays). The comma marks direct address. Use when speaking directly to the person or entity; choose the noun to match gender/role. Pronunciation: mon is pronounced [mɔ̃].
target_language_example: Vous, mon ami, vous savez la vérité.
native_language_example: You, my friend, you know the truth.

meaning: 'go away' (formal/plural imperative with the pronoun 'en' attached)
additional_notes: Used after the imperative verb allez (Allez-vous-en) to tell one or more people politely or firmly to go away/leave. The construction is impérative + reflexive pronoun (vous) + particle en; in speech the full phrase is often written together (Allez-vous-en) or more commonly Allez-vous en. Equivalent informal forms: Va-t'en (singular). Can be softened with s'il vous plaît. Tone can be firm or angry depending on context.
target_language_example: Allez-vous-en, je veux être seul.
native_language_example: Go away, I want to be alone.

meaning: yourself (formal or plural).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the action is done by the person addressed (formal singular vous) or by a group (vous = you plural). Often follows the verb or is used after a preposition: «Demandez-lui vous‑même», «Voyez par vous‑même». Use «toi-même» for informal singular (tu).
target_language_example: Faites-le vous-même si vous voulez le contrôle.
native_language_example: Do it yourself if you want control.

meaning: yourselves (plural or formal singular).
additional_notes: Reflexive/emphatic pronoun used to emphasize that the action or state applies to the people addressed. Used with vous (plural 'you' or formal singular). In affirmative commands it can add insistence (e.g., "Voyez vous-mêmes" = "See for yourselves"). Note the hyphen in affirmative imperative and pronoun agreement in gender/number not marked here.
target_language_example: Pensez par vous-mêmes avant de décider.
native_language_example: Think for yourselves before deciding.

meaning: 'I admire you' (formal or plural 'you').
additional_notes: Used to express admiration or respect for someone. 'Vous' can be formal (to one person you don't know well or to show respect) or plural (to several people). The verb form 'admire' is first-person singular present (« j'admire ») but often in full phrase speakers say 'Je vous admire' — in the given input the subject 'Je' is implied. You can add a reason with 'pour' (e.g. 'pour votre courage').
target_language_example: Je vous admire pour votre travail acharné.
native_language_example: I admire you for your hard work.

meaning: I brought you a... / I have brought you a...
additional_notes: Polite/formal construction using 'vous' (formal you or plural). 'Je vous ai apporté un...' uses passé composé (je + avoir + past participle) to say you brought something to the person. Replace 'un' with the appropriate article + noun (un, une, du, de la, des, un peu de, etc.). For informal singular 'you' use 't' (je t'ai apporté...).
target_language_example: Je vous ai apporté un livre.
native_language_example: I brought you a book.

meaning: I told you that I... (used to introduce what the speaker has already said about themselves).
additional_notes: This is part of the construction Je vous ai dit que je + [verb/clause]. Je vous ai dit = 'I told you' (formal/plural you). The clause after que begins with je and gives the content previously stated. Tense in the clause can vary (imperfect, present, etc.) depending on the meaning (e.g., Je vous ai dit que je détestais = I told you I hated/used to hate; Je vous ai dit que je déteste = I told you I hate). Useful for reminding or insisting that you already said something.
target_language_example: Je vous ai dit que je préfère partir maintenant.
native_language_example: I told you that I prefer to leave now.

meaning: 'have/has never (to you)' — part of the perfect tense construction meaning 'I have never ... you' or 'I never ... you'.
additional_notes: This sequence combines the pronoun 'vous' (you, formal or plural), the auxiliary 'ai' (first-person singular of avoir) and 'jamais' (never). It's used in the passé composé to say you have never done/seen/said something to or about 'vous' (often idiomatically 'I have never ... you' or 'I have never ... to you'). Word order can vary: more common is 'Je ne vous ai jamais ...' (negative), but in casual spoken French the 'ne' is often dropped: 'Je vous ai jamais ...'. Ensure the past participle follows the auxiliary: e.g. 'Je ne vous ai jamais vu.'
target_language_example: Je ne vous ai jamais vu ici avant.
native_language_example: I have never seen you here before.

meaning: '(I) have not (to) you' — part of the negated passé composé with vous as object (e.g. I did not ... you / I have not ... you).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a sequence that appears inside negated sentences in the passé composé: subject + ne + pronoun (vous) + auxiliary (ai) + pas + past participle. In English it usually corresponds to 'I did not [verb] you' or 'I have not [verb] you.' Word order and agreement of the past participle depend on the direct object: with direct object pronouns placed before the past participle, the past participle may agree in gender and number (e.g. 'Je ne vous ai pas vue' when speaking to one female).
target_language_example: Je ne vous ai pas appelé hier.
native_language_example: I did not call you yesterday.

meaning: 'took you for' or 'mistook you for' (I thought you were...)
additional_notes: Part of the passé composé of the verb prendre used with 'pour' to indicate a mistaken identity or assumption: 'je vous ai pris pour...' = 'I took/mistook you for...'. The full construction is typically 'je vous ai pris pour + noun/pronoun'. Formal register is fine; can be used with tu (je t'ai pris) or il/elle (je l'ai pris).
target_language_example: Excusez-moi, je vous ai pris pour un de mes amis.
native_language_example: Sorry, I mistook you for one of my friends.

meaning: you
additional_notes: This is a grammatical fragment, not a fixed expression. Here, vous means 'you' (formal singular or plural), and ait is the subjunctive form of avoir. It often appears after que with a past participle in the past subjunctive: que ça vous ait plu = 'that you liked it', que ça vous ait échappé = 'that you missed it'.
target_language_example: Je suis content que le film vous ait plu.
native_language_example: I'm glad you liked the movie.

meaning: (formal or plural) you learned to do/make — used with passé composé (avez appris) + à + infinitive to ask about acquiring a skill.
additional_notes: This appears inside questions using the auxiliary avoir in passé composé: (Comment/Où/Quand) avez-vous appris à faire... 'Vous' can be formal singular or plural. In spoken French the word order in questions often uses inversion (avez-vous appris) or est-ce que (vous avez appris). The exact sequence 'vous appris à faire' occurs when the auxiliary and subject are separated in written contexts or in embedded clauses (e.g., je vois que vous appris à faire is nonstandard; prefer 'que vous avez appris à faire').
target_language_example: Où avez-vous appris à faire des pizzas ?
native_language_example: Where did you learn to make pizzas?

meaning: 'I was waiting for you' (formal/plural 'you'), or 'I expected you'.
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of attendre (j'attendais) with the object pronoun vous placed before the verb. Used to describe a past ongoing action — that you were waiting for someone (vous = formal singular or plural). Can also mean 'I expected you' in contexts of surprise or mild reproach. In spoken French the subject 'je' is often included: 'Je vous attendais.'
target_language_example: Je vous attendais depuis une heure au café.
native_language_example: I was waiting for you at the café for an hour.

meaning: you (plural or emphatic) — used to emphasize or distinguish the group being addressed (you folks/you guys).
additional_notes: Informal/regional way to emphasize the second-person plural. Common in spoken French in some regions and in familiar contexts. Equivalent to 'vous' or 'vous autres' used contrastively (e.g., 'vous autres, vous faites ça' = 'you people, you do that'). Not used in formal writing. Can indicate a contrast with 'nous' or with another group.
target_language_example: Vous autres, vous êtes prêts ?
native_language_example: You guys, are you ready?

meaning: ‘you need something’ (start of the phrase used to offer help: 'if you need anything').
additional_notes: This fragment appears in the common expression «si vous avez besoin de quelque chose» = 'if you need anything'. Used to offer help or ask whether someone needs something. Formal/plural 'vous' can be used with one person (polite) or with multiple people. To complete the phrase, add 'chose' (something) or a specific noun (e.g. 'de pain').
target_language_example: Si vous avez besoin de quelque chose, dites-le-moi.
native_language_example: If you need anything, tell me.

meaning: to have made you (do/wait/etc.)
additional_notes: Commonly appears in apologetic phrases meaning 'sorry for having made you wait' (e.g. désolé de vous avoir fait attendre). Structure: "vous" = you (object), "avoir fait" = to have made/caused — followed by an infinitive or noun (here, 'attendre' is often omitted after 'fait' because it's understood). Use when apologizing for causing someone inconvenience. Not a fixed idiom beyond this causative use.
target_language_example: Désolé de vous avoir fait attendre hier.
native_language_example: Sorry for having kept you waiting yesterday.

meaning: 'to have you with (us)' — a polite way to say 'glad you're here' or 'pleased to have you among us'.
additional_notes: Commonly used in greetings or formal welcome phrases (often completed as «vous avoir parmi nous»). It expresses pleasure that someone has joined a group, event, or organization. Can be used in singular or plural forms (ravi/ ravis). Tone ranges from friendly to formal depending on context.
target_language_example: Nous sommes ravis de vous avoir parmi nous aujourd'hui.
native_language_example: We are delighted to have you with us today.

meaning: ‘that you were able to’ (subjunctive form used after expressions of feeling or judgment).
additional_notes: This is the subjunctive perfect (avoir au subjonctif + pouvoir au participe passé) used after phrases expressing emotion, opinion, or reaction (e.g., content que, heureux que). It emphasizes that someone was able to do something in the past and is dependent on a main clause that triggers the subjunctive. Use with 'tu aies pu' (informal) or 'ils/elles aient pu' for other subjects.
target_language_example: Je suis content que vous ayez pu venir hier.
native_language_example: I'm glad that you were able to come yesterday.

meaning: '(make) yourself comfortable' or '(sit) comfortably' (polite/formal or plural you).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs like s'asseoir/installer: 'Asseyez-vous confortablement' / 'Installez-vous confortablement' meaning 'Please sit/make yourself comfortable.' 'Vous' here is polite singular or plural. Often said by a host before a show or when welcoming guests. Word order: verb + vous + confortablement (adverb).
target_language_example: Installez-vous confortablement, le film commence dans cinq minutes.
native_language_example: Make yourself comfortable, the movie starts in five minutes.

meaning: 'to (you) agree to take' or 'to ask someone to take/accept' (polite/formal construction)
additional_notes: This sequence appears inside polite or formal constructions: "Acceptez-vous de prendre... ?" (Do you accept/agree to take...) and "Que diriez-vous de prendre... ?" (How about taking...). It also appears in instructions with "Assurez-vous de prendre..." meaning "Make sure to take..." The phrase combines a polite subject form (vous) with the infinitive prendre; exact translation depends on the surrounding verb (accepter, assurer, dire). Use in questions for proposals or in imperatives for instructions.
target_language_example: Acceptez-vous de prendre ce poste à temps plein ?
native_language_example: Do you agree to take this full-time position?

meaning: 'to tell you this' or part of a clause meaning 'to tell you [this/that/what]'. Often appears before 'que' or as part of 'vous dire ce que...'.
additional_notes: This sequence alone is not a complete standalone sentence in French; it usually appears within a larger clause. Common full forms: 'je veux vous dire ce que...' (I want to tell you what...), 'je vais vous dire ce qui s'est passé' (I'll tell you what happened). If followed by 'que' it becomes 'vous dire que...' (to tell you that...). 'Vous dire ce' is compositional and can be translated literally, but you must include the following words ('que', 'qui', 'que' + clause, or 'que' + subordinate) to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire ce que j'ai vu hier soir.
native_language_example: I'll tell you what I saw last night.

meaning: part of a phrase meaning 'to tell you a ...' (directed to vous)
additional_notes: This is not a complete fixed expression by itself. It appears when the speaker addresses someone formally or plural (vous) and begins a clause: 'vous dire un ...' = 'to tell you a ...' Usually followed by a noun or clause (e.g. 'je voulais vous dire un secret' or more commonly 'je voulais vous dire que...'). In spoken French you are more likely to hear 'je veux vous dire...' or 'je voulais vous dire...' or the shorter 'je vous dis...' depending on tense and politeness.
target_language_example: Je voulais vous dire un secret important.
native_language_example: I wanted to tell you an important secret.

meaning: to tell you a (story/joke/thing) — the start of a phrase meaning 'to tell you one...'
additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself; it's the beginning of a sentence like «je vais vous dire une histoire» (I'll tell you a story) or «je vais vous dire une chose» (I'll tell you one thing). The structure is: (je/je vais) + vous dire + une + [noun]. Use it when offering to tell someone one item (a story, a secret, a joke). If addressing multiple people or formal singular, 'vous' is appropriate.
target_language_example: Je vais vous dire une histoire intéressante.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell you an interesting story.

meaning: I owe you a (something) / I owe you (an explanation, a favor...).
additional_notes: Literal structure: je vous dois une + noun. Used to say you are indebted to someone for something (an explanation, a favor, etc.). Formal subject pronoun vous is used for polite you or plural you. Context determines the noun (explication, faveur, etc.). Not used with indefinite articles omitted: must include the owed thing. Can be used figuratively (e.g. «je vous dois une fière chandelle» = I owe you big time).
target_language_example: Je vous dois une faveur pour m'avoir aidé hier.
native_language_example: I owe you a favor for helping me yesterday.

meaning: I give you my... / I give you (female noun) — a fragment used when offering or promising something belonging to the speaker (feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase on its own but a common word order: Je vous donne ma + [feminine noun]. Used to offer, hand over, or promise something. In examples, ma carte (my card), ma parole (my word/promise), ma promesse (my promise), ma fille (my daughter). You must add a feminine noun after 'ma'. For masculine nouns use 'mon' (je vous donne mon...) and for plural use 'mes' (je vous donne mes...). 'Je vous donne ma parole' is an idiom meaning 'I give you my word / I promise'.
target_language_example: Je vous donne ma confiance si vous êtes honnête.
native_language_example: I give you my trust if you are honest.

meaning: 'I (or someone) give(s) you everything that...'/ 'I give you all that...'
additional_notes: A phrase that begins a clause meaning the speaker gives the listener everything that follows (e.g. everything they ask for). 'Vous' can be formal singular or plural. Verb agreement and past/tense change with subject (je donne = I give). The clause 'tout ce que' = 'everything that/whatever'. Common in sentences like 'Je vous donne tout ce que vous demandez.'
target_language_example: Je vous donne tout ce que vous demandez, mais cela ne suffit pas.
native_language_example: I give you everything that you ask for, but that's not enough.

meaning: I will give you
additional_notes: Future tense of donner with the polite/plural object pronoun vous. Used to promise or state that the speaker will give something to 'you' (formal singular or plural). In everyday speech the subject je may be dropped in short answers, but in full sentences keep it: Je vous donnerai. Can be followed by a direct object (cet argent, quelques exemples, une bicyclette, etc.).
target_language_example: Je vous donnerai le livre demain.
native_language_example: I will give you the book tomorrow.

meaning: 'Have you ever been (to...)?' (asking if someone has visited a place)
additional_notes: Polite/formal question using inversion (êtes-vous). 'déjà' = 'already/ever' here means 'ever' in experience questions. Use 'allé' (masculine past participle) with être; with 'vous' the past participle doesn't agree in spoken French when 'vous' is used for 'you' (agreement optional/formal). For a casual form use 'Vous êtes déjà allé(e) à... ?' (with rising intonation) or 'T'es déjà allé(e) à... ?' for informal 'tu'. Include the destination after 'à' (or 'au/à la/aux' depending on the place).
target_language_example: Êtes-vous déjà allé à Paris ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Paris?

meaning: 'have you ever done' (polite/formal or plural)
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself but a fragment appearing in polite questions using 'Avez-vous déjà fait...?' or the reflexive inversion 'Vous êtes‑vous déjà fait...?' meaning 'Have you ever...?' Use to ask if someone has ever performed an action. 'Déjà' = 'already/ever'. Verb after 'fait' varies (faire vos devoirs, faire une liste, se faire des amis). The form 'vous' can be formal singular or plural. Word order changes in questions (inversion or 'Est‑ce que').
target_language_example: Avez‑vous déjà fait un voyage en train de nuit ?
native_language_example: Have you ever taken a night train trip?

meaning: 'Have you ever read...?' (polite/formal).
additional_notes: Avez-vous déjà lu is the formal/polite inversion question using 'vous'. Use to ask if someone has at any time read something. 'Déjà' = ever/before. Commonly followed by a book, poem, author, or 'ça'/'cela'. In informal speech you can say 'Est-ce que vous avez déjà lu...' or with 'tu' use 'As-tu déjà lu.../Tu as déjà lu...?'. The verb 'lu' is the past participle of 'lire' (to read) and pairs with 'avoir' in passé composé.
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà lu ce roman de Camille?
native_language_example: Have you ever read this novel by Camille?

meaning: 'Have you already eaten?' or 'Have you ever eaten?' depending on context.
additional_notes: This is the polite/formal inversion question using 'vous'. 'Déjà' with the passé composé can mean 'already' (something that happened before now) or 'ever' (in experience questions) depending on context. Use 'Avez-vous déjà mangé ?' to ask politely if someone has already eaten (e.g., today) or in questions about experience add a specific food/item (e.g., 'Avez-vous déjà mangé des huîtres ?' = 'Have you ever eaten oysters?'). Informal spoken French often uses 'Vous avez déjà mangé ?' or 'Tu as déjà mangé ?' (for friends/family).
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà mangé ce plat traditionnel ?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten this traditional dish?

meaning: 'have you ever been' (used to ask if someone has had the experience of being somewhere or feeling something)
additional_notes: This is the inversion question form (formal or polite) using the verb être in the passé composé with 'déjà' (ever). Commonly used to ask about experiences: locations (en Europe, à Rio) or states/feelings (amoureux). In casual spoken French you may also hear 'Vous avez déjà été… ?' or 'Tu as déjà été… ?' (informal).
target_language_example: Avez-vous déjà été en Italie ?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

meaning: part of the phrase 'je vous en ai parlé' — 'I told you about it' (literally 'I have told you of it').
additional_notes: Not a standalone phrase; 'vous en ai' appears in constructions with a subject (je/je vous en ai parlé) or other pronouns. 'En' replaces 'about it/of it' (something previously mentioned). 'Vous' is the indirect object meaning 'to you'. The full form is usually 'je vous en ai parlé' (perfect tense) or 'je vous en ai déjà parlé' (I already told you about it).
target_language_example: Je vous en ai parlé hier.
native_language_example: I told you about it yesterday.

meaning: Please (I beg you), don’t ... — polite plea asking someone not to do something.
additional_notes: Formal/polite/formulaic phrase: 'Je vous en prie' is a polite expression meaning 'please' or 'you're welcome' depending on context; here it's used as a strong polite request or plea followed by 'ne' + verb to ask someone not to do something. Use with the formal 'vous' (can be plural or polite singular). Often appears as 'Je vous en prie, ne ...' or simply 'Je vous en prie' plus the negative command or request.
target_language_example: Je vous en prie, ne partez pas maintenant.
native_language_example: Please, don't leave now.

meaning: 'have you heard of' or 'have you heard about' (formal/plural you).
additional_notes: This is part of the question construction Avez-vous entendu parler de ... ? used to ask if someone (formal singular or plural) knows about or has heard news of a person, thing, or topic. The full phrase includes Avez- before vous (Avez-vous entendu parler de ... ?). Use entendu parler de + noun/pronoun. Informal alternative: Tu as entendu parler de ... ?
target_language_example: Avez-vous entendu parler de ce film ?
native_language_example: Have you heard of that movie?

meaning: 'did you do that' (formal or polite 'you')
additional_notes: This is the inversion question form using the formal/plural vous + passé composé of faire (avez-vous fait = have you done/did you do). Used to ask whether the person did something. In everyday speech, French speakers often use 'Est-ce que vous avez fait cela ?' or the informal 'tu as fait ça ?'. 'Cela' is slightly more formal than 'ça'.
target_language_example: Pourquoi avez-vous fait cela ?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

meaning: 'you do this' or 'you are doing this' (polite/plural 'you')
additional_notes: Literal combination of polite/plural subject pronoun vous + verb faire + demonstrative ce. In practice, native speakers are more likely to say 'vous faites ça', 'vous faites ceci', or 'vous faites cela' rather than 'vous faites ce' alone. Use 'vous faites ce' only when followed immediately by a noun or clause (e.g. 'Vous faites ce travail ?').
target_language_example: Vous faites ce projet ensemble ?
native_language_example: Are you doing this project together?

meaning: 'what you do is' (part of a sentence: points to actions performed by 'you')
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom but a sequence used to form sentences like 'Ce que vous faites est...'. 'Ce que' = 'what' or 'that which'; 'vous faites' = 'you do' (formal/plural); 'est' = 'is'. Use to comment on or evaluate someone's actions. In spoken French, you may also hear 'ce que tu fais est...' with 'tu' for informal singular. The word order is important: 'Ce que vous faites est...' (not 'Vous faites ce que est...').
target_language_example: Ce que vous faites est très utile pour l'équipe.
native_language_example: What you do is very useful for the team.

meaning: you need
additional_notes: This is the impersonal construction from falloir: il vous faut = you need / you must have. Often used as il vous faut or il vous faudra (future). Alone 'vous faut' typically appears after 'il' or in colloquial omission: 'Ça vous faut?' (less common). Use with a noun or infinitive: il vous faut un passeport / il vous faut partir. Not the same as 'vous faut' meaning someone is needed (rare).
target_language_example: Il vous faut un billet pour monter dans le train.
native_language_example: You need a ticket to get on the train.

meaning: 'could/would you (please) close it/the ...' (polite request to close something)
additional_notes: This is part of polite requests using vous + verb (Pouvez-vous / Pourriez-vous / Voudriez-vous) followed by an object (la porte, la fenêtre, etc.). The phrase itself is not complete alone; 'la' refers to a feminine noun previously mentioned (la porte, la fenêtre). Common verbs: fermer (to close). Use 'fermez la...' for the informal/imperative or 'Pouvez-vous fermer la...' for polite requests.
target_language_example: Pouvez-vous fermer la porte, s'il vous plaît ?
native_language_example: Could you close the door, please?

meaning: 'to trust' or 'to rely on' (reflexive: se fier à quelqu'un/quelque chose).
additional_notes: Always used with à before the person or thing trusted: se fier à quelqu'un/à quelque chose. In polite/formal address use vous (vous fier à). It is reflexive in French (se fier) but in English you say 'trust' or 'rely on'. Common in instructions or reassurances: Je vous demande de vous fier à moi = I ask that you trust me.
target_language_example: Vous pouvez vous fier à moi pour garder votre secret.
native_language_example: You can trust me to keep your secret.

meaning: 'have you finished (doing something)?' (formal/plural)
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has completed an action. In correct French the full phrase is Avez-vous fini de + infinitive (e.g. Avez-vous fini de lire?). In past contexts use Aviez-vous fini de...? With reflexive verbs include the reflexive pronoun (Avez-vous fini de vous habiller?). Formal or plural 'vous' is implied; informal singular uses 'as-tu fini de...'.
target_language_example: Avez-vous fini de préparer le repas ?
native_language_example: Have you finished preparing the meal?

meaning: 'have you ever eaten' (formal / plural 'you')
additional_notes: Polite/formal question using inversion (avez-vous) with jamais to mean 'ever'. Used to ask if someone has at any time eaten somewhere or something.
